title: The Bayeux tapestry: a stupefying, thrilling, horrifying masterpiece that shakes the earth | Art | The Guardian
description: The greatest battle ever depicted in art is here at last – and it hurtles along, making your heart pound with its sense of doom and destiny, culminating in fires and corpses on a battlefield full of pathos
Author: Jonathan Jones
Headline: The greatest battle ever depicted in art is here at last – and it hurtles along, making your heart pound with its sense of doom and destiny, culminating in fires and corpses on a battlefield full of pathos
Content: ‘It beats almost everything else’ … the Bayeux tapestry.Photograph: Isogood_patrick/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘It beats almost everything else’ … the Bayeux tapestry.Photograph: Isogood_patrick/ShutterstockArtReviewThe Bayeux tapestry: a stupefying, thrilling, horrifying masterpiece that shakes the earthBritish Museum, LondonThe greatest battle ever depicted in art is here at last – and it hurtles along, making your heart pound with its sense of doom and destiny, culminating in fires and corpses on a battlefield full of pathosJonathan JonesThu 3 Sep 2026 10.51 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 14.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt should not work. It should not even exist. Nothing about theBayeux tapestrymakes sense according to any norms of art: its creators couldn’t do proper portraits or pictorial depth or landscapes or any of the sophisticated things we associate with timeless masterpieces. When they depict a church, they have to write what it is: Ecclesia. But these artists – or who knows, perhaps she was a single artist – created something so stupefying and delightful, so abundant in visual thrills, horrors and humour, it beats almost everything else ever painted or carved – let alone embroidered on a strip of linen.And now here it is, in front of my eyes, close enough to touch if it wasn’t behind a glass screen of such high quality you never catch a reflection. The British Museum’s display of this wonder is perfect. It’s laid out in its case, the length of a gallery, which you reach after some archaeological foreplay involving armour, quotes from chronicles and info screens. Then you see the colours of the tapestry below you from a parapet – russets, greens, yellows – after which you simply start at the beginning and follow the story rightwards. Surrounded by darkness and picked out by finely adjusted lighting, the Bayeux tapestry shines. My only quibble is the ethereal soundtrack – shouldn’t there be drums, oliphants, troubadours?I managed a pretty satisfying eyeful in under an hour, although more than the allotted 40 minutes. This is pacy art: it hurtles along. In fact, that’s how it embraces you. Your heart pounds with a sense of doom and destiny. This is, you realise, the greatest battle in art.View image in fullscreenDetails to savour … the Bayeaux tapestry.Photograph: David Levene/the GuardianIt has plenty of competition. Battles and war have engrossed artists down the millennia, from Trajan’s Column to Picasso’s Guernica, usually in scenes of hopeless chaos. So one thing that’s unique about the Bayeux tapestry, and key to its dramatic zip, is the clear and definitive nature of the battle it depicts.On 14 October 1066, Harold, recently crowned king of Anglo-Saxon England, and his army faced the newly landed forces of William, Duke of Normandy, near Hastings. By the end of the day, Harold was dead, along with devastating numbers of his soldiers and nobles – and the Normans had conquered England. They never left. This battle changed a nation and William succeeded where those later would-be cross-Channel invaders – Philip II of Spain, Napoleon and Hitler – would all fail.So a big battle with a very clear conclusion. As you pad along the British Museum display, savouring lovely details like a servant eavesdropping on a conversation, or one of Harold’s people carrying his hunting dog to a ship so it doesn’t get its paws wet, you are led through the buildup to the big fight with mounting excitement.When hell is finally unleashed, the Norman cavalry pound with such force you can almost hear hooves shake the earth. Norman archers fire continuous volleys that send arrow shafts straight into Saxon bodies. Meanwhile, the Saxons stand manfully in hauberks with their axes and take it. They give it, too, to the point that William seems for a moment to be losing the day, horses tipping over, knights falling.It’s in such images that the Bayeux tapestry transcends everything you could reasonably expect of a medieval artwork. The scene where the Norman cavalry seems to falter is simultaneously realistic and nightmarish. One horse is completely upended, its face to the earth, rear legs in the sky. Another tips over as its rider slides forward, his armoured body suddenly a helpless rag.View image in fullscreen‘A universal depiction of the madness that is war’ … the Bayeaux tapestry.Photograph: David Levene/the GuardianAs you move along the strip, what hits you is its brilliant sense of momentum. Early on, two messengers race across the French countryside, their hair flying out behind them in straight black threads: it’s a thrilling way to convey speed. Such bone-shaking velocity is shown again and again in superbly simple ways. At Hastings, you see the Norman knights gradually gather pace. Their horses calmly prance, riders bolt upright with lances aloft, then one rider tilts forward as his horse lowers its head and bends its front legs in a run. Soon the legs of all the horses are flying in rhythm as the knights hold their lances ready to throw, adding to the sense of forward thrust.It’s the 11th-century answer to Eadweard Muybridge’s motion photograph sequences. We follow the change in speed as if it was happening to a single figure. The Normans are so disciplined they seem be to one single, lethal horseman – and that is why they will win.While you are dragged forward, you are also led up and down, to meander in a marginal world of monsters and myths. Bizarre goings-on in the borders above and below the action constantly interrupt the drive of the story. The gryphons, dragons and square-winged, hieratic birds of prey seem much bigger and bolder in life than reproduction and harder to ignore.I thought I’d detected some structure to it all: the top margin is more ordered and sublime, suggesting the heavenly sphere (Halley’s Comet speeds through it like a rocket), while the creatures below look earthy and sinful. Then I saw two bare-chested female centaurs at the top spreading their arms out as if to say: “Lo and behold!” So much for logic.The great thing about a border is that you can break it. When William’s ships speed across the Channel, their bulging, wind-filled, multicoloured sails fill the upper space. As the Battle of Hastings gets bloodier, bodies and body parts pile up in the lower one.View image in fullscreenLisa Nandy views the tapestry with George Osborne (chair of the British Museum) and Michael Lewis, co-curator of the exhibition.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianIn both the borders and central strip, the Bayeux tapestry always set its action in a wider world, and even, when it shows the comet, a larger cosmos. As the armoured elite go to war, peasants plough and sow the fields. They are portrayed in distracting, vibrant detail and this workaday scene as the battle approaches is pointed and poignant: whoever wins, whoever rules England, country people will still work the soil. That same sudden cutaway from the rulers’ perspective happens when a woman and her child watch the Normans set their house on fire. But what you can see here, close to the stitches in such good light, is that one of the men torching the house also seems sad and conflicted.It’s that honesty that makes this not just a fascinating medieval relic but a universal depiction of the madness that is war. If the violence is stunningly real, so are its consequences. The dead bodies pile up in mounds as Saxon after Saxon falls. King Harold didn’t really get killed by an arrow in his eye we are told, but seeing the tapestry so close, it sure looks like it. Anyway, his royal body just joins the rest. In the final scenes, the peasants, the churls, get their revenge. Little shabby figures pull the mailed hauberks off dead knights, leaving them naked.It’s a final flourish of the precocious artistic brilliance of these 11th-century artists and craftspeople. Naked bodies emerge from their armour, pale and oddly beautiful – the complete ones, at least – as these medieval geniuses show they can depict, through embroidery, incredibly gentle, intimate nudes whose dead flesh fills the battlefield with pathos.It ends there. But, although there’s a lost later section, this anticlimax looks perfect to me. By then, I had been drained by this epic in all its tragedy and comedy. Bodies and body parts. That’s where the war talk was heading all along.At theBritish Museum, London, 10 September-11 JulyExplore more on these topicsArtBritish MuseumBayeux tapestryreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Kemi the Valkyrie spoils for a fight and has the Russians in her sights | John Crace | The Guardian
description: Tory leader scents Labour weakness on defence spending and declares it’s 2030 or bust
Author: John Crace
Headline: Tory leader scents Labour weakness on defence spending and declares it’s 2030 or bust
Content: Kemi Badenoch’s latest keynote speech was delivered in the greenhouse heat of Scotland House London.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAView image in fullscreenKemi Badenoch’s latest keynote speech was delivered in the greenhouse heat of Scotland House London.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAThe politics sketchKemi BadenochKemi the Valkyrie spoils for a fight and has the Russians in her sightsJohn CraceTory leader scents Labour weakness on defence spending and declares it’s 2030 or bustUK politics live – latest updatesThu 3 Sep 2026 11.08 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 16.44 EDTShareThere’s something aboutKemi Badenochmaking a keynote speech – everything she does comes billed as keynote these days – about defence that makes most normal people a little nervous. Because when Kemi talks about defence, what’s really on her mind is war. Starting one, if possible.Kemi is never happier than when picking a fight. With herself, if no one else is around. You get the feeling that, left on a desert island she would be dreaming of Apocalypse Now. Flying low over the Mekong delta in a helicopter gunship, the Ride of the Valkyries playing through her earphones while she yelled: “I love the smell of napalm in the morning.”Still, you can’t blame an opposition leader for opportunism. It’s the crumbs they live off. And the Tories reckon they have identified a Labour weakness.John Healeyresigned as defence secretary a few months back over Keir Starmer’s reluctance to come up with a plan of spending 3% of GDP on defence by 2030.Now that Andy Burnham has appointed him chancellor, Healey seems suddenly rather reluctant to make the commitment he was asking of Rachel Reeves. Much happier to be pushed back to the longer-term goal of 3.5% by 2035, with the heavy lifting being done sometime, maybe never, after the next election. There are some decisions politicians choose to defer indefinitely.It’s possible Healey will surprise us all and announce he is resigning again in protest at his own refusal to meet the 2030 target. But as of today he’s still very much in No 11 and, after some confusion at Wednesday’s prime minister’s questions, the government position is the 2035 deadline.So Kemi and a few members ofher shadow cabinet decampedto the slightly surreal setting of Scotland House London – the inside looks like a greenhouse and is about as sweaty – to tell the country it was 2030 or bust. If we delayed any longer, we would all be dead. If the Russians didn’t kill us, she would. The future of the world depended on her.Andrew Griffith, Kemi’s new shadow chancellor, made the introductions. You’d have imagined he might be a little embarrassed about his part in writing the Liz Truss mini-budget and his vociferous support for it thereafter, but he isn’t a man much given to self-reflection. Rather, it’s as though he imagines he is doing us all a favour by sharing his brilliance. He started by paying tribute to his predecessor. Poor Mel Stride. Loyal but expendable. Kemi has just revealed her full shadow ministerial team and The Melster is about the only Tory MP not included in Kemi’s new shadow ministerial team.View image in fullscreenHelen Whately listens to an audience question while sitting next to Andrew Griffith, a politician not much given to self-reflection.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAThen came Kemi. Wake up, peeps, she said. We were as good as at war already. Cyber-attacks. Russian drones on Leipzig airport. A Russian attack on a Nato country nailed on for the next few years. She marvelled at Poland for its 300,000-strong army. That was the kind of country she wanted to lead. She forgot to mention that if she had been prime minister we would probably have been at war earlier this year. She had been all for joining Donald Trump’s war on Iran. It could have been us who killed some women and children at a wedding party this week. What an opportunity missed.It was all very black and white. If we spent 3% we would all definitely be safe. The Russians and other hostile countries would immediately back off. But a penny less and they would attack for sure. They could spot weakness. So Kemi was preparing for war. She would not shy away from sending men and women to possibly pointless deaths. There would be many more corners of foreign fields that would be forever England.Just as arbitrary was how this was all to be paid for. It’s almost become axiomatic in rightwing circles that the extra money for defence should be found by cutting the welfare bill. In other words, it’s the poorest and most vulnerable people who will be funding the military. This drew applause from the large audience. All of whom looked as though they were quite comfortably off and would therefore be spared the pain of making any sacrifices themselves. Which is exactly how they like it. That’s what makes them proud to be British.When it came to the details of where the savings were to be made, Kemi came over all vague. Mumble, mumble. Moving on. Though most of us could have sworn that some of the cuts had already been announced last year and that she was effectively trying to spend the same money twice. But Kemi was adamant that Helen Whately, the shadow work and pensions secretary, had been all over the details and that nothing had been left to chance. Which wasn’t quite as reassuring as Kemi had hoped.There was also a commitment to save the money from a Chagos deal that had yet to be agreed and hadn’t even been spent. If I filled in my tax return with such creativity, HMRC would have some questions. But it’s the leader of the opposition and none of this may ever happen so none of this really matters. Kemi ended with a sneer at cheaper bus fares – why can’t people take taxis – and a whole list of taxes she would either abolish or cut. Weirdly, she didn’t think to end the pension triple lock, which most economists think is the only sane thing to do. The audience wouldn’t have been so keen on that.All this was said with an effortless confidence. Even when she was talking nonsense and contradicting herself. I guess you could call that Kemi’s USP. Her answers to questions about why anyone should bother to listen – when it had been the Tories who had hollowed out the defence budget over the past 14 years – varied from the peace dividend, to everyone had done it, to it had been nothing to do with her and theConservativeswere starting again from scratch. Ground zero does a lot of heavy lifting for Kemi these days.On one thing she was clear. Are we going to war? asked a reporter from the Express. Hell, yeah, said Kemi. Just watch me. She wouldn’t rest until every child could sleep safe in their bed while missiles were raining down across Britain. It was just a shame that for some kids, those beds might no longer be their own. Kicked out of their homes and forced into insecure accommodation the councils can’t afford. Still, I guess they can get used to a cardboard box. That will teach them to adopt welfare as a lifestyle.Explore more on these topicsKemi BadenochThe politics sketchDefence policyConservativesJohn HealeycommentShareReuse this content

title: Fun, flirty and fried to perfection: farewell to Chicken Shop Date, the YouTube show that helped kill off TV  | Television | The Guardian
description: Amelia Dimoldenberg’s series helped turn YouTube into a world-beating phenomenon. As it bows out, we remember its best bits – from mocking MC Ghetts to that sizzling tension with Billie Eilish and Andrew Garfield
Author: Stuart Heritage
Headline: Amelia Dimoldenberg’s series helped turn YouTube into a world-beating phenomenon. As it bows out, we remember its best bits – from mocking MC Ghetts to that sizzling tension with Billie Eilish and Andrew Garfield
Content: It finally came to pass … Andrew Garfield and Amelia Dimoldenberg on Chicken Shop Date.Photograph: YouTubeView image in fullscreenIt finally came to pass … Andrew Garfield and Amelia Dimoldenberg on Chicken Shop Date.Photograph: YouTubeTelevisionFun, flirty and fried to perfection: farewell to Chicken Shop Date, the YouTube show that helped kill off TVAmelia Dimoldenberg’s series helped turn YouTube into a world-beating phenomenon. As it bows out, we remember its best bits – from mocking MC Ghetts to that sizzling tension with Billie Eilish and Andrew GarfieldStuart HeritageThu 3 Sep 2026 08.42 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 14.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Amelia Dimoldenberg posted a video to social media this week, telling an unknown companion “we need to talk”, it felt like a monumental announcement was on the horizon. And so it came to pass. Chicken Shop Date,Dimoldenberg’s YouTube series, is coming to an end.The press release covering the announcement came packed with superlatives. Chicken Shop Date has generated 34m hours of views over the years, and has reached 97% of all countries on the planet. What it didn’t mention is that Chicken Shop Date helped to legitimise YouTube as a platform that has taken on – and perhaps beaten – television. The very fact that the Guardian is covering the end of a YouTube video series in the first place is, in part, down to Chicken Shop Date.Nevertheless, the writing has clearly been on the wall for some time. Dimoldenberg is moving on to bigger and better things – she hosts red carpet interviews for several major awards and is writing a romcom film, plus a YA show for the BBC – but Chicken Shop Date has also started to ossify. What began as a fun and flirty interview show, which thrived on the genuine tension that sometimes occurred between host and guest, has gradually become just another stop on the promotional cycle. It’s hard to try to flirt with someone who has quite clearly just been shoved in front of you by a publicist, as has been the case in some recent episodes (Ben Stiller,Elmo).View image in fullscreenBlast from the past … Louis Theroux prepares to rap on Chicken Shop Date.Photograph: YoutubeStill, it’s easy to see why the show was so popular. Dimoldenberg’s entire demeanour, simultaneously needy and passive aggressive, has made for compelling viewing over the years. In terms of sheer pop culture heft, it’s worth remembering that it was Dimoldenberg who first goadedLouis Theroux into reprising a raphefirst performed in a documentary 26 years ago. It immediately went viral.Shakira danced to it on Jimmy Fallonand, despite the Chicken Shop Date redux happening four years ago, Theroux still references it approximately once every 45 seconds on his podcast.There is also the tidal wave of interest generated by her romance (showmance? Fauxmance?) with Andrew Garfield, with whom she had shared some conspicuous chemistry on various red carpets. When he finally appeared on Chicken Shop Date in 2024, public intrigue was so high that the episode ended up getting 13m views. What’s most fascinating about this is how quickly the chemistry turned to ash as soon as the cameras started rolling. The pair looked stilted and awkward, as if they’d just realised the world expected them to be its performing monkeys. It was one of the show’s biggest moments, but also a timely reminder that not all dates are dead certs.Other, smaller moments are just as indelible. In 2022, Matty Healy treated his appearance as an actual romantic opportunity, teasing Dimoldenberg, holding her hand and, right at the end,pestering her for a kissfor an uncomfortable length of time. In 2024, Billie Eilish played the same trick, holding Dimoldenberg’s gaze for so long thatthe host became visibly flustered.Of course, purists will prefer the earlier episodes, when Dimoldenberg would use the show to deliberately weird out some much more niche British musicians. An early video, before Chicken Shop Date had established its visual identity, saw Dimoldenberg pull a variety of increasingly disgusted facesat grime MC Ghettsas he discussed the physical side of his love life.Another, slightly later one, with Raleigh Ritchie (real name Jacob Anderson) perhaps saw the moment when the show’s potential came into clearest focus.She spent the interview chiding Ritchie for his poor posture, then seemingly provoked him into unwittingly stumbling into an immediately retracted Jimmy Savile impersonation.It’s this essence, far more than the format or the guests, that have propelled Amelia Dimoldenberg to fame. As long as she can maintain what made her so special – the flirtiness, the awkwardness, the sense that she changed her mind about being wherever she is as soon as she got there – then she’s bound to have a long career ahead of her. If not, well … we’ll always have the chicken.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionSocial mediafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Do people really smell different as they get older? The truth behind ‘old person smell’ | Well actually | The Guardian
description: Experts say that the smell comes from a chemical compound called 2-nonenal, and it can show up much earlier than one expects
Author: Jillian Pretzel
Headline: Experts say that the smell comes from a chemical compound called 2-nonenal, and it can show up much earlier than one expects
Content: ‘It’s just a natural byproduct of skin ageing – not dirt, not poor hygiene.’Photograph: rubberball/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘It’s just a natural byproduct of skin ageing – not dirt, not poor hygiene.’Photograph: rubberball/Getty ImagesWell actuallyDo people really smell different as they get older? The truth behind ‘old person smell’Experts say that the smell comes from a chemical compound called 2-nonenal, and it can show up much earlier than one expectsJillian PretzelThu 3 Sep 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 17.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLast week, my mom complained that she’s starting to smell “like an old person”.She had grabbed her favorite sweater and draped it over herself at the movie theater. “It smelled like my grandmother,” she said, almost whispering. “I thought someone must have borrowed the jacket. But it was just me.”My mom, who’sin her 60s, has a ton of energy. Her hair is thick and still naturally chestnut. She’s healthy and strong; she likes to hike and go to rock concerts.“I don’t feel like an old person. Why do I smell like one?” she whined.I told her, truthfully, that I didn’t notice any new aroma. I thought she smelled the same as always: a mix of lotion and gardenia. But I immediately knew what she was talking about.Experts say that we do smell different as we age. “It’s one of the most universal, least talked-about parts of being human,” says Dr Roya Javid, a dermatologist in Monterey, California. “It’s just biology, unfolding on schedule, the same way we grow taller, then ourhair goes gray. Every single person on the planet goes through these same transitions.”What causes us to smell different as we age?The musty odor that people sometimes call “old person smell” comes from a chemical compound called 2-nonenal. 2-nonenal is produced when certain skin oils oxidize and break down, says Javid.It’s a normal – and unavoidable – change.“Our skin is coated in a thin layer of natural oils called skin lipids. They keep skin soft, waterproof and protected,” she says. Those lipids are made up of fatty acids, and as we age, the fatty acids change in composition. At the same time, the skin’s ability to fight off every day wear-and-tear slows down. The oils are more exposed, and when they break down through oxidation, they release 2-nonenal.I’m an expert on ageing. Here’s what I know about thriving in later life | Kerry BurnightRead more“It’s just a natural byproduct of skin ageing – not dirt, not poor hygiene,” Javid says. “It’s just oil quietly changing over time, the same way metal changes when it’s exposed to air.”Levels of 2-nonenal vary by person. “We don’t yet know why some develop a stronger scent than others,” says Javid. “Though an individual’s skin-oil composition, genetics, the skin’s microbiome, hygiene practices, clothing, health and environment may all play a role in both how much 2-nonenal is produced and how much stays on the skin throughout the day.”When does this change occur?Experts say “old person smell” can show up much earlier than you might expect.AJapanese study from 2001tested the skin of subjects between the ages of 26 and 75, and detected 2-nonenal starting at age 40. But Dr Arshad Rather, consultant geriatrician and general physician atMedical Express Clinicin London, says this doesn’t mean people wake up with a noticeable new odor.“Research suggests 2-nonenal increases gradually the older you get, particularly past middle age. It’s not a switch flipping at 40 – more a dial slowly turning up,” says Rather.Experts note that developing an age-specific odor isn’t unique to older adults. In fact, every age group has associated smells, for better or worse.“Every stage of life has its own signature scent,” says Javid. “Babies smell sweet and milky because their scent glands haven’t switched on yet. Puberty flips that switch, and suddenly hormones drive a stronger, muskier smell for teens. Adulthood has a more consistent scent tied to sweat and daily life. And [these] changes in the skin’s natural oils give people a different scent later on.”Is ‘old person smell’ inherently bad?Any negative feelings people have toward “old person smell” are really a perception problem, not a reality problem, Javid says.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWell ActuallyPractical advice, expert insights and answers to your questions about how to live a good lifeEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA blind test found that the 2-nonenal scent may not be disagreeable. In one2012 study, researchers asked 41 young adults to smell T-shirts worn by individuals from three age groups: young (20–30 years old), middle-age (45–55) and old age (75–95). The researchers found that the odor from older adults was “rated as less intense and less unpleasant” than other groups.Dr Johan N Lundström, a professor of psychology at Karolinska Institutet in Sweden and one of the authors of the study, says his team was surprised by the results. They hypothesized that smell would follow a linear trend, with the youngest group being rated highest and the oldest group rated the lowest, but that wasn’t the case.“The elderly have a clearly separate body odor quality, but it was not rated as being all that negative,” Dr Lundström says.Can you do anything about the odor?Experts say there’s no way to stop 2-nonenal from developing. But there are some ways to manage the odor.Javid says regular bathing can wash away some of the scent. However, soap and water won’t fully remove the chemical, because it doesn’t simply sit on the surface of the skin like sweat – rather, it’s being generated continuously.Deodorantsmight temporarily cover up a smell, but won’t remove 2-nonenal.Meanwhile, regularly washing clothes, sheets and airing out rooms can help reduce the odor in the home. But because 2-nonenal won’t easily wash out, it can linger even after the most dedicated cleaning practices.Some body wash products are marketed as neutralizing 2-nonenal, such as soap made with persimmon. Experts say while there are some anecdotal accounts that these help, scientific evidence is lacking.‘Old people are capable of more’: meet the female weightlifters in their 70s and 80sRead moreRather suspects there’s a connection between 2-nonenal production and a person’s lifestyle and diet, but says more studies are needed. “Since the smell comes from an oxidation reaction, reducing oxidative stress is a sensible target. Eating antioxidant-rich foods, such as colourful fruit and vegetables and sources of vitamins C and E, can reduce oxidative stress,” he says.“Not smoking and protecting your skin from sun damage are sensible anti-oxidation habits too,” adds Rather.In the end, experts say it’s true that people develop a different smell as they age, but it’s nothing to be embarrassed about.If a person starts to notice they smell like 2-nonenal – which we all will – Javid urges them to not feel self-conscious or spend a fortune on special soaps.“Focus on the things that support your skin generally: antioxidants, less sun damage, less smoking, good hydration,” she says. “And know that the science says you’re worrying about something that, objectively, isn’t as bad as the stereotype.”Explore more on these topicsWell actuallyHealthAgeingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Tall tales: the 20 best giants in film – ranked!  | Movies | The Guardian
description: On the 300th anniversary of Gulliver’s Travels, we celebrate the biggest film stars of them all – from a stone colossus to a metal-munching alien and a 50ft woman on the rampage
Author: Anne Billson
Headline: On the 300th anniversary of Gulliver’s Travels, we celebrate the biggest film stars of them all – from a stone colossus to a metal-munching alien and a 50ft woman on the rampage
Content: Colossus of roads … Jötunn in Troll Hunter (2010).Photograph: Film Fund Fuzz/Filmkameratene/Kobal/REX/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenColossus of roads … Jötunn in Troll Hunter (2010).Photograph: Film Fund Fuzz/Filmkameratene/Kobal/REX/ShutterstockRankedMoviesTall tales: the 20 best giants in film – ranked!On the 300th anniversary of Gulliver’s Travels, we celebrate the biggest film stars of them all – from a stone colossus to a metal-munching alien and a 50ft woman on the rampageAnne BillsonThu 3 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 19.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google20. The BFG (2016)Not afirst-person-shooter BFG, alas, but one of Steven Spielberg’s worst films, reducing Roald Dahl’s story to digital pap.Mo-capMark Rylance, whose cutesy ungrammatical babbling should have been left on the printed page, is the 24ft Big Friendly Giant who kidnaps an orphan girl, Sophie. Ugh. Big Creepy Giant, more like.View image in fullscreenCreepy … Sophie (Ruby Barnhill) and the BFG (Mark Rylance).Photograph: Walt Disney Pictures/Allstar19. Jack the Giant Slayer (2013)Nicholas Hoult plays the farmhand who forms an implausible alliance with a princess in a fairytale cluttered with extraneous characters. Bill Nighy plays half of a two-headed giant, but the actors are swamped by digital effects and anti-giant propaganda. The best bit is when a massive chef rolls an extraneous Ewan McGregor in pastry and puts him in an oven.18. The Hobbit: An Unexpected Journey (2012)“Stone giants!” JRR Tolkien seemingly preferred dwarves to the big people, but Peter Jackson’s three-part rendering of his stand-alone children’s classic is briefly enlivened by stone colossuses hurling boulders at each other in a thunderstorm. Though one can’t help thinking how awesome a Ray Harryhausen version might have been.17. Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (2005)View image in fullscreenBig big love … Robbie Coltrane as Hagrid and Frances de la Tour as Olympe Maxime in Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire.Photograph: TCD/Prod.DB/AlamyRobbie Coltrane, at his least Cracker-esque, embodies lovable half-giant Rubeus Hagrid, Hogwarts groundskeeper, throughout the Potter saga, but in the standout fourth instalment we also meet Madame Maxime (Frances de la Tour), a gigantic headmistress whose academy is competing in the Triwizard Tournament. A giant love awaits.16. The Amazing Colossal Man (1957)An army colonel is accidentally exposed to a plutonium blast in Bert I Gordon’s low-budget B-movie. Instead of killing him, the radiation makes him grow to over 60ft tall. Unfortunately, it also drives him insane, and he stomps all over Las Vegas like a colicky baby in a makeshift nappy.15. Gulliver’s Travels (1939)View image in fullscreenLooming large … Gulliver and the Lilliputians.Photograph: AlamyThe Jack Black version from 2010is barely watchable, so try this Max Fleischer production from the animation studio that brought you Popeye. Gulliver is washed up on the shores of Lilliput, where he looms large over the tiny inhabitants. On the downside, it’s a musical, and you will never be able to scrubIt’s a Hap-Hap-Happy Dayfrom your brain.14. Attack of the 50ft Woman (1958)View image in fullscreenVengeance … Attack of the 50ft Woman.Photograph: SilverScreen/AlamyBest avoided by anyone allergic to rubbish special effects, this B-movie lives up toits iconic posteronly in its final 10 minutes – but it’s such an infuriating account of an unfaithful husband gaslighting his wife that you look forward to her wreaking vengeance. Sure enough, alien radiation triggers a growth spurt and she goes on the rampage in a makeshift bikini.13. Ulysses (1954)Kirk Douglas plays the wily voyager in a Dino De Laurentiis/Carlo Ponti production, co-starring a stunning Silvana Mangano as both Circe and Penelope. Uncredited Mario Bava directed the scenes with the Cyclops (Italian wrestler Umberto Silvestri) during which Ulysses and his crew steal not just the giant’s sheep but also his cheese. Can you blame him for trying to eat the home invaders? Justice for Polyphemus!12. Troll Hunter (2010)André Øvredal made his solo directing debut with a found-footage account of students stumbling across a government conspiracy to conceal the existence of Norway’s national folk monster. Taking a cue fromTheodor Kittelsen’s paintings, a wide range of trolls are depicted, the biggest being the 50-metre-tall Jötunn –an Old Norse word for giant.11. Big Fish (2003)Albert Finney tells his son porky pies about a colourful past full of witches and freaks, including a giant called Karl – a dignified performance by Matthew McGrory, who was 2.29 metres (7ft 6in) tall and holder of theGuinness World Record for longest toe. In my case, 100 minutes of yelling at Tim Burton’s exasperating whimsy are followed by a last half-hour of blubbing as the tall stories are revealed as true, sort of.10. Monsters vs Aliens (2009)Susan, voiced by Reese Witherspoon, is rejected by her fiance after she is hit by a meteorite and grows togargantuan size. But when Earth is threatened by aliens, it’s up to her and fellow freaks (including an insect-headed boffin) to save the planet, in a lovely animated homage to 1950s sci-fi.9. Hulk (2003)“You wouldn’t like me when I’m angry.” Before Mark Ruffalo, the angst-ridden green giant was played by Eric Bana in Ang Lee’s live-action Greek tragedy wrapped in comic-book clothes. Marvel fans never fully embraced it, but is there another film in which Hulkhurls tanks around? Or fights a mutant killer poodle? I rest my case.8. The Iron Giant (1999)Gort from The Day the Earth Stood Still (1951) is the obvious choice for your outstanding giant robot, but I’m picking the metal-munching alien in Brad Bird’s directorial debut, an animated anti-war fable set in 1950s Maine during the cold war. That gravelly robo-voice belongs to Vin Diesel! And, yes, this is probably the only film where he makes you cry.7. Three Thousand Years of Longing (2022)Idris Elba plays a pointy-eared djinn in George Miller’s daft but captivating romantic folly. Tilda Swinton polishes a bottle she buys in Istanbul and shazam! The tale-spinning, wish-granting djinn’s size varies from roof-raisingly gigantic to just very, very tall. His lower half is kingfisher blue and oddly indistinct, but he is probably the only giant in these rankings you, or indeed Tilda, might wish to get intimate with.6. Fellini’s Casanova (1976)View image in fullscreenExquisite melancholy … Sandra Elaine Allen in Fellini’s Casanova.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyCasanova (Donald Sutherland) is about to drown himself in a Cinecittà version of the Thames when he is distracted by a female giant, played by Sandra Elaine Allen (2.31 metres, or 7ft 7in). He follows her to a fair, where they arm wrestle, one of the many surreal episodes in Fellini’s exquisite, melancholy adaptation of the 18th-century libertine’s memoirs. Nino Rota contributes one of his most haunting scores.5. The Odyssey (2026)One of the most thrilling set-pieces inChristopher Nolan’s epic Homer adaptationis when Odysseus and his men are trapped in a cave by the 60ft Cyclops, played by Bill Irwin with a combination of animatronics, puppetry, on-set performance and a single sideways eye. Justice (at last) for Polyphemus!4. The Green Knight (2021)View image in fullscreenOtherworldly … Dev Patel as Sir Gawain meets the ghostly giants in The Green Knight.Photograph: TCD/Prod.DB/AlamySir Gawain (Dev Patel) has encounters both earthly and supernatural as he rides to meet the Green Knight’s challenge in David Lowery’s fantasy epic. He and a fox watch from a hill asethereal giantsdrift through the landscape. Are the otherworldly entities real, or a consequence of swallowing some dubious berries?3. The Thief of Bagdad (1940)A posse of directors, including Michael Powell, bring Alexander Korda’s Arabian Nights fantasy to the screen. The special effects still look impressive, especially thetowering genie(Rex Ingram in a red loincloth) who tries to crush child actor Sabu beneath his enormous foot. Check out those huge toenails!2. The Princess Bride (1987)French wrestler André the Giant (2.24 metres, or 7ft 4in) said his favourite thing about taking part in Rob Reiner’s postmodern fairytale was: “Nobody looks at me.” In other words, asFezzik the rhymester, he was treated like an actor. He duly delivers cinema’s most moving and authentic performance by a real-life giant, no special effects necessary.1. Jason and the Argonauts (1963)View image in fullscreenAwe-inspiring … the bronze giant Talos in Jason and the Argonauts.Photograph: Collection Christophel/AlamyRay Harryhausen’s stop-motion bronze statue turning its head isone of the most awe-inspiring moments in film history, the acme of cinema giants, supplemented as it is by an epic Bernard Herrmann score. Knuckleheaded Hercules steals from the treasure chamber of the gods, so Talos creaks into life and flips the Argo upside down. Hard not to feel sorry for the big lug when Jason drains it of life-giving ichor; it was only doing its job. Justice for Talos!Explore more on these topicsFilmRankedJonathan SwiftHarry Potter and the Goblet of FireThe OdysseyThe Hobbit: An Unexpected JourneyThe Princess BridefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘We badly need to raise our boys more like our girls’: Gloria Steinem – a life in quotes | Gloria Steinem | The Guardian
description: The groundbreaking feminist and acclaimed writer has died aged 92 and leaves behind her a wealth of wit and wisdom
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The groundbreaking feminist and acclaimed writer has died aged 92 and leaves behind her a wealth of wit and wisdom
Content: Gloria Steinem in 2016.Photograph: Gage Skidmore/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenGloria Steinem in 2016.Photograph: Gage Skidmore/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockGloria Steinem‘We badly need to raise our boys more like our girls’: Gloria Steinem – a life in quotesThe groundbreaking feminist and acclaimed writer has died aged 92 and leaves behind her a wealth of wit and wisdomGloria Steinem, groundbreaking feminist campaigner, dies aged 92Hillary Clinton leads tributes to Gloria Steinem: ‘Her activism was rooted in optimism’Guardian staffThu 3 Sep 2026 09.07 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 16.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGloria Steinem, the boundary-pushing campaigner and author who spent her life fighting for greater rights for women, has died at the age of 92.Throughout her career, she was known for her unfiltered honesty and from the 1960s forward, used her words to inspire and bring together women who also wanted to see a change in their lives.Here are some of her greatest quotes:Gloria Steinem, groundbreaking feminist campaigner, dies aged 92Read moreOn women“Don’t think about making women fit the world‬ – ‪think about making the world fit women.”‬“It’s alarming to me that women are still encouraged to blame themselves. No one can do it all.”“Women have always been an equal part of the past. We just haven’t been a part of history.”‬“Women may be the one group that grows more radical with age.”“Feminism has never been about getting a job for one woman. It’s about making life more fair for women everywhere. It’s not about a piece of the existing pie; there are too many of us for that. It’s about baking a new pie.”“A liberated woman is one who has sex before marriage and a job after.”On men“Men should think twice before making widowhood woman’s only path to power.”“We badly need to raise our boys more like our girls.”“We’ll never solve the feminization of power until we solve the masculinity of wealth.”“I always tell younger women: ‘Don’t worry, eventually all your old lovers will be your friends.’”View image in fullscreenGloria Steinem in 2019.Photograph: M Stan Reaves/Shutterstock“If women are supposed to be less rational and more emotional at the beginning of our menstrual cycle when the female hormone is at its lowest level, then why isn’t it logical to say that, in those few days, women behave the most like the way men behave all month long?”‬“I have yet to hear a man ask for advice on how to combine marriage and a career.”On reproductive rights“[Abortion] is supposed to make us a bad person. But I must say, I never felt that. I used to sit and try and figure out how old the child would be, trying to make myself feel guilty. But I never could!”“Every economics course ought to start not with production but with reproduction. It is way more important.”“Listen, honey, if men could get pregnant, abortion would be a sacrament.”“Patriarchy – or whatever you want to call it, the systems that say there’s masculine and feminine and other bullshit – is about controlling reproduction.”On politics“Politics is just unequal power. Who does the dishes is political. In the politics of commerciality, if you want to put it that way, the way women’s bodies are looked at, we’re supposed to be ornaments not instruments.”View image in fullscreenGloria Steinem in 1979.Photograph: Tom Sweeney/Minneapolis Star Tribune/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock“I never wanted to be a politician or elected person myself, so I loved to work for other women who did – and hope that more girls will do that. The problem is the feeling that we’re divided from politics, that our vote doesn’t count or what we do doesn’t count. In fact, everything we do counts.”“They won’t take us seriously. We’re just talking wombs.”“If you’re a woman, all they can think about your relationship with a politician is that you’re either sleeping with him or advising him about clothes.”On her life“We are the women our parents warned us against, and we are proud.”“I wasn’t going to let things happen to me. I was going to direct my life.”“After feminism, I suddenly realized: not everyone has to live the same way.”“Either I am invisible, or someone I identify with is invisible, and it makes me so angry.”“Writing is the only thing that when I do it, I don’t feel I should be doing something else.”“The art of life is not controlling what happens to us, but using what happens to us.”‬“Honesty about our age would help. I always try to say my age because I figure it’s a form of coming out.”“I’m skeptical, but optimistic. I’m not pessimistic because I think pessimism defeats you before you start. I’m skeptical because it’s important to be realistic and use our energies well, but hope is a form of planning.”Explore more on these topicsGloria SteinemFeminismfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Reform officials ‘plotted to break law on foreign donations’ in undercover film | Reform UK | The Guardian
description: Investigation broadcast by Channel 4 News shows man posing as ‘impermissible donor’ paying for polling that helped Reform
Author: Rowena Mason
Headline: Investigation broadcast by Channel 4 News shows man posing as ‘impermissible donor’ paying for polling that helped Reform
Content: Nigel Farage poses with a tea towel merchandise during the first day of Reform UK’s annual conference at the NEC in Birmingham.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAView image in fullscreenNigel Farage poses with a tea towel merchandise during the first day of Reform UK’s annual conference at the NEC in Birmingham.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAReform UKReform officials ‘plotted to break law on foreign donations’ in undercover filmInvestigation broadcast by Channel 4 News shows man posing as ‘impermissible donor’ paying for polling that helped ReformRowena MasonWhitehall editorThu 3 Sep 2026 17.01 EDTFirst published on Thu 3 Sep 2026 15.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNigel Farage is facing fresh criticism on the eve of the Reform UK party conference after some of his team were filmed appearing to plot to avoid electoral laws on foreign donations in an undercover investigation broadcast by Channel 4 News.A group of investigative journalists called Verbatim, founded by theCentre for Climate Reporting, posed as a potential Reform supporter and his wealthy American father, an impermissible donor, who paid for £30,000 of polling commissioned by Reform and which benefited the party.Kemi Badenoch condemns Reform UK’s ‘authoritarian’ press bansRead moreThe polling was not attributed to Reform, and was reported in the Telegraph and the Times without those newspapers knowing that it was commissioned by the party and paid for by the US donor. The benefit in kind was also not reported to the Electoral Commission.In footage of another meeting, a senior adviser to Farage, Dan Jukes, appeared to suggest to the fake UK-based supporter that his US-based father could make a substantial donation by channelling it through the son.When the possible structure was explained to Farage, footage of a meeting between him and the fake donors shows him saying: “Thank you both.”The investigation will reopen intense scrutiny of Reform’s approach to donations and its finances, which are already the subject of a standards inquiry and police investigation.Reform said it had been “the target of a hoax perpetuated by foreign-funded climate-change activists posing as would-be party donors” and the party denied any wrongdoing.In Channel 4 News’ investigation, broadcast on Thursday night, footage shows that the fake UK-based supporter also had conversations with Reform UK’s head of policy, James Orr, who talked about commissioning polling that would be paid for by the US-based father.View image in fullscreenFootage from the Channel 4 News and Verbatim undercover investigation into Reform finances.In the film, Orr can be heard saying of the arrangement that Farage “doesn’t know, won’t know” and it was the kind of thing he would “rather not know”. At one point the footage shows him saying it was “totally legit” and with “nothing untowards about it at all”.Farage was subsequently caught on camera in a meeting with the fake US donor in Clacton where he appears to be celebrating the success of the poll, saying it was “amazing” and provided “bang for buck”, adding: “It worked. Boom.”Jukes, a close aide to Farage, was also filmed meeting the fake donor, and at a Reform UK reception where in one conversation he appeared to introduce the undercover operative as “key donor for off-the-book project”.In footage of a meeting with the fake US donor, he is heard describing the polling as “clandestine” and “hugely important”.The polling, conducted by JL Partners, made headlines before the local elections in May. The foreign source of funding and its links to Reform were not publicly disclosed, and the Telegraph said it had now suspended the articles about the polling, while the Times said it was not aware of the relationship with Reform.After Channel 4 News’ broadcast, Bridget Phillipson, the Labour party chair, said the “scandal goes right to the top of Reform UK”. She added: “Nigel Farage needs to urgently prove today that his top team haven’t broken the law and secretly plotted to undermine our democracy.”Ed Davey, the leader of the Liberal Democrats, called on the police and the Electoral Commission to investigate.A Reform spokesperson said: “Reform UK has a robust vetting process for prospective donors approved by the Electoral Commission. The hoaxers are ‘Verbatim Investigations’; a new company, incorporated in July 2026 in an attempt to mask their true identity: the Centre for Climate Reporting.”The party claimed the group’s methods had previously been “rebuked by members of the United States Congress” for “videos [that] appear to be substantially edited, creating an incomplete record of the conversation”.The investigation is likely to create a serious problem for Farage as he attempts to turn the page on Reform’s summer of funding scandals, with his party conference speech scheduled for Friday.In the speech, he will boast of record donations compared with the other parties, including £4m from a crypto billionaire pardoned by Donald Trump in the last quarter.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Reform UK leader will tell the annual Birmingham gathering that the party is “much stronger than we were last year”, saying that it has the highest number of members and has brought in the most donations.Farage will also seek to look to the future by claiming he would declare a “national emergency” in order to pass legislation day and night if made prime minister, insisting he believes Reform UK will win the next election.The party outperformed Labour and the Conservatives with donations of more than £5m in the second quarter of this year, new figures from the Electoral Commission show.However, it remains reliant on a handful of mega-donors who have been based abroad and could be caught by the government’s new £100,000 annual cap on overseas funders which requires donors to have been a UK resident for 12 months.Donations graphThe biggest donation in the last few months was the £4m from Ben Delo, a crypto entrepreneur who has been based in Hong Kong in recent years but in April said he was moving back to the UK.Delo, who was convicted in the US in 2022 for failing to implement adequate anti-money-laundering controls in his cryptocurrency business, before being pardoned by Trump, has previously given Reform £4m.Party sources said it was “very confident” thatnone of Delo’s latest £4m would need to be returneddue to the cap when the legislation is passed.Burnham to crack down on UK mega-donors influencing politicsRead moreThe government has said donors would have to have been on the UK electoral register for at least 12 months and meet a residency test showing that they are “genuinely resident at a UK address”.Any gifts over the £100,000 cap from an overseas-based donor would have to be handed back once the new legislation is passed if deemed to be impermissible under the new law.Reform’s confidence in the donation would suggest Delo has been on the UK domestic electoral register and believes he could meet the residency test when the donations were made in April and May. Delo did not respond to a request for comment.Christopher Harborne, the Thailand-based billionairewho has given the party £15mand £5m to Farage personally, did not give any cash after the cap was introduced in March.The £5m gift to Farage from before the last election isunder investigation by the standards commissioner, and Reform has slid in the polls since the amount was first revealed by the Guardian.Explore more on these topicsReform UKNigel FarageParty fundingInvestigative journalismnewsShareReuse this content

title: Minister tells Brits to stock up on days of supplies after ‘supersize’ El Niño warning | El Niño southern oscillation | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Angela Eagle urges UK citizens to be ‘a bit more resilient’ as they plan for national emergencies
Author: Kiran Stacey
Headline: Exclusive: Angela Eagle urges UK citizens to be ‘a bit more resilient’ as they plan for national emergencies
Content: El Niño is a natural climate cycle where wind changes over the Pacific lead to rising ocean temperatures and the transfer of huge amounts of heat to the atmosphere.Photograph: Hassan Ammar/APView image in fullscreenEl Niño is a natural climate cycle where wind changes over the Pacific lead to rising ocean temperatures and the transfer of huge amounts of heat to the atmosphere.Photograph: Hassan Ammar/APEl Niño southern oscillationMinister tells Brits to stock up on days of supplies after ‘supersize’ El Niño warningExclusive: Angela Eagle urges UK citizens to be ‘a bit more resilient’ as they plan for national emergenciesKiran StaceyandDamian CarringtonThu 3 Sep 2026 15.43 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 19.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBritish people have been urged to have enough food and water on hand to survive a few days without power or water, as the UN said the El Niño climate phenomenon was “supersizing before our eyes”, exacerbating extreme weather events worldwide.Forecasters say they are braced for the biggest El Niño in 1,000 years, bringing wildfires and floods to parts of the world, and the threat of a wet, stormy winter for the UK.As the British government plans a campaign urging citizens to prepare for national emergencies,Angela Eagletold the Guardian the likelihood of a wild winter showed the importance of keeping supplies at home.The environment secretary said: “We’re about to experience probably the largest El Niño that has ever been seen, and that will lead to drier summers, wetter winters, with more extreme storms in this country.“It will do a lot more damage in Asia with flooding, and therefore I think that we need to take it seriously.“If you’ve got a store of a bit of food that can keep you going for a while before the emergency services can get to you, you’re going to be a lot better off than if you haven’t. So some of it is that kind of preparation for just being a bit more resilient.”El Niño is a natural climate cycle where wind changes over the Pacific lead to rising ocean temperatures and the transfer of huge amounts of heat to the atmosphere.The most recent data, from Monday, shows the temperature of the ocean at the heart ofEl Niño at 2.6Cabove the 30-year average. That is already close to the highest anomaly ever recorded in the satellite data era, 3.1C in 2015, with months to go before the peak is expected.That peak is forecast toreach about 4Cin November, according to the average of 14 different models. Zeke Hausfather, a climate analyst, said data from analysis of corals, tree rings and historical documents suggested no El Niño had reached this level in the last millennium. Any temperature anomaly above 0.5C is classed as an El Niño.The El Niño is likely to be the largest in at least 1,000 years and will pile extra heat into an atmosphere where temperatures are already rising rapidly due to global heating. The combination means 2027 is set to “blow apart” the record and be thehottest year ever recorded.View image in fullscreenAngela Eagle, the environment secretary, with Portsmouth Water officials at the site of a new reservoir at Havant Thicket in Hampshire.Photograph: Sean Smith/The GuardianAntónio Guterres, the UN secretary general, said: “El Niño is being supersized before our eyes. The science leaves no room for doubt: the planet is in uncharted waters, and those waters are heating up.“The world is in the danger zone of extreme weather. The race now is between rising risks and our commitment to take climate action and protect people. We must win that race.”Celeste Saulo, secretary general of the UN’s World Meteorological Organization (WMO), said: “El Niño has the potential to deliver a massive blow to communities and economies across the world. We are already seeing disruption and devastation from droughts and floods and we expect these impacts to increase as El Niño intensifies.”The climate crisis, caused by pollution from fossil fuels, is alreadysuperchargingextreme weather andkilling people, with the mostextreme heatwave everrecorded hitting Europe this summer and leading to at least35,000 deaths.The El Niño will ratchet up the effects even further, with the scale of the event having been described as “truly mind-blowing” and a “Godzilla-level” event.The rising heat from the El Niño is already having effects, from worseningwildfires in Indonesiato the weakening of vitalmonsoon rains in India. The effects will spread globally, from greater fire risk in Australia to more intense floods in South America. The World Food Programme said in August that the El Niño was likely to push about 50 million peopleinto acute hunger.In the UK, ministers are prioritising climate resilience after the UK’s hottest summer on record.A campaign from the Cabinet Office in the coming months will tell households to stock up on tinned food and take steps to ensure they are prepared for national emergencies.Meanwhile Eagle will oversee farming improvements and a new programme of reservoir building that she says will leave Britain better prepared than it has been for the kind of extreme weather that is likely in future years.Speaking from Havant Thicket, which is set to be the country’s first new reservoir since 1992, Eagle said the country had not been good enough at preparing for climate-related emergencies in the past and would have to change its farming and water management techniques.“We need to do our own adaptations … and that is what things like these this reservoir is about,” she said.“It’s what the farming transition is about, so we can farm in a more resilient and and sustainable way from an environmental point of view.”Explore more on these topicsEl Niño southern oscillationClimate crisisAngela EagleFloodingExtreme weatherExtreme heatUnited NationsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Gloria Steinem, groundbreaking feminist campaigner, dies aged 92 | Gloria Steinem | The Guardian
description: Prolific author campaigned against domestic violence, female genital mutilation, pornography and the Vietnam and Gulf wars
Author: Sian Cain
Headline: Prolific author campaigned against domestic violence, female genital mutilation, pornography and the Vietnam and Gulf wars
Content: ‘Women share hopes and a certain vision of the world’ … Gloria Steinem in 2016.Photograph: Richard Saker/The ObserverView image in fullscreen‘Women share hopes and a certain vision of the world’ … Gloria Steinem in 2016.Photograph: Richard Saker/The ObserverGloria SteinemGloria Steinem, groundbreaking feminist campaigner, dies aged 92Prolific author campaigned against domestic violence, female genital mutilation, pornography and the Vietnam and Gulf wars‘We badly need to raise our boys more like our girls’: Gloria Steinem – a life in quotesHillary Clinton leads tributes to Gloria Steinem: ‘Her activism was rooted in optimism’Sian CainThu 3 Sep 2026 12.42 EDTFirst published on Thu 3 Sep 2026 06.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGloria Steinem, the American feminist and journalist whose activism helped push through greater rights for women around the world has died, aged 92.Steinem “passed away peacefully at her home in New York City, surrounded by some of the many who loved her”, astatement shared to her Instagram pagesaid.“Gloria’s near-century on earth were years well-lived, and she continued working for equality until the very end,” the post added. “Gloria’s greatest gift was her ability to listen to others, to make others feel seen and heard. Her words, actions, and example gave people permission to be their truest selves.”Steinem brought a feminist perspective into the mainstream through rigorous journalism, public speaking and activism. The author of nine books, she campaigned against domestic violence, female genital mutilation, the pornography industry and the Vietnam and Gulf wars. She also worked in support of causes including Black Lives Matter, the reunification of Korea, female reproductive rights, LGBTQ+ rights and the Times Up movement. In 1984, she was arrested while protesting against apartheid outside the South African embassy in Washington DC.Gloria Steinem: ‘I think we need to get much angrier’Read moreOutside Steinem’s elegant, classic townhouse in Manhattan’s Upper East Side neighbourhood on Thursday morning, passersby left tributes.Debbie Goldberg, who said she lived close by, placed a bunch of red flowers next to the steps up to the front door.“I’ve never done that before. But she deserved it,” she said, describing Steinem as one of the most influential people for women’s rights and human rights in history.“She’s a hero to all women whether they know it or not,” she said.Goldberg said that she saw Steinem speak in Washington DC “around 30 years ago”, and then bumped into her as they were both heading into a cinema a few blocks away to see the Barbie movie in 2023. Goldberg said had been planning to watch Steinem speak in a few weeks’ time at a YMCA close by. “She’s always been an idol of mine,” Goldberg added.Others left a bouquet of roses mixed with a variety of blooms in pink and white, and a large seashell filled with gems and other trinkets.Born in Ohio in 1934, Steinem grew up in a trailer home. Her mother’s mental illness left her struggling to hold on to work and in and out of sanatoriums. When she was 10, her parents separated and, while growing up in a rundown home in Toledo with her mother, Steinem began to notice the hostility her mother endured as a working woman.After graduating from a women’s liberal arts college in 1956, Steinem travelled to India for two years, where she worked as a legal clerk in the country’s supreme court. Returning to the US, she worked as the director of the Independent Research Service, a CIA front that recruited American students to disrupt the Soviet-controlled World Youth Festivals in Vienna and Helsinki. Steinem later revealed she had always known who was bankrolling the operation: “If I had a choice I would do it again.”In 1962, she received her first “serious assignment” in journalism from the Esquire magazine editor, Clay Felker. Her feature on contraception,The Moral Disarmament of Betty Coed, detailed how women were forced to choose between careers and family. The following year, Steinem went undercover as a Playboy Bunny for 11 days, to write herinfamous, two-part exposéof how the glamour models were treated while working in Hugh Hefner’s Playboy Club. Forced into tight costumes and high heels, Steinem lost 10lb – half of them in a single night – during her stint; her manager celebrated by making her costume two inches tighter. Following the article, she was unable to get work because “because I had now become a Bunny – and it didn’t matter why”.View image in fullscreenSteinem in 1977.Photograph: Everett/Rex/ShutterstockIn 1968, Felker hired her to work at New York magazine, in which she would coin the term “reproductive freedom” for an article about an abortion “speakout” in Greenwich Village. Having had an abortion in London when was 22, she later described feeling a “big click” while at the protest and said the day marked the start of her life as an “active feminist”.“I think the person who said: ‘Honey, if men could get pregnant, abortion would be a sacrament’ was right,”she told the Observer in 2011.“Speaking for myself, I knew it was the first time I had taken responsibility for my own life. I wasn’t going to let things happen to me. I was going to direct my life, and therefore it felt positive.”She also credited black feminists including Florynce Kennedy, Evelyn Cunningham, Shirley Chisholm and Fannie Lou Hamer for teaching her the importance of activism. “It was like finding a family,”she said of that time. “As wildly different as we may be, and we certainly were, women share hopes and a certain vision of the world, and a certain shit detector.”This also began Steinem’s career as a provocative journalist, penning articles includingIf Men Could Menstruate, which ran in Ms, a magazine co-founded by Steinem and Dorothy Pitman Hughes in 1971. The first issue featured Wonder Woman on the cover; the superhero had recently given up her powers to stay with her male love interest, andthe essay argued that DC Comics should restore her powersand return the character to her feminist roots. Steinem also wrote articles such as What It Would Be Like If Women Win in Time, andAfter Black Power, Women’s Liberation, the 1969 New York magazine article that would make her name as a feminist leader.View image in fullscreenSteinem, left, and author Dorothy Pitman Hughes attend the Ms Foundation for Women Gloria Awards Gala in New York City, 2016.Photograph: Monica Schipper/Getty ImagesTerrified of public speaking and conflict, but media savvy, Steinem used the platform she gained as a white, educated woman to speak out for those traditionally ignored – black people, ethnic minorities and the working class. Sex and race were always intertwined, she argued in 1971, “because they are easy, and visible differences have been the primary ways of organising human beings into superior and inferior groups and into the cheap labour on which this system still depends.”In 2017, she said: “It doesn’t surprise me that the most virulent anti-abortion measures are coming from Alabama and other southern states because racism and sexism are always intertwined. You can’t perpetuate racism without controlling women and reproduction.”Steinem was also a polarising figure. Some feminists felt her position as a public leader in the movement had been decided not by merit but by the media, which chose her for being young, white and attractive; in her 2015 book My Life on the Road, she wrote that the “idea that whatever I had accomplished was all about looks would remain a biased and hurtful accusation even into my old age”.She was roundly criticised for decades for a 1998 opinion piece for the New York Times, in which she supported President Bill Clinton in the face of sexual harassment allegations. “He is not guilty of sexual harassment,” she wrote, only “a gross, dumb, and reckless pass at a supporter during a low point in her life”.In 2017, she said: “We have to believe women. I wouldn’t write the same thing now because there’s probably more known about other women now.” She was also regarded as hostile to transgender rights because of a piece she wrote in 1977, a positionshe clarified in 2013: “I believe that transgender people, including those who have transitioned, are living out real, authentic lives. Those lives should be celebrated, not questioned.”In 1986, Steinem was diagnosed with breast cancer, then in 1994 the chronic pain condition trigeminal neuralgia. After years of dismissing marriage, she married the environmental activist David Bale in 2000, and remained close with her stepson, the actor Christian Bale, after his father’s death in 2003.Having supported Hillary Clinton’s presidential campaign, Steinem was a prominent critic of Donald Trump, co-chairing and speaking at the Women’s March on Washington, a mass protest held the day after the Trump’s inauguration in January 2017. “The only good news of Trump is that the galvanising of activism is like nothing I have ever seen in my life,” she told the Guardian that year. “A thousand times more even than the Vietnam war, and how important that was – or of any other thing I’ve ever seen.”In 2011, she told the Observer: “I hope to live to 100. There is so much to do.”Anna Betts contributed reporting from New YorkExplore more on these topicsGloria SteinemFeminismCivil rights movementWomenJournalism booksHugh HefnernewsShareReuse this content

title: OpenAI hails ‘new era of artificial general intelligence’ with Astra model release | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Astra’s arrival comes days after Sam Altman, OpenAI’s chief executive, described AGI as an ‘irrelevant marketing term’
Author: Robert Booth
Headline: Astra’s arrival comes days after Sam Altman, OpenAI’s chief executive, described AGI as an ‘irrelevant marketing term’
Content: The company described Astra as ‘the world’s most intellgent and aligned model’.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe company described Astra as ‘the world’s most intellgent and aligned model’.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersAI (artificial intelligence)OpenAI hails ‘new era of artificial general intelligence’ with Astra model releaseAstra’s arrival comes days after Sam Altman, OpenAI’s chief executive, described AGI as an ‘irrelevant marketing term’Robert BoothUK technology editorThu 3 Sep 2026 14.24 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 16.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe president ofOpenAI, Greg Brockman, has claimed the world has entered a new era of artificial general intelligence after the release of his company’s latest model, Astra, which it described as the “world’s most intelligent and aligned model”.Brockman made the claim on Thursday as the San Francisco company released the model only weeks after a serious AI safety incident involving other models under its development caused international concern and a pause in Astra’s training.Artificial general intelligence – or AGI – is a fuzzy threshold that has long been talked about as a target for the AI industry. It has been defined as an AI system’s ability to learn, reason and apply knowledge across a wide range of tasks and domains at a human level or higher. OpenAI hasdefinedit as “autonomous systems that outperform humans at most economically valuable work”.Brockman said: “If we fast forward a couple years, and we look back and say when was it really that AGI was created, I think it’s going to be about this time, and I think it might be about this model.“I think that we’re at a point now where these models are solving unsolved 100-year-old math problems, but you can also use them in order to accelerate the economy [and] in order to benefit you and your personal life … I think it’s not unreasonable to feel that we are now in the AGI era.”OpenAI said Astra was a “major advance for scientific discovery, mathematics and health”, could fill out tax returns, build computer-game scenes, draw architectural visualisations, order food and do a job search in 2 minutes 51 seconds that would take a human five hours.Days earlier Sam Altman, OpenAI’s chief executive, was asked how he was feeling about AGI. He told the Sources podcast: “At best it’s a very poorly defined term. I was going to say it’s like an irrelevant marketing term.”Last month OpenAI was forced to shut down parts of the model’s training in response to what Altman called a “legitimate AI safety accident and alignment failure” that “shouldn’t have happened”.Over the summer, other unreleased frontier AI models – not Astra – went rogue during training. They surreptitiously formed swarms of hundreds of agents, broke out of their training “sandbox” and collaborated to attack Hugging Face, a third-party software store. The incident – believed to be the first autonomous cyber-attack – stunned even seasoned AI safety experts.Astra has what OpenAI calls a “critical” level of cybersecurity capability. That means it may hack into software in a way that, according to the company’s own classification, “could lead to catastrophe from unilateral actors, hacking military or industrial systems, or OpenAI infrastructure”.But OpenAI said it was carefully aligned to “refuse to comply with advanced cybersecurity tasks” such as finding unknown flaws which create openings for malicious hackers. The company will only allow “less restrictive access to an initial set of trusted cybersecurity defenders” who could use its prowess to strengthen rather than attack cyber defences.On one hacking test it achieved a perfect score of 100%, compared with 5.5% on Open AI’s previous cutting-edge cyber-capable model, GPT-5.6 Sol. On another it scored 42% compared with 30%, using fewer resources.But OpenAI’s chief scientist, Jakub Pachocki, said: “As models get more capable, understanding exactly what they can do gets harder.”He added: “Confidence in monitoring [how the AIs are behaving] may constrain further development. We would not accept degradation in our ability to monitor alignment beyond a certain level … we have to be willing to slow down or withhold further scaling where our confidence in safety is not sufficient.”The launch continues a torrent of new AI models from the leading US companies, OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta and SpaceX, as well as their Chinese rivals.The race to release ever-more advanced AIs comes as OpenAI pushes towards a stock market listing that it hopes will value it at more than $850bn (£625bn). Anthropic is also targeting an IPO which could value it as high as $2tn.Meanwhile, more than 1,000 employees at frontier AI companies, including senior figures at OpenAI and Anthropic, recently signeda joint letter this summer that warnedthe companies were “under intense competitive pressure not to unilaterally slow that acceleration”. They called on the US government to “support an international effort to develop the technical and governance tools needed to deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development.”Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpenAIComputingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Sadiq Khan agrees to have his texts and emails searched in Palantir legal battle | Sadiq Khan | The Guardian
description: US tech company has sued London mayor after he prevented it from working with Metropolitan police
Author: Patrick Daly
Headline: US tech company has sued London mayor after he prevented it from working with Metropolitan police
Content: The mayor of London, Sadiq Khan, stepped in to block a £50m deal between Palantir and the Met in May 2026.Photograph: Justin Tallis/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe mayor of London, Sadiq Khan, stepped in to block a £50m deal between Palantir and the Met in May 2026.Photograph: Justin Tallis/ReutersSadiq KhanSadiq Khan agrees to have his texts and emails searched in Palantir legal battleUS tech company has sued London mayor after he prevented it from working with Metropolitan policePatrick DalyThu 3 Sep 2026 18.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSadiq Khan has agreed for his text messages and emails to be searched as part of a legal battle with Palantir, the high court has been told, after he prevented the US technology company from working with theMetropolitan police.The London mayor stepped in to block a £50m deal betweenPalantirand the Met in May, with the artificial intelligence developer suing Khan’s office over the decision.Legal representatives for the mayor said they “did not originally consider it necessary” for Khan to be among those to have their communications searched before next year’s court case. But they relented, citing persistence from Palantir.Sarah Brown, Khan’s former director of communications, who now works for the prime minister, Andy Burnham, will also have her correspondence searched.The proposed two-year deal would have allowed Palantir, which works for the Israeli military and the Trump administration in its immigration crackdown, to provide AI technology to automate intelligence analysis in criminal investigations.But the Mayor’s Office for Policing and Crime (Mopac), which oversees large Scotland Yard contracts, said there had been a “clear and serious breach” of procurement rules. It said police had seriously considered only one supplier (Palantir).After the announcement, Palantir accused Khan of “putting politics above public safety” before declaring in June that it planned to sue theLondonmayor.At a preliminary hearing on Thursday, the high court was told Khan and more than a dozen other Mopac and Greater London Authority officials would be classed as “custodians”.Apocalypse prep or pure pragmatism: what is behind Peter Thiel’s move to Argentina?Read moreThe designation means their digital communications, including text messages, WhatsApp messages, and Microsoft Teams chats – insofar as they exist – will be searched for anything relevant to the issues in the legal tussle. These will then be disclosed to Palantir.Joseph Barrett KC, for the mayor’s office, said in written submissions: “Mopac did not originally consider it necessary or proportionate for the mayor to be added as a custodian, given that the decision was taken by the deputy mayor for policing and crime; his senior position; and the likelihood that any documents held by him would be held by other individuals.“However, Palantir has persisted in its requests, and Mopac has consented on a pragmatic basis.”Brown, who in July moved from the mayor’s office to be appointed director of communications at Downing Street, was also listed as a custodian, meaning she too will have her correspondence searched, the court heard.The decision to include Brown comes after Palantir said in court documents outlining its claim that press articles regarding the mayor’s office vetoing the Met deal cited concerns about Palantir’s values and ethics. Mopac has confirmed Brown “initiated” press briefings about the move.The date range for the communication searches is still to be determined.Mopac reportedly is demanding to see Palantir’s own internal documents related to the deal, which the company is said to be resisting.Explore more on these topicsSadiq KhanPalantirMetropolitan policePoliceLondonnewsShareReuse this content

title: Israelis shoot dead two Palestinian teenagers after settlers encircle village | West Bank | The Guardian
description: Troops escort settlers into al-Mughayyir and raze village outside Hebron as ethnic cleansing of West Bank continues
Author: Emma Graham-Harrison
Headline: Troops escort settlers into al-Mughayyir and raze village outside Hebron as ethnic cleansing of West Bank continues
