Content: Relatives of Khalil Abu Alia grieve during his funeral in al-Mughayyir after the 16-year-old was shot on his doorstep by an Israeli rooftop sniper.Photograph: Zain Jaafar/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRelatives of Khalil Abu Alia grieve during his funeral in al-Mughayyir after the 16-year-old was shot on his doorstep by an Israeli rooftop sniper.Photograph: Zain Jaafar/AFP/Getty ImagesWest BankIsraelis shoot dead two Palestinian teenagers after settlers encircle villageTroops escort settlers into al-Mughayyir and raze village outside Hebron as ethnic cleansing of West Bank continuesEmma Graham-Harrisonin JerusalemThu 3 Sep 2026 15.33 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 16.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIsraelis have shot dead two teenagers in a Palestinian village encircled by settlers, and Israeli troops have razed an entire village outside Hebron, in the latest attacks in a surge of Israeli terror and ethnic cleansing across the occupiedWest Bank.The shootings targeted Khalil Abu Alia, 16, who was about to start 11th grade at the al-Mughayyir boys school, and 19-year-old Omar al-Nassan, who graduated from the same institution with top marks this summer.The teenagers were killed soon after sunset, when a group of settlers entered the village under police and military escort to steal dozens of sheep from a Palestinian home, village residents and Israeli activists said.Snipers took up position on rooftops and one shot Abu Alia in the neck, his English teacher, Waheed Abu Naim, said in a phone interview. The boy was on the doorstep of his home when he was targeted.View image in fullscreenMourners at the funeral ceremony of Khalil Abu Alia, 16, and Omar al-Nassan, 19.Photograph: Zain Jaafar/AFP/Getty ImagesAl-Nassan was shot twice, the second time in the back, residents and activists said. Both had died before they made it to hospital.A spokesperson for the Israeli military said Israeli police, army and settlers entered the village to take sheep claimed by settlers from a Palestinian home. The spokesperson provided no evidence of ownership, theft or investigation into stolen goods.When Palestinians resisted seizure of the sheep by throwing stones and cinder blocks, the troops shot them, the spokesperson said. “The forces responded by firing at key instigators in order to remove the threat. Hits were identified.”Abu Alia was killed by a soldier. It was not clear whether Al-Nassan was shot by a soldier or a settler.View image in fullscreenMourners at the funeral ceremony of Abu Alia and al-Nassan in al-Mughayyir.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesIsraeli soldiers and militants had already killed three other students from their school’s 470-strong student body this year.The other victims werea 17-year-old player from the Palestinian youth football teamshot in June,a 14-year-old gunned down at the school gatein April, and another14-year-old killed outside the village mosquein January.“We don’t know how long these crimes are going to continue,” said Abu Naim, who had taught all five boys, and said many more of his students had been injured by Israeli attacks. His brother was also killed by settlers in April.“This week we are making extra security preparations for the new semester which starts in three days,” he said. They have built a higher wall around the school, topped by a fence, and strengthened gates to the compound.They are also making teaching contingency plans, because the village has been under tightening siege for the past two weeks.View image in fullscreenFuneral attenders look out from their village of al-Mughayyir at an Israeli hilltop settlement.Photograph: Léo Corrêa/APSince late 2023, Israeli barricades blocked all but one road into the village, and at least eight settler outpostssurround it in all directions.In late August soldiers and settlers began closing the one remaining lifeline out of al-Mughayyir for hours at a time, setting up a temporary checkpoint near the school in the morning and evening.At least eight families have fled in the past week because they were unable to commute to work, renting flats in other places, Abu Naim said.The school has 26 teachers but only nine live in the village, and they fear the other two-thirds may not be allowed to reach their classrooms on Monday.View image in fullscreenIsraeli troops raiding al-Mughayyir in July after settler attacks.Photograph: Mohammed Torokman/ReutersIn the south Hebron hills Israeli forces spent the day razing the homes of 12 Palestinian families who lived in the community of Khirbet al-Taban. All 70 residents are now homeless, including 28 children.Israeli troops demolished all buildings and destroyed water cisterns, storage, livestock pens and caves, the Israeli-Palestinian rights group B’Tselem said in a statement.It is the 66th Palestinian community that has been wiped off the map since October 2023, with 18 others partly displaced, the group said. Nearly 5,000 people have been forced from their homes, almost half of them children.“Israel is continuing to erase Palestinian communities at an accelerating pace as part of the ethnic cleansing it is carrying out in the West Bank,” saidYuli Novak, the executive director of B’Tselem. “The world continues to stand by as Palestinians and their lives are left completely exposed to Israeli violence.”A spokesperson for Cogat, the Israeli military agency which manages civilian affairs in occupiedPalestine, said troops were carrying out “enforcement activity” against illegal construction in a military training zone.In 1981 Israel designated the Masafer Yatta area, including Khirbet al-Taban, asFiring Zone 918. It has been working since to push out the roughly 1,200 Palestinian residents who remain. They have been fighting expulsion in Israeli courts for decades, slowing but not stopping demolitions.As Palestinian communities have been wiped out, illegal Israeli settlements have expanded, with 11 outposts inside the firing zone, housing some of the mostnotoriously violentIsraeli settlers. None have been targeted for removal.Explore more on these topicsWest BankPalestineMiddle East and north AfricaIsraelnewsShareReuse this content

title: Higher education regulator apologises for imposing £585,000 fine on university | Higher education | The Guardian
description: Office for Students made decision to punish University of Sussex last year after claiming it breached free speech regulations
Author: Richard Adams
Headline: Office for Students made decision to punish University of Sussex last year after claiming it breached free speech regulations
Content: The OfS investigation began after Kathleen Stock’s resignation, following campus protests for her views on transgender rights and gender identity.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe OfS investigation began after Kathleen Stock’s resignation, following campus protests for her views on transgender rights and gender identity.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianHigher educationHigher education regulator apologises for imposing £585,000 fine on universityOffice for Students made decision to punish University of Sussex with fine last year after claiming it breached free speech regulationsRichard AdamsEducation editorThu 3 Sep 2026 15.01 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 17.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEngland’s higher education regulator has apologised for a string of mistakes in its decision to punish theUniversity of Sussexwith a record fine that was later overturned by the high court.TheOffice for Students(OfS) tried to impose a £585,000 fine against Sussex last year after claiming the university breached free speech regulations involving its former professor Kathleen Stock. It was forced to back down in April after a judicial review initiated by Sussex found the OfS “had closed its mind” and acted with bias.University of Sussex overturns £585,000 fine as high court rejects free speech breach claimRead moreIn a statement, the regulator said: “The OfS made mistakes in the Sussex case, which we regret. The actions we are announcing today show our continuing commitment to learning the lessons from this case with humility and honesty.”Among the changes promised by the OfS in a“lessons learned” reportwere “ensuring respectful relationships with higher education providers” and in the future using “alternative forms of intervention where possible to effect change” before taking enforcement action such as fines.Prof Sasha Roseneil, Sussex’s vice-chancellor, said she welcomed the OfS’s acknowledgement of its mistakes but was concerned that its plans for reform “fell short” in a number of areas.Roseneil said: “[The report] reveals deep cultural problems within the OfS in relation to freedom of expression and internal challenge, and it is heartening to see the new leadership setting different expectations for the organisation, expectations that are more appropriate for a public institution, trusted to regulate one of the most important sectors in a democratic society.“However, the report does not fully reflect the breadth or the seriousness of the high court’s findings or all the lessons that could be learned from the case.View image in fullscreenSasha Roseneil.“It is also disappointing that the review missed the opportunity to engage with the University of Sussex when their lack of engagement was roundly criticised by the high court.”The high court’s findings were backed up by an internal review by KPMG commissioned by the OfS, published in summary on Thursday. KPMG’s findings criticised the regulator for being adversarial, allowing gaps in its written records, and lacking clear accountability.“It appears that insufficient emphasis was placed on maintaining constructive engagement and dialogue with higher education providers, which contributed to relationships becoming increasingly adversarial,” according to the review’s summary.View image in fullscreenKathleen Stock.KPMG also criticised the OfS’s leadership at the time for becoming blinkered: “The investigation team was made up of particularly senior staff, reflecting the case’s novelty, complexity and profile.“However, the concentration of decision making and delivery responsibilities within a relatively small group reduced the opportunity for independent challenge and fresh perspectives.”The OfS’s chair, Edward Peck, and chief executives Ruth Hannant and Polly Payne, thanked the University of Sussex’s leadership “for the frank discussions and insightful commentary leading to this point”.Hannant and Payne took over as the OfS’s chief executives in June and had no prior involvement with the decision to fine Sussex. The OfS investigation began after Stock’s resignation from Sussex in 2021, following campus protests for her views on transgender rights and gender identity.Explore more on these topicsHigher educationUniversity of SussexOffice for StudentsFreedom of speechUniversity administrationUniversitiesnewsShareReuse this content

title: JD Vance reacts to airstrike that killed four at Iran wedding: ‘Things happen’ | US-Israel war on Iran | The Guardian
description: The vice-president says he’s ‘extremely skeptical’ of Iran reports when asked whether US was responsible for deaths
Author: Joseph Gedeon
Headline: The vice-president says he’s ‘extremely skeptical’ of Iran reports when asked whether US was responsible for deaths
Content: Vice President JD Vance talks to reporters at a news briefing at the White House on Thursday.Photograph: Chip Somodevilla/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenVice President JD Vance talks to reporters at a news briefing at the White House on Thursday.Photograph: Chip Somodevilla/Getty ImagesUS-Israel war on IranJD Vance reacts to airstrike that killed four at Iran wedding: ‘Things happen’The vice-president says he’s ‘extremely skeptical’ of Iran reports when asked whether US was responsible for deathsJoseph Gedeonin WashingtonThu 3 Sep 2026 17.04 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 20.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US vice-president,JD Vance, said “sometimes things happen” when asked on Thursday whether an American strike was responsible for killing four people, including a child, at a wedding celebration in southern Iran this week.Iran accuses US of ‘war crime’ after missile blast kills four people at weddingRead moreThe strike hit Kuhestak, a town in Sirik county on the strait of Hormuz. The toll was reported not by the Iranian government but bythe Iranian Red Crescent,a member of the International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement that operates independently of Tehran and is generally treated by international monitors as a credible source on casualty figures.Asked at a White House press briefing whether the US was responsible, Vance dismissed the reporting.“I will say that the Iranian state media has not been a very good scribe about what’s happened in the conflict thus far, so I’m extremely skeptical of this,” he said, offering no acknowledgment that the killings had been confirmed by an internationally recognized humanitarian body.“What I can say with 100% confidence is that, unlike the [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps] IRGC, the United States never targets civilians in combat,” Vance continued. “We never will do that. We never have done that, and unfortunately, obviously, sometimes things happen.”Vance told reporters that he had no new information on the specific strike, but that the US was investigating and, unlike Iran, learns from its mistakes.He also said that the conflict between the US and Iran, which has now stretched into a seventh month and led to the deaths of 18 US service members, was not presently “a war”. The comment sparked immediate backlash from Democrats and critics.“It’s unbelievable gaslighting,” congressman Ro Khanna, a Democrat from California, said in avideo posted to X.“This is war,” he added. “You know who understands it’s a war? Donald Trump. He claims that we’re winning the war.”Earlier on Thursday, Trump claimed in a social media post that the US had “virtually unlimited” amounts of mid- to high-grade munitions, and called journalists who have reported on the Pentagon’s dwindling stockpiles “treasonous SCUM”.The remarks come amid a broader US-Iran war that continues with no sign of a lasting peace despite months of halting negotiations.The US and Iranexchanged fireearlier this week, renewing fears of greater escalation across the region. US Central Command (Centcom) has said the broader strike package that Tuesday night targeted Iranian air defense sites, radar systems, maritime assets and communications facilities, without specifying whether the wedding venue was among the intended targets. The Red Crescentsaidshrapnel from the US missile strike hit the residential home where the wedding celebration was under way, killing four people and wounding more than 50 others.Iranian authorities have previously put the overall death toll from US and Israeli strikes in the thousands, figures that outside observers, including US-based monitoring groups, have broadly corroborated.The strike also revives scrutiny of a 28 February US attack roughly 23 miles away, in Minab, that hit a school compound and killed at least 156 people, most of them schoolchildren. A preliminaryUS militaryinquiry reportedly found that the strike resulted from a targeting error, after outdated coordinates identified the school as part of an adjacent Revolutionary Guard naval base. The Pentagon said at the time it was investigating; a full report has not been made public.Explore more on these topicsUS-Israel war on IranTrump administrationJD VanceIranUS militaryUS foreign policyUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Genetically modified pig kidney keeps man alive for record nine months  | Medical research | The Guardian
description: Organ kept Tim Andrews off dialysis and acted as a ‘bridge’ while he waited for a human transplant in the US
Author: Andrew Gregory
Headline: Organ kept Tim Andrews off dialysis and acted as a ‘bridge’ while he waited for a human transplant in the US
Content: Tim Andrews in his room at Massachusetts general hospital four days after receiving the genetically modified pig kidney.Photograph: Kate Flock/Massachusetts general hospital/PAView image in fullscreenTim Andrews in his room at Massachusetts general hospital four days after receiving the genetically modified pig kidney.Photograph: Kate Flock/Massachusetts general hospital/PAMedical researchGenetically modified pig kidney keeps man alive for record nine monthsOrgan kept Tim Andrews off dialysis and acted as a ‘bridge’ while he waited for a human transplant in the USAndrew GregoryHealth editorThu 3 Sep 2026 18.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA genetically modified kidney from a pig called Wilma has kept a 66-year-old man with kidney failure alive for a record nine months and successfully acted as a “bridge” to a human transplant in a world first.Tim Andrews was seriously ill with end-stage kidney disease caused by type 2 diabetes and had only a 9% chance of receiving a human kidney within five years, against a more than 40% risk of dying or being removed from the waiting list.Kidney transplantation provides the best survival and quality of life for patients with end-stage kidney disease, but global demand for human organs far exceeds supply.Surgeons in the US successfully transplanted a kidney from Wilma, a Yucatan miniature pig, into Andrews, after genetically engineering it to be compatible with his immune system.The kidney kept Andrews free of dialysis for a record nine months, the longest period ever recorded, before it began failing and he received one from a dead human donor. It was also the first time a pig’s kidney had been used as a temporary “bridge” to a human transplant.Details of the breakthrough, which offers hope to millions of people whose kidneys have failed, werepublished in the Lancet medical journal.Andrews, from New Hampshire, described the pig kidney transplant as a “miracle”, adding: “I was alive, and I hadn’t been in a long time.” He was able to cook, vacuum and take long walks with his dog, Cupcake, he said.View image in fullscreenSurgeons during the procedure at Massachusetts general hospital on 25 January 2025.Photograph: Kate Flock/Massachusetts general hospital/PATransplanting genetically engineered pig organs has long been proposed as a solution to the organ shortage. But the first pig kidney transplant into a living person, in 2024, ended after 52 days whenthe patient died from unrelated heart problems, and no previous studies had documented xenograft survival beyond two months,according to the Lancet.Before the transplant in January 2025, Wilma the pig had received 69 edits to her genome. Some of these were designed to dodge viruses that might pose a risk to humans, while others made the organ more compatible with humans, reducing the odds of immune rejection.The team behind the transplant at Mass General Brigham, a non-profit, integrated academic healthcare system inMassachusetts, said Andrews successfully lived with the genetically edited kidney for 271 days before receiving a human kidney from a donor.His case represents the longest dialysis-free survival following pig kidney xenotransplantation in a living human, and the world’s first transition to human kidney transplantation, the team said.“The organ shortage is the greatest crisis we have right now in transplantation,” said Dr Leonardo Riella, of the Center for Transplantation Sciences and the Division of Nephrology at Mass General Brigham. “We know that the best treatment option for patients with end-stage kidney disease who have developed renal failure is transplantation, but we simply don’t have enough human organs to transplant in a timely manner.“Our vision is that xenotransplantation could help address this gap – initially as a bridge to get patients off dialysis while they wait for a human donor kidney, and potentially, as we establish long-term safety and durability, as a destination therapy in its own right.”View image in fullscreenAndrews with nurse Melanie Brodner at Massachusetts general hospital on 29 January  2025, four days after his pig kidney transplant.Photograph: Kate Flock/Massachusetts general hospital/PAAfter roughly six months, damage developed in the pig kidney’s blood vessels which progressed to organ failure and the kidney was removed nine months after transplantation.After several months back on dialysis, Andrews received a kidney from a dead human donor, which worked well during six months of follow-up,according to the Lancet.There were no new antibodies against human tissue detected, indicating the pig kidney had not made it harder for the human kidney transplant to work successfully. No pig viruses or other pig pathogens were detected at any point.The team cautioned that this was a single patient with no comparison group, and that the outcome reflected careful patient selection and intensive specialist care that may not be available elsewhere.Further clinical trials such as the one Andrews participated in will be needed. But the success opens the door to pig kidney transplants as a bridge for other people facing long waits for a human kidney, they said.“The patients are the true pioneers here,” Riella said. “By stepping forward and being willing to participate in these early stage studies, they are advancing the science. Without their trust and courage, we would not be able to do what we do.”Explore more on these topicsMedical researchHealthGeneticsMassachusettsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Sabotage, leaks and political ties: the story of the Daphne Caruana Galizia murder trial | Daphne Caruana Galizia | The Guardian
description: Maltese businessman cleared of involvement in journalist’s death, but trial revealed challenges faced by those leading search for killers
Author: Juliette Garside
Headline: Maltese businessman cleared of involvement in journalist’s death, but trial revealed challenges faced by those leading search for killers
Content: Flowers and a candle lie in front of a portrait of Daphne Caruana Galizia outside the court in Valletta, Malta.Photograph: Jonathan Borg/APView image in fullscreenFlowers and a candle lie in front of a portrait of Daphne Caruana Galizia outside the court in Valletta, Malta.Photograph: Jonathan Borg/APDaphne Caruana GaliziaSabotage, leaks and political ties: the story of the Daphne Caruana Galizia murder trialA Maltese businessman has been cleared of involvement in the journalist’s death, but his trial revealed the challenges faced by those leading the search for her killersJuliette Garsidein VallettaThu 3 Sep 2026 13.13 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 16.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe conclusion of the longest-running murder trial in Maltese history has left a country in turmoil, and a grieving family still searching for answers.At 7.30pm on Wednesday, gasps and cheers echoed around hall 22 of the courts of justice in Valletta, as a jury pronounced a businessman accused of ordering the murder of the investigative journalist Daphne Caruana Galizianot guilty.Yorgen Fenech, 44, had been facing a life sentence if convicted. Now, after nearly seven years in and out of custody, he is free to return to a gilded life as the heir to one of Malta’s biggest fortunes.In her reporting, Caruana Galizia had taken aim at many powerful figures, including Fenech and the politicians he was close to. Her revelations, and the fallout from her violent death in a car bombing in October 2017, had ultimately led to the resignation of the prime minister, Joseph Muscat, and several members of his government.Within weeks, three hitmen accused of planting the bomb were arrested. Two weresentenced to life in prisonafter pleading guilty to murder, while the third wasgiven a reduced 15-year sentencein exchange for evidence against his accomplices.After Wednesday’s decision, the long search for whoever was responsible for hiring them must begin again.The opposition leader, Alex Borg, has demanded the recall of parliament from its summer recess, and called for the government to act to strengthen press protection and anti-corruption measures. “We believe journalism is the backbone of a democracy,” he told the Guardian, describing the failure to find the culprits as a black mark against the Labour government. The party has been in power since 2013.Caruana Galizia’s family described the verdict as “justice denied”.The attorney general is considering whether to appeal for a retrial. The chances of success may be slim: both charges brought against Fenech were dismissed by an 8-1 majority.It had taken nine years, a relentless family campaign and a determined judge to bring Fenech before a jury. In the end, they took him at his word. During his evidence, he was adamant: “I never ordered Daphne Caruana Galizia’s murder, or anyone else’s. I had no role in her murder.”View image in fullscreenYorgen Fenech was cleared by a jury of complicity in voluntary homicide and association with the intention of committing a crime.Photograph: Darrin Zammit Lupi/ReutersWhile the identity of the mastermind remains a mystery, what the trial did reveal was the full extent of the challenges faced by those leading the search for Daphne’s killers.Witness after witness spoke of attempts to block and sabotage the murder investigation. As detectives worked to identify all of those involved, from the bomb makers to the hitmen to their ultimate client, they heard evidence that the most sensitive details were being leaked. Most disturbingly of all, the jury was told much of the information was coming from the prime minister’s right-hand man.“Don’t worry about me, nobody can touch me,” Fenech was heard saying in secret recordings that formed a cornerstone of the case against him, and played to the jury.View image in fullscreenA court artist’s sketch of Yorgen Fenech during the trial.Illustration: Anna Calleja DayThe man who had made those recordings was a taxi driver, Melvin Theuma, who testified to acting as the middleman between Fenech and the bombers. He was the key prosecution witness, having secured a pardon two years after the murder in return for giving evidence.In July 2020, he was taken to hospital in a critical condition. Overcome with remorse, he had attempted suicide while staying at a safe house, and it took intensive support to get him back in the stand.What follows is the story of the search for those responsible, based on pre-trial hearings, the trial itself, and related court cases.Consumed by an investigation that would kill herIn the last summer of her life, Caruana Galizia was deeply isolated.As a younger woman, she had not only been brilliant, but strikingly beautiful, with big statement earrings and shining black hair. She had co-founded a national newspaper, was a lifestyle magazine publisher, and had become one of Malta’s most-read columnists, all while raising three sons.View image in fullscreenDaphne Caruana Galizia in 1989 at Lisbon zoo with her sons Paul, Andrew and Matthew.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesIn later life, it was the investigative work that consumed her.‘I knew it was a car bomb straight away’: the day my mother Daphne Caruana Galizia was murderedRead moreHer blog Running Commentary was among the most-read news sites in Malta, but its popularity, and her often scathing satires of public figures, made her a target.She had as many detractors as fans, and on social media she was vilified as a “witch”. There were arson attacks, and the family dogs were killed.“I was worried about her,” her middle son, Andrew, told the trial. “The atmosphere around her was horrible. People would stare at her in Valletta. She wouldn’t leave the house.”Caruana Galizia knew she was at risk and had already started varying her routine. For added security, she drove a rental car.It was in that car that she died on 16 October 2017, aged 53, metres from her house. A bomb placed under the driver’s seat ripped through the vehicle, scattering burning remains across the road and into a field.View image in fullscreenForensic experts examine the field where a bomb blew up Daphne Caruana Galizia’s rental car.Photograph: Darrin Zammit Lupi/ReutersBarricaded inside their home, sheltering from the media storm, Daphne’s sons and her widow, Peter, wondered who they could trust. They felt sure her work would hold clues, but also that they could not hand sensitive source material to the police. Her eldest son, Matthew, a software engineer who had been part of the reporting team that won a Pulitzer prize for the Panama Papers, a giant leak of offshore company data, suggested contacting journalists outside Malta.“I didn’t have the resources to do the investigation on my own,” he told the jury at Fenech’s trial.He reached out to the Guardian, which joined Reuters, the non-profitForbidden Storiesand others to formthe Daphne Project.Before her death, Caruana Galizia had published a series of stories that plunged the Maltese government into scandal. She had found evidence in the Panama Papers that the energy minister, Konrad Mizzi, and the prime minister’s chief of staff, a businessman turned political fixer called Keith Schembri, had set up offshore companies held via anonymous trusts.Posts she published, read out during the trial, suggested she thought they were planning to use these to receive kickbacks.View image in fullscreenCaruana Galizia’s sons Matthew, Paul and Andrew and her husband, Peter, take part in a protest march in Valletta in 2019.Photograph: Darrin Zammit Lupi/ReutersThose allegations are now the subject of acriminal case,in which Fenech, Schembri, Mizzi and others are pleading not guilty to corruption, trading in influence and criminal association.At the time she died, Caruana Galizia was receiving a leak of information about a large government contract – a concession to build a €500m gas power plant that would supply electricity for the national grid. The leak came from the servers of the company building the plant, Electrogas. One of its shareholders was Fenech, and the email traffic suggested he was a driving force, handling communications with the government, and the refinancing of a crucial bank loan.The jury heard how, in her blog, Caruana Galizia had described the venture as a “magic new corruption power station”.View image in fullscreenGrafitti on a wall in rural Malta highlights Caruna Galizia’s murder.Photograph: Simon Leigh/AlamyThe prosecution had claimed, in its closing submissions, that Fenech’s motive for ordering her murder was to prevent any further revelations.The Electrogas data was shared with the Daphne Project. As reporters combed the files, following the money trails, Keith Arnaud, a homicide detective, searched for the killers. At first he made rapid progress, thanks to the FBI. The agency’s cellphone analysis team had been inEuropewhen the bomb went off, and they diverted to Malta, landing there within hours.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe hitmen, brothers George and Alfred Degiorgio, and their accomplice Vincent Muscat, had used burner phones but they had been careless, often carrying them alongside their usual mobiles. The FBI made the link, tracing a text message sent by George to detonate the bomb. In December 2017, the trio were arrested.In April 2018, Vincent Muscat told police he was ready to turn on his accomplices, in exchange for a shorter sentence. While the hitmen had never known the identity of their ultimate client, Muscat had the name of the middleman: Melvin Theuma.View image in fullscreenA makeshift memorial to Caruana Galizia in Valletta, Malta.Photograph: Darrin Zammit Lupi/ReutersThe mosquito and the lionFor Theuma, a fatherless teenager, the Malta Racing Club was a home from home. He started as a groom, tending to the ponies that pull small carts around the bare-earth track. Before long he was working as a scout for a bookmaker. The old betting shop still stands across the street from the Fenech family stables.View image in fullscreenMelvin Theuma, a key witness who was granted a presidential pardon, with Judge Edwina Grima visiting the site where Caruana Galizia was killed.Photograph: Darrin Zammit Lupi/ReutersTheuma and Fenech became friends, but it was not a relationship of equals. As the taxi driver said in court: “I was hanging out with a lion, and I’m a mosquito.”Police said in court they had identified Fenech as a suspect by September 2018. But it would take until February 2019 for a warrant to be authorised to intercept his calls.The person signing the warrants was the prime minister, Joseph Muscat. From the beginning, Muscat had been receiving updates about the investigation directly from Arnaud and his colleagues. That decision was controversial because, along with his ministers, he had been one of the main subjects of Caruana Galizia’s reporting.Muscat has indicated it was customary for the prime minister to sign warrants in cases of national importance. He has previously said he fulfilled his duties “without fear, prejudice or favour”. In a statement on Thursday, he said that from the beginning, and while he was still in office, “no one was protected from or immune to justice”.Schembri was allowed to attend the police briefings and told the trial he was kept informed throughout.The two men were close – Schembri had started out as Muscat’s campaign manager – but Schembri had another good friend: Fenech. They had played football together as children, and when Fenech, a few years younger, stepped up to run his family business, Schembri had mentored him. They would often holiday together and gather for family events.Schembri is accused of repeatedly leaking sensitive details about the homicide investigation to Fenech. He denies the allegations, and is being prosecuted over the matter in aseparate criminal case.During his trial, Fenech sought to paint Schembri as the ultimate mastermind, describing himself as a go-between, passing messages to Theuma. Fenech’s lawyers depicted the taxi driver as a blackmailer and a liar, and accused the police of framing Fenech because they had failed to properly follow other leads. They said the searches at Schembri’s home and his office had been bungled. His phone, active 28 minutes before the raid, was never found.“All roads lead to Keith and all bridges leading to Keith were burnt,” Fenech’s lawyer said. “And so a bridge had to be built to Yorgen Fenech.”Schembri denies any involvement in the murder. In their evidence, police said he was never a murder suspect.View image in fullscreenMalta’s former chief of staff, Keith Schembri, was a close childhood friend of Yorgen Fenech.Photograph: Matthew Mirabelli/AFP/Getty ImagesUnder questioning, Fenechadmitted paying €400,000, via Theuma, to the hitmen to cover their legal bills. He said this was to keep Theuma calm, and that the cab driver had “drained” him of money. He also admitted giving Theuma money before the murder, but said he warned that it should not go ahead, telling the taxi driver to “stop it here”.He admitted passing information about the police investigation from Schembri to Theuma, starting soon after the assassination.“Keith Schembri was continuously informed and in a way you can say real time,” Fenech told a court in 2019, in a constitutional case regarding his right to a fair trial. “The information was passed to me by Keith Schembri but it came from Mr Arnaud, and he used to tell me that it came from Mr Arnaud.”Recordings, messages and testimony from Fenech himself indicate that in the first months after the murder he had passed on to Theuma the identity of who had made the bomb and the date on which the police were planning to arrest the hitmen. When the police raided their shed by the docks, they had already thrown their mobile phones into the water, and one of them had written his wife’s number on his wrist.In April 2018, Fenech also shared that Vincent Muscat was offering to become a witness for the prosecution. The news sent Theuma into a spin and he started to record his exchanges with Fenech, using a spare phone switched to airplane mode so it would not ring.View image in fullscreenVincent Muscat is serving a 15-year prison sentence for his part in the murder of Caruana Galizia.Photograph: Darrin Zammit Lupi/ReutersIt was around this time that Arnaud’s investigation seemed to lose momentum. Eventually, details of what had been uncovered began to leak. By May 2019, reporters had Theuma’s name.Europol, which had been supporting Arnaud and his team, threatened over the summer of 2019 to withdraw unless arrests were made. The family were also losing patience. “We had known what was being alleged about Melvin Theuma for months,” Matthew Caruana Galizia has said. “And it reached a point where I just wanted to go into the street and spraypaint his name on a wall. I wanted the world to know that he was the middleman, to just push the police into action.”While the walls around the prime minister and his friends looked strong from the outside, when the police finally went for Theuma, Joseph Muscat’s administration crumbled.Theuma had been warned of his planned arrest date but police swooped two days early, on 14 November 2019. Fenech had urged him in messages beforehand to dispose of the evidence. The jury saw one message in which he said: “Be 100% sure everywhere is clean.”But Theuma held on to his recordings. On 19 November, the prime minister signed a memorandum guaranteeing Theuma immunity from prosecution in exchange for testimony. Within hours, Fenech was making preparations to flee, messages seen by the jury suggest. “Go while you’re still in time,” his uncle texted. He planned to sail to Sicily, and then head for France. However, the police had been tipped off. His yacht was intercepted a mile off the coast, and he was arrested. The interrogation tapes, played at his trial, showed he offered to implicate Schembri in return for a pardon.View image in fullscreenA mass in memory of Caruana Galizia in Valletta.Photograph: Matthew Mirabelli/AFP/Getty ImagesAs Fenech talked, heads rolled. Schembri was arrested in relation to the suspected leaks, and resigned. The economy minister, a frequent subject of Caruana Galizia’s blog, suspended himself and Mizzi, by now reassigned from energy to tourism minister, quit, citing “political, extraordinary and general circumstances in the country”.Public outrage brought hundreds on to the streets, filling the grand plaza outside the prime minister’s office, chanting: “Mafia, mafia.”Fenech’s pardon request was rejected and on 30 November, he was charged. Two days later, Joseph Muscat resigned. Defiant to the end, he insisted: “This case cannot define everything that our country is.”The saga is once again drawing attention from outside Malta. Shami Chakrabarti, the British Labour peer, has been appointed rapporteur of a Council of Europe investigation into the Maltese government’s response to the murder. Caruana Galizia’s family members intend to give evidence at the first hearing next week.“The failure to ensure individual accountability for the murder risks perpetuating a culture of impunity,” Chakrabarti said on Thursday. “A culture where … those who try to shine a light in the darkness pay the ultimate price.”Explore more on these topicsDaphne Caruana GaliziaMaltaEuropeJournalist safetyInvestigative journalismNewspapersNewspapers & magazinesfeaturesShareReuse this content

Author: Zoe Hitch
Headline: The UN has warned that the El Niño climate phenomenon is ‘supersizing before our eyes’, with the event forecast to be the largest in at least 1,000 years – and making it near certain 2027 will be the hottest year ever recorded. Lucy Hough speaks to environment correspondent Damien Gayle

title: Grinding up fish to feed to fish is ‘absurd’: fears over UN aquaculture plan | Fishing | The Guardian
description: Huge rollout of fish farms could harm ecosystems and threaten vulnerable communities’ food sources, say experts
Author: Matthew Pearce
Headline: Huge rollout of fish farms could harm ecosystems and threaten vulnerable communities’ food sources, say experts
Content: Fish farmers remove dead fish at a fish farm in South Korea amid a high water temperature warning off the country’s west coast.Photograph: Yonhap News Agency/ReutersView image in fullscreenFish farmers remove dead fish at a fish farm in South Korea amid a high water temperature warning off the country’s west coast.Photograph: Yonhap News Agency/ReutersFishingGrinding up fish to feed to fish is ‘absurd’: fears over UN aquaculture planHuge rollout of fish farms could harm ecosystems and threaten vulnerable communities’ food sources, say expertsMatthew PearceThu 3 Sep 2026 12.59 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 13.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNearly half of the world’s wild fish catch will be ground into animal feed for farmed fish if plans to expand aquaculture go ahead, a report has found.The UN’sFoodand Agriculture Organization (FAO) is aiming to increase aquaculture – where fish are farmed rather than caught in the wild – production by 75% by 2040.The plans form part of its “blue transformation” agenda to meet growing global demand for seafood, improve food security and eradicate world hunger by 2030.But an analysis by Changing Markets Foundation found the plans would potentially pull tens of millions of tonnes of fish from the oceans each year to feed species such as salmon and shrimp.Aquaculture adds to the intense pressure on overexploited fisheries because food is removed from marine ecosystems and the coastal communities that rely on them.Aquaculturesupplies more than half of the aquatic animals consumed worldwide, according to the report. Carnivorous farmed species are commonly fed fishmeal and fish oil made by grinding down smaller wild fish such as anchovies and sardines.“These fish are naturally carnivorous species, so that is what they would eat in the wild,” said Tara Ganesh, a senior campaigner at Changing Markets Foundation. “You can’t suddenly raise a salmon overnight that is vegetarian.”Although producers had reduced the amount of wild fish used for each kilogram of farmed fish, she said this did not mean the industry’s total consumption was falling.View image in fullscreenCage fish farming facilities in Ordu, Turkey, where about 6,000 tonnes of fish production were reported in 2025.Photograph: Hayati Akcay/Anadolu/Getty ImagesModelling produced with the University of British Columbia found that, if industry trends continued, up to 34.6m tonnes of wild fish could be caught and fed to farmed species annually by 2040.The FAO has not specified which species or farming systems should deliver the 75% increase in aquaculture. Changing Markets Foundation modelled several possible routes to the target and found that, under a scenario weighted towards feed-intensive species such as salmon and shrimp, demand for wild fish could rise to 41.4m tonnes – equivalent to 46% of the global wild-fish catch in 2020.Muhammed Oyinlola, an aquatic ecologist at the University of British Columbia, said: “Our modelling shows that the outcome is not inevitable. A more diversified option favours growth in lower-input species, while ambiguity leaves the door open to growth that threatens communities, fisheries and the climate.”The scale of the impact would depend heavily on which species and production systems were expanded, the research said. But neither the FAO’s roadmap nor its guidelines for sustainable aquaculture specify how its growth target should be met.The report also says safeguards addressing the nutritional and food security effects of aquaculture trade and consumption were removed from successive drafts of the guidelines without explanation.Changing Markets Foundation examined a December 2023 workshop in Ghana organised by the FAO in collaboration with the Global Roundtable on Marine Ingredients, an industry coalition. “Small-scale fisheries representatives instead called for sardinella to be reserved for direct human consumption and for fishmeal factory expansion to be halted,” it said.West African participants later said the official account of the workshop did not reflect what they regarded as broad opposition among African groups to turning edible wild fish into fishmeal.View image in fullscreenFishers off Tanji beach, one of Gambia’s busiest fishing spots. There is opposition among African groups to turning edible wild fish into fishmeal.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesIn a reportpresented to the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva in June, Elisa Morgera, the UN special rapporteur on climate change, said using nutritionally valuable fish to produce fishmeal and fish oil raised “serious human rights concerns” because it could reduce people’s access to food.Changing Markets Foundation said the consequences were already visible in Senegal, a west African centre for fishmeal and fish oil production, where factories compete with local communities for the same fish.Ganesh said: “A large share of those fish come from much poorer communities where that fish is an essential source of nutrition, but also really essential for the livelihoods of coastal communities and artisanal fishers.” Women who process, smoke and sell fish also risk losing an important source of income.Annual fish consumption per person in Senegal fell by more than 10kg between 1999 and 2019, according to the report. A 2021Changing Markets Foundation investigationestimated that enough fish to feed 33 million people across west Africa was instead being turned into animal and aquaculture feed each year.The foundation said the FAO’s target could be met while keeping demand for whole wild fish well below 2020 levels by reducing fishmeal and fish oil use and directing more growth towards species requiring fewer marine ingredients.Changing Markets Foundation is urging the FAO to introduce safeguards that prioritise edible wild fish for human consumption and direct aquaculture growth towards species requiring little or no fishmeal or fish oil.“There is an urgent need for safeguards in the FAO’s policy to explicitly preserve wild fish for human consumption,” Ganesh said.She said the modelling exposed “the absurdity of production systems that essentially rely on other fish to make fish”, adding: “It’s a net loss of fish – a net loss of nutrition.”The FAO was approached for comment.Explore more on these topicsFishingFood securityFish (Environment)Fish (Food)Food (global)United NationsFood (Environment)newsShareReuse this content

title: An Unexpected Life by Gloria Steinem review – a fitting tribute to a feminist icon | Autobiography and memoir | The Guardian
description: The activist’s memoir, due to be published this month, now stands as a posthumous testament to her remarkable life
Author: Emma Brockes
Headline: The activist’s memoir, due to be published this month, now stands as a posthumous testament to her remarkable life
Content: Gloria Steinem at Ms magazine in 1980.Photograph: New York Daily News Archive/NY Daily News/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGloria Steinem at Ms magazine in 1980.Photograph: New York Daily News Archive/NY Daily News/Getty ImagesAutobiography and memoirReviewAn Unexpected Life by Gloria Steinem review – a fitting tribute to a feminist iconThe activist’s memoir, due to be published this month, now stands as a posthumous testament to her remarkable lifeEmma BrockesThu 3 Sep 2026 10.16 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 16.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGloria Steinem was due to speak at a women’s lunch in New York at the end of this month and at more events in October, illustrating the central theme of An Unexpected Life, her new memoir, which, when it’s published a few weeks from now, will stand as posthumous testament to the 92-year-old icon: just keep going. So it is, after herdeath on Wednesday, that the book’s opening pages unfold with a deep, added poignancy and when Steinem expresses gratitude for a life that has been both happier and longer “than I ever imagined”, one is struck by the greater gratitude we probably owe her.An Unexpected Life is a follow-up of sorts toMy Life on the Road, the activist’s memoir of a decade ago, and as the tributes pour in, the book offers us an opportunity to go back over Steinem’s hardscrabble origins in Toledo, Ohio, and the roots of her activism. This is where it all happened, the formation of a woman who would come to define second wave feminism by combining a tough-as-they-come stance with something that looked a lot like serenity. Reading the first half of the book, one is reminded of Steinem’s original power and the improbability and iconoclasm of her journey, in which a childhood governed by poverty and dysfunction turned into a lifelong mission to resist the narrow templates laid out for her.It’s a cracking backstory. Steinem’s rackety father was a travelling salesman of sorts, touring the country with a dance pavilion that saw Steinem spend long stretches of her childhood with him on the road, which, she writes, conditioned her to enjoy a similarly unconventional existence in adulthood. When she was at home, the young Steinem was a carer for her increasingly mentally unwell mother, who was frequently to be found wandering the town in her nightdress, and Steinem writes movingly about what it is to grow up ashamed of your house and your family. “I learned I could survive almost anything,” she writes, “including a sad mother who was called the Crazy Lady of the neighborhood. We are all one human family, and we are responsible for one another.”Raised on instability, Steinem grew up remarkably free of the pressure weighing on most of her female peers to knuckle down into conventional marriage and motherhood, leaving her free to pursue a life as a freelance writer and, later, an activist. After college, she went to India for two years, a defining period that informed her outlook to the very end, and on return, began her career as a campaigning journalist, which culminated in her co-founding of Ms magazine in 1971 and eventual ascent to the head of the women’s movement.These periods of her life are well documented. What I found interesting in the book were Steinem’s asides about the cost of pursuing the life she chose. “Though I managed to support myself,” she writes, “I didn’t save money until I was past fifty. I was sure that I’d end up as a bag lady, like women I saw sleeping in subway stations. I used to handle that fear by thinking, It’s a life like any other. I’ll organize the other bag ladies.” She eventually became somewhat financially secure, largely thanks to buying part of a 19th-century brownstone on the Upper East Side of Manhattan, the beloved home in which she died this week – although a throwaway line towards the end of the book suggests she was still paying off her mortgage well into her 80s, an astonishing fact given her fame.double quotation markIt is useful to be reminded by Steinem of how bad things were so very recentlySteinem is the real thing, of course; she was never in it for the money. She makes a strong case that she wasn’t in it for the attention, either, although, as a talented speaker and organiser, she drew on great reserves of magnetism that over the years caused her a lot of problems with jealousy from within the movement, and condescension from without. Right until the end, Steinem was stewarding large groups of women – famous and otherwise – at “talking circles” in her house and putting herself at the centre of a conversation she had in some ways begun.A big strand of these debates was the shoe-horning of women into flat, unfulfilled lives, which they are conditioned to believe are the only desirable option. This is where the book’s startling honesty comes into play, a habit Steinem seems to have had from the get-go. Some years after graduating, she wrote to her Smith College classmates in an alumni newsletter: “I’m quite broke, not at all who I thought I would be – and consciously happy.”She writes powerfully about women who made different, unhappier choices under pain of social death: “I remember one woman, married to a socially acceptable man much older than she, who explained, ‘After he dies, I’ll be free.’ The cost of freedom seemed to mean she was able to live only in the future.” It is useful to be reminded of how bad things were so very recently. As the book informs us, “in the 1960s Columbia Law School had a 5% quota for women” – in an era in which American women were earning, on average, 59 cents on each dollar earned by men. (“Now,” she writes, “they typically earn 82 cents for every dollar earned by men. At the going rate, it will be fifty years before we reach parity overall, and seventy-five years for African American women to reach parity with African American men.”)There are glowing, drive-by sketches of some of the famous figures Steinem encountered on the road, including James Baldwin and Annie Leibovitz. She is disinclined to offer anything but praise for the people she admires and so the book’s only waspish assessment is reserved for Andy Warhol, whose smirking sensibility really flies up Steinem’s nose and sits poorly alongside her earnestness. I like her for this – having a crack at the immensely irritating Warhol, about whom, she sniffs, “It seems a low point of the art world that Andy Warhol’s is considered valuable.”As we enter the post-Steinem era – a statement that seems outlandish, given the length and ardour of her service – it’s a pleasure, simply, to spend time in her company, and her role as an elder is one she takes seriously, evoking her deep relationship with Native Americans as the basis for many of her insights. “The patriarchal nuclear family, the one that we are supposed to think is the only kind of family, is really only about 150 years old, and almost entirely a function of industrialization and capitalism.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt wasn’t until she was much older, she writes, that she realised so much of her life “was spent doing what was expected of me, and not enough doing what I loved”. Counterintuitively, this included her hard line on marriage, which she set herself against as a matter of principle, only marrying her great love, David Bale, at 66 and staying with him until he died three years later. This is the old Steinem we love, the combination of absolute force and, hard on its heels, admission of error.After all the doubt and indecision, Steinem at 92 had a very clear idea of what she was supposed to be doing, and my God she did it right to the end. “My role as an older person is to remind us how far we have come, and with age comes the responsibility to keep learning. As Robert Browning wrote: ‘The best is yet to be, / The last of life, / for which the first was made.’” Or as Steinem put it, with a hard-won smile it’s impossible to resist, “Now even my jeans are much older than many people I work with.” We should all be so lucky; what a life.An Unexpected Life by Gloria Steinem is published by Ebury in the UK and Random House in the US. title: Nessun Dolore review – sketchy Roman fable of liberal white guilt | Venice film festival | The Guardian
description: A white man’s eyes are opened to cruelty and racism when a young boy is thrust into his life in Gianni Amelio’s bold but ultimately naive drama
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: A white man’s eyes are opened to cruelty and racism when a young boy is thrust into his life in Gianni Amelio’s bold but ultimately naive drama
Content: Pain free? … Valeria Golino and Alessandro Borghi in Nessun Dolore.Photograph: Claudio IannoneView image in fullscreenPain free? … Valeria Golino and Alessandro Borghi in Nessun Dolore.Photograph: Claudio IannoneVenice film festivalReviewNessun Dolore review – sketchy Roman fable of liberal white guiltVenice film festivalA white man’s eyes are opened to cruelty and racism when a young boy is thrust into his life in Gianni Amelio’s bold but ultimately naive dramaPeter BradshawThu 3 Sep 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 16.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFrom the heart of Rome, and broadly in an Italian tradition of sentimentalist realism, film-maker Gianni Amelio brings us a fairytale of the city, about the liberal white guilt of those who live a prosperous pain-free existence and those whom Frantz Fanon called the wretched of the earth.There is some incidental interest and the film is beautifully shot, but finally it buckles under the weight of its own preposterousness and naivety. It is also sketchy about how and why people go into and come out of prison; the final shot, a supposedly heartwarming visionary moment of redemption and reconciliation, looks absurd.Davide is a secondhand book dealer with a little-visited stall: who on earth reads books nowadays? He is played by Alessandro Borghi with something of that troubled decency that Peter Sarsgaard often projects. Evidently, Davide has got enough family money (and a handsome book-lined flat) that he doesn’t have to worry about sales. He flirts with a literature professor (Valeria Golino) but doesn’t quite have the maturity to pursue a relationship.Davide’s world falls apart one day when he is approached in the street by a north African man (Ramzi Lafrindi) – perhaps a migrant or asylum seeker – hand-in-hand with a nine-year-old boy (Beidja Yahiaoui), whom he is clearly trying to be rid of. This man shoves the small boy into Davide’s arms, insisting that he is Davide’s responsibility.Is he? Or is this a desperate stratagem on the man’s part, gambling that there are enough white men nursing guilty sexual secrets for this ruse to have a chance of succeeding? Either way, the kid follows the increasingly alarmed Davide around, until he furiously orders the boy to back off, which he does, off the pavement, with terrible results.From there, Davide embarks on an odyssey of guilt and shame, red-pilled by his close encounter with poverty, his eyes opened to cruelty and racism, visiting the shantytown quarters where poor migrants are to be found and makes a muddied and disastrous attempt to open his heart and his flat.It is a bold and interesting high-concept premise – though audiences might have been expecting more twists and turns in the narrative. In the end, the film settles for a placid sense of personal unhappiness and self-forgiveness on the hero’s part, which supersedes any larger sense of poverty or injustice in society.Nessun Dolore screened at theVenice film festival.Explore more on these topicsVenice film festivalDrama filmsItalyreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I have an obsession with barber shops’: kd lang on her prairies upbringing, Patsy Cline and being shaved by Cindy Crawford | Pop and rock | The Guardian
description: The Canadian singer-songwriter answers your questions about her trailblazing career, her spirituality, and collaborations with the likes of Neko Case, Laura Veirs and Pee-wee Herman
Author: Laura Snapes
Headline: The Canadian singer-songwriter answers your questions about her trailblazing career, her spirituality, and collaborations with the likes of Neko Case, Laura Veirs and Pee-wee Herman
Content: ‘The sky was very important to me’ … kd lang.Photograph: Jeri HeidenView image in fullscreen‘The sky was very important to me’ … kd lang.Photograph: Jeri HeidenFilm & Music reader interviewPop and rockInterview‘I have an obsession with barber shops’: kd lang on her prairies upbringing, Patsy Cline and being shaved by Cindy CrawfordAs told toLaura SnapesThe Canadian singer-songwriter answers your questions about her trailblazing career, her spirituality, and collaborations with the likes of Neko Case, Laura Veirs and Pee-wee HermanThu 3 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 11.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI left the Canadian prairies many years ago, but they remain my home. How do you feel about that part of westernCanada, where the prairies meet the Rockymountains, whichshaped us both? What does Alberta mean to you now?NicholasLittleAll of my artistic preferences were formed by the minimalism of the prairies, by the affordable space and the stillness. There weren’t many things around, so a field with bales would be this incredibly graphic moment, or a tree or a certain hill – very small increments of beauty placed in vast amounts of space. The sky was very important and a feeling of – I wouldn’t say loneliness, but solace, perhaps. That’s my bottom line, my basic instinct. It’s the frame that that informs all of my art, the way I decorate my house, the way I sing, the way I dress. That sort of minimalist nature is embedded in me.Many people can sing a song well, but you’re a vocalist who emotes raw vulnerability. Do you work like a method actor – entering, or reliving, the reality of the song during the practice period?verdantearthI try to sink myself into the lyrics for sure. I try to create visuals, sort of an emotional internal movie of what the lyrics possess, to relive it emotionally. With [Case/Lang/Veirs track] Honey and Smoke, for example, I imagine watching somebody I’m in love with dancing with somebody else and feeling jealousy.How proud are you of that infamous Vanity Fair cover shoot [in which Cindy Crawford“shaves”kd in a barber’s chair]?TrumansdadView image in fullscreen‘It was magical’ … Herb Ritts’ Vanity Fair cover.Photograph: Herb Ritts/Vanity FairVery. I was friends with Herb [Ritts] and somehow I got the opportunity to do the Vanity Fair cover, and he was shooting it. I was obsessed with a French movie called The Hairdresser’s Husband at the time. I have kind of an obsession with cutting hair and barber shops. I don’t know where that came from – actually, I just realised why, and I’ve never told anyone this! My dad’s drugstore in the really small town I grew up in – the next business over was a barber shop, so I used to watch the barber cutting hair all the time. It must be some sort of childhood visualisation imprint or something. I suggested to Herb, maybe we can do it in a barber’s chair. He phoned me a few days later and said, “I have Cindy Crawford.” I was like, “OK!” We shot it on the roof of his building in downtown Hollywood, up on the roof at golden hour. It was magical. Cindy was super professional, as you can imagine. She’s a model, so it was her realm. I was trying to behave and not be an idiot. It was incredible, and I knew that it had a certain gravity to it. After all these years, I feel like we made a piece of art and a significant social statement, and I really have such pride about it.LS: You have a very cheeky look on your face on the cover.Yeah. I mean, come on!Could you name some of your favourite visual artists and explain why you love them?Do you own art?SimotherI can’t afford to be a collector, but I’m certainly a fan. I love everything; some of my favourite painters areFranz Kline, because I love the confidence with which he painted, andAgnes Martinbecause I love patterns and simplicity. She’s also from Alberta. I really gravitate towards abstract expressionism just because I love that the emotion is driving it. That’s how I relate to art, emotionally rather than intellectually.View image in fullscreen‘They’re both incredible songwriters’ … (from left) Laura Veirs, kd lang and Neko Case in 2016.Photograph: Don Ryan/APLooking back 10 years on, what do you remember most about Case/Lang/Veirs? And would you be tempted to work with Neko Case and Laura Veirsagain if the stars aligned?VerulamiumParkRangerI remember how excited I was when I had the idea to collaborate with them. When I texted them, they both answered within half an hour. And then the work began. I remember it being quite difficult in terms of having three major artists, who had been bosses their whole lives, coming together – we had to navigate and reformulate how we worked, the structure of writing and creativity. They’re both incredible songwriters. I’m in awe of their songwriting ability, and I had to stay out of the way because I felt like they were so much more prolific than I was. We ended up being real good friends, and we had an exciting but short tour.What was it like being part of the Vancouver music scene and performing at the Railway Club in the 80s?budthespudYou must be a Canadian. The Railway Club and the Savoy Club in Vancouver were extremely important to my career. They were both really great small alternative independent music venues. The person who booked the music, Janet Forsyth, booked me very early, and the buzz started happening. It was an incredibly vibrant and buzzy time for me. The shows were extremely formative because I was trying out a lot of different material, learning how to be a stage performer. To this day, Janet Forsyth is my best friend.View image in fullscreenPee-wee’s Playhouse Christmas Special.Photograph: Everett Collection/AlamyWhat was it like to be a part of thePee-wee’s Playhouse Christmas Special(AKA the greatest, gayest Christmas special ever made)? My little brother and I have watched it together every year since 1988!AlexisHidellIt was amazing – it was magical because it was so unbridled. I just sang a Christmas carol – it was all carols, but he had really contrasting artists like Grace Jones and Doris Day. It was like he had all these different kites and he was flying them all at once. You could do whatever you wanted and it was joyful and wise and sardonic – it contained everything. It’s not unlike the paintings we were talking about: it’s emotional expression without any constraints, artistic freedom. Paul [Reubens, AKA Pee-wee Herman] and I became friends. I lovedthe documentary Matt Wolf made on him. Paul was serious and very deliberate.Would you ever consider a follow-up to [lang’s 2004 album of cover versions]Hymns of the 49th Parallel? Hearing Canadian music treated with that kind of deep respect and understanding – the individual songs and the way they exist in conversation with each other – changed something for a lot of people, I think.MarnaNightingaleI have been asked that by my record company and my manager, but I really try to honour my muse and my instincts. It hasn’t happened yet, but maybe it will. Certainly the material is there. There’s an embarrassment of riches of great Canadian songwriting.kd lang on Tony Bennett: ‘It was a salve for society to see an older man and a young dyke in a happy relationship’Read moreWhat was it like appearing on the Larry Sanders show?CaptainLibIt was fun. He was a beautiful guy. [The show was] an intense niche to be put into because they have their own vernacular and rhythm and way of being. I tried to inhabit my own space with it and be natural, but man, the energy there was kind of like being placed in the middle of a football game, and somebody’s vacuuming naked … I don’t totally remember what happened.You’ve described your connection withPatsy Clineas “otherworldly”. What is it about her – and the emotional landscapes of songs such asLeavin’ on Your Mind– that gives her such enduring appeal?Bopalena_now_JohnnyThe emotional connection is inexplicable. Emotion is something ethereal and indescribable. Patsy contained an empathy, an earthiness, a vulnerability, a sense of humour – all the essential parts of humanity. She just sang from an open place, and let people feel comfortable immersing themselves in her.View image in fullscreenStage presence … lang with accordionist Teddy Borowiecki in 2006.Photograph: Mark Mainz/Getty ImagesThe accordion is prominent not just in thebeautiful Constant Craving but in multiple other recordings of yours. Can you tell us more about your accordionist, Teddy Borowiecki, and do you have a particular fascination with this instrument?BirtyDankersIt was around in my upbringing because in the Canadian prairies there were a lot of German and Polish eastern Europeans who had migrated to Canada, so it was prevalent in dance bands and so forth. And Teddy, who is Polish, was a very good accordion player, so I wanted to utilise his talent.What can you share about your meditation practice, and how ithas affected you, the living of your life, and your music?SillyputtyMy spiritual practice is inseparable from anything I do, and is of utmost importance. It’s taken precedence over all things in my life. So I don’t even know where to start or how to describe it. It’s given me a different point of reference that has anchored me in motivation and purpose. Just taking my contribution to the universe very seriously – not self-righteously, but the desire to be authentic and uncontrived.The 10th anniversary edition of Case/Lang/Veirs is released via Anti- on 4 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsPop and rockFilm & Music reader interviewCountryCanadainterviewsShareReuse this content

title: I own six guns. Here’s how to talk to conservatives about firearms | US gun control | The Guardian
description: In rural America, guns are a fact of life. But even conservatives agree that properly locking them up is crucial in preventing deaths
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: In rural America, guns are a fact of life. But even conservatives agree that properly locking them up is crucial in preventing deaths
Content: ‘I’ve been working with liberal volunteers to find common ground with conservative gun owners, beginning with something remarkably simple: giving away gun locks.’Illustration: Antoine Maillard/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘I’ve been working with liberal volunteers to find common ground with conservative gun owners, beginning with something remarkably simple: giving away gun locks.’Illustration: Antoine Maillard/The GuardianUS gun controlI own six guns. Here’s how to talk to conservatives about firearmsIn rural America, guns are a fact of life. But even conservatives agree that properly locking them up is crucial in preventing deathsMeredith DeanThu 3 Sep 2026 09.30 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 11.54 EDTShareI have six guns in my house.The first was a vintage Winchester 12-gauge. It was the winter of 1990, and my husband and I had just moved from an urban block in north-west Philadelphia to a 100-year-old farmhouse in Appalachian Virginia, where my family goes back seven generations.That spring, we started sitting out back every night with the two outdoor dogs and 13 feral barn cats we had adopted since moving in. Invariably, our new neighbor Jimmy would drive by and stop for a beer.One evening in March, the three of us looked up to see a bat flying out of the old attic. Then another, and another. We stopped counting at 100. Since our only access to the attic was through a 2ft hole in the closet ceiling, we installed a door in the hallway with a drop-down ladder.After clearing out countless piles of hidden guano, we began to worry about histoplasmosis – not to mention rabies – as the vexatious critters clawed at the edges of the new entrance, trying to squeeze their way into the house. By mid-summer, we still had not succeeded in humanely relocating what was clearly a firmly established colony.In exasperation, we turned to our newfound repository of rural knowledge – Jimmy – who brought over his old shotgun and suggested we shoot in the air to scare them away. The bats made an immediate 180 and proceeded to chase after the shot, as if they were tracking down moths and mosquitoes.We lost no bats, but we did gain a gun.‘These deaths are not inevitable’: state gun control laws reduce children’s firearm deaths, study showsRead moreOur second came the next fall. As with many rural homesteads, when the Department of Transportation straightened out the road decades earlier, they located it 20ft from our front porch. My husband was out of town a good bit that summer, and someone set up a ratty old trailer at one end of our two-mile, gravel road. An abandoned farmhouse sat at the other end, and a group of single male squatters moved in.Foot traffic grew between the two, and we suspected meth was changing hands. While I was alone one night, a particularly rough-looking fellow from the trailer stumbled up the front steps to “borrow the phone”. That weekend we took a trip to Walmart and added a 20-gauge Remington youth model to our collection.When my mom died 10 years later, I inherited her old BB gun and Remington 22; my husband also inherited one of each. He says the two childhood BB guns don’t really count, but I think they do.When I told a second amendment-supporting friend about our collection, she said: “You need to lock them up or get rid of them.”I don’t disagree.In rural America, guns are a fact of life. But the preventable deaths that come with unsecured firearms don’t have to be.That is why, for the past two years, I’ve been working with liberal volunteers to find common ground with conservative gun owners, beginning with something remarkably simple: giving away gun locks.As national director ofCommunity Works, a program of theRural Urban Bridge Initiative, I bring together volunteers across political differences to address practical needs in their home communities.Progressives won’t gain traction in rural areas by showing up at election time and asking people to change their politics. We have to earn trust year-round by acting locally alongside our conservative neighbors to make things better for everyone: cleaning up rivers, repairing homes, distributing food – even saving lives.When working shoulder-to-shoulder with fellow volunteers one day, it’s harder to turn around and demonize them the next. National depictions of Democrats as godless baby-killers or Republicans as gun-waving racists just don’t hold up when those same folks are standing next to you handing out diapers and school supplies, or packing food for students in the free-lunch program.Promoting gun safety put that concept to an unusually difficult test. Guns, after all, are one of the subjects widely considered unbridgeable in rural politics.I was aware of that when I asked volunteers to hand out free gun locks in some of Virginia’s most conservative counties. I also knew the stakes: firearms are the leading cause of death among American children and teenagers, killing 2,581 children under 18 in 2023 alone.But decades of polarization have made it near impossible to agree on even the simplest measures. Liberals caricature gun owners as uneducated rednecks or reckless young men stockpiling AR-15s; gun owners see liberals as bleeding hearts determined to confiscate their weapons. But keeping guns away from children seemed like the one place where we might meet.View image in fullscreenKeeping guns away from children seemed like the one place where us liberals and conservatives might meet.Illustration: Antoine Maillard/The GuardianTheGun Aware Project(Gap) was founded by Karen and Nick Fischer after a local high school murder-suicide in 2023. Gap organizes free gun-lock distributions during fall back-to-school events in public schools, and volunteers from Community Works were eager to help.One of the first distributions took place in Giles county, on the West Virginia border. There, a growing number of residents support seceding from Virginia and joining West Virginia, in part because they believe Virginia’s new gun laws threaten their second amendment rights.It would be easy to dismiss such a group with the “ignorant hillbilly” stereotype, except for the fact that my physical therapist and her doctor husband were thinking about joining. Despite the gun lobby’s success in pitting gun owners against those who aren’t – always leading to bigger gun sales – the “sides” are often more fluid than we’ve been led to believe.Maybe that’s why the Giles county sheriff’s office, a strong defender of second amendment rights, agreed to collaborate with the Gun Aware Project. Sheriff W Morgan Millirons issued a statement describing firearm safety as part of responsible gun ownership.To date, Gap has given away more than 4,000 locks, 1,000 of those to local departments like Millirons’. Volunteers have spoken with more than 15,000 people in a four-county area. No proselytizing – just sharing storage safety information along with the locks.The Fischers say they have been surprised by the number of people in NRA hats and camo who say: “I really like what you’re doing, we need to protect our kids.” The second most common response is more what they expected: “I have a right to have a weapon. Why are you people trying to take it away?”Attuned to the rural gun culture in which they are operating, the Fischers acknowledge the second amendment, and then redirect the conversation back to safety.Karen explains that removing the magazine from a semi-automatic firearm does not necessarily unload it: a live round may remain in the chamber, something most children – and even some gun owners – do not realize. After listening to Karen, and learning the locks were free, one woman asked for enough locks to secure 12 guns, saying it would be a Christmas gift to her husband.“The issue is not about taking away the second amendment,” says Nick. “The issue is how we deal with living with the second amendment.”In the same vein, the goal of Community Works is not to overcome, or try to change, rural culture. It’s about understanding, respecting and learning to live alongside our conservative rural neighbors.Early research suggests the approach may be working. More than 4,400 surveys were conducted before and after the launch of Community Works in six pilot counties in Virginia and Georgia, along with nearby counties without the new program.According to the study’s author, the Colby College social scientist Dr Nicholas Jacobs, residents in participating counties became less influenced by national partisan divisions and more likely to judge parties by how well they governed locally. They began to view local Democrats as distinct from national party stereotypes, instead judging people based on their contributions to the community.What we did not foresee is that Community Works would also change the way rural Democrats viewed and interacted with their communities.One Democratic volunteer who helped to hand out gun locks at a rural high school event reflected: “I was actually kind of scared to do this in gun country. I thought they’d call me ‘woke’ and walk right on by. But all the kids and parents were really nice, and they totally agreed with me about gun safety.”View image in fullscreen‘The issue is not about taking away the second amendment,’ says Nick Fischer, co-founder of Gun Aware Project. ‘The issue is how we deal with living with the second amendment.’Illustration: Antoine Maillard/The GuardianHer apprehension was understandable. For generations, rural people – and particularly Appalachians with guns – have been portrayed as violent and backward. If you’ve seen the 1972 movie Deliverance or the more recent Netflix series Justified,you know what I’m talking about.Historically, the Appalachian hillbilly stereotype was created in the late 1800s by “local color” travel writers to sell their stories to urban readers. Shotguns, moonshine, bad teeth and dirty overalls were all part of the image. The timber, coal and railroad industries soon adopted the negative caricature as justification for their abusive exploitation of Appalachian landowners.It worked.
