He is very much the face of modernIsraeland his vision for the country accurately reflects the reality on the ground.“Israeli policy is directed toward making life unbearable for Palestinians wherever they live, so that their emigration can be described as an act of free will,” the Israeli journalist Amira Hasswrote in Haaretzthis week. “‘Erasure’ is the nightmare solution being written into reality every day.” Settler violence is escalating, more land in the West Bank and Gaza is being seized, and there has been widespread dehumanization of Palestinians inIsraeli society.Hass writes: “Together, these and similar forces are creating the material, ideological and psychological infrastructure within Israeli-Jewish society for another mass expulsion of Palestinians and for what might accompany it: mass slaughter.”I’m quoting Hass because she is a brilliant journalist. But, I’ll be honest, I’m also quoting her because I’m part-Palestinian and she’s Israeli. I’m quoting Hass because, by virtue of being Israeli, she is seen as someone worth listening to. The world has made it very clear that it doesn’t want to listen to Palestinians, that we are barbarians who should not be believed.And it is this sort of widespread dehumanization that has resulted in the complete shamelessness of a man like Ben-Gvir. He did not come into power in a vacuum: he was helped into his position by an international community which has afforded Israel complete impunity. He has been aided and abetted by international media organizations that have helpeddemonize Palestinians, cast doubt on our claims, and manufacture consent for erasure and expulsion.He has been bolstered by lawmakers who tell us that we must defend Israel at all costs. And now, in the wasteland that is Gaza, in thenightlypogromsby Israeli settlers in the West Bank, and in Ben-Gvir’s brazen bloodlust, we are seeing the inevitable outcome of this unconditional support. Ben-Gvir is no aberration; he is the international community’s creation.Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian US columnistExplore more on these topicsIsraelOpinionGazaPalestinecommentShareReuse this content

title: Queens of the Stone Age’s Josh Homme kicked a woman and his ex-wife alleged domestic abuse. Why the cosy makeover? | Josh Homme | The Guardian
description: Like Johnny Depp and Chris Brown before him, Homme has got past his chequered history to retain an adoring fanbase. Almost a decade post-#MeToo, audiences no longer seem to care
Author: Laura Snapes
Headline: Like Johnny Depp and Chris Brown before him, Homme has got past his chequered history to retain an adoring fanbase. Almost a decade post-#MeToo, audiences no longer seem to care
Content: Josh Homme performing with Queens of the Stone Age last year.Photograph: Mondadori Portfolio/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJosh Homme performing with Queens of the Stone Age last year.Photograph: Mondadori Portfolio/Getty ImagesJosh HommeQueens of the Stone Age’s Josh Homme kicked a woman and his ex-wife alleged domestic abuse. Why the cosy makeover?Laura SnapesLike Johnny Depp and Chris Brown before him, Homme has got past his chequered history to retain an adoring fanbase. Almost a decade post-#MeToo, audiences no longer seem to careThu 3 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 07.02 EDTShareAs part of the promo for Queens of the Stone Age’s new album Perfecth, the band has set up a novelty complaints hotline for fans to call. “No bitching too big, no whiny too tiny,” it promises. I’ll bite: how about the fact that frontman Josh Homme’s ex-wife Brody Dalle testified in court that hehead-butted her so hard that she “saw stars”and said he had fantasised about killing her? Or that hekicked a female photographer in the face? It’s certainly not what anyone’s talking about as part of Homme’s friendly neighbourhood rock star image rehabilitation: duetting on Shania Twain’s new album, taking the couch on Celebrity Gogglebox, teatime BBC 6 Music interviews.Homme and Dalle clearly had a complicated relationship: he allegedly tried to throw her boyfriend off a balcony; he claims that she was violent towards him; both have taken outrestraining orders against one another; Homme has full custody of their kids after Dalle’s boyfriend was found to have forged her signature on an application for a restraining order. Homme has recently talked about coming through a dark period, includingsuccessful treatment for cancer, and getting a handle on his vices. Nevertheless, there is clear footage of him brutally kicking the camera of photographer Chelsea Lauren back into her face, which he acknowledged in an apology video, and court testimony from Dalle alleging that a drunk Homme told her “I want to fucking strangle you right now” on one occasion, and head-butted her on another.Their situation shares resonances with Johnny Depp and Amber Heard’s messy relationship breakdown, which prompted a British judge to deem that the Sun was in fact accurate inlabelling Depp a “wife-beater”despite his libel claim against them; althougha US jury ruled in his favour against Heard, who was found guilty of defamation. You only have to see the grim trailer for Ebenezer, Depp’s forthcoming Scrooge trauma plot movie, to see how much any of this really damaged his career. “It’s good to be back,” Depp-as-Scrooge tee-hees in his first spoken scene. Subtext, as Garth Marenghi told us, is for cowards. Text appears proclaiming “the master of misfits returns”; the entire aesthetic seems skimmed from former Depp hits Sweeney Todd, Pirates of the Caribbean and Edward Scissorhands. As someone says in the comments: “This entire trailer is just, ‘You like Johnny Depp right?’” You could sum up most of the rest of the comments as: we sure do! Nothing says future Christmas classic like big-budget reputation laundering.You get the hopeless feeling that none of this matters any more. Chris Brown is currently on a high-profile US tour with Usher that has had guest appearances from trailblazing female artists such as Alicia Keys and Mary J Blige – despite him beating then-girlfriend Rihanna in 2009 and another ex being granted a five-year restraining order after he threatened her. “For years, traditional media has been tiptoeing around the popularity of Chris Brown, and in reality, that benefits nobody but him,” critic Alphonse Pierre wrote ina pan of Brown’s latest album, Brown. “The lack of critical engagement with his music has allowed him to contextualise his own redemption with statistic and sob stories.” And yet, as Doreen St Felixwrote in the New Yorker, the tour’s audience is full of adoring women.Almost a decade after the mainstream#MeToo movement, it’s clear that audiences’ nostalgia for artists who made art that meant something to them at a formative age overrides the inconvenience of violence against women. Couple that fondness with an expensive publicity campaign and the counternarrative never stands a chance, easily dismissed as the shrill cries of cranks. I believe firmly in rehabilitation and second chances, but haven’t been able to shake a sense of horror that millions of people can apparently look past allegations and evidence of violence against women when engaging in supposedly feelgood pop culture.Last month, Homme made headlines during a Detroit show where he flouted the venue’s smoking ban, risking a $10,000 fine to take a stand against“fuckin’ corporate assholes”who “tell you what to do” (while his band, um, voluntarily play those corporate assholes’ corporate venue for a fat pay cheque). This sort of limp rock’n’roll cosplay is just as cosy in its own way as reviewing crap British TV on primetime Channel 4: vanilla rebellion figures offering the comforting reassurance that rock stars still walk among us, boldly reminding us that rules are made to be broken.The notion of so-called rock’n’roll behaviour, many have theorised, was partly why music never had much of a “#MeToo moment”, that hopeless relic of a phrase. When bad behaviour isn’t just accepted but venerated, real wrongdoing can be brushed under the same whisky-stained rug. Blind eyes are turned, offenders are remade as outlaws, myths are upheld, party lines toed: “It’s so safe to play along / Little soldiers in a row,” as Homme sang in Go With the Flow. The jokey complaints hotline might be the most honest part of QOTSA’s return: a grim reflection of the fact that nobody is taking this shit seriously any more.Explore more on these topicsJosh HommePop and rockQueens of the Stone AgeJohnny Depp#MeToo movementcommentShareReuse this content

title: The Ceuta border breach was leapt on by Europe’s right. That doesn’t absolve Spain | María Ramírez | The Guardian
description: The government’s sluggish response has been disastrous for everyone involved – and for Sánchez’s message on immigration, says María Ramírez, deputy managing editor of Spanish news outlet elDiario.es
Author: María Ramírez
Headline: The government’s sluggish response has been disastrous for everyone involved – and for Sánchez’s message on immigration, says María Ramírez, deputy managing editor of Spanish news outlet elDiario.es
Content: Dozens of people by makeshift tents on the beach, a day after a violent protest during which some tents were set alight.Photograph: Antonio Sempere/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDozens of people by makeshift tents on the beach, a day after a violent protest during which some tents were set alight.Photograph: Antonio Sempere/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionSpainThe Ceuta border breach was leapt on by Europe’s right. That doesn’t absolve SpainMaría RamírezThe government’s sluggish response has been disastrous for everyone involved – and for Sánchez’s message on immigrationThu 3 Sep 2026 09.29 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 09.32 EDTShareMore than a month after an estimated 72,000 people suddenly crossed from Morocco into the Spanish territory of Ceuta, the city remains in chaos and the damage inflicted on the Spanish government is becoming clearer. Most of those who made the crossing have returned to Morocco. The scale of the incident was nevertheless extraordinary, and about 140 peopleare thought to have died.Also extraordinary was the response of the22 EU governmentsthat rounded on the Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, rather than demonstrate the solidarity one might expect from allies. Perhaps less surprising was the exploitation of the crisis by rightwing and far-right parties in Spain and beyond,Donald Trump’s attacksand the interventions ofRussian state-linked actorsandIsraeli criticson social media tofuel division.But this opportunism by Europe’s rightwing governments – Italy suspended its Schengen arrangements with Spain for no good reason – does not absolve Spain of blame. What has unfolded since 30 July is tragic for Ceuta, which has a permanent population of only about 84,000 people, and for the thousands of people, including an estimated 1,200 unaccompanied children, left on its streets and beaches. Sánchez’s government must take responsibility for some of the damage it is now belatedly trying to mop up.Ceuta was a carnival of anti-migrant content for hateful opportunists on the right – and a lesson for the left | Jonathan LiewRead moreOn 1 August, in the aftermath of the border breach, Sánchez reassured the EU that“virtually all”of the people who had arrived in Ceuta had returned to Morocco. The overwhelming majority did indeed leave, but thousands did not – and they are still in the city. Official numbershave fluctuated. The Spanish government’s estimate is that 5,000 of those who arrived are still in Ceuta; the region’s local governmenthas suggestedit could be double that. For weeks, there was no accommodation available, and hundreds are still camped on beaches or near the overcrowded migrant centres.View image in fullscreenWomen and children picking from donated clothes in a sports field set up by local residents as an improvised shelter.Photograph: Violeta Santos Moura/ReutersPeople living near these centrescomplainthey cannot leave their apartments out of fear, and that their children are unable to play on the beach or in the street. Businesses have had to close for days on end, incurring losses. Summer festivities had to be cancelled. Many migrants, including women and children, have survived on charity from local NGOs, the Red Cross and neighbours, and have little food, water and shelter.Yet as the situation deteriorated, the Spanish government failed for weeks to appoint anyone to coordinate a response. This would have been essential in Spain’s decentralised system, with powers divided between the central government and local and regional authorities. Now Madrid is finally funnelling resources and money into the matter, but only after the situation had deteriorated dangerously.Tensions have been evident in recent days, with local people crying in front of TV cameras, and politicians pleading for help. Protests directed against migrants have been constant. They have been mostly peaceful, but there have been outbreaks of violence. In one incident, a group of protesterstried to drive migrants off the beachand burned their tents before they were dispersed by the police with teargas. In another, military police were allegedly assaulted by a group from Morocco. At least 23sexual assaultsagainst migrants have been reported, including nineagainst children.View image in fullscreenCeuta residents protesting in late August by the beach where migrants have made makeshift camps.Photograph: REDUAN/EPACeuta was already fragile. The city, smaller than the site of Madrid airport, is home to a multicultural community that has been part of Spain since the 17th century. But even before this,its citizens complainedabout feeling abandoned. And now Morocco isreviving claims of sovereignty.Sánchez’s defence of Morocco –telling parliamenton Thursday that there was “no evidence” that Rabat had orchestrated events at the border – is at odds with popular sentiment in Ceuta and with most of the parties in parliament, including hisleftwing allies Sumar, the minority partner in the governing coalition.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Spanish government’s slow response and state of denial are damaging not only for Ceuta, but for Madrid’s own message on immigration. Spain has quite successfully promoted immigration as a force for good in recent years, even as most governments in Europe have moved in the opposite direction. What happened in Ceuta should not diminish the case for immigration as a factor driving economic growth and social dynamism, as Spain has shown over the past decade. But the mismanagement of Ceuta on the ground will inevitably impair that message.Even now, the Spanish government is backtracking, tightening its migration rules and pointing to disinformation around asupreme court decisionthat protected migrants’ rights against speedy returns as a cause for the rush on Ceuta. It has said it will stop transferring unaccompanied minors out of the territory and distributing them around the country for their protection, and isapproving restrictionsin line with the hardlineEU pact on migration and asylumpushed by rightwing governments.Regional politicians, who are mostly conservative, refuse to help out. The conservative People’s party (PP), which is leading inthe pollsbefore next year’s general election, is always better at attacking the government than clarifying what it would do differently. But even some local politicians from theSocialist Workers’ partyhave recently joined demonstrations in solidarity with Ceuta.The Ceuta episode has landed Spain with an almost impossible situation to resolve. But a combination of passivity and blaming everyone butMoroccohas not helpedthe city’s residents, Sánchez’s political position or the positive case for immigration in Spain and beyond.María Ramírez is a journalist and deputy managing editor of elDiario.es, a news outlet in SpainDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on press freedom: to defend democracy, stand up for journalists | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: The lack of justice for Daphne Caruana Galizia in Malta casts a shadow on reporters everywhere
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: The lack of justice for Daphne Caruana Galizia in Malta casts a shadow on reporters everywhere
Content: Flowers lie in front of a portrait of the investigative journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia, during a vigil outside the law courts in Valletta, Malta, in October 2018.Photograph: Jonathan Borg/APView image in fullscreenFlowers lie in front of a portrait of the investigative journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia, during a vigil outside the law courts in Valletta, Malta, in October 2018.Photograph: Jonathan Borg/APOpinionPress freedomThe Guardian view on press freedom: to defend democracy, stand up for journalistsEditorialThe lack of justice for Daphne Caruana Galizia in Malta casts a shadow on reporters everywhereThu 3 Sep 2026 13.50 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 14.02 EDTShareTheacquittal of Yorgen Fenech, who was on trial in Malta for involvement in the murder of the journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia, is a devastating blow for justice and press freedom. Nine years after her car was blown up, it seems increasingly unlikely that anyone will be held to account for ordering and paying for her death. Mr Fenech’s admissions that he knew about the murder before it happened, and gave money to the middle-man who paid the killers, make it hard to understand why he was found not guilty on the lesser charge of association.All killings of journalists are wrong. The bomb placed in Caruana Galizia’s car was especially shocking, as such brazen violence is usually associated with war zones or states overrun by organised crime. The fact that this acquittal came two months after those ofthree men accused of murdering another journalist, Lyra McKee, in Northern Ireland, adds to a grim impression of impunity for killers. While McKee is not thought to have been targeted in the way that Caruana Galizia was, the inability of police and prosecutors to secure convictions in either case points to wider problems.View image in fullscreenReform UK leader Nigel Farage.Photograph: Victoria Jones/ShutterstockJoseph Muscat resignedas Malta’s prime minister in 2019. But his party, Labour, remains in power, raising questions as to whether the corrupt networks alleged to have been behind the plot have been broken up. The EU and countries including the UK – which has close ties with Malta – must apply pressure. This is all the more urgent given the global context of intensifying attacks on the press, including in Donald Trump’s US. Reporters Without Borders recently warned that political hostility combined with financial pressures could lead tojournalism “being asphyxiated”.Physical safety should be regarded as a bare minimum. As well as addressing threats of violence, politicians and others should stand up for press freedom – even when they don’t approve of every outlet or editorial choice. In the UK, a private member’s bill currently seems the most likely route tooutlawing strategic lawsuits against public participation(known as Slapps), which are used – by those who can afford them – to block media investigations and silence whistleblowers.But while Labour’s record in office on this issue is weak, recent actions by Reform UK are an anti-democratic disgrace. Nigel Farage’s party kicked off party conference season by refusing to give the Guardian’s city editor, Anna Isaac, and two other journalists passes. While itrefused to give an explanationfor barring Ms Isaac, the obvious one is that the party wants to punish her. Ms Isaac broke the story that Mr Farage accepted an undeclared £5m gift from Christopher Harborne, a cryptocurrency billionaire. She also found out that donations to Reform UK caused bankers to report potential money-laundering concerns to the National Crime Agency.There is a clear public interest in news about the way that political parties are funded. But as in Nottinghamshire, where Reform UKbanned its councillors from speaking to the Nottingham Post,the party has shown its oft-trumpeted commitment to free speech to be a sham. Singling out journalists for bans is not the same as threatening them. But it is part of a populist strategy that combines hollow rhetoric about liberty with an authoritarian approach to people and institutions that place obstacles on the path to power. Pluralism must be defended at home and abroad – and this includes journalists.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on Nigeria’s kidnappings: a country can’t prosper when going to school is a danger | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Abductions are resurging and may be spreading to new areas – with young children among the victims. A military response alone won’t work
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Abductions are resurging and may be spreading to new areas – with young children among the victims. A military response alone won’t work
Content: A poster at a rally in Lagos in June demanding the government rescue people who have been kidnapped.Photograph: Sunday Alamba/APView image in fullscreenA poster at a rally in Lagos in June demanding the government rescue people who have been kidnapped.Photograph: Sunday Alamba/APOpinionNigeriaThe Guardian view on Nigeria’s kidnappings: a country can’t prosper when going to school is a dangerEditorialAbductions are resurging and may be spreading to new areas – with young children among the victims. A military response alone won’t workThu 3 Sep 2026 13.44 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 13.52 EDTShareEarly last month, Nigeria’s government announced the largest single-day hostage rescue in its history, withthe freeing of 300 peoplewho had been taken in raids in two north central states. Celebrations were short-lived. Barely a fortnight later, gunmen abducted up to 600 worshippers from a mosque in Niger state. Nigerians paid kidnappers nearly $6m in ransoms in the year to June,according to a new reportfrom the Lagos-based consultancy SBM Intelligence – more than triple the total in the previous 12-month period. More than 7,800 people were abducted, a two-thirds increase, and more than 1,100 killed, including almost 900 civilians.When Boko Haramabducted almost 300 schoolgirlsfrom their school in Chibok, Borno state in 2014, it made headlines worldwide. Yet around 45 children, mostly aged between two and five, remain missing after theywere snatched from schools in Mussa, in north-eastern Borno state, in May. There is growing concern that kidnappingsmay be spreadingto new areas. Forty-six students and staffwere abducted from three schoolsin the south-western state of Oyo in the same month; they were rescued in July.View image in fullscreenPresident Bola Tinubu.Photograph: Jean Bizimana/ ReutersThe kidnappings are just one facet of Nigeria’s multiple and overlapping security crises, which may be key to January’s presidential election.Boko Haram, its Islamic State West Africa Province offshoot and other jihadist groups are battling each other as well as terrorising civilians.In themiddle beltand parts of the south-west, violence pits predominantly Muslim Fulani herders against largely Christian farming communities. Climate stress and environmental despoliation are intensifying competition over land and resources. Because the two sides fall largely along religious lines, Donald Trump and American evangelicals have presented this conflict as if it were Nigeria’s entire security crisis, rather than one part of it.The repercussions of abductions can be devastating even if hostages come home. Around100 Chibokgirls remain missing, while some returnees face rejection. Kidnapping also drives displacement, economic disruption and school closures, especially affecting girls in a country with a median age of just 18 and pervasive mass youthunemployment.Many schools in Africa’s most populous countryhave simply closed. A safe schools protection initiative was laudable, buthas limited effectwithout broader security improvements. Successive governments have failed to curb the violence. An overly centralised state and an overstretched security apparatus leave too many of Nigeria’s 240 million people unprotected. State abandonment isforcing communitiesto seek their own accommodation with the perpetrators.US strikes and a short-lived troopdeploymentwere misconceived, with Mr Trump casting thecomplexviolence, which has killed many Muslims too, as “Christian genocide”. Nigeria needs outside support rather than intervention. President Bola Tinubu announced amajor military expansionand pay rise in July. But Christopher Musa, the country’s defence minister, has said that the military can only be 30% of the solution; 70% is socioeconomic. The army’s operational failures and grim human rights record, and the danger of other essentials being cut to pay for boosting defence, also counsel caution. Nigeria’s children and adults can’t be protected without better intelligence, improved collaboration among security institutions and with communities, and, above all, a fairer social and economic deal.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Climate injustices have been laid bare in the Nepal-Tibet flood disaster | Nepal-Tibet flood disaster | The Guardian
description: Letters: Prof Lyla Mehta says the glacial floods and loss of life are a stark reminder that climate disruption is global and highly unequal. Plus letters from Lynda McDonald and Jan Bengtsson
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Prof Lyla Mehta says the glacial floods and loss of life are a stark reminder that climate disruption is global and highly unequal. Plus letters from Lynda McDonald and Jan Bengtsson
Content: A woman retrieves personal belongings from the mud in a community impacted by the glacial flood in Nuwakot, Nepal.Photograph: Suryams Upreti/AAPView image in fullscreenA woman retrieves personal belongings from the mud in a community impacted by the glacial flood in Nuwakot, Nepal.Photograph: Suryams Upreti/AAPNepal-Tibet flood disasterLettersClimate injustices have been laid bare in the Nepal-Tibet flood disasterProf Lyla Mehtasays the glacial floods and loss of life are a stark reminder that climate disruption is global and highly unequal. Plus letters fromLynda McDonaldandJan BengtssonThu 3 Sep 2026 12.52 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 13.16 EDTShareThe recent glacial collapse and catastrophic floods in Nepal and Tibet are not isolated tragedies (Report, 28 August). They reflect accelerating climate disruption that disproportionately affects the countries and people that are least responsible for global emissions.As climate change intensifies, glaciers around the world, including in the Himalayas, are melting at unprecedented rates, destabilising ecosystems and causing glacial collapse and ice-and-rock landslides, destroying settlements, villages and livelihoods in minutes. No one died when a Swiss glacier collapsed last year, owing to early-warning systems that were in place. But a lack of early-warning systems means that the disaster in Nepal and Tibet has led to hundreds of deaths and thousands missing.Events like these are not “natural disasters”. They are due to global warming and climate injustices, and also flawed development policies, includingrampant property developmentson vulnerable floodplains. They call for better disaster preparedness and investment in early-warning systems. Most importantly, they require global action.The UK has long positioned itself as a leader in international development and climate action. Yet recent UK commitments have fallen far short of what is required – including the decision toraid the diminished aid budgetto switch international climate finance grants to loans, to fund a bus-fare cap.The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, recentlyspoke compellinglyabout the need to put the climate crisis and overseas development at the heart of UK international relations. These words must now translate into action. The UK must step up its development commitments and funding for climate adaptation, and loss and damage, to support those living on the frontlines of climate change.The recent glacial floods remind us that climate disruption is global, and highly unequal. The UK must act urgently. Anything less is a failure of responsibility.Prof Lyla MehtaInstitute of Development StudiesSunil Acharya is correct when he states: “The countries that benefited most from fossil fuel-driven growth have a responsibility to cut emissions rapidly”(Nepal-Tibet flood: this is the cost of not acting in the face of the climate crisis, 28 August).This was the founding principle of the global “contraction and convergence” framework, tabled by India, China and the African Group of Nations in Kyoto at Cop3 in 1997.Had we enacted this, we would now be on a safe, and equitable, 30-year contraction path, avoiding the worst of the climate crisis and ensuring our survival. Instead, we remain adrift, with no viable solution or plan. Is it really too late to adopt this framework?Lynda McDonaldPortaferry, County DownThe key question is: who should pay for this disaster? Yes, the rich world should pay, but the bills should be sent to all the fossil-fuel companies that have known this risk for at least half a century and have ignored it. If they refuse to pay, all of us in countries that have profited from the fossil-driven benefits of “progress” should, through our governments, pay a progressive tax on all things based on fossil fuels, to cover the past, present and future costs of climate change.Jan BengtssonUppsala, SwedenHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: How 20mph on our roads benefits everyone | Transport | The Guardian
description: Letters: The advantages of 20mph speed limits are celebrated by Rod King, while John Hopkin says drivers who speed won’t be deterred unless tougher action is taken against them
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: The advantages of 20mph speed limits are celebrated by Rod King, while John Hopkin says drivers who speed won’t be deterred unless tougher action is taken against them
Content: A street with 20mph speed limit signs in Rhayader, Powys.Photograph: Kara Thomas/Athena PicturesView image in fullscreenA street with 20mph speed limit signs in Rhayader, Powys.Photograph: Kara Thomas/Athena PicturesTransportLettersHow 20mph on our roads benefits everyoneThe advantages of 20mph speed limits are celebrated byRod King, whileJohn Hopkinsays drivers who speed won’t be deterred unless tougher action is taken against themThu 3 Sep 2026 12.52 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 13.16 EDTShareThanks to Christian Wolmar for his insightful article on a 20mph limit and how it would be a good thing for Birmingham (Dear culture-war motorists, look to the future. We’ll all be driving at 20mph soon, 28 August). He is right to identify that the world has changed from when the car was king and we planned our city mobility almost exclusively around automobiles.At 20’s Plenty for Us we have seen our movement developing from being classed as radical in the 2000s, to progressive in the 2010s and the new normal in the 2020s. As 20mph limits have been adopted by progressive authorities, we have seen the significant benefits extend beyond pedestrians and cyclists to those who drive.There is clear evidence that when implemented on a wide scale, as in Wales, the average motorist benefits. Journeys for drivers took less than a minute more on average, and journey times were more reliable; car, van and taxi occupant casualties on urban and village roads were reduced by 29.6% in the first year; and insurance costs were reduced by £45 for the average driver owing to 20% fewer damage claims.These are real gains for the average motorist, who also benefits from 20mph being the foundation for people to choose to walk or cycle instead of being in another car in front of them. Of course, when they are not in their car, the same people benefit, and their community becomes a safer and less stressful place.Some drivers will always object to community needs being placed above their own judgment. But the world has changed, and soon a 20mph speed limit will be the urban and village norm, making all of our places better places to be.Rod KingFounder and chair, 20’s Plenty for UsCICGood luck to Birmingham city council with their plan for a blanket 20mph speed limit. However, many speed cameras were turned off a decade ago to make austerity savings. As a result, current speed limits are widely (and sometimes enthusiastically) ignored with apparent impunity – particularly, it seems, the existing 20mph limits on residential roads.If there’s a war on motorists here, it is one that motorists are now winning: if existing limits are not enforced, it seems unlikely that simply extending the zone will result in a change in behaviour.John HopkinMoseley, BirminghamHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Donald Trump’s shallow renaming of the Great Lakes | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers respond to the Trump administration’s decision to change Lake Ontario to ‘Lake America’
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers respond to the Trump administration’s decision to change Lake Ontario to ‘Lake America’
Content: Has Donald Trump has ruined a Great Lakes acronym?Photograph: Anadolu/GettyView image in fullscreenHas Donald Trump has ruined a Great Lakes acronym?Photograph: Anadolu/GettyDonald TrumpLettersDonald Trump’s shallow renaming of the Great LakesReaders respond to the Trump administration’s decision to change Lake Ontario to ‘Lake America’Thu 3 Sep 2026 12.52 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 13.16 EDTShareI think too much is being made of this (Apple Maps renames Lake Ontario as ‘Lake America’ for US users after Trump order, 2 August). It is common for geographical features straddling borders to receive different names in different jurisdictions.Consider, for example, Lac Léman and the Bodensee, La Manche and Les Îles Malouines.Waleshas only recently reclaimed Yr Wyddfa and Bannau Brycheiniog, and for a reminder and dramatisation of how renaming played out in Ireland, look no further than Brian Friel’s Translations. Perhaps we can look forward to Lake Cleveland (previously Erie) and Lake Trump (previously Superior)?Owen StewartGatley, Greater ManchesterDonald Trump’s renaming of Lake Ontario to Lake America (Report, 27 August) could be an ominous precedent for this country if Reform UK or Restore Britain come to power. In his dystopian vision of the future, the novelist Islwyn Ffowc Elis foresaw Wales being renamed Western England by the government in 2033.David PopeRoyal Wootton Bassett, WiltshireMost Americans will have learned the mnemonic HOMES for the Great Lakes (Huron, Ontario, Michigan, Erie, Superior). With Donald Trump’s renaming, what will this be replaced by? SHAME, perhaps?James LindesayLeicesterA new name for America (Letters, 30 August)? Trumpton, with its cast of characters including Musk, Musk, Altman and Thiel, Bezos, Zucky and Huang.Rob HorneCoventryHow about SouthCanada? Or, alternatively, North Mexico?Andy CookHonley, West YorkshireHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Abundant common fossils don’t need to be protected | Fossils | The Guardian
description: Letters: Museums have countless examples of the common fossils from these Lower Jurassic rocks, says the Charmouth Heritage Coast Centre’s Phil Davidson
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Museums have countless examples of the common fossils from these Lower Jurassic rocks, says the Charmouth Heritage Coast Centre’s Phil Davidson
Content: The Dorset coastline. ‘Allowing tourists to collect and take home their discoveries helps them foster a sense of curiosity.’Photograph: Gordon Hulmes/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe Dorset coastline. ‘Allowing tourists to collect and take home their discoveries helps them foster a sense of curiosity.’Photograph: Gordon Hulmes/AlamyFossilsLettersAbundant common fossils don’t need to be protectedMuseums have countless examples of the common fossils from these Lower Jurassic rocks, says the Charmouth Heritage Coast Centre’sPhil DavidsonThu 3 Sep 2026 12.52 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 12.53 EDTShareThe vast majority of the fossils revealed on this rapidly eroding part of the Jurassic Coast hold very little scientific importance and are not in need of protection or recording (Letters, 28 August). Museums around the world have countless examples of the common fossils from these Lower Jurassic rocks, thanks to the efforts of fossil collectors, who since the pioneering palaeontologist Mary Anning (1799–1847) have saved fossils from the same process that reveals them, the action of the sea.The majority of these scientifically important fossils are saved from destruction after the winter storms, not during the peak tourist season in the summer. Allowing tourists to collect and take home their discoveries helps them foster a sense of curiosity and encourages an interest in the natural world, which is especially important for future generations.As in any busy tourist destination, there will always be ill-informed tourists. Some visitors have not worked out which rocks to crack open successfully yet, but the next rough sea or storm will wash new fossils out of the mudslides, and if they are not collected they will be damaged and destroyed by the sea.Here at the Charmouth Heritage Coast Centre, our educational charity welcomes in excess of 100,000 visitors a year. It is free for all to enter and learn more about the past, present and future of our amazing coast through our award-winning displays of recent fossil finds. We also maintain the westDorsetand Undercliffs Fossil Recording Schemes and have records of over 600 fossils of scientific importance that have been discovered here, many by members of the public. We work with academics, researchers, landowners and the public to deliver ethical collecting guidelines (fossil codes), which are management tools on this part of the world heritage site.Phil DavidsonPalaeontologist, Charmouth Heritage Coast CentreHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today?
