title: Premier League: 10 things to look out for this weekend | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Florian Wirtz has a chance to shine, there’s a Red Bull reunion at St James’ Park and Chelsea face a litmus test at Arsenal
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: Florian Wirtz has a chance to shine, there’s a Red Bull reunion at St James’ Park and Chelsea face a litmus test at Arsenal
Content: Bournemouth’s Alex Scott, Manchester City’s Nico O’Reilly and Liverpool’s Florian Wirtz.Composite: Getty, ShutterstockView image in fullscreenBournemouth’s Alex Scott, Manchester City’s Nico O’Reilly and Liverpool’s Florian Wirtz.Composite: Getty, ShutterstockTen things to look out for this weekendPremier LeaguePremier League: 10 things to look out for this weekendFlorian Wirtz has a chance to shine, there’s a Red Bull reunion on Tyneside and Chelsea face litmus test at ArsenalGuardian sportThu 3 Sep 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 19.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCan Wirtz find his best for Liverpool?Florian Wirtz is easing himself into his second season at Liverpool after a forgettable first. There were signs of promiseagainst Nottingham Forest, where he set up the second equaliser and would have had a goal of his own if not for an offside in the buildup. It is clear the German needs to become more influential as a No 10 given the quality of players he has around him, especially afterthe expensive arrival of Bradley Barcolathis week. Bruno Fernandes showed there is plenty of fun for an attacking midfielder to have against Ipswich and Wirtz can follow suit as a protagonist. Liverpool have drawn both their opening fixtures 2-2 and need something to kickstart their campaign, with a Friday night visit to promoted opposition a fine place to start. Wirtz should cause problems but, if he does not, the internal competition will be after his spot.Will UnwinIpswich vLiverpool(Friday 8pm, all times BST)Red Bull gives you wingsVerticality, intensity and hard pressing are likely to be the order of the day at St James’ Park, where two German graduates of the Red Bull stable meet on Saturday at lunchtime. Newcastle’s new manager, Matthias Jaissle, is a former head coach of Red Bull Salzburg, while Bournemouth’s Marco Rose has managed Salzburg and, more recently, RB Leipzig. “We have the same idea of how we want to play football,” said Jaissle – and Rose knows what to expect from Eddie Howe’s successor. “Matthias and me were several years in the style of Red Bull,” he said. “Everyone knows how we work. You can see it clearly. He’s a good coach. He’s brought his ideas really quickly into the Newcastle team. They are playing quite intense, they have clear pressing patterns that are different from before.”Louise TaylorNewcastle v Bournemouth (Saturday 12.30pm)View image in fullscreenMatthias Jaissle is looking for his first back-to-back league wins with Newcastle.Photograph: MI News/NurPhoto/ShutterstockBees plot left-wing raid on Black CatsSaturday’s meeting between two of the Premier League’s best-run clubs, Brentford and Sunderland, promises to one of the best contests of the weekend, with both sides physical, technical and superbly coached. Brentford, in particular, have made a terrific start to the season, the left side of their team looking especially dangerous. Keane Lewis-Potter provides impetus from full-back, with Mamadou Sangaré backing up strong ball-winning and carrying with intelligent passing, while Kevin Schade offers a threat in behind and, increasingly, in front of goal. All of which suggests a difficult afternoon for Thomas Meunier, Sunderland’s likely right-back who, at 34, has plenty of experience but might struggle with the athletic questions asked of him. He will, though, be able to rely on assistance from Noah Sadiki, whose nous, work ethic and running power will be invaluable in defending Sunderland’s right flank. How that battle plays out will go a long way towards deciding the game.Daniel HarrisBrentford vSunderland(Saturday 3pm)Chema looks another astute Brighton buyWe can be sure any player Brighton buy has delivered the data metrics employed by the owner, Tony Bloom. But Chema Andrés, the 21-year-old midfielder just signed from Stuttgart, also nails the eye test. Signed for £18.9m, it’s already tempting to speculate how sizeable the mark-up will be when Brighton sell him on. If we remember we’re talking about a sport, it’s impossible not to be excited about what the former Real Madrid academy midfielder brings to Fabian Hürzeler’s team. A No 6 of the old school, Chema offers economical movement but extravagant intelligence, evident in his passing and anticipation. Even if this weekend’s game against Leeds comes too early for him to be handed a start, he will make an impact soon enough.DHBrighton v Leeds (Saturday 3pm)An early basement battle at the CottageIt’s been a tricky summer for Crystal Palace despite their Conference League win. Oliver Glasner has gone, with two key defenders in Daniel Muñoz and Maxence Lacroix also departing and Jean-Philippe Mateta and Ismaïla Sarr trying their best to join them. This upheaval has left Pierre Sage, whose existing relationship with Malick Fofanawasn’t enough to secure the Lyon winger’s signature, with major problems. The former Lens coach is seeking to replace the club’s most successful manager while learning what works in a new league, with new players and without three mainstays. It wasn’t especially surprising to see Palace lose their first two matches, while Fulham have also been beaten twice while seeking to bed in a new coach and arrivals. More troubling for both teams is that the promoted sides look competitive. Hull and Ipswich have performed well and won games, while Coventry are better than they’ve shown so far. Though it’s far too early to talk about relegation, this already feels like a game of significance for two sides struggling for momentum.DHFulham vCrystal Palace(Saturday 3pm)Graphic showing Fulham and Crystal Palace second and fourth respectively among the favourites for relegation, according to Opta dataO’Reilly to step into Rodri role for City?Manchester City spent more than £300m on new midfielders in this transfer window, but look light in the No 6 role, with Rodri and Nico González both departing. Ayyoub Bouaddi, bought as Rodri’s long-term successor, is only 18, so Enzo Maresca’s plan is to ease him into first-team action. TheManchester Citymanager deployed Marc Guéhi in a holding midfield role against Bournemouth, and is also confident Nico O’Reilly can switch from left-back to operate there. O’Reilly may line up at the base of midfield for Coventry’s visit, with City seeking a third straight win. Maresca is also not fazed by Omar Marmoush’s departure on an initial loan to Spurs, with Iliman Ndiaye arriving on deadline day and Antoine Semenyo also an able deputy centre-forward if Erling Haaland is unavailable.Jamie JacksonManchester City v Coventry (Saturday 3pm)Delap to be thrown in against shaky SpursLiam Delap came off the bench against Liverpool and helped create Nottingham Forest’s second goal with quick thinking from a throw-in. The striker cost £45m from Chelsea but missed out on an intense pre-season after Xabi Alonso decided he was surplus to requirements, so needs to build fitness. Considering Tottenham’s major flaws thus far, it would make sense for Delap to be given the chance to spearhead the Forest attack. The former England Under-21 international is the ideal No 9, quick, strong and a capable finisher, but needs to get all these attributes sharpened up. An outing against a fragile opponent could speed up the process. Tottenham are bottom of the league having conceded five and scored none in two games, and compared to Chris Wood or Igor Jesus, Delap is a far scarier foe, as Oliver Glasner will know.WUNottingham Forest v Tottenham (Saturday 3pm)Six points, seven signings for happy HullThey may have nabbed two wins in as many games upon their return to the Premier League but Hull were still not happy with their squad, seven new players arriving in the final week of the window. That means the Tigers have made 19 signings since promotion, which is an impressive turnover in personnel. Sergej Jakirovic needs to decide whether to incorporate these potential upgrades into his starting XI as soon as possible or make them earn the shirts from those who have accumulated six points. No one has let down the head coach or the fans over 180 minutes, so it would be harsh to drop anyone but, equally, having spent so much money on acquisitions, it could be argued that the sooner they get on the pitch, the quicker they will gel. It is not an easy decision for Jakirovic to make but he values loyalty and will want to challenge the mentality of the new arrivals – no one will walk into the side he has built.WUHullvAston Villa(Saturday 5.30pm)View image in fullscreenElliot Stroud, one of Hull’s 19 summer signings, in action during their 1-0 win at Coventry.Photograph: Neal Simpson/Getty Images/AllstarEverton fans react to dismal deadline dayThere are parallels between Manchester United’s visit to Hill Dickinson Stadium and their 3-0 win at Goodison Park in 2023 in the sense they will face a furious Everton crowd, and for the second time in four seasons the anger will not be directed towards them. Three years ago it was the Premier League in Evertonians’ sights following the record 10-point deduction that had just been imposed on the club. This time it is Everton’s owners, the Friedkin Group, in the firing line following the club’s shambolic end to the transfer window.There will be no flag displays inside the stadium after the group responsible for organising them, the 1878s, withdrew their support and there are calls for a “not a pound in the ground” campaign in response to the owners making a profit on transfers while leaving David Moyes with a weaker squad. Everton have started the season positively on the pitch, but are now surrounded by problems of their owners’ making.Andy HunterEverton v Manchester United (Sunday 2pm)Chelsea face litmus test in London derbyYou have to go back to the start of the 2021-22 season, when Arsenal had Rob Holding and Pablo Marí in central defence, for the last time thatChelseabeat their north London rivals, a run of 11 matches in all competitions. But having come close to ending that sequence in the 1-1 draw at Stamford Bridge last season before things began to unravel for Enzo Maresca, the Italian’s successor, Xabi Alonso, will head to the Emirates to face his old friend Mikel Arteta in a competitive match for the first time as a manager full of confidence after winning his opening two games. Chelsea’s new-look front three of Cole Palmer, João Pedro and Morgan Rogers can certainly cause Arsenal problems, although the question is whether a defence that has already conceded five goals can keep out the champions at the other end.Ed AaronsArsenal v Chelsea (Sunday 4.30pm)PosTeamPGDPts1Man City2462Arsenal2463Hull2364Chelsea2265Brentford2346Newcastle2247Everton2248Leeds2149Brighton23310Man Utd21311Sunderland20312Ipswich2-2313Liverpool20214AFC Bournemouth2-1115Nottm Forest2-1116Fulham2-2017Coventry2-4018Crystal Palace2-5019Aston Villa2-5020Tottenham Hotspur2-50Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueTen things to look out for this weekendIpswich TownLiverpoolNewcastle UnitedBournemouthBrentfordSunderlandfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Naomi Osaka grinds it out to see off Siniakova’s stubborn US Open challenge | US Open Tennis 2026 | The Guardian
description: Naomi Osaka recovered from a mid-match slump to beat Katerina Siniakova 6-2, 5-7, 6-1 and reach the third round of the US Open
Author: Tumaini Carayol
Headline: Naomi Osaka recovered from a mid-match slump to beat Katerina Siniakova 6-2, 5-7, 6-1 and reach the third round of the US Open
Content: Naomi Osaka had some nervous moments on the way to victory.Photograph: Robert Deutsch/IMAGN IMAGES/ReutersView image in fullscreenNaomi Osaka had some nervous moments on the way to victory.Photograph: Robert Deutsch/IMAGN IMAGES/ReutersUS Open Tennis 2026Naomi Osaka grinds it out to see off Siniakova’s stubborn US Open challengeFormer champion into third round with 6-2, 5-7, 6-1 win‘I hope to continue making good memories here’Tumaini Carayolat Flushing MeadowsThu 3 Sep 2026 17.06 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 19.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor a second consecutive match at the US Open,Naomi Osakaappeared to be cruising. Everything was in hand as the two-time champion established a set and a break lead in her round two match against Katerina Siniakova, an uneventful return to the third round beckoning.Instead of carrying that great momentum forward until the end, though, Osaka was overcome by tension in the final stages of the second set and she soon found herself in a decider. It took a significant amount of resilience and restraint for her to reset and find a way through to the third round with a comprehensive final set to win 6-2, 5-7, 6-1.US Open 2026: Auger-Aliassime out; Keys, Osaka and Swiatek through; Sweeny and Popyrin in action – liveRead moreBefore the North American hard-court swing, a period that yielded US Open titles in 2018 and 2020, Osaka finally looked like a grand slam contender again. After years of struggling through the clay- and grass-court seasons, seemingly just waiting for the hard courts to return, this year Osaka produced career-best showings on those surfaces to the fourth round at the French Open and quarter-finals at Wimbledon.Her level on grass at Wimbledon, a surface she has toiled on for much of her career, was particularly impressive as she defeated the world No 1, Aryna Sabalenka, in round four. Osaka ran out of steam in the quarter-finals, fatigue seeping in after she reached the Bad Homburg final a week earlier, but it was some of the best tennis she had played since winning her last grand slam title at the Australian Open in 2021. She headed back to North America full of confidence.Elevated expectations can naturally lead to greater pressure and Osaka’s first two wins in New York this year are perhaps a reflection of the additional weight on her shoulders. In her 7-6 (6), 7-6 (3) first-roundwin over Anastasia Zakharova, a nervous Osaka squandered a break in both sets before barely dragging herself over the line in two tie-breaks. This time her nerves cost her a set. The most important thing about the early stages of the grand slam tournaments for the top players, though, is simply finding a way to win and offering themselves an opportunity to unleash their top form in later rounds.“I’m quite fortunate to have a lot of high-quality matches that went in my favour,” said Osaka. “Especially whenever I think of going into the third set and I need to regroup, I literally only specifically think of the [2019] Australian Open Final [a three-set win against Petra Kvitova]. Then it’s just like you can just pull from your memory bank for every certain situation that you need to get finished.“I think that’s the best thing about being a more experienced player. You’ve been able to play so many different matches in different situations. Here, obviously, I’ve had a lot of good memories, and I hope to continue making them.”It is increasingly difficult to speak only of tennis when discussing Osaka. At the same time that her overall form has improved, every grand slam appearance this year has featured dramatic walk-on outfits and match kit reveals that have generated their own headlines. Her outfits at the US Open this year are a homage to Allen Iverson, the former basketball player. Her elaborate outfit choices, and the discussion around them, have often been the source of conversation and also ample scorn.For such a reserved and inoffensive person, Osaka’s mere existence seems to enrage some of her detractors. Some describe her as an attention seeker who should focus only on her tennis. Her mental health difficulties in 2021, when she struggled with public scrutiny, are often referenced as hypocritical considering the way her choice of attire even though she is at a completely different stage in her life half a decade on. So much of the criticism she receives is in bad faith, driven by people who will never forgive her anti-racist activism during the early 2020s.View image in fullscreenIga Swiatek enjoyed a comfortable win against Nadia Podoroska.Photograph: Robert Prange/Getty ImagesAlthough Osaka has matured, growing in confidence and stature, she is introverted at heart. She believes fashion allows her a far easier avenue for her to express herself. Most of all, she is an entertainer who runs around a court and hits tennis balls for the pleasure of her audience. This is not a matter of life and death. Wearing elaborate dresses while playing tennis is no outrage.Osaka has been handed one of the toughest draws of the many title contenders, with the second seed, Elena Rybakina a potential fourth-round opponent. The first objective, though, is simply making it there.Meanwhile, Iga Swiatek, the eighth seed and 2022 champion, continued to build momentum in New York as she reached the second round with a 6-3, 6-2 win over Nadia Podoroska. British qualifier Harriet Dart was comprehensively defeated 6-2, 6-2 by the 25th seed, Marie Bouzkova. In the men’s draw, Félix Auger-Aliassime, the third seed and a semi-finalist last year, struggled with dizziness and illness as he was defeated 6-7 (5), 6-3, 6-2, 6-2 by Karen Khachanov.Explore more on these topicsUS Open Tennis 2026Naomi OsakaUS Open tennisTennisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Women’s Super League 2026-27 preview No 14: West Ham | West Ham United Women | The Guardian
description: Rita Guarino has been backed in the transfer market after turning around the club’s fortunes last season but concerns remain over a lack of resources
Author: Suzanne Wrack
Headline: Rita Guarino has been backed in the transfer market after turning around the club’s fortunes last season but concerns remain over a lack of resources
Content: West Ham’s Katie Zelem enters the pitch surrounded by bubbles before the WSL match against Manchester City. Photograph: Naomi Baker/WSL/Getty ImagesRita Guarino has been backed in the transfer market after turning around the club’s fortunes last season but concerns remain over a lack of resourcesBySuzanne WrackThu 3 Sep 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 19.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGuardian writers’ predicted position:11th (NB: this is not necessarily Suzanne Wrack’s prediction but the average of our writers’ tips)Last season’s position:10thProspectsWest Ham were in big trouble last December, with half the season gone and one win in 11 games. Rehanne Skinner was dismissed and the former Italy forward Rita Guarino came in to steady the ship. There were questions over how much any manager would be able to do without the club giving a bit more support to the women’s setup, but Skinner, fairly or not, had lost the dressing room and heads were down. The impact of Guarino wasn’t instant, a 5-0 defeat by Chelsea was a cruel introduction. It took a little time to rebuild the confidence of the team and get them playing the way she believed they could, but back-to-back wins against Newcastle in the FA Cup and Leicester in the Women’s Super League followed the Chelsea game, before a huge 3-2 win against Brighton and battling draws with Manchester United and London City Lionesses contributed to 14 points from their final 11 WSL games, taking their total to 19.As players started to depart in the summer, the situation looked bleak. Among the 14 departures were the forward Shekiera Martinez, who joined Tottenham, Katrina Gorry, who decided to take a break from football, and Shelina Zadorsky, who left at the end of her contract before signing for AFC Toronto. Then the signings started to arrive and suddenly the dark clouds were parting.The Hammers have had a hugely productive and impressive window with 10 signings, including the forwards Kelly Gago, recruited from Everton, and Ebony Salmon, who joined from Aston Villa, the defenders Estelle Cascarino, whose loan was made permanent, and Nadine Riesen and Laia Codina, who joined from Eintracht Frankfurt and Arsenal respectively, and the young English talents Sienna Wareing and Niamh Peacock who signed from Manchester United and Arsenal. Guarino has been backed in this window and West Ham have a real opportunity to make a statement in the WSL.Graphic showing how West Ham finished in the past five seasonsOff-field pictureWest Ham’s relative indifference towards their women’s team has been long known. There has been a steady decline since the departure of the enthusiastic Jack Sullivan as managing director of the women’s team in 2021 – the son of David Sullivan having been handed control of the side at 18. Little is known of how cash strapped the women’s setup is compared with other WSL sides. The club have not published detailed financial figures throughout their time in the WSL, with their most recent Companies House submission saying they are entitled to exemption from audit under section 479A of the Companies Act 2006. According to Football Association figures they were the WSL’s lowest spenders on agents’ fees in the year to February 2026, at £97,000, and one of only two clubs – Manchester United were the other – whose spend was down year on year.The managerGuarino was a relative unknown when she arrived in the WSL, having managed only in Italy. In the second half of the season West Ham didn’t quite experience a new manager bounce, but Guarino was able to guide them to another four wins and a 10th-place finish above Liverpool and Leicester. Guarino has impressed. Codina told the BBC of her transfer talks: “I remember having my first conversation with Rita. It was at the beginning of everything. I had my agent next to me and I was like: ‘Wow.’ The feeling that I got in this meeting is what I want in my future; it is what I want for my next steps.”Star signingGago scored 10 goals in 30 games for Everton but was frustrated there, handing in a written transfer request in January. The 27-year-old has praised West Ham, saying: “The family feel of the club really appealed to me and I’m excited to join that family. I’m going to give everything in order to help the team reach our ambitions and I’m really looking forward to getting started.”Stat attackWest Ham were the most direct team last season. They moved the ball upfield quicker than anyone and only Leicester averaged fewer passes per possession sequence. There is no right way to play; everyone needs a style. But after West Ham collected fewer points than in three of the preceding four campaigns, is it time for a change of approach?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGraphic showing West Ham were the most direct team in 2025-26Set for a breakthroughInès Belloumou played 18 times for West Ham last season after a long wait following her recruitment from Bayern Munich in July 2024. She was sent out on loan straight away, first to Lazio then to Malmö to build up the points to meet the governing body endorsement criteria for international player visas. This summer the 25-year-old, who was born in France and represented the country up to under-23 level before switching allegiance to Algeria, shone at the Women’s Africa Cup of Nations. Named in the team of the tournament, Belloumou started all six Algeria games as they finished third, with the full-back scoring the winning penalty in the shootout at the end of the third-place playoff. Full of confidence, she is ready to kick on in the WSL.View image in fullscreenFull-back Inès Belloumou crunches into a challenge with Arsenal’s Smilla Holmberg.Photograph: Pedro Porru/MB Media/Getty ImagesWhat they say“I want to put the club in the highest position in the table and go as far as we can in the cups. For me, the WSL is the best league in the world at the moment and anything can happen. Anything is possible. We need to have a lot of consistency, which is not easy, but it’s why we work hard every day” – Viviane Asseyi, after signing a new contractWhere are they playing their home games?If you spend too much time dwelling on this you’ll feel as if you’re in Waiting for Godot. The team have not played at the club’s main stadium since a 2-0 loss to Tottenham in front of close to 25,000 fans in September 2019. There has been talk since of it being a priority, including from Skinner, but every year another season ticks on without the team playing at the club’s main home. Instead, the team continue to call Dagenham and Redbridge’s Victoria Road stadium home.On Friday 4 September at 1pm Suzanne Wrack will be answering readers’ questions about the new WSL season for GuardianConversationsExplore more on these topicsWSL season previews 2026-27West Ham United WomenWomen's Super LeagueWomen's footballfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Fifa calls Uefa’s legal threat a ‘smear campaign’ in US federal filing | Fifa | The Guardian
description: Fifa has filed a motion opposing Uefa’s request for discovery for use in a potential criminal case against president Gianni Infantino
Author: Alexander Abnos
Headline: Fifa has filed a motion opposing Uefa’s request for discovery for use in a potential criminal case against president Gianni Infantino
Content: Fifa president Gianni Infantino and Uefa president Alexander Ceferin pictured in 2024.Photograph: Nick Potts/PAView image in fullscreenFifa president Gianni Infantino and Uefa president Alexander Ceferin pictured in 2024.Photograph: Nick Potts/PAFifaFifa calls Uefa’s legal threat a ‘smear campaign’ in US federal filingFifa filed motion opposing Uefa’s request for discoveryUefa said to be considering criminal case v Gianni InfantinoAlexander Abnosin New YorkThu 3 Sep 2026 15.41 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 17.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAttorneys representing Fifa have hit back atUefa’s request for discoveryin a US federal filing earlier this week. The lawyers called Uefa’s legal efforts “little more than press releases in further support of [a] smear campaign against Fifa and its leadership” and requested the judge assigned to the case dismiss the request.The filing requests thatFifaUS, a subsidiary business unit of Fifa, be permitted to officially opposite the request for discovery by 30 September.Thierry Henry says players ‘have more power than they think’ amid Fifa scandalsRead moreUefa filed four separate requests for subpoena in different US courts at the end of August, arguing in each that discovery was needed as itcontemplated initiating criminal proceedingsagainst Fifa president Gianni Infantino over the proposed Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) plan thatcaused uproar across football. The requests sought information, including documents and communications from Fifa as well as Joshua Kushner and the investment firm he oversees, Thrive Capital, which had been set to be the lead investor in Infantino’s plan. Uefa’s filing also requests information from other related parties, including JP Morgan.Fifa submitted a request to intervene in one of those four filings, which came in the state of Florida. A judge granted the request late last week.Filing on behalf of Fifa, attorney H Christopher Boehning argues that the request for discovery should be delayed or denied in part becauseUefadoes not have any active legal proceedings against Fifa in Switzerland. The filing also argues that discovery would in effect “use the legal process and public US filings to expose information that [Fifa] is obligated to keep confidential under [its] governing rules.”The document also retells the history of the FFE plan, and suggests that Uefa’s threatened boycott of Fifa competitions after the FFE proposal was economically motivated.“If soccer is strengthened in the developing world, global competition increases, which ultimately reduces Uefa’s market power and provides more competition for its flagship tournaments,” the document reads. “By raising funds to allow some of Fifa’s smaller member associations to better develop soccer, FFE would lead to more players from those nations choosing to represent their countries of origin and playing in their home leagues rather than playing abroad.”The filing quotes Cameroon federation president Samuel Eto’o to support this assertion, but refers to him only as “one of the greatest African players in history.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice weeklySign up toSoccer DeskJonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe filing also asserts that Uefa does not have the authority to initiate any criminal proceeding in Switzerland, as it is contractually bound by Fifa statutes to resolve any disputes with Fifa itself via arbitration.Explore more on these topicsFifaFootball politicsGianni InfantinoUefanewsShareReuse this content

title: Wong’s five wickets lead England to rampant victory over Ireland and ODI series win | England women's cricket team | The Guardian
description: Issy Wong’s career-best five for 33 set up England’s six-wicket win over Ireland that sealed the three-match ODI series with a game to spare
Author: Raf Nicholson
Headline: Issy Wong’s career-best five for 33 set up England’s six-wicket win over Ireland that sealed the three-match ODI series with a game to spare
Content: England's Issy Wong celebrates with teammate Alice Capsey after removing Gaby Lewis, one of her five wickets for 33 – career-best figures.Photograph: Mike Egerton/PAView image in fullscreenEngland's Issy Wong celebrates with teammate Alice Capsey after removing Gaby Lewis, one of her five wickets for 33 – career-best figures.Photograph: Mike Egerton/PAEngland women's cricket teamWong’s five wickets lead England to rampant victory over Ireland and ODI series winIssy Wong’s five for 33 sets up win with 27 overs to spareVictory seals series with a match still to playRaf Nicholsonat The OurCoop County Ground, DerbyThu 3 Sep 2026 13.38 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 15.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEngland sealed victory in their one-day international series against Ireland with a straightforward six-wicket win at Derby on Thursday, after seamer Issy Wong took a career-best five for 33.Wong, again handed the new ball in the absence of Lauren Bell, bowled with accuracy and control to knock over the leg stump of the Ireland captain, Gaby Lewis, then ran through the lower-middle order as they tried to hit out, but were dismissed for 165.England beat Ireland by six wickets: second women’s cricket one-day international – liveRead moreWong said: “Any time you get to represent England is a really proud feeling, and any time you do well in a cricket match is also a proud feeling, so to put the two together probably for the first time in my international career, if I’m being honest with myself, is really nice.”It was in marked contrast to her performance in the first ODI, when she sent down four consecutive wides in her opening spell and sparked hopes she may be recovering some of the mojo she lost when discarded by England three summers ago.Wong credited her performance to a recent decision to embrace wobble seam, as advised by the head coach, Charlotte Edwards. “It’s something I’ve bowled for six or seven years,” Wong said. “The switch in mindset is that it probably now sits as my stock ball. Previously I was trying to swing it out, try and find the edge, whereas I guess that little flip is actually trying to wobble it and keep really tight to the stumps.”Ireland’s Orla Prendergast described Wong’s wobble ball as “challenging”. “It’s hard to see and it’s hard to pick,” she said.The 20-year-old Amy Hunter anchored the Ireland effort with a battling half-century but eventually became Wong’s fifth victim, caught at deep midwicket on 64 in the final throes of the innings.In reply, Maia Bouchier ran out her opening partner, Sophia Dunkley, and then holed out to short fine leg five runs short of a half-century, while Alice Capsey was trapped lbw by Kia McCartney’s fizzing off-break. Jodi Grewcock struck a patient 24 but lost concentration and pulled Cara Murray straight into the hands of Lewis.Grewcock, though, was praised by Wong after holding on to two catches on the ring off her bowling. “It was like prime Kevin De Bruyne out there from Jodi,” Wong joked. “I said to her: ‘Thanks for the assist.’ And she said she was just threading through-balls for me and I was running on and tapping them in.”Freya Kemp and Dani Gibson then showed a glimpse of England’s ODI future by firing England to a rapid win. Far from holding back, they attacked: Gibson wrapped things up with two sixes over Murray’s head in the 23rd over to seal the win with more than half their overs to spare.In comparisonwith the first ODI, this was a much more convincing all-round performance by England, albeit in bowler-friendly conditions with an outfield made squelchy by overnight rain. The England captain, Charlie Dean, fell victim to the conditions, slipping over in her follow-through while trying to stop the ball and badly grazing her knee. Her absence from the field, though, only lasted for one over – just long enough to change out of the pair of trousers she had ripped at the knee.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEngland squandered their two DRS reviews after poor communication between Dean and Capsey, who also put down an edge off Louise Little – a move which will do nothing to decrease the scrutiny of her keeping role.But Dean’s bowling changes proved effective, with off-spinner Mady Villiers taking wickets in consecutive overs in her first spell, including the key scalp of Prendergast, who – for the second game in a row – misjudged the boundary size and was caught on the rope.Prendergast said: “We left runs out there, we probably could have rotated better through the middle and maybe taken the game on a little bit earlier.”Earlier, Dunkley celebrated her 50th ODI with the direct-hit run out of Alice Tector from mid-off, as Ireland’s innings began with a stutter. Dunkley’s stay at the crease, though, ended prematurely when she was run out by Prendergast from cover after a poor call from Bouchier. The series concludes at Worcester on Sunday.Explore more on these topicsEngland women's cricket teamIreland women's cricket teamWomen's cricketCricketmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Daniel Kretinsky to become biggest West Ham shareholder in blow to Amanda Staveley | West Ham United | The Guardian
description: Daniel Kretinsky is to become the biggest shareholder at West Ham in a blow to Amanda Staveley
Author: Jacob Steinberg
Headline: Daniel Kretinsky is to become the biggest shareholder at West Ham in a blow to Amanda Staveley
Content: Daniel Kretinsky has been a shareholder at West Ham since 2021.Photograph: David W Černý/ReutersView image in fullscreenDaniel Kretinsky has been a shareholder at West Ham since 2021.Photograph: David W Černý/ReutersWest Ham UnitedDaniel Kretinsky to become biggest West Ham shareholder in blow to Amanda StaveleyRoyal Mail owner made agreement with David SullivanStaveley was pushing to buy  stake in the clubJacob SteinbergThu 3 Sep 2026 18.39 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 18.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDaniel Kretinsky is set to become the biggest shareholder at West Ham after striking an agreement withDavid Sullivan, dealing a blow to Amanda Staveley’s hopes of buying a stake in the Championship club.Staveley was a guest at the London Stadium for West Ham’s 4-2 win over Wolves earlier this week and was pushing to buy Vanessa Gold’s 25.1% stake in the club. The British businesswoman, previously a director at Newcastle, had struck a deal with the Gold family in July and was fronting a consortium looking for a way on to the east London club’s board.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWest Ham fight off Wolves as Divine Mukasa double eases pressure on NunoRead moreHowever that arrangement sparked a process allowing West Ham’s other shareholders to exercise their pre-emption rights over the Gold family’s stake before a 5.30pm deadline on Thursday evening. It is believed that Kretinsky, a Czech billionaire and the owner of Royal Mail, and Sullivan have come to an agreement that will see the former increase his 27% stake to 46%. Sources have said there is unlikely to be a way back for Staveley’s group.Sources have consistently said that Kretinsky, who will surpass Sullivan as the biggest shareholder, is determined to increase his interest in West Ham as they look to rebuild after their relegation from the Premier League last season. His plans were complicated by Staveley entering the picture.However it is understood that Sullivan rebuffed an inquiry from Staveley about buying his stake during the summer. The 77-year-old privately indicated a preference to deal with Kretinsky, who first bought a stake in West Ham in November 2021. The arrangement will see Sullivan increase his stake from 38.8% to 40%, making him the second largest shareholder. The American businessman Tripp Smith’s stake will go from 8% to 11% and the remaining shareholders will rise from 1.1% to 3%. Staveley would need shareholders not to take up their pre-emption rights to have a chance of making a separate offer for the Gold shares.Sullivan stepped down as a director and co-chair of West Ham in June, before a joint investigation by the Times and Panorama reporting on seven women abusing his power and preying on them for sex in claims that date back to the 1980s and 90s. The 77-year-old categorically denies the allegations. Sullivan has been present at West Ham’s home games this season but does not have a seat on the board and is no longer the most powerful person at the club.Explore more on these topicsWest Ham UnitedDavid SullivannewsShareReuse this content

title: Thierry Henry says players ‘have more power than they think’ amid Fifa scandals | Thierry Henry | The Guardian
description: The former Arsenal, Barcelona and France star says players shouldn’t underestimate their ability to change how football works
Author: Jeff Rueter
Headline: The former Arsenal, Barcelona and France star says players shouldn’t underestimate their ability to change how football works
Content: Thierry Henry (left) and Kate Scott both have commented on Fifa’s recent scandals.Photograph: dpa Picture-Alliance Archive/AlamyView image in fullscreenThierry Henry (left) and Kate Scott both have commented on Fifa’s recent scandals.Photograph: dpa Picture-Alliance Archive/AlamyThierry HenryThierry Henry says players ‘have more power than they think’ amid Fifa scandalsThe former Arsenal, Barcelona and France star says players shouldn’t underestimate their ability to change how football worksJeff RueterThu 3 Sep 2026 15.10 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 15.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs Fifa continues to face scrutiny from some confederations and fans,Thierry Henryhas encouraged players to use their voice as the political battle for control of international soccer unfolds. The former Arsenal and Barcelona forward turned pundit spoke with the Guardian on Tuesday alongside Kate Scott and Jamie Carragher as CBS and Paramount prepare for this season’s Champions League broadcasts.“For me, the players have more power than they think they have,” Henry said when asked for his thoughts on the situation. “And if they want it to change, they can make it happen – especially nowadays.”Fifa has been under public duress in the wake of multiple scandals surrounding the 2026 World Cup, exacerbated further after reports of Gianni Infantino’s effort to sell the World Cup’s commercial rights. The ensuing month has seen the Fifa president face significant criticism, withUefa exploring potential legal optionsagainst Infantino.Scott, who anchors the CBS panel comprising Henry, Carragher and Micah Richards, spoke extensively about 2021’s attempted Super League project and the ensuing debacle in an Apple TV documentary. The Super League saga seemed to pit the business interests of the sport’s business class against the game’s heart, represented by players, coaches and fans. The latest situation involvingFifahas progressed in a similar spirit.“I think it’s going to be really interesting to see [what comes next],” Scott said. “I think probably a large portion of world football has come to a point where they would like to see a change in [the Fifa presidency], similarly to the way we felt about [the Super League] … I think if you’re invested in the game and you love the game, it just kind of leaves a bad taste.”Infantino has been re-elected twice since 2016, both times without a challenger. The next vote is slated for 18 March 2027, with no alternative having declared their candidacy.“I have no idea which way that will go, because obviously one thing that Gianni Infantino has proven to be within world football is a very smart power broker and has understood how to make allies, use those allies to his benefit,” Scott said.For Henry, though, the voice of the players can – and should – be a bigger part of the conversation.“Players have all the power if they want to, and sometimes they don’t, I think, use it or realize actually the power that they have,” Henry said. “You guys in the US know fully well: when the player wants to do something, the league listens. You saw it with the NBA. You saw it with the NFL … At one point, the players are always on the side: go entertain, take your money, leave.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice weeklySign up toSoccer DeskJonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Us debating about it here, what’s going to change? We can all have a view whether it’s a good one or a bad one … But for me, the players have more power than they think they have. And if they want it to change, they can make it happen – especially nowadays.”This is an extract from Soccer Desk, a newsletter from the Guardian US.Subscribe for free here.Explore more on these topicsThierry HenryFifaFootball politicsUS sportsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Nick Kyrgios enters treatment program after accepting one-month ban for cocaine use | Nick Kyrgios | The Guardian
description: Fallen Australian tennis star Nick Kyrgios has entered a treatment program after accepting a one-month ban for testing positive to cocaine
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Fallen Australian tennis star Nick Kyrgios has entered a treatment program after accepting a one-month ban for testing positive to cocaine
Content: Nick Kyrgios is free to play tennis again after his ban for cocaine use was reduced by the International Tennis Integrity Agency.Photograph: Amr Alfiky/ReutersView image in fullscreenNick Kyrgios is free to play tennis again after his ban for cocaine use was reduced by the International Tennis Integrity Agency.Photograph: Amr Alfiky/ReutersNick KyrgiosNick Kyrgios enters treatment program after accepting one-month ban for cocaine useAustralian free to play again after having suspension reducedITIA accepts Kyrgios’s use of cocaine was outside of competitionAustralian Associated PressThu 3 Sep 2026 19.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFallen Australian tennis starNick Kyrgioshas entered a treatment program after accepting a one-month ban for testing positive to cocaine.After admitting his “huge mistake” wheninitially suspended for failing a drugs teston June 22 at an ATP 250 tournament in Spain, Kyrgios is allowed to compete again from Friday.Kyrgios, who had been provisionally suspended since 4 August, had faced a ban ranging from a baseline three-month period to up to four years.Stefanos Tsitsipas says Nick Kyrgios’s cocaine ban was ‘pretty much expected’Read moreDuring an interview with InternationalTennisIntegrity Agency (ITIA) investigators, Kyrgios explained his use of cocaine had occurred socially during a night out, days before he was due to play in Mallorca.The ITIA consulted an independent scientific expert at a World Anti-Doping Agency (Wada)-accredited laboratory, who stated the explanation was consistent with the level of cocaine found in his sample.As a result, the ITIA accepted Kyrgios’s use of cocaine was outside of competition.Under Wada rules, the default suspension for a breach of this type is three months, which can be further reduced to one month if the individual commits to a treatment program approved by the ITIA.The 2022 Wimbledon finalist also forfeited the 6570 euros he won in Mallorca for losing in the first round to countryman Adam Walton.But his suspension was reduced for agreeing to enter a treatment program.The International Tennis Integrity Agency (ITIA) said Kyrgios, whose career world ranking peaked at No 13, could appeal against the provisional suspension but he opted against doing so.“I recently failed a drug test in Mallorca after testing positive for cocaine,” Kyrgios posted on Instagram last month. “I made a huge mistake and I take full responsibility for it.“I’m sorry to my fans, my family, my sponsors and everyone close to me. Above all, I’m sorry to the kids who follow me. I know the example this sets and I’m deeply disappointed in myself.”Kyrgios, who played only four official singles matches on the elite ATP Tour this year, has battled knee and wrist injuries in recent years and has all but conceded he is finished as a singles force.The ITIA said Kyrgios was suspended for a ‌positive test for benzoylecgonine, a cocaine metabolite, with a World Anti-Doping Agency laboratory confirming the positive result on 17 July.The 31-year-old was banned from playing, coaching or attending any tournaments sanctioned by the men’s and women’s tennis tours worldwide and national-level events in Australia.Kyrgios last played in the men’s doubles at Wimbledon in London on July 2, when he and partner Alexander Bublik lost in the first round.Explore more on these topicsNick KyrgiosTennisAustralia sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Lewis Hamilton ready to rock Monza with ‘phenomenal’ Italian GP win for Ferrari | Lewis Hamilton | The Guardian
description: Lewis Hamilton said a win for Ferrari at the team’s home race in the Italian Grand Prix would be ‘phenomenal’
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: Lewis Hamilton said a win for Ferrari at the team’s home race in the Italian Grand Prix would be ‘phenomenal’
Content: Lewis Hamilton in the paddock at Monza with his Ferrari F40.Photograph: Kym Illman/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLewis Hamilton in the paddock at Monza with his Ferrari F40.Photograph: Kym Illman/Getty ImagesLewis HamiltonLewis Hamilton ready to rock Monza with ‘phenomenal’ Italian GP win for FerrariScuderia bring upgraded engine to their home raceWinning at Monza would be ‘new territory’Giles Richardsin MonzaThu 3 Sep 2026 13.05 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 16.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLewis Hamilton believes that a win for Ferrari at the team’s home race in the Italian Grand Prix would be a phenomenal moment in an already storied career for the seven-time champion.The British driver, who would make history if he takes the flag at Monza, endured a torrid time with the Scuderia last season but goes into the race this weekend with a win under his belt and a very competitive car that may prove to be even quicker on the high-speed blast around the famous track.Lando Norris launches LN4 Fusion team to develop young drivers in F1 and motorsportRead moreFerrari are bringing their second engine upgrade this weekend in expectation of narrowing the gap to title leaders Mercedes. Hamilton trails the championship leader, Kimi Antonelli, by 59 points, alongside Mercedes’ George Russell.If Hamilton wins the Italian GP he will pass Michael Schumacher’s record of five wins at Monza, all of which the German scored with Ferrari. The team are honouring him this weekend with a special livery to mark 30 years since Schumacher joined.Hamilton was more than aware of quite what a Ferrari home win in front of thetifosiwould mean. “I’ve really thought coming into this weekend, I pondered just thinking of the sheer magnitude of the concept that I’m coming to this grand prix,” he said.“Firstly, I didn’t know that I was equal with Michael for wins at Monza and then there’s the thought of a first ahead of me in the sense of potentially winning at Monza for Ferrari and going into new territory. That would be phenomenal.“If I did do that, I will be the only black driver to have ever done that for Ferrari in Italy, and possibly in history, too. So, a lot of those thoughts have been going through my mind.”Hamilton, always aware of the import of history and in making an impact, did so in no little style when he arrived at the track on Thursday. The 41-year-old pulled up at the paddock in his new Ferrari F40, suited and booted to make a photocall to echo the one he made on his first appearance for Ferrari at Maranello in January last year, where he also posed in front of one of Ferrari’s F40s.He has long coveted an F40 and finally succumbed to purchase what he called the car of his dreams earlier this year, which it transpired was a very special one he felt had been destined for him.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |FortnightlySign up toThe HotspotA new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisisEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I wanted to find the most authentic one and managed to come across this one that the owner had bought, drove it from Maranello to his home, 69km away, and then parked it and never started it again,” he said. “The passenger door had never been opened, it just had this cover on it and all this dust.“When they were taking the car apart to check it they took the engine out, they found out the engine’s number 44. It’s got stamped on the engine number 44 [Hamilton’s car number]. I couldn’t believe it. So, it feels very much like fate.“I thought it was a real opportunity to kind of highlight the history of Ferrari in their home country, at their race and when am I ever going to get to do that again?”Explore more on these topicsLewis HamiltonFormula One 2026Formula OneMotor sportFerrarinewsShareReuse this content

title: Iran targets US bases as Israel warns sanctions could drive Tehran to ‘desperate steps’ | US-Israel war on Iran | The Guardian
description: Air bases used by US in UAE and Kuwait hit as Israeli defence chief says Iran’s regime fears collapse due to economic pressures
Author: Peter Beaumont
Headline: Air bases used by US in UAE and Kuwait hit as Israeli defence chief says Iran’s regime fears collapse due to economic pressures
Content: A woman crosses the road in front of an anti-US billboard in Tehran. The Iranian army said it targeted bases used by the US in the UAE and Kuwait on Thursday.Photograph: Atta Kenare/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA woman crosses the road in front of an anti-US billboard in Tehran. The Iranian army said it targeted bases used by the US in the UAE and Kuwait on Thursday.Photograph: Atta Kenare/AFP/Getty ImagesUS-Israel war on IranIran targets US bases as Israel warns sanctions could drive Tehran to ‘desperate steps’Air bases used by US in UAE and Kuwait hit as Israeli defence chief says Iran’s regime fears collapse due to economic pressuresPeter BeaumontSenior international correspondentThu 3 Sep 2026 10.16 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 15.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIran has continued to demonstrate an ability to target bases in the Gulf used by the US despite six months of war and a new sanctions regime described by the Trump administration as an “economic D-day”.As Iran’s military targeted US bases in theUnited Arab Emiratesand Kuwait, despite threats of further strikes by the US president, Israel’s defence chief warned that economic pressures from the sanctions could lead Tehran to escalate to more “extreme measures”.“This morning, the army hit the satellite communication systems, equipment depots and fighter aircraft hangars of the terrorist US army at the Ahmad al-Jaber air base inKuwaitwith missiles and drones,” the Iranian military said on Thursday in a statement carried by state television.The “location of forces and radar systems of the child-killing US army at the Al Minhad air base in the UAE were also attacked by missiles and drones of the army”, it added.In a post on X, Kuwait’s ministry of defence said its air defences had intercepted missile and drone attacks during a “blatant Iranian aggression”.The Kuwaiti statement came after the US allies Bahrain and Jordan said their air defence systems intercepted several Iranian air attacks on Wednesday.Fighting between the US and Iran has increased this weekafter the US hit Iranian rocket launchers on an island in the strait of Hormuz on Sunday, claiming that Iran was planning to use them to shoot mines into the waterway.View image in fullscreenDamage to a residential building after an Iranian drone attack, according to Kuwaiti authorities, in Kuwait City on Thursday.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesThe latest flare-up in the conflict comes amid little evidence that the Trump administration is succeeding in advancing its nebulous war aims either on the battlefield or via mediation, despite the US president’s repeated claims to have opened the strait of Hormuz to oil traffic.Instead, traffic through the key maritime passageway remains far below prewar levels, with oil prices remaining stubbornly elevated ahead of US midterm elections. Oil prices jumped again on Thursday after the Iranian strikes.Among the weapons Iran has used this week is its Kheibar Shekan medium-range ballistic missile system. The cheap and accurate missile can be launched within minutes and has become a staple of Iranian strikes.The rocket’s solid fuel motor means it does not require lengthy fuelling. It can be deployed very quickly to avoid detection and can be armed with a powered and steerable final stage to help beat anti-missile systems.Despite claims by the Trump administration that Tehran is running out of rockets, Iran continues to fire missiles that are considerably cheaper to produce than the US interceptors used to shoot them down.Iran has claimed as recently as the end of August that it maintained both missiles stockpiles and the ability to manufacture them.“Initially, some believed that Iran had only a limited number of missiles and that its stockpiles would eventually be depleted as the war continued,” the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps spokesperson Brig Gen Hossein Mohebbi said.“However, that assumption proved incorrect, as Iran’s missile capability has remained sustained and its missile production has continued.” Mohebbi’s characterisation of Iranian missile stockpiles could not be verified.The continued strikes came as Israel’s defence minister,IsraelKatz, said that while the new US economic sanctions appeared to be effective, the increased pressure could lead Tehran into extreme measures.“We see signs indicating that the heavy economic pressure they are under, and the fear of an uprising and the collapse of the regime, may push them to desperate steps,” Katz said at a ceremony for defence ministry employees.The hawkish minister reiterated the threats against the Islamic Republic that he has made in recent months.“An Iranian attack on Israel will free Israel from any existing constraint,” he said. “We will strike all of Iran’s national military and civilian infrastructure – including energy infrastructure – and push Iran deep back into the stone age.”Explore more on these topicsUS-Israel war on IranIranStrait of HormuzUS foreign policyMiddle East and north AfricaDonald TrumpIsraelnewsShareReuse this content

title: Federal judge blocks Trump’s latest attempt to restrict birthright citizenship | US immigration | The Guardian
description: Supreme court ruled in June against president’s earlier order to change citizenship rules for babies born in US
Author: Maanvi Singh
Headline: Supreme court ruled in June against president’s earlier order to change citizenship rules for babies born in US
Content: A woman holds a flag and her citizenship packet during a naturalization ceremony at the New York public library in July 2018 in New York City.Photograph: Drew Angerer/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA woman holds a flag and her citizenship packet during a naturalization ceremony at the New York public library in July 2018 in New York City.Photograph: Drew Angerer/Getty ImagesUS immigrationFederal judge blocks Trump’s latest attempt to restrict birthright citizenshipSupreme court ruled in June against president’s earlier order to change citizenship rules for babies born in USMaanvi SinghThu 3 Sep 2026 17.50 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 21.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA federal judge has temporarily blockedDonald Trump’s latest attempt to restrictbirthright citizenship– thelongstanding principlethat all babies born in the US are guaranteed American citizenship.The decision came nearly a month after the presidenttried for a second timeto limit via executive order which people born in the US can become American citizens. The supreme courtruled in late Junethat Trump’s previous sweeping order denying birthright citizenship to the children of undocumented immigrants or temporary visitors wasunconstitutional.US could ask parents to prove citizenship or immigration status to obtain passports for childrenRead moreTrump’s latest order, issued on 6 August, denied automatic citizenship not only to the children of ambassadors or “foreign ministers” but to the children of other foreign citizens. Including employees at a foreign embassy and employees of international organizations including the United Nations and the World Bank. The new order also denied birthright citizenship to children of parents the government deemed “alien enemies” and parents who “engage[d] in a commercial transaction to ensure that the person’s mother is present in the United States, or a territory of the United States, to give birth”.The federal government has yet to issue guidelines on how these restrictions would work in practice. For instance, how the government would discern between a parent that buys plane tickets to visit on vacation and one who is engaging in what the administration called “birth tourism” – visiting the country for the sole purpose of giving birth in the US.Judge Deborah Boardman ruled on Wednesday that the supreme court had already settled some of the questions raised by Trump’s new order, writing: “No presidential executive order can undo what the Supreme Court has done.”In a 35-page opinion, she also wrote that the new executive order could have the effect of rescinding citizenship from children who were already protected by the supreme court decision, if – for instance – the administration arbitrarily moved to designate parents as “alien enemies”. The government has already used the sweeping label of “alien enemy” todesignate dozens of Venezuelan nationalswith no criminal records as terrorists, justifying their deportation to aSalvadoran megaprisonlast year.“The Supreme Court has spoken: Children in the certified class are ‘citizens at birth’,” she wrote. The court’s decision, she said, “is the law of the land. The President must follow it.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTrump signs new orders targeting birthright citizenshipRead moreThe plaintiffs in this latest challenge include Casa and the Asylum Seeker Advocacy Project (Asap), two non-profits that provide immigrant services, as well as individuals who could be affected by the new executive order. The new orders are worryingly vague, said Conchita Cruz, co-founder of Asap – which was also part of the lawsuit challenging the president’s original birthright restrictions last year.“Immigrant families should not have to rush back into court on an issue that has already been resolved by the supreme court,” she said.The pregnant women who partook in that first suit, who gave birth as the supreme court wasdeciding the fatesof their newborns, have once again been plunged into uncertainty, she said.One of the original plaintiffs, a Venezuelan asylum seeker, had told the Guardian she felt relief after the country’s highest court ruled that her baby boy was unambiguously a US citizen.“But I know this isn’t over,” she said in a statement after the ruling on Thursday. “The threat to birthright citizenship is still out there. I’ll keep fighting for permanent protection for my child, and for every child born in this country.”Explore more on these topicsUS immigrationDonald TrumpTrump administrationLaw (US)US politicsUS supreme courtnewsShareReuse this content

title: We’re prepared to change the law to reform water industry, says Angela Eagle | Thames Water | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: New environment secretary insists ‘nothing is off the table’ in dealing with ailing Thames Water
Author: Kiran Stacey
Headline: Exclusive: New environment secretary insists ‘nothing is off the table’ in dealing with ailing Thames Water
Content: The future of Thames Water has been hanging in the balance for months as it struggles under a £20bn debt pile.Photograph: Maureen McLean/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe future of Thames Water has been hanging in the balance for months as it struggles under a £20bn debt pile.Photograph: Maureen McLean/ShutterstockThames WaterWe’re prepared to change the law to reform water industry, says Angela EagleExclusive: New environment secretary insists ‘nothing is off the table’ in dealing with ailing Thames WaterKiran StaceyandSandra LavilleThu 3 Sep 2026 15.49 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 17.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBritain’s insolvency laws cannot deal with the aggressive behaviour shown by the companies that controlThames Water, the environment secretary has said, as she confirmed ministers were prepared to take it into public ownership.Angela Eagle told the Guardian she was determined to reform the water industry after being told by Andy Burnham to make it her top priority.But she warned that could mean a change in law to factor in the way in which the US hedge funds that own much of Thames Water have kept it running while seeking a deal to renegotiate its debts.The battle over Thames looks set to become the first test of the prime minister’s determination to bring Britain’s utilities into public control even in the face of concerted corporate lobbying and the threat of legal action.In her first big interview since becoming environment secretary, Eagle said putting Thames Water into special administration – a likely first step to deprivatisation – could prove more complicated than some activists think.“A lot of people think you can just choose [special administration] … [but] you either are, or you aren’t, insolvent. And whatever people think of Thames at the moment, it isn’t technically insolvent,” she said.“The Water Act didn’t really envisage this kind of behaviour and this kind of corporate presence behaving in particular ways.“But we have a water bill coming along, and nothing is off the table. We’ve got a legislative vehicle coming along soon to enable us to do what we decide to do.”Burnham has repeatedly promised to take public utilities into public control, focusing especially on energy and water. He told the Guardian before becoming MP for Makerfield thathe intendedto nationalise Thames.The prime minister’s focus on utilities puts Eagle at the centre of much of what he is trying to do in government, including reforming the water industry andcleaning up illegal dumping sites.She is taking part in weekly meetings of the National Drought Group, which is coordinating the response to the country’s fifth drought in three years.Speaking from Havant Thicket in Hampshire, which is due to be the country’s first new reservoir since 1992, she said the country had become less resilient under previous governments and she would speed up the pace of new infrastructure.“The system has got more clogged up,” she said, comparing the situation with the one she faced as a minister in the governments of Tony Blair and Gordon Brown.“Trying to get anything done from start to finish is now much slower, much more difficult. It seems to somehow be that people always give you loads of reasons why you can’t do anything, rather than [saying] strategically, we need nine reservoirs or this reservoir, or whatever the infrastructure is.”One of her first tasks will be to decide what to do about Thames Water, which is struggling under a £20bn debt pile and has been given a record £122.7m fine for sewage spills and unlawful shareholder payouts.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIts owners, which include some of the world’s biggest hedge funds – among them Elliott Management and Apollo Global Management – are seeking a £10bn deal to renegotiate its debt and stave off nationalisation.Eagle’s predecessor, Emma Reynolds,objected to the deal, warning it would not give taxpayers value for money but the investors are still seeking regulatory approval.One option is to put the company into special administration, which can be triggered if a company is either insolvent or failing in its legal duties to provide water and sewerage services.Those calling for such a move argue there are clear signs the company is failing in this way. But the Guardianrevealed last monththat senior government officials believe a change in the law may be needed.Ewan McGaughey, professor of law at King’s College London, said: “The government doesn’t need to wait for the creditors of Thames Water to admit they are insolvent, while they charge ever more to billpayers.“The law says ministers can take away Thames Water’s licence for breaching their principal duties, namely to put all sewage through secondary treatment before release, and keep taps and hosepipes running.”Thames’s creditors have been contacted for comment.Explore more on these topicsThames WaterWater industryUtilitiesNationalisationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Volkswagen announces it will cut 100,000 jobs by 2030 | Volkswagen (VW) | The Guardian
description: Under-pressure carmaker will shed 15% of workforce and halve its product line in sector’s biggest ever restructure
Author: Patrick Daly
Headline: Under-pressure carmaker will shed 15% of workforce and halve its product line in sector’s biggest ever restructure
Content: Protesters against proposed VW job cuts outside the company’s Zwickau factory in Saxony in July. The plant is one of four at risk of closure.Photograph: Jens Schluter/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenProtesters against proposed VW job cuts outside the company’s Zwickau factory in Saxony in July. The plant is one of four at risk of closure.Photograph: Jens Schluter/AFP/Getty ImagesVolkswagen (VW)Volkswagen announces it will cut 100,000 jobs by 2030Under-pressure carmaker will shed 15% of workforce and halve its product line in sector’s biggest ever restructurePatrick DalyThu 3 Sep 2026 18.30 EDTFirst published on Thu 3 Sep 2026 18.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe car company Volkswagen has announced it will shed 100,000 jobs by the end of the decade after being hit by US tariffs and fierce competition from Chinese rivals.The German manufacturer said management and unions had agreed as part of a sweeping cost-cutting plan to cut a further 50,000 positions by 2030, bringing total job losses in the pipeline to 100,000.The number of car models the Volkswagen group produces, which includes the Bentley and Audi brands, will be slashed by half, while four production plants inGermanycould also be shuttered within the next eight years.“It is essential to systematically align workforce levels with economic realities,” Volkswagen group said in a statement.The company said it had approved a plan that involved “the reduction of about 50,000 jobs”, on top of another 50,000 already agreed.Volkswagen’s chief executive, Oliver Blume, was booed last month by staff during a tour of the company’s headquarters in Wolfsburg, northern Germany, as part of a company dialogue about the need to address its financial challenges.At the time, Blume’s restructuring plans, which were rumoured to envisage increasing the reduction in headcount from 50,000 to 100,000, were yet to be approved by the VW group’s powerful supervisory board, which represents the labour force and shareholders.But on Thursday, the company, Europe’s largest carmaker, said the board had signed-off on the proposals.“The supervisory board has unanimously approved the executive board’s future plan presented today,” Blume said. “This is a strong signal for the future of the Volkswagen group.”The total of 100,000 cuts will be the largest restructuring ever carried out in the global automotive industry, amounting to about 15% of the carmaker’s employees.Volkswagen employs more than 650,000 people across all its brands, which also includes Skoda, Seat, Porsche, Cupra and Lamborghini.On Thursday, Volkswagen also said that management and unions agreed that the future of four German plants – in Hanover, Emden, Zwickau and Neckarsulm – could not be guaranteed into the 2030s.VW has facedincreasing pressure from rampant Chinese competition in Europe, decreasing sales in China and hefty US tariffs. Even before that, it was struggling for years with falling profits and overproduction in Europe.The tough market in China has also hit other carmakers, with BMW cutting its profit guidance for this year because of the disruption caused by the Iran war and the company’s struggles in the Chinese market.Explore more on these topicsVolkswagen (VW)Automotive industryGermanyEuropeJob lossesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Rich people more likely to steal children’s sweets, finds Ig Nobel prize-winning study | Ig Nobel prizes | The Guardian
description: We round up the winners at awards for achievements that ‘first make people laugh and then make them think’
Author: Ian Sample
Headline: We round up the winners at awards for achievements that ‘first make people laugh and then make them think’
Content: Volunteers were left alone with a jar of sweets ostensibly meant for children; when researchers returned, upper-class people had snaffled far more.Photograph: Nitat Termmee/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenVolunteers were left alone with a jar of sweets ostensibly meant for children; when researchers returned, upper-class people had snaffled far more.Photograph: Nitat Termmee/Getty ImagesIg Nobel prizesRich people more likely to steal children’s sweets, finds Ig Nobel prize-winning studyWe round up this year’s winners at awards for achievements that ‘first make people laugh and then make them think’Ian SampleScience editorThu 3 Sep 2026 13.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 14.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s that time of year again: a select group of scientists have been summoned to a ceremony to receive coveted prizes, be showered in paper planes, and leave with a 10tn dollar bill, albeit in the form of a phased-out note from Zimbabwe. It is, of course, the annual Ig Nobel awards.Not to be confused with the more prestigious and career-changing Nobel prizes that will be announced in Scandinavia next month, the satiricalIg Nobelsare awarded for achievements that “first make people laugh and then make them think”.On Thursday, real Nobel laureates were on stage to hand out the awards and winners were giving “24/7” lectures: describing their work in 24 seconds and then in seven words. Here are the 2026 winners.1.Economics: evil rich peopleAre rich people really worse behaved than the rest of us? Through a series of experiments, psychologists amassed evidence that the upper classes are indeed more prone to behaving badly, from being oblivious to other road users, lying at work and taking treats meant for children. “I’ve followed the Ig Nobels since my early college days. I didn’t think I’d ever win one,” said Dr Paul Piff, a social psychologist at the University of California, Irvine.Piff and his colleagues found that upper-class drivers were more likely to cut other cars off at junctions and ignore pedestrians at crossings. Wealthier people also appeared more willing to lie at work. In one experiment, volunteers were left alone with a jar of sweets ostensibly meant for children. When the researchers returned, upper-class people had snaffled nearly twice as many candies as lower-class people.“The general pattern seems to be that with wealth and rising power, you become less engaged with the needs of others and less burdened by the needs of social relationships,” Piff said. “Taking candy from children might be the least of our worries but it’s emblematic of the tendency to prioritise one’s own needs over those of others.”2.Biomechanics: the definition of kissingResearchers at Oxford University ensured the UK could hold its head high after winning the biomechanics prize. “The whole team is thrilled,” said Dr Matilda Brindle. She and her colleagues investigated theevolution of kissingand needed a scientific definition of the act. They settled on “non-agonistic interactions involving directed, infraspecific oral-oral contact with some movement of the lips/mouthparts and no food transfer”.Brindle, who is writing a book on non-reproductive sexual behaviour, has also studied theevolution of masturbation, making her a strong contender to become theMarie Curieof Ig Nobels by winning more than once. “We’re so focused on penises, what they do and why they are important, but all these other sexual behaviours are important,” she said.3.Physics: The splashless urinalA team of students led by Kavee Thurairajah at the University of Waterloo inCanadaworked out that urinal splash is almost entirely eradicated if the stream strikes the urinal at less than 30 degrees. They went on to design a urinal whose shape ensures minimal splash regardless of the user’s aim. “I am very proud,” said Dr Zhao Pan, who runs the lab.View image in fullscreenResearchers at Canada’s University of Waterloo designed an optimal urinal (not pictured).Photograph: Mevans/Getty Images4.Peace: The power of mutual enemiesIt is natural to want friends that are kind to us, but our friends interact with others in the world in ways that can affect our lives. Dr Jaimie Krems at the University of California, Los Angeles, showed there’s plenty of room for attack dogs in our friendship groups, as long as they target those we dislike. “Sometimes we want our friends to be more vicious and indifferent when they interact with our enemies,” she said. “I’ve felt, in many instances, incredibly loved when people have carried my hate for me and been willing to have my back.”5.Biology: The science of stepping on snakesResearchers in Brazil donned safety boots to explore what made venomous snakes bite in defence by softly stepping on different parts of their bodies. Pressure on the head triggered most bites, they had found, but the study had beenretracted by theScientific Reportsjournalas the team did not have ethical approval to step on the creatures.6.Ig notable mentionsThe chemistry prize went to an international team that found cockroach milk contains three times as much energy as cows’ milk, while the olfaction prize went to scientists who discovered babies smell wonderful to their parents, but teenagers do not. Other researchers landed prizes for turning mosquito proboscises into 3D printing nozzles, clarifying the aerodynamics of nose blowing, andburying underpantsto monitor soil quality.Explore more on these topicsIg Nobel prizesScience prizesEconomicsBiologyPhysicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: There’s a quick way to slow climate change. Why isn’t everyone doing it? - video | Climate crisis | The Guardian
description: Methane is a potent greenhouse gas that traps more than 80 times as much heat than carbon dioxide over a 20-year period and causes 25% of global heating today. We definitely don’t want this gas spewing needlessly into the atmosphere, but in 2023 that’s exactly what environment editor Damian Carrington found was happening when he reported on 1,000 super-emitting methane leaks across the globe. Now Turkmenistan, the worst country for mega-leaks, has begun to plug them. Damian tells Madeleine Finlay why some experts call stopping leaks the climate ‘emergency brake’ and reveals which countries are still failing to act.

title: A sun goddess, hundreds of devotees – and polluted water: the Nigerian festival threatened by gold mining | Global development | The Guardian
description: Each year, people from across the world gather in a grove sacred to the Yoruba goddess Osun to be healed, conceive or realise their deepest wishes. But toxic lead, mercury and cyanide is leaching into the river
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Each year, people from across the world gather in a grove sacred to the Yoruba goddess Osun to be healed, conceive or realise their deepest wishes. But toxic lead, mercury and cyanide is leaching into the river
Content: Devotees gather by the Osun River with offerings including animals near a fetish of Osun, the Yoruba goddess of fertility, beauty and healing. All photographs by Pelumi SalakoEach year, people from across the world gather in a grove sacred to the Yoruba goddess Osun to be healed, conceive or realise their deepest wishes. But toxic lead, mercury and cyanide is leaching into the riverByPelumi SalakoSupported byAbout this contentThu 3 Sep 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 09.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google7Devotees in white clothing line the riverbank, praying as they carry offerings of fruit, kola nut and sacrificial animals in supplication to Osun, the Yoruba goddess of fertility, beauty and healing, whose carved form stands with arms outstretched a few metres away in the Osun River.It is the final day of Nigeria’s annualOsun Osogbo festivalin honour of the African deity, in a tradition that has existed for hundreds of years and draws people from across the diaspora.Except this year the water was once again a discoloured brown. Until 2018, the river ran clear, but then mining several miles upstream began to pollute it, introducing heavy metals and sediment into the watercourse.View image in fullscreenYeye Omifunto Ojo performs a sacrifice at the Osun RiverThe river, named after the goddess, runs through theOsun-Osogbo sacred grove, a 75-hectare (185-acre) Unesco world heritage site since 2005.
