The water is believed to possess healing powers and women who have trouble conceiving, or people in search of promotion or prosperity, often come to pray at the riverbank; the water is drunk or used for bathing, depending on the “directions” of the goddess.Yemi Elebuibon, a writer who is also the chiefIfá priestof Osogbo, is among those who have been campaigning against the mining and pollution.“What we are telling them [those running the mining operations] is for them to turn the mining in another direction so it can stop polluting Osun. Osun is naturally pure; it should not be polluted,” he says.View image in fullscreenDevotees carry offerings on their head at the Osun Osogbo festivalView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenDrummers at the festival; Sango fire dancers,who honour the Yoruba deity of thunder, lightning and fire through their performances; devotees at the shrine; and kola nut offerings at the festivalOsun is a gold-rich state inNigeria, where small-scale and artisanal miners often operate illegally due to lax enforcement. When they dig for gold along the 132-mile (213km) river, they let the runoff leach back into the water, polluting it.In 2021, Urban Alert, a social and environmental justice group, launched a#SaveOsunRiver campaignand commissioned independent testing of the water, drawing samples from six locations along the river. The tests confirmed there wereunsafe levels of lead, mercury and cyanide, which are especially dangerous to children and pregnant women.View image in fullscreenFashola Osungbemi Oladepo, who is anaworo,or Osun priest, in the shrine, surrounded by wooden fetishesThe authorities responded by arresting prospectors and closing some illegal mining sites, but campaigners say there has been no remediation plan, no independent verification, and no measurable improvement in water quality.Fashola Osungbemi Oladepo, an Osun priest, says he is concerned about the pollution of the river, which is central to their traditions and the festival.“We’ve been complaining to the government, but it has to do with the state’s economy,” he says.New mining sites have sprung up, including one less than four miles from the grove, Urban Alert says.“That gap between announcement and action is itself part of the story,” says Anthony Adejuwon, Urban Alert’s founder and team lead.Although the authorities publicised the fact thatwater was unsafe for drinkingbefore this year’s festival, many devotees continued to drink it.“We see it as an herbal concoction; it is not ordinary water to us. Any harmful substance in it has been removed by Osun,” says one devotee, Yeye Omifunto Ojo.Some worshippers and tourists arrived with kegs and bottles to take the river water home.View image in fullscreenWorshippers continue to drink and take home the water, despite the muddiness and pollution in the riverAdejuwon says the contamination puts devotees in an impossible position between honouring a centuries-old tradition and facing real health risks that threaten the continuity of a living heritage practice at a site the world has formally recognised as globally significant.The contamination also poses great risks to the wider environment and aquatic species. Sekinat Ojeniyi, an analyst at the business consultancyAfricaPractice, notes that heavy metals persist in river sediments, accumulate in fish and aquatic vegetation, and biomagnify – whereby pollutants accumulate up the food chain – meaning their ecological impacts can continue long after mining ceases.“This has implications not only for public health, but also for aquatic biodiversity, fisheries and the long-term economic resilience for communities that rely on the river ecosystem,” she says.View image in fullscreenA priestess uses a chicken to pray over a woman at the riverbankDevotees travel to the festival from across Nigeria and the diaspora, including Brazil, Cuba and the United States, regarding it as a pilgrimage. But the unsafe water represents a profound loss for practitioners, not only an environmental one.The ceremonies also attract tourists. Pippa Mistry-Norman, from London, had been planning her trip this year for six months because the idea of a goddess who grants wishes appealed to her.“A couple of my friends are Nigerian, and I sit opposite them every day. They have such a rich, deep and spiritual culture and I wanted to experience it first-hand, but you can’t do that from the office in London,” the 33-year-old says.View image in fullscreenTwo men restrain a devotee ‘possessed by a spirit’During last year’s festival, Osunfunmito Eyeyemi, 31, prayed to the goddess for a property and a car. This year, she returned to show her appreciation, having achieved everything she prayed for.Sacred ground: the ancient grove where Yoruba traditions are rebornRead more“Here I am to give my own testimony because I am now a landlady and I drive my own car,” she says. “There is nothing you ask [Osun] that she will not do for you.”Experts say the government must show political will to tackle the contamination of the Osun by tightening its enforcement measures.“They must not wait until it is too late, when the impact starts to reflect on people’s health. The authorities must independently characterise and map the full extent of the contamination along the river, which would give way for a comprehensive, time-bound and well-funded remediation plan. The remediation cannot happen if mining does not stop,” Adejuwon says.View image in fullscreenThe fetish of Osun in the river“A gold deposit can be mined over decades; a living cultural landscape that has evolved over more than 700 years cannot simply be restored once its ecological and spiritual integrity has been compromised,” adds Ojeniyi.Explore more on these topicsNigeriaAfricaReligionRiversPollutionMiningfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: From ‘psyops’ to ‘hysterical hysteria’: how GB News and Talk TV lost their cool in the heatwaves | Climate science scepticism and denial | The Guardian
description: Thousands of heat-related deaths in record-breaking temperatures appeared to only intensify hosts’ climate denials
Author: Damian Carrington
Headline: Thousands of heat-related deaths in record-breaking temperatures appeared to only intensify hosts’ climate denials
Content: GB News presenter Bev Turner said sending children home from overheated schools was ‘priming them for climate lockdowns – that is all this is’.Photograph: GBNView image in fullscreenGB News presenter Bev Turner said sending children home from overheated schools was ‘priming them for climate lockdowns – that is all this is’.Photograph: GBNClimate science scepticism and denialAnalysisFrom ‘psyops’ to ‘hysterical hysteria’: how GB News and Talk TV lost their cool in the heatwavesDamian CarringtonEnvironment editorThousands of heat-related deaths in record-breaking temperatures appeared to only intensify hosts’ climate denialsThu 3 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 12.51 EDTShareAs the first heatwave of the record-breaking summer arrived on 23 May, GB News hostCristo Foufas was not happy: “I am sick to death of the naysayers saying firstly that we’re all going to die and that we have to put out heat alerts, because, you know, just drink some water and drink a bit less rosé in the sunshine.”“We used to call it Darwinism,” replied co-host Renée Hoenderkamp. She is a medical doctor.The arrival of the intense heatwave in late June – themost extreme recorded in Europe– didn’t change the tone. “People die each year from vending machines falling on them, and coconuts hitting their heads. People die, unfortunately, that’s a reality of life, and things get hot,”said Will Kingston, a presenter and contributor on GB News, a free-to-air television news channel. “It doesn’t mean you have to go about changing your life in ways big and small to accommodate for it.”Over on TalkTV, a British streaming news channel, there was also little empathy as the country sweltered in deadly heat. “I’m very sorry if someone dies because of the heat, but I don’t think that’s a reason for us never to be allowed to take a flight again, or stop being allowed to eat meat,”said the presenter Julia Hartley-Breweron 24 June, citing policies no one is putting in place. Her guest, the conservative commentator Benedict Spence, agreed: “One way or another, something’s going to get you.”As that heatwave reached its peak, the TalkTV host Kevin O’Sullivan wasgetting hot under the collarabout the “asinine snowflakery” of climate concern: “Our hysterical hysteria over climate change because we’ve had a few nice days … It’s a nice day. Now we call it … a death risk.”Then the numbers came in. The May and June heatwaves hadkilled about 2,700 people prematurelyin England and Wales, according to an analysis based on the relationship established between heat and mortality in previous data, published on 13 July.Cue a meltdownfrom O’Sullivan: “No such thing happened. They’ve sort of qualified it – and said 2,700 peoplemighthave died – and this has been apparently gamed by computer programmes and God knows what.” The report was “justdisgraceful climate change scaremongering” and “absolute poppycock”, he said.View image in fullscreenTalkTV’s Kevin O’Sullivan reacting to the premature, heat-related deaths of 2,700 people.Photograph: Talk TVOn GB News, the presenterKingston was also deeply unimpressed: “If there is one thing that Covid taught us, it is that modelling is effectively guesswork from clever-sounding people with an ideological agenda.”These hot takes did not age well. On 30 July, the UK Health Security Agency announced that2,877 people had diedbecause of the May and June heatwaves, using data on actual recorded deaths.Many heat-related deaths are among elderly people and those who are already unwell, factors that apparently made their premature demise less important for some contributors, such asRoss Clark, who had told TalkTVon 25 June that they were “perhaps on the point of dying anyway”.10:27‘Godzilla-level’ El Niño could cause hottest year on record - The LatestPresenters and guests on both channels frequently pointed to the higher level of deaths from cold in winter. None were asked why any reduction in winter deaths due to global heating would mean the rising number of heat deaths in summer was acceptable. And it’s not even true any more: the most recent figures from the Office of National Statistics show2,805 heat-related deaths in England and Walesin 2025 compared with 2,244 cold-related deaths.Instead, one TalkTV presenter,André Walker, decided that one manin particular had blood on his hands: “I believe by the end of his career, Ed Miliband will have killed 100,000 people because of his crazy green energy policies that freeze people in the winter and cook them in the summer.” He offered no evidence for this attack on every climate-denier’s bogeyman, the former energy secretary.You might think it would be hard to deny the basic reality of climate change as the temperatures soared outside. You’d be wrong.There was straightforward denial on GB News with, for example, the presenterNana Akua calling the climate crisis a “scam”as thehottest May ever recordedended; Hoenderkamp blaming the sun(an ancientclimate myth); and the fashion designer andregular contributor Jeff Bankssaying,wrongly, that: “The facts are that carbon dioxide in the atmosphere has been declining for the last 150 million years.” Over on TalkTV,Hartley-Brewer blithely told viewersin late June: “We’ve always had freak weather.” Not like this we haven’t, according tohundreds of scientific studies.View image in fullscreenTalkTV presenter Julia Hartley-Brewer, pictured with commentator Benedict Spence, claimed falsely that it was illegal to fit air conditioning in new-build houses.Photograph: Talk TVLet’s take a short break, for a fact check. The world’s climate scientists, in reports signed off by 192 national governments, have been clear for more than a decade that100% of global heating since 1950has been caused by human emissions and activities. Every heatwave is being mademore intense and more likelyas a result of fossil fuel burning, and rising global heatkills one person a minutearound the world, according to a major recent report in the Lancet.Back to the channels, where the heat the country was enduring, if not its cause, was undeniable. Cue the presenters turning their fire on the weather forecasts. “The weather maps, they used to go orange and red. They’ve now lowered the threshold so it’s bright red. It’s obviously … a psyops operation,”said the TalkTV host Ash Gould. Who was behind this conspiracy was not revealed.Another TalkTV host,Alex Armstrong, was also frothingabout maps: “They’ve literally coloured the country black – because it’s like a nuclear holocaust level. They’ve gone nuts, these climate fanatics.” He did not explain what maps he meant, and they were not shown to viewers of the programme.One issue that got the TV stations hot under the collar was air conditioning, which, ironically enough, was barely needed in the UK until the climate crisis drove up temperatures.Foufas said on GB News: “Here in the UK, remember we’ve all been told to rip out our air conditioning because it’s not conducive to net zero.” This blanket statement appears to be based on asingle planning dispute in Camden.“It’s actually still illegal in new-build homes to fit air con,” chimed inHartley-Brewer on TalkTV.It’s notillegal, for either new or existing homes.And the unrelenting attacks on net zero, a policy now at the heart of the right’s culture war, carried on. “The biggest psychosis of our age is climate alarmism and net zero,” the contributorPaul Cox told TalkTV. “Net zero being a product of the monetisation of climate alarmism.” The presenter Alex Phillips did not challenge him. Instead, she insulted Miliband as “a meme and a congested ukulele player”.A few more examples: net zero is a “deranged religion”, a “crazy ideology”, a “fallacy [that] doesn’t exist”, “lunacy” and “madness”, meaning “we all have to eat insects rather than beef and lamb”.View image in fullscreenGB News presenter Jacob Rees-Mogg claimed it would be cheaper to deal with the consequences of climate change than to try to prevent them. The government’s independent adviser’s have shown this to be wrong.Photograph: GBNJust to be clear, net zero is the principle, dictated by the laws of basic physics, that until we stop adding greenhouse gases to the atmosphere, it will continue to get ever hotter. But even if net zero was admitted as necessary, excuses for inaction abound on the channels.For example: theUK emits only 1% of global emissions, making action pointless. What about all theother countries that only emit a small percentage? Another favourite: the supposed cost of net zero, often backed byfiguresconjured up by analyses which ignore the costs of maintaining the status quo or climate damage. Net zero will have “smashed the economy to bits”, according toCox on TalkTV.“It’s going to be less expensive to deal with the consequences,” said the GB News presenterJacob Rees-Mogg. Despite being a former energy and net zero secretary, he is also wrong: a multitude of serious assessmentsover decadeshave shown reaching net zero is cheaper than not doing so, including work by thegovernment’s own official independent advisers.For those on GB News and TalkTV, the answer to high energy bills is drill, baby, drill! TalkTV’sJeremy Kyle quotes Donald Trump: “We have, in his words, liquid gold under the North Sea.” In fact, according to the UK Energy Research Centre, the idea that more North Sea oil and gas could cut energy bills for UK consumers or improve energy security is a “delusion”.Perhaps the conspiratorial mindset that sometimes leaks out on the channels can explain all this cognitive dissonance in the face of record heat, thousands of deaths and all the hard evidence? Commentators on the channels call net zero “a road to communism” and “socialist-style, communist-style control”. Apparently, it is easier for some to deny reality than accept that some big problems require a collective response.The GB News presenterBev Turner is particularly enragedwhen her kids are sent home fromoverheated schools: “When the weather gets warm and the government says it’s too hot to go out, stay at home – we are priming them for climate lockdowns, that is all this is.”There’s a lot of talk on these billionaire-owned,heavy-loss-makingTV channels about deranged ideologues. But reviewing the summer meltdown on GB News and TalkTV, I think I found them – right there in the studios.Note: The research was conducted for the Guardian byStop Funding Heat, which used a combination of manual and AI-assisted research to monitor broadcasts for relevant content. Each instance was then checked by a researcher and a Guardian reporter.The Guardian’s climate forum 2026On Tuesday 20 October, join Damian Carrington, and our panel of experts – including Prof Andy Haines, Katie White MP, Asad Rehman, Shruti Suresh Gareth Thomas and Amy Fairman – for a hopeful and solutions-focused evening.Book ticketshereor atguardian.liveExplore more on these topicsClimate science scepticism and denialClimate crisisGB NewsTalkTVJacob Rees-MogganalysisShareReuse this content

title: Zack Polanski announces plans to fight byelection in Keir Starmer’s old seat  | Zack Polanski | The Guardian
description: Green party leader says he will ‘stand up for people struggling to pay their bills’ if he becomes MP for Holborn and St Pancras
Author: Alexandra Topping
Headline: Green party leader says he will ‘stand up for people struggling to pay their bills’ if he becomes MP for Holborn and St Pancras
Content: Polanski has said the byelection is a chance for the community to ‘make history’ by electing London’s first Green MP.Photograph: Ben Montgomery/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPolanski has said the byelection is a chance for the community to ‘make history’ by electing London’s first Green MP.Photograph: Ben Montgomery/Getty ImagesZack PolanskiZack Polanski announces plans to fight byelection in Keir Starmer’s old seatGreen party leader says he will ‘stand up for people struggling to pay their bills’ if he becomes MP for Holborn and St PancrasAlexandra ToppingandPeter WalkerThu 3 Sep 2026 05.08 EDTFirst published on Thu 3 Sep 2026 04.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleZack Polanski has announced his intention to fight for the Commons seat vacated by Keir Starmer, setting up a high-stakes byelection pitting the mass campaigning of his Greens against a resurgent Labour under Andy Burnham.Local Greens in Holborn and St Pancras still have to formally select their candidate under a process that will not be completed until next Friday. But itseems inevitablethey will endorse Polanski, under whose leadership the party has soared in the polls, with membership more than tripling.Polanski told the Camden New Journal newspaper that he wanted to “stand up for people struggling to pay their bills”, adding he was confident that the Greens could win the seat.He lives in east London and had been expected to target a parliamentary seat there. Polanski, whowas electedleader of the Greens in England and Wales a year ago, previously lived in Holborn and St Pancras and is a London assembly member. “I know it well and I love it,” he told the newspaper. “It represents so many of the things that make London so special.”View image in fullscreenPolanski with supporters at a Green party rally in south London in June.Photograph: Henry Nicholls/AFP/Getty ImagesThe area had “been held back by governments who have failed to make the changes to improve people’s lives”, he added.The Greens are planning to flood the north London constituency with campaigners this weekend, building on the mobilisation modelused to overturna 13,000-plus Labour majority in Greater Manchester’s Gorton and Denton in February.Starmer, who announced on Tuesday that he was stepping down from the seat he has represented since 2015, in the wake of his departure as prime minister, saw his majority slip at the last election from nearly 28,000 to 11,500 amid a challenge from the left.The Greens came third, with Starmer’s main competitor being Andrew Feinstein, a leftwing independent. In a boost to Polanski, Feinsteinconfirmed on Thursdaythat he would not stand, indicating that the Camden People’s Alliance, the group which emerged from his campaign, would most likely back the Greens.It will nonetheless be a huge challenge for the Greens, which will face a highly organised and motivatedLabourcampaign and a national party buoyed up by higher polling since Burnham took over in No 10.Labour has not yet selected a candidate, but one hopeful could be Sagal Abdi-Wali,who is leader of the local council, Camden, and well known in the constituency.One Green source said the byelection would be a chance for the party to use its increased campaigning resources and knowhow in an area where it won 10 seats in May’s local elections.“The Labour machine is very good, but it is an engaged electorate, and we’re going to go all out,” they said. “There’s not really a downside for Zack doing this. If he loses it’s likely to be narrow, and he looks brave and committed. And if he wins, it would be against a huge Labour operation.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnother source in the party, however, said that while many members welcomed the move, some would have preferred a more local candidate and had concerns about how Polanski could combine being an MP with his campaigning duties as leader.The battle for Holborn and St Pancras would be “genuinely consequential”, said the pollster Luke Tryl, chief executive of pollsters More in Common.“It is totally fascinating because it will define the contours of the electoral landscape on the left of British politics,” he said. “If the Greens win they get their mojo back; if Labour win then Burnham is a step closer to dealing with the challenge on his left.”While the Greens were surging in popularity inLondonat the start of the year, polling has changed significantly since, making the outcome of the race far more uncertain, said Tryl.“Earlier this year I would probably have said that the seat would be an easy Green gain, but since then two things have happened,” he said.“One, Zack Polanski’s personal missteps have taken some of the shine off his appeal. Secondly, the Burnham bounce has not come from winning back voters from Reform but winning those on the left who were disillusioned withKeir Starmer. This is a huge test to see whether that shift holds.”Explore more on these topicsZack PolanskiKeir StarmerByelectionsLabourLondonGreen partyLocal politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Thieves steal more than 70,000 pints’ worth of Guinness from depot in Cheshire | Crime | The Guardian
description: Police say two lorries were driven into industrial estate in Runcorn and attached to trailers holding about 800 barrels
Author: Kevin Rawlinson
Headline: Police say two lorries were driven into industrial estate in Runcorn and attached to trailers holding about 800 barrels
Content: Cheshire police have appealed for witnesses who may have seen a lorry entering the Aston Lane area.Photograph: John Keeble/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCheshire police have appealed for witnesses who may have seen a lorry entering the Aston Lane area.Photograph: John Keeble/Getty ImagesCrimeThieves steal more than 70,000 pints’ worth of Guinness from depot in CheshirePolice say two lorries were driven into industrial estate in Runcorn and attached to trailers holding about 800 barrelsKevin Rawlinsonand agencyThu 3 Sep 2026 13.18 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 14.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe famous tagline “Guinness is good for you” applies only when the drink is bought and paid for, police have said, after thieves made off with more than 70,000 pints’ worth inCheshire.Officers said they believed two lorries were driven into a depot in Runcorn on Monday and attached to waiting trailers holding a combined total of about 800 barrels before being driven away.Cheshire police said they hoped for a full recovery of the stolen barrels, and had appealed for witnesses who may have seen a lorry entering the Aston Lane area at about 7.45pm.The first lorry was said to have connected to the HGV trailer before leaving the depot at about 7.55pm in the direction of the Mersey Gateway bridge. The second lorry arrived at the same site at 9.12pm and connected to another trailer before leaving at 9.30pm in the direction of Rainhill and Watkinson Way, police said.View image in fullscreenOne of the two HGV trailers pictured before it was stolen from Whitehouse industrial estate in Runcorn.Photograph: Cheshire Constabulary/PADS McClatchy said: “It is famously said that ‘Guinness is good for you’, but that is only the case when it has been bought and paid for.“It is with this in mind that we have wasted no time in launching inquires to identify those responsible for the theft of £115,000 worth of Guinness and the two trailers that housed the barrels. We will settle for nothing less than the full recovery of all the items stolen.”When including the value of the trailers, the total value of the items stolen is estimated at about £205,000.McClatchey asked anyone with information to speak to officers. “We would also ask any motorists who were driving in the area at the time of either of the incidents to please review any dashcam footage to see if you have captured anything that could aid our investigation.”The stolen barrels, containing about 70,400 pints of Guinness, had been intended for delivery to pubs. Diageo, which owns the brand, has a packaging warehouse on the Whitehouse industrial estate on Aston Lane.Police believe both HGVs were driven by men. The first driver was described as white with a short dark beard, and wearing a beanie hat. The second was believed to have been wearing a cap.The trailers were described as white tri-axle curtain-side trailers with branding for the logistics company GXO on the curtains and rear doors. The trucks have the unique ID numbers DL736 and DL542 on the top left corner of their rear doors.Explore more on these topicsCrimeCheshirePubsFood & drink industryBeerFoodnewsShareReuse this content

title: Hundreds gather to urge Scottish government to pause datacentre boom | Datacentres - UK | The Guardian
description: Opposition mounts as at least 20 projects proposed, including one in Fife billed as second largest in world
Author: Aisha Down
Headline: Opposition mounts as at least 20 projects proposed, including one in Fife billed as second largest in world
Content: Campaigners say moratorium needed while the Scottish government analyses the environmental impact of datacentres.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenCampaigners say moratorium needed while the Scottish government analyses the environmental impact of datacentres.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianDatacentres - UKHundreds gather to urge Scottish government to pause datacentre boomOpposition mounts as at least 20 projects proposed, including one in Fife billed as second largest in worldPatrick GreenfieldandAisha DownThu 3 Sep 2026 13.48 EDTFirst published on Thu 3 Sep 2026 13.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKat Jones may be the closest thingScotlandhas to Erin Brockovich in 2026. Standing in the shadow of Arthur’s Seat outside Holyrood, the 52-year-old is revving up the crowd of protesters around her. “Who is here from Lammermuir? Ayrshire? What about Aberdeen?” she calls to the crowd.On Thursday, hundreds travelled toEdinburghto call for an immediate moratorium on Scotland’s datacentre boom, which includes one project in Auchtertool, Fife, that has been billed as the second largest in the world.UK government does not know what datacentres are being used for, FoI request showsRead moreJones, the director of the NGOAction to Protect Rural Scotland, is spearheading a campaign demanding a pause while the Scottish government produces analysis on the environmental impact of the centres, and clear planning guidance on the definition of a “green” datacentre.She is a whirr of action: greeting, encouraging, emailing and introducing. Thursday’s protest was the biggest yet.In John Swinney’s programme for government on Tuesday, Scotland’s equivalent to the king’s speech, the first minister said he would take a strategic approach to datacentres with “expectations around environmental sustainability, resource use, community benefit”, but stopped short of agreeing to a moratorium.For the campaigners, this is not enough. From Dubar to Greenock, there is fierce anger at the speed and scale of the projects in the planning pipeline. At least 20 are proposed so far, with more rumoured. Some are planned in the countryside not far from small villages, others next to care homes and residential housing.Kathleen White, who is campaigning against a proposed £2bn datacentre in Lammermuir hills in the Scottish borders, said the project did not make any sense in her area.“We are from a small village of about a hundred people. The project is planned about a mile up the road,” she said.View image in fullscreenCampaigners say Scotland needs a national strategy before allowing the buildout to become too bigPhotograph: Murdo MacLeod/The Guardian“There’s a reservoir and an angling spot. It’s an upland area with dark skies. The datacentre buildings would cover eight hectares [20 acres] of mostly concrete in a greenfield area. It is going to be a monstrosity.”Therising public anger about the datacentre buildoutthat underpins the global AI boom is a growing threat to the UK’s strategy. Keir Starmer’s government leaned heavily on AI as a means to turbocharge a limp economy while he was prime minister.Wednesday briefing: ​What’s behind the global backlash against datacentres?Read moreCrucial to this were “AI growth zones”, which were areas where Britain planned to build massive AI datacentres in the hope that jobs and growth would follow. The Guardian’sinvestigationshave called intoquestion the numbers and reasoningbehind this strategy.The UK’s grid is strained, and proposed datacentres are meeting stiff resistance in London and elsewhere in the south of England.This spring, British officials pushed would-be AI datacentre developers to look north – suggesting Scotland, with its renewable energy and abundant water resources, is better-equipped to support the country’s efforts to keep up in the AI race. One of the UK’s five AI growth zones will be in Lanarkshire, a rural area outside Glasgow.Mounting public anger – and a potential moratorium – could jeopardise this pivot. But Jones rejects any suggestion that the moratorium campaign is standing in the way of progress.“People who are campaigning locally on issues that matter to them a lot get accused of being nimbys. But this is a campaign that has national and international consequences. Datacentres are some of the biggest buildings on the planet, they use so much energy.“Local campaigners are the most motivated to oppose them because they are a direct existential threat to the places they love, right near their homes, near hospitals, near schools.”View image in fullscreenProtesters in Edinburgh say they fear the environmental impact of large, energy-hungry datacentres.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianThe opposition to large-scale datacentres has also been backed by the Scottish Greens and by Reform UK. Reform has raised concerns about the number of projects, while the Scottish Greens have backed the moratorium – echoing the campaigners’ demands for a national framework.Ross Greer, co-leader of the Scottish Greens, who was outside Holyrood with protesters, said: “If we want to have the internet, we need datacentres and Scotland already has plenty of them.Tell us: do you live near the site of a planned AI datacentre in the UK?Read more“But some of these new hyper-scale datacentres of 120MW to 200MW – in total, those proposed would require more energy than all of Scotland needs at its peak at the moment. That is clearly not possible.”The Scottish government has said that all planning authorities must notify ministers of new datacentre applications exceeding 50MW within a week to help monitor their impact on infrastructure, but underscored that the centres are important for economic growth.The public finance minister for Scotland, Hannah Mary Goodlad, said: “We must balance the economic and employment interests in developing datacentres with national energy, climate and community wealth building ambitions, which are vital to our future prosperity, as well as the potential impact on local communities.“I am clear that voices of communities that will be affected will be central to any considerations on datacentres.”But Jones and the campaign want more. She fears that Scotland could be overwhelmed without a formal national strategy. “We are not saying everything needs to stop for ever. But it’s moving so fast. We need a pause.”Explore more on these topicsDatacentres - UKScotlandAI (artificial intelligence)EdinburghnewsShareReuse this content

title: Manchester synagogue attack: ministers seek to block MI5 files from inquest | UK news | The Guardian
description: Government lawyers tell coroner disclosing intelligence would pose serious risk to national security
Author: Josh Halliday
Headline: Government lawyers tell coroner disclosing intelligence would pose serious risk to national security
Content: Members of the community gather at Heaton Park Hebrew Synagogue in Crumpsall, Manchester, a week after the terror attack in October last year.Photograph: Peter Byrne/PAView image in fullscreenMembers of the community gather at Heaton Park Hebrew Synagogue in Crumpsall, Manchester, a week after the terror attack in October last year.Photograph: Peter Byrne/PAUK newsManchester synagogue attack: ministers seek to block MI5 files from inquestGovernment lawyers tell coroner disclosing intelligence would pose serious risk to national securityJosh HallidayNorth of England editorThu 3 Sep 2026 11.07 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 16.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMinisters are seeking to block intelligence material from being heard at an inquest into the death of two men killed in the 2025 Manchester synagogue attack.Lawyers for Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, told a coroner on Thursday that disclosing the MI5 files would pose a serious risk to national security.Melvin Cravitz, 66, died as a result of multiple knife wounds inflicted by the attacker, Jihad al-Shamie. Adrian Daulby, 53, was killed by a single police gunshot wound as he held the building’s doors shut against the terrorist.A senior coroner is due to examine the deaths of the two men at the Heaton Park Hebrew synagogue on 2 October last year during Yom Kippur, the holiest day in the Jewish calendar.The full inquest will focus on al-Shamie’s background, as well as what the state knew about him before the attack. It will also examine security at the synagogue, the role of the state in assessing the risks to the Jewish community in Greater Manchester, and the response to the attack.Mahmood told the Commons on 13 October that al-Shamie was “never referred to the Prevent programme, nor was he known to counter-terrorism policing or the security services”.At a pre-inquest review on Thursday, barristers for the families of Cravitz and Daulby said they were concerned that the emergence of MI5 material “may contradict” that statement.Anna Morris KC, representing Daulby’s family, said there had been a “demonstrable lack of candour” by the security services in other proceedings, including the inquiry into the Manchester Arena attack.She said Daulby’s family were “concerned that this application [by the Home Office] and the information behind it may contradict statements made public by security services and counter-terrorism police that the suspect was not known to counter-terrorism police”.The deaths of Daulby and Cravitz are being examined by Alexia Durran, the chief coroner of England and Wales, at Manchester coroner’s court.Edward Pleeth, counsel to the inquest, told the hearing the government was seeking to withhold “potentially relevant security sensitive material held by MI5” and “potentially relevant security sensitive material held by counter-terrorism police”.Pleeth said this unspecified material was judged by the government to “cause serious harm to national security” if it was disclosed publicly.He said the inquest legal team was satisfied that the information was so sensitive it could not be aired even in a redacted form.There was “no adequate alternative to complete non-disclosure”, Pleeth said, describing the concerns about its disclosure as “well-evidenced”.Durran is now considering whether to ask the government to convert the inquest into a statutory public inquiry to allow the MI5 material to be heard in private.Unlike public inquiries, coroner’s inquests cannot legally consider evidence given in secret hearings.Neil Sheldon KC, representing the Home Office, described the MI5 material as a “discrete body of information” that had been “identified as relevant and has the potential to impact the inquest”.The application to block the information from being heard publicly was not an “extreme approach” but was “cogent, compelling and supported by detailed analysis”, he told the court.Victoria Ailes, representing Cravitz’s family, said his family had “questions in this entire area” and were concerned that this new material came after “statements by the secretary of state to the House of Commons [that al-Shamie] was not known to counter-terrorism police or the security services”.Al-Shamie, a Syrian-born UK citizen, launched the attack while wearing what seemed to be a suicide vest. Before police arrived, the 35-year-old called 999 and pledged allegiance to Islamic State.Last month, a man who conducted hostile reconnaissance at a military base alongside al-Shamie was jailed for life with a minimum term of 16 years, after admitting preparing acts of terror.Mohammad Asim Bashir, 31, and al-Shamie travelled by car to the UK Defence Academy in Shrivenham, Swindon, in August last year, two months before the synagogue attack.Bashir was identified when counter-terrorism officers searched al-Shamie’s mobile devices after the Heaton Park attack.However, Greater Manchester police said last month that officers had seized his phones months earlier in 2025 after unrelated arrests, but that they were not examined until after the attack.Another man, Hekmat Omar Ali Hakim, was charged on 21 August with failing to disclose information in relation to the synagogue attack. Hakim, 49, pleaded not guilty at Westminster magistrates court. He is due to attend a hearing at the Old Bailey on 25 September.Explore more on these topicsUK newsEnglandManchesterUK security and counter-terrorismMI5Home OfficePolicenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘We need a touch of humanity’: Swedish opposition pledges to help Britons facing deportation | Sweden | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Centre party says it will change law to end plight of those hit by post-Brexit policy if it gains power in upcoming election
Author: Lisa O’Carroll
Headline: Exclusive: Centre party says it will change law to end plight of those hit by post-Brexit policy if it gains power in upcoming election
Content: Joyce Thomas, 78, has told how she is ‘sick’ with worry at the prospect of having to leave her home and family.Photograph: Felix AndlerView image in fullscreenJoyce Thomas, 78, has told how she is ‘sick’ with worry at the prospect of having to leave her home and family.Photograph: Felix AndlerSweden‘We need a touch of humanity’: Swedish opposition pledges to help Britons facing deportationExclusive: Centre party says it will change law to end plight of those hit by post-Brexit policy if it gains power in upcoming electionEurope live – latest updatesLisa O’CarrollSenior correspondentThu 3 Sep 2026 08.38 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 13.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA leading Swedish opposition party has promised an urgent reprieve for British nationals facing deportation from the country overBrexitadministrative issues.Niels Paarup-Petersen, the migration spokesperson for the Centre party, said it would introduce laws to end the suffering of peoplesuch as the 78-year-old British widow Joyce Thomasif, as polls project, it forms a new centre-left coalition after the general election in 10 days’ time. Thomas has been told to leave by next Wednesday after 21 years in Sweden.Paarup-Petersen said if his party got into power it would reopen the application process so British citizens threatened with deportation could reapply to stay inSweden.View image in fullscreenNiels Paarup-Petersen: ‘There is no middle ground here on migration.’Photograph: Centerpartie, SwedenHe said: “We have seen many appalling cases, people who are in a vulnerable state who have every right to be here but are being denied that right because of a minor administrative problem. There has been no leeway whatsoever.“People are paying the price, but Sweden doesn’t win either. We need a slight touch of humanity here.”His declaration comes aftera British man was detained in Stockholmby police on Tuesday ahead of a threatened deportation, the latest in a string of cases involving British citizens in the past month.The man’s wife pleaded with Andy Burnham to intervene, but so far no British politician, or official at the European Commission, has commented on the controversy which the Left party has saidwas “damaging” relations with the UKat the time of a potential reset with the EU.View image in fullscreenJohn Sellers with his wife, Caroline. He was deported from Sweden in January despite living there since childhood.Photograph: John SellersAl Pinkerton, theEuropespokesperson for the UK’s Liberal Democrat party, also called on Burnham to intervene: “This is the human cost of Brexit: British citizens who built their lives in Europe decades ago now facing detention and deportation.“The extraordinarily high refusal rate in Sweden should set alarm bells ringing in Downing Street. Andy Burnham must urgently raise these cases with the Swedish government and demand that the protections promised to British citizens under the withdrawal agreement are being honoured.”Paarup-Petersen’s intervention comes amid growing controversy over what he says is the “appalling” approach of Sweden’s current right-wing government towards British citizens caught out by Brexit.He said Sweden’s hardline approach to immigration seemed to have infected the approach taken to its obligations under the EU-UK withdrawal agreement, which was a legally binding treaty designed to give lifelong rights to EU citizens in the UK before Brexit and British nationals living in the EU before the end of the transition period in 2021.“Unfortunately I am not surprised because there is no middle ground here on migration. It is just hard rules and there is little consideration of the way people live in reality,” he said. “I was surprised to hear about the number of British people living here who did not know about the application deadline and that is a big issue.”Paarup-Petersen said theEuropean Commissionshould be able to help but “this is a problem that we can solve in Sweden” quickly with the help of the British embassy.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenGeorge Mason, who has dementia and faces deportation, with his daughter Michelle.Photograph: Copyright: The Mason family“We have an election in a week and I hope we can change things quickly because this is very much a Swedish problem as it looks like other countries in the EU do not have the same problem.”Sweden goes to the polls next Sunday with recent polling showing four centre-left parties including the Centre party and the Social Democrats on track to unseat the government’s centre-right coalition.Two weeks ago the centre left held a 10 percentage point lead for the 13 September ballot, according to an opinion poll by the public broadcaster SVT.Paarup-Petersen’s promise comes after weeks of revelations about British citizens who had made Sweden their home long before Brexit who had received removal orders or had already been deported.They include Thomas, a former nurse who has told how she is“sick” with worryat the prospect of leaving her home and proximity to her son, grandchildren and her husband’s grave.Othersinclude 34-year-old John Sellers,who was deported in January even though he had lived in Sweden since he was 10 years old, andGeorge Mason, 74, who needs round-the-clock care for dementiaand who has lived in Sweden for 25 years.Paarup-Petersen said the wider immigration system in Sweden was “messed up”, with one case ofa 95-year-old wheelchair-bound Iraqi womanwho was told she would be deported after 20 years in the country.Explore more on these topicsSwedenBrexitMigrationEuropeEuropean UnionEuropean CommissionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Shootout in Kyiv between Ukrainian spy services ‘disgraceful’, says Zelenskyy | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Domestic security service says clash with military intelligence directorate ‘definitely shouldn’t have happened’
Author: Amy Hawkins
Headline: Domestic security service says clash with military intelligence directorate ‘definitely shouldn’t have happened’
Content: Hours after the shootout, Volodymyr Zelenskyy (above) fired the SBU’s head of the department for the protection of state secrets.Photograph: DTS News Agency Germany/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenHours after the shootout, Volodymyr Zelenskyy (above) fired the SBU’s head of the department for the protection of state secrets.Photograph: DTS News Agency Germany/ShutterstockUkraineShootout in Kyiv between Ukrainian spy services ‘disgraceful’, says ZelenskyyDomestic security service says clash with military intelligence directorate ‘definitely shouldn’t have happened’Amy Hawkinsin KyivThu 3 Sep 2026 10.04 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 14.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSeveral people have been injured in a shootout in central Kyiv between two branches of Ukraine’s security services, in an incidentVolodymyr Zelenskyydescribed as “disgraceful”.The shootout, which took place on Wednesday morning in a downtown area of the capital, was between officers from the domestic security service, the SBU, and the military intelligence directorate, the HUR.The SBU said in a statement on Thursday that the shootout “definitely shouldn’t have happened” and that it was assisting state investigators.The clash appears to have been sparked by the SBU’s recent arrest of a Russian man fighting forUkraineunder the supervision of the HUR. Local media reported that while the SBU was searching an apartment linked to the investigation, HUR officers arrived and shots were fired; three HUR officers were injured.The SBU said that, together with the HUR, it had foiled a Russian-backed terrorist plot targeting a Russian opposition leader who had recently arrived in Ukraine. In a separate statement, the SBU said its officers had come under armed attack while conducting an investigation and they had used their weapons in response.On Thursday, the SBU releaseda videoof the Russian national fighting for Ukraine who had been arrested last month. In the video, the man says he was contacted by a person from Russia acting for Moscow’s intelligence agency who wanted to recruit him to assassinate Ukrainian defence personnel and other individuals. The man’s lawyer told local media that the video had been recorded under pressure and was being released to “whitewash” the shootout. The man has since been released from SBU custody.Hours after the shootout, Zelenskyy fired the SBU’s head of the department for the protection of state secrets, Oleh Khramov.“Shooting here in Ukraine is permitted only at Russian occupiers, in defence of Ukraine. Our state will never regard any other shootout as acceptable,” Zelenskyy wrote in a social media post.The incident comes at a delicate moment for Zelenskyy. He has recently faced down calls from a sacked defence ministerto hold wartime elections. The demand, from Mykhailo Fedorov – whose dismissal triggered a wave of protests – was the biggest challenge to Zelenskyy’s authority from inside Ukraine since the start of the Russian invasion.Zelenskyy also recentlysacked a presidential deputy chief of staffamid reports she was being investigated in connection to an alleged money-laundering scheme.The president said the shooting on Wednesday needed to be investigated by both the SBU and the HUR. Ukraine’s main investigative agency has also opened an investigation.In a separate incident, a 71-year-old man was shot outside a medical clinic on Thursday morning inKyivand remains in a “serious condition”, according to the the Kyiv city prosecutor’s office. An investigation has been launched into an attempted murder.The shootings come as Kyiv withstandsan intense period of Russian bombardment. Air raid alerts have been active for extended periods in the daytime as well as overnight in the capital. Across the country, at least five people were killed in strikes on Wednesday night. Ukraine is facing a critical shortage of US-made ​Patriot interceptors capable ⁠of shooting down Russian ballistic missiles.Ukraine has also increased its use of long-range drones to target deep into Russian territory. This week Zelenskyysaidthat Russian airspace was becoming unsafe for commercial airlines because of the growing number of drone attacks.On Thursday, Russian media reported that the military officer who ordered a missile strike on theOkhmatdyt children’s hospital in Kyivin July 2024 had been shot. Maj Gen Nikolai Varpakhovich was reportedly shot twice by an assailant riding a motorbike and wearing a helmet. The officer remains in a critical condition.Explore more on these topicsUkraineVolodymyr ZelenskyyKyivRussiaEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Spain’s PM says no evidence ‘whatsoever’ Morocco behind Ceuta border breach | Spain | The Guardian
description: Pedro Sánchez continues to defend Rabat after police report claiming border forces helped 70,000 cross border
Author: Stephen Burgen
Headline: Pedro Sánchez continues to defend Rabat after police report claiming border forces helped 70,000 cross border
Content: Sánchez addresses parliament on the government's handling of a massive border breach in the Spanish territory of Ceuta.Photograph: Olmo Blanco/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSánchez addresses parliament on the government's handling of a massive border breach in the Spanish territory of Ceuta.Photograph: Olmo Blanco/Getty ImagesSpainSpain’s PM says no evidence ‘whatsoever’ Morocco behind Ceuta border breachPedro Sánchez continues to defend Rabat after police report claiming border forces helped 70,000 cross borderEurope live – latest updatesStephen Burgenin BarcelonaThu 3 Sep 2026 08.52 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 08.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSpain has seen no evidence “whatsoever” that Morocco planned or facilitated a mass border breach into its north African territory of Ceuta, the Spanish prime minister,Pedro Sánchez, has told parliament.The address on Thursday followed the emergence of a police report, commissioned by a judge and widely quoted in the media, claiming Moroccan border forces had actively aided about 70,000 people to cross the border in late July.“I ‌can assure you ‌that no institution – not the diplomatic service, nor theEuropean Commission, ‌nor any international body – has provided the Spanish government with any solid evidence that Morocco planned or carried out the incident. None whatsoever,” Sánchez told parliament.Speaking the morning after about 50,000 people marched in Madrid to protest his handling of the Ceuta crisis, the socialist prime minister also denied the government had received any warning of the mass breach, saying no reports to authorities had anticipated “the scale or probability of what eventually happened”.View image in fullscreenA protest against the Spanish government’s handling of the recent border breach at Ceuta.Photograph: Francesco Militello Mirto/NurPhoto/ShutterstockSánchez has repeatedly defendedMoroccoduring the crisis, highlighting Rabat’s cooperation in returning most of the migrants in the days after the surge.But he said on Thursday that Spain had summoned Morocco’s ambassador on 21 August because of “unacceptable statements” made by two ministers over Ceuta and Melilla, another Spanish north African territory. Last month, Morocco’s justice minister, Abdellatif Ouahbi, publicly reiterated Rabat’s sovereignty claims over the cities.Sánchez said he had “for now” ruled out Moroccan government involvement but conceded that Moroccan forces had allowed crossings to occur during a key 10-hour period on 30 July.Many of those who crossed said in interviews they had been actively encouraged to do so. Moroccan officials have denied enabling the crossing.Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the leader of the conservative People’s party, called on Sánchez to resign for his “incompetence and complicity”.In response to Sánchez summoning the Moroccan ambassador to discuss the crisis, Santiago Abascal, the leader of the far-right Vox party, said: “Morocco doesn’t need an ambassador inSpain– you are its ambassador.”View image in fullscreenPeople who entered Ceuta from Morocco in late July on hunger strike last month to demand asylum.Photograph: Laura Rincon/EPAAs many as141 people are thought to have diedtrying to enter Ceuta at the end of July. The influx unleashed a political crisis, a humanitarian emergency andreignited tensions within the EU over immigration.On Thursday, Sánchez appealed for European solidarity over the crisis. He did not single out any countries by name but, in a pointed passage apparently aimed at Italy and Denmark, the two countries that had led public criticism of Spain, said the principle of solidarity should apply to Ceuta as much as it applies to Greenland and Lampedusa.Ceuta showed just how easily Europe can be dividedRead moreAlthough 90% of the people had returned to Morocco within 24 hours, several thousand, including at least 500 minors, are thought to remain, either living on the street or in makeshift shelters.Amid calls from Vox to return them to Morocco, Sánchez reminded parliament that under Spanish, European and international law, migrants had a right to be treated as individuals. “You can’t just grab someone by the arm and drag them across the frontier as though they were a sack of dirt,” he told MPs.In reference to the hundreds of destitute minors, Aina Vidal of the leftwing group Sumar, said: “They’re children, not invaders, not soldiers. They didn’t come carrying bombs, they arrived wearing water wings, in tears.”‘We want to find a better future’: teenage girls on why they risked their lives to reach SpainRead moreIt seems likely the government will invest in facilities in Ceuta to accommodate the remaining migrants rather than risk the political backlash both in Spain and across Europe were they to bring them to the mainland.There is also evidence that, faced with hunger as well as hostility from many local people, some migrants have already begun going back to Morocco.However, as Sánchez told parliament, the per capita income of Ceuta is eight times that of Morocco and “even if we build a wall 100 metres high there will still be people prepared to throw themselves into the sea to get across”.“We will not stop working until Ceuta emerges from this difficult situation: stronger, more prosperous, and more integrated with the rest of Spain and the EU,” he added.Additional reportingby Jakub KrupaExplore more on these topicsSpainMoroccoMigrationPedro SánchezEuropean CommissionEuropean UnionEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘We continue to suffer’: victims of apartheid-era Sharpeville massacre demand compensation | South Africa | The Guardian
description: Claim relating to 1960 attack on hundreds of protesters part of wave of litigation over apartheid crimes in South Africa
Author: Rachel Savage
Headline: Claim relating to 1960 attack on hundreds of protesters part of wave of litigation over apartheid crimes in South Africa
Content: Protesters flee after police opened fire on a peaceful crowd in Sharpeville on 21 March 1960. At least 91 people were killed and 238 injured.Photograph: Ian Berry/c/o Atlas GalleryView image in fullscreenProtesters flee after police opened fire on a peaceful crowd in Sharpeville on 21 March 1960. At least 91 people were killed and 238 injured.Photograph: Ian Berry/c/o Atlas GallerySouth Africa‘We continue to suffer’: victims of apartheid-era Sharpeville massacre demand compensationClaim relating to 1960 attack on hundreds of protesters part of wave of litigation over apartheid crimes in South AfricaRachel Savagein SharpevilleThu 3 Sep 2026 06.11 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 15.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe day dawned brightly on 21 March 1960, as residents of the South African township of Sharpeville gathered to protest against pass laws, which forced “Black, Indian and Coloured” South Africans to carry documents at all times specifying where they were allowed to be.Abraham Mofokeng joined the march, one of dozens organised nationwide by the Pan Africanist Congress (PAC), a breakaway group from the African National Congress (ANC). “The weather was very nice, the sun was out. You could not have suspected that the day would go so horribly,” said Mofokeng, who was then a 20-year-old factory worker.View image in fullscreenAbraham Mofokeng, who was shot in the foot and back during the Sharpeville massacre on 21 March 1960.Photograph: Rachel Savage/The GuardianMofokeng, now 86, was among the thousands gathered peacefully outside the police station in Sharpeville, which is about 40 miles south of Johannesburg in a heavily industrialised region known as the Vaal Triangle.The crowd was singing, he said, when officers opened fire without warning. At least91 people were killed and 238 injured, in what became known as the Sharpeville massacre.As Mofokeng fled, a bullet grazed the inside of his right foot, ripping his shoe off. A woman fell to the ground before him; he jumped over her and kept running. Only later, when he noticed blood running down his legs, did he realise he had been shot in the back, where a bullet remains lodged in his spine.Mofokeng is among three claimants suing the South African government, in a case filed on Thursday, for compensation for the massacre. If the case is successful, dozens more could file claims.The case is part of a wave of litigationdemanding justice for apartheid-era crimes, amid widespread disillusionment with ANC-led governments that have failed to rectify South Africa’s huge racial inequality and poverty since the end of apartheid over three decades ago.View image in fullscreenDead and wounded South Africans lie outside the Sharpeville police station.Photograph: PN2In January 2025, 25 survivors and relatives of victims of apartheid state violencesued South Africa’s governmentfor failing to prosecute cases referred to it by the post-apartheid Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC). That May, the president, Cyril Ramaphosa, announced a judicial inquiry into potential political interference, which is still ongoing.Spokespeople for South Africa’s justice department did not respond to a request for comment on the Sharpeville compensation case.In the immediate aftermath of the Sharpeville massacre, police claimed protesters had been throwing rocks at them. “I don’t know how many we shot,” said Col J Pienaar, the local police commander, according to astory published by the Guardianthe following day. “It all started when hordes of natives surrounded the police station. My car was struck with a stone. If they do these things they must learn their lesson the hard way.”In July 1961, in response to victims filing compensation claims, the white minority regime passeda lawindemnifying the government and anyone acting under its authority for any actions taken “in good faith for the prevention or suppression of internal disorder, the maintenance or restoration of good order, public safety or essential services, or the preservation of life or property”.View image in fullscreenPerformers re-enact the Sharpeville massacre at the memorial site for victims on 3 September.Photograph: Phill Magakoe/AFP/Getty ImagesThe law, which was made effective retrospectively from the date of the massacre, is still in force today. The claimants’ legal team is arguing that the law is unconstitutional.The claimants are hoping to get compensation of about 500,000 rand (£23,000), said Daniel Leader, a partner with the UK law firm Leigh Day, which is advising the South African legal team, led by Lawyers For Human Rights, an NGO.Mafokeng was awarded 30,000 rand as a one-off payment, after the TRC concluded in 2003. The TRC hadrecommended annual reparations payments of about 20,000 rand for six years.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe Long WaveNesrine Malik, Micha Frazer-Carroll and the team guide you through the biggest Black stories from around the worldEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“We continued to suffer,” said Mofokeng, who still lives in Sharpeville. “Especially now … I am struggling and my health is not up to standard.”View image in fullscreenPaulina Mathinye, whose father, Samson, was killed by police in the Sharpeville massacrePhotograph: Rachel Savage/The GuardianThe other two test claimants were children when their fathers were killed in the massacre. Paulina Mathinye was five when her father, Samson, was shot. “Every time he came back from work, I would be so happy to see him that I would run to him, and then he would pick me up,” she said.Mathinye did not initially understand what had happened that day in 1960. “I kept on asking my mum: ‘Mummy, why are you crying?’”Mathinye’s mother struggled to raise her five children on a domestic worker’s wages and Mathinye, who had wanted to train as a teacher but could not afford the bursary, had to leave education at 17 to find work.View image in fullscreenAbraham Mofokeng visiting the memorial site on Thursday.Photograph: Phill Magakoe/AFP/Getty ImagesMathinye, who is now 71, said she hoped for compensation that would make up for some of what she lost when her father died. “Some of my friends are teachers, some of them are nurses, and I’m staying in the same house that my father did,” she said.Sharpeville’s problems did not begin with the massacre in 1960, but with the dispossession of Black South Africans from productive land, their forced removals to townships and their exclusion from the economy, said Vincent Thamae, a PAC member who supports the massacre victims and their families.“When people talk about compensation now,” he said, “compensation is a concept to them that includes all the land that they lost, the economy that they were taken out of and even how they have been treated in the new democracy.”Explore more on these topicsSouth AfricaAfricaRaceProtestnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK mortgage borrowers brace for rate jump amid global bond sell-off | Mortgage rates | The Guardian
description: Swap rates rise to three-year high as increase in oil prices leads to fears of higher inflation
Author: Julia Kollewe
Headline: Swap rates rise to three-year high as increase in oil prices leads to fears of higher inflation
Content: The five-year swap rate rose above 4.52% on Wednesday, which is expected to result in higher interest rates on fixed-term mortgages.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe five-year swap rate rose above 4.52% on Wednesday, which is expected to result in higher interest rates on fixed-term mortgages.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesMortgage ratesUK mortgage borrowers brace for rate jump amid global bond sell-offSwap rates rise to three-year high as increase in oil prices leads to fears of higher inflationBusiness live – latest updatesJulia Kollewe,Graeme WeardenandHeather StewartThu 3 Sep 2026 13.21 EDTFirst published on Thu 3 Sep 2026 04.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHomeowners in the UK are braced for a jump in mortgage rates, driven by higher inflation and interest rate increase expectations amid turmoil in the global bond markets.UK swap rates, which lenders use to price mortgages, have risen to a three-year high, as this week’s global bond market sell-off ripples through the economy.The five-year swap raterose above 4.52%this week, the highest level since October 2023. This is expected to result in higher interest rates on fixed-term mortgages.A jump in oil prices as the US and Iran exchanged fire this week for the first time in a month has led to fears of higher inflation, leading investors to sell bonds, which pushes up their yield, or interest rate. The moves in gilts, as UK government bonds are known as, have been bigger than those in other countries.Coventry Building Society has become the first mainstream lender to increase mortgage rates. It raised rates across its entire range of fixed-rate mortgages for new and existing residential and buy-to-let borrowers.View image in fullscreenFixed-year mortgage rates were unchanged on Thursday.Photograph: Amer Ghazzal/ShutterstockAlthough the turmoil in the bond markets eased on Thursday, the consequences of the jump in bond yields could be serious for borrowers.That is because UK swap rates – the interest rates that banks charge when they borrow from each other – have been pushed up by the rise in gilt yields.Markets are not expecting the Bank of England to raise interest rates at its policy meeting later this month, though its chief economist, Huw Pill, used a speech on Thursday to underscore his argument for higher rates.In a speech in Edinburgh, Pill argued: “We cannot wait for uncertainties to resolve themselves before acting.”Rather than taking a “wait and see” approach, as the Iran war pushes up on inflation, he said, “I see benefit in acting clearly, promptly and decisively … This would cut through the noise inherent in the current uncertain environment in a way that bolsters the clarity and effectiveness of our policy choices.”Pill was among three members of the Bank’s monetary policy committee to call for a rate rise in July, but they were outvoted.Russ Mould, the investment director at the trading platform AJ Bell, said: “Credit card, mortgage and auto loan interest rates will rise if bond yields rise, as the lenders seek to preserve loan book margins and manage their risk.”If the cost of government borrowing continues to remain high, it could undermine Andy Burnham’s efforts to ease cost of living pressures.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe new prime ministerattempted to calm volatile bond marketson Wednesday, using his first appearanceat prime minister’s questionsto promise decisions for the autumn budget would be “grounded in fiscal responsibility”.He spoke as the yield on UK 10-year government debt hit its highest level since 2008 for a second day, before retreating thanks to a drop in the oil price. On Thursday, Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, dipped 0.6% to $95 a barrel.Oil has been one of the key factors driving the bond market sell-off, as inflationary pressures from high prices could force central banks to raise interest rates, along with worries over high government spending. Government bonds are also competing with a flurry of corporate debt issuance by technology companies keen to fund their spending on AI infrastructure.Tom Simpson, the managing director of homes at Yorkshire Building Society, said swap rates were now 0.7% above where they were a year ago, but there was “much more volatility” in March, at the start of the Iran war.“All things being equal, you would expect a modest increase in mortgage rates based on what we’ve seen so far,” he told the BBC, advising people who were worried about this to speak to an independent mortgage adviser.“When there is a movement in the market, that can pull forward demand. People will try to lock those rates in.” However, he added that the 0.1 percentage point increase over the past week was below the 0.5 percentage point increase in the 10 days after the US and Israel first launched airstrikes on Tehran.Fixed-year mortgage rates were unchanged on Thursday, according to the latest figures from Moneyfacts. The average two-year fix is 5.59%, while a typical five-year fixed deal costs 5.63%.Explore more on these topicsMortgage ratesMortgagesBondsGiltsInflationInterest ratesEconomicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Housebuilder Crest Nicholson warns of annual loss in ‘subdued’ property market | Construction industry | The Guardian
description: Firm will complete fewer homes than expected in year to 31 October – between 1,350 and 1,400
Author: Julia Kollewe
Headline: Firm will complete fewer homes than expected in year to 31 October – between 1,350 and 1,400
Content: Crest Nicholson now expects to slide into the red, with an operating loss of about £10m.Photograph: Maureen McLean/Rex/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenCrest Nicholson now expects to slide into the red, with an operating loss of about £10m.Photograph: Maureen McLean/Rex/ShutterstockConstruction industryHousebuilder Crest Nicholson warns of annual loss in ‘subdued’ property marketFirm will complete fewer homes than expected in year to 31 October – between 1,350 and 1,400Julia KolleweThu 3 Sep 2026 06.02 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 12.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe British housebuilder Crest Nicholson has warned of a surprise loss this year as it bemoaned difficult trading in a “subdued” property market.In an unscheduled trading update, the company said it would complete fewer homes than expected in the year to 31 October – between 1,350 and 1,400, down from its previous estimate of 1,400 to 1,500.Conditions in the property market have been “more subdued” than expected during the summer, which is typically quieter as many people go on holiday. Crest said its sales rate had slowed over the past six weeks compared with the first half of the year as “affordability constraints and competitive pricing” dragged down demand.The company now expects to slide into the red, with an operating loss of about £10m, reversing an earlier forecast of a profit of between £5m and £10m. It is the third profit warning since April. The Crest share price plunged more than 10% on Thursday morning.Building material prices remain about 3% to 4% higher on average. Crest hasclosed one divisional officeand cut 50 jobs in recent months.It reported a pre-tax loss of £35.2m for the six months to the end of April. However, it is reducing its borrowings faster than expected, and expects net debt of £70 to £90m at the end of October, down from the £100m to £120m flagged previously.The Surrey-based company has been trying to renegotiate its banking covenants with lenders for some time to ensure it has enough funding in the future. It described the talks as constructive but anticipated “some slippage in the current timetable”, indicating the negotiations were taking longer than expected.Martyn Clark, the chief executive, said: “While the trading backdrop has remained difficult through the summer, we are making tangible progress on the actions within our control.“Although the timing of a broader market recovery remains uncertain, the group is taking the right actions to protect liquidity and improve operational execution, while positioning the business for recovery when market conditions normalise.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe outlook for the property market has been clouded this year by the impact of the US-Israel war on Iran. The conflict has pushed up oil prices, stoking fears over inflation and this week leading to turmoil in bond markets.UK swap rates, which lenders use to price mortgages, haverisen to a three-year high, as this week’s global bond market sell-off ripples through the economy.Explore more on these topicsConstruction industryHousing marketReal estatePropertyProfit warningsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Nvidia to buy developer platform Hugging Face in $12.9bn deal | Nvidia | The Guardian
description: Semi-conductor giant bets that support for open AI models could offset potential slowdown in demand for chips
Author: Nick Robins-Early
Headline: Semi-conductor giant bets that support for open AI models could offset potential slowdown in demand for chips
Content: Nvidia’s acquisition of Hugging Face will give it direct access to platform developers use to collaborate, test and share tools.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersView image in fullscreenNvidia’s acquisition of Hugging Face will give it direct access to platform developers use to collaborate, test and share tools.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersNvidiaNvidia to buy developer platform Hugging Face in $12.9bn dealSemi-conductor giant bets that support for open AI models could offset potential slowdown in demand for chipsNick Robins-Earlyand agenciesThu 3 Sep 2026 12.59 EDTFirst published on Thu 3 Sep 2026 09.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNvidiawill buy the popular developer platform Hugging Face for nearly $13bn, betting that support for ⁠open AI models could offset a potential slowdown in demand for the semiconductor giant’s chips.Shares ⁠inNvidiawere ⁠slightly lower ​after the $12.93bn (£9.57bn) deal – which ranks among its biggest ever – was announced for the database of AI models on Thursday.Hugging Face, based in New York and backed by the likes of Intel, Advanced Micro Devices and Amazon, was founded in 2016 by the French entrepreneurs Clément Delangue, Julien Chaumond and Thomas Wolf.Nvidia is already a major open AI player in the US with ⁠its widely used Nemotron model and vocal support for the technology.Nvidia’s quarterly revenue doubles to nearly $100bn as CEO declares ‘golden age’Read moreAcquiring Hugging Face will give it direct access to a platform developers use to ⁠collaborate and test and share tools, potentially providing insight and data that could help it narrow the ​technology gap with top American and ‌Chinese labs.“Nvidia gains visibility into customer’s preferences and the AI models they use,” said Naveen Chhabra, principal analyst at Forrester. “They can see which models are trending, what datasets customers are downloading, and the architectures that are gaining traction weeks before they hit mainstream tech news.”Demand for open-weight models ‌has surged from businesses balking at the steep bill of deploying generative AI. Chinese companies ‌such as DeepSeek, Moonshot and Z.ai have emerged as crucial players with models that can match the best from the US in tasks including generating computer code at a lower cost.There are fears that some US firms could become reliant on Beijing’s models even as both countries race to dominate a technology they see as crucial to their future. The Trump administration hasscrambled to respondto the wave of open models from China, weighing whether to restrict their use while also worrying about stifling American businesses that have taken to using them.Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s chief executive, was a signatory of an open letter earlier this year from major tech firms that advocated for open models and warned against government regulation that would stifle their use. Huang pledged that Nvidia would keep Hugging Face open after acquiring it.“Hugging ‌Face will remain an open platform for the entire AI ecosystem,” said Huang, adding that his company’s chips would not be required to ​build on or deploy through Hugging Face.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUnder the deal, Nvidia will pay about $11.9bn to Hugging Face investors, while offering an equity-based retention program of up to $1bn for employees who join Nvidia.For Nvidia, building up its open source business may help it cushion a demand slowdown from customers such as ⁠Meta, OpenAI and Microsoft, which are developing their own AI chips to cut reliance ​on its costly and ​supply-constrained processors. Several Chinese chip-making firms have alsomade recent advancementsthat could further disrupt the balance of power within big tech, though they face strict international export controls.It has been a volatile year in the market for chipmakers, with a chip stockselloff in Julywiping $1tn from the market caps of leading firms. Nvidia shares bounced back in August, though, with a strong revenue forecast leading to the second-biggest one-day gain in market history – adding $442bn to the company’s market value.Hugging Face has also been ​in the news recently after ahack by rogue AI agentsthat ​escaped OpenAI’s testing ‌environment. Beyond hosting AI ​models, it offers datasets, ​software libraries and cloud services used to build and deploy AI applications.Explore more on these topicsNvidiaAI (artificial intelligence)ComputingTechnology sectornewsShareReuse this content

title: John Lewis to launch YouTube chatshow to improve AI search results | John Lewis | The Guardian
description: Department store chain’s Gift List ‘vodcast’ will be hosted by TV presenter Angela Scanlon
Author: Sarah Butler
Headline: Department store chain’s Gift List ‘vodcast’ will be hosted by TV presenter Angela Scanlon
Content: John Lewis’s YouTube show comes after the success of Waitrose’s Dish podcast.Photograph: Mike Egerton/PAView image in fullscreenJohn Lewis’s YouTube show comes after the success of Waitrose’s Dish podcast.Photograph: Mike Egerton/PAJohn LewisJohn Lewis to launch YouTube chatshow to improve AI search resultsDepartment store chain’s Gift List ‘vodcast’ will be hosted by TV presenter Angela ScanlonBusiness live – latest updatesSarah ButlerThu 3 Sep 2026 09.08 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 15.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJohn Lewis is launching an online chatshow and social media studio to help make itself and its products more visible to chatbots and more prominent in AI search results.The department store chain’s Gift List “vodcast” hosted by the TV presenter Angela Scanlon will air onYouTubewith clips disseminated via other social media channels and comes after the success of its sister chain Waitrose’s Dish podcast.View image in fullscreenAngela Scanlon will host the Gift List ‘vodcast’.Photograph: Ken McKay/ITV/ShutterstockThe premise is guests discussing good and bad presents they have given and received, with the broadcaster Louis Theroux appearing on the first show.
