There will be six episodes running up to Christmas, with more planned if the series takes off.Shoppers are increasingly influenced by the likes of ChatGPT and Gemini to find and recommend products and also by information on social media such as Instagram and TikTok. The AI large language models tend to prioritise third-party advice and live content when formulating their responses, which isforcing retailers to changetheir marketing plans.The department store’s outgoing boss, Peter Ruis, said that a year ago just 0.3% of its customers were searching for products via AI large language models such as ChatGPT, but that had already risen to 2.5%, and usage was growing exponentially with all ages using the technology.Being able to rapidly respond to trends and interests with clips of influencers or experts filmed for social media – such as the opening of the British Museum’s Bayeux tapestry exhibition, which is expected to spur an interest in cross stitching, or the launch of the Harry Potter TV series before Christmas – has become just as important as the group’s festive TV ad or its‘never knowingly undersold’ price pledge.Ruis,who departs John Lewis this weekendafter almost three years as managing director, said John Lewis had to move with the times as it faced an economy which was “a bit swirly”.He said the chancellor’s budget announcements next month would come at a “critical period” for retailers and he wanted to see more help on business rates.View image in fullscreenPeter Ruis, the outgoing managing director who leaves this weekend, said he was optimistic for John Lewis in the run-up to Christmas.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianRuis said strong trading this week and a string of recent innovations, including modernised cafes and sports departments as well as the social media push and a recent “toy boom”, made him optimistic about the run-up to Christmas.Details of John Lewis’s half-year figures will be released next week. Ruis said it had been a “summer of winners and losers” but indicated there was now “decent momentum” as shoppers still had money to spend.The chain rang up record sales of garden furniture, fans and air conditioning over the summer but Ruis said it was not yet clear if the “Burnham bounce” over the summer would last. “People are not going to splurge when you have got inflation swirling,” he said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“It’s not an easy economy. It’s not easy for customers and inflation is kicking in and the fuel pump is costing people a lot of money.”Ruis last month announcedhis abrupt departure, saying he was going to “pursue new projects”. He gave no further clue on his future plans on Thursday but said there was “no misalignment” on strategy with John Lewis’s relatively new chair, Jason Tarry.“We are getting things done at pace,” Ruis said, adding there was “never a good time” to leave but it was “far better to leave a winning team at the top of its game and all that excitement with events next year to unveil, rather than finishing bottom of the league and running out of the door”.Ruis insisted his departure did not indicate that he had lost hope in the future of John Lewis, saying it was not a traditional department store reliant on fashion and beauty like Harvey Nichols, which wasbought out of administrationby Sports Direct founder Mike Ashley’s Frasers Group last month.He said John Lewis sold a third of all UK prams and pushchairs, garden furniture and the latest technology and “this is not stuff Harvey Nichols can sell”.Explore more on these topicsJohn LewisYouTubeSocial mediaChatbotsAI (artificial intelligence)Retail industryDigital medianewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I don’t chase the dollar. I never did’: the astonishing hidden life of Mr T | Culture | The Guardian
description: He grew up in the ghetto, became a global superstar – then gave it all up. Why did he step away from the spotlight?
Author: Simon Hattenstone
Headline: He grew up in the ghetto, became a global superstar – then gave it all up. Why did he step away from the spotlight?
Content: ‘My job is to love people’ … Mr T.Photograph: Nolis Anderson/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘My job is to love people’ … Mr T.Photograph: Nolis Anderson/The GuardianThe big interviewCulture‘I don’t chase the dollar. I never did’: the astonishing hidden life of Mr THe grew up in the ghetto, became a global superstar – then gave it all up. Why did he step away from the spotlight?Simon HattenstoneThu 3 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 07.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMr T explains why he’s late, but he wants to make one thing clear – this is not an apology. “You caught me in my devotion, and nothing comes before God. So I won’t say I apologise for the delay. I just want you to know that God comes first in all my life. For allowing my success, I give God the glory.”He is here to discuss a new Netflix documentary, Untold Mr T: I Pity the Fool. At 74, he rarely gives interviews. But when Mr T decides to talk, he really does talk. What Mr T thinks, Mr T says. And I’ve never heard anyone trash the very thing they’re here to promote quite like Mr T does today.The actor, former wrestler and cultural icon is full of surprises. Perhaps the most surprising is that he’s still famous. As he says, he has no right to be. It’s more than 32 years since he participated in a wrestling match. Thirty-five years since he had a significant acting role in a TV show. Thirty-nine years since he starred as BA Baracus in The A-Team, and 44 years sinceRockyIII – the only TV show and movie he’s really remembered for. And yet, somehow, he’s still a household name.View image in fullscreen‘I don’t need gold now.’Photograph: Nolis Anderson/The GuardianIn the 80s, many boys and girls wanted to grow up to be Mr T. The A-Team was shown all over the world. This action-adventure TV series about four US army special forces commandos turned mercenaries became a huge hit and helped define the era.The movie star George Peppard was supposed to be the show’s headliner. But much to Peppard’s chagrin, Mr T proved far more popular. His BA (Bosco Albert or Bad Attitude, take your pick) Baracus was a mechanical genius and problem-solver; a peerless brawler and human battering ram, who wore an African Mandinka-style haircut, rattled with gold chains and had a pain threshold second to none. In some ways, BA Baracus and Mr T were similar. In others, they couldn’t have been more different.Born Lawrence Tureaud, Mr T grew up on the south side of Chicago, in poverty. His minister father left home when he was five, leaving his mother, Willie, to bring up their 12 children. The family survived on her work scrubbing floors for the wealthy, and welfare. Lawrence was known to his brothers and sisters as Little T. When he was growing up, everyday racism had a devastating impact on him. He was horrified by the disrespect most white people showed his family.View image in fullscreenThe A-Team. From left standing: Dwight Schultz, Melinda Culea, Dirk Benedict. Front: Mr T, George Peppard.Photograph: Pictorial Press Ltd/AlamyAged 18, he changed his name to Mr T. “Let me explain that,” he says. “See, everything I do there is a reason behind it. My father was a minister and I watched him being called Boy. And I watched my uncle being called Boy. I watched one of my brothers who was a marine come home from Vietnam in his beret and uniform, and some white guys were calling him Boy. So at 18 I had to register for the draft. I said, if I’m old enough to fight and die for my country, I’m old enough to be respected as a man, so I self-ordained myself Mr T at first. Then I legally changed my name to Mr T later on, so the first word out of everyone’s mouth would be Mr.”We meet on a video call. At 74, he looks wonderful. He’s wearing a stars and stripes bandana and a T-shirt that says Lord’s Gym, illustrated with a picture of Jesus doing press-ups with the crucifix on his back. His face, less full than it once was, is magnificently creased and creviced, with laughter lines galore.double quotation markMy mother taught me to take the high roadMr T is part preacher, part poet, part pugilist. Close your eyes and you could be chatting to Muhammad Ali in his prime. It’s all there in the rhythm of his speech, the wit and wisdom, the fighting talk. And yet, over the decades, he has often been portrayed as a muscle-bound meathead. He says if he had been that, his mother would never have forgiven him.He takes me back to his earlier years at school. Sure, he wanted to be tough like his bigger brothers, and hoped to be a successful footballer or boxer. But even more importantly, he wanted to pass his exams, because Willie had taught him the importance of education. She told him how the abolitionist Frederick Douglass, who was born into slavery, had been taught to read by the wife of his enslaver, “and then his slave master told her: ‘Don’t teach a slave to read, because if you do, he won’t be a slave much longer.’” Education was the route to freedom.What did he study? “Philosophy and theology. A teacher in high school said, there’s no money in that, and I said: ‘Sir, that’s disrespectful. That’s insulting, because not everybody’s about money.’ They didn’t take the time to know who I am.” I tell him I’ve been reading a lot about him, but it’s the first I’ve heard of him studying philosophy and theology. “See, that’s the problem. I’ve told journalists the same thing I’ve told you, but they don’t print that. They didn’t want people to know what Mr T is like. I was born and raised in the ghetto, but the ghetto was not born and raised in me. We was poor financially, but we was rich spiritually. I never robbed nobody, I never raped nobody, I never broke into nobody’s house. I never snatched a purse.”By the age of 15, he was a celebrated school athlete and looked like an adult bodybuilder. But his peers mocked him. “Growing up in the ghetto, even though I played football and wrestled, the thugs called me a sissy. You know why? Because I never robbed nobody.” He talks louder and louder. Soon he’s shouting. “They called me a sissy for listening to my mother, for listening to the teachers, for doing my homework. They didn’t go to school. They was dropouts. They was thugs. They’re in jail now or dead. They didn’t become nothing. As the Bible says, ‘Unless two agree, they can’t walk together.’ I told my mother I was going to be something in life. I was going to buy her a house and pretty dresses. They wasn’t going anywhere.” At times like this, he reminds me less of Ali and more of Samuel L Jackson’s Jules Winnfield in Pulp Fiction. Except Mr T’s Bible quotes are for real, and they focus on the loving aspect of the Old Testament rather than the hellfire and damnation.Despite all this, the new Netflix film zeroes in on a violent incident that happened when Mr T was in his teens. In the documentary, he describes how some local thugs robbed his mother of her welfare money, and he knocked their teeth out with the butt of a rifle, and told them that was just the start of it. He leaves the story hanging.View image in fullscreenIn the Netflix documentary, Untold Mr T: I Pity the Fool.Photograph: Courtesy of NetflixI mention this and he scowls. “There is too much emphasis on that scene. These thugs kept on robbing poor black women, who didn’t have no recourse. So we did what we was supposed to do. We’ll leave it like that. We don’t have to get into gory detail. You touch my mother, you got to pay. Bottom line. Then I would have been a real sissy if Ididn’ttake care of it.” But he’s not proud of what he did. “Revenge on the guys went against my God’s teaching, because Jesus said, vengeance is mine. But then we wasn’t dealing with the Bible stuff. It’s Dodge City. Somebody got to pay. Case closed. There’s nothing else to talk about. We’re going on to the next thing.”Did the guys live to tell the tale? “We’re going on to the next thing.” Silence.After college, he won a football scholarship to Prairie View A&M University, a predominantly Black college in Texas, where he majored in maths and was deputy president of the freshman year. But he was thrown out in 1971 for being part of a protest and uprising against the expulsion of the editor of the student newspaper, The Prairie View Panther. Photographs from the timeshow a very different Mr T– a smart-suited, clean-shaven student.View image in fullscreenA yearbook photo of Mr T.Photograph: AlamyHe returned to Chicago, did manual jobs (janitor at a local bank; housekeeping at a hotel) while attending local colleges on athletic scholarships. In 1975, he joined the military police corps of the US army and was named top trainee out of 6,000 recruits. He left the army in 1978 with an honourable discharge and, after a knee injury destroyed his dream of playing in the National Football League, he started working as a bouncer.This is when he developed his look. He was working at Dingbats nightclub, and accumulated gold chains from patrons who dropped jewellery or left it behind after late-night fights. His image was carefully cultivated. The gold, he says, was his way of reclaiming history. Instead of wearing chains of steel, as his forefathers had, he’d wear chains of gold. “People were concerned that I had too much gold and they asked me if it was too heavy. Nobody said to my ancestors: ‘That pregnant lady shouldn’t be in chains.’ Nobody cared about that, but all of a sudden they’re worried about this Black man, Mr T.”The jewellery and haircut were a way to attract attention, he says. “See, my mother and father taught me it takes a smart man to play dumb. In order to catch a rat, you gotta have cheese,so they want to see this man with the gold, with this funny haircut. Who is this guy? So they give me a chance, and I slip my message in. Maybe he looks crazy, but he’s not crazy. Now I’ve got your attention, I can tell you about me.”He explains why he used to wear seven earrings – three in his right ear, four in the left. “The three is symbolic of the father, son and the holy ghost; the three wise men; the three Hebrew boys – Shadrach, Meshach and Abed-nego; the three parts of the day – morning, noon and night; the three graces – faith, hope and love; the three civil rights workers that was killed in Mississippi trying to register blacks – James Chaney, Mickey Schwerner and Andrew Goodman. And the four in my left ear are symbolic of the four seasons – spring, winter, summer and fall; the four directions – north, east, south and west; the four gospel writers – Matthew, Mark, Luke and John. You put the three and the four together, it’s seven. There were seven times the Israelites marched around the walls of Jericho, Samson had seven locks of hair, there are seven colours in the rainbow, there are seven musical notes, God made heaven and Earth in six days, and rested on the seventh. I am the seventh son. So everything I do, there is a reason behind it.”Mr T became a personal bodyguard to the stars, including Michael Jackson, Diana Ross, Steve McQueen and Ali. I ask who he was closest to. He gives me an I’d-have-to-kill-you-if-I-told-you look. “No, I don’t want to name names. Everybody protected was important to me, ’cos it’s a life. If there was a gun, I’d take the bullet; if there was a knife, I’d be stabbed.” Did he ever have to take a bullet or knife for anybody? “No, no, no, it didn’t come to that. But if it had, I was ready.”He had first met Ali as a 16-year-old. “I was a sophomore in high school. One of my teachers knew Muhammad Ali, and told him about me and he came to my school. He said, ‘I want the baddest kid in the school to meet me in the gym’, because I’d just won the city wrestling championship. Ali became my hero because he stood up during the Vietnam war and said: ‘I have no quarrel with the Viet Cong, they never called me nigger, so why are we fighting the Viet Cong?’”View image in fullscreenAs Clubber Lang in Rocky III in 1982.Photograph: Collection Christophel/AlamyIn 1980, Mr T won an NBC show called America’s Toughest Bouncer. The thing is, he says, there were tougher men than him in the competition, but they didn’t have the right motivation. “I didn’t win because I was the roughest or toughest or baddest – there were sometoughguys there. True, you had to be a little tough, a little physical, but I won because I had a greater cause than the other guys. One guy said, if I win I’m gonna buy a car, another said he was gonna party. I said, when I win I’m gonna feed the homeless in the community.”It was on this show that casting director Rhonda Youngspotted him and suggested him to Sylvester Stallone for Rocky III as his antagonist Clubber Lang. Mr T’s performance is astonishing, not least because he had never acted before and many of his lines were improvised. (Most famously, when he taunts Rocky by telling his wife, “Bring your pretty little self over to my apartment tonight, and I’ll show you a real man.”) It was in Rocky III that he first said “I pity the fool,” which became his catchphrase. The film was the second highest grossing movie of 1982, ranking only behind ET the Extra-Terrestrial.View image in fullscreenIn character as BA Baracus in The A-Team.Photograph: NBC/NBCUniversal/Getty ImagesMr T was on a mission, but he insists it had nothing to do with stardom. “My pastor, Reverend Henry Hardy, said: ‘When you are in Los Angeles filming Rocky III find a place that you can minister to.’ So when I was out there I got connected to this homeless centre called the Midnight Mission.” Half a century on, he can still reel off the names of the other shelters he worked with when making Rocky – the Fred Jordan centre and Union Rescue Mission. “I brought them food and clothes. They didn’t know who I was. Because we were filming Rocky III, I brought a lot of Nike stuff. I left it at the door. Eventually at the Midnight Mission they found out who I was and they asked if I’d come in and pray and deliver a sermon, so I started preaching there.”A year later, in 1983, the A-Team started and Mr T became a global superstar. It was shown in more than 70 countries, and he soon became the best paid cast member, much to Peppard’s annoyance. He then became a global superstar twice over as the figurehead for the US’s most high-profile anti-drugs campaign.“The president and his wife, Nancy Reagan, hear about me telling the kids ‘don’t do drugs’, telling the kids ‘don’t rob and steal’, and Nancy Reagan says ‘Mr T would be good for my programme Just Say No’. So they check your background. And when they check my background, it blew them away. They said ‘Wow! He grew up in the ghetto, his mother brought them up on welfare and food stamps and they have no police record! Run that check again!’ They run that check again. ‘And one of his brothers is a Chicago police officer, another brother is a Chicago fireman, how do they do that?’” Mr T answers his own question for me. “Because we love and respected our mother.” There is a famous campaign photograph, taken in December 1983 at the White House, with Mr T dressed as Father Christmas, while Nancy Reagan sits on his knee and kisses his forehead.View image in fullscreenNancy Reagan with Mr T in December 1983.Photograph: Diana Walker/Getty ImagesIn 1985, he became a global superstar thrice over when he starred in the first WrestleMania with Hulk Hogan at Madison Square Garden. Liberace was the guest timekeeper and Ali was the special “outside” referee. By now, you couldn’t move for Mr T merchandise. There were Mr T dolls, Mr T fancy dress sets, Mr T cereal, Mr T lunchboxes, and a Mr T cartoon series.Does he think Peppard, who reportedly called him “the worst actor on the set” and refused to address Mr T by his name, was jealous of him? “My mother taught me to take the high road. I don’t want to get into that. My job is to love people, and I did. I always respected him. See, I don’t have to hate nobody. How can I claim to be a man of God if I’m hating somebody?”I was surprised, before our interview, when Netflix told me how much Mr T loved the documentary and how keen he was to promote it. The film suggests that his descent was as rapid as his rise, fuelled by poor decisions and bad behaviour. When I mention this, he tells me it’s a fake narrative. The truth is, he says, he didn’t want to act any more. “I don’t want to sound cocky or conceited, but if I never made another dollar, if I was never on TV again, all I ever wanted to do is done.” What was that? “All I wanted to do was buy my mother a beautiful house and pretty dresses. I done that in the 80s, so the game was over. It was done. I was already walking away. When they called me for the A-Team, I was at the wrap party for Rocky III. I was told, ‘the producer wants to meet you’, and I was like ‘I’m going home, my work is done. I’ve done Rocky III, I’m going back to what I did.’ My mother told me, ‘Son, there are some things that money just can’t buy.’ Like the poem says, if you can walk with kings and queens and not lose your common touch then you will be a man my son. How many people have sold their soul to the devil, chasing money? I’m not chasing the dollar. I never did.”The problem with the Netflix film, he says, is it focuses on the hardman stereotype and ignores the real Mr T. “The documentary pissed me off, because they didn’t cover a lot of stuff. When I saw it I was like: ‘What the heck?’ It’s garbage. You build me up, then you try to punk me out. I said: ‘Wow man, I’m more than that.’ Two days they interviewed my pastor, and he gets 30 seconds [on screen].” In his view, “That’s what we call, in the black community, a white man wanting to change the story and control the narrative. If you don’t know me, you’re gonna think I’m some monster.”View image in fullscreenMr T and Hulk Hogan backstage during WrestleMania 1 at Madison Square Garden on 31 March 1985.Photograph: WWE/Getty ImagesMr T appears most unhappy about the prominence given to his former agent, Peter Young. He says they fell out and claims he sued him after discovering that Young was allegedly putting his name to contracts Mr T knew nothing about.Meanwhile, in the documentary, Young says Mr T made terrible decisions, citing the film Freaked, a comedy set in a sideshow, in which he played the Bearded Lady. Young says Mr T walked away three days before the film wrapped.“I didn’t have no problem playing Freaked, because we were going against the typecast,” Mr T insists. “Brooke Shields was in it, Keanu Reeves was in it, Randy Quaid was in it. It was a fine role, but he’s putting me down for being in it. He wants to cut Mr T down. The time that it took to put that part [of the documentary] on, you could have had my pastor speaking about the people I changed in the community, but you don’t show that.” To be fair, the documentary does show a bit of that. He starts addressing me as if I made the film. “You see what I mean? Why don’t you show Mr T working with the Make-A-Wish kids, why don’t you show Mr T being in the army? So we show Mr T tough, and then you show Mr T as the Bearded Lady. See, that’s an agenda. It was a hidden agenda, they had to undercut what I’m about. What a joke!”He’s not done yet. “Here’s the bit that really pisses me off. Me and my manager did a conference call with Scott [Weintrob, the director] and he says, ‘what about Peter Young?’ and I said, ‘we had to sue him, so no, nothing to do with him’. Then we started to ask Scott, ‘OK, we wanna see some footage of what we’re doing, because when we do a movie we see dailies’. But he didn’t show it to me. We started filming last year at Easter. I didn’t see the finished product until a month ago. I didn’t see nothing on film. So now I see it, I say: ‘Goddammmmmmmmnmn, ain’t this something.’ We told them ‘Don’t put Peter in my doc’, but he did.”View image in fullscreen‘I’m doing what my calling is.’Photograph: Nolis Anderson/The GuardianWhen he finally saw the film, he says he had to pray for self-control. “I said: ‘Lord, don’t let me go off.Don’t let me go off.’’Cos I wanted to go off on Netflix. And I thought: ‘If I go off in here, it’s not going to be pretty.’ I said: ‘Take the high road.’ So I took the high road.”A message is flashing on my screen from the Netflix rep, who is listening in on the interview, pleading with me to change the subject. But Mr T isn’t quite done. I’ve asked about the comment in the film that he would only turn up to events if a white limousine was booked for him. “What’s wrong with white limousines? Shouldn’t I have a choice of colour? I wear white underwear. That makes me a bad guy? Let’s get real here. I wear white T-shirts sometimes, does that make me a bad person? I wear white socks. So what’s the beef about that? Sure, I like a white limousine. When Elvis Presley died he had a white limousine, so why can’t I have one while I’m living? But Mr T’s a bad guy. We don’t care about him feeding the homeless, but, you know, ‘He wanteda white limousine,he wanted acertainkind of soap in his hotel room.Wow, he’s a bad guy.’”Mr T is spitting with fury. “I’m not supposed to tell you what I like? I’m just supposed to take what you give me? No, no, no, no, brother, it don’t go like that. ‘When he became successful, he told ’em if they don’t fly his whole family, he ain’t flying,’” he says, as if quoting his critics. “That’s what I told them, too. My family is coming along. If they’re not part of it, I don’t do the deal.” Sure, he got the best deal he could, he says, because he was in a position to, and he knew his worth.We asked Netflix, Weintrob and Young whether they wanted to comment on the views Mr T has expressed about the film. Young replied: “Please give Mr T my best, and let him know I forgive him.” Netflix and Weintrob have so far declined to comment.I try to change the subject, and I tell him I love his daughter Erica’s comedy. (She is one of his three children, and a former teacher.) “I don’t go to see the comedy because it’s got four letter words in it and stuff,” he says. He’s still seething at Netflix. I ask him what he’s doing at the moment, and he tells me he’s visiting family in Chicago and spending time with the Pacific Garden Mission. “Once or twice a week I take them hand and foot warmers, ’cos it’s so cold. See, my life is like a rose. You gotta get past the thorns to get to the beautiful rose. So I take all the garbage, the lies, the lawsuits. As my brother would say, in a fight, ‘That’s all you got?’” Somehow the anger has dissipated and calm is restored.He says he’s so grateful for the difficulties he has faced in life – his childhood poverty and the T-cell lymphoma that almost did for him in the 1990s. And there’s been plenty worse than a film that doesn’t treat him with sufficient respect. “You ain’t gonna hear me crying the blues about ‘we was treated rough’. Life ain’t supposed to be easy. That made me who I am. I think of Maya Angelou’s poem. She said: ‘Still I rise.’ So, whatever you throw at me, I gonna rise from that. If you give me lemons, I’m gonna make lemonade. If you give me crap, I’m gonna make fertiliser.”I ask him if it’s true that he stopped wearing gold after Hurricane Katrina in 2005. Yes, he says. After helping with relief work in Louisiana, he felt it would be disrespectful to display his wealth while thousands of people had lost everything. Has he started wearing it again? “Sometimes I wear gold. Maybe one earring. I don’t need gold now. My heart is gold. You know why I don’t need to wear gold? The gold got you attention. Like making an announcement ‘Attention! Attention! Attention!’” And now he’s grinning like a little boy. “So, now you got the attention, slowly people know about this guy Mr T. They know his rap; they know what he stands for.”I tell him I’m going to expose him for having a cute smile, and it will ruin his reputation. I get another flash of it before it turns into a hammy snarl. “Then I’m gonna say: ‘Don’t believe what they say.’”Netflix asks me to wind up, though it seems as if he could chat for ever. He’s barely taken a breath in almost two hours. I’ve never met a septuagenarian with a set of lungs like Mr T. OK, just a few more questions I say.Is there a lady in his life at the moment? (In the mid-80s he and Phyllis Clark, the mother of his three children, divorced.) “Oh, there are a lot of ladies in my life. There’s my daughter, my sisters, my nieces. And then there’s the ladies at church.” I ask Mr T if he is teasing me? “Yes, I am. Actually, there is a lady in my life, yes. We’re about to get married. Yes. Now, go with that.” What’s her name? “I ain’t gonna tell you. I gave you enough now.”If you got offered a decent role in the next Rocky film would you take it? “No, no, no. I’m doing what my calling is. The money I made allowed me to have this free time.”Has he got much money left? “No. Let’s say I’m broke, because that sells better. People want to hear, he’s broke and he’s run out of money. It works better.” I tell him I don’t want to say it if it’s not true. He’s grinning. “You have no choice. I’m not going to open my wallet to you. See, if I’ve got God I’ve got all I need anyway. All I wanted to do is done – buy my mother a house and pretty dresses. I am complete. I. Am. Complete. All right brother, God bless you.”Untold Mr T: I Pity the Fool premieres globally on Netflix on 8 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsCultureThe big interviewTelevisionRockyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Bucking Fastard review – Herzog’s starry twins soap provokes a syncing feeling  | Movies | The Guardian
description: Venice film festival: Rooney and Kate Mara play the real-life Chaplin sisters who spoke in unsettling unison in this silly, pointless drama
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Venice film festival: Rooney and Kate Mara play the real-life Chaplin sisters who spoke in unsettling unison in this silly, pointless drama
Content: Double trouble … Rooney and Kate Mara in Bucking Fastard.Photograph: Courtesy Venice Film FestivalView image in fullscreenDouble trouble … Rooney and Kate Mara in Bucking Fastard.Photograph: Courtesy Venice Film FestivalMoviesReviewBucking Fastard review – Herzog’s starry twins soap provokes a syncing feelingVenice film festival:Rooney and Kate Mara play the real-life Chaplin sisters who spoke in unsettling unison in this silly, pointless dramaPeter BradshawThu 3 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 11.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWerner Herzog is such a unique film-maker that even a dud from him has some interest, but sadly a dud is what this is. It is a fiction feature based on a true story which – despite a few laughs – systematically wastes the audience’s time, as well as the talents of its formidable female leads, real-life sisters Rooney and Kate Mara. You can almost feel this pointless, aimless film making it up as it goes along, losing its way, line by line, scene by scene.It is inspired by the story oftwins Freda and Greta Chaplinfrom York in the UK; they eerily spoke in unison and in the 1980s were the subject of a highly publicised court case for harassing a neighbour. Herzog’s movie transplants their story to Ireland, in which the Maras play weirdly but comically interdependent sisters Jean and Joan Holbrook whose lives are sent in all sorts of loopy directions. Orlando Bloom plays the roguish neighbour who breaks the women’s hearts (Herzog imagines them as a short-lived throuple), and Domhnall Gleeson is a caring social worker who tries to make them less dysfunctional by taking their case after they move away from the scene of their sexual resentment and legal shame. (During the trial they shout out the spoonerism of the title.)Eventually the Holbrooks live with an aunt in the country where they (bafflingly) conceive a desire to extend a tunnel they find in a hillside cave, believing it will take them fromIrelandto the supposed utopia of Orkney where they will be happy. There is a (sort of) entertaining touch of Jules Verne in the outcome to all this. But when the film finally fades to black, after an eventful but also dull story, it’s almost difficult to credit how inconsequential and throwaway it’s all been. The women’s lives are theoretically poignant and fascinating and the Mara sisters show that they are more than capable of showing something like this. But the characters they’re given to play are essentially just silly. Perhaps Herzog could have made a fascinating documentary about the real Chaplin sisters while they were still alive. But Bucking Fastard is a Dumping Thisappointment.Bucking Fastard screened at the Venice film festivalExplore more on these topicsFilmVenice film festivalWerner HerzogRooney MaraKate MaraDomhnall GleesonYorkreviewsShareReuse this content

title: By Any Means review – Mark Wahlberg and Yahya Abdul-Mateen II drama provokes with horror of 1960s racism | Drama films | The Guardian
description: Elegance Bratton’s civil rights drama in the Jim Crow south confronts you with almost unbearable brutality
Author: Owen Myers
Headline: Elegance Bratton’s civil rights drama in the Jim Crow south confronts you with almost unbearable brutality
Content: Mark Wahlberg and Yahya Abdul-Mateen II in By Any Means.Photograph: Courtesy of Paramount PicturesView image in fullscreenMark Wahlberg and Yahya Abdul-Mateen II in By Any Means.Photograph: Courtesy of Paramount PicturesDrama filmsReviewBy Any Means review – Mark Wahlberg and Yahya Abdul-Mateen II drama provokes with horror of 1960s racismElegance Bratton’s civil rights drama in the Jim Crow south confronts you with almost unbearable brutalityOwen MyersThu 3 Sep 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 13.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBlack people officially won the unrestricted right to vote in the US in 1965 but many still encountered hurdles on their path to the ballot box: 11 states in the south quickly introduced a poll tax requiring an annual fee to be allowed to vote. The practice unambiguously targeted poor Black communities in an early form of thinly veiled racist voter suppression. Vernon Dahmer wouldn’t stand for it. In January 1966 the Hattiesburg, Mississippi-based Black activist and NAACP chapter head promised to cover the fee for those struggling to afford it. “It’s a proclamation that we here, that we matter,” he says in an early scene in By Any Means, a considered, if blunt, drama inspired by the real-life aftermath of Dahmer’s murder by the Ku Klux Klan.The Runner review – Gal Gadot stumbles through derivative high-speed, low-rent thrillerRead moreIt is Mississippi in the mid-60s and Wayne Strider (a sturdyYahya Abdul-Mateen II) is new to the local FBI unit, having recently moved back to his home state from Chicago, and is dealing with bosses who turn a blind eye to racist crimes. “White guys can get away with murder,” says one Black colleague while shaking his head. After his boss receives a message from President Johnson to prioritize the Dahmer murder case, Strider is teamed up with a widely feared mobster, Gregory Scarpa (Mark Wahlbergwith a rather distracting prosthetic nose), who has been shipped in from Brooklyn as part of an off-book mission to track down the Klansmen and bring justice to the killers.By Any Means is loosely based on historical events: the Scarpa character is real but Strider is a composite of multiple local FBI agents that he worked with (the agency has never clarified the names or acknowledged that they worked with Scarpa). There’s initially a boisterous likability to the unlikely pair, at least when Scarpa isn’t inviting Strider to watch his hook-ups at a crummy motel, and the actors’ banter provides the film with a few welcome moments of comic relief amid an onslaught of violence as Wahlberg’s character encourages the initially buttoned-up Strider to take justice into his own hands and he educates the mafioso about what it means to call someone a “cracker” (“Salty, no flavor,” the agent explains).Director Elegance Bratton brings a visual flair to By Any Means that is a welcome change from the sludgy palette of his previous feature, the gay military dramaThe Inspection. Mississippi has rarely looked so lush, kissed with the sun and saturated with color, with thoughtfully designed home interiors that give richness to the world. Yet there is also an overreliance on an emotive score (the original song over the credits is written by queen of schmaltzDiane Warren) and a tendency to overexplain the film’s themes: an establishing shot to a Klan meeting shows a man entering a door reading “whites only” later shows it again in closeup, in case we missed it the first time. Other choices are downright odd, such as when the film abruptly switches to a first person shooter style à la Call of Duty for little discernible reason; you often find yourself wishing for less machismo and rather more of, say, Nicole Beharie, underused as Strider’s wife and local community leader.View image in fullscreenAbdul-Mateen II in By Any Means.Photograph: Courtesy of Paramount PicturesIt’s no debate that better movies are made when film-makers look at the ugliness of American history with clear eyes. (While director Kathryn Bigelow has faced criticism for depictions of torture in her films, others such as Jafar Panahi have proved that showing theechoes of its traumacan be more effective.) Audiences may find Bratton’s vision particularly hard to endure: early on in the film Dahmer is shown engulfed in flames, filmed unflinchingly by Britton’s static camera as he burns to death after his home is firebombed by the Klan. Torture scenes include blood, baseball bats to the kneecaps, pistol-whipping and the threat of sexual assault. Racist abuse hurled at black characters ranges from spiteful slurs to sickening taunts about lynching. As if her husband’s death scene wasn’t enough, Dahmer’s elderly, defenceless wife is next in line for the Klan. Here Bratton breaks from history for dramatic effect: the real Ellie Dahmer has lived a rich life of activism and celebrated her 101st birthday this year. (Dahmer’s youngest son has called for a boycott of the film,describingit as “mostly fiction” and pushing “white hero savior” tropes.)Bratton aims to both expose and underline the racism that the US was built on by embellishing history with his own imagination. “I’m not interested in a prescriptive historical take,” the directorsaidin a recent interview. “My film is not history. My film is using history in a way to comment on the contemporary condition.” The result is grimly effective while also being one of the most grisly and upsetting films in recent memory. As a provocation, By All Means is hard to forget.By Any Means is out in Australia now and in the US on 4 September with a UK release to followExplore more on these topicsDrama filmsMark WahlbergreviewsShareReuse this content

title: La Mesías review – this utterly bizarre TV show is unforgettable  | Television | The Guardian
description: Finally landing on Mubi, this Spanish mega-hit about six sisters drilled into becoming viral Christian pop stars is wildly ambitious, blackly funny and a true triumph. Oh, and there are UFOs too
Author: Hannah J Davies
Headline: Finally landing on Mubi, this Spanish mega-hit about six sisters drilled into becoming viral Christian pop stars is wildly ambitious, blackly funny and a true triumph. Oh, and there are UFOs too
Content: Holy pop … La Mesías on Mubi.Photograph: MubiView image in fullscreenHoly pop … La Mesías on Mubi.Photograph: MubiTV reviewTelevisionReviewLa Mesías review – this utterly bizarre TV show is unforgettableFinally landing on Mubi, this Spanish mega-hit about six sisters drilled into becoming viral Christian pop stars is wildly ambitious, blackly funny and a true triumph. Oh, and there are UFOs tooHannah J DaviesThu 3 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 11.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt Primavera Sound festival in Barcelona in 2024, nestled alongside the likes of Pulp and Charli xcx was an unusual addition to the bill. Stella Maris arrived on stage as haunting home movies, religious iconography and glittery gifs popped up on the screen behind them. Part-Haim, part-Heaven’s Gate, the six sisters performed their hits: “Christian electronic dance music” that their late mother, apparently, believed would help them to save the world.The performance was very real, but the band was not. It was a stunt for the Spanish TV mega-hit La Mesías or The Messiah, which was released there in 2023. Its seven episodes centre on an estranged brother and sister, Enric and Irene, who discover that their siblings have become a viral pop band. Cue a soft-focus, flashback-heavy trip into the family’s past, thick with emotional neglect, parental narcissism and religious fanaticism. Oh, and there are UFOs, too.La Mesías is nothing if not singular in its vision, and was masterminded by Los Javis, the Spanish duo who won best director at Cannes film festival earlier this year for their upcoming queer drama film La Bola Negra. Certainly, this isn’t a series you will forget in a hurry. As well as being incredibly long (some episodes clock in at close to an hour and 20 minutes, making it less of an outlier on the usually cinema-focused streamer Mubi), it is – and I mean this lovingly – truly bizarre. Sometimes, it feels like two or three different series have been smooshed together, with timelines that jostle for your attention. There are the early years, with a young Enric and Irene played with poise and maturity by child actors Bruno Núñez Arjona and Carla Moral, plus Ana Rujas as Montserrat – part Cher in Mermaids, part Mommie Dearest who drunkenly tells her kids that “mamá tiene que vivir” (“mum needs a life, too”). Then there are the sheltered adolescent years, with the siblings now played by Biel Rossell and Irene Balmes and known by the names Isaías and Resurrección. They’re coerced by their mother into performing religious music in the 90s, while wearing clothes that look as if they’re from the 1920s. Finally, we have Enric and Irene in the present (Roger Casamajor and Macarena García), traumatised by their childhood but also determined to save their younger sisters.View image in fullscreenA rather ambitious feat … La Mesías.Photograph: sophiekoehler/MubiIf this wasn’t already clear, it is a rather ambitious feat. And if you thought Pedro Almodóvar had a lot to say about mothers, then just wait to see what Los Javis have in store here as Montserrat (also played by Lola Dueñas and Carmen Machi) inflicts all of her own psychic chaos and religious mania on to her children. The pairing of Dueñas as the middle Montserrat and Albert Pla as her super-conservative husband, Pep, is a casting coup, as they play some of the most horrendous (but also often the most farcical) parents imaginable. For all its horrors, La Mesías is blackly funny, finding its humour in unexpected places, like a visit from social services, or the aforementioned performance by the two teenage siblings, who are met with a horrible mixture of indifference and laughter on stage. The Stella Maris tunes are funny, too, but they’re also rather catchy thanks to some canny writing from the Catalan pop band Hidrogenesse.There are some aspects of La Mesías that don’t quite work. The apparent internet ubiquity of Stella Maris is never quite squared with just how sheltered the sisters apparently are (although, in fairness, they were heavily inspired by the real-life group Flos Mariae). There are about 10 plotlines too many, and some of the episodes drag. And while the music budget was clearly high, some of the needle-drops – among them Hozier’s Take Me to Church and Everytime You Go Away by Paul Young – can feel rather on-the-nose (an exception should probably be made for Pink Floyd’s Mother (“mama’s gonna make all your nightmares come true”) which is spot-on but also chilling here). But as a work of art, this series is a triumph – a nightmare-inducing thriller with the kind of ambition that shows exactly why Los Javis would go on to win at Cannes. Enric and Irene’s aunt tells them that “your mum met many men, but the worst of them was God”, which feels too simplistic an explanation for what we see here. This isn’t a show that critiques religion, so much as the dogma, destruction – and sometimes even the poppy indoctrination – that mere mortals bring to it.La Mesías is on Mubi now.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewMubireviewsShareReuse this content

title: Chad Powers season two review – Glen Powell’s sweet sports comedy scores a touchdown | Television | The Guardian
description: The Hollywood hottie is back as the quarterback in disguise, in an oddball comedy that is naughty, lovable and disarmingly unique
Author: Jack Seale
Headline: The Hollywood hottie is back as the quarterback in disguise, in an oddball comedy that is naughty, lovable and disarmingly unique
Content: The man behind the mask … Colton Ryan as Gerry in a Chad Powers mask.Photograph: DisneyView image in fullscreenThe man behind the mask … Colton Ryan as Gerry in a Chad Powers mask.Photograph: DisneyTV reviewTelevisionReviewChad Powers season two review – Glen Powell’s sweet sports comedy scores a touchdownThe Hollywood hottie is back as the quarterback in disguise, in an oddball comedy that is naughty, lovable and disarmingly uniqueJack SealeThu 3 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 11.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the first episode of season two of Chad Powers, there is but one concern: the main character’s nose has fallen off.The TV outlet for the wacky side of movie hottieGlen Powell, Chad Powers presents itself to us having willingly taken on the burden of a ludicrous premise. Powell is Russ Holliday, a former hotshot college-football quarterback who, eight years ago, committed a career-cancelling faux pas during the televised game that was meant to make him a star. With his sporting dreams suddenly vaporised, he became an obnoxious playboy. But then, just as he felt his feet starting to scrape rock bottom, he heard that a university in Georgia was holding open tryouts for a new quarterback. Donning prosthetic whiskers, teeth, hair and an occasionally unreliable nose – a slightly more sophisticated version of a joke-shop disguise – Russ became “Chad Powers”, a southern oddball and the new star of the team, while constantly dealing with the threat of being found out and sent home.The series has been compared toEastbound & Down, on account of its love of cartoonish characters being crass in a sporting context, and to the show that surely influenced its commissioning,Ted Lasso. Both Powers and Lasso feature a main character who is winging it, and both play off a naughty sense of humour against a weakness for sweet, folksy wisdom. In its overall structure, though, Powers most recallsSuits, the legal drama where one of the lawyers was secretly an unqualified impostor, and where the narrative was destined to destroy itself: the only thing that could really happen was someone finding out, but the more people who found out, the less room the story had to breathe.View image in fullscreenAn underdog to cheer for … Glen Powell is Chad Powers.Photograph: DisneyBy the end of season one, the Chad/Russ deception was known to team mascot Danny (Frankie Rodriguez), who recognised Russ on day one but vowed to assist him, because it suited his thwarted theatrical flair; and assistant coach Erika, AKA “Ricky” (Perry Mattfeld), a potential love interest who went cold on adorable Chad when toxic, selfish Russ made a reappearance and had sex with Ricky’s stepmother in his Tesla Cybertruck. (Incidentally, the show’s prominent featuring of the Cybertruck might make you think it was paid product placement, but instead it is visual shorthand for Russ being an agonisingly embarrassing loser, and one of its best gags.)What next? The task for Chad Powers is to not be the TV equivalent of a bad Adam Sandler/Will Ferrell movie, with a funny first act and then a long, boring plateau as the novelty of the premise wears off. Season two has a few solutions.One is just Chad carrying on being Chad, who, because his creator is frantically making everything up as he goes along, has a disarmingly unique imagination: he tries to get out of attending an event by claiming his Venus flytrap needs attention, and asks philosophical questions like: “What if balloons were afraid of heights?” Another is the looming threat of displaced and now dangerously disgruntled wannabe quarterback Gerry (Colton Ryan). Suits fans will spot that Gerry is the Louis Litt of the piece, as he tries to bring Chad down with increasingly manic recklessness, despite being a softie at heart.View image in fullscreenClue’s in the name … the South Georgia Catfish football team’s stars, Chad (Powell) and coach ‘Ricky’ (Perry Mattfeld).Photograph: Disney+There is also an attempt to lean into the serious dramatic potential of the mask Russ wears. Are all of us not, Chad Powers asks, wearing a mask in the workplace, and in relationships? And since everything Chad says and does is really Russ, which is the fiction and which the real man? That question gets more complex when we glimpse the damaged soul behind the crass preening of Russ, and we see that Russ’s overconfidence was a fake trait to hide behind long before Chad came along.‘I don’t know how anyone takes themselves seriously in this job’: Hollywood hotshot Glen Powell talks to Marina HydeRead moreCelebrities, meanwhile, have another layer of artifice that they place between themselves and the world. Picking up on this, the show has the college capitalise on Chadmania by selling Chad face masks. To hide his temporary lack of a nose, Chad himself ends up wearing a mask for a heart-to-heart with Ricky, which means Powell has to act with just his eyes through solid plastic. He manages it, though he’s at his best when Chad removes all his disguises and reverts to Russ: Powell’s face mixes matinee-idol looks with a boyish vulnerability that’s perfect for showing us that Russ is not awful at all, just lost.None of that is allowed to weigh heavily on what is still a stupid sports comedy peopled by charming doofuses, but this slightly more serious Chad Powers has given itself a shot at surviving for longer than it really should. It’s an underdog that’s worth cheering for.Chad Powers is on Disney+Explore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewGlen PowellTV comedyreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Gesualdo Six/Colin Currie Group review – surely the year’s most atmospheric Prom | Classical music | The Guardian
description: The Gesualdo Six brought focus and luminous tone to a sequence of early devotional music; Reich’s Tehillim made a mesmeric and ecstatic pairing
Author: Erica Jeal
Headline: The Gesualdo Six brought focus and luminous tone to a sequence of early devotional music; Reich’s Tehillim made a mesmeric and ecstatic pairing
Content: Mesmeric and devotional… Colin Currie conducts Steve Reich’s Tehillim at the Proms.Photograph: Chris ChristodoulouView image in fullscreenMesmeric and devotional… Colin Currie conducts Steve Reich’s Tehillim at the Proms.Photograph: Chris ChristodoulouClassical musicReviewThe Gesualdo Six/Colin Currie Group review – surely the year’s most atmospheric PromRoyal Albert Hall, LondonThe Gesualdo Six brought focus and luminous tone to a sequence of early devotional music; Reich’s Tehillim made a mesmeric and ecstatic pairingErica JealThu 3 Sep 2026 13.21 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 19.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhenSteve Reichwrote Tehillim, half his long life ago, it was a very modern contribution to the ancient tradition of psalm singing. In this late-night Prom celebrating Reich’s 90th birthday, Tehillim was presented next to a sequence of devotional music from medieval Europe, making for what was surely one of this year’s most atmospheric Proms.For the first half the stage was held by the singers of the Gesualdo Six, who brought intense focus, luminous tone and consistently outstanding vocal quality to polyphonic works by Machaut, Ockeghem, Dunstable and Josquin des Prez, all sung from memory, interspersed with solo melodies by Pérotin and Hildegard of Bingen. Odd one out, in theory, was a version of Hail Gladdening Light written in 2017 by Owain Park, the Gesualdo Six’s bass and director; but this brief chant-like solo for countertenor, with harmonies filled in by the rest of the singers’ humming, fitted in almost seamlessly.View image in fullscreenOutstanding vocal quality: the Gesualdo Six at the Proms.Photograph: Chris ChristodoulouTehillim may be from a different sonic world entirely, and yet the mesmeric, devotional aspect of the medieval music endured throughout Reich’s half-hour piece. The work set four Hebrew psalm verses, with four gently amplified soprano voices skipping from syllable to syllable, underpinned harmonically by a small orchestra and rhythmically by half a dozen percussionists, whether clapping, drumming or relentlessly shaking maracas – the latter creating an irresistibly restless sonic aura. Colin Currie and his group have a long association with Reich and his music, and their performance here was authoritative: mesmeric, energised and finally ecstatic.Available on BBC Soundsuntil 12 October. The Promscontinue until 12 September.Explore more on these topicsClassical musicProms 2026Steve ReichreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Adéla: Prima review – Slovakian star smashes the fourth wall to bask in pop’s cynicism and seduction | Music | The Guardian
description: The 22-year-old is impressively frank about indulging industry sleaze in her pursuit of fame on a debut that puts a distinctive spin on the best of 00s hedonism
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: The 22-year-old is impressively frank about indulging industry sleaze in her pursuit of fame on a debut that puts a distinctive spin on the best of 00s hedonism
Content: ‘Meta commentary on what it is to be a female pop star’ … Adéla.Photograph: Ryley  PaskalView image in fullscreen‘Meta commentary on what it is to be a female pop star’ … Adéla.Photograph: Ryley  PaskalAlexis Petridis's album of the weekMusicReviewAdéla: Prima review – Slovakian star smashes the fourth wall to bask in pop’s cynicism and seduction(Polydor)The 22-year-old is impressively frank about indulging industry sleaze in her pursuit of fame on a debut that puts a distinctive spin on the best of 00s hedonismAlexis PetridisThu 3 Sep 2026 10.30 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 12.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere’s something very striking about hearing a pop star in 2026, their voice larded with Auto-Tune, opening a song with the line “I can’t really sing”. We live in an era where fans seem more aware than ever of the nefarious music business machinations that lurk within the star-making process, one where you’re never far away from online outrage decrying some artist or other as an industry plant. Nevertheless, admitting that the ubiquitous audio processing software is sometimes deployed for a helping hand, not a futuristic aesthetic, feels strangely jarring. On one hand, well of course it is. On the other, actually announcing that without it, you might be honking like a despondent goose, in the first line of a song, still amounts to a dramatic breaking of the fourth wall.View image in fullscreenThe artwork for Prima.Photograph: PR IMAGEThat said, it’s very much on brand for Adéla Jergová, who started her career as a contestant on a TV talent show – she failed to make the cut for crumbling “global girl group” Katseye, as documented on Netflix’s Pop Star Academy – before established names alighted on her as a more left-field solo proposition: Grimes co-produced her early single Machine Girl. New artists are well advised to have a USP, something that helps them cut through the mass of peers vying for public attention on streaming services. The 22-year-old Slovakian has chosen to differentiate herself from the serried ranks of post-Brat female pop stars by spiking her songs about hedonism and messy sexual encounters (“no bed frame, we can do it on the carpet … you eat real good for a starving artist”) with a kind of meta commentary on what it is to be a female pop star.Her debut EP, 2025’s The Provocateur, came in a sleeve that featured Jergová urinating in the street and boasted a selection of songs that depicted the cynicism of the music business and Jergová’s willingness to indulge it in her pursuit of fame. “I bring you body and my energy / Calculate my attitude and my identity … you found your monetary fantasy / Stop, pose, drop, I’ll make your wallet sing,” offered Superscar. There’s plenty more where that came from on Prima. Songs about smoking weed then having it off in a car (Marijuana) coexist with stuff like KGB – “you want a pop star with a big bra for them big hits”; songs that flippantly compare a budding romance to a pair of Christian Louboutin heels (Red Bottoms) with Therapy, home to the aforementioned line about Auto-Tune. “I’ll have to talk to the people I have to talk to,” it continues. “They are old white men / They’re so annoying, but they hold the keys to my future / So I have to do it anyway because that’s how life works.”Adéla: Ain’t in LA – videoYou could decry all this as hopelessly cynical, or place it in a longstanding lineage of pop stars revealing the industry’s workings. The Monkees decried their career as “a manufactured image with no philosophies” on the soundtrack of the 1968 film Head; boyband ‘NSync depicted themselves as puppets on the sleeve of 2000’s No Strings Attached. Although perhaps Jergová’s most pertinent spiritual forebear, given how often she drops her name in the lyrics, is mid-80s Madonna, who was happy to wear a belt-buckle that read BOY TOY if it aided her stated ambition to “rule the world”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSleeve NotesGet music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTrash hits! Why a wave of hedonistic, feral female pop stars are rejecting respectabilityRead moreIf it’s an old trick, it still feels impressively bracing and frank, its effect amplified by the fact that it’s set to sharply written melodies and music that frequently evokes the 00s, a decade that apparently seems like a hedonistic pre-social media nirvana to those too young to remember it first-hand. Nicole Kidman revolves around the kind of sped-up old soul sample that automatically evokes Kanye West’s productions circa The College Dropout and Late Registration; the rattling tabla-driven rhythm of Boys has a distinct flavour of Timbaland’s productions for Missy Elliott; KGB is co-produced by Harrison Smith, better known as the Dare, the sometime Charli xcx collaborator praised and reviled in equal measure for his role in the indie sleaze revival.Prima was apparently made in a hurry so that Jergová would have enough material to warrant a support slot with Demi Lovato. It definitely feels like a debut album. There are moments where it sinks into boilerplate pop: Hitachi is a standard-issue piano ballad about a failing relationship; Fantasize isn’t particularly interesting beyond the fact that its hook is played on a trombone and the opening line unexpectedly features the word “reciprocity”. But failing to be a perfectly turned finished product on arrival is hardly a crime: rather, it suggests an artist who has room to grow and develop. On the basis of what’s here – which is frequently sharp, funny and daring – watching Adéla do just that should be fascinating.This week Alexis listened toAlabama Shakes – GardenNew album I Must Be Dreaming more or less picks up where Alabama Shakes left off a decade ago: not a problem at all if the results are like Garden’s distorted, gently psychedelicised southern soul.Explore more on these topicsMusicAlexis Petridis's album of the weekPop and rockreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I want to go further’: Justin Broadrick on retiring Godflesh, playing with Phoebe Bridgers – and his new band | Music | The Guardian
description: A hernia may mean his screaming days are over, but the Napalm Death alum’s influence on metal echoes on in unexpected places – and with ‘heavy, ugly’ experiments in the pipeline, his passion for ‘outsider music’ remains strong
Author: Matt Mills
Headline: A hernia may mean his screaming days are over, but the Napalm Death alum’s influence on metal echoes on in unexpected places – and with ‘heavy, ugly’ experiments in the pipeline, his passion for ‘outsider music’ remains strong
Content: ‘We were being exposed to a metal audience that had never experienced anything like us’ … (from left) Ben Green and Justin Broadrick of Godflesh.Photograph: Kim SølveView image in fullscreen‘We were being exposed to a metal audience that had never experienced anything like us’ … (from left) Ben Green and Justin Broadrick of Godflesh.Photograph: Kim SølveMusicInterview‘I want to go further’: Justin Broadrick on retiring Godflesh, playing with Phoebe Bridgers – and his new bandMatt MillsA hernia may mean his screaming days are over, but the Napalm Death alum’s influence on metal echoes on in unexpected places – and with ‘heavy, ugly’ experiments in the pipeline, his passion for ‘outsider music’ remains strongThu 3 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn 4 October 2024, Justin Broadrick felt a pop. The singer and guitarist of pioneering industrial metal duo Godflesh had felt pain in his groin for several years. After a coughing fit following a show in Sofia, Bulgaria, he knew he had a hernia. “It was a small knob in my groin,” says Broadrick. “I got back home and told my partner, and she was like, ‘Let’s watch how it goes.’” He continued to perform live for another year, wearing up to two hernia belts at a time. By the time he got it surgically treated in February this year, it was 13cm long.The next month, Broadrick shared a picture of himself in hospital and announced that Godflesh’s near-four-decade career will soon end. His condition had been caused by the physicality of shouting over their music since he was 18; he just turned 57. If he were to do so again, he would risk blowing out his abdominal wall entirely. There will be two more studio albums – starting with this autumn’s reliably crushing Decay, recorded pre-surgery – and possibly some archival releases and remixes. But beyond that? Nothing.“I’m still in a lot of discomfort, even now,” says Broadrick, talking to me by phone in mid-August. “I’m not the toughest guy in the world, I’m very sensitive to pain, so it’s going to be nine to 12 months [after surgery] before potentially feeling no negative sensations whatsoever.”Godflesh: Living/Ending – videoBroadrick received support from all over the heavy metal world, including current or former members of Megadeth, Slipknot, Fear Factory, Neurosis, Sunn O))) and Killing Joke. It was just a small glimpse of the impact Godflesh have made. When Broadrick and bassist Ben “GC” Green formed the band in 1988, their cacophonous beats, programmed on a £500 drum machine, were unprecedented in the genre. Broadrick’s riffs were immediate, dense and unsettling. From top to bottom, they were the heaviest band ever.Metallica were fans: guitarist Kirk Hammett got Andres Serrano to design their Load and Reload album covers after Broadrick showed him a Godflesh video directed by the provocative artist. Mike Patton praised them as “ridiculously heavy” and invited Broadrick to audition for Faith No More in 1993. He turned the offer down. “There’s no way I can join someone else’s band,” he reasons today. And many of nu metal’s frontrunners idolised Godflesh. Founding Slipknot drummer Joey Jordison once blared their music during an interview at his house; when Broadrick first heard Korn’s debut single Blind, he thought: “I quite like it, but it sounds like Godflesh meets Faith No More.”View image in fullscreen‘Among the distress [of touring] and the feeling of wanting to kill everyone, there is transcendence’ … Broadrick and Green in 1992.Photograph: Johnny Greig/AlamyDespite his widespread influence, Broadrick eschews the limelight. Born in Birmingham, he now lives with his partner, 15-year-old son and many, many pets in a north Wales village so remote that it doesn’t have as much as a pub. He avoids social situations, rarely granting interviews, but gives long, sometimes meandering answers. He says that these are symptoms of his autism, which went undiagnosed until 2022, when he was in his early 50s.“I’m generalising, but the psychiatrist pretty much said to me that there are two types of autistic people,” he explains in his undiluted Brummie accent. “A lot of people who used to get diagnosed with Asperger’s generally have the cold, don’t speak, sit-in-a-corner type of autism. My autism is the other one, where, they said, people can get hyperemotional and hypersensitive and talk all the time, trying to get themselves understood.”Broadrick’s hypersensitivity shaped Godflesh’s music. Their beats echo the clanging he heard from nearby factories while growing up on a council estate, and his anguished shouts and misanthropic lyrics are rooted in childhood trauma. His mum and stepdad were punk musicians who hosted wild parties with drugs and alcohol while he was home. “I was exposed to all manner of shit,” he says, “but at school, I was totally isolated. I couldn’t communicate with kids. I was virtually mute. Two very different, polarising existences there. As soon as I became obsessive about music at the age of eight, that’s all I could communicate about.”He began making music under the pseudonym Final when he was 13. At 15, he walked out of his first exam and never went back to school. After meeting Nicholas Bullen of West Midlands grindcore agitators Napalm Death at a market, he joined the band and wrote “90%” of the music on side A of their debut album, Scum. It became a cult classic, inspiring a legion of copycats. The 1.3-second track You Suffer holds the Guinness world record for the shortest song ever recorded.Godflesh: Crush My Soul – videoCome the release of Scum in 1987, however, Broadrick had already grown bored and left. “I love what we created, but I felt restricted. We said, ‘Let’s play as fast as we can.’ I remember saying to [drummer] Mick Harris, ‘Faster! Faster!’, and he was laughing, and we just got faster and faster. It was very momentary – very temporary, almost.”In 1988, Broadrick and Green, who grew up on the same estate, started Godflesh. They were both signing on at the time, and talked Green’s mum into taking out a bank loan to cover that £500 drum machine. Their formula of playing distorted guitar over huge beats was inspired by Run-DMC’s single King of Rock, which Broadrick heard on The Old Grey Whistle Test. The angular riffs were pulled from Killing Joke, while the discordance and rhythmic vocal patterns evoked early Swans. That unique blend resonated widely, getting the pair off the dole “relatively quickly”. Their 1989 debut album, Streetcleaner, was released by popular death metal label Earache (then also home to Napalm). After initially only reaching No 19 on the UK indie chart, it became a sleeper hit and seminal release.Godflesh proved especially popular in the US, where they scored their breakthrough by supporting Napalm in 1991. However, the tour triggered Broadrick’s hypersensitivity. From his first gig, he had used drink or substances to cope with the sensory overload of performing. Still, he had to play. Music is the only job he’s ever had, and, “among the distress and the feeling of wanting to fucking kill everyone, there is transcendence”, he says.“I hated the overwhelm, everything about it. Two-and-a-half months, that fucking tour! I spent two-and-a-half months trying to get off,” he admits. “But here’s the thing: you could tell we were being exposed to a metal audience that had never experienced anything like us.”View image in fullscreenBanned … Broadrick on the set of the video for Crush My Soul in 1994.Photograph: Karjean Levine/Getty ImagesThanks to a deal by Earache, Sony-backed juggernaut Columbia Records agreed to distribute Godflesh’s 1994 album Selfless in the US. But then MTV banned the Serrano-directed Crush My Soul video – not only did it contain religious imagery and end with red liquid being poured on to Broadrick, but the artist had previously flared tempers with his 1987 photographPiss Christ, which depicted a crucifix submerged in urine. Broadrick believes that the rise of nu metal not long after Selfless “buried” Godflesh: “Labels that wanted to sign Godflesh two years before were not interested any more. They just wanted anyone who sounded like Korn or Slipknot.”He also expresses his frustration over certain high-profile artists not acknowledging him. He claimed in a 90s interview that Metallica’s Hammett never publicly gave him the credit for introducing him to Serrano’s work. “Kirk promptly fell out with me and got friends of his to write me nasty letters and shit,” he alleges today. “That was the end of that.”Were you ever able to mend that relationship? “Eventually, he admitted that it was taken from the influence of Godflesh. It’s now public knowledge that it was inspired by a Godflesh video, but he didn’t say that for many, many years. And I got made the bad guy for daring to suggest that that concept was taken from the band. I’m pretty upset now, to be honest, that people turned on me about it.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSleeve NotesGet music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGodflesh suffered another, ultimately fatal blow when Green left in 2001, two weeks before a tour. After rushing to replace his longtime partner and once again hitting the road, Broadrick collapsed. He ended Godflesh in April 2002, ahead of a scheduled North American run, and put together a new shoegaze project, Jesu.More ambient and melodic than Godflesh, Jesu broadened Broadrick’s influence. Heremixed Julien Baker’s song Favorin 2021. Baker’s Boygenius bandmate Phoebe Bridgers did backing vocals. Recently, Bridgers emailed Broadrick about doing some “Jesu-style stuff” on her chart-topping new album,Lost Weekend. “I thought I was being scammed,” he admits, but he played guitar on the tracks Bobby and Best Dressed.Was it intimidating, collaborating with a pop star? “The fact that she was so personable and we were immediate friends was brilliant for me, but I was overwhelmed by how big she is. I was literally sending music to Taylor Swift’s personal engineer! I’m catapulted into this huge, mainstream world, and I’m like, ‘How the fuck am I here?!’” They’re still working together, as recently as three weeks before we speak. “She wanted me to play guitar and bass on a song for a film. She said to me a few months ago, ‘I’m just going to keep hitting you up.’”View image in fullscreen‘It will always be a beacon’ … Broadrick playing in Norway in 2023.Photograph: Gonzales Photo/AlamyAfter performing across Europe and North America as Jesu in 2007, Broadrick quit drink and drugs and gave up touring. “I ended up drinking a bottle of Jack Daniel’s every night,” he says. “Total self-destruction. I was killing myself, so I had to address it. I had to stop touring.”Two years later, craving a heavier counterpart to Jesu, he restarted Godflesh with Green. They’ve experimented plenty since the early days: they’ve done dub remixes, some of their later beats took from hip-hop and breakbeat, and new album Decay contains two of their longest, most claustrophobic compositions in Master and Slave and Consume Me.But Broadrick feels trapped by the band’s framework. His hernia didn’t cause their impending split as much as confirm it.“The Godflesh template has become dated to me,” he says. “It’s very 80s and 90s, like a noise rock band. For want of a better analogy, it’s very meat and potatoes. I always wanted to go much further than that. You can step outside the template, but it won’t be Godflesh any more.”‘I don’t want to die in a hotel room somewhere’: Black Sabbath on reconciling for their final gig – and how Ozzy is living through hellRead moreHe hopes to record Godflesh’s final album, aptly entitled The End, in November and December and release it as soon as possible. It’ll feature vocals, but they’ll be higher-pitched screams and spoken-word sections that he can handle safely. He reveals that the music will mark a “sideways step” for the band, as he plans to use a guitar with a tremolo arm: something Godflesh haven’t touched since their debut album.After Godflesh are put to bed, Broadrick, as well as continuing with Jesu and his electronic solo project JK Flesh, will form a new “brutal, industrial, heavy” solo band called White Light District. There’ll be sampled percussion and electronic textures. Live, he’ll be joined by a session drummer.“I wouldn’t dare call it a Godflesh replacement,” he says. “Because it’s heavy, ugly music, people may venture that it is, but it will be less rock based. It’s not confined by that instrumentation. It will sound like Glenn Branca with metal guitars, except it’s not metal: 15 layers of guitar that create this ultra-cluster of fucking hallucinatory dissonance, which could not be created by a band.”As he readies The End and this new pursuit, Broadrick admits that Godflesh’s retirement hasn’t sunk in yet. He believes, in a way, that the band will live for ever. “I’m not saying this arrogantly, but I think it will always be a beacon. It was a vehicle for my alien way of writing things, and I will still be writing shit like that. It’s outsider music. It doesn’t belong, and I don’t belong, and I’m happy to not belong. I don’t want to belong.”Decay is released via Relapse on 25 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsMusicMetalPop and rockinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Berlin Philharmonic/Petrenko review – insightful Elgar and Tchaikovsky holds Proms audience in thrall | Proms 2026 | The Guardian
description: Elgar’s Enigma Variations sounded fresh and striking in the German orchestra’s reading, while Tchaikovsky’s fourth symphony was thrilling and monumental
Author: Erica Jeal
Headline: Elgar’s Enigma Variations sounded fresh and striking in the German orchestra’s reading, while Tchaikovsky’s fourth symphony was thrilling and monumental
Content: Freshness… Kirill Petrenko conducts the Berlin Philharmonic at the BBC Proms.Photograph: Lena LaineView image in fullscreenFreshness… Kirill Petrenko conducts the Berlin Philharmonic at the BBC Proms.Photograph: Lena LaineProms 2026ReviewBerlin Philharmonic/Petrenko review – insightful Elgar and Tchaikovsky holds Proms audience in thrallRoyal Albert Hall, LondonElgar’s Enigma Variations sounded fresh and striking in the German orchestra’s reading, while Tchaikovsky’s fourth symphony was thrilling and monumentalErica JealThu 3 Sep 2026 10.31 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 10.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIs the Berlin Philharmonicthe best orchestra in the world? Quite possibly. The only potential disappointment about the first of their two Proms under their chief conductor Kirill Petrenko was that there were just two works. Elgar’s Enigma Variations and Tchaikovsky’s Symphony No 4 made an insightful pairing, though, sharing an autobiographical aspect that, in different ways, reveals much about their composers.The Elgar – bread-and-butter repertoire for UK orchestras but not yet for German ones – was approached with a freshness that made these portraits of the composer’s friends and family seem particularly affectionate. The opening can sound like merely a warm-up for what’s to come; here, though, from the very start the string tone was sumptuous and pregnant with possibility, the phrasing meaningful. This attention to detail continued throughout a performance that gloried in the richness of the orchestra’s sound and the full extent of its range, from the softest of melancholy cello solos to the floor-shaking throb of the Royal Albert Hall organ in the finale. A particularly striking moment came with the stark timpani rolls in the penultimate variation, conjuring the sound of a ship’s engine to honour a friend who was then on a long sea voyage – or, reading deeper, perhaps a lost love who had emigrated years before.There is no room for friends and family in the Tchaikovsky – just implacable Fate breathing down the composer’s neck during an especially turbulent time in his life. The Fate theme came at us like a juggernaut at the opening thanks to the Philharmonic’s outstanding brass section. This work was where Petrenko’s mastery of the long view paid off – in each movement Tchaikovsky’s repetitious figurations were sculpted into long lines that built and receded to create something huge. The third movement had similar scope but came as a kind of light relief: its long passages of gossamer plucked strings were dispatched with pinpoint accuracy, and Petrenko seemed barely to need to conduct it at all. When Fate thundered back in to disrupt the finale, the quality of the silence in the pauses afterwards spoke volumes: this was an orchestra holding its audience in thrall.Available on BBC Soundsuntil 12 October. The Promscontinue until 12 September.Explore more on these topicsProms 2026Classical musicBerlin PhilharmonicreviewsShareReuse this content

title: What we’re reading: Irvine Welsh, Janice Hallett and Guardian readers on the books they enjoyed in August | Books | The Guardian
description: Writers and Guardian readers discuss the titles they have read over the last month. Join the conversation in the comments
Author: Irvine Welsh
Headline: Writers and Guardian readers discuss the titles they have read over the last month. Join the conversation in the comments
Content: Photograph: PRView image in fullscreenPhotograph: PRWhat we're readingBooksWhat we’re reading: Irvine Welsh, Janice Hallett and Guardian readers on the books they enjoyed in AugustWriters and Guardian readers discuss the titles they have read over the last month. Join the conversation in the commentsIrvine Welsh,Janice Hallettand Guardian readersThu 3 Sep 2026 08.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIrvine Welsh, authorI’ve been enjoyingContrappostobyDave Eggers. The premise that love and art are the only things that make life worthwhile pulses beautifully through this novel and its two protagonists, spanning decades of their obsession with both, and each other. The tragedy is they are not sufficient alone for a relationship to survive to the exclusion of everything else (namely capitalism, which always has a place at the table), but they remain essential and enduring. Nowhere is this better evoked than here. Think John Williams’s Stonerbut with art instead of literature and stuffed with more memorable characters.View image in fullscreenIrvine Welsh.Photograph: Europa Press News/Europa Press/Getty ImagesInRaveheart, Graeme Armstrong confronts the twin promises of utopia and madness in a time before the internet’s colonisation of the mind, when people still dared to dream and lived to party. This book made me want to call some heads, rent a farmhouse, get a sound system and neck several pills.
