In fact, I might just do that.Finally, another one for creatures of the night in all their disparate glory.Overnightby Dan Richards is more than a tribute to the people (and other critters) who operate in the hours of darkness to ensure we have everything we need – it’s a discourse on the very nature of night-time itself, and its essential relationship to our humanity. This is a beautifully written work of startling brilliance, astonishing the reader page after page.Can Nothing Save Us? by Irvine Welsh is published by Jonathan Cape (£20). To support the Guardian, buy a copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Jean, Guardian readerI am readingThe Shampoo Effectby Jenny Jackson. My only regret is not saving this book until my late summer beach vacation, because this book is best read with sand betwixt your toes. The story follows a group of lifelong friends in their thirties in their Massachusetts home town as they navigate marriage, parenthood, and careers. A newcomer from New York City arrives to work on what she hopes will be her big break as a writer and becomes irrevocably interwoven in the group’s complicated dynamics. It’s funny, sharp, and has me wondering as a child-free woman if many parents are self-medicating with weed on a regular basis to get through the day.Janice Hallett, authorI’ve been diving deep into true crime lately.London Fallingby Patrick Radden Keefe is a book that examines so much more than its central crime story: that of a young man whose big dreams and relentless drive took him in a deadly direction. Keefe elevates the tragedy by placing it in the context of our capital’s criminal history. I’ve also revisited Carol Ann Lee’s exceptionally researched and presentedThe Murders at White House Farm.For someone fascinated by criminal psychology and the legal system, this book is without a doubt a core text on the Jeremy Bamber case. Meanwhile, I was hooked for a whole weekend onDead Fashion Girlby Fred Vermorel. Described as “a situationist detective story” it starts with the 1954 murder of a young fashion designer in Ruislip, not far from where I live, and splays outwards and downwards into London’s postwar criminal underbelly.The Silent Appeal by Janice Hallett is published by Profile (£20). To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Barbara, Guardian readerYou wouldn’t think that an account of a ten-month long legal process would be a page-turner, but that is exactly what Emmanuel Carrère has achieved inV13,the book based on his weekly magazine columns covering the trial of the surviving perpetrators of the terror attacks in Paris on Friday (ie Vendredi) 13, 2015. He delves into the lives of the victims, the perpetrators, the lawyers, and produces an all-round picture of the human beings involved in this horrific event. It is written with compassion, empathy, and a genuine curiosity about motivation.Light-years away (or perhaps not) is the deceptively simple tale told by Iain Crichton Smith inConsider the Lilies,a short novel about an elderly woman’s treatment at the hands of the Duke of Sutherland as he evicted tenants during the Highland Clearances – one woman, representing the fates of 150,000. A note at the front of the book tells me that I bought it on North Uist more than half-a-century ago, and now that I’m older I find it possibly even more moving than it was then.Explore more on these topicsBooksWhat we're readingIrvine WelshDave EggersfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A Death of One’s Own by Terry Eagleton review – meditations on arriving at a full stop | Terry Eagleton | The Guardian
description: The literary critic brings his vast reading to bear on life’s most inescapable fact
Author: Kathryn Hughes
Headline: The literary critic brings his vast reading to bear on life’s most inescapable fact
Content: Terry Eagleton in 2018.Photograph: Tracey Paddison/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenTerry Eagleton in 2018.Photograph: Tracey Paddison/ShutterstockBook of the dayTerry EagletonReviewA Death of One’s Own by Terry Eagleton review – meditations on arriving at a full stopThe literary critic brings his vast reading to bear on life’s most inescapable factKathryn HughesThu 3 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 02.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTerry Eagleton is not a fan of sloppy thinking, especially when it comes to the granite fact of death. He particularly doesn’t like the attitude ofDylan Thomaswho famously urged his ailing father to “not go gentle into that good night”. If the “night” – death – is so “good” then why, asks Eagleton reasonably, would Thomas want his dad to dawdle? Shouldn’t DJ Thomas, rather, be encouraged to trot towards his lovely end like an ecstatic marathon runner on the home straight?Eagleton’s reproach to Thomas’s doublethink should not be read as panicky denial about the reality of his own mortality. To the contrary, Eagleton, who at 83 admits that he wasn’t sure whether this book would end up being published posthumously, finds it hard to think or write about much else. After a 60-year academic career spent tussling with Marxist literary theory, not to mention the epistemological void at the heart of postmodernism criticism, these days Eagleton is more interested in pondering death and how it “lacks a sense of occasion”. It might visit, for example, while you happen to be dressed in a giraffe outfit.Not, Eagleton clarifies, that it would really matter being found dead disguised as a long-necked ungulate since you would be beyond all caring. Indeed, this not mattering is, as he sees it, one of the great pleasures of being deceased. You’re beyond the reach of moral and social obligation: you can cheat your creditors, fail to turn up at your mother’s funeral and ignore increasingly hysterical demands to pay a parking fine. There might even be something sexy about being dead, a certain “pornographic pleasure” in decomposition, what Eagleton calls “the erotic bliss of yielding to an impregnable power”. Practically speaking, you’re no longer required to hold it all together.Until that moment of blessed release, though, we are obliged to trundle on as best we can. Eagleton mildly advocates trying to live each day in the full knowledge that death is just around the corner. Done right, this should in theory release us “from the mortal anxiety that compels us to clutch, seize and despoil”. Instead, we would experience the world around us with the visionary intensity of a William Blake, savouring every raindrop, ray of sunlight and crunch of apple to the point of almost painful lucidity. Lovely in principle, but as Eagleton puts it with a typically bathetic side-swipe, the mental contortion required to attain this state of ecstasy may end up being “more trouble than it’s worth”.For the fact remains that we are time-trapped creatures, forever casting back to the past and projecting forward to an imagined future, refusing to live in the reality of now. For this reason, our meagre deaths tend to arrive like an unexpected insult, a monstrous unfairness that we weren’t expecting. Eagleton is consoling here about the fact that when death arrives we probably won’t say the right or splendid thing. Thomas’s final words were apparently “the End is in Eden” which, as Eagleton tartly points out, is just one more of the old windbag’s “metaphysical vacuities”.As far as deathbed utterance goes, better instead to recall Steve Jobs’s less prescriptive “Oh wow. Oh wow. Oh wow”, which doesn’t strain for “sham grandeur” and leaves the listener free to fill in the blank according to their own fantasies. Personally, I’ve always liked to imagine that Jobs was being shown a vision of a heavenly Apple store, with serried ranks of angels in cobalt-coloured T-shirts tip-tapping away on futuristic Macs.A Death of One’s Own is in no sense an argument about its subject or even a sustained inquiry into death’s terrors and odd consolations. Instead, Eagleton lets his capacious mind, vast reading and wicked wit loose over the whole business of arriving at a full stop. In his introduction he explains that he has included ideas and individuals that have been central to his “spiritual and intellectual life” of the past six decades. Marx, Freud and cradle Catholicism are all invited to troop on stage to take a final bow “before the curtain comes down”. I found that the best way to read this book, which is undeniably dense, is to take in a bit each night before going to sleep, that “little death” from which, God willing, we awake refreshed each morning.A Death of One’s Own: Reflections on Mortality by Terry Eagleton is published by Yale (£18.99). To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. title: ‘Ruin and decay bring a chance of rebirth’: Hidetaka Miyazaki on uniting players in a damaged world | Games | The Guardian
description: As FromSoftware’s new multiplayer game The Duskbloods nears release, the legendary game director behind Dark Souls talks connection, pessimism and of course, feet
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: As FromSoftware’s new multiplayer game The Duskbloods nears release, the legendary game director behind Dark Souls talks connection, pessimism and of course, feet
Content: ‘Of all the things Miyazaki and his team do well, creating a sense of mystery is the greatest’ … The Duskbloods.Photograph: NintendoView image in fullscreen‘Of all the things Miyazaki and his team do well, creating a sense of mystery is the greatest’ … The Duskbloods.Photograph: NintendoGamesInterview‘Ruin and decay bring a chance of rebirth’: Hidetaka Miyazaki on uniting players in a damaged worldKirk McKeandAs FromSoftware’s new multiplayer game The Duskbloods nears release, the legendary game director behind Dark Souls talks connection, pessimism and of course, feetThu 3 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 12.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSince 2009’s Demon’s Souls, Japanese video game director Hidetaka Miyazaki has shown the world a different way to think about game design. His games defy convention with punishing fights, obscure rules, and unknowable, inhospitable worlds. The “Soulslike” genre – named afterDemon’s Soulsand its sequelDark Souls– is now ubiquitous, influencing multimillion-sellers from God of War and Star Wars: Jedi to Hollow Knight. Miyazaki’s most recent success, 2022’sElden Ring, which credited Game of Thrones author George RR Martin as a co-creator, sold over 30m copies and inspired Alex Garland to adapt it for the big screen at A24. It earned Miyazaki a spot on Time magazine’s “most influential” list, an accolade he shares with just one other game developer: Mario creator Shigeru Miyamoto.Miyazaki is now 51 and has been FromSoftware’s president since 2014, elevated from game designer to CEO after the success of the Souls series. He has a cherubic face that could pass for 35. He rarely speaks publicly, and never on camera. When he does speak, he answers questions like one of his characters – softly, sadly, his head bowed, making eye-contact only when I am speaking. Outside the studio where we speak is the sprawl of Tokyo’s Shinjuku, an ever-changing maze where tourists get lost and pop-up stores appear and vanish without a trace. Today, a J-pop band performs in the square as the cicadas scream from the trees. A gilded statue of Malania, one of Elden Ring’s toughest bosses, looms over this dimly lit conference room inside From’s headquarters, a bonfire checkpoint away from the chaos.View image in fullscreenHe creates an ‘atmosphere of wonder’ … Hidetaka Miyazaki accepts a Bafta games award for Elden Ring in 2023.Photograph: Stuart Wilson/Bafta/Getty Images for BaftaFromSoftware’s in-game universes are filled with clues – enemies, places and scraps of information from item descriptions paint a vague image of the world, and the player fills the blank space. You never fully understand these domains, although countless YouTube video game theorists have tried – as have other developers in awe of his work. “Of all the many things Miyazaki and his team do well, creating a sense of mystery is the greatest,” explains Dishonored directorHarvey Smith, who has more than 40 days’ playtime in Elden Ring. “It’s so incredibly hard to do in video games, which are technical systems … But Miyazaki somehow creates an atmosphere of wonder. Even when finishing, you are left ruminating on fun, murky elements that feel half understood. It’s a delicious sense of intrigue.”Rather than the single-player action game that Miyazaki’s audience craves (fans are desperate for a sequel to his 2015 gothic masterpiece Bloodborne,for instance), hislatest project The Duskbloodsis a multiplayer Switch 2 exclusive. Eight players face off against ghoulish horrors, fighting each other to avoid being culled at the end of each round. The survivors are whittled down over three phases culminating in a final three-way battle. The Duskbloods is releasing to an audience with shifting tastes and trends, and it is certainly a risk. “I’m very nervous,” Miyazaki says. “With every title we release there is this mounting tension.”The game opens with an arresting image: one hand reaching out for another. A male character is slumped on a chair, dejected; the shot moves in close to focus on their draped fingers. From below the frame, a pale hand slowly reaches out and caresses them before gently clasping his wrist. Hands are a recurring motif in Miyazaki’s games; in Elden Ring, massive crawling hands burrow up from underground to attack you, and hand-like giants are revered as deities.“It’s not necessarily something I’m consistently aware of – maybe it’s something subconscious coming through,” Miyazaki says when I ask about this imagery. “Take a look online and there’s a rumour that I have a bit of a thing for feet, but I’m not honestly sure where this comes from. I feel like I’m trying to depict some side of human nature or the human existence that is difficult to describe.” (His games have featured, by my count, at least six barefoot female characters.)View image in fullscreen‘It’s rumoured I have a bit of a thing for feet’ … Elden Ring Nightreign.Photograph: Bandai NamcoPerhaps all the hands and feet are symbolic of human connection. One hand reaches for another; bare feet connect skin with earth.Miyazaki has been exploring that theme since Demon’s Souls, whose novel, stranger-centric multiplayer was inspired by a time his car slipped on an icy hill and a stranger helped to push him to safety. In Demon’s Souls and the Dark Souls series, players paint runes on the ground, which other players can then use to summon help in a fight, creating moments of spontaneous togetherness before an inevitable parting.While The Duskbloods primarily puts players in opposition, it also explores temporary alliances and conflicting objectives, buoyed by Miyazaki’s love for tabletop role-playing games and board games. Players can even become betrothed to each other, forming an alliance. “I feel it’s less a traditional romance and more a sense of secure trust with a character in the world, and that’s something I personally yearn for,” he says. “It’s not necessarily a romantic pairing – it’s having someone that you can ultimately rely on. This concept is carried through from characters like the maidens in Elden Ring … it’s a transient, ephemeral love, which is maybe a motif I’m striving for.”The Duskbloods is preoccupied with ruin and rebirth, a thematic cornerstone of From’s games – much as Godzilla was a product of nuclear paranoia in Japan. Even as Miyazaki and I talk, a deadly magnitude 6.8 earthquake hits the Kumamoto prefecture on Kyushu island, a thousand miles away. If the very ground beneath your feet is unreliable, that can shape your outlook on life, a concept explored extensively in Japanese literature and entertainment, recently on the hit television showShōgun.“[Ruin and rebirth] is an ongoing theme in a lot of my games, I realise,” Miyazaki says. “That theme on a cosmological scale applies to The Duskbloods as an interesting philosophical area to explore.”View image in fullscreen‘If we have two ideas of a brighter or dark future, I would tend to sway towards the darker one,’ …Bloodborne.Photograph: Sony Computer EntertainmentMiyazaki describes himself as a pessimist, a tendency that he believes comes across in his output. That should be obvious to anyone who’s finished any of his games, in which you keep throwing body and blade against seemingly impossible odds, reborn each time you die at a bonfire checkpoint, to try again. Even when you triumph, nothing ultimately seems to change: these games culminate in bleak, morally ambiguous gut-punches, leaving you not as a conquering hero but as the perpetuator of a hopeless cycle. “If we have two ideas of a brighter or dark future, I would tend to sway towards the darker one,” Miyazaki says. “[But] if you explore the ruin and the decay in those worlds, it also lets you explore some chance of rebirth, and I think having that tiny pinprick of light or hope can be something beautiful, something fleeting.”Sekiro, Dark Souls, Bloodborne, and Elden Ring are all separate series, but they share the same bones. They’re reborn in different forms, to explore fresh ideas, places and perspectives while still playing, feeling and sounding like a FromSoftware game. While it’s immediately clear The Duskbloods is a Miyazaki game, it too wears a different skin, inspired by extraction shooters like Escape from Tarkov and those tabletop role-playing games the director loves. “There’s no intentional FromSoftware [mantra] – ‘this is the way we make our games’ – because if you start to do that it becomes stale and conservative, and you start having to adhere to a set of rules and philosophies, and it just doesn’t become interesting, you can’t make anything that’s as fun,” Miyazaki says.“So I feel like at least what’s worked for us philosophically is trying to adhere to what we find interesting first. I think that has created a good throughline through our games, and that’s what we concentrate on to [conceive] a new title.”Back in his early days at the studio, when he was only a coder on the Armored Core series of games, Miyazaki volunteered to take on a struggling project at From – the game that would become Demon’s Souls. (The game was already in trouble, so he felt he had nothing to lose.) He changed everything about the game, and then the game changed everything about his life, as he climbed from coder to company president. From failure was born a game that changed the landscape of video games. Ruin and rebirth.But does Miyazaki think he has changed? “I don’t intend to,” he says, a smile curling on his lips. “But I probably have.”This article was amended on 3 September 2026 to correct the release year of the original Demon’s Souls.Explore more on these topicsGamesAction gamesRole playing gamesinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I was never taught Welsh history’: Michael Sheen on reclaiming rebel leader Owain Glyndŵr  | Michael Sheen | The Guardian
description: Actor will play 15th-century hero in sweeping production about Welsh rebellion against English crown
Author: Steven Morris
Headline: Actor will play 15th-century hero in sweeping production about Welsh rebellion against English crown
Content: Michael Sheen at the Wales Millennium Centre, Cardiff. One of the actor’s main reasons for staging Owain & Henry is because Glyndŵr’s story has never been told on an epic scale.Photograph: Dimitris Legakis/Athena PicturesView image in fullscreenMichael Sheen at the Wales Millennium Centre, Cardiff. One of the actor’s main reasons for staging Owain & Henry is because Glyndŵr’s story has never been told on an epic scale.Photograph: Dimitris Legakis/Athena PicturesMichael SheenInterview‘I was never taught Welsh history’: Michael Sheen on reclaiming rebel leader Owain GlyndŵrSteven MorrisActor will play 15th-century hero in sweeping production about Welsh rebellion against English crownThu 3 Sep 2026 02.17 EDTFirst published on Thu 3 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere are myriad films, plays and books focusing on heroes of English, Scottish and Irish history but far fewer that tell the stories of the great figures ofWales.A major new play about the Welsh nobleman Owain Glyndŵr’s early 15th-century rebellion against the English crown will help redress the balance this autumn.Michael Sheen, who will play Glyndŵr, said one of the main rationales for staging the show was simply that the rebel leader’s story had never before been told on such a large scale.“We’re talking about a figurevoted the second most important Welsh person of all time, only behind Aneurin Bevan [the architect of the NHS],” Sheen said. “But nobody’s ever done anything about him on this scale before. That tells a story in itself.”Sheen said when growing up in south Wales he had not been taught about Glyndŵr’s rebellion against Henry IV. “He meant absolutely nothing. I was never taught about him. He’s in the cultural collective consciousness so at some point I became aware of his name but I knew nothing about his story,” he said.“I was never taught Welsh history. It wasn’t on the curriculum. And again, that tells you something.”View image in fullscreenMichael Sheen said Owain Glyndŵr was in the cultural collective consciousness but he had known little about his story.Photograph: Dimitris Legakis/Athena PicturesOwain & Henry, will be performed at the Donald Gordon theatre atWales Millennium Centre, the second biggest stage in Europe, by Sheen’s fledgling company,Welsh National Theatre.The Millennium Centre is also co-producing the play.Sheen said there were very few ambitious, large-scale Welsh plays written for big theatre spaces. “For most Welsh playwrights, the reality of getting your play produced is that you probably have to write for a studio space. Maybe a couple of weeks’ run. And maybe a cast of maybe two or three. Beyond that, it becomes very difficult.”Sheen said the Olivier award-winning Welsh playwright Gary Owen had only felt able to create a sweeping version of the Glyndŵr story when the pandemic seemed to make it unlikely that it would ever be produced.He said: “During Covid, during the lockdown, he thought, no one’s going to ever see this play anyway, so I might as well write it the way I want to write it.”View image in fullscreenA painting of Owain Glyndŵr in battle by AC Michael.Photograph: Lordprice Collection/AlamySheen described Glyndŵr as a very unlikely rebel. “He was born into privilege. He inherited estates. He worked in the service of English noblemen. Fought on behalf of the English king, Richard II, in Scotland. Fought against the French. He was taught at the Inns of Court.“But then he got into a land dispute with his neighbour [the Englishman Reginald de Grey]. And this land dispute grew and grew and grew until eventually he was essentially being called a traitor.“He wasn’t the big crusading rebel leader. He found himself in a position where he had to fight back, otherwise really bad things were going to happen for him and his family. So he was sort of forced into it.”Sheen said he thought the Glyndŵr story, which will be performed in English, was relevant today. “Just putting it on is important, I think, but also the story is a kind of catalyst for a conversation that we very much need to have at the moment.”Earlier this year, the Welsh nationalist partyPlaid Cymru won the Welsh Senedd electionsin spectacular fashion, ending 100 years of Labour rule in Wales.It means that two governments – the devolved Plaid Welsh administration and the Labour UK government – have a say in the life of Welsh citizens.Sheen said: “The old has been swept away. And the immediate future of Wales is essentially in the hands of two very different visions of what it is to be Welsh, what Welsh identity is, what Welsh nationhood can be.“This play speaks to that absolutely. Even though we’re talking about events in the early 1400s, it speaks to us right now in a more urgent way than I could ever have imagined.View image in fullscreenOwain & Henry will be staged at the Donald Gordon theatre at the Wales Millennium Centre from 5 November.Photograph: Geography Photos/Universal Images Group/Getty“But also beyond Wales, it’s looking at what is it to be a leader? What is leadership? What is a responsible use of power? Is might right? They’re all things that feel very, alive right now.”Sheen said Glyndŵr’s world was a brutal one. “It was a world where everything was changing. You’ve got a man on the throne [Henry IV] where there are questions of legitimacy around him. And therefore there is a kind of febrile nature to the politics of that time. It feels very of now where the political floor is shifting all the time.”Sheen said it was “early days” for the new Plaid government. He has invited the Welsh administration toengage with him over the dumping of toxic waste in Wales, a subject the actor has highlighted in a documentary.Buried With Michael Sheen review – this vital look at a toxic waste scandal is deeply enraging TVRead more“But as yet, that has not happened. There’s also been a lot of talk about wanting to support the arts. But, you know, we’ll see what happens. This is the thing, isn’t it? When you actually get into power, then it’s not about talk any more, it’s about doing stuff.”Does he hope that Welsh ministers will come and watch the play? “Oh, they will come and watch it. It’ll ask a lot of questions. This is not in any way a sort of cloaked support for any particular party. It’s about values and beliefs, but they’ll come and watch it.”Owain & Henry is atWales Millennium Centre, 5-28 NovemberExplore more on these topicsMichael SheenWalesHeritageTheatreCardiffActinginterviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Finally, a victory for the middle-aged white man!’ Chris Cantrill on winning the Edinburgh comedy award | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: The ex-marketing manager’s win, for his spoof Sycamore Gap-inspired whodunnit Rewilding, arrives just as he’s gearing up for a new season of hit sketch show SNL UK – which he calls ‘the hardest job of my life’
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: The ex-marketing manager’s win, for his spoof Sycamore Gap-inspired whodunnit Rewilding, arrives just as he’s gearing up for a new season of hit sketch show SNL UK – which he calls ‘the hardest job of my life’
Content: ‘In my head, I’m a plucky young upstart still’ … Chris Cantrill.Photograph: Rebecca Need-MenearView image in fullscreen‘In my head, I’m a plucky young upstart still’ … Chris Cantrill.Photograph: Rebecca Need-MenearEdinburgh festival 2026Interview‘Finally, a victory for the middle-aged white man!’ Chris Cantrill on winning the Edinburgh comedy awardBrian LoganThe ex-marketing manager’s win, for his spoof Sycamore Gap-inspired whodunnit Rewilding, arrives just as he’s gearing up for a new season of hit sketch show SNL UK – which he calls ‘the hardest job of my life’Thu 3 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 09.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor the last month, Chris Cantrill has been performinghis fringe show Rewildingdaily in a lunchtime slot. And yet, when we plan to speak about hisvictory in the Edinburgh comedy awards, the interview is arranged – on the festival’s penultimate day – for lunchtime. Can he really have won the fringe’s major prize, and – hell of a mic drop, this – immediately sacked off his last two shows? “I couldn’t be happier not to be at the festival today,” he says, on video call from his Northumberland home. But the cancellation, it transpires, is long-standing, because work starts immediately post-fringe on the new series ofSNL UK, for which he writes.“But I’m absolutely over the moon not to be doing my show right now,” he admits. “I’ve got a lot of adrenaline in my body slowly seeping out, and I feel like I’ve been hit by a train.” The Edinburgh comedy award (it used to be the Perrier, and was won in the past by Steve Coogan, The League of Gentlemen and Frank Skinner) has been a long time coming for Bradford-born Cantrill. This year’s was his fourth nomination, twice as a solo act, and twice as part of his duoThe Delightful Sausage, alongside2024 winner Amy Gledhill. He is, as I tease him when we speak, a comparatively senior winner, the oldest since Bridget Christie, also 42, 13 years ago. “Finally, a victory for the middle-aged white man!,” he retorts, then bursts into laughter. “Common sense at last!”View image in fullscreenChris Cantrill performing Rewilding at the 2026 Edinburgh fringe.Photograph: Jack Kirby“But in my head, I’m a plucky young upstart still.” And you can see why. Cantrill didn’t take up comedy until he was 28, having “worked in an office as a marketing manager. I wasn’t a good fit for that.” He sidelined as a comedian, but was going nowhere fast when in 2016 his first child was born. By way of a last resort, he then asked Gledhill whether she fancied “trying something a little bit different” – and The Delightful Sausage came into being. This raucous and surreal double act, a slacker northern Mighty Boosh, was Cantrill’s unlikely meal ticket, a mates-having-a-laugh confection that went unexpectedly mainstream. “We used to come to Edinburgh and hang out with comics we knew from Glasgow, Newcastle, the regions. Then we started getting nominated [for the award] and found ourselves in the orbit of switched-on, ruthlessly ambitious, twentysomethings. I remember thinking, ‘oh God, that’s a bit intense, isn’t it?’”Cantrill has always styled himself an outsider, speaking (whenthe Guardian interviewed The Delightful Sausage in 2022) about his hard-to-shake impostor syndrome. One might think winning the award, againstfellow nominees including Lara Ricote and upcoming Last One Laughing star Harriet Dyer, would put paid to that self-image. But Cantrill doesn’t see it that way. Edinburgh’s comedy awards, he says, “have undoubtedly altered the trajectory of my life. Being nominated took me from part-time while working in an office to doing comedy full-time.” But winning won’t be transformative. “What this means is that when I send an email, there’s 30% more chance someone will respond to it. If I’m working on other stuff, it might move that stuff forward slightly more favourably.”View image in fullscreen‘Oh God, that’s a bit intense’ … Cantrill performing with Amy Gledhill as The Delightful Sausage.Photograph: James Darcey / J Darcey imagesThe show for which Cantrill won the prize, meanwhile, seems designed to confirm the Yorkshireman as a fish out of water. Rewilding continues the story of his move to rural Northumberland, first related in2024’s Easily Swayed. In this year’s show, we meet fellow residents of the fictionalised “Gaskill village” as an act of vandalism is perpetrated on a local landmark. The tale, a thinly veiled take on the global outrage caused bythe felling of the Sycamore Gap tree, becomes a spoof whodunnit, in which Cantrill, a city boy still adapting to countryside life – not to mention a child trapped in a grown man’s body – plays a key role.Rewilding is about “how I observed that [Sycamore Gap story] at a grassroots WhatsApp level,” says Cantrill. “I just thought it was fascinating.” How do such incidents affect communities – and why do we care so much about trees? “One of them [ie the two men convicted of the crime] was obsessed with it. From when he was a kid, he had a string that measured the circumference of it. Then when he got arrested, he said, ‘it’s just a tree’. And I was like, you wouldn’t have driven through the night in a storm to cut it down if you thought it was just a tree that had a no effect on anyone.”Cantrill trialled the show in front of his fellow villagers, many of them depicted in it. “They like laughing at themselves,” he reports. “Hopefully the comedy award doesn’t change their perspective on it, and I’ll be hearing from their lawyers soon.” Taken as a pair, the two city-boy-in-the-country shows feel like a sitcom in utero – but Cantrill is cautious of that thinking. (A long-planned Delightful Sausage sitcom has yet to come to fruition.) One benefit of being older when success comes your way, he says, is that you enjoy the moment rather than fret about next steps. “There’s this award. There’s me and Amy working on a show for BBC Radio 4 [Icklewick FM] and it’s the most joy of my life. So I’m just trying to be like: this is happening now for a bit, let’s savour it.”View image in fullscreen‘This needs to end, whatever the decision’ … Chris Cantrill, seventh from left, with the writers for Saturday Night Live UK in March.Photograph: Saturday Night Live UK/PAThere’s also SNL UK, whose success has been a huge boon to British comedy – and to which Sky TV recently committed long-term. When the creative team was first assembled, Cantrill recalls, “I went in for a casting, I went in as a writer, I submitted a tape. Then I did a showcase in Soho theatre, then several screen tests. And they kept going, ‘Can you come back and do it again?’ Eventually I said to the producer, ‘it’s been lovely seeing you every three weeks for the last six months. But this needs to end, whatever the decision.’” It ended with a writing job that he now describes as “great”, but also “the hardest of my life”.“They started by giving us ‘corporate resilience training’,” says Cantrill, wrinkling his nose: “about how to stay resilient in a pressured environment. And I remember saying toJonno [head writer Daran Johnson], ‘I’m a veteran performer. I donotneed resilience training.’ And then we did the first read-through, and my sketch either was cut or completely died. I’ve had both happen to me. And I turned to Jonno and said, ‘Please, can I have a top-up of the resilience training?’” It’s a competitive environment, in short, with no guarantee your work will ever make it to the screen.“I’ve always been hard on myself. At no point do Amy and I ever think we’re good and comfortable with our comedy. So SNL has been challenging.” But it’s also been “the closest thing I’ve done to what you think in your head the job [of comedy writing] will be. It’s sort of magical.” And off he goes on a rhapsody about filming SNL, the glamour of “storming around Television Centre, dressed as Victorians”, changing Riz Ahmed’s lines at the last minute, arranging cue cards, conferring with the director. “It feels like you’re in a film. It’s a rush.”View image in fullscreen‘Just surreal’ … Cantrill collects his Edinburgh comedy awardPhotograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianSNL also changed his experience of the fringe – in ways that surely spell the end for his outsider self-image. “I was part of a two-person team for years, and it was a closed shop. We’d work relentlessly and never see anyone else’s shows. But suddenly because of SNL, I’ve got all these wayward children all over the city. I’m going to see [SNL co-writers]Bella [Hull]andAyo [Adenekan]andOmar [Badawy], and I’m so invested in their success. It’s a really nice feeling.”In one of the funniest sections of Rewilding, Cantrill makes indiscreet jokes about SNL, teasing that its cast may not be “one big happy family”, and that his relationship is strained with the “private schoolboys” who run the show. But that’s just him being “a little cheeky boy”, he now tells me. “I do still feel on the outside of things. When I meet the upper echelons of the taste-makers, to those people, with my accent, I do sound basically like Kes.”“But I’m old enough to know what an opportunity looks like. So, when something like this pops up, it’s time to knuckle down and make the most of it.” That knuckling down, on season two of SNL, begins the day after we speak – leaving just 24 hours more to process the dream-come-true of winning the Edinburgh comedy award. “On no level have I processed it yet. It just happened yesterday. My phone has melted. My wife is keeping an eye on all the messages. I completely lost it on stage at my last performance and it all caught up with me. It was just surreal.” But Cantrill has been round the block too many times to get carried away. “I’ll be back in SNL dying on my arse on Wednesday, having a script read to silence,” he says. “And I can’t wait.”This article was amended on 3 September. A caption wrongly described Chris Cantrill’s comedy partner Amy Gledhill as his wife.Explore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Comedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)Edinburgh festivalinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Present Laughter review – gender-switched Coward comedy dazzles in 70s New York | Stage | The Guardian
description: Antihero actor Garry becomes a magnificent new kind of beast as Gerri, played with blistering hilarity by Tracy-Ann Oberman
Author: Mark Lawson
Headline: Antihero actor Garry becomes a magnificent new kind of beast as Gerri, played with blistering hilarity by Tracy-Ann Oberman
Content: Peter McKintosh’s Manhattan loft design has walls decorated with  mock-Warhols.Photograph: Simon AnnandView image in fullscreenPeter McKintosh’s Manhattan loft design has walls decorated with  mock-Warhols.Photograph: Simon AnnandGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.StageReviewPresent Laughter review – gender-switched Coward comedy dazzles in 70s New YorkTheatre Royal BathAntihero actor Garry becomes a magnificent new kind of beast as Gerri, played with blistering hilarity by Tracy-Ann ObermanMark LawsonThu 3 Sep 2026 08.08 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 08.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe reputation of Noël Coward’s plays has involved escaping restrictions: his recorded clipped, waspish tone in key roles and a perception that, at a time when gay men’s careers and lives were at risk, the dramatist could not be socially and emotionally truthful.Seven years ago, in an Old Vic revival of Coward’s 1942 off-stage comedy Present Laughter, Andrew Scott – as actor Garry Essendine, a gorgon of priapic self-importance – memorably banished the parodic playing style and probed forbidden subtext. Changing Joanna, one of Garry’s love interests, into Joe made characters bisexual or in sham marriages.That seemed the limit of new life to be found in the play, especially as Matthew Warchus’s production survives in the NationalTheatreat Home archive. But the Coward estate has authorised a differently radical transformation directed by Lindsay Posner, starting an appetising national tour in Bath.View image in fullscreen‘The adaptation’s primary purpose is expanding the classical canon for women’ … Tracy-Ann Oberman and Seb Carrington.Photograph: Simon AnnandGarry is now Geri, an actress-singer played by Tracy-Ann Oberman, who previously feminised Shylock in The Merchant of Venice. Whereas Garry had a fantasy of playing Peer Gynt, Geri’s Ibsen vanity is being cast as Hedda Gabler. As dramaturg, Oberman reverses six other characters, with Essendine’s secretary morphing from Monica to Monty, and the ex-spouse being Len not Liz.These re-gendered characters also have a new calendar and atlas, moving from mid 20th century London to New York in the 1970s (Studio 54 has just opened). Peter McKintosh’s Manhattan loft design has walls decorated with mock-Warhols of the star and a poster for a cabaret show called Geri With a G, a nod to Ms Minnelli’s recent Liza With a Z. Coward’s ghastly avant garde playwright Roland Maule is here Rosina, an intense cross-genre experimentalist for whose work no theatre is far enough off-Broadway.View image in fullscreen‘Oberman poignantly recalls 70s American power women Dolly Parton and Farrah Fawcett’.Photograph: Simon AnnandMultiple line revisions interestingly reflect the sexism of language. Whereas Garry was rather admired as a “cad”, Geri is denigrated as a “cow”, although, stingingly, his disparagement of women as “bitches” stays in her mouth. Local and time references are smoothly retooled: Maule comes not from Uckfield but Yonkers and Essendine’s impending trip to take culture to the colonies bypasses Coward’s rather patronised “Africa” for “Australia”. The equivalent of Garry’s terror of soon requiring toupees is Geri’s fear of needing work on her face.These translations are not as politically powerful as allowing Garry to be gay, although the time shift is vital because no 1940s showbiz woman could have been as sexually ruthless as Geri.The adaptation’s primary purpose, though, is expanding the classical canon for women. Oberman, playing an actor less good than she thinks, makes it hard to think of many better than her, surpassing even last year’s Hampstead turn as a rude, ruthless matriarch over 20 years in Richard Greenberg’sThe Assembled Parties.In a sequinned pantsuit fighting teeth for maximum dazzle – blond tresses piled as high as the platform shoes that make even funnier the running in the farcical finale – Oberman poignantly recalls 70s American power women Dolly Parton and Farrah Fawcett (both painted by Warhol) in a performance that vocally samples Coward’s clicky diction. James Dreyfus’s enjoyable Monty is, like Lear’s Fool, alone licensed to speak truth to the tyrant. The show is, paradoxically, a daring Coward.AtTheatre Royal Bathuntil 5 September,then touring.Explore more on these topicsStageTheatreTheatre Royal BathNoel CowardreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Martin McDonagh says CIA has ‘done awful things all around the world’ | Movies | The Guardian
description: McDonagh’s new film, Wild Horse Nine, stars John Malkovich as an agent in 1970s Chile who feels ‘guilt and regret’ over his role in global interventions
Author: Philip Oltermann
Headline: McDonagh’s new film, Wild Horse Nine, stars John Malkovich as an agent in 1970s Chile who feels ‘guilt and regret’ over his role in global interventions
Content: ‘We don’t question the CIA’s activity as much as we ought to’ … Martin McDonagh, centre, in Venice with Wild Horse Nine stars Sam Rockwell and John Malkovich.Photograph: Anthony Harvey/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘We don’t question the CIA’s activity as much as we ought to’ … Martin McDonagh, centre, in Venice with Wild Horse Nine stars Sam Rockwell and John Malkovich.Photograph: Anthony Harvey/ShutterstockMoviesMartin McDonagh says CIA has ‘done awful things all around the world’McDonagh’s new film, Wild Horse Nine, stars John Malkovich as an agent in 1970s Chile who feels ‘guilt and regret’ over his role in global interventionsPhilip Oltermannin VeniceThu 3 Sep 2026 10.21 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 10.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US’s history of intervening in democratic processes around the world deserves more attention in the light of current political developments, playwright and film-makerMartin McDonaghhas said, as his Oscar-tipped film about a rueful CIA agent premieres at the Venice film festival.“I’ve been very interested in the truth of what the CIA has been doing over the last 60 years, and the awful things they’ve done all around the world,” McDonagh said about Wild Horse Nine, his first film since his 2022 tragicomedyThe Banshees of Inisherin.“I think maybe something that’s not talked about enough. We know what the KGB are like, but we probably don’t question the CIA’s activity as much as we ought to.”In Wild Horse Nine,John Malkovichplays Chris, a veteran agent for the foreign intelligence service who is stationed in Santiago, Chile, on the eve of the US-supported coup against Salvador Allende – Latin America’s first democratically elected Marxist president – in 1973. Recently diagnosed with cancer and acting erratically, Chris is dispatched to Easter Island with his protege Lee (Sam Rockwell), where he starts to reflect critically on his role in other CIA interventions, including the Guatemalan coup d’état of 1954, the 1961 assassination of revolutionary Congolese prime minister Patrice Lumumba and – according to the film’s telling – the killing of John F Kennedy.View image in fullscreen‘Sadder and darker’ … John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell in Wild Horse Nine.Photograph: Diego Araya Corvalán/Searchlight PicturesMcDonagh said he had originally set out writing a screenplay about a father and son who were both actors, but the story had only started to gel when he tied the story to theCIAoverthrow of Allende. “I realised that the story could be about a guy who [feels] guilt and regret about the things he has done,” he said. “It took it away from something a bit corny to somewhere much sadder and darker.”As well as Rockwell and Malkovich, who has already been tipped as an Oscar contender for his leading turn, Wild Horse Nine stars Steve Buscemi, Parker Posey and Tom Waits.double quotation markOne of the frightening things is that they don’t seem to be making it covert any moreMcDonagh on US in VenezuelaAsked at the press conference what they thought of the Trump administration’s illegal capturing of Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro in January, the US members of the cast looked reluctant to answer. “I can’t think any more,” said Malkovich.London-born Irish national McDonagh took over the mic instead. “I think, for me, one of the frightening things is that they don’t seem to be making it covert any more, which is very strange,” he said. “Like in the 70s, at least these horrible people had the intelligence to keep their acts secret, but it just feels like things are getting stupider and stupider and stupider.”“When I wrote the film and we made it, it was to talk about 1973 and Chile at that point,” McDonagh added. “But watching it now, it does feel like it does seem to have a bit of a commentary on present day geopolitics.”Explore more on these topicsFilmVenice film festivalMartin McDonaghJohn MalkovichCIASam RockwellFestivalsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Margaret Preston: Australia’s most beloved and contested artist? | Australian art | The Guardian
description: The Ian Potter Centre: NGV Australia has staged the first Preston retrospective in 20 years, exploring what was gained and flattened in her quest to create a singular Australian aesthetic
Author: Oliver Giles
Headline: The Ian Potter Centre: NGV Australia has staged the first Preston retrospective in 20 years, exploring what was gained and flattened in her quest to create a singular Australian aesthetic
Content: Margaret Preston’s Self-Portrait, 1930, oil on canvasView image in fullscreenMargaret Preston’s Self-Portrait, 1930, oil on canvasAustralian artMargaret Preston: Australia’s most beloved and contested artist?The Ian Potter Centre: NGV Australia has staged the first Preston retrospective in 20 years, exploring what was gained and flattened in her quest to create a singular Australian aestheticOliver GilesThu 3 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 20.03 EDTShareHanging at the entrance of the new Margaret Preston exhibition at the National Gallery of Victoria are three of her instantly recognisable still lifes. Each depicts a vase brimming with native flora: bell-shaped gumnuts, silvery eucalyptus leaves and bristly banksias. These are identifiably Australian plants, painted in what might be described as an Australian style, reflecting Preston’s lifelong ambition to define a national aesthetic. Look more closely, though, and this simplistic story begins to unravel.View image in fullscreenNative Honeysuckle, 1933, oil on canvasHer 1928 painting Western Australian Gum Blossom features a blocky background of creamy rectangles that gesture to the modernist and abstract movements that were flourishing in Europe at the time, as well as the flattened forms of Japanese woodblock prints. The black and white geometry of the second work, Native Honeysuckle, echoes cubist paintings by the French artist Fernand Léger. And all three point to Preston’s interest in Indigeneity, a fascination intertwined with her appreciation and appropriation of Aboriginal art.“Preston was working towards a unified art for Australia,” says Michael Gentle, the NGV’s former curator of Australian and First Nations art, who co-curated the exhibition alongside Beckett Rozentals, the gallery’s senior curator ofAustralian art.“That was her mandate, yet it was saturated with contradictions because she’s actively pulling from multiple sources.”This paradox lies at the heart of this retrospective, the first dedicated to Preston in more than 20 years. Featuring more than 200 of her works – including three long-lost paintings the NGV tracked down through a public appeal – as well as pieces by her peers and contemporary artists responding to her, the show takes you on a loosely chronological journey through the artist’s life.View image in fullscreenThe three paintings at the entrance to the exhibition.Photograph: Phoebe PowellAlong the way, it navigates the tangled web of what she wanted her work to be, what it actually became and why it remains both beloved and contested as a symbol of Australian identity today.Preston was born in Port Adelaide in 1875. Her family later moved to Sydney, then, as Preston’s talent became apparent, toMelbourneso she could enrol in the National Gallery of Victoria Art School in her late teens. Stories of her student days reveal the confidence that would characterise her throughout her life; the artist Hans Heysen remembered Preston positioning herself right in front of a model in a life-drawing class, irritating her peers, most of whom were men.View image in fullscreenAn early Preston, titled Still Life, from 1901 …View image in fullscreen… and her 1927 still life, Implement Blue, after her time in EuropeTall tales: the gumtree in art – in picturesRead moreHer devotion to still life painting also set her apart at a time when landscape painting was considered the pinnacle of artistic achievement in Australia. Several early paintings demonstrate Preston’s skill at bringing sedate scenes to life. A gleaming glass bowl full of unblemished eggs sits next to a cracked shell oozing a sticky yolk. Milk pools from an upended jug. Onions appear to dance across a kitchen surface, as though they have just been poured out of a bag. “One of our art handlers said, ‘I love this one. You can almost smell the onions cooking,’” Rozentals says.The following rooms trace how Preston’s style developed during two formative trips to Europe, the first from 1904 to 1906 and the second from 1912 to 1919. In London, Paris and the many other cities she visited, she encountered the latest developments in modernism, Fauvism, post-impressionism and the Arts and Crafts movement, among others.View image in fullscreenAboriginal Flowers, 1928, oil on canvasThese discoveries transformed Preston’s art. Upon returning home, she began incorporating techniques she’d learnt overseas into her work, becoming a local authority on woodblock printmaking. At the same time, she started publishing essays that articulated her desire to create a unique Australian style. She shifted her focus to capturing local flora and, less famously, urban scenes, shown here in a selection of striking Sydney cityscapes.View image in fullscreenMosman Bay, Sydney Harbour, circa 1927As she strove to create a singular Australian aesthetic, Preston embarked on what is now her most contentious practice: her appropriation ofIndigenous art. Her vocal admiration of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander art was unusual in a period when it was often dismissed as a curio for tourists, or exhibited in ethnographic museums rather than galleries. But “she specifically asked people not to consider the spiritual, cultural or ceremonial significance”, Gentle says. Having divorced Aboriginal art from its context, Preston inserted elements from it into her work, flattening and assimilating hundreds of Indigenous cultures into her nationalist project.View image in fullscreenAboriginal Still Life, 1940, oil on canvasHere, the chronological journey is interrupted by the restaging of a display from the Documenta 13 exhibition in Germany in 2012, where the Birri Gubba and Darumbal artist Gordon Bennett showed paintings from his series Home Décor (After M Preston). These were dramatic enlargements of small gouaches by Preston that featured Indigenous designs she had taken from an Aboriginal shield with the intention of using them to decorate household items. Bennett’s reproductions tower over Preston’s paintings, exposing a chain of appropriation that runs through Australian art history to the present.View image in fullscreenPreston’s 1952 work The Expulsion 1952 (left), beside Tony Albert’s The Expulsion 2021 (right), in the exhibition.Photograph: Phoebe PowellConversations between Preston’s work and that of First Nations artists continue throughout the rest of the exhibition, which includes pieces by Trevor Nickolls, Deanne Gilson and Tony Albert, as well as new works commissioned from Marilyn Russell, Kaye Brown, Raelene Kerinauia Lampuwatu, Mary Elizabeth Moreen and Jimmy Frank. These artists rarely solely condemn or celebrate Preston but instead illuminate the complexity of her legacy as an advocate for Aboriginal art whose actions still have consequences today:Indigenous artcontinues to be used as visual shorthand to represent Australia across culture, entertainment and advertising.View image in fullscreenA selection of Preston’s largest works on display.Photograph: Phoebe PowellThe exhibition embraces this multiplicity of viewpoints, rather than declaring a definitive conclusion about Preston and her art. One of the few certainties that emerges is that Preston was intensely driven, which is palpable from her early still lifes right through to her late landscapes, and in painting after painting after painting of lush Australian flora. “She believed in herself and her vision and her art,” Rozentals says. “There were a lot more male artists at the time getting their moment in the sun. She was successful in her lifetime.”Preston’s works do not provide, however, the unified vision of Australia she hoped for. Ultimately, they tell a more interesting story: that Australian art and identity are rich and ever-changing tapestries of influences from across the country and around the world. That is even more true today than it was when Preston died in 1963, leaving behind a body of work that, more than 60 years later, prompts difficult questions but remains full of beauty.Margaret Preston is at the Ian Potter Centre: NGV Australiauntil 31 January 2027

title: ‘My work has always been serious’: Maurizio Cattelan on his $6m banana, his gold toilet – and bringing Hitler to Berlin | Maurizio Cattelan | The Guardian
description: He is famed for creating a golden loo that was stolen and a $6m banana that was eaten. But, says the sculptor ahead of a major new show in Germany, there’s more to his work than pranks and provocation
Author: Deborah Cole
Headline: He is famed for creating a golden loo that was stolen and a $6m banana that was eaten. But, says the sculptor ahead of a major new show in Germany, there’s more to his work than pranks and provocation
Content: ‘The problem is, people often stop at the joke’ … Maurizio Cattelan at the Neue Nationalgalerie in Berlin.Photograph: Christian Jungeblodt/the GuardianView image in fullscreen‘The problem is, people often stop at the joke’ … Maurizio Cattelan at the Neue Nationalgalerie in Berlin.Photograph: Christian Jungeblodt/the GuardianMaurizio CattelanInterview‘My work has always been serious’: Maurizio Cattelan on his $6m banana, his gold toilet – and bringing Hitler to BerlinDeborah Colein BerlinHe is famed for creating a golden loo that was stolen and a $6m banana that was eaten. But, says the sculptor ahead of a major new show in Germany, there’s more to his work than pranks and provocationThu 3 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 11.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMaurizio Cattelan, the art world’s merriest prankster, pauses when asked which object in his sprawling new Berlin show is most likely to be defaced, stolen or eaten, then emits a foghorn of a laugh. “There is no need to vandalise anything,” says the trim, soulful Italian, explaining that he has already taken care of all that, given how the work cuts villains, imposters and straw men down to size. “But,” he says, referring to the show’s more daring works, “maybe we need someone to resuscitate people.”Cattelan, who speaks in a lilting English, grins broadly, a mischievous glint in his brown eyes. Speaking on the subterranean level of Mies van der Rohe’s weightlessNeue Nationalgalerie(NNG) in Berlin, he darts between the impish and the profound in conversation, mirroring the dizzying range of his work. The silver-haired sculptor is best known for duct-taping a banana to a wall in 2019 and calling it Comedian, in a droll commentary on the excesses of the art market. The joke became even funnier when it sold for $6.2m, then hilarious when its buyer took abite out of his purchase and swallowed it.View image in fullscreenComedian, 2019, the $6.2m banana.Photograph: © 2025 Maurizio CattelanThere was also the gold toilet, called America, that was installed in New York’s Guggenheim in 2016, its curatorslater offering the piece to Donald Trump’s White Houseinstead of the Van Gogh that it requested.Thieves later made off withthe 18-carat loo when it went on display at Blenheim Palace, Winston Churchill’s Oxfordshire birthplace.“It’s rare to be with an artist who’s recognised on the street,” says NNG director Klaus Biesenbach. “He reached a level of accessibility with these very easy-to-communicate ideas: ‘Oh God, a person puts a banana on the wall and it’s sold for six million!’ He is a very deep thinker who camouflages seriousness with humour, and who camouflages the sublime with irony.”Night, Cattelan’s first major solo exhibition in Germany, was granted to him as winner of this year’s Neue Nationalgalerie prize honouring influential contemporary artists. Cattelan collaborated with curator Lisa Botti on new commissions, as well as selecting historic works from the past three decades, noticeably skipping over his greatest hits. “They were part of a different conversation,” he says. “My work has always been serious. The problem is people often stop at the joke.”The show spotlights the wax and wane of power, the contentiousness of collective memory, and the horror and hope of history, as symbolised by its scarred and vibrant host city. “Night,” he says, “is a beautiful title. We sleep, we love, we dream, we fear. It’s a moment where things get fuzzy. And after night, there is dawn and another day. But it’s definitely a suspended moment – a magic moment.”double quotation mark‘I suffer when making a show – but I love the rush. It’s a fix, a dependency’At the entrance, peering down from the roof, the 2003 work Never features Oskar, Günter Grass’s eerie child witness to the Nazi era from his novelThe Tin Drum, silently beating out his warning. Purgatory, created for the show, presents a stunted-scale version of Berlin’s Brandenburg Gate as an ambivalent landmark, a portal for visitors to rethink their engagement with European history.View image in fullscreenKneeling for $17m … Him, from 2001, is Cattelan’s most controversial – and lucrative – sculpture.Photograph: Attilio Maranzano/Maurizio CattelanHim, from 2001, features a diminutive kneeling man who is revealed to be Adolf Hitler in a prayer-like pose, facing off against 2007’s Dawn, a female figure with real human hair, her hands pinned in a crucifixion pose. Overhead, thousands of stuffed pigeons are absorbed by the black ceiling. They, for Cattelan, are “a menacing presence”, though Botti adds: “It’s also about the holy spirit, about looking up. It’s a bit of optimism.” It all calls to mind La Nona Ora, or The Ninth Hour, an infamous work from 1999 (sadly not in the show) depicting Pope John Paul II resplendent in ceremonial garb, having been struck down by a meteorite.The Hitler piece Him has been Cattelan’s most lucrative, selling for $17.2m in 2016. It had courted controversy in Warsaw, where it was displayed on the site of the wartime ghetto, recallingthe day in 1970 when West German chancellor Willy Brandt dropped to his kneesin front of the city’s Monument to the Ghetto Heroes to beg forgiveness for the crimes of the Nazi era. The Simon Wiesenthal Centercalled Cattelan’s work“a senseless provocation”.Cattelan is satisfied the Night exhibition is in the right place at the right time, lending the works fresh power. He confesses to a certain obsession with the darkest chapters of German history, but primarily for the universality of their nightmarish resonance. “Hitler in this case represents evil,” he says. “It could have been Genghis Khan or another very popular, very famous leader.” He is unafraid of the possibility of a Berlin audience questioning his right to borrow from German iconography, “like if I was wearing rasta hair or something”. Cultural appropriation, he believes, is a “very American” accusation.View image in fullscreen‘My Catholicism comes out when I don’t want it to!’ … The Ninth Hour (1999).Photograph: Dominik Pluess/APCattelan calls the NNG “an incredible building” and considers this modernist masterpiece with its famously windswept plaza “a major contributor” to the show. “There is no separation between inside and outside here,” he says. “I had to find a way not to dominate it, not to be dominated but to have a conversation. I connected with the idea of a church. My Catholicism comes out when I don’t want it to! But this time it came out as a structure, on this idea of central axes through the exhibition.” Botti describes Cattelan’s work as “comic existentialism”, saying: “You laugh about something, but then the laugh gets stuck in your throat.”His work comments on an era of crumbling social structures and disinformation, created by an artist who divides his time between Trump’s US and Italy under hard-right prime ministerGiorgia Meloni, choosing New York and Milan as his bases. “Internationally, there is now a resurgence of people asking for more strong leadership: Meloni is a very cunning and astute politician.” Expressing a grudging admiration for her unusual staying power, he says: “It’s disappointing to think that the left weren’t able to produce, in all the occasions they had, such stability. What didn’t they have that she has?” He suggests an answer: scapegoats. “We have always these enemies that are offered to us. They give us problems that probably we don’t have. But nobody has the magic wand.”Cattelan was born to a working-class family in Padua, a historic city 40km west of Venice, and famously had no formal art training. Having Berlin put on one of his most ambitious exhibitions in years has felt like a kind of homecoming, given it’s now 20 years since he co-curated thefourth Biennale, a barn-burner of a show that made the most of the now-restored capital’s“poor but sexy” era.“Maurizio really participated in Berlin becoming Berlin,” says Klaus Biesenbach, director of the NNG, calling that 2006 biennale “a watershed moment for this city” and its creative scene. Cattelan believes Berlin “still carries scars, history, contradictions – it’s a sort of outdoor experiment”. He credited it with helping him recapture part of his youth, his days spent as a postman, a mortuary attendant and a sperm donor. “Berlin definitely was about clubbing,” he says. “It was very interesting because in Berlin stuff can grow overnight, last like a mushroom for a few days and then disappear. [Clubbing] was something I didn’t experience during my 20s or 30s. I had a serious … well, four or five years of taking back lost time. It was beautiful, it was very raw. Now it’s over again. The city became more mature.”View image in fullscreenNovecento (1997), showing in the Castello di Rivoli in Torino.Photograph: Paolo Pellion di Persano/Maurizio CattelanFor Cattelan, the 2010s brought a highly publicised retirement, then a ferocious comeback. “At that time, it was like that pressure, the anxiety, the making of the shows we were producing – you reach a level where it’s like” – he makes a drowning sound – “where you have to raise a white flag.”Each major exhibition sends him on a rollercoaster of exhilaration and panic, he says, admitting to being “extremely desperate” while planning Night. “Do I suffer? Yes, I don’t like it. It’s always a challenge. I still need the rush. It’s a contradiction, but I love the hate of making a show. It’s a fix. It’s a dependency. Maybe a therapist would say, ‘We can solve your addiction problem.’ And I’d say, ‘No, no, I love it.’”I wonder, given the death ofDavid Hockney, another epochal figure of the art world, if Cattelan has given any thought to his own legacy, but he does not seem to envision a future in which his work endures. “I don’t have a foundation,” he says. “I don’t have a studio, never had. I also don’t have a family. A legacy would be like being so conscious about yourself that you have these constructions.”However, now being in his 60s, he says: “Maybe I should think about who I want to pass my problems to. I’m super lucky. I did have doubts [as an artist]. But I jumped into the void and said, ‘If we overcome fear, there will be a fantastic dawn. A fantastic dawn.’”Maurizio Cattelan: Night is atNeue Nationalgalerie, Berlin, from 10 September to 7 MarchExplore more on these topicsMaurizio CattelanArtSculptureExhibitionsInstallationinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: New musical to give intimate portrait of Marilyn Monroe and Arthur Miller’s marriage | Stage | The Guardian
description: Misfits Together, by Bastille’s Dan Smith and To Kill a King’s Ralph Pelleymounter, is set amid the 1950s’ ‘red scare’
Author: Chris Wiegand
Headline: Misfits Together, by Bastille’s Dan Smith and To Kill a King’s Ralph Pelleymounter, is set amid the 1950s’ ‘red scare’
Content: Marilyn Monroe with her husband Arthur Miller in New York in 1957.Photograph: New York Daily News Archive/NY Daily News/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMarilyn Monroe with her husband Arthur Miller in New York in 1957.Photograph: New York Daily News Archive/NY Daily News/Getty ImagesStageNew musical to give intimate portrait of Marilyn Monroe and Arthur Miller’s marriageMisfits Together, by Bastille’s Dan Smith and To Kill a King’s Ralph Pelleymounter, is set amid the 1950s’ ‘red scare’Chris WiegandStage editorThu 3 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 07.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was lampooned as the union of the “hourglass” and the “egghead” – the marriage, in the summer of 1956, between Hollywood superstarMarilyn Monroeand Pulitzer-winning playwright Arthur Miller. Now, a new stage musical is to give a nuanced and intimate portrait of that famous relationship, treat each as trailblazers in their own way and reveal parallels between the volatile state of the US during the 50s “red scare” and now.The production, which opens next autumn atLeicester’s Curve, is called Misfits Together, a reference to the film Miller wrote for Monroe that was released shortly after their divorce in 1961. It is a foray into musical theatre by two indie musicians, Dan Smith of the band Bastille and Ralph Pelleymounter from To Kill a King, who have recorded the score as a studio album. The first track, Oh America, is out on Thursday.Smith and Pelleymounter had originally envisaged it as a musical about 50s America. They shared their songs with Charlotte Bogard Macleod, who has written the book, and had long been fascinated by the relationship that caught the public’s imagination.View image in fullscreenArthur Miller, Laurence Olivier and Marilyn Monroe at the Savoy hotel, London, in 1956.Photograph: PA“I’d always wanted to exploreArthur Millerand how he had this integrity that cut through everything,” she said. “He refused to name names [before the House Un-American Activities Committee] and he stood up at a huge personal cost. When we started doing research, we just couldn’t believe that Marilyn was so central to this. She was supporting him. She had her own production company. And we were thinking, why hasn’t this been talked about or celebrated?” Each empowered the other, she added – “fighting [the anti-communist senator Joe] McCarthy or fighting misogyny”.Smith said that the musical would deal with how Monroe was pigeonholed. “Here’s a working-class woman who was in foster care and created the persona of Marilyn Monroe and became one of the most successful and known people ever in the world,” he said. “And still at the height of her success and fame, she was constantly questioned and denigrated and patronised.”Despite her many achievements, Monroe had been “reduced and reduced and reduced” to the image of a bombshell, Pelleymounter said. The musical, he added, would look at how her fame eclipsed Miller’s.Presented with Tila Arts, Misfits Together will be staged by Curve’s artistic director, Nikolai Foster, who said the company had been watching Monroe’s films for research. He praised her “innate understanding of the art of film-making” and “the craft of acting”. Foster said the musical showed the couple’s lives in such closeup that at times during the workshops they almost forgot that the main characters were two of the 20th century’s most famous cultural figures.View image in fullscreenFrom left, Curve chief executive Chris Stafford, librettist Charlotte Bogard Macleod, Dan Smith, Ralph Pelleymounter and Curve artistic director Nikolai Foster.Photograph: Phil TragenPelleymounter said he had returned to the phrase “history doesn’t repeat, but it rhymes” throughout their work on the project. Seventy years after the red scare, othering was still being used to create “fear and anger in order to maintain the status quo” in the US, he said. One song written for the musical expresses Miller and film directorElia Kazan’s frustration at “seeing politicians say things on the news that are so blatantly not true, that are manipulative and scaremongering”.Other famous figures in the musical include Laurence Olivier, Monroe’s co-star in The Prince and the Showgirl. “He says: ‘Stop trying to act, just be sexy,’” said Bogard Macleod. “His one note is: ‘Be sexy!’ He was frustrated with her wanting lots of takes, and she was just trying to get it right. But then when you see the film, she’s the one that shines.”Marilyn Monroe and Arthur Miller: a year in their lives - in picturesRead moreSmith and Pelleymounter wrote more than three dozen songs for the musical and have been whittling them down to under half that number. The pair, longtime friends, “have always loved writing narrative songs and using songwriting to dive into character and story and history and culture”, said Smith. “I want the songs to be epic and instant and nuanced and move the story along, to sweep across history and then zoom into someone’s psychology.”One song takes surprising inspiration from Eminem’s hit Stan, as it tells an “incredibly complex story via their correspondence”. Pelleymounter said they had also drawn inspiration from famous photos of the pair. “Bicycle rides have definitely made it into at least one song.”Pelleymounter and Smith will be following in the footsteps of fellow indie musician Passenger (Michael David Rosenberg), who recently had a musical theatre success with theOlivier award-nominatedThe Unlikely Pilgrimage of Harold Fry. Smith has also written the music and lyrics for Young Romantics, a musical in development whose characters include Mary Shelley and Lord Byron.Misfits Together will run at Curve’s Studio theatre from 4 September until 2 October 2027.Explore more on these topicsStageTheatreMusicalsArthur MillerMarilyn MonroeCurve theatreBastillenewsShareReuse this content

title: My dad died suddenly with no will. Am I morally obliged to share his estate with my estranged half-sibling? | Money | The Guardian
description: It’s kind of you to wonder if you should change the way things were left, writes advice columnist Eleanor Gordon-Smith. But it’s possible his preference is already clear
Author: Eleanor Gordon-Smith
Headline: It’s kind of you to wonder if you should change the way things were left, writes advice columnist Eleanor Gordon-Smith. But it’s possible his preference is already clear
Content: ‘Whatever you decide to do, it’s worth – as much as you can – trying not to let any possible tensions with your sister play out through money,’ writes Eleanor Gordon-Smith. Painting: Pandora’s Box by Charles Edward Perugini.Illustration: Wikimedia CommonsView image in fullscreen‘Whatever you decide to do, it’s worth – as much as you can – trying not to let any possible tensions with your sister play out through money,’ writes Eleanor Gordon-Smith. Painting: Pandora’s Box by Charles Edward Perugini.Illustration: Wikimedia CommonsLeading questionsMoneyMy dad died suddenly with no will. Am I morally obliged to share his estate with my estranged half-sibling?It’s kind of you to wonder if you should change the way things were left, writes advice columnistEleanor Gordon-Smith. But it’s possible his preference is already clearRead moreLeading questionsEleanor Gordon-SmithThu 3 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 20.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMy dad died suddenly earlier this year, with no will, and I am unsure as to how I should distribute the estate. We are talking about very modest sums of money – about £5,000 (US$6,750, A$9,500) in total.My dad was a very ethical person. While his death was unexpected, he had a sense it was coming. About six months before he died, he arranged for the disposal of many personal effects. The lack of a will, given his self-discipline and preferences for forward planning, is odd.My dad has two daughters from a previous relationship, who he was not in contact with until I was in my mid-30s. Their mum had remarried after separating from our dad, and her new husband had formally adopted both her girls. My dad was delighted to resume contact with one half-sister. Another, two years younger, wanted nothing to do with him and firmly disapproved of her sister’s choice to re-establish contact.Some 10 years ago, I started my own family, relocated to remove myself from domestic abuse, and joined the league of parents of children with additional needs. My dad mentioned that he had a little money put aside that could go towards legal costs, should courts ever become involved in arrangements for my son.I don’t get along with my sister-in-law. Should I try to address the dynamic? | Leading questionsRead moreBefore it became apparent that there was no will, my initial expectation was that my dad would have split his estate three ways. But that lack of clear direction introduces uncertainty. Did my dad deliberately leave no will, with knowledge that under intestacy laws, biological children that have been adopted have no claim? Did he intend me to distribute his estate in the way we initially assumed? If so, why not make that clear? Do I have a moral obligation to share the estate with my half-siblings? And does the presumption that their legal dad intends to provide for his children equally, and significantly more generously, have any bearing on this?Eleanor says:It sounds like the process of making this decision has as much significance as the outcome. Partly, deciding ethically is a way of honouring your dad: it’s clearly important to you that he was a profoundly moral man.And partly, as long as we’re thinking through the estate, it’s not over. We have unfinished business with the person we’ve lost. There’s one more interaction to be had, we’re still in conversation with them; it’s not done. I think that’s part of why estate disputes can get so bloody. Fighting for years over where Mum would have wanted the teaspoons to go can somehow feel preferable to having nothing left to figure out or say about her. Figuring out the details of the estate can, as much as anything else, be a way of keeping the person you loved alive.I can’t know with total certainty what your dad intended. It’s too particular. How much did he know about estate law? The only possible answer is, “I’m not sure.” But we can know something else: he had the opportunity to find out. He knew they’d been adopted; he wasn’t totally unable to plan for death.Ifit was very important to him that your sisters receive part of his estate, he could have taken steps to make sure of that.It sounds as if you won’t feel OK about inheriting more if it feels like your decision. (You are your father’s daughter, when it comes to ethics.) You receiving more needs to feel like honouring his wishes, not just you deciding what’s fair alone. He could have done more to make his wishes explicit, you’re right – but it’s absolutely possible that thiswashis preference.He raised you alone, your child has additional needs, your sisters have material resources elsewhere, and there’s the complication that one sister didn’t have a relationship with him, and if you leave some to one sister, you have to leave some to the other. The way he left things produces the result that it all goes to you, without him saying out loud that that’s his wish. If he wanted to rule out that possibility, he could have.Whatever you decide to do about the estate, it’s worth – as much as you can – trying not to let any possible relationship tensions with your sister play out through money. She has another father figure. You’ve just lost your only one. She has other material inheritance. You’re thinking through your only one. That’s bound to cause some tension, and themes about relative advantage in the rest of life are wont to play out through money. But money isn’t a good proxy for interpersonal issues: it will exacerbate them instead of providing symbolic resolution.It’s very kind of you to ask whether you should change the way things were left. But another way of looking at it is that the decision’s been made: the law says what happens to people’s estates when they die intestate, and you don’t have clear evidence that he wanted something else instead.This letter has been edited.Ask Eleanor a questionShare your questionTell us hereYour responses, which can be anonymous, are secure as the form is encrypted and only the Guardian has access to your contributions. We will only use the data you provide us for the purpose of the feature and we will delete any personal data when we no longer require it for this purpose. For alternative ways to get in touch securely please see ourtips guide.NameWhat is your question for Eleanor?Email addressYour contact details are helpful so we can contact you for more information. They will only be seen by the Guardian.By submitting your response, you are agreeing to share your details with us for this feature.SubmitShow moreExplore more on these topicsMoneyLeading questionsFamilyDeath and dyingAustralian lifestyleSiblingsParents and parentingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: You be the judge: should my girlfriend stop letting the recycling pile up? | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Robin keeps used packaging on the kitchen ledge. Benny thinks that’s unhygienic. You decide who’s talking rubbish
Author: Georgina Lawton
Headline: Robin keeps used packaging on the kitchen ledge. Benny thinks that’s unhygienic. You decide who’s talking rubbish
Content: Illustration: Igor Bastidas/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Igor Bastidas/The GuardianYou be the judgeLife and styleYou be the judge: should my girlfriend stop letting the recycling pile up?Robin keeps used packaging on the kitchen ledge. Benny thinks that’s unhygienic.
