You decide who’s talking rubbishFind out how to get a disagreement settled or become a jurorInterviews byGeorgina LawtonThu 3 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 06.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheprosecution: Bennydouble quotation markWe’ve had little flies buzzing around–I know they’re coming from the recyclingMy girlfriend, Robin, likes to keep the recycling on a ledge above the counter in our kitchen, instead of taking it straight outside. I absolutely hate it. It’s not just empty cereal boxes or clean bottles – we have a dog, so there are often empty dog food cans too. There’s always a bit of food left around the edges, and if they’re left for long enough they start to smell and attract flies. It’s gross.If recycling has any food residue in it, you can’t leave it sitting around in the kitchen for days. We’ve had little flies buzzing around before and I know they’re coming from the recycling. Robin thinks I’m making too much of a fuss and that it’s only there temporarily until there’s enough to justify taking it outside, but I think it needs to go out immediately.double quotation markWhen the ledge starts attracting wildlife it’s not an environmental initiative, it’s a biohazardWe live in a flat on the third floor, so I understand not wanting to make a trip to the bin every time we finish something, but there has to be a limit. If the cans are growing mould or attracting flies, we’ve passed it. I don’t want to be preparing food while there’s a collection of old things sitting above the counter.I’ve suggested rinsing the cans as soon as we’ve used them, which Robin does sometimes, but not often. We have a small kitchen and clear surfaces make it feel calmer and cleaner. Twelve pieces of recycling lined up along the wall is an eyesore.Robin is not as environmentally conscious as me and I think she would put a lot of things in the rubbish bin if it wasn’t for me. She likes pointing out the stuff on the ledge as if to say: “See, I recycle.”But we all should recycle.Sometimes I take individual items downstairs to the recycling bin because I can’t stand looking at them any more. Robin never does this because she says it’s inefficient. My options are therefore to become the household recycling porter or accept that the ledge has been totally annexed by empty packaging.I’m willing to compromise: we can collect clean recycling in a box, bag or container, and take it down when it’s full. But Robin needs to relinquish that ledge. When the ledge starts attracting wildlife, it’s not an environmental initiative, it’s a biohazard.You be the judge – send us your domestic disputesRead moreThedefence: Robindouble quotation markI don’t understand Benny’s obsession with buying a recycling box. Where would it go?Benny is making our kitchen sound like a landfill site when it’s not. We live on the third floor of a block of flats and the recycling bins are all the way downstairs, so I’m not going to make a special trip every time the dog finishes a tin of food.The ledge is practical and out of the way. Benny says it’s unhygienic to have recycling above a kitchen counter, but we don’t use that counter, so if they fall off it doesn’t matter. When a reasonable amount accumulates we take everything downstairs together.I disagree that Benny takes all the recycling down. I do it when I can, but he goes in and out of the building more as the bins are on his route to work and I work from home.double quotation markIf something is genuinely dirty, I’ll get rid of it. I just don’t agree that every piece of packaging needs to leave the flat immediatelyThe ledge is dead space. We have a small kitchen with hardly any storage, floor or counter space, which is why I don’t understand Benny’s obsession with buying a recycling box. Where would it go? It wouldn’t fit on the ledge, there’s no room on the counter and I don’t want a big box taking up the limited floor space. We’d be replacing some cans neatly lined up against a wall with a massive container we’d have to manoeuvre around every day. How is that better?Benny is exaggerating about the dog food cans. I do rinse them. He makes it sound as though we have mushrooms sprouting out of them. If something smells or is genuinely dirty, obviously I’ll get rid of it. I just don’t agree that every piece of packaging needs to leave the flat immediately, especially if it’s cardboard or plastic I’ve rinsed. Benny thinks any old packaging has germs. I think it can stay on the ledge if it doesn’t have food debris on it.I also reject the idea that I don’t recycle. Benny might be more militant about it, but me putting something on the ledgeismaking sure it gets recycled. His real problem is that he hates seeing things on surfaces. I’m just not as bothered by a few cans or bits of cardboard waiting to go downstairs.I’m not giving up the ledge for a box we don’t have room for. If Benny wants every single tin removed the moment the dog finishes eating, he’s welcome to keep making those journeys down three flights of stairs. I will wait until there’s enough recycling to make the trip worthwhile.Names have been changedskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe jury of Guardian readersSounds like the best option is to find a recycling bin that fits the space, whether that’s a plastic bag hanging off a door knob, or something else. Having open empty tins of dog food in the kitchen is nasty, whether they’ve been rinsed or not. Also, rubbish should not be above food prep areas.Sebastian, 33Perhaps Robin could look on this not so much as an inefficient use of her time, but as an opportunity to be kind, get some exercise and improve the hygiene of her kitchen. Get a can crusher – and a small container to mount inside the under-sink door.Elizabeth, 63Abolish the ledge! However, making a trip downstairs for individual items is unworkable in the long term. Shop around and find a container that is tall rather than wide, to minimise the floor space it takes up, and fill the ledge with a painting, a houseplant, or literally anything other than dirty tins.Morag, 29Benny’s request to have a box or bag is completely reasonable. Surely a small box is better than having mouldy cans tumbling on to the counter?! Even if Robin doesn’t see the issue with it, it should matter to her that it’s making Benny uncomfortable.Lucy, 32Why can’t Robin rinse out her recycling, put it in a canvas bag and hang it on the back of the kitchen door? Then she can take it down once there’s a bag collected.Mike, 54Now you be the judgeIn our online poll, tell us: who’s getting canned?The poll closes onWednesday 9 September at 9am BSTLast week’s resultsWe asked ifBill should stop eating off other people’s plates?79%of you said yes –Bill is guilty21%of you said no –Bill is not guiltyExplore more on these topicsLife and styleYou be the judgefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The best fans to keep you cool in 2026 – tried and tested | Summer | The Guardian
description: Missed out on a fan this summer? Chill your space with our pick of the best still in stock, including tower and misting models
Author: Caramel Quin
Headline: Missed out on a fan this summer? Chill your space with our pick of the best still in stock, including tower and misting models
Content: View image in fullscreenGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterSummerReviewThe best fans to keep you cool in 2026 – tried and testedMissed out on a fan this summer? Chill your space with our pick of the best still in stock, including tower and misting modelsThe best portable neck and handheld fansDyson HushJet Mini Cool fan reviewCaramel QuinThu 3 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOur world is gettinghotter. Summer heatwaves are so frequent, they’re stretching the bounds of what we think of as summer. Hot-and-bothered home working and sweaty, sleepless nights are now alarmingly common.Get a good fan and you can dodge the temptation of air conditioning. Aircon is incredibly effective, but it uses a lot of electricity … and burning fossil fuels is how we got into this mess in the first place. Save money and carbon by opting for a great fan instead.Fans are more energy efficient than aircon. A typical portable air conditioner uses 1,000W of electricity, which would cost about 26p an hour to run. The fans I tested used between 8W and 60W; my favourite, theAirCraft Lume, used 18W on its top setting. You could run it on max for 56 hours, and it would still use no more electricity (money, carbon) than a single aircon unit going for an hour.I tested 20 fans of all shapes and sizes, so you can pick the best one for you. I tested them for size, noise, power use and, of course, how much they cool you down. I also tested a few “evaporative coolers”, which use water to cool the air blowing at you while using significantly less energy than aircon.Still in stockFollowing this summer’s fossil-fuel charged heatwaves, many of our favourite fans are out of stock. Our favourite misting fan, the Shark FlexBreeze Pro Mist, is still in stock in blush pink, however.£259.99 at SharkOur best powerful tower fan, the Meaco Sefte Smart 36in, is also available. It’s slim, quiet and one of the most powerful fans we tested.£99.99 at MeacoFor smaller spaces, our best mini tower fan, the Meaco Sefte 19in, is compact and energy efficient, while still packing a decent cooling punch.£69.99 at MeacoWhy you should trust meI’m an award-winning consumer tech journalist with decades of experience testing gadgets. I’m also a menopausal woman in her 50s who honestly can’t remember the last time she felt cold: I think that might be why we gravitate towild swimmingin middle age. Oh, and I have a degree in engineering. So I’m triply qualified to put these fans through their paces, scientifically and subjectively.How I testedView image in fullscreenAn anemometer was used to measure the air speed each fan generates on its top setting.Photograph: Caramel Quin/The GuardianI chose 20 fans, each from different brands, aiming for a mix of new and highly rated models plus a few stellar bargains. I wanted to make sure there was something for everyone before I put them through their paces.I used a power meter to measure how much electricity (and therefore money and carbon) the fans use, an anemometer to measure the air speed they generate on the top setting, and the Sound Meter app to measure the noise on the top setting (they were all too quiet to register on their lowest).I measured everything from 1m away, although in reality, you’ll probably position a tower or pedestal fan farther away and a desk fan closer to you. That means the noise a desk fan makes matters more.I also measured them myself, as sometimes the official specs can be misleading or wrong. For example, I measured a tower fan that was supposedly 17cm wide, only to find that wasn’t including the base. Here I’ve stuck with each fan’s largest dimensions, including their footprint.I used a thermometer to measure the impact of the evaporative coolers I tested, and took note of everything from how cooling each of the fans felt, how annoying the noise was and how good the controls were. I also considered how they looked and how small they packed away, as well as the price tag.All the fans that weren’t returned to the manufacturers were donated toFurnishing Futures, a charity that furnishes the empty social homes in which women and children are placed after domestic abuse.The best fans in2026View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Caramel Quin/The GuardianBest quiet fan for the bedroom and best overall:AirCraft LumeAirCraftLume£149£149 at AirCraftWhat we loveQuiet, elegant, powerful cooling and a backlightWhat we don’t loveSo quiet, it’s easy to forget to turn it offView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Caramel Quin/The Guardian£149 at AirCraftPreorder now for delivery inearly SeptemberThis pedestal fan was hard to fault, with an elegant design that boasts a dimmable backlight (three brightness levels or you can turn it off, all with the remote control). It’s billed as height adjustable, but rather than scooting up and down, you can remove the bottom pole to convert it into a 63cm desk fan. There’s an LED display and touch controls on the front, and other features include a 12-hour timer and a sleep mode.Of all I tested, this is probably the best fan for sleeping: it’s the best for low noise relative to wind speed. Pick a lower setting for silent cooling, a higher setting if you’re happy to doze off to the white noise, or use the sleep button if you’d like it to gradually reduce power in the night. Not just its simple, circular air multiplier, but every single detail. The display is small but readable. The oscillation (15, 40 or 70 degrees) works well. The magnetic storage on top for the remote control is clever. The controls work well and let you easily set the timer and sleep mode. I couldn’t hear this bladeless fan on the first six of its 10 speeds, and I found the noise easy to live with even at higher speeds.It didn’t make the final cut because …the price is hard to justify. Go for it!Style:desk;dimensions:36 x 16 x 55cm (WDH);number of speeds:10;remote control?Yes;peak noise level on test:35dB;power use on top setting:20W;air speed on top setting:2.9m/sDysonCool CF1£249.99£249.99 at DysonWhat we loveAttractive design and works wellWhat we don’t loveIt’s a bit priceyMeaco Sefte 8in portable air circulatorMeacoSefte 8in portable air circulatorfrom£79.99£79.99 at Meaco£79.99 at CurrysWhat we loveCordless, fairly quiet, good warrantyWhat we don’t loveIt doesn’t fold up for portabilityView image in fullscreen£79.99 at Meaco£79.99 at CurrysCurrently out of stockBest for:acordless fanThis is an impressive, cordless desk fan with a battery life of four to 17 hours, depending on fan speed. I couldn’t hear the first seven of its 12 speeds. It oscillates and you can manually point it up or down, and features include a timer, Night and Eco modes. Its three-year warranty is a bonus, too (most have two).Overall, I liked it. It’s good-looking and pretty strong, although it’s weaker when cordless; for example, air speed dropped from an impressive 4.6m/s to 3.1m/s when I unplugged it. Still, if you want a desk fan that can sometimes be cordless, it’s a good buy.It didn’t make the final cut because …the USB-powered Morphy Richards is even handier.Style:desk;dimensions:26 x 20 x 38cm (WDH);number of speeds:12;remote control?Yes;peak noise level on test:55dB;power use on top setting:10W;air speed on top setting:4.6m/sMeacoSefte 8in portable air circulatorfrom£79.99£79.99 at Meaco£79.99 at CurrysWhat we loveCordless, fairly quiet, good warrantyWhat we don’t loveIt doesn’t fold up for portabilityBlueair ComfortPure 3-in-1 T20iBlueairComfortPure 3-in-1 T20ifrom£499£499 at Blueair£499 at BootsWhat we loveIt’s also an air purifier and a fan heaterWhat we don’t loveIt’s expensive if you just want a fanView image in fullscreen£499 at Blueair£499 at BootsCurrently out of stockBest for:hay fever and allergy sufferersThis is also afan heater(so it’s useful all year round) and anair purifier(ideal for allergy sufferers). It cleans the air in a room in 12.5 minutes or a small house in an hour, removing airborne particles such as pollen, odours, dust and smoke.On test, it created a good breeze, even though the anemometer only read 0.8m/s. And on cooler days, it can send purified air upwards instead, circulating air in the room as well as cleaning it.The controls and display are on top, making them hard to see from across the room. But there’s an app and Alexa control as well as a remote. The three-year warranty is nice, too.It didn’t make the final cut because …it’s expensive as a fan (but great as an air purifier).Style:tower;dimensions:35 x 35 x 70cm (WDH);number of speeds:4;remote control?Yes;peak noise level on test:35dB;power use on top setting:21W;air speed on top setting:0.8m/sBlueairComfortPure 3-in-1 T20ifrom£499£499 at Blueair£499 at BootsWhat we loveIt’s also an air purifier and a fan heaterWhat we don’t loveIt’s expensive if you just want a fanWhat you need to knowView image in fullscreenFor personal comfort, simply point a fan towards you.Photograph: Caramel Quin/The GuardianWhat are the different types of fan?Pedestal fansare tall fans where all the hard work happens at the top. They don’t have to be old-fashioned; some have modern designs. And some are convertible, with a pole you can remove to turn them into a desk fan. They can be good for a focused blast of cooling wind.Bladeless fansaren’t magic; they just don’t have visible blades. The work is done in the body of the fan, and then air is pushed out of a nozzle. The Dyson, Vortex Air and Shark on test are all bladeless. They look modern and are easy to clean. And there are no moving parts on show, meaning zero chance of getting your hair caught.Tower fansare tall and narrow. They produce a lot of wind and oscillate from side to side, making them good for a room like an office.Desk fansare like pedestal fans without the pole. They’re not only for desks, they’re good on a bedside table too. And they take up less storage space over the winter.Evaporative coolersuse water from a reservoir to cool the air that blows at you. They don’t produce a powerful wind like a fan, but they genuinely cool the room and are much more energy efficient than air conditioning. Note that they only cool the room a little – they won’t turn it fridge cold like aircon.Handheld fansare lightweight, portable fans to cool you on the move. We’ve tested a wide range of handheld and neck fans.What does oscillation mean?Most fans oscillate (move back and forth) by swivelling on their base, and some let you select how wide an angle you want. If it’s just for you, pick a narrow angle; if you’re cooling the whole office, go wide. Some fans achieve the same effect in other ways, such as by moving louvres. Some also oscillate up and down, so the fan can circulate air all over the room to create a gentle breeze.What’s sleep mode?Most fans have a sleep mode, where every 30 or 60 minutes the fan lowers its setting until it reaches a certain point. This is a good compromise that helps you get to sleep without wasting energy, minimising the risk of waking up in the middle of the night suddenly cold.Start by lowering the fan speed to the point where you don’t find it annoying. In fact, some people find the white noise of a fan helpful at bedtime. Then switch to sleep mode.The best eye masks in the UK to help you sleep better – testedRead moreWhere is the best place to position a fan?For personal comfort, simply point it towards you. The cooling feeling is because the moving air from the fan displaces the warm, humid air near your skin, which in turn helps your sweat evaporate, cooling down your body. It’s like a breeze rather than a still day. Or why it feels colder swimming in a river than in a lake, even if the water temperature is the same. Evaporative coolers, of which I’ve included two above, use water to actively cool the air.Never place a fan up against a wall because air needs to flow into the back. If the air’s cooler outside, put the fan in front of an open window or door to bring in the cooler air.How energy efficient are fans?Fans are very energy efficient compared with the electricity used by tech such as air conditioning. Fans cost pennies to use but can make you feel much cooler. Note that they circulate air rather than actively cooling it. The effect is like turning a still day into a breezy one.How much does a fan cost to use?I’ll set out the maths. For each fan here, I’ve measured its power use on the top setting, in watts (W). Electricity costs are in kilowatt hours (kWh). If, for example, you were using a 30W fan for five hours, it would use 150Wh. Divide by 1,000 to convert it to kilowatt hours: 0.15kWh.The energy price cap for 1 July to 30 September 2026 is 26.11p per kWh. Multiply this by the last figure and you’ll discover it will cost just under 4p to run that fan for five hours. Or just over £14 to run it for five hours every day for a year.Running fans is pretty cheap, then, and a good fan will keep you cool enough to dodge buying any kind of air conditioning. An evaporative cooler is a good alternative to aircon. The Swan Nordic here used 26W, so less than 3% of the electricity of a typical portable air conditioner (1,000W). The effect isn’t the same: you can’t turn your bedroom into a fridge. But you can cool the air enough to make a big difference when there’s a heatwave.Do I need air conditioning?For most of us, there are good energy-saving alternatives to aircon. It’s tempting to turn your bedroom into a walk-in fridge on a hot day – or night – but fans are great and use much less electricity (and therefore money and carbon) than aircon. We are in a climate crisis. We got into this mess by burning fossil fuels, and we continue to do so, so the carbon footprint of your cooling matters.There are valid reasons to own air conditioning though, even during a climate crisis. Older people, young children and those with health conditions are more vulnerable to extreme heat, and some homes are simply much harder to keep cool.My guide to portable air conditioners and alternativestakes in how much energy they use, as well as how well they cool the room and their refrigerant’s global warming potential.Note that the electricity you use won’t contribute as much towards climate breakdown if you’re on a good renewable tariff – or even better, producing it yourself with solar panels. Solar panels and batteries are becoming a popular choice for homeowners as they become more affordable.How to clean your fanFan blades tend to gather dust. Make sure the fan is unplugged, then remove the front grille and wipe the blades with a microfibre cloth. If the grille doesn’t come off then a dry paintbrush or a small cleaning brush (like a bottle brush but smaller) might let you dust through the grille. Never use water on electricals. Acan of compressed airis also good for blowing off dust – keep your fingers away, though, because it will of course make the fan blades spin.What to do with your old fanIf your old fan works, try to find it a good home on a local swap site or street WhatsApp – they work better than the front wall, where it might get rained on. If it’s not working, you could take it to a localrepair cafe. And if it’s beyond repair, check your council website or checkRecycle Your Electricals: they don’t belong in general waste.If you’re wondering whether you need air conditioning, read our guide thebest portable aircon units, plus the pros, cons and alternativesCaramel Quin is ajournalist specialising in consumer technology. She prides herself on real-world testing and plainlanguage. Her pet hates are jargon, pointless products and overcomplicated instruction manuals. Caramel is an engineering graduate who has won awards for communicating hi-tech subjects to normal people. When she’s not testing gadgets, she’s feeding pets (16 beasts at the time of writing) or pottering at the allotmentThis article was originally published on 17 June 2025. title: Are there any drinkable canned cocktails?  | Food | The Guardian
description: Palatable premix cocktails – well, ones that adults like, at least – are far and few between
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Palatable premix cocktails – well, ones that adults like, at least – are far and few between
Content: Moth is one of the drinkable brands – try the mango one in our recs.Photograph: Moth/PRView image in fullscreenMoth is one of the drinkable brands – try the mango one in our recs.Photograph: Moth/PRGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.FoodAre there any drinkable canned cocktails?Palatable premix cocktails – well, ones that adults like, at least – are far and few betweenMina HollandThu 3 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor somebody whose children recently learned how to crack open a tinnie, this week’s tasting was a perilous one. Cans covered in seductive, brightly coloured pictures of parasols, palm trees and their favourite fruits filled the kitchen, and both the seven- and the five-year-old tried to take a swig. Premix cocktails are disproportionately marketed to young drinkers – gateway booze, if you will, as the likes of Bacardi Breezer pineapple was for me – and often have a one-note, cloying taste.Absolut’s passionfruit martiniandMalibu’s piña coladaare cases in point: both have sugary, synthetic fruit flavours that mask, or even eliminate, the taste of the base spirits. Is it any wonder that, in 2024, Britain had theworst rate of child alcohol consumption in the world? These drinks make it easy to forget that you’re even drinking alcohol.Perhaps more than any other theme, writing about premix cocktails has made me confront the very question of why we drink alcohol. Take me as an example. My Bacardi Breezer years were undoubtedly a question of booze for function; it loosened my teenage inhibitions and I had a laugh. The fact that this so-called “alcopop” was so saccharine chimed with my childish predilection for sweetness, and conveniently masked the flavour of the rum, which may at the time have offended my uninitiated palate. Twenty-five years on, and my palate is a different place, and I welcome the notes and nuances of a well-mixed drink. I now drink alcohol to savour it, and I like what I’m drinking to give me pause; it doesn’t need to be hard work, but I do like it to make me think.That’s not to say there aren’t premix cocktails out there that can do this, and I tasted several that I found interesting. The Reina Mezcalita in today’s pick, for instance, is delicious – smoky mezcal meets zippy lime soda – and I’d happily sip it from the can in the park or, even better, from a glass rimmed withTajìnat home.Whitebox and Moth both produce good iterations of premix drinks (and in reassuringly small, potent formats) and are widely available in supermarkets; they feel a bit more grown up, too, both on the sugar front and because their ABVs skew higher, which you can taste (in the premix realm, quality seems to align with a higher ABV).Marks & Spencer has the widest own-brand selection, some of them better than others, but, on the whole, its premium Served range has more character and acidity (a good thing) than you’ll find elsewhere – I enjoyed the mojito and the lychee martini especially.Spritz cocktails, meanwhile, work particularly well in cans.M&S’s limoncello oneis a crowdpleaser, while Aperol Spritz To Go is everything you want and need it to be: a failsafe, bittersweet symphony.Five canned cocktails worth cracking openWhitebox Cosmo£5 (100ml) Ocado, 16.8%. Vodka, cranberry, lime and triple sec: cosmopolitans are making a comeback, and this one has me here for it.Reina Mezcalita£4.99 (200ml) Mex Grocer, 10%. A smoky, citrussy delight, and my favourite of the lot.M&S Served Mojito£3.35 (250ml) Ocado, 8%. Unlike this store’s cheaper premixes, this one has some complexity. Rum, mint and lime.Aperol Spritz To Go£3 (250ml) Waitrose, 5%. Inarguably good and utterly dependable. Literally does what it says on the tin.Moth Mango Margarita£4.15 (125ml) Waitrose, 14.9%. Ripe mangoes meet Tequila Enemigo and triple sec: 100% toothsome.Explore more on these topicsFoodCocktailsSpiritsFruitMexican food and drinkItalian food and drinkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Jam season is here - bottle that sunshine now to brighten up the winter | Food | The Guardian
description: September’s preserving season is a race to capture the heady flavours of summer fruit
Author: Itamar Srulovich
Headline: September’s preserving season is a race to capture the heady flavours of summer fruit
Content: Sunshine in a jar … Felicity Cloake's strawberry jam.Photograph: The GuardianView image in fullscreenSunshine in a jar … Felicity Cloake's strawberry jam.Photograph: The GuardianFeastFoodJam season is here - bottle that sunshine now to brighten up the winterSeptember’s preserving season is a race to capture the heady flavours of summer fruitSign up here for our weekly food newsletter, FeastItamar SrulovichandSarit PackerThu 3 Sep 2026 07.35 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 07.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe ideal time to make lemonade, when lemons are juicy and plentiful and cheap, is in the dead of winter, when the last thing you want is a cooling glass of lemonade. Similarly, jam-making is best done on a grey November afternoon, when the windows are steamed up and the kitchen is the warmest place in the house. Winter is exactly when you want to be standing over a great pot of bubbling fruit and boiling sugar, but much less so in summer, which is when all the good fruit is in season. From May until mid-October, our fruit supplier bills spike exponentially as boxes and boxes of seasonal fruit in its absolute prime make their way to our kitchen for a jam session, and the practice of turning them into a sweet spread is part profession, part obsession. Jam is very much our jam.Early in the season, we can just about cope. Thesoft fruitsstart to come in when the weather is still behaving itself, and we love giving them a little seasonal accent – elderflower comes with the last rhubarb, as well as with the first strawberries and apricots, and it pairs wonderfully with all of them (if you are starting there, Felicity Cloake has a very thorough guide tothe perfect strawberry jam). Cherries, meanwhile, go with just about anything, while young bay leaves often find themselves heading into the blackcurrant pot. Fennel fronds and peaches are another favourite, and we make some whenever we can get those two at the same moment. It is an amazing combination: sweet, perfumed and just a little bit green.View image in fullscreenIntriguing … Lillie O’Brien’s fig and earl grey jam.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianFor us, the realpreserving frenzybegins round about now, at the deep, sticky end of summer. In fact, September may well be the best jam month of all. The days are not too hot and the produce – figs, plums, grapes – are the ultimate jammers. Plums offer near endless possibilities and, depending on the variety, can take a surprising amount of spice: cassia bark, star anise, perhaps a clove or two. Nigel Slater’s collection oflate-summer jams and picklesis exactly the sort of thing to read when the fruit bowl begins to look threatening.Grapes, meanwhile, are a bit of a challenge, not least because most of the varieties grown commercially are chosen for their sweetness, whereas you want something else for jam: there needs to be some acidity, some funk, some flavour in there. Fragola grapes, with their musky, intoxicating, wild strawberry flavour, are a rare treat – we usually get only one delivery of them each year, which makes them all the more special, and all the more worthy of preserving for the rest of the year.Figs, especially those beautiful, black bursa ones, make the best jam of all, and the one that we and our customers crave the most. The fruit hardly needs any help, either, although its honeyed sweetness loves nothing more then a few pods of cooling cardamom for balance (that said, we are more than a little intrigued byLillie O’Brien’s earl grey combo).Our annual September challenge, then, is simple: make enough fig jam to last until Christmas. Every year, we make what looks like an absurd quantity. And every year it disappears far too quickly, which is exactly the point – spend a bit of the summer sweating over the pots so that in winter, when we aren’t sweating at all, there’s a little bit of jarred sunshine ready for us when it is most desperately needed.Our month in foodView image in fullscreenHappy new year … Claudia Roden’s honey cake.Photograph: Romas Foord/The ObserverThe sweet spot|Jams aside, our pastry kitchen currently smells heavily of honey and spice as we get busy baking loaves and loaves of honey cake in readiness for the Jewish new year next week, which this year is coming round earlier than usual. It is traditional to start the year with something sweet, be that an apple dipped in honey, dates,sweet challah breadand, of course,honey cake. You don’t need to be Jewish to enjoy this delicious tradition: on the 11th, wish your Jewish friends a happy new year, and have something sweet for yourself.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFeastRecipes from all our star cooks, seasonal eating ideas and restaurant reviews. Get our best food writing every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLocal attraction|Our love for Jackson Boxer’s cooking knows no bounds, and even though hisBrunswick Houseis so close to our home in south London that we are there more often that is OK to admit, whenever he opens a new place, we go.Vesperis on Exmouth Market in the centre of London, and it made us question our loyalty not only to Brunswick House, but also to our own home and our beloved neighbourhood, because the fried potato pizzette is something we need to live closer to.Book marks|We got a sneak preview of two new books that are already making our autumn look much more delicious, and both of which are published today.Simple Too by Yotam Ottolenghiis full of mouthwatering recipes that look and taste as good as they are easy to make, and promises to add a touch of glamour to our midweek meals. The second is the new one by Fuchsia Dunlop, a perennial favourite of ours, andFive Tastes: The Magic of Flavour in a Chinese Kitchenis a deep and delicious dive into the flavours that are the cornerstones of Chinese cooking. We are into all of them.If you want to read the complete version of this newsletterplease subscribeto receive Feast in your inbox every Thursday.Explore more on these topicsFoodFeastPickling, fermenting and preservingFruitVegetablesSummer food and drinkAutumn food and drinknewslettersShareReuse this content

title: Rachel Roddy’s summer minestrone with pesto – recipe | Food | The Guardian
description: A fresh, seasonal vegetable soup that can be made in advance and only improves in texture and flavour over time
Author: Rachel Roddy
Headline: A fresh, seasonal vegetable soup that can be made in advance and only improves in texture and flavour over time
Content: Rachel Roddy’s summer minestrone with pesto.Photograph: Rachel Roddy/The GuardianView image in fullscreenRachel Roddy’s summer minestrone with pesto.Photograph: Rachel Roddy/The GuardianA kitchen in RomeFoodRachel Roddy’s summer minestrone with pesto – recipeA fresh, seasonal vegetable soup that can be made in advance and only improves in texture and flavour over timeRachel RoddyThu 3 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNow that I am an accomplished sourdough maker, soon to start my own micro-bakery and YouTube channel … Only joking! Now that I can make half-decent, variable loaves of sourdough, I have become more aware of how the temperature in the kitchen affects food. Not that I was completely unaware, of course – I have curdled enough milk and neglected enough eggs – but feeding, then watching the sourdough starter in a jar, and then the dough itself, seeing how the process takes hours in winter, speeds up in spring, then takes on a foaming, bubbling and at times terrifying life of its own in summer, are lessons in living microorganisms and fermentation.It is a shame, then, that I didn’t give the same attention to the pan of summer minestrone I had felt so pleased with myself for cooking, cutting the courgettes carefully so they looked like Trivial Pursuit scoring wedges, while drinking tea and listening for the bottle bank lorry to drop the glass into its box, and before the sun (or anyone else) was up. Even though the combined taste of minestrone and milky Yorkshire tea is interesting, I knew it had turned out particularly well. I put on the lid, left the pan at the back of the stove and went out.It must have been 11am by the time I got back home with a plant of basil quietly suffocating behind its plastic cone. The kitchen was already hot and the minestrone was only slightly, but unequivocally, fizzy. A spoonful of pesto did not balance it out – but please don’t let my neglect put you off making this abundantly fresh-green and creamy-white courgette, green and white bean minestrone, inspired by three recipes in Laura Ragoni’s Profumi e Sapori di Liguria.If you are eating the minestrone straight away, leave it to sit for 10 minutes before serving. If you have prepared the minestrone in advance, not only will it sit for hours, but resting improves the flavour and texture.That said, learn from my mistake: if you are experiencing hot weather and the rest is longer than an hour, that rest needs to take place in a cool spot, or in the fridge to avoid a spoiled, fizzy soup. The minestrone can then be reheated gently until warm rather than hot.Summer minestrone with pestoServes65 tbspolive oil1 onion, peeled and diced small1 stick celery, trimmed and diced1 small bunch flat-leaf parsley, stems separated from the leaves (save the leaves for the pesto), and mincedSalt6 cherry tomatoes, quartered2 large courgettes, trimmed, cut into quarters lengthwise, then into quarter-moons200g green beans, cut into 2½cm lengths1 large potato, peeled and cut into cubes1 parmesan rind2400g tinswhite beans, drainedFor the pesto1garlic clove, peeled20g pine nuts, or almonds50gparsley leaves and basil100g olive oil50g cheese(pecorino, grana padano, parmesan, or a mixture), gratedHeat the olive oil in a heavy-based pan or casserole dish and gently fry the onion, celery, minced parsley stems and a pinch of salt, stirring often, until soft – about eight minutes.Add the tomatoes, stir for a minute or two, then add the courgettes, green beans and potatoes, and a pinch of salt, stirring to prevent sticking and so each chunk glistens with oil. Add one and a half litres of water and a parmesan rind, if you have one, then raise the heat so the soup nearly boils. Reduce to a simmer for 30 minutes, or until the vegetables are tender.Meanwhile, make the pesto. Pulse or pound the garlic, nuts and a pinch of salt, until they form a rough paste. Add the parsley and basil leaves, and pulse again until creamy. Gradually stir in the cheese and oil.About 10 minutes before the end of the cooking time, add the drained white beans, then leave the minestrone to sit for at least 10 minutes before serving, passing around the pesto so everyone can add the amount they like.Explore more on these topicsFoodA kitchen in RomeItalian food and drinkVegetablesSoupMain courseStarterCheeserecipesShareReuse this content

title: I camped in one of Britain’s last remaining rainforests | Devon holidays | The Guardian
description: After years of conservation work, this campsite on the edge of Dartmoor now offers the opportunity to pitch next to a fragile ecosystem
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: After years of conservation work, this campsite on the edge of Dartmoor now offers the opportunity to pitch next to a fragile ecosystem
Content: Ancient woodland surrounds the Wray Valley campsite.Photograph: Greydog ImagesView image in fullscreenAncient woodland surrounds the Wray Valley campsite.Photograph: Greydog ImagesDevon holidaysI camped in one of Britain’s last remaining rainforestsA fragment of temperate rainforest lies on the edge of Dartmoor, and following years of conservation work, its owners have now opened up a sustainable campsite next to this fragile ecosystemKirsten AmorThu 3 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 04.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMist blankets the valley as I wheel my camping gear down the small hill towards a clearing ringed by trees and shrubs. A picnic bench sits at its edge, angled towards the reason why I’m here: one of the last remaining fragments of temperate rainforest in Britain. I’m pitching my tent at Wray Valley Camping, a low-impact site on Dartmoor’s eastern edge between Lustleigh and Moretonhampstead, where I’ll spend five days on one of the site’s “nearly wild” pitches.Also known as Atlantic woodland, temperate rainforests depend on a rare combination of high humidity, rainfall and consistently mild coastal temperatures where the sea moderates the climate. They once stretched from the western Highlands of Scotland down to Cornwall,covering 20% of the UK, and sheltering rare and delicate lichens and plants. Today more than 95% of our temperate rainforest cover is gone, but Devon’s near-constant dampness and its exposure to the Atlantic make it one of the last strongholds for this rare habitat.Wray Valley Camping owners Michelle Grist and her partner Kevin Chamberlain have spent seven years restoring this fragile ecosystem while developing the adjacent campsite.View image in fullscreenHound Tor is an easy cycle from the campsite.Photograph: Paul Biggins/Alamy“We always intended to run a sustainable campsite from here,” says Michelle, a retired environmental consultant, admitting that neither she nor Kevin (a member of the Dartmoor search and rescue Ashburton team) had ever run one previously. “We did not take it over,” she adds. “We built it from scratch.” Years of camping, both in the UK and abroad, gave them enough experience to know what they liked and what they didn’t. The valley’s topography dictated their designs from the start, Kevin explains – tents only, nothing driven in.The early years were slow-going: Kevin built a compost toilet by hand before a shower block and other facilities arrived. Running alongside it all was the harder, longer graft of coaxing the temperate rainforest back to life.“It was actually difficult getting on to the land,” Michelle tells me. “While the drains upland had been cleared, our land was completely flooded.” Michelle and Kevin worked along with several other organisations to restore the woodland, adding 1,200 native plants, 200 metres of new hedgerow and 45 native saplings as well as removing invasive species.double quotation markIf you’re asking people to make a bit more effort to protect this environment, it tends to attract those who appreciate itTheir efforts culminated in February this year, when Wray Valley Camping saw six acres of its 4-hectare (10-acre) estate designated a Devoncounty wildlife site (CWS), recognising its importance as one of Dartmoor’s fragile remnants of temperate rainforest and wet woodland. The campsite now offers a unique opportunity to sleep beside this rare ecosystem in one of its four Nearly Wild camping pitches.A short signposted sustainability trail around the campsite and woodland explains the restoration work. Along the way, I spot a pied flycatcher between the oaks, hazels, rowans and willows while stonechats call to each other and an oil beetle meanders across a mossy stone in search of food.In the distance, the whiz of bike chains and children’s voices echo from theWray Valley Trail. This 7-mile (11km) walk and cycle track snakes along the edge of the temperate rainforest, retracing where the Moretonhampstead and South Devon Railway steam train once ran. Today it links the historic villages of Moretonhampstead and Lustleigh, and beyond to Bovey Tracey.View image in fullscreenKirsten Amor and her husband John Higgins camping at Wray Valley.Photograph: Kirsten AmorAs I walk along the old trackbeds of the valley trail, I imagine iron cleaving the valley and clouding it with steam and soot. When once the scream of the train whistle heralded fallen timber and quarried stone, today it’s given way to the shrill call of the treecreeper. It’s a small measure of how fast this corridor has recovered since industry nearly gutted it in the 19th century.double quotation markWithout the white noise of everyday life, every splash and wingbeat becomes audibleThe Wray Valley Trail acts as a low-impact gateway for exploring eastern Dartmoor, and it is worth building a few days’ itineraries around it. From the Wray Valley campsite, it’s an easy cycle or walk to Lustleigh and on towards Hound Tor, where towering granite boulders guard the low moss-strewn walls of abandoned medieval settlements. Waymarked paths from here weave between Dartmoor’s scattered prehistoric monuments and weatherworn waycrosses.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA 40-minute drive away, Dartmoor’smost popular temperate rainforest, Wistman’s Wood, is a cautionary lesson on what happens when these fragile environments go viral: eroded paths, damaged mosses and trampled roots from footfall they were never intended to sustain. Even as conservationists work there to double the woodland’s size, it remains under pressure from its popularity.For Michelle and Kevin, restoring the woodland is only part of the challenge. The harder task is ensuring that welcoming visitors help protect the landscape rather than putting it under pressure. Their approach is simple: keep visitor numbers low and deliberately limit the impact they have on the landscape, even if that means sacrificing some of the conveniences of modern camping. There are no electric hookups, cars are left in the parking area and campers wheelbarrow their kit to their pitch. Kevin admits that the arrangements can divide opinion but says the extra effort is intentional: “If you’re asking people to make a bit more effort to protect this environment, it tends to attract those who appreciate it.”View image in fullscreenDartmoor is a rare UK stronghold of Atlantic woodland.Photograph: Nigel Hicks/AlamyThat philosophy runs through the rest of the carbon-negative site, from borehole water and solar power to discounts for guests arriving on foot, by bike or by public transport. The result feels as close to wild camping as you can get with a hot shower.Both Michelle and Kevin say they’re surprised by the enthusiasm of the campsite guests. One horticulturist recently helped catalogue its plants, while scout groups have joined woodland management activities.The dying embers of sunlight fade behind our tent as we position our chairs towards the rainforest and sit, whisky in hand, and wait. A stoat dashes past liverworts into the undergrowth. An owl hoots in the distance and bats swoop and dart in the starlight above us. Without the white noise of everyday life, every splash and wingbeat becomes audible.Wray Valley may only be a small site, but it sits in a much larger mosaic of habitats. Ancient woodland lies on either side, while the nearby site of special scientific interest (SSSI) at Bovey Tracey supports species such as adders and ground-nesting birds. Camping here offers more than a place to pitch a tent – it provides a glimpse of how a small patch of land can contribute to the wider recovery of Dartmoor’s nature.Nearly Wild stays atWray Valley Campinginclude small pitches at£10/£8 (adult/child) per personor large pitches priced per pitch (from £40 forfour people). Both includehot showers and toilets. title: Country diary: A stranded traveller that looks more plastic than animal  | Coastlines | The Guardian
description: Appledore, Devon: By-the-wind sailors have been washed up in great numbers this summer. I stumble on a single one of these bright blue beauties
Author: Elizabeth-Jane Burnett
Headline: Appledore, Devon: By-the-wind sailors have been washed up in great numbers this summer. I stumble on a single one of these bright blue beauties
Content: The by-the-wind-sailor (Velella Velella) is not a single animal but rather collections of polyps working together.Photograph: Nature, food, landscape, travel/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe by-the-wind-sailor (Velella Velella) is not a single animal but rather collections of polyps working together.Photograph: Nature, food, landscape, travel/Getty ImagesCountry diaryCoastlinesCountry diary: A stranded traveller that looks more plastic than animalAppledore, Devon:By-the-wind sailors have been washed up in great numbers this summer. I stumble on a single one of these bright blue beautiesElizabeth-Jane BurnettThu 3 Sep 2026 02.33 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 02.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAmid the hot grit of the estuarine beach, a cool light glints. Not the habitual shade of mussel shells, nor even the shimmer of sea glass, this is a blue so bright that at first I mistake it for a kind of plastic, perhaps the discarded part of a pair of goggles.I’m about to pick it up when something prompts me to pause, mid-swoop; an inkling that this is not synthetic, but animal.Looking closer, I see an intricate pattern of concentric circles like a carved inscription on a wave-blue disc. A translucent “sail” rises from the middle. This is the marine hydrozoan,Velella velella.Like aportuguese man o’war, it is not a single animal, but rather collections of polyps working together. They feed on planktonic organisms using tentacles beneath their floating disc. The concentric circles are air chambers, aiding buoyancy. Largely harmless to humans, they don’t share the man o’war’s sting, but can still cause irritation if touched.View image in fullscreenBy-the-wind sailors more typically arrive in numbers during stormy winter weather.Photograph: Jonathan Smith/Marine Conservation SocietyThis pelagic species doesn’t swim, but instead uses its tiny sail to catch the wind and move with ocean currents, giving rise to its common name by-the-wind sailor. This evocative term, recalling maritime vernacular, highlights its sailing prowess, as do its other common names of purple sail, sea raft and little sail.The distinctive blue of its disc comes from the carotenoid pigment astaxanthin. As well as providing camouflage against the ocean waves, these pigments can absorb and reflect harmful ultraviolet rays – particularly helpful when you travel along the surface of the sea rather than through its colder depths, and when temperatures are at a record high.An occasional visitor to UK shores, mass by-the-wind sailor strandings have been reported along the Welsh coast and atSt Bees in Cumbriathis summer. Driven by strong winds, they more typically arrive in numbers during stormy winter weather, but their increased presence further inshoremay be due to calmer waters and favourable winds.Here, there is only one. Grounded, this listless sailor rests, startling in its blueness and veneer of coolness.Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now atguardianbookshop.comExplore more on these topicsCoastlinesCountry diaryRural affairsMarine lifefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The place that never freezes: the Arctic habitat where global heating threatens more ice, not less | Sea ice | The Guardian
description: The race to study the North Water between Canada and Greenland before it changes has led to a bold plan for an Inuit-run protected area
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The race to study the North Water between Canada and Greenland before it changes has led to a bold plan for an Inuit-run protected area
Content: Terry Noah and Silas Pijamini return from a sampling run on the sea ice near Grise Fiord, Nunavut.Photograph: Jimmy ThomsonView image in fullscreenTerry Noah and Silas Pijamini return from a sampling run on the sea ice near Grise Fiord, Nunavut.Photograph: Jimmy ThomsonSeascape: the state of our oceansSea iceThe place that never freezes: the Arctic habitat where global heating threatens more ice, not lessThe race to study the North Water between Canada and Greenland before it changes has led to a bold plan for an Inuit-run protected areaSeascape: the state of our oceans is supported byAbout this contentWords and pictures by Jimmy Thomson in Nunavut, CanadaThu 3 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 09.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleElectric-blue meltwater sprays up under Terry Noah’s snowmobile as he races across sea ice extending out from Canada’s northernmost public community: Grise Fiord in Nunavut, a hamlet of 144 people closer to Murmansk in Russia than the Canadian city of Toronto. The bay’s cliffs loom higher and higher like stone icebergs as he approaches his destination across the bay.Noah pulls his sled carefully over a seal’s breathing hole, about the circumference of a basketball. Using a custom-made winch, he lowers a submersible instrument into the sea below the ice.Noah will bring the data it collects back to his shipping container-based mobile lab and beam the data to the south, where his collaborator, research scientist Andrew Hamilton at the University of Alberta, can review it.View image in fullscreenWater that stays ice-free all year – a ‘polynya’ – helps all life, from algae to whales needing airAs the climate emergency thins the ice, jumbles up the seasons and forces millennia-old Inuit cultures to adapt, Noah is part of a scientific effort that extends far beyond Grise Fiord. He says: “This science work, it’s the first step to preparing.”The data Noah is collecting will help Hamilton and Noah understand changes taking place in Jones Sound, which empties into Baffin Bay to the east. There, in the bay’s northern reaches, one of the Arctic’s most important ecosystems is in the midst of a political and environmental upheaval – and Noah, Hamilton and a coalition of scientists have plans to better understand the changing waters before they’re beyond recognition.It is an area of 85,000 sq km (33,000 sq miles), bigger than Austria, that goes by at least three names: 19th-century whalers called it the North Water; Kalaallit (Inuit of Greenland) call it Pikialasorsuaq, or “the great upwelling”; and to the Inuit of Nunavut, it is Sarvarjuaq, “the place that never freezes”.Map showing the extent of North Water between Canada and GreenlandGreenland and Canada have proposed that they jointly manage the stretch of year-round open water as an internationally protected areaA stretch of year-round open water (known as a polynya) this far north is a boon to life of all kinds, from the algae that bloom in the summer and feed an entire web of other creatures to the whales that need access to the air in the depths of winter. Polar bears are drawn in by thewhales, seals and walruses that migrate there; seabirds, too, have flown and paddled their way thereby the millions, over millennia.All of that activity is why the polynya is the focus of a unique proposal to become an internationally protected area jointly managed by Greenland and Canada. A 2017 reportby the Pikialasorsuaq commission recommendedthe two countries create an Inuit-managed protected area. Canada followed up in March this year bydesignating the Sarvarjuaq marine protected areaon its half of the zone,stretching 1,000kmfrom just south of the open Arctic Ocean to northern Baffin Island.But Greenland has fallen behind on its promises for protection.Sara Olsvig, a former member of the Greenlandic parliamentand chair of the Inuit Circumpolar Council until earlier this year, says it is not wise to move too quickly when the fundamental cultural rights of Inuit could be at stake.View image in fullscreenAn estimate in one study carried out in 2014 suggested that more than 2,500 walruses spent the winter in the North Water polynya, as well as large numbers of bearded seals and narwhals“Some of the very good initiatives within conservation and nature preservation, and so forth, have unfortunately also resulted in violations of the rights ofIndigenous peoples,” she says.As negotiations slow, the physical process of change continues unabated, and the efforts to understand the polynya are accelerating.The polynya’s size and shape ebb and flow with the seasons – depending, in part, on an “ice arch” that forms across its northern tip in Nares Strait. The arch, a strong crescent-shaped bridge of ice, jams the strait, preventing sea ice from being blown south from the Arctic Ocean. The lack of ice keeps the polynya open to the sunlight and the air, allowing algae to grow, the seabirds to dive and the whales to blow.View image in fullscreenTerry Noah and Silas Pijamini collect data through the sea ice near Grise Fiord, NunavutNearly 20 years ago, the Nares Strait ice arch failed to take shape for the first time. Now it often does not form – and in those years, the polynya itself has a harder time staying open through the spring. Instead, the sea ice drifts down to cover the water’s surface. It is an unusual and perverse effect of warming: more ice, not less, could ultimately become the problem here.“I would say that at some point, when the ice bridge disappears, you’re probably going to have a drastic reduction in productivity – a collapse of the polynya,” saysDavid Harning, a climate scientist at the University of Colorado, Boulder.Finding out what is happening beneath the surface has become critical as the planet warms, and the Inuit experience that change first-hand. Researchers met in Nuuk in the autumn of 2025 and had initial conversations about developing what Hamilton calls an “observatory” to monitor the polynya from all sides.That would require the involvement of a lot more people like Noah on both sides of Baffin Bay, but many Inuit do not have passports, and bringing them together physically is proving to be a problem.View image in fullscreenTerry Noah in his mobile lab. A note saying ‘Don’t forget gun’ is taped to the door as a reminder to take protection against polar bears“Being able to connect the knowledge of these communities between Canada and Greenland is super important in order to really understand how that environment is changing, because they’re the ones that are there every day of the year, all year long,” says Hamilton.“The scientific aspect is important because it’s very difficult to understand how the ocean temperature is changing 300 metres below the surface unless you have particular instruments that you can deploy to measure those changes. But there are many other observations that I think are super critical to understand holistically what’s happening there.”A few minutes after dropping his submersible to take measurements, Noah is packing it up for the return trip. Today’s journey was just off the coast of Grise Fiord, but others take him further afield, sometimes with his 13-year-old daughter, Madison, but often alone, hopping from station to station like a hunter checking his traps.But Noah’s circle is widening. Wearing smart glasses that beam images to social media via portable satellite internet, he is a globally connected Inuk, part of a generation that grew up sharing hunting stories on Facebook.Now, they are sharing data, too, recreating the knowledge transfer that helped Grise Fiord survive those hard early years. It is data that can help Inuit – and the rest of the world – understand their vast and rapidly changing home.View image in fullscreenAqamutik, or traditional Inuit wooden sled, loaded with the two vital types of fuel for travel on the Arctic ice: petrol for the snowmobiles and a seal for the sled dogsNoah has already been in talks with Hamilton about becoming a trainer for other communities, building a network across the High Arctic from Pond Inlet to Resolute to Arctic Bay, to monitor their home waters. The hunting and the science are all part of the same reconnection to the land.“I get to take my friends out here,” says Noah. “And while we’re hunting, we’re collecting data.”A version of this article wasoriginally publishedin Canada’s National Observer and has been republished by Seascape as part of the Guardian’sClimateDeskpartnership. title: Spain’s PM says no evidence ‘whatsoever’ Morocco behind Ceuta border breach | Spain | The Guardian
description: Pedro Sánchez continues to defend Rabat after police report claiming border forces helped 70,000 cross border
Author: Stephen Burgen
Headline: Pedro Sánchez continues to defend Rabat after police report claiming border forces helped 70,000 cross border
Content: Sánchez addresses parliament on the government's handling of a massive border breach in the Spanish territory of Ceuta.Photograph: Olmo Blanco/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSánchez addresses parliament on the government's handling of a massive border breach in the Spanish territory of Ceuta.Photograph: Olmo Blanco/Getty ImagesSpainSpain’s PM says no evidence ‘whatsoever’ Morocco behind Ceuta border breachPedro Sánchez continues to defend Rabat after police report claiming border forces helped 70,000 cross borderEurope live – latest updatesStephen Burgenin BarcelonaThu 3 Sep 2026 08.52 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 08.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSpain has seen no evidence “whatsoever” that Morocco planned or facilitated a mass border breach into its north African territory of Ceuta, the Spanish prime minister,Pedro Sánchez, has told parliament.The address on Thursday followed the emergence of a police report, commissioned by a judge and widely quoted in the media, claiming Moroccan border forces had actively aided about 70,000 people to cross the border in late July.“I ‌can assure you ‌that no institution – not the diplomatic service, nor theEuropean Commission, ‌nor any international body – has provided the Spanish government with any solid evidence that Morocco planned or carried out the incident. None whatsoever,” Sánchez told parliament.Speaking the morning after about 50,000 people marched in Madrid to protest his handling of the Ceuta crisis, the socialist prime minister also denied the government had received any warning of the mass breach, saying no reports to authorities had anticipated “the scale or probability of what eventually happened”.View image in fullscreenA protest against the Spanish government’s handling of the recent border breach at Ceuta.Photograph: Francesco Militello Mirto/NurPhoto/ShutterstockSánchez has repeatedly defendedMoroccoduring the crisis, highlighting Rabat’s cooperation in returning most of the migrants in the days after the surge.But he said on Thursday that Spain had summoned Morocco’s ambassador on 21 August because of “unacceptable statements” made by two ministers over Ceuta and Melilla, another Spanish north African territory. Last month, Morocco’s justice minister, Abdellatif Ouahbi, publicly reiterated Rabat’s sovereignty claims over the cities.Sánchez said he had “for now” ruled out Moroccan government involvement but conceded that Moroccan forces had allowed crossings to occur during a key 10-hour period on 30 July.Many of those who crossed said in interviews they had been actively encouraged to do so. Moroccan officials have denied enabling the crossing.Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the leader of the conservative People’s party, called on Sánchez to resign for his “incompetence and complicity”.In response to Sánchez summoning the Moroccan ambassador to discuss the crisis, Santiago Abascal, the leader of the far-right Vox party, said: “Morocco doesn’t need an ambassador inSpain– you are its ambassador.”View image in fullscreenPeople who entered Ceuta from Morocco in late July on hunger strike last month to demand asylum.Photograph: Laura Rincon/EPAAs many as141 people are thought to have diedtrying to enter Ceuta at the end of July. The influx unleashed a political crisis, a humanitarian emergency andreignited tensions within the EU over immigration.On Thursday, Sánchez appealed for European solidarity over the crisis. He did not single out any countries by name but, in a pointed passage apparently aimed at Italy and Denmark, the two countries that had led public criticism of Spain, said the principle of solidarity should apply to Ceuta as much as it applies to Greenland and Lampedusa.Ceuta showed just how easily Europe can be dividedRead moreAlthough 90% of the people had returned to Morocco within 24 hours, several thousand, including at least 500 minors, are thought to remain, either living on the street or in makeshift shelters.Amid calls from Vox to return them to Morocco, Sánchez reminded parliament that under Spanish, European and international law, migrants had a right to be treated as individuals. “You can’t just grab someone by the arm and drag them across the frontier as though they were a sack of dirt,” he told MPs.In reference to the hundreds of destitute minors, Aina Vidal of the leftwing group Sumar, said: “They’re children, not invaders, not soldiers. They didn’t come carrying bombs, they arrived wearing water wings, in tears.”‘We want to find a better future’: teenage girls on why they risked their lives to reach SpainRead moreIt seems likely the government will invest in facilities in Ceuta to accommodate the remaining migrants rather than risk the political backlash both in Spain and across Europe were they to bring them to the mainland.There is also evidence that, faced with hunger as well as hostility from many local people, some migrants have already begun going back to Morocco.However, as Sánchez told parliament, the per capita income of Ceuta is eight times that of Morocco and “even if we build a wall 100 metres high there will still be people prepared to throw themselves into the sea to get across”.“We will not stop working until Ceuta emerges from this difficult situation: stronger, more prosperous, and more integrated with the rest of Spain and the EU,” he added.Additional reportingby Jakub KrupaExplore more on these topicsSpainMoroccoMigrationPedro SánchezEuropean CommissionEuropean UnionEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘We continue to suffer’: victims of apartheid-era Sharpeville massacre demand compensation | South Africa | The Guardian
description: Claim relating to 1960 attack on hundreds of protesters part of wave of litigation over apartheid crimes in South Africa
Author: Rachel Savage
Headline: Claim relating to 1960 attack on hundreds of protesters part of wave of litigation over apartheid crimes in South Africa
Content: Protesters flee after police opened fire on a peaceful crowd in Sharpeville on 21 March 1960. At least 91 people were killed and 238 injured.Photograph: Ian Berry/c/o Atlas GalleryView image in fullscreenProtesters flee after police opened fire on a peaceful crowd in Sharpeville on 21 March 1960. At least 91 people were killed and 238 injured.Photograph: Ian Berry/c/o Atlas GallerySouth Africa‘We continue to suffer’: victims of apartheid-era Sharpeville massacre demand compensationClaim relating to 1960 attack on hundreds of protesters part of wave of litigation over apartheid crimes in South AfricaRachel Savagein SharpevilleThu 3 Sep 2026 06.11 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 15.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe day dawned brightly on 21 March 1960, as residents of the South African township of Sharpeville gathered to protest against pass laws, which forced “Black, Indian and Coloured” South Africans to carry documents at all times specifying where they were allowed to be.Abraham Mofokeng joined the march, one of dozens organised nationwide by the Pan Africanist Congress (PAC), a breakaway group from the African National Congress (ANC). “The weather was very nice, the sun was out. You could not have suspected that the day would go so horribly,” said Mofokeng, who was then a 20-year-old factory worker.View image in fullscreenAbraham Mofokeng, who was shot in the foot and back during the Sharpeville massacre on 21 March 1960.Photograph: Rachel Savage/The GuardianMofokeng, now 86, was among the thousands gathered peacefully outside the police station in Sharpeville, which is about 40 miles south of Johannesburg in a heavily industrialised region known as the Vaal Triangle.The crowd was singing, he said, when officers opened fire without warning. At least91 people were killed and 238 injured, in what became known as the Sharpeville massacre.As Mofokeng fled, a bullet grazed the inside of his right foot, ripping his shoe off. A woman fell to the ground before him; he jumped over her and kept running. Only later, when he noticed blood running down his legs, did he realise he had been shot in the back, where a bullet remains lodged in his spine.Mofokeng is among three claimants suing the South African government, in a case filed on Thursday, for compensation for the massacre. If the case is successful, dozens more could file claims.The case is part of a wave of litigationdemanding justice for apartheid-era crimes, amid widespread disillusionment with ANC-led governments that have failed to rectify South Africa’s huge racial inequality and poverty since the end of apartheid over three decades ago.View image in fullscreenDead and wounded South Africans lie outside the Sharpeville police station.Photograph: PN2In January 2025, 25 survivors and relatives of victims of apartheid state violencesued South Africa’s governmentfor failing to prosecute cases referred to it by the post-apartheid Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC). That May, the president, Cyril Ramaphosa, announced a judicial inquiry into potential political interference, which is still ongoing.Spokespeople for South Africa’s justice department did not respond to a request for comment on the Sharpeville compensation case.In the immediate aftermath of the Sharpeville massacre, police claimed protesters had been throwing rocks at them. “I don’t know how many we shot,” said Col J Pienaar, the local police commander, according to astory published by the Guardianthe following day. “It all started when hordes of natives surrounded the police station. My car was struck with a stone. If they do these things they must learn their lesson the hard way.”In July 1961, in response to victims filing compensation claims, the white minority regime passeda lawindemnifying the government and anyone acting under its authority for any actions taken “in good faith for the prevention or suppression of internal disorder, the maintenance or restoration of good order, public safety or essential services, or the preservation of life or property”.View image in fullscreenPerformers re-enact the Sharpeville massacre at the memorial site for victims on 3 September.Photograph: Phill Magakoe/AFP/Getty ImagesThe law, which was made effective retrospectively from the date of the massacre, is still in force today. The claimants’ legal team is arguing that the law is unconstitutional.The claimants are hoping to get compensation of about 500,000 rand (£23,000), said Daniel Leader, a partner with the UK law firm Leigh Day, which is advising the South African legal team, led by Lawyers For Human Rights, an NGO.Mafokeng was awarded 30,000 rand as a one-off payment, after the TRC concluded in 2003. The TRC hadrecommended annual reparations payments of about 20,000 rand for six years.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe Long WaveNesrine Malik, Micha Frazer-Carroll and the team guide you through the biggest Black stories from around the worldEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“We continued to suffer,” said Mofokeng, who still lives in Sharpeville. “Especially now … I am struggling and my health is not up to standard.”View image in fullscreenPaulina Mathinye, whose father, Samson, was killed by police in the Sharpeville massacrePhotograph: Rachel Savage/The GuardianThe other two test claimants were children when their fathers were killed in the massacre. Paulina Mathinye was five when her father, Samson, was shot. “Every time he came back from work, I would be so happy to see him that I would run to him, and then he would pick me up,” she said.Mathinye did not initially understand what had happened that day in 1960. “I kept on asking my mum: ‘Mummy, why are you crying?’”Mathinye’s mother struggled to raise her five children on a domestic worker’s wages and Mathinye, who had wanted to train as a teacher but could not afford the bursary, had to leave education at 17 to find work.View image in fullscreenAbraham Mofokeng visiting the memorial site on Thursday.Photograph: Phill Magakoe/AFP/Getty ImagesMathinye, who is now 71, said she hoped for compensation that would make up for some of what she lost when her father died. “Some of my friends are teachers, some of them are nurses, and I’m staying in the same house that my father did,” she said.Sharpeville’s problems did not begin with the massacre in 1960, but with the dispossession of Black South Africans from productive land, their forced removals to townships and their exclusion from the economy, said Vincent Thamae, a PAC member who supports the massacre victims and their families.“When people talk about compensation now,” he said, “compensation is a concept to them that includes all the land that they lost, the economy that they were taken out of and even how they have been treated in the new democracy.”Explore more on these topicsSouth AfricaAfricaRaceProtestnewsShareReuse this content

title: Nobel laureate Machado: ‘Illegitimate’ Venezuela regime has no right to strike US oil deal | Venezuela | The Guardian
description: Opposition leader says interim government lacking democratic mandate to negotiate on natural resources
Author: Tom Phillips
Headline: Opposition leader says interim government lacking democratic mandate to negotiate on natural resources
Content: María Corina Machado addressing the Venezuelan diaspora during a rally in Panama City in May.Photograph: Martin Bernetti/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMaría Corina Machado addressing the Venezuelan diaspora during a rally in Panama City in May.Photograph: Martin Bernetti/AFP/Getty ImagesVenezuelaNobel laureate Machado: ‘Illegitimate’ Venezuela regime has no right to strike US oil dealOpposition leader says interim government lacking democratic mandate to negotiate on natural resourcesThe US and Venezuela: a century-old relationship drenched in oilTom PhillipsLatin America correspondentThu 3 Sep 2026 12.17 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 16.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado has questioned Donald Trump’s oil deal with Venezuela’s interim government, saying the country’s natural resources do not belong to “an illegitimate regime”.In her first public comments sinceTrump announcedwhat he called “the biggest oil deal in world history” with Venezuela last Friday, Machado walked a diplomatic tightrope between challenging the agreement and trying not to rile the White House.In a video posted on social media, the Nobel peace prize winner said: “Of course the United States is the principal partner Venezuela needs to fully develop its strategic potential. This is what the majority of Venezuelans believe … and it is something I’ve spent my whole life defending.”However, Machado said, the current occupants of the Miraflores presidential palace in Caracas were “enemies of the US”, saying they did not have the right or the democratic mandate to negotiate Venezuela’s natural resources. “The wealth of our subsoil does not belong to an illegitimate regime – it belongs to the Venezuelan people,” she said, adding that supporters felt “sadness and anger” at being excluded from the decision-making process.Venezuela has the world’s largest proven crude oil reserves with an estimated 303bn barrels, of which more than 65bn barrels are involved in the agreement.Trump’s deal was struck with the un-elected interim president, Delcy Rodríguez, who took power in January after her predecessor, Nicolás Maduro, was abducted by US special forces.Many observers expected Trump to replace Maduro with Machado, a conservative democracy activist who later gave the US president her Nobel prize award. But instead Trump backed Rodríguez, threatening: “If she doesn’t do what’s right, she is going to pay a very big price – probably bigger than Maduro”, and sidelined Machado.The White Houseclaimsthe oil deal will help secure US “energy dominance for the next century” as well as “purging foreign malign influence from our back yard” by excluding China and Russia.Speaking outside the Miraflores palace on Wednesday, the US energy secretary, Chris Wright, said the aim was “to massively grow production and economic opportunities in Venezuela”, adding: “President Trump has a clear mission in Venezuela. The mission is to bring peace, freedom, opportunity, and prosperity to everyone in Venezuela.”But there has been widespread condemnation of what critics call a predatory and colonial-style land grab. Machado’s supporters fear the deal makes Washington far less inclined to push for fresh presidential elections.Machado’s movement is widely believed to have beaten Maduro by a landslide in the last such vote, in 2024, but he refused to accept the result and clung to power until his dramatic rendition on 3 January this year.On Wednesday, Trump and Rodríguez brushed off questions about when an election might be held. “You had a very powerful, very nasty dictatorship in Venezuela – and they’re just not going to be ready for it yet,” Trump told reporters, before adding vaguely: “But soon.”Rodríguez said: “There will be an electoral process, but when Venezuela is ready.“I don’t set dates,” she added.Explore more on these topicsVenezuelaAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Apocalypse prep or pure pragmatism: what is behind Peter Thiel’s move to Argentina? | Peter Thiel | The Guardian
description: Relocation coincides with proposed laws that opponents say would entrench power of US tech billionaires in country
Author: Aisha Down
Headline: Relocation coincides with proposed laws that opponents say would entrench power of US tech billionaires in country
Content: Protesters marching to Peter Thiel’s mansion in Buenos Aires this week. There is broad unease about the tech magnate’s presence in the country.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenProtesters marching to Peter Thiel’s mansion in Buenos Aires this week. There is broad unease about the tech magnate’s presence in the country.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesPeter ThielApocalypse prep or pure pragmatism: what is behind Peter Thiel’s move to Argentina?Relocation coincides with proposed laws that opponents say would entrench power of US tech billionaires in countryAisha DownGlobal technology reporterThu 3 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 08.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDozens of protesters converged on Peter Thiel’s mansion in Buenos Aires this week after a congressional session raised questions about the billionaire’s presence in the country.In white masks, they held signs saying “Peter Thief” and “No to the Peter Thiel law” in front of the wrought-iron gates of the $12m (£8.9m) residence, which Thiel bought in April as he moved his family toArgentina.There is broad unease at the tech magnate’s presence in the country.
