His move has been characterised as part of a plan to hedge against world war three: Argentina, agriculturally rich and deep in the southern hemisphere, might just be the ideal place for a tech billionaire towait out the apocalypse.But recent developments in the country suggest Thiel could have more pragmatic considerations.View image in fullscreenProtesters marched to the gates of the $12m residence Peter Thiel bought when he moved his family to Argentina in April.Photograph: Tomás Cuesta/ReutersLast week, Argentina’s chamber of deputies held a six-hour debate on a set of sweeping regulatory changes put forward by Javier Milei’s rightwing government shortly after Thiel moved to Buenos Aires. They invited Thiel, Milei and an official linked to Argentina’s intelligence services to answer questions.“None of them answered, and none of them came to the meeting,” said Juan Marino, a member of the chamber of deputies and the leader of the Piquetero party.Marino said the new laws amounted to a “technofascist legislative package” aimed at entrenching the power of US tech billionaires in the country. Thiel has not publicly advocated for them, but Marino and others have said that their timing was suggestive.The meeting in the chamber of deputies came after Argentinian deputies from several parties made public requests to the government for information about Thiel, his meetings and his businesses. None have been answered.View image in fullscreenPeter Thiel held closed-door meetings with Javier Milei and key presidential advisers in the months after he moved to Argentina.Photograph: Gage Skidmore/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockOne of the laws, the “super RIGI”, would put in place an investment regime offering foreign companies a minimal tax rate and a 30-year guarantee against regulatory change. It specifically names AI datacentres among investments it hopes to attract.Another, which failed,aimed to eliminatemost of the restrictions around foreigners buying land in Argentina. A final decree would require some civilian government departments to share vast amounts of personal data on Argentinian citizens with the state intelligence services.There is no evidence that Thiel has advocated for these laws directly. But in the months after he moved to Buenos Aires, he held closed-door meetings with Milei and key presidential advisers. It is uncommon for a foreign investor to have this degree of access.In the regulatory package, Marino and others see the footprint of Thiel’s larger techno-libertarian interests.The decree that gives vast amounts of Argentinians’ personal data to state intelligence services comes as Argentinian deputies have asked increasinglypointedquestionsabout whether Palantir, the company Thiel co-founded, has undisclosed contracts with the state, which have gone unanswered.View image in fullscreenOne of the proposed laws protesters oppose would offer foreign companies a minimal tax rate and a 30-year guarantee against regulatory change.Photograph: Tomás Cuesta/ReutersThe land law, said Marino, could have paved the way for semi-autonomous “startup cities” – such as the controversialPróspera development in Honduras– that Thiel has advocated as a way for libertarians to carve out zones outside state control.“Argentina is kind of a laboratory,” said Cecilia Nicolini, who represents Argentina at the Mercosur regional parliament. US tech billionaires, she said, “are using Argentina as a laboratory, because they have a person in power, Milei, who is even more crazy than they are”.Over the summer Milei wrote an article in the Financial Times advocating the creation of “non-human corporations” – “entities operated by AI agents or robots”.It parallels a vision put forward by OpenAI’s chief executive, Sam Altman, whopredicted in 2024that the world could soon be run by AI-owned companies. It also raises dark, thorny questions about the legal liabilities of those entities.Nicolini said: “It’s not just that [Thiel] chose Argentina in terms of, it’s a secure place to live in a world that is facing a number of wars, etcetera.“But really, behind it, I think there is a clear plan. And it is related to reforms that Milei is trying to pass, with some success in some cases, and in others, backlash.”Thiel was approached for comment.Explore more on these topicsPeter ThielArgentinaJavier MileiPalantirAmericasData protectionnewsShareReuse this content

title: The US and Venezuela: a century-old relationship drenched in oil | Venezuela | The Guardian
description: A visual look at how Washington’s relationship with Caracas has gone from cordial to ‘predatory’
Author: Lucy Swan
Headline: A visual look at how Washington’s relationship with Caracas has gone from cordial to ‘predatory’
Content: Venezuela’s importance to the US has been proven time and time again over the past century. Composite: Prina Shah for the Guardian/AP/AFP/Getty ImagesA visual look at how Washington’s relationship with Caracas has gone from cordial to ‘predatory’Trump ally defends Venezuela oil deal amid ‘gunpoint diplomacy’ criticismNobel laureate Machado: ‘Illegitimate’ Venezuela regime has no right to strike US oil dealByOliver Holmes,Seán ClarkeandLucy SwanThu 3 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 16.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWritten in the middle of the last century, the US Department of State memo conveys its message in a curt and undiplomatically honest tone: the glue that binds Washington to Caracas is, and is always likely to be, oil.“All US policies toward Venezuela are affected in greater or less degree by the objective of assuring an adequate supply of petroleum for the US,”the 1950 documentreads.Decades later, little appears to have changed. After a brazen night-time kidnapping of the country’s leader earlier this year, Donald Trumpannouncedlast week that the US was taking majority control over about a fifth of Venezuela’s oil reserves. That deal,accordingto the White House, “secures our energy dominance for the next century”. How much it will benefit Venezuelans is yet to be seen.The country’s importance to the US has been proven time and time again over the past century. Home to what are now known to be the world’s largest known oil reserves,Venezuelakept allied planes, ship and tanks well fuelled during the second world war.Global oil reserves by country in 2026.Washington and Caracas largely cooperated over the following decades, with US energy companies heavily involved in Venezuela’s oil industry, and profiting from it immensely. But relations took a nosedive in 1999, whenHugo Chávezbecame president.A self-professed socialist and anti-imperialist, Chávez made alliances, and often oil deals, with China, Iran and Russia. Venezuela switched 180 degrees to become a natural adversary of the US, alongside its ally Cuba.View image in fullscreenHugo Chávez pictured in 2010.Photograph: ReutersRelations deteriorated further when Chávez wasbriefly detained by his own militaryafter a deadly crackdown on mass anti-government protests. The attempted overthrow lasted only two days andhe was soon back in the presidential palace, accusing Washington ofinvolvement in the failed coup.Chávez deepened Venezuela’sdependence on oil exportsin the years that followed. In 2007, he stepped up his battle with Washington with a wave of nationalisation in which he seized oilfields, including those that US firms had operated.Caracas had nationalised the oil industry decades before, but had allowed US companies to profit from the extraction. Under Chávez’s new terms, however, the state oil company was given control of a majority share and foreign firms were offered minority stakes.Scenes from 2002 demonstrations in VenezuelaNational guard officers shoot teargas at protesters in April 2002Among US oil companies, Chevron agreed to the worse terms, but ExxonMobil and ConocoPhillips refused and were in effect pushed out of the industry.Only Chevron, the second largest US oil company, has continued to operate in the country. ExxonMobil and ConocoPhillips engaged in a years-long legal battle with Venezuela for compensation. The World Bank’s international centre for the settlement of investment disputes awarded them billions of dollars, but Venezuela has never paid the money in full.PartnershipsStill, much of the country’s oil infrastructure was built with foreign involvement, and foreign companies are still active in the exploitation of the fields, among them Russian, Chinese and Cuban firms, as well as UK and European companies, including Shell, BP, Italy’s Eni and Spain’s Repsol.When Chávez died in 2013, Nicolás Maduro rose to power. Theformer bus driverhad worked as his foreign minister and continued an antagonistic policy towards the US.Maduro’s rule was considered dictatorial. The UN estimated in 2019 that more than 20,000 Venezuelans had died in extrajudicial killings. Key institutions, such as the judiciary, were eroded under Maduro and the rule of law deteriorated.View image in fullscreenSupporters of Venezuela’s government protesting in Caracas on 3 January 2026 after the US seized Nicolás Maduro.The US has portrayed the Maduro government as illegitimate. A Washington-led sanctions campaign compounded widespread corruption, and the Venezuelan economy suffered.It did not help the relationship that Maduro kept close ties with Moscow and Beijing. About 80% of the crude oil Venezuela produced was exported to China before the US-imposed blockade in December.Venezuelan oil exportsChina is the world’s biggest oil importer, and takes the shipments as repayment for loans it previously gave to Caracas, often at low prices.Chinese loans to VenezuelaSince the start of his second term, Donald Trump had repeatedly called for Maduro to be ousted, accusing him of sending drugs and criminals to the US – a claim experts say lacks evidence. He also claimed Maduro was stealing US oil, a reference to Chávez’s seizure.In July last year, Washington announced a $50m (£37m) bounty on Maduro’s head, accusing him of being one of the biggest drug traffickers in the world.Trump’s administration began to carry out airstrikes against alleged drug traffickers in the Caribbean Sea and then to seize Venezuelan tankers, while building up the US military presence in the waters surrounding the country.Footage shows US special forces boarding a tanker off VenezuelaFootage shows US special forces boarding a tanker off VenezuelaTrump gave Maduro an ultimatum to relinquish power in late November, offering him safe passage out of the country. But Maduro refused the offer, telling supporters he did not want “a slave’s peace” and accusing the US of wanting control of his country’s oil reserves.This January, in the ultimate expression of a relationship breakdown, US forces carried out a pre-dawn raid on Caracas,capturing Maduroand his wife, Cilia Flores, who are now on trial in New York.Venezuela’s acting president, Delcy Rodríguez, initially denounced Maduro’s capture as a kidnapping, but has since shown she is willing to work with Washington.In the aftermath of Maduro’s abduction, Trump said the US would take control of Venezuela’s oil industry. And in August, after months of secret talks, Washington’s longstanding oil-focused policy was on display again when the US presidentannouncedthe agreement to control millions of barrels of oil.A White House press release described the agreement as the “biggest oil deal in world history” that gave the US government “powerful governance rights” over reserves. Further down in the document, the White House claimed private-sector growth would help drive a democratic transition in Venezuela, though few in Caracas will be holding their breath. Rodríguez has already been forced todefend herselfagainst claims she is surrendering Venezuela’s natural resources to a foreign power.One prominent Venezuelan economist has called the deal “predatory”, saying it was “done at gunpoint”. Francisco Rodríguezwrotethat Washington’s actions in Venezuela had turned the country into “a protectorate in all but name”.“Trying to run a country from the capital of an imperial power has been tried before,” he said. “And it has not ended well.”​Additional reporting by Jillian AmbroseExplore more on these topicsVenezuelaUS foreign policyTrump administrationNicolás MaduroHugo ChávezAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Yen soars as Bank of Japan tipped to raise interest rates | Yen | The Guardian
description: Jump lifts currency to highest level against dollar in a month, while global markets remain jittery
Author: Heather Stewart
Headline: Jump lifts currency to highest level against dollar in a month, while global markets remain jittery
Content: The Tokyo skyline. Investors have been reassessing their expectations for the future path of interest rates in Japan and other major economies.Photograph: Yuichi Yamazaki/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Tokyo skyline. Investors have been reassessing their expectations for the future path of interest rates in Japan and other major economies.Photograph: Yuichi Yamazaki/AFP/Getty ImagesYenYen soars as Bank of Japan tipped to raise interest ratesJump lifts currency to highest level against dollar in a month, while global markets remain jitteryBusiness live – latest updatesHeather StewartandGraeme WeardenThu 3 Sep 2026 10.33 EDTFirst published on Thu 3 Sep 2026 07.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Japanese yen has soared by more than 2% against the dollar amid speculation the Bank ofJapanis set to raise interest rates.The latest jump on Thursday lifted the yen to its highest level against the dollar in a month, at 155.57, and followed a 0.9% move the previous day.Global markets remain jittery after this week’sdramatic government bond sell-off– caused by fears of a fresh inflation increase as a result of higher oil prices.Investors have been reassessing their expectations for the future path of interest rates, in Japan and across other major economies.Remarks by a Bank of Japan policymaker, Hajime Takata, suggesting it needs to move more “nimbly”, appeared to have heightened the prospects of a decisive move.The chief executive of the financial adviser deVere, Nigel Green, said the scale of the yen appreciation over such a short time period underlined the febrile state of markets. “Markets this jumpy don’t need a shock to move hard, a rumour is enough,” he said.Citi said in a note to clients that Takata’s remarks were the “strongest messaging we’ve heard from the board and reintroduces the idea of an expedited rate hike trajectory”.The Bank of Japan has been incrementally raising rates for the past two years, after the economy finally shrugged off decades of deflation, or falling prices – but its main policy rate was left unchanged at 1% in July.Markets now believe there is a 77% chance of a rate rise at the BoJ’s next meeting, which starts on 17 September.Commenting on the latest market moves, Japan’s vice-finance minister for international affairs, Atsushi Mimura, said he was “neither satisfied nor reassured”, and policymakers “remain on a state of heightened alert”.The global bond market sell-off – pushing up the yield, or interest rate, on government borrowing – intensified earlier this week after the US Federal Reserve chair, Kevin Warsh, used a speech last Friday to indicate that he was determined to bring inflation back to target.Warsh had previously baffled some investors by withdrawing the Fed’s approach of signalling future rate moves, known as “forward guidance” – but in Friday’s speech at the central bankers’ conference in Jackson Hole, he said that if inflation did not move towards the 2% targetthe Fed would have “more to do”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe dollar weakened on Thursday after the Fed governor Christopher Waller indicated he was leaning towards keeping interest rates steady at this month’s meeting of Fed rate-setters.“I’m going to paraphrase John Lennon here: ‘give disinflation a chance’. We can wait one meeting,” Waller told Reuters.The dollar dropped further against the yen after his comments, and was also weaker against the pound and the euro.The bond sell-off appeared to have eased on Thursday, with yields on 10-year UK government bonds, known as gilts, hovering at about 5.1% in morning trading – having touched the highest level since 2008, close to 5.3%,earlier this week.Explore more on these topicsYenJapanInterest ratesCurrenciesEconomicsAsia PacificDollarnewsShareReuse this content

title: BoM forecasts strongest El Niño on record as research points to ‘alarming’ climate change influence | Australia news | The Guardian
description: Bureau of Meteorology suggests El Niño has already broken records, with Pacific Ocean temperature change exceeding 2C in six months
Author: Graham Readfearn
Headline: Bureau of Meteorology suggests El Niño has already broken records, with Pacific Ocean temperature change exceeding 2C in six months
Content: Bushfires in the area around the Nowra, New South Wales in December 2019.Photograph: Saeed Khan/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBushfires in the area around the Nowra, New South Wales in December 2019.Photograph: Saeed Khan/AFP/Getty ImagesAustralia newsBoM forecasts strongest El Niño on record as research points to ‘alarming’ climate change influenceBureau of Meteorology suggests El Niño has already broken records, with Pacific Ocean temperature change exceeding 2C in six monthsFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesSign up for climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s free Clear Air newsletter hereGraham ReadfearnEnvironment and climate correspondentThu 3 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 18.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe growing El Niño weather phenomenon to Australia’s east is already breaking heat records, with forecasts showing it will likely easily surpass previous events, according to Australia’s Bureau of Meteorology.Separate research suggests climate change has greatly shortened the odds of the event hitting record extremes.On Thursday,the UN’s weather agency said the event in the Pacific was continuing to strengthenand would probably persist until early 2027, warning it had the “potential to deliver a massive blow to communities and economies across the world”.The UN secretary general, António Guterres, said: “El Niño is being supersized before our eyes. The science leaves no room for doubt: the planet is in uncharted waters, and those waters are heating up.”‘Supersizing before our eyes’: UN warns of record El Niño approachingRead moreIn an update this week, the Bureau of Meteorology said the El Niño was now forecast to peak in late spring or summer and “reach levels above the warmest observed since reliable records began in 1950”.El Niño events tend to mean hotter and drier conditions for Australia’s south and east in winter and spring, and can increase the risk of heatwaves, drought and bushfires.El Niño strength is assessed by analysing sea surface temperatures in a region of the equatorial Pacific known as Niño 3.4. The bureau has said the strength of an El Niño does not necessarily mean stronger effects for the continent.10:27‘Godzilla-level’ El Niño could cause hottest year on record - The LatestHowever, bureau analysis of the unfolding event suggested this El Niño had already broken records.“We have been looking at the rate of warming observed in the last two months and it has been faster than any other event. Not only is it strong, but it has escalated rapidly,” said Felicity Gamble, a senior climatologist at the BoM.Gamble said the relative sea surface temperatures in the Niño 3.4 region for the month of August were likely to be between 2.2C and 2.3C above average – higher than any previous August since 1950 (the year after which records are considered to be more reliable).Sign up to get climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s Clear Air column as a free newsletterShe said forecasts were suggesting relative sea surface temperatures in that region could peak over 3C above average, compared with the highest previous figure of 2.6C observed in January 1983.Gamble said the relative sea surface temperatures in the Niño 3.4 region had warmed by more than 2C between February and July.She said: “No other period in the historical record exceeds that. This is the first event where we have had that change exceed 2C in the space of six months.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When he publishesSign up toClear Air AustraliaAdam Morton brings you incisive analysis about the politics and impact of the climate crisisEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“We could be seeing a record in terms of the strength, and also the rate of warming and the duration.”Climate experts have said El Niño will likely combine with climate change to push global temperatures to record highs next year.Gamble said in the Pacific region El Niño was already contributing to droughts in Papua New Guinea, with food and water shortages and major wildfires in Indonesia.This winter was Australia’sthird-warmest on record and the hottest on record for New South Wales, Tasmania and Victoria.Scientists at the University of Melbourne have released preliminary research into the influence of climate change on the predicted peak of the El Niño. By analysing historical records and comparing climate models with and without the influence of greenhouse gas emissions, the scientists found climate change had made “an event of this magnitude” six times more likely.Thestudy has been submitted to a journalfor peer review, but the authors said they had used a methodology common to many other published studies.Dr Andrew King, one of the co-authors of the research, said: “This points to the fact that there is likely a climate change role here in the chance of having these extreme El Niño conditions. It seems likely there is a human fingerprint emerging in this event.“We are seeing something that does not appear to have happened before and that is alarming.”The bureau’s long-range forecast for September to November points to an increased chance of below average rainfall for the south and east, but above average for most of the continent’s western half. Temperatures are also likely to be above average south of the tropics.Explore more on these topicsAustralia newsClimate crisisEl Niño southern oscillationClimate scienceAustralia weathernewsShareReuse this content

title: Australian science prize awarded to researcher studying memory accuracy of domestic violence survivors | Science | The Guardian
description: Helen Paterson’s work on advancing how police and courts understand memory is recognised in prestigious Eureka prizes
Author: Donna Lu
Headline: Helen Paterson’s work on advancing how police and courts understand memory is recognised in prestigious Eureka prizes
Content: Assoc Prof Helen Paterson was awarded a Eureka prize in recognition of her work in advancing how police and courts understand victim-survivor memories and testimony.Photograph: Emlyn Crockett/Australian MuseumView image in fullscreenAssoc Prof Helen Paterson was awarded a Eureka prize in recognition of her work in advancing how police and courts understand victim-survivor memories and testimony.Photograph: Emlyn Crockett/Australian MuseumScienceAustralian science prize awarded to researcher studying memory accuracy of domestic violence survivorsHelen Paterson’s work on advancing how police and courts understand memory is recognised in prestigious Eureka prizesFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastDonna LuThu 3 Sep 2026 08.30 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 17.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMemory is an imperfect thing:research showsthat recollections of single events – a purse being snatched, say – differ from those about repeated or ongoing events, such as incidents of domestic and family violence.“What our research shows is that compared to a single-event witness, a repeated-event witness tends to report more gist-like details, the overall details of what typically would happen, and the things that remain constant between the episodes,” said Helen Paterson, an associate professor in forensic psychology at the University of Sydney.Two women and two girls dead in four days. Australian experts yet again call for actionRead more“Sometimes they confuse one episode with another.”Paterson’s work has important implications for victim-survivors of domestic and family violence and how their testimony is received.“If they’re saying this in trial, it’s defence 101 to say … they’ve made this inconsistency, therefore their whole memory is unreliable,” she said. “But we do know what they do report tends to be highly accurate in that it did happen to them. It’s just they might mix up the episode in which it happened.”Paterson’s work has also found that repeated-event witnesses are perceived to be “less honest, less cognitively competent, and less overall credible than the single-event witnesses – which is pretty concerning that the more repeatedly you are victimised, the less credible you appear to others”.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailIn recognition of her work in advancing how police and courts understand victim-survivor testimony in such cases, Paterson was awarded a prestigious Eureka prize on Thursday night.Established in 1990, the Australian Museum Eureka prizes recognise the work of Australian scientists and science communicators.Paterson was recognised for excellence in forensic science – one of 19 categories – at an event at Sydney town hall.She hopes the award will help elevate the voices of victim-survivors. “Often we don’t give them the support and encouragement, and we don’t believe them and see them as credible as we should.”View image in fullscreenAssoc Prof Jane Tiller was recognised at the Eureka prizes for driving national legislative change that bans life insurers from discriminating against people due to genetic test results.Photograph: Michelle McFarlane/Australian MuseumAlso among the winners was Assoc Prof Jane Tiller of Monash University, recognised for driving national legislative change that bans life insurers fromdiscriminating against people due to genetic test results.Passed into law in April, the ban will come into effect on 8 October. The legal change will enable scientists to use genomics more effectively to prevent conditions such as cancer and heart disease, Tiller said.“The biggest reason that people don’t want this testing is because of fear of insurance discrimination,” she said. The legal change was a “critical barrier that we needed to remove”.“We want to … start finding young people who we know have very high risks of diseases that we can prevent, and give them the screening, the surveillance, the health tools available to them to prevent or treat those diseases early.”Prof Georgina Long, who alongside the lateProf Richard Scolyerwas named Australian of the Year in 2024, won the Eureka prize for scientific research, for her pioneering melanoma work. Four other Australians of the Year have previously received Eureka prizes: Prof Tim Flannery, Prof Ian Frazer, Prof Michelle Simmons, and the late Prof Alan Mackay-Sim.Also among Thursday night’s winners were Australia’s marine heatwaves forecasting tool, developed by the CSIRO and Bureau of Meteorology; the Women’s Microbiome Innovation Group, a Melbourne-based research collaboration that discovered thatbacterial vaginosisis sexually transmitted between partners; and Prof Yansong Shen of the University of New South Wales, who developed a scalable low-cost process to recover valuable metals and silicon from used solar panels.The Australian Museum director and chief executive, Kim McKay, said: “This year’s winners are tackling some of our greatest challenges: protecting our environment, advancing healthcare, informing public policy and inspiring the next generation of scientists.“World-changing discoveries do not happen overnight. They are built on years of dedication, collaboration and sustained investment.”In Australia,domestic and family violence counsellingis available from Full Stop Australia on 1800 385 578. Other international helplines may be found viawww.befrienders.org.Explore more on these topicsSciencePsychologyDomestic violenceInsurance (Australia)GeneticsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Off-grid UK-Australian couple describe ‘anguish’ at removal of children by Italian court | Italy | The Guardian
description: After judge allows partial access rights, Catherine Birmingham and Nathan Trevallion say the enforced separation ‘broke each of our hearts’
Author: Tory Shepherd
Headline: After judge allows partial access rights, Catherine Birmingham and Nathan Trevallion say the enforced separation ‘broke each of our hearts’
Content: ‘We are deeply saddened’ … Nathan Trevallion and Catherine Birmingham were raising their three children off-grid in ItalyView image in fullscreen‘We are deeply saddened’ … Nathan Trevallion and Catherine Birmingham were raising their three children off-grid in ItalyItalyOff-grid UK-Australian couple describe ‘anguish’ at removal of children by Italian courtAfter judge allows partial access rights, Catherine Birmingham and Nathan Trevallion say the enforced separation ‘broke each of our hearts’Tory ShepherdThu 3 Sep 2026 06.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA couple have told of their heartache, trauma and stress after fighting for two years for their right to parent their children as they choosein the glare of the world’s attention.The three children of a Melbourne woman, Catherine Birmingham, and her British partner, Nathan Trevallion, were removed from their “dilapidated” off-grid home in Italy last year.It sparked global conversations about state intervention and alternative lifestyles.They were raising the children on a property in the woods in the Abruzzo region, where they grew their own food and homeschooled the children.Off-grid UK-Australian couple given more access to children who were removed from home in ItalyRead moreIn September 2024, the family was hospitalised after eating poisonous mushrooms they had picked, which brought them to the attention of authorities.In November 2025, the juvenile court ordered the removal of Utopia Rose, nine, and six-year-old twins Galorian and Bluebell to a residential care facility, citing a lack of hygiene, social interaction, toilet facilities and schooling.Birmingham stayed with them until March, when she was ordered to leave under a new court ruling.On Wednesday, an Italian court approved a staged process that would allow a “gradual reunification process”, and could eventually allow the children to leave the facility.“The ruling partially revises previous court decisions and sets out a ‌gradual reunification process, ‌allowing the children to return home for daytime visits immediately and, from October, for weekend ‌overnight stays with their family,” theirlawyer, Simone Pillon, said.In a statement released on Thursday, the couple said the “long-awaited decision, which our entire family awaited with anguish, arrived with a harshness that broke each of our hearts”.They asked whether forcing school attendance was “fair, legal, and respectful” of their parental rights and the rights of their children, saying they choseItalyfor reasons including its homeschooling rights and support for family bonds.The parents have said that doctors say the children’s health is at “serious risk” and “the only way to reduce this risk is to return them home immediately”.“We are deeply concerned for their health,” the parents wrote.“How will they be well if they are forced to travel back and forth from their home to the foster home, then to school, and then back to the foster home again, all while still being kept apart from their parents?“How will they fare in the evening when, after an afternoon spent at home with their friends and pets, they must return to the foster home?”Even Italy’s hard-right prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, has weighed in. Sheexpressed “alarm”over the children being taken into care, while the deputy prime minister, Matteo Salvini, compared the case to a kidnapping.But the judiciary’s union said the court’s decision was based on factors including the children’s safety, sanitary conditions and education.After the latest decision, social services will monitor the process and make an assessment before any permanent reunion can happen.The couple wrote that the authorities wanted to impose a standard. “And those who don’t follow it lose their children,” they wrote.“We are deeply saddened by this.“We have continued to collaborate and engage with everyone, even under extreme trauma, stress, exasperation and concern for our children knowing their daily suffering but we will always demand respect for our parental rights and, above all, for our children’s rights, especially their right to health – mental, physical and emotional.”The couple plan to appeal for a complete and faster reunification.Explore more on these topicsItalynewsShareReuse this content

title: Property developer claimed ‘the premier is my best friend’ in tapped phone call, Icac hears  | Independent Commission Against Corruption | The Guardian
description: Charles Perrottet, the younger brother of the former premier, tells Icac that claims made by Jean Nassif in the call were ‘bravado’ and ‘far-fetched’
Author: Penry Buckley
Headline: Charles Perrottet, the younger brother of the former premier, tells Icac that claims made by Jean Nassif in the call were ‘bravado’ and ‘far-fetched’
Content: Developer Jean Nassif claimed ‘the premier is my best friend’ in a secretly recorded phone call.Photograph: PR IMAGEView image in fullscreenDeveloper Jean Nassif claimed ‘the premier is my best friend’ in a secretly recorded phone call.Photograph: PR IMAGEIndependent Commission Against CorruptionProperty developer claimed ‘the premier is my best friend’ in tapped phone call, Icac hearsCharles Perrottet, the younger brother of the former premier, tells Icac that claims made by Jean Nassif in the call were ‘bravado’ and ‘far-fetched’Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastPenry BuckleyThu 3 Sep 2026 05.14 EDTFirst published on Thu 3 Sep 2026 02.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA property developer who allegedly made prohibited donations to support factional Liberal work claimed “the premier is my best friend” in a secretly recorded phone call the day after Dominic Perrottet was chosen asNew South Walespremier, an inquiry has heard.Charles Perrottet, the younger brother of the former premier, told theIndependent Commission Against Corruption(Icac) on Thursday that claims made by property developer Jean Nassif in a phone call lawfully intercepted by police were “bravado” and “far-fetched”.Dominic Perrottet is not named as a person of interest in Icac’s allegations and is not accused of any wrongdoing. Nassif, who fled Australia for Lebanon in 2022, has withdrawn from an expected video appearance on Friday after providing a medical certificate. He has previously denied any wrongdoing.As part of its inquiry into alleged corruption in the NSW Liberals, Icac is investigating the allegation that conservative factional figures Charles Perrottet, Jeremy Greenwood and Christian Ellis received prohibited donations totalling $2m from Nassif or his company Toplace between 2020 and 2023 in exchange for political outcomes.The outcomes included damage to the career of former NSW Liberal minister, David Elliott, who had opposed Nassif’s developments, and the removal of former building commissioner, David Chandler, who was scrutinising defects in Toplace apartments.Ellis is overseas and has not responded to Icac’s allegations, while Greenwood will appear before the commission again next week. Charles Perrottet has repeatedly denied he accepted payments from Nassif in exchange for political outcomes.On Thursday, the commission heard phone call between Nassif and a friend in which the developer claimed: “The premier is my best friend … They’re my friends and my boys”.“I only started yesterday. You’re gonna be surprised soon, no jokes, no jokes. I’ve got my hand on the state government, and you’re gonna see changes. You’re gonna see DA approvals for me, like every second week, one DA approved,” he said.Inside knowledge or ‘making stuff up’? Charles Perrottet’s advice to Jean Nassif put under microscope by IcacRead moreCharles Perrottet, who described a phone conversation between Nassif and his younger brother Jean-Claude Perrottet, in which the developer claimed he had “forced the boys” to get rid of the Liberal branch of Baulkham Hills in Elliott’s seat as “bravado”, said the October 2021 call was “even more far-fetched”.On Tuesday,the commission heardabout a May 2021 meeting between him and Nassif at the Nobu fine-dining restaurant in Melbourne’s Crown Casino. Afterwards, Charles Perrottet wrote he had told the told the developer “the best way to get the building commissioner off his back is to take the fight to Elliott and dismantle his infrastructure”, with the result that Elliott would “be on his knees”.Referencing the Nobu dinner, counsel assisting, Peggy Dwyer SC, suggested on Thursday it was “little wonder … that Jean Nassif thought that he had the right [faction] in his pocket immediately after your brother got the premiership.”“I think it’s just bravado. He says he’s the premier’s best friend,” said Charles Perrottet.The inquiry has previously heard that Charles Perrottet, who texted his wife Anita about a plan to remove Elliott from his ministry once the Perrottet government had formed – writing “we execute the prick once party room is over” – shared a secret phone recording in which Elliott could allegedly be heard criticising Dominic Perrottet.On Thursday, the commission heard the recording, during which speaking was faintly audible beneath a loud, rhythmic sound, which Dwyer suggested was a “a heartbeat that suggests a recording device”. Charles Perrottet suggested it was a pocket dial, saying he did not recall having the recording until it wasmentioned in evidence last week, or how he had obtained it.The commission heard evidence that he passed it into another NSW Liberal MP and that Ellis shared it with a private investigator employed by Toplace in the hope of improving the audio quality.‘Charles fucked this whole thing’Charles Perrottet has previously said he would regularly mislead Nassif, adding a “political flavour” to advice in order to chase up payments for genuine lobbying work by Beckington, a company controlled by Ellis and Greenwood.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOn Thursday, the commission heard an exchange sent by Greenwood to Ellis in April 2020, expressing concern about losing Toplace as a client when Nassif’s Cherrybrook development proposal was refused after the Hills shire council did not support it. Charles Perrottet said he did not know what the message – in which Greenwood wrote “Charles fucked this whole thing” – meant.He was asked about a subsequent exchange between him and Ellis in which he detailed steps to assist with Toplace developments, including a call he wrote he would make to the NSW Liberal MP and former Hills shire councillor Robyn Preston.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailOn Thursday, Charles Perrottet said he could not recall calling Preston. The counsel assisting, Peggy Dwyer SC, asked if he would “regularly lie to Christian Ellis at that time to tell him you were doing some things and not others?”“I may have,” said Charles Perrottet, suggesting it might have been “to sound supportive”.Dwyer, noting he had also said he would lie to Nassif, suggested that “actually the fabrication is the evidence you’re giving to the commission because you want to make it sound like you didn’t take the active steps that are clearly set out in this text”.“No,” said Charles Perrottet.Later, he was asked about a message from Greenwood to the Toplace executive Sharangan Maheswaran, also named in Icac’s allegations, in 2021, asking for payment from Nassif, or “Charles is just going to cut the relationship”. After Maheswaran offered to pass on the message, Greenwood expressed concern that Nassif might see it as a threat.Maheswaran, who is named in a separate allegation, has previously denied any wrongdoing. He will appear before Icac next week.Under repeated questioning from Dwyer, Charles Perrottet rejected the suggestion it was “clear as day … that Mr Greenwood shared your view, as expressed to Jean Nassif, that he had to hand over the money in order to achieve the political outcomes”.Icac’s inquiry continues.Explore more on these topicsIndependent Commission Against CorruptionNew South Wales politicsLiberal partyNew South WalesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Volkswagen announces it will cut 100,000 jobs by 2030 | Volkswagen (VW) | The Guardian
description: Under-pressure carmaker will shed 15% of workforce and halve its product line in sector’s biggest ever restructure
Author: Patrick Daly
Headline: Under-pressure carmaker will shed 15% of workforce and halve its product line in sector’s biggest ever restructure
Content: Protesters against proposed VW job cuts outside the company’s Zwickau factory in Saxony in July. The plant is one of four at risk of closure.Photograph: Jens Schluter/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenProtesters against proposed VW job cuts outside the company’s Zwickau factory in Saxony in July. The plant is one of four at risk of closure.Photograph: Jens Schluter/AFP/Getty ImagesVolkswagen (VW)Volkswagen announces it will cut 100,000 jobs by 2030Under-pressure carmaker will shed 15% of workforce and halve its product line in sector’s biggest ever restructurePatrick DalyThu 3 Sep 2026 18.30 EDTFirst published on Thu 3 Sep 2026 18.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe car company Volkswagen has announced it will shed 100,000 jobs by the end of the decade after being hit by US tariffs and fierce competition from Chinese rivals.The German manufacturer said management and unions had agreed as part of a sweeping cost-cutting plan to cut a further 50,000 positions by 2030, bringing total job losses in the pipeline to 100,000.The number of car models the Volkswagen group produces, which includes the Bentley and Audi brands, will be slashed by half, while four production plants inGermanycould also be shuttered within the next eight years.“It is essential to systematically align workforce levels with economic realities,” Volkswagen group said in a statement.The company said it had approved a plan that involved “the reduction of about 50,000 jobs”, on top of another 50,000 already agreed.Volkswagen’s chief executive, Oliver Blume, was booed last month by staff during a tour of the company’s headquarters in Wolfsburg, northern Germany, as part of a company dialogue about the need to address its financial challenges.At the time, Blume’s restructuring plans, which were rumoured to envisage increasing the reduction in headcount from 50,000 to 100,000, were yet to be approved by the VW group’s powerful supervisory board, which represents the labour force and shareholders.But on Thursday, the company, Europe’s largest carmaker, said the board had signed-off on the proposals.“The supervisory board has unanimously approved the executive board’s future plan presented today,” Blume said. “This is a strong signal for the future of the Volkswagen group.”The total of 100,000 cuts will be the largest restructuring ever carried out in the global automotive industry, amounting to about 15% of the carmaker’s employees.Volkswagen employs more than 650,000 people across all its brands, which also includes Skoda, Seat, Porsche, Cupra and Lamborghini.On Thursday, Volkswagen also said that management and unions agreed that the future of four German plants – in Hanover, Emden, Zwickau and Neckarsulm – could not be guaranteed into the 2030s.VW has facedincreasing pressure from rampant Chinese competition in Europe, decreasing sales in China and hefty US tariffs. Even before that, it was struggling for years with falling profits and overproduction in Europe.The tough market in China has also hit other carmakers, with BMW cutting its profit guidance for this year because of the disruption caused by the Iran war and the company’s struggles in the Chinese market.Explore more on these topicsVolkswagen (VW)Automotive industryGermanyEuropeJob lossesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Serbians targeted with spyware in country’s ‘largest documented wave of surveillance’ | Serbia | The Guardian
description: Student protesters among those hacked, says digital rights group, though Aleksandar Vučić’s government denies spying
Author: Aisha Down
Headline: Student protesters among those hacked, says digital rights group, though Aleksandar Vučić’s government denies spying
Content: A student protest movement has been raging in opposition to Aleksandar Vučić’s government since 2024.Photograph: Đorđe Kojadinović/ReutersView image in fullscreenA student protest movement has been raging in opposition to Aleksandar Vučić’s government since 2024.Photograph: Đorđe Kojadinović/ReutersSerbiaSerbians targeted with spyware in country’s ‘largest documented wave of surveillance’Student protesters among those hacked, says digital rights group, though Aleksandar Vučić’s government denies spyingAisha DownGlobal technology reporterThu 3 Sep 2026 18.10 EDTFirst published on Thu 3 Sep 2026 13.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt least 14 people from across Serbian civil society were targeted with advanced spyware earlier this year in what the digital rights group Share Foundation said was the largest documented ​wave of such infection inSerbiato date.The wave of spyware infections was discovered in August afterApplenotified people in 110 ⁠countries that they had probably been victims ⁠of mercenary spyware.The Citizen Lab, which carries out forensic analyses of spyware attacks, released an analysis on Wednesday showing that at least one of the Serbians had been targeted with the NSO Group’s Pegasus spyware, which wouldhave giventhe attacker “total access to the device”.Share said those targeted included members of a Serbian student movement that has been a thorn in the side of the government of Aleksandar Vučić since 2024. Coalescing out of countrywide protests that followed the collapse of a train station that winter, it is one of the largest student movements inEurope.Vučić has been in power for more than a decade, during which time critics have said he has overseen a hollowing-out of institutions while steering the countrycloser to Moscow.There is no evidence that Vučić’s government was the entity that targeted the student with the Pegasus spyware. However, other spyware used against the students, including a software called NoviSpy, has been previously connected to Serbian authorities.In an interview with Euronews Serbia TV on Wednesday, Ana Brnabić, the parliamentary speaker and a ranking member of the ruling Serbian Progressive party, denied that students had been spied on. “Absolutely not,” she said. “I do not believe a single word they’ve [students, Share] said.”View image in fullscreenAna Brnabić, right, next to Serbia’s president, Aleksandar Vučić, said of the claims students had been spied on: ‘I do not believe a single word they’ve said.’Photograph: Marko Djokovic/EPAShare said the timing – during March’s local elections – may have been a practice run beforesnap electionsset for this October.“This is the largest documented wave of surveillance in Serbia so far,” said Andrijana Ristic, a policy adviser at Share. “We imagine … that the local elections were basically used as a test for the ruling party to see [the spyware’s] strengths, but also to see the amount of pressure they are able to exert over the students and the opposition.”John Scott-Railton, a senior researcher at the Citizen Lab, said: “Our forensic findings, and this fresh wave of Apple threat notifications reveal that Serbia’s peaceful pro-democracy movement is being aggressively targeted with mercenary spyware ahead of key 2026 election cycles.”Milica Popović, one of the students who was targeted, called the attacks “cruel”. She said: “Thinking that someone may have entered my private space without my knowledge made me feel so exposed.”But, she said, the attack, as uncomfortable as it was, would not deter her or the student movement. “If their intention was to frighten us, or make us stop, it will not work.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNSO Group, which makesPegasus, a spyware that has been leveraged by authoritarian states to target journalists, human rights campaigners and dissidents, began as an Israeli company with close ties to the military.It is now under USownership, and appears to be searching for a way into the US market, including through efforts to get off the US Commerce Department’s blacklist. However, this and otherincidentswill raise questions about what has been described as their attempt to rebrand as an “ethical spyware company”.NSO Group has been permanentlybarredby a US court from targeting WhatsApp users and Meta products. It is unclear if this most recent Pegasus attack happened via WhatsApp.“Today, Pegasus is still being used to hack people campaigning for democracy. NSO spent a decade promising reform, yet their spyware is still an instrument of political repression,” said Railton.NSO Group was approached for comment.Explore more on these topicsSerbiaSurveillanceEspionageEuropeProtestApplenewsShareReuse this content

title: Sabotage, leaks and political ties: the story of the Daphne Caruana Galizia murder trial | Daphne Caruana Galizia | The Guardian
description: Maltese businessman cleared of involvement in journalist’s death, but trial revealed challenges faced by those leading search for killers
Author: Juliette Garside
Headline: Maltese businessman cleared of involvement in journalist’s death, but trial revealed challenges faced by those leading search for killers
Content: Flowers and a candle lie in front of a portrait of Daphne Caruana Galizia outside the court in Valletta, Malta.Photograph: Jonathan Borg/APView image in fullscreenFlowers and a candle lie in front of a portrait of Daphne Caruana Galizia outside the court in Valletta, Malta.Photograph: Jonathan Borg/APDaphne Caruana GaliziaSabotage, leaks and political ties: the story of the Daphne Caruana Galizia murder trialA Maltese businessman has been cleared of involvement in the journalist’s death, but his trial revealed the challenges faced by those leading the search for her killersJuliette Garsidein VallettaThu 3 Sep 2026 13.13 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 16.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe conclusion of the longest-running murder trial in Maltese history has left a country in turmoil, and a grieving family still searching for answers.At 7.30pm on Wednesday, gasps and cheers echoed around hall 22 of the courts of justice in Valletta, as a jury pronounced a businessman accused of ordering the murder of the investigative journalist Daphne Caruana Galizianot guilty.Yorgen Fenech, 44, had been facing a life sentence if convicted. Now, after nearly seven years in and out of custody, he is free to return to a gilded life as the heir to one of Malta’s biggest fortunes.In her reporting, Caruana Galizia had taken aim at many powerful figures, including Fenech and the politicians he was close to. Her revelations, and the fallout from her violent death in a car bombing in October 2017, had ultimately led to the resignation of the prime minister, Joseph Muscat, and several members of his government.Within weeks, three hitmen accused of planting the bomb were arrested. Two weresentenced to life in prisonafter pleading guilty to murder, while the third wasgiven a reduced 15-year sentencein exchange for evidence against his accomplices.After Wednesday’s decision, the long search for whoever was responsible for hiring them must begin again.The opposition leader, Alex Borg, has demanded the recall of parliament from its summer recess, and called for the government to act to strengthen press protection and anti-corruption measures. “We believe journalism is the backbone of a democracy,” he told the Guardian, describing the failure to find the culprits as a black mark against the Labour government. The party has been in power since 2013.Caruana Galizia’s family described the verdict as “justice denied”.The attorney general is considering whether to appeal for a retrial. The chances of success may be slim: both charges brought against Fenech were dismissed by an 8-1 majority.It had taken nine years, a relentless family campaign and a determined judge to bring Fenech before a jury. In the end, they took him at his word. During his evidence, he was adamant: “I never ordered Daphne Caruana Galizia’s murder, or anyone else’s. I had no role in her murder.”View image in fullscreenYorgen Fenech was cleared by a jury of complicity in voluntary homicide and association with the intention of committing a crime.Photograph: Darrin Zammit Lupi/ReutersWhile the identity of the mastermind remains a mystery, what the trial did reveal was the full extent of the challenges faced by those leading the search for Daphne’s killers.Witness after witness spoke of attempts to block and sabotage the murder investigation. As detectives worked to identify all of those involved, from the bomb makers to the hitmen to their ultimate client, they heard evidence that the most sensitive details were being leaked. Most disturbingly of all, the jury was told much of the information was coming from the prime minister’s right-hand man.“Don’t worry about me, nobody can touch me,” Fenech was heard saying in secret recordings that formed a cornerstone of the case against him, and played to the jury.View image in fullscreenA court artist’s sketch of Yorgen Fenech during the trial.Illustration: Anna Calleja DayThe man who had made those recordings was a taxi driver, Melvin Theuma, who testified to acting as the middleman between Fenech and the bombers. He was the key prosecution witness, having secured a pardon two years after the murder in return for giving evidence.In July 2020, he was taken to hospital in a critical condition. Overcome with remorse, he had attempted suicide while staying at a safe house, and it took intensive support to get him back in the stand.What follows is the story of the search for those responsible, based on pre-trial hearings, the trial itself, and related court cases.Consumed by an investigation that would kill herIn the last summer of her life, Caruana Galizia was deeply isolated.As a younger woman, she had not only been brilliant, but strikingly beautiful, with big statement earrings and shining black hair. She had co-founded a national newspaper, was a lifestyle magazine publisher, and had become one of Malta’s most-read columnists, all while raising three sons.View image in fullscreenDaphne Caruana Galizia in 1989 at Lisbon zoo with her sons Paul, Andrew and Matthew.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesIn later life, it was the investigative work that consumed her.‘I knew it was a car bomb straight away’: the day my mother Daphne Caruana Galizia was murderedRead moreHer blog Running Commentary was among the most-read news sites in Malta, but its popularity, and her often scathing satires of public figures, made her a target.She had as many detractors as fans, and on social media she was vilified as a “witch”. There were arson attacks, and the family dogs were killed.“I was worried about her,” her middle son, Andrew, told the trial. “The atmosphere around her was horrible. People would stare at her in Valletta. She wouldn’t leave the house.”Caruana Galizia knew she was at risk and had already started varying her routine. For added security, she drove a rental car.It was in that car that she died on 16 October 2017, aged 53, metres from her house. A bomb placed under the driver’s seat ripped through the vehicle, scattering burning remains across the road and into a field.View image in fullscreenForensic experts examine the field where a bomb blew up Daphne Caruana Galizia’s rental car.Photograph: Darrin Zammit Lupi/ReutersBarricaded inside their home, sheltering from the media storm, Daphne’s sons and her widow, Peter, wondered who they could trust. They felt sure her work would hold clues, but also that they could not hand sensitive source material to the police. Her eldest son, Matthew, a software engineer who had been part of the reporting team that won a Pulitzer prize for the Panama Papers, a giant leak of offshore company data, suggested contacting journalists outside Malta.“I didn’t have the resources to do the investigation on my own,” he told the jury at Fenech’s trial.He reached out to the Guardian, which joined Reuters, the non-profitForbidden Storiesand others to formthe Daphne Project.Before her death, Caruana Galizia had published a series of stories that plunged the Maltese government into scandal. She had found evidence in the Panama Papers that the energy minister, Konrad Mizzi, and the prime minister’s chief of staff, a businessman turned political fixer called Keith Schembri, had set up offshore companies held via anonymous trusts.Posts she published, read out during the trial, suggested she thought they were planning to use these to receive kickbacks.View image in fullscreenCaruana Galizia’s sons Matthew, Paul and Andrew and her husband, Peter, take part in a protest march in Valletta in 2019.Photograph: Darrin Zammit Lupi/ReutersThose allegations are now the subject of acriminal case,in which Fenech, Schembri, Mizzi and others are pleading not guilty to corruption, trading in influence and criminal association.At the time she died, Caruana Galizia was receiving a leak of information about a large government contract – a concession to build a €500m gas power plant that would supply electricity for the national grid. The leak came from the servers of the company building the plant, Electrogas. One of its shareholders was Fenech, and the email traffic suggested he was a driving force, handling communications with the government, and the refinancing of a crucial bank loan.The jury heard how, in her blog, Caruana Galizia had described the venture as a “magic new corruption power station”.View image in fullscreenGrafitti on a wall in rural Malta highlights Caruna Galizia’s murder.Photograph: Simon Leigh/AlamyThe prosecution had claimed, in its closing submissions, that Fenech’s motive for ordering her murder was to prevent any further revelations.The Electrogas data was shared with the Daphne Project. As reporters combed the files, following the money trails, Keith Arnaud, a homicide detective, searched for the killers. At first he made rapid progress, thanks to the FBI. The agency’s cellphone analysis team had been inEuropewhen the bomb went off, and they diverted to Malta, landing there within hours.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe hitmen, brothers George and Alfred Degiorgio, and their accomplice Vincent Muscat, had used burner phones but they had been careless, often carrying them alongside their usual mobiles. The FBI made the link, tracing a text message sent by George to detonate the bomb. In December 2017, the trio were arrested.In April 2018, Vincent Muscat told police he was ready to turn on his accomplices, in exchange for a shorter sentence. While the hitmen had never known the identity of their ultimate client, Muscat had the name of the middleman: Melvin Theuma.View image in fullscreenA makeshift memorial to Caruana Galizia in Valletta, Malta.Photograph: Darrin Zammit Lupi/ReutersThe mosquito and the lionFor Theuma, a fatherless teenager, the Malta Racing Club was a home from home. He started as a groom, tending to the ponies that pull small carts around the bare-earth track. Before long he was working as a scout for a bookmaker. The old betting shop still stands across the street from the Fenech family stables.View image in fullscreenMelvin Theuma, a key witness who was granted a presidential pardon, with Judge Edwina Grima visiting the site where Caruana Galizia was killed.Photograph: Darrin Zammit Lupi/ReutersTheuma and Fenech became friends, but it was not a relationship of equals. As the taxi driver said in court: “I was hanging out with a lion, and I’m a mosquito.”Police said in court they had identified Fenech as a suspect by September 2018. But it would take until February 2019 for a warrant to be authorised to intercept his calls.The person signing the warrants was the prime minister, Joseph Muscat. From the beginning, Muscat had been receiving updates about the investigation directly from Arnaud and his colleagues. That decision was controversial because, along with his ministers, he had been one of the main subjects of Caruana Galizia’s reporting.Muscat has indicated it was customary for the prime minister to sign warrants in cases of national importance. He has previously said he fulfilled his duties “without fear, prejudice or favour”. In a statement on Thursday, he said that from the beginning, and while he was still in office, “no one was protected from or immune to justice”.Schembri was allowed to attend the police briefings and told the trial he was kept informed throughout.The two men were close – Schembri had started out as Muscat’s campaign manager – but Schembri had another good friend: Fenech. They had played football together as children, and when Fenech, a few years younger, stepped up to run his family business, Schembri had mentored him. They would often holiday together and gather for family events.Schembri is accused of repeatedly leaking sensitive details about the homicide investigation to Fenech. He denies the allegations, and is being prosecuted over the matter in aseparate criminal case.During his trial, Fenech sought to paint Schembri as the ultimate mastermind, describing himself as a go-between, passing messages to Theuma. Fenech’s lawyers depicted the taxi driver as a blackmailer and a liar, and accused the police of framing Fenech because they had failed to properly follow other leads. They said the searches at Schembri’s home and his office had been bungled. His phone, active 28 minutes before the raid, was never found.“All roads lead to Keith and all bridges leading to Keith were burnt,” Fenech’s lawyer said. “And so a bridge had to be built to Yorgen Fenech.”Schembri denies any involvement in the murder. In their evidence, police said he was never a murder suspect.View image in fullscreenMalta’s former chief of staff, Keith Schembri, was a close childhood friend of Yorgen Fenech.Photograph: Matthew Mirabelli/AFP/Getty ImagesUnder questioning, Fenechadmitted paying €400,000, via Theuma, to the hitmen to cover their legal bills. He said this was to keep Theuma calm, and that the cab driver had “drained” him of money. He also admitted giving Theuma money before the murder, but said he warned that it should not go ahead, telling the taxi driver to “stop it here”.He admitted passing information about the police investigation from Schembri to Theuma, starting soon after the assassination.“Keith Schembri was continuously informed and in a way you can say real time,” Fenech told a court in 2019, in a constitutional case regarding his right to a fair trial. “The information was passed to me by Keith Schembri but it came from Mr Arnaud, and he used to tell me that it came from Mr Arnaud.”Recordings, messages and testimony from Fenech himself indicate that in the first months after the murder he had passed on to Theuma the identity of who had made the bomb and the date on which the police were planning to arrest the hitmen. When the police raided their shed by the docks, they had already thrown their mobile phones into the water, and one of them had written his wife’s number on his wrist.In April 2018, Fenech also shared that Vincent Muscat was offering to become a witness for the prosecution. The news sent Theuma into a spin and he started to record his exchanges with Fenech, using a spare phone switched to airplane mode so it would not ring.View image in fullscreenVincent Muscat is serving a 15-year prison sentence for his part in the murder of Caruana Galizia.Photograph: Darrin Zammit Lupi/ReutersIt was around this time that Arnaud’s investigation seemed to lose momentum. Eventually, details of what had been uncovered began to leak. By May 2019, reporters had Theuma’s name.Europol, which had been supporting Arnaud and his team, threatened over the summer of 2019 to withdraw unless arrests were made. The family were also losing patience. “We had known what was being alleged about Melvin Theuma for months,” Matthew Caruana Galizia has said. “And it reached a point where I just wanted to go into the street and spraypaint his name on a wall. I wanted the world to know that he was the middleman, to just push the police into action.”While the walls around the prime minister and his friends looked strong from the outside, when the police finally went for Theuma, Joseph Muscat’s administration crumbled.Theuma had been warned of his planned arrest date but police swooped two days early, on 14 November 2019. Fenech had urged him in messages beforehand to dispose of the evidence. The jury saw one message in which he said: “Be 100% sure everywhere is clean.”But Theuma held on to his recordings. On 19 November, the prime minister signed a memorandum guaranteeing Theuma immunity from prosecution in exchange for testimony. Within hours, Fenech was making preparations to flee, messages seen by the jury suggest. “Go while you’re still in time,” his uncle texted. He planned to sail to Sicily, and then head for France. However, the police had been tipped off. His yacht was intercepted a mile off the coast, and he was arrested. The interrogation tapes, played at his trial, showed he offered to implicate Schembri in return for a pardon.View image in fullscreenA mass in memory of Caruana Galizia in Valletta.Photograph: Matthew Mirabelli/AFP/Getty ImagesAs Fenech talked, heads rolled. Schembri was arrested in relation to the suspected leaks, and resigned. The economy minister, a frequent subject of Caruana Galizia’s blog, suspended himself and Mizzi, by now reassigned from energy to tourism minister, quit, citing “political, extraordinary and general circumstances in the country”.Public outrage brought hundreds on to the streets, filling the grand plaza outside the prime minister’s office, chanting: “Mafia, mafia.”Fenech’s pardon request was rejected and on 30 November, he was charged. Two days later, Joseph Muscat resigned. Defiant to the end, he insisted: “This case cannot define everything that our country is.”The saga is once again drawing attention from outside Malta. Shami Chakrabarti, the British Labour peer, has been appointed rapporteur of a Council of Europe investigation into the Maltese government’s response to the murder. Caruana Galizia’s family members intend to give evidence at the first hearing next week.“The failure to ensure individual accountability for the murder risks perpetuating a culture of impunity,” Chakrabarti said on Thursday. “A culture where … those who try to shine a light in the darkness pay the ultimate price.”Explore more on these topicsDaphne Caruana GaliziaMaltaEuropeJournalist safetyInvestigative journalismNewspapersNewspapers & magazinesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: EU’s ability to defend against invasion remains in doubt, finds official report | European Union | The Guardian
description: Fragmented infrastructure and reliance on US continue to hinder ‘defence readiness’, says European court of auditors
Author: Jennifer Rankin
Headline: Fragmented infrastructure and reliance on US continue to hinder ‘defence readiness’, says European court of auditors
Content: The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, and Donald Trump. EU countries’ purchase of US hardware went up after invasion of Ukraine.Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, and Donald Trump. EU countries’ purchase of US hardware went up after invasion of Ukraine.Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/ReutersEuropean UnionEU’s ability to defend against invasion remains in doubt, finds official reportFragmented infrastructure and reliance on US continue to hinder ‘defence readiness’, says European court of auditorsEurope live – latest updatesJennifer Rankinin BrusselsThu 3 Sep 2026 11.09 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 14.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe EU’s ability to respond to a foreign invasion by 2030 remains in doubt due to a continuing reliance on the US and fragmented national defence systems, according to a report from its official auditor.The European court of auditors (ECA) said the EU was much better prepared than before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine of 2022, but achieving its goal of defence readiness by the end of the decade would be difficult.“Achieving defence preparedness in the EU by 2030 remains challenging,” said Marek Opioła, an ECA member who led the review of the EU’s defence policy published on Thursday. “There are still major difficulties such as fragmented national systems or industrial bottlenecks. We also still rely on the United States.”Speaking to the Guardian, he stressed the EU could “still make major progress” if it sharply increased defence spending and rapidly expanded ammunition production.Between 2020 and 2025, EU member states increased defence spending by 79%, a response to the Russian threat and a belated effort to meet Nato spending targets. In November 2024, the EU met itspledge of providing 1 million rounds of ammunition to Ukraine– eight months behind schedule.The EUset the goal of defence readiness by 2030 last year, after intelligence services warned that Russia could be ready to wage a large-scale war in Europe around that time.The bloc’s financial watchdog said major difficulties had to be overcome to reach this target, defined by a senior auditor as “having strategic autonomy” and “the ability to independently sustain high-intensity warfare”. The senior auditor said the EU was better prepared than 2019 when a similarreviewwas conducted, but warned that fragmented national defence industries and “insufficient cooperation” between EU governments contributed to a risk of duplication in spending or persistent gaps in military capabilities.Emblematic of the dysfunction – although not mentioned in the report – is France and Germany’s decisionto abandon a €100bn project to build a joint fighter jet,because the lead companies were unable to resolve disputes over leadership and control.The report highlighted a possible tension between short-term battlefield needs and a “Buy European” policy that aims to reduce dependencies on foreign suppliers. Between February 2022 and June 2023, 78% of EU governments’ defence acquisitions were sourced outside the bloc, with the US alone representing 63%, according to one study cited by the ECA.The senior auditor said purchases from the US went up after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine “which was understandable because the EU needed to find capabilities that were available quickly”. The official added that “early signs of improvement in that situation” were visible, although the auditors did not have complete data to draw conclusions.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe EU has set requirements that common defence spending should benefit domestic defence industries or those of closely-associated countries, such as Ukraine and Norway. But some flexibilities have been allowed where Europe is unable to produce critical supplies in time.After a brutal summer of deadly Russian missile and drone attacks, this week Ukraine asked for an exemption from Buy European procurement rules to acquireUS-made Patriot interceptorsusing the EU’s €90bn support loan. The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said on Wednesday that Ukraine had requested funding “worth several billion euros” for air defences, including Patriot air-defence systems. A commission spokesperson said Ukraine’s request for Patriot interceptor missiles “would require a derogation” from rules requiring majority European content in military purchases under the loan. “The final say is with the member states and of course our hope would be that this would soon be granted,” the spokesperson said.The senior auditor said sometimes “it may make sense” to buy outside “when you have a short-term urgent need”. The person added: “Even if you buy something that you don’t have in-house, you [should] always have a plan how to develop that critical capacity in the long-term within theEuropean Union.”Explore more on these topicsEuropean UnionEuropeNatonewsShareReuse this content

title: Rise of far-right leader Roberto Vannacci challenges Meloni as she celebrates Italian milestone | Italy | The Guardian
description: Futuro Nazionale party’s speedy poll rise poses questions whether PM will return to her roots before election
Author: Angela Giuffrida
Headline: Futuro Nazionale party’s speedy poll rise poses questions whether PM will return to her roots before election
Content: Roberto Vannacci’s far-right Futuro Nazionale party has risen to about 8% in polls since its launch in February.Photograph: Remo Casilli/ReutersView image in fullscreenRoberto Vannacci’s far-right Futuro Nazionale party has risen to about 8% in polls since its launch in February.Photograph: Remo Casilli/ReutersItalyAnalysisRise of far-right leader Roberto Vannacci challenges Meloni as she celebrates Italian milestoneAngela Giuffridain RomeFuturo Nazionale party’s speedy poll rise poses questions whether PM will return to her roots before electionEurope live – latest updatesThu 3 Sep 2026 10.25 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 14.11 EDTShareGiorgia Meloni’s government has become the longest-running in Italy since the second world war – a milestone the prime minister is determined not to let pass unnoticed.In the port area of Bari, the capital of the southern Italian region of Puglia, where Meloni hosted the G7 in 2024 and where she spends her summer holiday, preparations are well under way for a festival-style showcase of her rightwing administration.On Friday, there will be food trucks, water stations and traditional Puglian light shows as part of celebrations to entertain an expected crowd of 10,000 people bussed in from acrossItaly. Militants from the youth wing of Meloni’s far-right Brothers of Italy party have fanned the city’s squares and beaches for days, handing out flyers promoting the celebrations while wearing T-shirts featuring the official slogan:Il Governo più stabile, l’Italia più forte(the most stable government, the strongest Italy).Meloni, who just a few weeks ago was booed at the opening ceremony of the Mediterranean Games in Taranto, farther south in Puglia, will address the audience in the evening, surrounded by her coalition allies – Matteo Salvini, the leader of the far-right League, and the conservative Forza Italia’s Antonio Tajani.“This moment will be written in the history books,” said Michele Picaro, a Brothers of Italy MEP and former Bari councillor. “We are the longest government in the history of the Italian Republic and this must be celebrated.”View image in fullscreenIn recent months the political landscape has become less settled for Giorgia Meloni.Photograph: Francesca Bolla/AGF/ShutterstockBeneath the triumph, however, the outlook for Meloni is less settled. True, she has enjoyed a political stability that eluded her predecessors. Brothers of Italy is still the country’s biggest party. But in recent months, the political landscape has shifted with the emergence of a challenger – not from the left or the centre, but from someone who is even further to the right than Meloni.Since its launch in February, Roberto Vannacci, a former army general, has seen his far-right party, Futuro Nazionale, rise to about 8% in the polls, surpassing his former compatriots in the League months ago and this week eclipsing Forza Italia, too.Vannacci first entered the public eye in 2023 after self-publishing a book filled with racism, homophobia, Islamophobia and antisemitism. The subsequent backlash cost him his army job, but propelled him to the top of the bestsellers list. Helped along by ample coverage in the Italian press, he capitalised on the notoriety and in 2024 was elected as an MEP for the League, later leaving Salvini’s party to set up his own.“I read his book because I always think you need to know the enemy,” said Giulia Pastorella, an MP and vice-president of the small centrist party Azione (Action). “And I thought, this is exactly the kind of thing you might hear people talking about in the bar. Here’s a military man, who is really a mirror of the worst impulses of people. The scary thing is, I think he’s genuine and not a PR construct.”Vannacci’s policies, such as they are, are extreme. Futuro Nazionale’s recently published manifesto says that “abortion is not a right” and calls for gay people to be banned from TV between 6am and 11pm so children aren’t exposed to what it describes as “homosexualist” content. It also proposes introducing military education in high schools and a “remigration” plan to remove irregular immigrants and foreign nationals who commit crimes.On foreign policy, Vannacci has campaigned to stop weapons and financial aid to Ukraine, saying if he could choose between Vladimir Putin or the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy,he would choose Putin.In July, he organised a “Futuristic Triathlon” in the northern seaside town of Sanremo, billed as an event to “temper the mind and body” in an echo of the fascist aesthetics and themes of the Mussolini era.View image in fullscreenRoberto Vannacci’s policies, such as they are, are extreme.Photograph: Remo Casilli/ReutersFar from being a treated as a pariah, however, Vannacci’s party has proved moderately successful, luring defectors from the three main ruling coalition parties. It is also actively courting disillusioned voters from the Five Star Movement, a key ally in a broad but perennially fractious leftwing coalition led by the Democratic party.For the government, he represents a dilemma.
