Meloni, whose Brothers of Italy has neofascist roots, has governed more moderately than many had expected, cultivating a pragmatic and, crucially, pro-Ukraine image abroad while still deploying hardline rhetoric on choice occasions for domestic audiences.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThat positioning, however, has left a vacuum on the far right that Vannacci has exploited. The question now is: how will Meloni respond? Until now her ruling coalition had mostly coasted along, propped up by a strong parliamentary majority. Her government is largely regarded to have been fiscally prudent, but has steered clear of major structural reforms. Instead, it has heavily focused on security and continues to vigorously expandlegislation on law and order.“This government has wasted the huge occasion that stability gave them,” said Lia Quartapelle, an MP with the Democratic party. “None of the core issues have been addressed – we have stagnant productivity and growth, salaries that have lagged behind for many years and an education system that is not up to the pace.”Pastorella said a focus on foreign policy had also contributed to Vannacci’s success. “Meloni hasn’t really done much at home but has been very present abroad,” she added. “The Italian electorate is tired of talking about foreign policy and would rather discuss national politics – this is precisely what Vannacci has understood.”Picaro batted away questions about recent polls. “This is a government that is more used to working than looking at percentages,” he said, citing lower unemployment, reduced irregular immigration, cutting taxes for the self-employed and an initiative in the south to boost entrepreneurial investment.Pastorella said that, far from being strong and stable, Meloni had struggled to keep her coalition united while dealing with various scandals, including ones that led toa tourismand aculture ministerbeing forced to resign.With the possibility of an election as early as April, time is now of the essence for the prime minister. In recent weeks she has pivoted back to hardline rhetoric,most notably in her reactionto the influx of migrants from Morocco into the Spanish north African enclave of Ceuta.She is also trying to push through a highly contentious electoral law that would give a majority bonus to any alliance winning more than 42% of the vote, which critics say is aimed at increasing her group’s chance of victory.If Vannacci continues to strengthen, Meloni might be tempted to accommodate him before the vote, a move that would risk repelling moderate supporters. Or she could clinch a post-election pact to maintain power, resulting in what many both inside and outside Italy would see as a frightening shift to the extreme right.As government supporters head to Bari, Alessandro Cattaneo, an MP with Forza Italia, thinks it won’t come to that. “We in Forza Italia believe that Vannacci is too far removed from our political culture,” he said. “It would not be possible to govern with him … the coalition needs to continue to work seriously for the remainder of this administration and explain better to people what we have done. The best antidote to the extreme right is to show our seriousness.”Explore more on these topicsItalyGiorgia MeloniEuropeThe far rightnewsShareReuse this content

title: Israelis shoot dead two Palestinian teenagers after settlers encircle village | West Bank | The Guardian
description: Troops escort settlers into al-Mughayyir and raze village outside Hebron as ethnic cleansing of West Bank continues
Author: Emma Graham-Harrison
Headline: Troops escort settlers into al-Mughayyir and raze village outside Hebron as ethnic cleansing of West Bank continues
Content: Relatives of Khalil Abu Alia grieve during his funeral in al-Mughayyir after the 16-year-old was shot on his doorstep by an Israeli rooftop sniper.Photograph: Zain Jaafar/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRelatives of Khalil Abu Alia grieve during his funeral in al-Mughayyir after the 16-year-old was shot on his doorstep by an Israeli rooftop sniper.Photograph: Zain Jaafar/AFP/Getty ImagesWest BankIsraelis shoot dead two Palestinian teenagers after settlers encircle villageTroops escort settlers into al-Mughayyir and raze village outside Hebron as ethnic cleansing of West Bank continuesEmma Graham-Harrisonin JerusalemThu 3 Sep 2026 15.33 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 16.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIsraelis have shot dead two teenagers in a Palestinian village encircled by settlers, and Israeli troops have razed an entire village outside Hebron, in the latest attacks in a surge of Israeli terror and ethnic cleansing across the occupiedWest Bank.The shootings targeted Khalil Abu Alia, 16, who was about to start 11th grade at the al-Mughayyir boys school, and 19-year-old Omar al-Nassan, who graduated from the same institution with top marks this summer.The teenagers were killed soon after sunset, when a group of settlers entered the village under police and military escort to steal dozens of sheep from a Palestinian home, village residents and Israeli activists said.Snipers took up position on rooftops and one shot Abu Alia in the neck, his English teacher, Waheed Abu Naim, said in a phone interview. The boy was on the doorstep of his home when he was targeted.View image in fullscreenMourners at the funeral ceremony of Khalil Abu Alia, 16, and Omar al-Nassan, 19.Photograph: Zain Jaafar/AFP/Getty ImagesAl-Nassan was shot twice, the second time in the back, residents and activists said. Both had died before they made it to hospital.A spokesperson for the Israeli military said Israeli police, army and settlers entered the village to take sheep claimed by settlers from a Palestinian home. The spokesperson provided no evidence of ownership, theft or investigation into stolen goods.When Palestinians resisted seizure of the sheep by throwing stones and cinder blocks, the troops shot them, the spokesperson said. “The forces responded by firing at key instigators in order to remove the threat. Hits were identified.”Abu Alia was killed by a soldier. It was not clear whether Al-Nassan was shot by a soldier or a settler.View image in fullscreenMourners at the funeral ceremony of Abu Alia and al-Nassan in al-Mughayyir.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesIsraeli soldiers and militants had already killed three other students from their school’s 470-strong student body this year.The other victims werea 17-year-old player from the Palestinian youth football teamshot in June,a 14-year-old gunned down at the school gatein April, and another14-year-old killed outside the village mosquein January.“We don’t know how long these crimes are going to continue,” said Abu Naim, who had taught all five boys, and said many more of his students had been injured by Israeli attacks. His brother was also killed by settlers in April.“This week we are making extra security preparations for the new semester which starts in three days,” he said. They have built a higher wall around the school, topped by a fence, and strengthened gates to the compound.They are also making teaching contingency plans, because the village has been under tightening siege for the past two weeks.View image in fullscreenFuneral attenders look out from their village of al-Mughayyir at an Israeli hilltop settlement.Photograph: Léo Corrêa/APSince late 2023, Israeli barricades blocked all but one road into the village, and at least eight settler outpostssurround it in all directions.In late August soldiers and settlers began closing the one remaining lifeline out of al-Mughayyir for hours at a time, setting up a temporary checkpoint near the school in the morning and evening.At least eight families have fled in the past week because they were unable to commute to work, renting flats in other places, Abu Naim said.The school has 26 teachers but only nine live in the village, and they fear the other two-thirds may not be allowed to reach their classrooms on Monday.View image in fullscreenIsraeli troops raiding al-Mughayyir in July after settler attacks.Photograph: Mohammed Torokman/ReutersIn the south Hebron hills Israeli forces spent the day razing the homes of 12 Palestinian families who lived in the community of Khirbet al-Taban. All 70 residents are now homeless, including 28 children.Israeli troops demolished all buildings and destroyed water cisterns, storage, livestock pens and caves, the Israeli-Palestinian rights group B’Tselem said in a statement.It is the 66th Palestinian community that has been wiped off the map since October 2023, with 18 others partly displaced, the group said. Nearly 5,000 people have been forced from their homes, almost half of them children.“Israel is continuing to erase Palestinian communities at an accelerating pace as part of the ethnic cleansing it is carrying out in the West Bank,” saidYuli Novak, the executive director of B’Tselem. “The world continues to stand by as Palestinians and their lives are left completely exposed to Israeli violence.”A spokesperson for Cogat, the Israeli military agency which manages civilian affairs in occupiedPalestine, said troops were carrying out “enforcement activity” against illegal construction in a military training zone.In 1981 Israel designated the Masafer Yatta area, including Khirbet al-Taban, asFiring Zone 918. It has been working since to push out the roughly 1,200 Palestinian residents who remain. They have been fighting expulsion in Israeli courts for decades, slowing but not stopping demolitions.As Palestinian communities have been wiped out, illegal Israeli settlements have expanded, with 11 outposts inside the firing zone, housing some of the mostnotoriously violentIsraeli settlers. None have been targeted for removal.Explore more on these topicsWest BankPalestineMiddle East and north AfricaIsraelnewsShareReuse this content

title: Far-right Israeli minister outlines plan for removal of all Palestinians from Gaza | Israel | The Guardian
description: Itamar Ben-Gvir claims proposal for illegal forced displacement of 2 million people is ‘realistic’ and ‘concrete’
Author: Peter Beaumont
Headline: Itamar Ben-Gvir claims proposal for illegal forced displacement of 2 million people is ‘realistic’ and ‘concrete’
Content: Displaced Palestinians queue for drinking water in al-Bureij refugee camp, in central Gaza.Photograph: Moiz Salhi/APAImages/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenDisplaced Palestinians queue for drinking water in al-Bureij refugee camp, in central Gaza.Photograph: Moiz Salhi/APAImages/ShutterstockIsraelFar-right Israeli minister outlines plan for removal of all Palestinians from GazaItamar Ben-Gvir claims proposal for illegal forced displacement of 2 million people is ‘realistic’ and ‘concrete’Peter BeaumontSenior international correspondentThu 3 Sep 2026 14.01 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 15.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIsrael’s far-right national security minister has set out a plan for the illegal forced expulsion of all Palestinians from the Gaza Strip, with the intention of sending them abroad.Speaking in the run-up to close-fought Israeli elections, Itamar Ben-Gvir said the plan aimed to remove 250,000 Palestinians fromGazain the first year, followed by the rest of its population of roughly 2 million over the next six years.“It’s realistic,” Ben-Gvir said, claiming there were countries that were “ready” to take in Palestinians from Gaza, without naming which ones.While the forced displacement of civilians in occupied territory is considered a war crime under the Geneva conventions, Israeli political figures have competed over the harshness of their visions for Gaza, rebuffing efforts by the US president, Donald Trump, to advance a half-baked and largely moribund ceasefire deal that has been marked by continuing Israeli attacks.Ben-Gvir said the far-right Jewish Power party would demand “a ministry in charge of emigration” during the formation of the next government, adding that his plan was “the result of a year and a half of work and … is concrete”.View image in fullscreenItamar Ben-Gvir speaks at a rally in the Israeli city of Netanya this week.Photograph: Amir Levy/Getty ImagesThe proposal is contained in a 20-page document with the euphemistic title of “National Work Plan for Voluntary Emigration from the Gaza Strip”.Despite the use of the word “voluntary”, the plan will be seen as coercive by the international community because of the dire conditions imposed on Gaza’s population by Israel and because of Ben-Gvir’s explicit intention: to remove Gaza’s Palestinian population.Earlier this year,an independent UN inquiryfound that Israel continued to commit genocide by deliberately targeting Palestinian children in Gaza.Ben-Gvir’s comments follow hard on the heels of comments by Israel’s defence minister, Israel Katz, who said Israel was seeking the approval of the Trump administration to displace Palestinians from Gaza, which he claimed was still under discussion after being “frozen” by Trump.Katz, at a conference hosted by the Israeli newspaper Yedioth Ahronoth, said Israel would facilitate the emigration “by any means”, implying a policy of coercion.Trump himself provoked international outrage at the beginning of his second term with a suggestion that all 2 million Palestinians leave Gaza and that the US redevelop the territory, a proposal he later walked back.Israel ‘seeking Trump’s support for plan to expel Palestinians from Gaza’Read moreWith elections in Israel in October, Ben-Gvir has made a series of inflammatory interventions aimed at his far-right base, includingsharing footage from a sitewhere Palestinians convicted of deadly attacks by Israeli military courts – but not Jewish extremists accused of similar crimes – are to be executed. In another video, he revelled in the mistreatment of Palestinian prisoners in Israeli custody.Polling suggests that Jewish Power, the party led by Ben-Gvir – who has convictions for incitement to racism and support for a terrorist organisation, and who has been put under sanctions by various countries – would gain about seven seats.The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, for his part staged a visit to a military outpost in Gaza on Wednesday to insist that Israel would not withdraw from the areas of Gaza that it occupies.“We are not withdrawing. We are staying on this line. We control 60% of the strip. And there is still more to come, because we are eliminating the terrorists who threaten us – we do this day in and day out,” he said.According to Israel’s deputy chief of general staff, Maj Gen Tamir Yadai, the country nowcontrols 65% of Gaza. This is far beyond the 53% agreed under the ceasefire brokered last year by Trump.As well as pushing for the expulsion of Gaza’s population, Ben-Gvir has called for the deportation of two MPs and others “who are disloyal to the state of Israel” – including Jews – saying he would promote such a policy if he is included in the next government.Explore more on these topicsIsraelPalestineGazaMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: US commerce secretary erroneously said no Americans have died in Iran war, Trump claims | US-Israel war on Iran | The Guardian
description: President said Howard Lutnick had Venezuela operation on his mind when he was discussing Iran war on CNBC
Author: Joseph Gedeon
Headline: President said Howard Lutnick had Venezuela operation on his mind when he was discussing Iran war on CNBC
Content: A carry team carries the remains of Private Isabella Gonzales, who was killed in an Iranian airstrike in Jordan, at Dover air force base in Delaware, on 22 July.Photograph: Jim Lo Scalzo/EPAView image in fullscreenA carry team carries the remains of Private Isabella Gonzales, who was killed in an Iranian airstrike in Jordan, at Dover air force base in Delaware, on 22 July.Photograph: Jim Lo Scalzo/EPAUS-Israel war on IranUS commerce secretary erroneously said no Americans have died in Iran war, Trump claimsPresident said Howard Lutnick had Venezuela operation on his mind when he was discussing Iran war on CNBCJoseph Gedeonin WashingtonThu 3 Sep 2026 10.38 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 10.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump has claimed his commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, erroneously stated that no Americans had been killed in the war with Iran because he was thinking about a previous US operation, in Venezuela.The claim, at odds with the Pentagon’s count of 18 US service members dead in theUS-Israel war on Iran, sparked a swift backlash as Trump struggles to end the conflict after six months.In a post on his Truth Social platform on Thursday, the US president wrote: “Sec. Lutnick had Venezuela on his mind when he said nobody was killed. 18 people were killed in Iran!”The rebuke came a day after Lutnick appeared on CNBC’s Squawk Box and framed the Trump administration’s approach to Iran as primarily economic. Describing the strategy as an “economic choke-out”, he erroneously told the network there had not been American deaths in the conflict, adding that he was optimistic bond markets would respond well to the approach.Lutnick this morning acknowledged the mistake,posting on Xthat he had misspoken and also claiming he had been thinking of the US operation in Venezuela, where US forces captured Nicolás Maduro in January with minimal US casualties. The Pentagon said seven US troops were injured and none were killed in that operation, while Venezuelan officials put their overall death toll at 47, and Cuba said 32 of its military and police personnel were killed.Trump’s post landed as Iranian authorities detailed heavy casualties from the latest US strikes. Iran’s health ministry said Tuesday night’s strikes killed 18 people and wounded 108, while the country’s Red Crescent identified that four people were killed and 67 wounded when a US strike hit a wedding ceremony near the coast of the strait of Hormuz, which also killed a child. Reuters said it was able toverify the locationof the damaged building using satellite imagery.A US Central Command spokesperson, Capt Tim Hawkins, said theUS militarydoes not target civilians and that the reports, which originated with Iranian state media, were being reviewed.The strikes were part of a broader operation that Central Command said hit Iranian air defense systems, radar installations, maritime assets, mine-laying equipment and communications sites near the strait of Hormuz, a strategic waterway through which a large share of the world’s oil passes.The Pentagon’s capacity to independently verify such claims has been sharply reduced. Its Civilian Protection Center of Excellence has been cut from 40 staff to nine since the start of last year, according to thePentagon’s own inspector general, while the department has also stopped developing a database meant to track civilian harm from US operations.The episode has exposed a wider tension in how the White House is presenting the conflict.Officials have sought to characterize the campaign (estimated to have costat least $37.5bnas of July) against Iran in economic terms even as it continues to produce US military deaths, mounting Iranian civilian casualties and rising oil prices.Polling fromUMass-Amherstin late August found that 54% of Americans disapprove of the war initiated by the US and Israel, and one in six Trump voters would go back and change their vote in 2024.The current round of fighting began after the US struck rocket launchers on Larak Island that officials said were being prepared to mine the strait, prompting Iranian missile and drone attacks on US and allied positions in Jordan, Bahrain, Kuwait and Iraq. Jordanian authorities said 13 ballistic missiles were fired at the country, of which 10 were intercepted.Trump described Iran’s retaliation as a “love tap”, but warned that further strikes remained an option. “It was a very heavy attack last night, and we’re prepared to do another one anytime we want,” he said earlier this week.Explore more on these topicsUS-Israel war on IranTrump administrationIranUS politicsMiddle East and north AfricaDonald TrumpUS militarynewsShareReuse this content

title: Iran targets US bases as Israel warns sanctions could drive Tehran to ‘desperate steps’ | US-Israel war on Iran | The Guardian
description: Air bases used by US in UAE and Kuwait hit as Israeli defence chief says Iran’s regime fears collapse due to economic pressures
Author: Peter Beaumont
Headline: Air bases used by US in UAE and Kuwait hit as Israeli defence chief says Iran’s regime fears collapse due to economic pressures
Content: A woman crosses the road in front of an anti-US billboard in Tehran. The Iranian army said it targeted bases used by the US in the UAE and Kuwait on Thursday.Photograph: Atta Kenare/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA woman crosses the road in front of an anti-US billboard in Tehran. The Iranian army said it targeted bases used by the US in the UAE and Kuwait on Thursday.Photograph: Atta Kenare/AFP/Getty ImagesUS-Israel war on IranIran targets US bases as Israel warns sanctions could drive Tehran to ‘desperate steps’Air bases used by US in UAE and Kuwait hit as Israeli defence chief says Iran’s regime fears collapse due to economic pressuresPeter BeaumontSenior international correspondentThu 3 Sep 2026 10.16 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 15.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIran has continued to demonstrate an ability to target bases in the Gulf used by the US despite six months of war and a new sanctions regime described by the Trump administration as an “economic D-day”.As Iran’s military targeted US bases in theUnited Arab Emiratesand Kuwait, despite threats of further strikes by the US president, Israel’s defence chief warned that economic pressures from the sanctions could lead Tehran to escalate to more “extreme measures”.“This morning, the army hit the satellite communication systems, equipment depots and fighter aircraft hangars of the terrorist US army at the Ahmad al-Jaber air base inKuwaitwith missiles and drones,” the Iranian military said on Thursday in a statement carried by state television.The “location of forces and radar systems of the child-killing US army at the Al Minhad air base in the UAE were also attacked by missiles and drones of the army”, it added.In a post on X, Kuwait’s ministry of defence said its air defences had intercepted missile and drone attacks during a “blatant Iranian aggression”.The Kuwaiti statement came after the US allies Bahrain and Jordan said their air defence systems intercepted several Iranian air attacks on Wednesday.Fighting between the US and Iran has increased this weekafter the US hit Iranian rocket launchers on an island in the strait of Hormuz on Sunday, claiming that Iran was planning to use them to shoot mines into the waterway.View image in fullscreenDamage to a residential building after an Iranian drone attack, according to Kuwaiti authorities, in Kuwait City on Thursday.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesThe latest flare-up in the conflict comes amid little evidence that the Trump administration is succeeding in advancing its nebulous war aims either on the battlefield or via mediation, despite the US president’s repeated claims to have opened the strait of Hormuz to oil traffic.Instead, traffic through the key maritime passageway remains far below prewar levels, with oil prices remaining stubbornly elevated ahead of US midterm elections. Oil prices jumped again on Thursday after the Iranian strikes.Among the weapons Iran has used this week is its Kheibar Shekan medium-range ballistic missile system. The cheap and accurate missile can be launched within minutes and has become a staple of Iranian strikes.The rocket’s solid fuel motor means it does not require lengthy fuelling. It can be deployed very quickly to avoid detection and can be armed with a powered and steerable final stage to help beat anti-missile systems.Despite claims by the Trump administration that Tehran is running out of rockets, Iran continues to fire missiles that are considerably cheaper to produce than the US interceptors used to shoot them down.Iran has claimed as recently as the end of August that it maintained both missiles stockpiles and the ability to manufacture them.“Initially, some believed that Iran had only a limited number of missiles and that its stockpiles would eventually be depleted as the war continued,” the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps spokesperson Brig Gen Hossein Mohebbi said.“However, that assumption proved incorrect, as Iran’s missile capability has remained sustained and its missile production has continued.” Mohebbi’s characterisation of Iranian missile stockpiles could not be verified.The continued strikes came as Israel’s defence minister,IsraelKatz, said that while the new US economic sanctions appeared to be effective, the increased pressure could lead Tehran into extreme measures.“We see signs indicating that the heavy economic pressure they are under, and the fear of an uprising and the collapse of the regime, may push them to desperate steps,” Katz said at a ceremony for defence ministry employees.The hawkish minister reiterated the threats against the Islamic Republic that he has made in recent months.“An Iranian attack on Israel will free Israel from any existing constraint,” he said. “We will strike all of Iran’s national military and civilian infrastructure – including energy infrastructure – and push Iran deep back into the stone age.”Explore more on these topicsUS-Israel war on IranIranStrait of HormuzUS foreign policyMiddle East and north AfricaDonald TrumpIsraelnewsShareReuse this content

title: Dozens of trapped hydropower tunnel workers in Nepal could still be alive, official says | Nepal-Tibet flood disaster | The Guardian
description: About 46 people believed to be trapped in ‘room-like’ structure inside hydro plant tunnel on Nepal-Tibet border
Author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen
Headline: About 46 people believed to be trapped in ‘room-like’ structure inside hydro plant tunnel on Nepal-Tibet border
Content: A week after the flash-flood hit the Nepal-Tibet border, some officials believe trapped workers at the Rasuwagadhi hydropower plant could still be alive.Photograph: Naveen Srivastava/X/ReutersView image in fullscreenA week after the flash-flood hit the Nepal-Tibet border, some officials believe trapped workers at the Rasuwagadhi hydropower plant could still be alive.Photograph: Naveen Srivastava/X/ReutersNepal-Tibet flood disasterDozens of trapped hydropower tunnel workers in Nepal could still be alive, official saysAbout 46 people believed to be trapped in ‘room-like’ structure inside hydro plant tunnel on Nepal-Tibet borderAfter the flood: human suffering on an unfathomable scale in Nepal’s worst-hit districtsHannah Ellis-PetersenandGaurav Pokharelin KathmanduThu 3 Sep 2026 07.25 EDTFirst published on Wed 2 Sep 2026 21.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNepal authorities have said they are “confident” that dozens of workers in Nepal’s Rasuwagadhi hydropower plant are still alive, more than a week after deadly flash floods left them trapped in an underground chamber.Authorities said that at least 639 workers were still missing from hydropower plants built along Nepal’s Bhote Koshi and Triushuli rivers.Most of the projects were destroyed when a surge of water, debris and mud came coursing down the river valley last week, triggered by ‌thecollapse of a melting glacieron the border between Nepal and China-controlled Tibet.After the flood: human suffering on an unfathomable scale in Nepal’s worst-hit districtsRead moreThe deadly flash floods reached up to 100mph (160km/h), according to scientists, and travelled more than 60 miles down the river valley, wiping away whole villages, bridges, and hydropower dams.At least 1,252 people have been confirmed dead from the floods. More than 4,200 remain missing.According to a preliminary estimate by the UN Development Programme, the disaster created at least 2.2m tonnes of debris, including parts of buildings, rocks and sediment. Large boulders and flood waters deluged the hydropower tunnels, blocking off the entrances, and some were buried deep in mud.Rescue efforts have increasingly centred on these tunnels, where authorities believe workers may ⁠have survived for more than a week due to air pockets. So far, more than 270 people have been rescued from the hydropower projects.View image in fullscreenA turquoise-green house stands tall amid sludge near Trishuli River in the aftermath of flash floods.Photograph: Arun Sankar/AFP/Getty ImagesSpeaking on Wednesday, officials said they believed 46 people were still alive in an underground room inRasuwagadhi hydropower plant,and efforts were ongoing to locate them using excavators and other heavy equipment.“We are very confident that they must be alive after one week because … they have food and water over there in the building,” Amhsu Kiran Shahi, a board member of the Nepal ⁠electricity authority, told Reuters.Durga Gurung, 60, said his brother Jhappad Bhujel was among those trapped in a hydropower tunnel. “Right now, we are just relying on God,” he told the Guardian. “We have not been given any information about whether the people inside are alive or not.“Neither the army nor the people from the electricity authority are telling us anything. So many days have passed that we have reached a point where it feels like all we can do is hope for a miracle.”“Our relatives are sitting inside a dark tunnel,” he added. “How long can they possibly survive?”View image in fullscreenThe area around Rasuwagadhi hydropower plant before the flash flood.Photograph: Maxar/DigitalGlobe/Getty ImagesMajor rescue operations were under way or planned at four hydropower projects. Two sites – the Rasuwagadhi hydroelectric project and the Upper Trishuli 3A facility – where about 90 people are missing, offered the strongest prospect of finding survivors because of the presence of air inside the tunnels, Shahi said.The Rasuwagadhi hydroelectric project is located in Rasuwa district, about three miles away from the border withTibet, which was one of the areas of Nepal hardest hit by the floods, and remains almost inaccessible except by helicopter. “This is the only project where it’s possible to walk through ‌the tunnel,” Shahi said. “The army tried doing that three days ago, but they didn’t find the room. We are going in again.”At the Upper Trishuli 3A facility, another project hit by the floods, it took rescue workers almost six days to find the tunnels ⁠because of the thick mud. The authorities believe about 30 to 40 people may still be alive in the tunnel. “We are expecting [survivors] in there because we ​are told there is a ​dry space inside. We are ​trying to break into the tunnel now,” said the Nepali army spokesperson Raja Ram Basnet on Wednesday.The army said the search and rescue operation would go on for as long as there was hope for survivors, but that efforts would also continue to recover the dead bodies. “We are using every technology ​available in Nepal ‌right now, and we ​are taking help ​from the Indians, Chinese, Koreans. We have experts from Australia too,” added Basnet.Families of those still trapped in the projects have returned to the Nepal electricity office for the past eight days, in the hope for information. Laxmi Adhikari’s brotherJeevanlal Adhikari had gone to the Trishuli 3A Hydropower Project to test the machines, when the floods hit.She accused the authorities of withholding information from the families, and of not acting fast enough to save their relatives. “We have been running from one ministry to another and from disaster management authority to another government office, trying to find my brother,” she said. “We keep going from place to place, but the rescue operation has not been accelerated.”She said the lack of answers made the wait even more painful: “When the water came rushing in, where did he go? Did he manage to get to safety? They haven’t even given us definite information about whether our people are alive or not.”Nepal has invested more than $9bn (£6.7bn) in building hydropower dams across the mountains, huge sums given the country’s small economy. According to preliminary surveys, the floods debilitated or destroyed 11 hydropower plants and knocked out about 10% of Nepal’s total electricity-generation capacity.According to the authorities, more than 20,000 houses will have to be rebuilt in the aftermath of the flood. Nepal has put the cost of recovery at more than $5bn (£3.7bn).Explore more on these topicsNepal-Tibet flood disasterNatural disastersNepalTibetChinaSouth and central AsianewsShareReuse this content

title: Sadiq Khan agrees to have his texts and emails searched in Palantir legal battle | Sadiq Khan | The Guardian
description: US tech company has sued London mayor after he prevented it from working with Metropolitan police
Author: Patrick Daly
Headline: US tech company has sued London mayor after he prevented it from working with Metropolitan police
Content: The mayor of London, Sadiq Khan, stepped in to block a £50m deal between Palantir and the Met in May 2026.Photograph: Justin Tallis/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe mayor of London, Sadiq Khan, stepped in to block a £50m deal between Palantir and the Met in May 2026.Photograph: Justin Tallis/ReutersSadiq KhanSadiq Khan agrees to have his texts and emails searched in Palantir legal battleUS tech company has sued London mayor after he prevented it from working with Metropolitan policePatrick DalyThu 3 Sep 2026 18.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSadiq Khan has agreed for his text messages and emails to be searched as part of a legal battle with Palantir, the high court has been told, after he prevented the US technology company from working with theMetropolitan police.The London mayor stepped in to block a £50m deal betweenPalantirand the Met in May, with the artificial intelligence developer suing Khan’s office over the decision.Legal representatives for the mayor said they “did not originally consider it necessary” for Khan to be among those to have their communications searched before next year’s court case. But they relented, citing persistence from Palantir.Sarah Brown, Khan’s former director of communications, who now works for the prime minister, Andy Burnham, will also have her correspondence searched.The proposed two-year deal would have allowed Palantir, which works for the Israeli military and the Trump administration in its immigration crackdown, to provide AI technology to automate intelligence analysis in criminal investigations.But the Mayor’s Office for Policing and Crime (Mopac), which oversees large Scotland Yard contracts, said there had been a “clear and serious breach” of procurement rules. It said police had seriously considered only one supplier (Palantir).After the announcement, Palantir accused Khan of “putting politics above public safety” before declaring in June that it planned to sue theLondonmayor.At a preliminary hearing on Thursday, the high court was told Khan and more than a dozen other Mopac and Greater London Authority officials would be classed as “custodians”.Apocalypse prep or pure pragmatism: what is behind Peter Thiel’s move to Argentina?Read moreThe designation means their digital communications, including text messages, WhatsApp messages, and Microsoft Teams chats – insofar as they exist – will be searched for anything relevant to the issues in the legal tussle. These will then be disclosed to Palantir.Joseph Barrett KC, for the mayor’s office, said in written submissions: “Mopac did not originally consider it necessary or proportionate for the mayor to be added as a custodian, given that the decision was taken by the deputy mayor for policing and crime; his senior position; and the likelihood that any documents held by him would be held by other individuals.“However, Palantir has persisted in its requests, and Mopac has consented on a pragmatic basis.”Brown, who in July moved from the mayor’s office to be appointed director of communications at Downing Street, was also listed as a custodian, meaning she too will have her correspondence searched, the court heard.The decision to include Brown comes after Palantir said in court documents outlining its claim that press articles regarding the mayor’s office vetoing the Met deal cited concerns about Palantir’s values and ethics. Mopac has confirmed Brown “initiated” press briefings about the move.The date range for the communication searches is still to be determined.Mopac reportedly is demanding to see Palantir’s own internal documents related to the deal, which the company is said to be resisting.Explore more on these topicsSadiq KhanPalantirMetropolitan policePoliceLondonnewsShareReuse this content

title: Reform officials ‘plotted to break law on foreign donations’ in undercover film | Reform UK | The Guardian
description: Investigation broadcast by Channel 4 News shows man posing as ‘impermissible donor’ paying for polling that helped Reform
Author: Rowena Mason
Headline: Investigation broadcast by Channel 4 News shows man posing as ‘impermissible donor’ paying for polling that helped Reform
Content: Nigel Farage poses with a tea towel merchandise during the first day of Reform UK’s annual conference at the NEC in Birmingham.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAView image in fullscreenNigel Farage poses with a tea towel merchandise during the first day of Reform UK’s annual conference at the NEC in Birmingham.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAReform UKReform officials ‘plotted to break law on foreign donations’ in undercover filmInvestigation broadcast by Channel 4 News shows man posing as ‘impermissible donor’ paying for polling that helped ReformRowena MasonWhitehall editorThu 3 Sep 2026 17.01 EDTFirst published on Thu 3 Sep 2026 15.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNigel Farage is facing fresh criticism on the eve of the Reform UK party conference after some of his team were filmed appearing to plot to avoid electoral laws on foreign donations in an undercover investigation broadcast by Channel 4 News.A group of investigative journalists called Verbatim, founded by theCentre for Climate Reporting, posed as a potential Reform supporter and his wealthy American father, an impermissible donor, who paid for £30,000 of polling commissioned by Reform and which benefited the party.Kemi Badenoch condemns Reform UK’s ‘authoritarian’ press bansRead moreThe polling was not attributed to Reform, and was reported in the Telegraph and the Times without those newspapers knowing that it was commissioned by the party and paid for by the US donor. The benefit in kind was also not reported to the Electoral Commission.In footage of another meeting, a senior adviser to Farage, Dan Jukes, appeared to suggest to the fake UK-based supporter that his US-based father could make a substantial donation by channelling it through the son.When the possible structure was explained to Farage, footage of a meeting between him and the fake donors shows him saying: “Thank you both.”The investigation will reopen intense scrutiny of Reform’s approach to donations and its finances, which are already the subject of a standards inquiry and police investigation.Reform said it had been “the target of a hoax perpetuated by foreign-funded climate-change activists posing as would-be party donors” and the party denied any wrongdoing.In Channel 4 News’ investigation, broadcast on Thursday night, footage shows that the fake UK-based supporter also had conversations with Reform UK’s head of policy, James Orr, who talked about commissioning polling that would be paid for by the US-based father.View image in fullscreenFootage from the Channel 4 News and Verbatim undercover investigation into Reform finances.In the film, Orr can be heard saying of the arrangement that Farage “doesn’t know, won’t know” and it was the kind of thing he would “rather not know”. At one point the footage shows him saying it was “totally legit” and with “nothing untowards about it at all”.Farage was subsequently caught on camera in a meeting with the fake US donor in Clacton where he appears to be celebrating the success of the poll, saying it was “amazing” and provided “bang for buck”, adding: “It worked. Boom.”Jukes, a close aide to Farage, was also filmed meeting the fake donor, and at a Reform UK reception where in one conversation he appeared to introduce the undercover operative as “key donor for off-the-book project”.In footage of a meeting with the fake US donor, he is heard describing the polling as “clandestine” and “hugely important”.The polling, conducted by JL Partners, made headlines before the local elections in May. The foreign source of funding and its links to Reform were not publicly disclosed, and the Telegraph said it had now suspended the articles about the polling, while the Times said it was not aware of the relationship with Reform.After Channel 4 News’ broadcast, Bridget Phillipson, the Labour party chair, said the “scandal goes right to the top of Reform UK”. She added: “Nigel Farage needs to urgently prove today that his top team haven’t broken the law and secretly plotted to undermine our democracy.”Ed Davey, the leader of the Liberal Democrats, called on the police and the Electoral Commission to investigate.A Reform spokesperson said: “Reform UK has a robust vetting process for prospective donors approved by the Electoral Commission. The hoaxers are ‘Verbatim Investigations’; a new company, incorporated in July 2026 in an attempt to mask their true identity: the Centre for Climate Reporting.”The party claimed the group’s methods had previously been “rebuked by members of the United States Congress” for “videos [that] appear to be substantially edited, creating an incomplete record of the conversation”.The investigation is likely to create a serious problem for Farage as he attempts to turn the page on Reform’s summer of funding scandals, with his party conference speech scheduled for Friday.In the speech, he will boast of record donations compared with the other parties, including £4m from a crypto billionaire pardoned by Donald Trump in the last quarter.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Reform UK leader will tell the annual Birmingham gathering that the party is “much stronger than we were last year”, saying that it has the highest number of members and has brought in the most donations.Farage will also seek to look to the future by claiming he would declare a “national emergency” in order to pass legislation day and night if made prime minister, insisting he believes Reform UK will win the next election.The party outperformed Labour and the Conservatives with donations of more than £5m in the second quarter of this year, new figures from the Electoral Commission show.However, it remains reliant on a handful of mega-donors who have been based abroad and could be caught by the government’s new £100,000 annual cap on overseas funders which requires donors to have been a UK resident for 12 months.Donations graphThe biggest donation in the last few months was the £4m from Ben Delo, a crypto entrepreneur who has been based in Hong Kong in recent years but in April said he was moving back to the UK.Delo, who was convicted in the US in 2022 for failing to implement adequate anti-money-laundering controls in his cryptocurrency business, before being pardoned by Trump, has previously given Reform £4m.Party sources said it was “very confident” thatnone of Delo’s latest £4m would need to be returneddue to the cap when the legislation is passed.Burnham to crack down on UK mega-donors influencing politicsRead moreThe government has said donors would have to have been on the UK electoral register for at least 12 months and meet a residency test showing that they are “genuinely resident at a UK address”.Any gifts over the £100,000 cap from an overseas-based donor would have to be handed back once the new legislation is passed if deemed to be impermissible under the new law.Reform’s confidence in the donation would suggest Delo has been on the UK domestic electoral register and believes he could meet the residency test when the donations were made in April and May. Delo did not respond to a request for comment.Christopher Harborne, the Thailand-based billionairewho has given the party £15mand £5m to Farage personally, did not give any cash after the cap was introduced in March.The £5m gift to Farage from before the last election isunder investigation by the standards commissioner, and Reform has slid in the polls since the amount was first revealed by the Guardian.Explore more on these topicsReform UKNigel FarageParty fundingInvestigative journalismnewsShareReuse this content

title: We’re prepared to change the law to reform water industry, says Angela Eagle | Thames Water | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: New environment secretary insists ‘nothing is off the table’ in dealing with ailing Thames Water
Author: Kiran Stacey
Headline: Exclusive: New environment secretary insists ‘nothing is off the table’ in dealing with ailing Thames Water
Content: The future of Thames Water has been hanging in the balance for months as it struggles under a £20bn debt pile.Photograph: Maureen McLean/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe future of Thames Water has been hanging in the balance for months as it struggles under a £20bn debt pile.Photograph: Maureen McLean/ShutterstockThames WaterWe’re prepared to change the law to reform water industry, says Angela EagleExclusive: New environment secretary insists ‘nothing is off the table’ in dealing with ailing Thames WaterKiran StaceyandSandra LavilleThu 3 Sep 2026 15.49 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 17.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBritain’s insolvency laws cannot deal with the aggressive behaviour shown by the companies that controlThames Water, the environment secretary has said, as she confirmed ministers were prepared to take it into public ownership.Angela Eagle told the Guardian she was determined to reform the water industry after being told by Andy Burnham to make it her top priority.But she warned that could mean a change in law to factor in the way in which the US hedge funds that own much of Thames Water have kept it running while seeking a deal to renegotiate its debts.The battle over Thames looks set to become the first test of the prime minister’s determination to bring Britain’s utilities into public control even in the face of concerted corporate lobbying and the threat of legal action.In her first big interview since becoming environment secretary, Eagle said putting Thames Water into special administration – a likely first step to deprivatisation – could prove more complicated than some activists think.“A lot of people think you can just choose [special administration] … [but] you either are, or you aren’t, insolvent. And whatever people think of Thames at the moment, it isn’t technically insolvent,” she said.“The Water Act didn’t really envisage this kind of behaviour and this kind of corporate presence behaving in particular ways.“But we have a water bill coming along, and nothing is off the table. We’ve got a legislative vehicle coming along soon to enable us to do what we decide to do.”Burnham has repeatedly promised to take public utilities into public control, focusing especially on energy and water. He told the Guardian before becoming MP for Makerfield thathe intendedto nationalise Thames.The prime minister’s focus on utilities puts Eagle at the centre of much of what he is trying to do in government, including reforming the water industry andcleaning up illegal dumping sites.She is taking part in weekly meetings of the National Drought Group, which is coordinating the response to the country’s fifth drought in three years.Speaking from Havant Thicket in Hampshire, which is due to be the country’s first new reservoir since 1992, she said the country had become less resilient under previous governments and she would speed up the pace of new infrastructure.“The system has got more clogged up,” she said, comparing the situation with the one she faced as a minister in the governments of Tony Blair and Gordon Brown.“Trying to get anything done from start to finish is now much slower, much more difficult. It seems to somehow be that people always give you loads of reasons why you can’t do anything, rather than [saying] strategically, we need nine reservoirs or this reservoir, or whatever the infrastructure is.”One of her first tasks will be to decide what to do about Thames Water, which is struggling under a £20bn debt pile and has been given a record £122.7m fine for sewage spills and unlawful shareholder payouts.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIts owners, which include some of the world’s biggest hedge funds – among them Elliott Management and Apollo Global Management – are seeking a £10bn deal to renegotiate its debt and stave off nationalisation.Eagle’s predecessor, Emma Reynolds,objected to the deal, warning it would not give taxpayers value for money but the investors are still seeking regulatory approval.One option is to put the company into special administration, which can be triggered if a company is either insolvent or failing in its legal duties to provide water and sewerage services.Those calling for such a move argue there are clear signs the company is failing in this way. But the Guardianrevealed last monththat senior government officials believe a change in the law may be needed.Ewan McGaughey, professor of law at King’s College London, said: “The government doesn’t need to wait for the creditors of Thames Water to admit they are insolvent, while they charge ever more to billpayers.“The law says ministers can take away Thames Water’s licence for breaching their principal duties, namely to put all sewage through secondary treatment before release, and keep taps and hosepipes running.”Thames’s creditors have been contacted for comment.Explore more on these topicsThames WaterWater industryUtilitiesNationalisationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Minister tells Brits to stock up on days of supplies after ‘supersize’ El Niño warning | El Niño southern oscillation | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Angela Eagle urges UK citizens to be ‘a bit more resilient’ as they plan for national emergencies
Author: Kiran Stacey
Headline: Exclusive: Angela Eagle urges UK citizens to be ‘a bit more resilient’ as they plan for national emergencies
Content: El Niño is a natural climate cycle where wind changes over the Pacific lead to rising ocean temperatures and the transfer of huge amounts of heat to the atmosphere.Photograph: Hassan Ammar/APView image in fullscreenEl Niño is a natural climate cycle where wind changes over the Pacific lead to rising ocean temperatures and the transfer of huge amounts of heat to the atmosphere.Photograph: Hassan Ammar/APEl Niño southern oscillationMinister tells Brits to stock up on days of supplies after ‘supersize’ El Niño warningExclusive: Angela Eagle urges UK citizens to be ‘a bit more resilient’ as they plan for national emergenciesKiran StaceyandDamian CarringtonThu 3 Sep 2026 15.43 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 19.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBritish people have been urged to have enough food and water on hand to survive a few days without power or water, as the UN said the El Niño climate phenomenon was “supersizing before our eyes”, exacerbating extreme weather events worldwide.Forecasters say they are braced for the biggest El Niño in 1,000 years, bringing wildfires and floods to parts of the world, and the threat of a wet, stormy winter for the UK.As the British government plans a campaign urging citizens to prepare for national emergencies,Angela Eagletold the Guardian the likelihood of a wild winter showed the importance of keeping supplies at home.The environment secretary said: “We’re about to experience probably the largest El Niño that has ever been seen, and that will lead to drier summers, wetter winters, with more extreme storms in this country.“It will do a lot more damage in Asia with flooding, and therefore I think that we need to take it seriously.“If you’ve got a store of a bit of food that can keep you going for a while before the emergency services can get to you, you’re going to be a lot better off than if you haven’t. So some of it is that kind of preparation for just being a bit more resilient.”El Niño is a natural climate cycle where wind changes over the Pacific lead to rising ocean temperatures and the transfer of huge amounts of heat to the atmosphere.The most recent data, from Monday, shows the temperature of the ocean at the heart ofEl Niño at 2.6Cabove the 30-year average. That is already close to the highest anomaly ever recorded in the satellite data era, 3.1C in 2015, with months to go before the peak is expected.That peak is forecast toreach about 4Cin November, according to the average of 14 different models. Zeke Hausfather, a climate analyst, said data from analysis of corals, tree rings and historical documents suggested no El Niño had reached this level in the last millennium. Any temperature anomaly above 0.5C is classed as an El Niño.The El Niño is likely to be the largest in at least 1,000 years and will pile extra heat into an atmosphere where temperatures are already rising rapidly due to global heating. The combination means 2027 is set to “blow apart” the record and be thehottest year ever recorded.View image in fullscreenAngela Eagle, the environment secretary, with Portsmouth Water officials at the site of a new reservoir at Havant Thicket in Hampshire.Photograph: Sean Smith/The GuardianAntónio Guterres, the UN secretary general, said: “El Niño is being supersized before our eyes. The science leaves no room for doubt: the planet is in uncharted waters, and those waters are heating up.“The world is in the danger zone of extreme weather. The race now is between rising risks and our commitment to take climate action and protect people. We must win that race.”Celeste Saulo, secretary general of the UN’s World Meteorological Organization (WMO), said: “El Niño has the potential to deliver a massive blow to communities and economies across the world. We are already seeing disruption and devastation from droughts and floods and we expect these impacts to increase as El Niño intensifies.”The climate crisis, caused by pollution from fossil fuels, is alreadysuperchargingextreme weather andkilling people, with the mostextreme heatwave everrecorded hitting Europe this summer and leading to at least35,000 deaths.The El Niño will ratchet up the effects even further, with the scale of the event having been described as “truly mind-blowing” and a “Godzilla-level” event.The rising heat from the El Niño is already having effects, from worseningwildfires in Indonesiato the weakening of vitalmonsoon rains in India. The effects will spread globally, from greater fire risk in Australia to more intense floods in South America. The World Food Programme said in August that the El Niño was likely to push about 50 million peopleinto acute hunger.In the UK, ministers are prioritising climate resilience after the UK’s hottest summer on record.A campaign from the Cabinet Office in the coming months will tell households to stock up on tinned food and take steps to ensure they are prepared for national emergencies.Meanwhile Eagle will oversee farming improvements and a new programme of reservoir building that she says will leave Britain better prepared than it has been for the kind of extreme weather that is likely in future years.Speaking from Havant Thicket, which is set to be the country’s first new reservoir since 1992, Eagle said the country had not been good enough at preparing for climate-related emergencies in the past and would have to change its farming and water management techniques.“We need to do our own adaptations … and that is what things like these this reservoir is about,” she said.“It’s what the farming transition is about, so we can farm in a more resilient and and sustainable way from an environmental point of view.”Explore more on these topicsEl Niño southern oscillationClimate crisisAngela EagleFloodingExtreme weatherExtreme heatUnited NationsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Higher education regulator apologises for imposing £585,000 fine on university | Higher education | The Guardian
description: Office for Students made decision to punish University of Sussex last year after claiming it breached free speech regulations
Author: Richard Adams
Headline: Office for Students made decision to punish University of Sussex last year after claiming it breached free speech regulations
Content: The OfS investigation began after Kathleen Stock’s resignation, following campus protests for her views on transgender rights and gender identity.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe OfS investigation began after Kathleen Stock’s resignation, following campus protests for her views on transgender rights and gender identity.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianHigher educationHigher education regulator apologises for imposing £585,000 fine on universityOffice for Students made decision to punish University of Sussex with fine last year after claiming it breached free speech regulationsRichard AdamsEducation editorThu 3 Sep 2026 15.01 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 17.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEngland’s higher education regulator has apologised for a string of mistakes in its decision to punish theUniversity of Sussexwith a record fine that was later overturned by the high court.TheOffice for Students(OfS) tried to impose a £585,000 fine against Sussex last year after claiming the university breached free speech regulations involving its former professor Kathleen Stock. It was forced to back down in April after a judicial review initiated by Sussex found the OfS “had closed its mind” and acted with bias.University of Sussex overturns £585,000 fine as high court rejects free speech breach claimRead moreIn a statement, the regulator said: “The OfS made mistakes in the Sussex case, which we regret. The actions we are announcing today show our continuing commitment to learning the lessons from this case with humility and honesty.”Among the changes promised by the OfS in a“lessons learned” reportwere “ensuring respectful relationships with higher education providers” and in the future using “alternative forms of intervention where possible to effect change” before taking enforcement action such as fines.Prof Sasha Roseneil, Sussex’s vice-chancellor, said she welcomed the OfS’s acknowledgement of its mistakes but was concerned that its plans for reform “fell short” in a number of areas.Roseneil said: “[The report] reveals deep cultural problems within the OfS in relation to freedom of expression and internal challenge, and it is heartening to see the new leadership setting different expectations for the organisation, expectations that are more appropriate for a public institution, trusted to regulate one of the most important sectors in a democratic society.“However, the report does not fully reflect the breadth or the seriousness of the high court’s findings or all the lessons that could be learned from the case.View image in fullscreenSasha Roseneil.“It is also disappointing that the review missed the opportunity to engage with the University of Sussex when their lack of engagement was roundly criticised by the high court.”The high court’s findings were backed up by an internal review by KPMG commissioned by the OfS, published in summary on Thursday. KPMG’s findings criticised the regulator for being adversarial, allowing gaps in its written records, and lacking clear accountability.“It appears that insufficient emphasis was placed on maintaining constructive engagement and dialogue with higher education providers, which contributed to relationships becoming increasingly adversarial,” according to the review’s summary.View image in fullscreenKathleen Stock.KPMG also criticised the OfS’s leadership at the time for becoming blinkered: “The investigation team was made up of particularly senior staff, reflecting the case’s novelty, complexity and profile.“However, the concentration of decision making and delivery responsibilities within a relatively small group reduced the opportunity for independent challenge and fresh perspectives.”The OfS’s chair, Edward Peck, and chief executives Ruth Hannant and Polly Payne, thanked the University of Sussex’s leadership “for the frank discussions and insightful commentary leading to this point”.Hannant and Payne took over as the OfS’s chief executives in June and had no prior involvement with the decision to fine Sussex. The OfS investigation began after Stock’s resignation from Sussex in 2021, following campus protests for her views on transgender rights and gender identity.Explore more on these topicsHigher educationUniversity of SussexOffice for StudentsFreedom of speechUniversity administrationUniversitiesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Judge rules 2,000 Catalina Island deer can be killed to save native plant species | California | The Guardian
description: Cull of animals that eat native shrubs, causing spread of fast-igniting grasses, to go ahead despite fierce opposition
Author: Sophie Sullivan
Headline: Cull of animals that eat native shrubs, causing spread of fast-igniting grasses, to go ahead despite fierce opposition
Content: A mule deer doe walks through a hillside behind the Descanso Beach Club in Avalon on Catalina Island.Photograph: Allen J Schaben/Los Angeles Times/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA mule deer doe walks through a hillside behind the Descanso Beach Club in Avalon on Catalina Island.Photograph: Allen J Schaben/Los Angeles Times/Getty ImagesCaliforniaJudge rules 2,000 Catalina Island deer can be killed to save native plant speciesCull of animals that eat native shrubs, causing spread of fast-igniting grasses, to go ahead despite fierce oppositionSophie Sullivanin Los AngelesThu 3 Sep 2026 19.19 EDTFirst published on Thu 3 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLocals and tourists have long fawned over Catalina Island’s mule deer population. For nearly a century, the ungulates have roamed the land’s waterfronts and woodlands, so comfortable around humans that it is not uncommon to spot deer roaming downtown Avalon.But that sight will soon disappear, after a judge this week paved the way for the island’s conservancy to kill nearly all the island’s 2,000 deer.A non-profit controlling 88% of the island off the southernCaliforniacoast has been trying for years to eliminate a non-native deer population. Experts statewide have expressed support for the Catalina Island Conservancy proposal, saying the deer’s consumption of a native shrub plant has led to a growth of an invasive grass species that ignites faster and spreads fire more easily.The prospect of killing so many deer hassparked fierce – and emotional – oppositionfrom the public, creating an unlikely coalition of animal activists and hunters that has tried to prevent the culling in court. Anonline petitionagainst the move has garnered more than 32,000 signatures.Los Angeles county supervisor Janice Hahn, an outspoken critic of the deer’s killing, asked California’s governor, Gavin Newsom, to intervene earlier this week. But the plea was to no avail, and on Thursday a county judge issued a final ruling denying a preliminary injunction filed by opponents.The conservancy said it would now move forward with a five-year plan to eliminate the island’s deer population, according to its director of communications, Pepe Barton, with an estimated 200 to be hunted with rifles over the next two months. Formally known as Santa Catalina Island, it is the last leg of the Channel Islands to remove non-native deer species.Barton said the conservancy’s decision was “never our first choice”.“We understand the gravity of the situation and the responsibility, and it’s a noble sacrifice on the part of the deer that didn’t ask for this,” Barton said. “But this is a necessary step to protect the island, the native plants and animals that are only found here, as well as the residents and livelihoods that depend on Catalina.”California officials move forward with plans to exterminate mule deer from islandRead moreHunters first introduced mule deer to Catalina for sport about a century ago. What began as a population of a few quickly grew to a few thousand, and save for minor dips in drought seasons, the island’s deer population has not dwindled.The animals developed an appetite for shrubs native to the island. That presented a unique ecological problem, according to Anna L Jacobsen, a professor and plant biologist atCaliforniaState University, Bakersfield, who studied the island deer’s relationship with its vegetation after its last major fires in 2006 and 2007.Jacobsen said when non-native deer eat shrubs already threatened by climate change, the native plants cannot regenerate or recover fast enough, and can become locally extinct. They are subsequently replaced by invasive grasses that ignite and spread fire faster than native species.In southern California, which has seen increasingly dangerous wildfire seasons in recent years, prevention “has shifted away from, say, fuel reduction to focusing on ignitions”, according to Max Moritz, a wildfire specialist who provides scientific advisory to California state and local governments.Seeing that loss, and increasingly concerned as wildfires becomemore frequent across California, scientists sought deer population control measures.The conservancy examined contraception and sterilization for the deer, which Barton said was infeasible for such a large population. They considered fencing the animals, but it “just isn’t a thing that would be approved”, he said. Four decades of regular hunting seasons have not been enough to reduce populations. And introducing new predators would create new risks to native animals and local people, Barton said.That leaves total extermination. The conservancy filed for a restoration management permit with the California department of fish and wildlife, which in January approved the plan.Only a small population of deer will be sterilized – those living near the town of Avalon – and all others will be killed. Island residents will be allowed one last hunting season from late October to mid-December of this year.The meat from the deer killing will go to the California condor recovery program or local tribal groups, and Barton said deer carcasses near trails or roads will be removed; only those in steep, dangerous terrain will be allowed to decompose naturally. People traveling or hiking the island will not regularly see deer carcasses, Barton said.Still, the question over what to do about Catalina’s deer has created a complex situation where “people feel some strong attachment to the deer” and it becomes difficult to see the science behind decisions, Moritz said. “But the fact is, you can’t realistically constrain the deer to graze only targeted areas ... From a scientific, ecological, and fire perspective, removal is the best way.”Explore more on these topicsCaliforniaWest CoastAnimalsLos AngelesWildlifenewsShareReuse this content

title: Nvidia to buy developer platform Hugging Face in $12.9bn deal | Nvidia | The Guardian
description: Semi-conductor giant bets that support for open AI models could offset potential slowdown in demand for chips
Author: Nick Robins-Early
Headline: Semi-conductor giant bets that support for open AI models could offset potential slowdown in demand for chips
Content: Nvidia’s acquisition of Hugging Face will give it direct access to platform developers use to collaborate, test and share tools.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersView image in fullscreenNvidia’s acquisition of Hugging Face will give it direct access to platform developers use to collaborate, test and share tools.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersNvidiaNvidia to buy developer platform Hugging Face in $12.9bn dealSemi-conductor giant bets that support for open AI models could offset potential slowdown in demand for chipsNick Robins-Earlyand agenciesThu 3 Sep 2026 12.59 EDTFirst published on Thu 3 Sep 2026 09.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNvidiawill buy the popular developer platform Hugging Face for nearly $13bn, betting that support for ⁠open AI models could offset a potential slowdown in demand for the semiconductor giant’s chips.Shares ⁠inNvidiawere ⁠slightly lower ​after the $12.93bn (£9.57bn) deal – which ranks among its biggest ever – was announced for the database of AI models on Thursday.Hugging Face, based in New York and backed by the likes of Intel, Advanced Micro Devices and Amazon, was founded in 2016 by the French entrepreneurs Clément Delangue, Julien Chaumond and Thomas Wolf.Nvidia is already a major open AI player in the US with ⁠its widely used Nemotron model and vocal support for the technology.Nvidia’s quarterly revenue doubles to nearly $100bn as CEO declares ‘golden age’Read moreAcquiring Hugging Face will give it direct access to a platform developers use to ⁠collaborate and test and share tools, potentially providing insight and data that could help it narrow the ​technology gap with top American and ‌Chinese labs.“Nvidia gains visibility into customer’s preferences and the AI models they use,” said Naveen Chhabra, principal analyst at Forrester. “They can see which models are trending, what datasets customers are downloading, and the architectures that are gaining traction weeks before they hit mainstream tech news.”Demand for open-weight models ‌has surged from businesses balking at the steep bill of deploying generative AI. Chinese companies ‌such as DeepSeek, Moonshot and Z.ai have emerged as crucial players with models that can match the best from the US in tasks including generating computer code at a lower cost.There are fears that some US firms could become reliant on Beijing’s models even as both countries race to dominate a technology they see as crucial to their future. The Trump administration hasscrambled to respondto the wave of open models from China, weighing whether to restrict their use while also worrying about stifling American businesses that have taken to using them.Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s chief executive, was a signatory of an open letter earlier this year from major tech firms that advocated for open models and warned against government regulation that would stifle their use. Huang pledged that Nvidia would keep Hugging Face open after acquiring it.“Hugging ‌Face will remain an open platform for the entire AI ecosystem,” said Huang, adding that his company’s chips would not be required to ​build on or deploy through Hugging Face.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUnder the deal, Nvidia will pay about $11.9bn to Hugging Face investors, while offering an equity-based retention program of up to $1bn for employees who join Nvidia.For Nvidia, building up its open source business may help it cushion a demand slowdown from customers such as ⁠Meta, OpenAI and Microsoft, which are developing their own AI chips to cut reliance ​on its costly and ​supply-constrained processors. Several Chinese chip-making firms have alsomade recent advancementsthat could further disrupt the balance of power within big tech, though they face strict international export controls.It has been a volatile year in the market for chipmakers, with a chip stockselloff in Julywiping $1tn from the market caps of leading firms. Nvidia shares bounced back in August, though, with a strong revenue forecast leading to the second-biggest one-day gain in market history – adding $442bn to the company’s market value.Hugging Face has also been ​in the news recently after ahack by rogue AI agentsthat ​escaped OpenAI’s testing ‌environment. Beyond hosting AI ​models, it offers datasets, ​software libraries and cloud services used to build and deploy AI applications.Explore more on these topicsNvidiaAI (artificial intelligence)ComputingTechnology sectornewsShareReuse this content

title: Fox News Media abruptly ousts longtime anchor Maria Bartiromo | Fox News | The Guardian
description: Bartiromo had been a host at the network for more than a decade and Fox gave no explanation for the decision
Author: Jeremy Barr
Headline: Bartiromo had been a host at the network for more than a decade and Fox gave no explanation for the decision
Content: Maria Bartiromo during Fox Business Network's show Mornings with Maria in Washington DC.Photograph: Paul Morigi/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMaria Bartiromo during Fox Business Network's show Mornings with Maria in Washington DC.Photograph: Paul Morigi/Getty ImagesFox NewsFox News Media abruptly ousts longtime anchor Maria BartiromoBartiromo had been a host at the network for more than a decade and Fox gave no explanation for the decisionJeremy BarrThu 3 Sep 2026 14.20 EDTFirst published on Thu 3 Sep 2026 13.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFox News Media on Thursday abruptly ousted one of its most well-known hosts and anchors, Maria Bartiromo, without providing an explanation.“Effective today, Maria Bartiromo is no longer with FOX News Media,” the network said in a press release, adding in a statement: “We thank Maria for her work over the last 12 and a half years and wish her all the best on her next chapter.”Bartiromo was one of the busiest anchors for the company, hosting a three-hour weekday morning show for theFoxBusiness Network and the Sunday morning Fox News show Sunday Morning Futures.But Bartiromo has been off the air since early August, with no reason given for her departure, though television hosts regularly take time off during the summer.CBS brings back Norah O’Donnell to co-anchor morning show amid ratings challengesRead moreBartiromo, who distinguished herself as a financial journalist for CNBC knownas “the money hunny” in the 1990s, had in recent years became known primarily for her fervent support for Donald Trump.Bartiromo has regularly been effusive in her praise of the president, and has dined with him on multiple occasions. In January 2025, she sat at Trump’s table for a dinner held for his inauguration. “The world is watching 47 as he is sworn in less than 3-hours thank you @potus47 for this honor and for your dedication and love of this great nation,”she wrote in a poston Instagram.A few months later, she posted a photo of her dining at the White House with Trump and Steven Cheung, his communications director. “Thank you Mr President for your graciousness, your leadership and your protection of this great nation,”she wrote in a captionon Instagram.Bartiromo was a prominent part of two separate defamation lawsuits against Fox News Media owing to the network’s coverage of the 2020 presidential election. One of those lawsuits, filed by Dominion Voting Systems, was settled in April 2023, while another case filed by Smartmatic remains ongoing.Internal communications released as part of the Dominion and Smartmatic lawsuits showed that Bartiromo was open to the theory that the 2020 election had been rigged in favor of Joe Biden. “#1 story all trump supporters want right now is stop the steal,”she wrote in a messageto a producer. “They do not believe the ejection [sic] was fair or honest. So fox needs to cover it.” (In depositions, Bartiromo denied knowledge that the claims of election fraud were false, as the voting technology companies had contended.)Documentsreleased in the Smartmatic casealso showed that Bartiromo had made $70m in her career at Fox.It’s unclear whether Bartiromo might be considered for a job in the Trump administration, as some of her fellow colleagues have been. Last spring, Bartiromo and her fellow Fox News host Laura Ingraham were appointed to the board of the Kennedy Center.Some conservatives have suggestedthat she could be a candidate for White House press secretary.“Everyone is wondering if she’s going to the administration or whether it was the Smartmatic lawsuit,” said one Fox News Media employee who was not authorized to comment.The network said on Thursday that Bartiromo’s daily Fox Business Network show will be called Mornings with FOX Business and will have rotating anchors for the time being. The network also said that her Sunday morning show on Fox News will be hosted this weekend by Jason Chaffetz, a contributor and former congressman, and a new host will be announced at a later date.The abrupt nature of her departure suggests that it was not voluntary. Fox News Media used similar language in announcing the departure of one-time star Tucker Carlson in 2023.By Thursday afternoon, Fox Business Network had already deleted Bartiromo’s staff page.Explore more on these topicsFox NewsTV newsFoxnewsShareReuse this content

title: Thieves steal more than 70,000 pints’ worth of Guinness from depot in Cheshire | Crime | The Guardian
description: Police say two lorries were driven into industrial estate in Runcorn and attached to trailers holding about 800 barrels
Author: Kevin Rawlinson
Headline: Police say two lorries were driven into industrial estate in Runcorn and attached to trailers holding about 800 barrels
Content: Cheshire police have appealed for witnesses who may have seen a lorry entering the Aston Lane area.Photograph: John Keeble/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCheshire police have appealed for witnesses who may have seen a lorry entering the Aston Lane area.Photograph: John Keeble/Getty ImagesCrimeThieves steal more than 70,000 pints’ worth of Guinness from depot in CheshirePolice say two lorries were driven into industrial estate in Runcorn and attached to trailers holding about 800 barrelsKevin Rawlinsonand agencyThu 3 Sep 2026 13.18 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 14.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe famous tagline “Guinness is good for you” applies only when the drink is bought and paid for, police have said, after thieves made off with more than 70,000 pints’ worth inCheshire.Officers said they believed two lorries were driven into a depot in Runcorn on Monday and attached to waiting trailers holding a combined total of about 800 barrels before being driven away.Cheshire police said they hoped for a full recovery of the stolen barrels, and had appealed for witnesses who may have seen a lorry entering the Aston Lane area at about 7.45pm.The first lorry was said to have connected to the HGV trailer before leaving the depot at about 7.55pm in the direction of the Mersey Gateway bridge.
