The second lorry arrived at the same site at 9.12pm and connected to another trailer before leaving at 9.30pm in the direction of Rainhill and Watkinson Way, police said.View image in fullscreenOne of the two HGV trailers pictured before it was stolen from Whitehouse industrial estate in Runcorn.Photograph: Cheshire Constabulary/PADS McClatchy said: “It is famously said that ‘Guinness is good for you’, but that is only the case when it has been bought and paid for.“It is with this in mind that we have wasted no time in launching inquires to identify those responsible for the theft of £115,000 worth of Guinness and the two trailers that housed the barrels. We will settle for nothing less than the full recovery of all the items stolen.”When including the value of the trailers, the total value of the items stolen is estimated at about £205,000.McClatchey asked anyone with information to speak to officers. “We would also ask any motorists who were driving in the area at the time of either of the incidents to please review any dashcam footage to see if you have captured anything that could aid our investigation.”The stolen barrels, containing about 70,400 pints of Guinness, had been intended for delivery to pubs. Diageo, which owns the brand, has a packaging warehouse on the Whitehouse industrial estate on Aston Lane.Police believe both HGVs were driven by men. The first driver was described as white with a short dark beard, and wearing a beanie hat. The second was believed to have been wearing a cap.The trailers were described as white tri-axle curtain-side trailers with branding for the logistics company GXO on the curtains and rear doors. The trucks have the unique ID numbers DL736 and DL542 on the top left corner of their rear doors.Explore more on these topicsCrimeCheshirePubsFood & drink industryBeerFoodnewsShareReuse this content

title: Yen soars as Bank of Japan tipped to raise interest rates | Yen | The Guardian
description: Jump lifts currency to highest level against dollar in a month, while global markets remain jittery
Author: Heather Stewart
Headline: Jump lifts currency to highest level against dollar in a month, while global markets remain jittery
Content: The Tokyo skyline. Investors have been reassessing their expectations for the future path of interest rates in Japan and other major economies.Photograph: Yuichi Yamazaki/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Tokyo skyline. Investors have been reassessing their expectations for the future path of interest rates in Japan and other major economies.Photograph: Yuichi Yamazaki/AFP/Getty ImagesYenYen soars as Bank of Japan tipped to raise interest ratesJump lifts currency to highest level against dollar in a month, while global markets remain jitteryBusiness live – latest updatesHeather StewartandGraeme WeardenThu 3 Sep 2026 10.33 EDTFirst published on Thu 3 Sep 2026 07.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Japanese yen has soared by more than 2% against the dollar amid speculation the Bank ofJapanis set to raise interest rates.The latest jump on Thursday lifted the yen to its highest level against the dollar in a month, at 155.57, and followed a 0.9% move the previous day.Global markets remain jittery after this week’sdramatic government bond sell-off– caused by fears of a fresh inflation increase as a result of higher oil prices.Investors have been reassessing their expectations for the future path of interest rates, in Japan and across other major economies.Remarks by a Bank of Japan policymaker, Hajime Takata, suggesting it needs to move more “nimbly”, appeared to have heightened the prospects of a decisive move.The chief executive of the financial adviser deVere, Nigel Green, said the scale of the yen appreciation over such a short time period underlined the febrile state of markets. “Markets this jumpy don’t need a shock to move hard, a rumour is enough,” he said.Citi said in a note to clients that Takata’s remarks were the “strongest messaging we’ve heard from the board and reintroduces the idea of an expedited rate hike trajectory”.The Bank of Japan has been incrementally raising rates for the past two years, after the economy finally shrugged off decades of deflation, or falling prices – but its main policy rate was left unchanged at 1% in July.Markets now believe there is a 77% chance of a rate rise at the BoJ’s next meeting, which starts on 17 September.Commenting on the latest market moves, Japan’s vice-finance minister for international affairs, Atsushi Mimura, said he was “neither satisfied nor reassured”, and policymakers “remain on a state of heightened alert”.The global bond market sell-off – pushing up the yield, or interest rate, on government borrowing – intensified earlier this week after the US Federal Reserve chair, Kevin Warsh, used a speech last Friday to indicate that he was determined to bring inflation back to target.Warsh had previously baffled some investors by withdrawing the Fed’s approach of signalling future rate moves, known as “forward guidance” – but in Friday’s speech at the central bankers’ conference in Jackson Hole, he said that if inflation did not move towards the 2% targetthe Fed would have “more to do”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe dollar weakened on Thursday after the Fed governor Christopher Waller indicated he was leaning towards keeping interest rates steady at this month’s meeting of Fed rate-setters.“I’m going to paraphrase John Lennon here: ‘give disinflation a chance’. We can wait one meeting,” Waller told Reuters.The dollar dropped further against the yen after his comments, and was also weaker against the pound and the euro.The bond sell-off appeared to have eased on Thursday, with yields on 10-year UK government bonds, known as gilts, hovering at about 5.1% in morning trading – having touched the highest level since 2008, close to 5.3%,earlier this week.Explore more on these topicsYenJapanInterest ratesCurrenciesEconomicsAsia PacificDollarnewsShareReuse this content

title: Will the Clippers’ $30m fine tame the NBA’s billionaire class? We’re about to find out | Los Angeles Clippers | The Guardian
description: The league is awash with ultra-wealthy owners. Adam Silver is hoping a hefty punishment for the Clippers will send them a message about who is in charge
Author: Oren Weisfeld
Headline: The league is awash with ultra-wealthy owners. Adam Silver is hoping a hefty punishment for the Clippers will send them a message about who is in charge
Content: Steve Ballmer and Kawhi Leonard found themselves in the middle of one of the biggest scandals in NBA history.Photograph: Katelyn Mulcahy/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSteve Ballmer and Kawhi Leonard found themselves in the middle of one of the biggest scandals in NBA history.Photograph: Katelyn Mulcahy/Getty ImagesLos Angeles ClippersWill the Clippers’ $30m fine tame the NBA’s billionaire class? We’re about to find outThe league is awash with ultra-wealthy owners. Adam Silver is hoping a hefty punishment for the Clippers will send them a message about who is in chargeOren WeisfeldThu 3 Sep 2026 08.18 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Steve Ballmer bought theLos Angeles Clippersfor $2bn in 2014, it was widely regarded as a coup for the NBA.Not only is Ballmer one of the richest men in the world –worth an estimated $152.7bn– but his passion and enthusiasm for the sport stood in stark contrast to the team’s embattled former owner. Donald Sterling, who bought the Clippers for $12.5m in 1981, was forced to sell after being handed a lifetime ban by the NBA in response to a series ofracist comments.Ballmer was the kind of owner NBA fans dream of, especially ones as downtrodden as the Clippers. He invested hundreds of millions of dollars towards improving the roster, growing the brand, and developing the new state-of-the-art Intuit Dome in Inglewood, California. When it opened in 2024, it gave the Clippers a home of their own for the first time since moving from San Diego in 1984. Ballmer’s Clippers constantly pushed the envelope, installing the first “halo” scoreboard, awall of a supporters’ section strategically positioned to throw off opponents, a team with future Hall of Famers Kawhi Leonard and Paul George. Ballmer turned a laughingstock that had been living in the shadows of the crosstown rival Lakers into a relevant organization.Clippers docked five first-round draft picks and fined $30m over Kawhi Leonard scandalRead moreBut Wednesday afternoon, after a year of allegations that Ballmer’s Clipperscircumvented the NBA’s salary capto pay superstar Leonard back in 2021, it was confirmed that Ballmer had taken it all a little bit too far. NBA commissionerAdam Silver handed downthe harshest punishment in league history, stripping the Clippers of five first-round draft picks and fining them $30m, while suspending Ballmer for a year.“The NBA’s collectively bargained system for determining player compensation is a fundamental component of the basketball competition that the league oversees for the benefit of the teams and players and ultimately the fans,” Silversaidin a statement. “I am deeply disappointed by the flagrant violations of our rules and by the Clippers’ institutional and leadership failures that led to this misconduct. The severity of the penalties reflects the seriousness of the violations.”NBA fans have been looking for clarity for a year. Last September, journalist Pablo Torre releasedthe first in a series of podcast episodesalleging that Ballmer’s Clippers violated the salary cap circumvention rules designed to punish teams for spending too much on player salaries. Citing legal documents, Torre claimed that Ballmer went under the table to sign Leonard to a no-show endorsement deal with Aspiration – a now-bankrupt sustainability services company that Ballmer invested in to pay Leonard $28m.The NBA-hired New York law firm of Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz has been conducting an independent investigation into the allegations since then,saying on Wednesdaythat the Clippers violated “the circumvention rules in numerous independent ways by (i) affirmatively initiating off-court income opportunities between Mr Leonard and four different companies doing business with the team: Aspiration, Boingo Wireless,Daktronics, and Lockton Insurance.” It also found that the Clippers facilitated the fulfillment of those endorsement agreements and induced the companies to enter into the agreements by offering and providing them with business from the Clippers, such as an Aspiration jersey patch and Daktronics scoreboard.The Clippers “vehemently reject the NBA’s punishments”, according to a statement released by the organization, calling them “the result of a heavily biased investigation seeking to justify a predetermined narrative rather than facts and evidence”. Leonard, meanwhile, announced onInstagramthat “I accept full responsibility for lapses in judgment by people within my inner circle,” referring to his uncle and former business manager, Dennis Robertson, who solicited these agreements on Leonard’s behalf and was banned from the league for five years as a result.Leonard appears to be on his way to Toronto, as the previously announced trade between the Clippers and Raptors is expected to go through within the next few days, according toESPN. The Raptors will send Brandon Ingram, Gradey Dick, two first-round picks, two second-round picks and a pick-swap to Los Angeles to reunite Leonard with the franchise he won an NBA championship with in 2019. The deal was put on hold in late July after the NBA announced that the Raptors had to commit in writing to assume any risk of penalties Leonard could incur from the investigation. But given that Leonard basically got off scot-free – his only punishment is to pay the league $700,000, probably because the league wanted to avoid a battle with its players association – the Raptors will be incentivized to see the deal through while the Clippers will have a hard time going back to the negotiating table given that most oftheir front office has been suspended.Still, the Clippers are desperate for a way out of this situation, and for good reason. After having to forfeit five first-round draft picks, the Clippers now have no natural pick in the draft from 2029 through 2033. It’s a dire situation considering that the franchise only recently pivoted to a rebuild after trading veterans James Harden, Ivica Zubac, and (almost certainly) Leonard – leaving them without any superstars or bluechip prospects to build around. They can’t really attract veteran talent given the damage this year-long soap opera has done to their brand, and finding good young players through the draft just became nearly impossible.“We intend to vigorously challenge these findings and penalties through every avenue available to us and look forward to an ethical and impartial arbitration process,” announced the Clippers, who also sent aletterto Silver confirming that “we are exploring every legal remedy to address this gross injustice.”Prolonged litigation between one of the world’s richest men and one of its wealthiest sports leagues could be ahead. But while this all may seem like a harsh penalty for an organization that only recently climbed out of the dregs of theNBA– one that could be forced to sell or relocate in the aftermath of this news in the worst-case scenario – Silver had no choice but to drop the hammer on Ballmer given what he represents not only to sports fans, but to the swell of big-pocketed owners who have recently bought into the NBA as well.“Many fans have expressed apathy about the entire cap circumvention fiasco,” Stephen Nohwrotein Sporting News. “But if the league simply gave a finger wag, then other deep-pocketed ownership groups would surely have started their own cap circumvention techniques.”Whether it’s Bob Iger andJosh Kushner buying the Lakers for $12.5bn this summer, or casino mogul andDonald Trump megadonor Miriam Adelsonbuying the Dallas Mavericks for $3.5bn in 2023, the new wave of NBA owners have a lot more in common with Ballmer than they do with the previous generation of NBA owners like Sterling and former Lakers owner Jerry Buss, who ran mom-and-pop-shop operations after buying their teams for, as ridiculous as this sounds, “mere” millions.Following in Ballmer’s footsteps, the new money entering the NBA is tied to tech billionaires,sovereign wealth funds in Gulf states, and private equity firms in the United States that have seemingly unlimited amounts of money and power. Silver had no choice but to make an example out of the Clippers, theoretically setting a precedent that is harsh enough to keep the rest of the owners in line to ensure parity and integrity for the NBA.Hopefully it’s not already too late.Explore more on these topicsLos Angeles ClippersNBABasketballUS sportsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Athletic investigation finds Dianna Russini-Mike Vrabel ties violated standards | US sports media | The Guardian
description: The NFL reporter resigned from the outlet after fallout from the publication of photos of her and the Patriots coach at an Arizona resort this spring
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: The NFL reporter resigned from the outlet after fallout from the publication of photos of her and the Patriots coach at an Arizona resort this spring
Content: Dianna Russini worked as an NFL reporter for ESPN before joining The Athletic.Photograph: Icon Sportswire/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDianna Russini worked as an NFL reporter for ESPN before joining The Athletic.Photograph: Icon Sportswire/Getty ImagesUS sports mediaAthletic investigation finds Dianna Russini-Mike Vrabel ties violated standardsNFL reporter resigned after fallout from photo scandalPatriots coach, Russini were pictured at Arizona resortInvestigation unable to find ‘exact nature’ of relationshipGuardian sportThu 3 Sep 2026 12.24 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 12.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Athletic’s internal investigation found thatthe relationshipbetween former NFL reporter Dianna Russini and New England Patriots coach Mike Vrabel was in “clear violation” of the newsroom’s standards.The outlet, which is owned by the New York Times, released a report Thursday detailing the findings of a five-months-longinvestigation. Mike Semel, the Athletic’s editorial director for standards and quality, wrote that he was unable to find signs of clear bias in her coverage or determine the exact “nature of their relationship”, but said it gave the appearance of a conflict of interest.The Dianna Russini fallout is less about scandal than who carries blame in the NFL | Melissa JacobsRead more“Russini’s relationship with Vrabel was in clear violation of The Athletic’s standards,” Semel wrote. “Regardless of whether the relationship was romantic, it was a breach and should have been disclosed.”Semel added: “I’ve not found a clear link to conclude that Russini used her platform to help promote Vrabel or help his teams during her time at The Athletic. That said, there are examples of Russini writing glowingly of Vrabel that in hindsight are awkward or even uncomfortable.”The investigation began after the New York Postpublishedphotos of Russini and Vrabel at an Arizona resort, taken around the time of the NFL owners meetings in March. Some appeared to show the two embracing and holding hands. Russini and Vrabel, who are married to other people, said the interaction was platonic. Russini said the photos did not reflect that they were part of a larger group gathering, and Vrabel called any suggestion of impropriety “laughable”.The Athletic initially defended Russini, with its executive editor saying the photos lacked context, but the outlet began a review of her work after additional photos and reporting raised questions about the nature of their relationship. Russini, who had joined The Athletic in 2023 after nearly a decade at ESPN, resigned on 14 April.“I have covered theNFLwith professionalism and dedication throughout my career, and I stand behind every story I have ever published,” Russini said in her resignation letter.The NFLoptednot to investigate Vrabel’s behavior, and the coach publicly addressed the situation soon after Russini’s resignation, saying it prompted“difficult conversations”and thathe would seek counseling.The New York Times Company and Russini declined comment toESPNand the New York Times.In the report, Semel said he reviewed 903 stories, 77 videos and more than 200 podcast episodes that contained Russini’s reporting. Russini, the report said, told editors that her and Vrabel’s relationship was “close” but “strictly professional”.“The vast majority of Russini’s work for The Athletic had nothing to do with Vrabel, the teams he was coaching or the players the team was pursuing,” Semel wrote. “Russini’s work was seldom reliant on Vrabel as a source or subject. In interviews with editors and reporters with whom she worked most closely, it was clear Russini was sourced up around the NFL, not just with Vrabel or the Patriots.”“But of course,” he wrote, “the appearances surrounding her relationship with Vrabel undermines our audience’s confidence in her impartiality.”Explore more on these topicsUS sports mediaNFLUS sportsNew England PatriotsUS press and publishingNew York TimesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Fifa calls Uefa’s legal threat a ‘smear campaign’ in US federal filing | Fifa | The Guardian
description: Fifa has filed a motion opposing Uefa’s request for discovery for use in a potential criminal case against president Gianni Infantino
Author: Alexander Abnos
Headline: Fifa has filed a motion opposing Uefa’s request for discovery for use in a potential criminal case against president Gianni Infantino
Content: Fifa president Gianni Infantino and Uefa president Alexander Ceferin pictured in 2024.Photograph: Nick Potts/PAView image in fullscreenFifa president Gianni Infantino and Uefa president Alexander Ceferin pictured in 2024.Photograph: Nick Potts/PAFifaFifa calls Uefa’s legal threat a ‘smear campaign’ in US federal filingFifa filed motion opposing Uefa’s request for discoveryUefa said to be considering criminal case v Gianni InfantinoAlexander Abnosin New YorkThu 3 Sep 2026 15.41 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 17.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAttorneys representing Fifa have hit back atUefa’s request for discoveryin a US federal filing earlier this week. The lawyers called Uefa’s legal efforts “little more than press releases in further support of [a] smear campaign against Fifa and its leadership” and requested the judge assigned to the case dismiss the request.The filing requests thatFifaUS, a subsidiary business unit of Fifa, be permitted to officially opposite the request for discovery by 30 September.Thierry Henry says players ‘have more power than they think’ amid Fifa scandalsRead moreUefa filed four separate requests for subpoena in different US courts at the end of August, arguing in each that discovery was needed as itcontemplated initiating criminal proceedingsagainst Fifa president Gianni Infantino over the proposed Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) plan thatcaused uproar across football. The requests sought information, including documents and communications from Fifa as well as Joshua Kushner and the investment firm he oversees, Thrive Capital, which had been set to be the lead investor in Infantino’s plan. Uefa’s filing also requests information from other related parties, including JP Morgan.Fifa submitted a request to intervene in one of those four filings, which came in the state of Florida. A judge granted the request late last week.Filing on behalf of Fifa, attorney H Christopher Boehning argues that the request for discovery should be delayed or denied in part becauseUefadoes not have any active legal proceedings against Fifa in Switzerland. The filing also argues that discovery would in effect “use the legal process and public US filings to expose information that [Fifa] is obligated to keep confidential under [its] governing rules.”The document also retells the history of the FFE plan, and suggests that Uefa’s threatened boycott of Fifa competitions after the FFE proposal was economically motivated.“If soccer is strengthened in the developing world, global competition increases, which ultimately reduces Uefa’s market power and provides more competition for its flagship tournaments,” the document reads. “By raising funds to allow some of Fifa’s smaller member associations to better develop soccer, FFE would lead to more players from those nations choosing to represent their countries of origin and playing in their home leagues rather than playing abroad.”The filing quotes Cameroon federation president Samuel Eto’o to support this assertion, but refers to him only as “one of the greatest African players in history.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice weeklySign up toSoccer DeskJonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe filing also asserts that Uefa does not have the authority to initiate any criminal proceeding in Switzerland, as it is contractually bound by Fifa statutes to resolve any disputes with Fifa itself via arbitration.Explore more on these topicsFifaFootball politicsGianni InfantinoUefanewsShareReuse this content

title: Bill Simmons’s embrace of ChatGPT is a breach of his website’s creative spirit | US sports media | The Guardian
description: The founder of The Ringer and Grantland was famous for discovering and developing writers. Now he is promoting a technology eroding the creative industries
Author: Owen Lewis
Headline: The founder of The Ringer and Grantland was famous for discovering and developing writers. Now he is promoting a technology eroding the creative industries
Content: Bill Simmons has been a dominant figure in US sports media for more than a decade.Photograph: Rebecca Sapp/Getty Images for The Recording AcademyView image in fullscreenBill Simmons has been a dominant figure in US sports media for more than a decade.Photograph: Rebecca Sapp/Getty Images for The Recording AcademyUS sports mediaBill Simmons’s embrace of ChatGPT is a breach of his website’s creative spiritThe founder of The Ringer and Grantland was famous for discovering and developing writers. Now he is promoting a technology eroding the creative industriesOwen LewisThu 3 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 06.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBill Simmons may have stopped writing with any regularity in the mid-2010s – he claims his fingers don’t work – but that won’t stop him from reminding you of his greatest hits. On a recent podcast aboutRussell Westbrook’s retirement, he couldn’t stop quoting his old columns. He first referenced an article from the 2012 NBA finals, and wasn’t finished until 11 minutes into the podcast. His guest, The Ringer contributor Kirk Goldsberry, deserved an award for patience. But the biggest blight on the episode came later, in the form of a bizarre ad read.“This episode,” Simmons announced, “is brought to you byChatGPT,the Bill Simmons PodcastAI sponsor.” (Emphasis mine; his overenthusiastic delivery mandates the italics.) Simmons said that he had asked ChatGPT what Westbrook’s defining game was. “That was a pretty good answer,” he said of ChatGPT’s offerings, as if it were a precocious, loveable nephew, before encouraging his listeners to try the platform.As ESPN cuts familiar faces, its retreat from serious NBA coverage is completeRead moreThe segment was instructive, not for its content but for Simmons’s ignorance of how he would be perceived. As large language models such as ChatGPT have become ubiquitous, they’veslashed website traffic across the internet, accelerating the decay of already imperiled media and creative industries. As the founder of The Ringer, a website and podcast network, Simmons should want to protect his company from those effects. It’s a strange look for someone who has historically sought out and promoted unique writing to suddenly trumpet the virtues of an LLM, and naturally raises questions. Is Simmons clueless about how the move is a betrayal of the industry – or does he not care?Unfortunately, Simmons is far from unique here. Countless podcasts promote AI, from the Joe Rogan Experience toThis American Life. Wondery’s The Lead: Starting Five evendebuted an AI host in 2023.What makes Simmons’s embrace of it particularly frustrating is that he used to champion human creativity.In 2011, Simmons founded Grantland under the ESPN umbrella.It rapidly became a dream platform for young writers.Simmons and his editors sought out writers across a variety of beats and writing styles, and encouraged them to do the most ambitious work possible, all funded by ESPN’s deep pockets. The results were oftenstartlingfortheirscope,style, and ambition. Providing the platform for such pieces is a significant part of Simmons’s legacy, and established him as an expert scout of talent on top of being a popular writer. At its best, Grantland was a place that held creativity as sacred, granting writers the trust to follow their storiesto the ends of the Earth, or to many thousands of words. Grantland had a spirit opposite to the voicelessness of ChatGPT. It was the exact spirit that LLMs are helping erode from the internet.Simmons’s own writing – and podcasting – always tended towards the irreverent, from deep dives into basketball history to bizarre pornography references. But even those who didn’t like his work had to concede he had a defined and influential voice. So it makes sense thatr/billsimmons, the alarmingly parasocial Reddit community of Simmons fans, reacted so negatively to his first ChatGPT-sponsored episode that the website Awful Announcingran a story about it.It’s not just his partnership with ChatGPT that signals Simmons’s move away from a promoter of excellent writing, though. The Spotify-owned Ringer has heavy focus on podcasts. The Ringer puts out an article or three per day – a strikingly low output that undersells thewealth of writing talentthat remains on staff. (Twenty-five people on its masthead are labeled as “staff writer”.) The Ringer’s biggest names are best known as podcast hosts and personalities rather than editors and bosses. (Mallory Rubin, director of content at The Ringer but more famous as a podcaster, recently threw out the first pitch at a Baltimore Orioles game.)And while there are still excellent writers at The Ringer, they don’t always stick around. Claire McNear (whosestoryabout former would-be Jeopardy! host Mike Richards ensured he didn’t get the job) and Miles Surrey (whowrotemore prolifically than anybody else on staff) were laid off recently. Then there’s the content itself. While Grantland had dedicated coverage for sports from baseball to boxing, the lone leagues The Ringer covers consistently via the written word are the NBA and the NFL.There are concerns, too, about Simmons as a boss. Before the sale to Spotify,employees say they were largely kept in the darkabout the deal; there have been allegations hetook steps to marginalize The Ringer’s unionandnumerous complaintsoflow payat a publication with plenty of revenue. That’s before we get to his recentadmissionsthat he doesn’t wear a seatbelt or the fact that heis under scrutiny for proxy betting.Media is a constantly mutating industry, necessitating constant evolution to stave off death. Still, if any place is capable of resisting trends to focus entirely on quality, it should be The Ringer.Spotify– a humongously popular and wealthy music streaming service – bought it for about $200m. (Simmons tweeted at the time: “More details to come down the road... but @ringer will remain @ringer in every respect. They appreciate what we do and they want us to be us.”) With Spotify commanding as much money as it does, the slow abandonment of writing is hard to justify.Meanwhile, Simmons’spromotion of AI suggests that he’s no longer concerned with quality in the way his reputation would have you believe. On aMarch episode of The Rewatchables, when Simmons announced, “Roger Ebert sadly passed away in 2013,” his co-hosts knew what was coming. Simmons quoted ChatGPT’s take on how Ebert would have reviewed The Nice Guys. Co-hosts Chris Ryan and Rob Mahoney expressed disapproval, but it’s always hard to tell how much of podcast material is banter, particularly when you’re sitting alongside your boss. So let’s turn instead to a recent episode of Talk Easy, in which two senior Ringer staffers, Sean Fennessey and Amanda Dobbins,were asked about Simmons’s use of AIby host Sam Fragoso.Fennessey and Dobbins immediately stressed that it had been Simmons trying to mimic Ebert through ChatGPT, not them. “I wouldn’t do that,” Fennessey said, adding that he and Ryan had told Simmons about their distaste for the segment. Dobbins claimed not to know that ChatGPT had been sponsoring Simmons’s podcast, and said she’d never used AI before. If lower-level Ringer employees share Fennessey’s and Dobbins’s feelings on the ChatGPT ad reads, they almost certainly do not feel comfortable expressing that disapproval, or the same proximity to Simmons.You can trace Simmons’s history as a scribe right through that Westbrook podcast: once a writer himself and still evidently proud enough of his body of work to relentlessly quote decade-old material, now willing to advertisea platform accelerating the demise of the profession.Simmons got to spend his entire writing career in an industry mostly free of existential threats. Now it seems like he doesn’t much care if anybody else gets that luxury again, including his own employees.The tragedy here is not of a once-energetic writer lapsing into lazy podcasting. It’s that employees at a well-funded outlet like The Ringer, which is run by someone with a history of rewarding ambitious writing, have to worry about layoffs and the fact that Simmons is promoting a technology eroding their profession.As with so many media stories, it did not have to be this way. When Grantland launched in June 2011, Simmons wrote anintroductory piece, briefly describing what the website would look like, while reminiscing on his days as a writer on Jimmy Kimmel’s show. Two lines stand out. The first: “I was born to write columns.” That didn’t age so well. The other: “Writing is a fundamentally lonely thing. It’s just you and a blank Microsoft Word document. The process can drive people crazy. (And has.)”That line aged beautifully. Simmons’s career as a writer and boss has not.Explore more on these topicsUS sports mediaUS sportsSpotifyInternetAI (artificial intelligence)featuresShareReuse this content

title: Lewis Hamilton ready to rock Monza with ‘phenomenal’ Italian GP win for Ferrari | Lewis Hamilton | The Guardian
description: Lewis Hamilton said a win for Ferrari at the team’s home race in the Italian Grand Prix would be ‘phenomenal’
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: Lewis Hamilton said a win for Ferrari at the team’s home race in the Italian Grand Prix would be ‘phenomenal’
Content: Lewis Hamilton in the paddock at Monza with his Ferrari F40.Photograph: Kym Illman/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLewis Hamilton in the paddock at Monza with his Ferrari F40.Photograph: Kym Illman/Getty ImagesLewis HamiltonLewis Hamilton ready to rock Monza with ‘phenomenal’ Italian GP win for FerrariScuderia bring upgraded engine to their home raceWinning at Monza would be ‘new territory’Giles Richardsin MonzaThu 3 Sep 2026 13.05 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 16.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLewis Hamilton believes that a win for Ferrari at the team’s home race in the Italian Grand Prix would be a phenomenal moment in an already storied career for the seven-time champion.The British driver, who would make history if he takes the flag at Monza, endured a torrid time with the Scuderia last season but goes into the race this weekend with a win under his belt and a very competitive car that may prove to be even quicker on the high-speed blast around the famous track.Lando Norris launches LN4 Fusion team to develop young drivers in F1 and motorsportRead moreFerrari are bringing their second engine upgrade this weekend in expectation of narrowing the gap to title leaders Mercedes. Hamilton trails the championship leader, Kimi Antonelli, by 59 points, alongside Mercedes’ George Russell.If Hamilton wins the Italian GP he will pass Michael Schumacher’s record of five wins at Monza, all of which the German scored with Ferrari. The team are honouring him this weekend with a special livery to mark 30 years since Schumacher joined.Hamilton was more than aware of quite what a Ferrari home win in front of thetifosiwould mean. “I’ve really thought coming into this weekend, I pondered just thinking of the sheer magnitude of the concept that I’m coming to this grand prix,” he said.“Firstly, I didn’t know that I was equal with Michael for wins at Monza and then there’s the thought of a first ahead of me in the sense of potentially winning at Monza for Ferrari and going into new territory. That would be phenomenal.“If I did do that, I will be the only black driver to have ever done that for Ferrari in Italy, and possibly in history, too. So, a lot of those thoughts have been going through my mind.”Hamilton, always aware of the import of history and in making an impact, did so in no little style when he arrived at the track on Thursday. The 41-year-old pulled up at the paddock in his new Ferrari F40, suited and booted to make a photocall to echo the one he made on his first appearance for Ferrari at Maranello in January last year, where he also posed in front of one of Ferrari’s F40s.He has long coveted an F40 and finally succumbed to purchase what he called the car of his dreams earlier this year, which it transpired was a very special one he felt had been destined for him.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |FortnightlySign up toThe HotspotA new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisisEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I wanted to find the most authentic one and managed to come across this one that the owner had bought, drove it from Maranello to his home, 69km away, and then parked it and never started it again,” he said. “The passenger door had never been opened, it just had this cover on it and all this dust.“When they were taking the car apart to check it they took the engine out, they found out the engine’s number 44. It’s got stamped on the engine number 44 [Hamilton’s car number]. I couldn’t believe it. So, it feels very much like fate.“I thought it was a real opportunity to kind of highlight the history of Ferrari in their home country, at their race and when am I ever going to get to do that again?”Explore more on these topicsLewis HamiltonFormula One 2026Formula OneMotor sportFerrarinewsShareReuse this content

title: Thierry Henry says players ‘have more power than they think’ amid Fifa scandals | Thierry Henry | The Guardian
description: The former Arsenal, Barcelona and France star says players shouldn’t underestimate their ability to change how football works
Author: Jeff Rueter
Headline: The former Arsenal, Barcelona and France star says players shouldn’t underestimate their ability to change how football works
Content: Thierry Henry (left) and Kate Scott both have commented on Fifa’s recent scandals.Photograph: dpa Picture-Alliance Archive/AlamyView image in fullscreenThierry Henry (left) and Kate Scott both have commented on Fifa’s recent scandals.Photograph: dpa Picture-Alliance Archive/AlamyThierry HenryThierry Henry says players ‘have more power than they think’ amid Fifa scandalsThe former Arsenal, Barcelona and France star says players shouldn’t underestimate their ability to change how football worksJeff RueterThu 3 Sep 2026 15.10 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 15.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs Fifa continues to face scrutiny from some confederations and fans,Thierry Henryhas encouraged players to use their voice as the political battle for control of international soccer unfolds. The former Arsenal and Barcelona forward turned pundit spoke with the Guardian on Tuesday alongside Kate Scott and Jamie Carragher as CBS and Paramount prepare for this season’s Champions League broadcasts.“For me, the players have more power than they think they have,” Henry said when asked for his thoughts on the situation. “And if they want it to change, they can make it happen – especially nowadays.”Fifa has been under public duress in the wake of multiple scandals surrounding the 2026 World Cup, exacerbated further after reports of Gianni Infantino’s effort to sell the World Cup’s commercial rights. The ensuing month has seen the Fifa president face significant criticism, withUefa exploring potential legal optionsagainst Infantino.Scott, who anchors the CBS panel comprising Henry, Carragher and Micah Richards, spoke extensively about 2021’s attempted Super League project and the ensuing debacle in an Apple TV documentary. The Super League saga seemed to pit the business interests of the sport’s business class against the game’s heart, represented by players, coaches and fans. The latest situation involvingFifahas progressed in a similar spirit.“I think it’s going to be really interesting to see [what comes next],” Scott said. “I think probably a large portion of world football has come to a point where they would like to see a change in [the Fifa presidency], similarly to the way we felt about [the Super League] … I think if you’re invested in the game and you love the game, it just kind of leaves a bad taste.”Infantino has been re-elected twice since 2016, both times without a challenger. The next vote is slated for 18 March 2027, with no alternative having declared their candidacy.“I have no idea which way that will go, because obviously one thing that Gianni Infantino has proven to be within world football is a very smart power broker and has understood how to make allies, use those allies to his benefit,” Scott said.For Henry, though, the voice of the players can – and should – be a bigger part of the conversation.“Players have all the power if they want to, and sometimes they don’t, I think, use it or realize actually the power that they have,” Henry said. “You guys in the US know fully well: when the player wants to do something, the league listens. You saw it with the NBA. You saw it with the NFL … At one point, the players are always on the side: go entertain, take your money, leave.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice weeklySign up toSoccer DeskJonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Us debating about it here, what’s going to change? We can all have a view whether it’s a good one or a bad one … But for me, the players have more power than they think they have. And if they want it to change, they can make it happen – especially nowadays.”This is an extract from Soccer Desk, a newsletter from the Guardian US.Subscribe for free here.Explore more on these topicsThierry HenryFifaFootball politicsUS sportsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: 606 miles in six days: teacher Megan Eckert chases ultrarunning history – and a men’s record | Sport | The Guardian
description: At this week’s world championship, the women’s record holder who once feared a 5K will try to top her own 144-hour distance – and beat the US men’s mark
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: At this week’s world championship, the women’s record holder who once feared a 5K will try to top her own 144-hour distance – and beat the US men’s mark
Content: Megan Eckert set the women’s world record in the six-day ultradistance event last May, running 603.156 miles in France.Photograph: Sam Lhermillier/Mount to CoastView image in fullscreenMegan Eckert set the women’s world record in the six-day ultradistance event last May, running 603.156 miles in France.Photograph: Sam Lhermillier/Mount to CoastSport606 miles in six days: teacher Megan Eckert chases ultrarunning history – and a men’s recordAt this week’s world championship, the women’s record holder who once feared a 5K will try to top her own 144-hour distance – and beat the US men’s markEmily HalnonThu 3 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 13.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhile many teachers head back to school this week, middle-school math teacher Megan Eckert will be 5,000 miles from her classroom in Santa Fe, New Mexico. She has a good reason to miss a few classes: she’ll be competing at the Global Organization of Multi-Day Ultramarathoners World Championship.On Thursday, more than 100 runners will gather on a start line in Balatonfüred, Hungary, and attempt to run as many miles as they can in six days.Eckert, who turned 40 last month, has one of the most audacious goals in the field. She wants to beat the women’s world record – and take down the US men’s record, as well.‘A cheeseburger worked really well’: the secrets behind a record-breaking 152-hour runRead moreEckert will be racing against herself for the women’s mark. Last May, she ran 603.156 miles (970.685km) at the world championships in Vallon-Pont-d’Arc, France, setting the world record (pending final ratification). She bested Camille Herron’s mark by more than 40 miles and became the first woman in history to run 600 miles in six days. That’s the equivalent of running nearly four marathons a day for six straight days.That performance earned her recognition as one of the top athletes in the sport last year. She was voted third inUltrarunningMagazine’s rankings for Worldwide Ultrarunner of the Year.Now, Eckert wants to one-up herself – and almost every man, too. But as she goes through her final preparations for the race, she has some doubts about whether she can actually do it. That’s exactly how she likes to race, and is how she’s built such an impressive running resume – which includes national teams, world records and podiums at Badwater 135, Cocodona 250, and Vermont 100, three notorious ultradistance races.Eckert likes to think about odds when she sets goals for herself. It’s fitting for someone who spends most weekdays teaching algebra and calculus, when she’s not using her vacation days to chase world records.“I like to choose goals where I have a 50% chance of success and a 50% chance of failure,” she says. “It’s amazing what can happen when you go after goals that scare you – and that just might not be possible.”She appreciates that when she takes a big swing, she gets more out of herself in training, racing, and life, even if she doesn’t nail every big goal.That wasn’t always Eckert’s strategy. She was once so afraid of failure that it almost stopped her from running at all.Eckert trained for months to run her first 5K in 2008. But on the morning of the run, she didn’t leave her house.“I was too afraid of failing,” she said. “I let my doubts win.”So she hung up her running shoes and walked away from the sport. It took years, and meeting her husband, Joe Eckert, before she decided to give running another try.View image in fullscreenMegan Eckert holds a shoe after her record-setting 603.156-mile run last May.Photograph: Sam Lhermillier/Mount to CoastWhen they started dating in 2016, Joe convinced her to run a half marathon with him. This time, she made it to the start line. And when she reached the point on the course where marathoners continued on while the half-marathoners turned towards the finish, she remembers thinking: “It would be fun to keep going.”“It would be fun to keep going” has become a theme of Eckert’s running career.Eckert, who is now sponsored by brands including shoe company Mount to Coast and apparel company Janji, has won races of most every distance, but she’s best known for the supersized runs.This will be her third six-day event. In 2024, she set the then-women’s world record for backyard ultra events, a last-man-standing format where runners finish a 4.16-mile (6.69km) loop every hour for as many hours as possible. Eckert lasted 88 hours and racked up 362 miles (582.583km) atBig Dog’s Backyard Ultra.Once Eckert gave running a second chance, she was hooked. She appreciated that it offered her an outlet to test her limits. And she realized the only way to actually find out what she could do was to try things that seem impossible.“There’s something about pushing your personal limits, seeing what you’re made of, and coming out the other side that keeps drawing me back,” she said. “I want to feel how I can do more than I think I can – again and again.”She didn’t start her running career with record-breaking runs. She finished that first half marathon in 1hr 57 min – for context, about 55 minutes shy of the current world record.But it wasn’t long before she realized she could be pretty good. She entered her first 100-mile run because she’d read a book about someone running 100 miles in one go and wanted to see if she could do it, too. She ended up winning the race – outright – beating all of the other women and the men, too.She tried every challenge she could get her feet on: 100-mile runs in 100-degree weather, mountain races through sole-sucking mud, and her first multiday events, where she covered more than 200 miles at a time.“I started dabbling in lots of different distances, different places, and different terrains and found that, regardless of where I went or how I performed, I loved it,” she said.The first time Eckert heard about six-day events, she thought they sounded a little too nutty, even for someone who loved a challenge.She signed up for email updates about an event in Wisconsin without any real intention of competing. When she got a notice that the price was about to increase, she turned to her husband and said: “Should we go try this stupid six-day thing? No one has ever hit 600 miles.”And then, the question that has shaped her running career: “Why not give it a shot?”View image in fullscreenThis week’s world championship will be Megan Eckert’s third six-day run.Photograph: Sam Lhermillier/Mount to CoastWhile ultradistance events carry runners past sweeping vistas or through miles of breathtaking mountains, six-day events generally involve a short, fixed-distance loop. As the clock runs for 144 hours, runners make quick stops to nap, eat and troubleshoot any issues that pop up, such as blisters, chafing or stomach problems. Last year, Eckert slept an hour or two every 12 hours and ate lots of rice cakes, pasta, eggs, gummy bears and barbecue potato chips.Eckert’s first six-day event was on an 0.275-mile (443m) indoor track. The course in Hungary is a 0.558-mile (898m) loop of a paved road. If Eckert hits her goal and beats the USmen’s record of 606.243 miles (975.654km), she’ll run the same loop at least 1,086 times.But Eckert, who says prioritizing joy is as integral to her success as taking big swings, thinks the six-day event may be her happiest place. She’s genuinely excited to run for six straight days – and for every high and low along the way.“I didn’t even know six-day runs existed until a few years ago, but I fell in love with them the minute I found them,” she said. “When I’m training for a big goal like the American men’s record, I don’t dwell on fear because I get so excited about how the goal is pushing me to train harder – and how I get to go and run with a community who’s turning the same 144-hour race into our own little world.”She set the world record last year with the help of short naps, turkey and pickle sandwiches, and breaking her big goal into smaller chunks. And leaving the math to her crew.“It’s such a long time to have to think about your pace, I trust them to tell me when I need to push,” she says. “I’m really good at being mindful and just staying in the moment on the course.”Sweat, tears and camaraderie as 20,000 runners take on world’s largest ultramarathonRead moreEckert even has a fish tattoo on her foot that was inspired by a splotch on the floor from her first six-day event. She’d look at it every lap and think about how it looked like a fish that was swimming along with her.When she goes after the record this week, she’s counting on her mind to do as much work as her body.“Sure, I go into races and have doubts, but it’s not the limiting factor or the loudest voice any more,” she said. “Failure isn’t the worst case scenario, it’s not having the experience of whatever thing I’m chasing.”She now knows the surest way to combat her doubts is to do exactly what she didn’t do back in 2008: “When you take your first step, they all dissipate and you can just be in the moment.”She just has to take that first step.Explore more on these topicsSportUltrarunningRunningUS sportsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Gabriel Martinelli leaves Arsenal for Saudi Arabian club Al-Hilal in £60m deal | Arsenal | The Guardian
description: Arsenal have confirmed Gabriel Martinelli has joined the Saudi Arabian side Al-Hilal for £60m
Author: Ed Aarons
Headline: Arsenal have confirmed Gabriel Martinelli has joined the Saudi Arabian side Al-Hilal for £60m
Content: Gabriel Martinelli’s sale to Al-Hilal is a record for Arsenal, surpassing the £40m they got in 2017 for Alex Oxlade-Chamberlain.Photograph: Al-HilalView image in fullscreenGabriel Martinelli’s sale to Al-Hilal is a record for Arsenal, surpassing the £40m they got in 2017 for Alex Oxlade-Chamberlain.Photograph: Al-HilalArsenalGabriel Martinelli leaves Arsenal for Saudi Arabian club Al-Hilal in £60m dealForward follows Gabriel Jesus out of championsRicharlison not in Tottenham’s Premier League squadEd AaronsandDavid HytnerThu 3 Sep 2026 13.26 EDTFirst published on Thu 3 Sep 2026 12.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleArsenal have confirmed Gabriel Martinelli has joined the Saudi Arabian sideAl-Hilalfor £60m. It is understood the deal for Brazil forward includes a sell-on clause.Martinelli, who joinedArsenalfrom Ituano in 2019, has fallen down the pecking order at the Emirates despite being part of the squad that won the Premier League title last season. His fee surpasses the previous record £40m received by Arsenal when they sold Alex Oxlade-Chamberlain to Liverpool in 2017.Quick GuideHow do I sign up for sport breaking news alerts?ShowIn the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from theiOS App Storeon iPhone or theGoogle Play storeon Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Martinelli is believed to have signed a four-year contract worth about £17m a season. His move was widely expected after Arsenal agreed a deal last week and has gone through before the transfer window in Saudi Arabia closes on Sunday.The 25-year-old joins his Brazil teammate Gabriel Jesus in leaving Arsenal this week, the striker having moved to Barcelona for £8.6m. The Premier League champions also sold Fábio Vieira to Hamburg on deadline day but decided against bringing in players.Arsenal are believed to have received about £3m from Brook Norton-Cuffy’s £14m move from Genoa to Hull owing to a sell-on clause in the England Under-21 defender’s contract but missed out on about £7m when Folarin Balogun move to Evertoncollapsed.Tottenham have omitted Richarlison from their Premier League squad, with the striker not a part of their plans for the season. They could have accommodated him for the first-half of the campaign because one of their 17 senior non-homegrown players – Xavi Simons – is out until March or April, according to the manager, Roberto Di Zerbi, with an anterior cruciate ligament injury.Spurs made clear to Richarlison before the closure of the transfer window in England on Tuesday night that he would not be included so he could arrange a move. He was unable to do so, with one to his former club, Everton, not happening. He is the subject offirm interest from Trabzonsporin Turkey, where the window remains open until Friday night.Richarlison posted a message on social media on Monday in which he said he would not allow anybody to decide his future for him. He talked about his commitment to Spurs; how “when everything here was falling apart and they needed me, I stayed and gave my life”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRicharlison was Spurs’ top scorer in the league last season with 11 goals. He also said: “So I hope they treat my situation with the same respect that I’ve always had for the Spurs and for all the people who worked with me during this period. Just don’t try to decide for me.”Explore more on these topicsArsenalAl-HilalSaudi Pro LeagueTransfer windowSaudi Arabia and sportTottenham HotspurnewsShareReuse this content

title: Premier League: 10 things to look out for this weekend | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Florian Wirtz has a chance to shine, there’s a Red Bull reunion at St James’ Park and Chelsea face a litmus test at Arsenal
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: Florian Wirtz has a chance to shine, there’s a Red Bull reunion at St James’ Park and Chelsea face a litmus test at Arsenal
Content: Bournemouth’s Alex Scott, Manchester City’s Nico O’Reilly and Liverpool’s Florian Wirtz.Composite: Getty, ShutterstockView image in fullscreenBournemouth’s Alex Scott, Manchester City’s Nico O’Reilly and Liverpool’s Florian Wirtz.Composite: Getty, ShutterstockTen things to look out for this weekendPremier LeaguePremier League: 10 things to look out for this weekendFlorian Wirtz has a chance to shine, there’s a Red Bull reunion on Tyneside and Chelsea face litmus test at ArsenalGuardian sportThu 3 Sep 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 19.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCan Wirtz find his best for Liverpool?Florian Wirtz is easing himself into his second season at Liverpool after a forgettable first. There were signs of promiseagainst Nottingham Forest, where he set up the second equaliser and would have had a goal of his own if not for an offside in the buildup. It is clear the German needs to become more influential as a No 10 given the quality of players he has around him, especially afterthe expensive arrival of Bradley Barcolathis week. Bruno Fernandes showed there is plenty of fun for an attacking midfielder to have against Ipswich and Wirtz can follow suit as a protagonist. Liverpool have drawn both their opening fixtures 2-2 and need something to kickstart their campaign, with a Friday night visit to promoted opposition a fine place to start. Wirtz should cause problems but, if he does not, the internal competition will be after his spot.Will UnwinIpswich vLiverpool(Friday 8pm, all times BST)Red Bull gives you wingsVerticality, intensity and hard pressing are likely to be the order of the day at St James’ Park, where two German graduates of the Red Bull stable meet on Saturday at lunchtime. Newcastle’s new manager, Matthias Jaissle, is a former head coach of Red Bull Salzburg, while Bournemouth’s Marco Rose has managed Salzburg and, more recently, RB Leipzig. “We have the same idea of how we want to play football,” said Jaissle – and Rose knows what to expect from Eddie Howe’s successor. “Matthias and me were several years in the style of Red Bull,” he said. “Everyone knows how we work. You can see it clearly. He’s a good coach. He’s brought his ideas really quickly into the Newcastle team. They are playing quite intense, they have clear pressing patterns that are different from before.”Louise TaylorNewcastle v Bournemouth (Saturday 12.30pm)View image in fullscreenMatthias Jaissle is looking for his first back-to-back league wins with Newcastle.Photograph: MI News/NurPhoto/ShutterstockBees plot left-wing raid on Black CatsSaturday’s meeting between two of the Premier League’s best-run clubs, Brentford and Sunderland, promises to one of the best contests of the weekend, with both sides physical, technical and superbly coached. Brentford, in particular, have made a terrific start to the season, the left side of their team looking especially dangerous. Keane Lewis-Potter provides impetus from full-back, with Mamadou Sangaré backing up strong ball-winning and carrying with intelligent passing, while Kevin Schade offers a threat in behind and, increasingly, in front of goal. All of which suggests a difficult afternoon for Thomas Meunier, Sunderland’s likely right-back who, at 34, has plenty of experience but might struggle with the athletic questions asked of him. He will, though, be able to rely on assistance from Noah Sadiki, whose nous, work ethic and running power will be invaluable in defending Sunderland’s right flank. How that battle plays out will go a long way towards deciding the game.Daniel HarrisBrentford vSunderland(Saturday 3pm)Chema looks another astute Brighton buyWe can be sure any player Brighton buy has delivered the data metrics employed by the owner, Tony Bloom. But Chema Andrés, the 21-year-old midfielder just signed from Stuttgart, also nails the eye test. Signed for £18.9m, it’s already tempting to speculate how sizeable the mark-up will be when Brighton sell him on. If we remember we’re talking about a sport, it’s impossible not to be excited about what the former Real Madrid academy midfielder brings to Fabian Hürzeler’s team. A No 6 of the old school, Chema offers economical movement but extravagant intelligence, evident in his passing and anticipation. Even if this weekend’s game against Leeds comes too early for him to be handed a start, he will make an impact soon enough.DHBrighton v Leeds (Saturday 3pm)An early basement battle at the CottageIt’s been a tricky summer for Crystal Palace despite their Conference League win. Oliver Glasner has gone, with two key defenders in Daniel Muñoz and Maxence Lacroix also departing and Jean-Philippe Mateta and Ismaïla Sarr trying their best to join them. This upheaval has left Pierre Sage, whose existing relationship with Malick Fofanawasn’t enough to secure the Lyon winger’s signature, with major problems. The former Lens coach is seeking to replace the club’s most successful manager while learning what works in a new league, with new players and without three mainstays. It wasn’t especially surprising to see Palace lose their first two matches, while Fulham have also been beaten twice while seeking to bed in a new coach and arrivals. More troubling for both teams is that the promoted sides look competitive. Hull and Ipswich have performed well and won games, while Coventry are better than they’ve shown so far. Though it’s far too early to talk about relegation, this already feels like a game of significance for two sides struggling for momentum.DHFulham vCrystal Palace(Saturday 3pm)Graphic showing Fulham and Crystal Palace second and fourth respectively among the favourites for relegation, according to Opta dataO’Reilly to step into Rodri role for City?Manchester City spent more than £300m on new midfielders in this transfer window, but look light in the No 6 role, with Rodri and Nico González both departing. Ayyoub Bouaddi, bought as Rodri’s long-term successor, is only 18, so Enzo Maresca’s plan is to ease him into first-team action. TheManchester Citymanager deployed Marc Guéhi in a holding midfield role against Bournemouth, and is also confident Nico O’Reilly can switch from left-back to operate there. O’Reilly may line up at the base of midfield for Coventry’s visit, with City seeking a third straight win. Maresca is also not fazed by Omar Marmoush’s departure on an initial loan to Spurs, with Iliman Ndiaye arriving on deadline day and Antoine Semenyo also an able deputy centre-forward if Erling Haaland is unavailable.Jamie JacksonManchester City v Coventry (Saturday 3pm)Delap to be thrown in against shaky SpursLiam Delap came off the bench against Liverpool and helped create Nottingham Forest’s second goal with quick thinking from a throw-in. The striker cost £45m from Chelsea but missed out on an intense pre-season after Xabi Alonso decided he was surplus to requirements, so needs to build fitness. Considering Tottenham’s major flaws thus far, it would make sense for Delap to be given the chance to spearhead the Forest attack. The former England Under-21 international is the ideal No 9, quick, strong and a capable finisher, but needs to get all these attributes sharpened up. An outing against a fragile opponent could speed up the process. Tottenham are bottom of the league having conceded five and scored none in two games, and compared to Chris Wood or Igor Jesus, Delap is a far scarier foe, as Oliver Glasner will know.WUNottingham Forest v Tottenham (Saturday 3pm)Six points, seven signings for happy HullThey may have nabbed two wins in as many games upon their return to the Premier League but Hull were still not happy with their squad, seven new players arriving in the final week of the window. That means the Tigers have made 19 signings since promotion, which is an impressive turnover in personnel. Sergej Jakirovic needs to decide whether to incorporate these potential upgrades into his starting XI as soon as possible or make them earn the shirts from those who have accumulated six points. No one has let down the head coach or the fans over 180 minutes, so it would be harsh to drop anyone but, equally, having spent so much money on acquisitions, it could be argued that the sooner they get on the pitch, the quicker they will gel. It is not an easy decision for Jakirovic to make but he values loyalty and will want to challenge the mentality of the new arrivals – no one will walk into the side he has built.WUHullvAston Villa(Saturday 5.30pm)View image in fullscreenElliot Stroud, one of Hull’s 19 summer signings, in action during their 1-0 win at Coventry.Photograph: Neal Simpson/Getty Images/AllstarEverton fans react to dismal deadline dayThere are parallels between Manchester United’s visit to Hill Dickinson Stadium and their 3-0 win at Goodison Park in 2023 in the sense they will face a furious Everton crowd, and for the second time in four seasons the anger will not be directed towards them. Three years ago it was the Premier League in Evertonians’ sights following the record 10-point deduction that had just been imposed on the club. This time it is Everton’s owners, the Friedkin Group, in the firing line following the club’s shambolic end to the transfer window.There will be no flag displays inside the stadium after the group responsible for organising them, the 1878s, withdrew their support and there are calls for a “not a pound in the ground” campaign in response to the owners making a profit on transfers while leaving David Moyes with a weaker squad. Everton have started the season positively on the pitch, but are now surrounded by problems of their owners’ making.Andy HunterEverton v Manchester United (Sunday 2pm)Chelsea face litmus test in London derbyYou have to go back to the start of the 2021-22 season, when Arsenal had Rob Holding and Pablo Marí in central defence, for the last time thatChelseabeat their north London rivals, a run of 11 matches in all competitions. But having come close to ending that sequence in the 1-1 draw at Stamford Bridge last season before things began to unravel for Enzo Maresca, the Italian’s successor, Xabi Alonso, will head to the Emirates to face his old friend Mikel Arteta in a competitive match for the first time as a manager full of confidence after winning his opening two games. Chelsea’s new-look front three of Cole Palmer, João Pedro and Morgan Rogers can certainly cause Arsenal problems, although the question is whether a defence that has already conceded five goals can keep out the champions at the other end.Ed AaronsArsenal v Chelsea (Sunday 4.30pm)PosTeamPGDPts1Man City2462Arsenal2463Hull2364Chelsea2265Brentford2346Newcastle2247Everton2248Leeds2149Brighton23310Man Utd21311Sunderland20312Ipswich2-2313Liverpool20214AFC Bournemouth2-1115Nottm Forest2-1116Fulham2-2017Coventry2-4018Crystal Palace2-5019Aston Villa2-5020Tottenham Hotspur2-50Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueTen things to look out for this weekendIpswich TownLiverpoolNewcastle UnitedBournemouthBrentfordSunderlandfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Women’s Super League 2026-27 preview No 14: West Ham | West Ham United Women | The Guardian
description: Rita Guarino has been backed in the transfer market after turning around the club’s fortunes last season but concerns remain over a lack of resources
Author: Suzanne Wrack
Headline: Rita Guarino has been backed in the transfer market after turning around the club’s fortunes last season but concerns remain over a lack of resources
Content: West Ham’s Katie Zelem enters the pitch surrounded by bubbles before the WSL match against Manchester City. Photograph: Naomi Baker/WSL/Getty ImagesRita Guarino has been backed in the transfer market after turning around the club’s fortunes last season but concerns remain over a lack of resourcesBySuzanne WrackThu 3 Sep 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 19.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGuardian writers’ predicted position:11th (NB: this is not necessarily Suzanne Wrack’s prediction but the average of our writers’ tips)Last season’s position:10thProspectsWest Ham were in big trouble last December, with half the season gone and one win in 11 games. Rehanne Skinner was dismissed and the former Italy forward Rita Guarino came in to steady the ship. There were questions over how much any manager would be able to do without the club giving a bit more support to the women’s setup, but Skinner, fairly or not, had lost the dressing room and heads were down. The impact of Guarino wasn’t instant, a 5-0 defeat by Chelsea was a cruel introduction. It took a little time to rebuild the confidence of the team and get them playing the way she believed they could, but back-to-back wins against Newcastle in the FA Cup and Leicester in the Women’s Super League followed the Chelsea game, before a huge 3-2 win against Brighton and battling draws with Manchester United and London City Lionesses contributed to 14 points from their final 11 WSL games, taking their total to 19.As players started to depart in the summer, the situation looked bleak. Among the 14 departures were the forward Shekiera Martinez, who joined Tottenham, Katrina Gorry, who decided to take a break from football, and Shelina Zadorsky, who left at the end of her contract before signing for AFC Toronto. Then the signings started to arrive and suddenly the dark clouds were parting.The Hammers have had a hugely productive and impressive window with 10 signings, including the forwards Kelly Gago, recruited from Everton, and Ebony Salmon, who joined from Aston Villa, the defenders Estelle Cascarino, whose loan was made permanent, and Nadine Riesen and Laia Codina, who joined from Eintracht Frankfurt and Arsenal respectively, and the young English talents Sienna Wareing and Niamh Peacock who signed from Manchester United and Arsenal. Guarino has been backed in this window and West Ham have a real opportunity to make a statement in the WSL.Graphic showing how West Ham finished in the past five seasonsOff-field pictureWest Ham’s relative indifference towards their women’s team has been long known. There has been a steady decline since the departure of the enthusiastic Jack Sullivan as managing director of the women’s team in 2021 – the son of David Sullivan having been handed control of the side at 18. Little is known of how cash strapped the women’s setup is compared with other WSL sides. The club have not published detailed financial figures throughout their time in the WSL, with their most recent Companies House submission saying they are entitled to exemption from audit under section 479A of the Companies Act 2006. According to Football Association figures they were the WSL’s lowest spenders on agents’ fees in the year to February 2026, at £97,000, and one of only two clubs – Manchester United were the other – whose spend was down year on year.The managerGuarino was a relative unknown when she arrived in the WSL, having managed only in Italy. In the second half of the season West Ham didn’t quite experience a new manager bounce, but Guarino was able to guide them to another four wins and a 10th-place finish above Liverpool and Leicester. Guarino has impressed. Codina told the BBC of her transfer talks: “I remember having my first conversation with Rita. It was at the beginning of everything. I had my agent next to me and I was like: ‘Wow.’ The feeling that I got in this meeting is what I want in my future; it is what I want for my next steps.”Star signingGago scored 10 goals in 30 games for Everton but was frustrated there, handing in a written transfer request in January. The 27-year-old has praised West Ham, saying: “The family feel of the club really appealed to me and I’m excited to join that family. I’m going to give everything in order to help the team reach our ambitions and I’m really looking forward to getting started.”Stat attackWest Ham were the most direct team last season. They moved the ball upfield quicker than anyone and only Leicester averaged fewer passes per possession sequence. There is no right way to play; everyone needs a style. But after West Ham collected fewer points than in three of the preceding four campaigns, is it time for a change of approach?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGraphic showing West Ham were the most direct team in 2025-26Set for a breakthroughInès Belloumou played 18 times for West Ham last season after a long wait following her recruitment from Bayern Munich in July 2024. She was sent out on loan straight away, first to Lazio then to Malmö to build up the points to meet the governing body endorsement criteria for international player visas. This summer the 25-year-old, who was born in France and represented the country up to under-23 level before switching allegiance to Algeria, shone at the Women’s Africa Cup of Nations. Named in the team of the tournament, Belloumou started all six Algeria games as they finished third, with the full-back scoring the winning penalty in the shootout at the end of the third-place playoff. Full of confidence, she is ready to kick on in the WSL.View image in fullscreenFull-back Inès Belloumou crunches into a challenge with Arsenal’s Smilla Holmberg.Photograph: Pedro Porru/MB Media/Getty ImagesWhat they say“I want to put the club in the highest position in the table and go as far as we can in the cups. For me, the WSL is the best league in the world at the moment and anything can happen. Anything is possible. We need to have a lot of consistency, which is not easy, but it’s why we work hard every day” – Viviane Asseyi, after signing a new contractWhere are they playing their home games?If you spend too much time dwelling on this you’ll feel as if you’re in Waiting for Godot. The team have not played at the club’s main stadium since a 2-0 loss to Tottenham in front of close to 25,000 fans in September 2019. There has been talk since of it being a priority, including from Skinner, but every year another season ticks on without the team playing at the club’s main home. Instead, the team continue to call Dagenham and Redbridge’s Victoria Road stadium home.On Friday 4 September at 1pm Suzanne Wrack will be answering readers’ questions about the new WSL season for GuardianConversationsExplore more on these topicsWSL season previews 2026-27West Ham United WomenWomen's Super LeagueWomen's footballfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Mike Dean claims he played secret games for a laugh while refereeing matches | Soccer | The Guardian
description: Mike Dean, the former Premier League referee, said he used to play secret games while officiating matches
Author: Paul MacInnes
Headline: Mike Dean, the former Premier League referee, said he used to play secret games while officiating matches
Content: Mike Dean stood down as a referee in 2022.Photograph: Reuters/AlamyView image in fullscreenMike Dean stood down as a referee in 2022.Photograph: Reuters/AlamySoccerMike Dean claims he played secret games for a laugh while refereeing matchesFormer official says he ‘tried to stay in the centre circle’Referees’ group thought to be puzzled by remarksPaul MacInnesThu 3 Sep 2026 11.22 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 18.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe formerPremier Leaguereferee Mike Dean claims he used to take part in secret challenges while officiating, including trying to stay in the centre circle for as long as possible, as he confessed to “just joking about” during matches. The remarks, made by one of the most well-known officials in the English game, have been met with bemusement by refereeing officials who say there is no evidence of any such behaviour having ever taken place.Dean was a member of the select group of referees for more than two decades before he retired in 2022 and a brief spell as a video assistant referee followed. In an interview on Jamie Vardy’s podcast this week, Dean shared anecdotes from his time as a top-flight official in the pre-VAR era. “We used to say, ‘We’ll kick off now. Right, see how long we can go without blowing a whistle,’” he said. “I’ve done that a few times in the Premier League, before VAR obviously – [I] went 20, 25 minutes without blowing a whistle.Football Daily | Mike Dean appears to blow the whistle on himself over in-match game claimsRead more“I used to do another thing. I used to stand in the centre circle – see how long I could stay in the centre circle before I had to leave. That was just me joking about. I got about 15 minutes once.”Officials within the refereeing organisation, Pro Ref, are understood to be puzzled by the claims, with the suggestion that a referee could stay in the centre circle for 15 minutes without someone noticing, for example, seen as highly improbable.This is not the first time that Dean has courted controversy in a post-retirement interview. Dean was stood down from his role as a VAR in 2023 after failing to intervene over an error in a match between Tottenham and Chelsea, refereed by Anthony Taylor. Describing Taylor as a “mate”, Dean told Simon Jordan’s podcast that he had chosen not to ask Taylor to review his decision on a VAR monitor because he didn’t want him to have “any more grief than he already had”.Dean earned notoriety during his time as a referee for his flamboyant mannerisms and apparent eye for the camera – as captured in the terrace chant “Mike Dean, it’s all about you”. But he was also held to be one of the best officials in the top flight, taking charge of 561 matches – and issuing a record 114 red cards – over the course of his 22-year career.Explore more on these topicsFootballRefereesPremier LeagueLaws of footballnewsShareReuse this content

title: Andoni Iraola defends Liverpool opting against throwing ‘crazy money’ at short-term fixes | Liverpool | The Guardian
description: Andoni Iraola believes Liverpool think it ‘better to look a little further than the next game’ and said he is happy with the wingers he has in the squad
Author: Andy Hunter
Headline: Andoni Iraola believes Liverpool think it ‘better to look a little further than the next game’ and said he is happy with the wingers he has in the squad
Content: New signing Bradley Barcola can play on the left or right, according to Andoni Iraola.Photograph: Liverpool FC/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenNew signing Bradley Barcola can play on the left or right, according to Andoni Iraola.Photograph: Liverpool FC/Getty ImagesLiverpoolAndoni Iraola defends Liverpool opting against throwing ‘crazy money’ at short-term fixes‘It’s better to look a little further than the next game’Head coach ‘happy with the four wingers we have’Andy HunterThu 3 Sep 2026 17.30 EDTFirst published on Thu 3 Sep 2026 08.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndoni Iraola has defended Liverpool’s summer transfer strategy and said the club were right not to pay “crazy money” for short-term fixes while Hugo Ekitiké, Conor Bradley and Giovanni Leoni are recovering from serious injuries.Liverpool had the highest net spend in the Premier League, with Bradley Barcola, signed for a potential £123m, added on Monday to a front line that includes the £125m Alexander Isak and £116m Florian Wirtz.
