Barcola could make his debut at Ipswich on Friday, despite not featuring for Paris Saint-Germain this season.Quick GuidePlay our football trivia game, On the ballShowThe Guardian'sdaily football game, On the ball, is now live in the app for both iOS and Android. Can you identify the Premier League star from the clues?Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Liverpool’s outlay did not include a right-back, defensive midfielder or right-winger but Iraola, who believes Barcola could be deployed in Mohamed Salah’s old position on the right, insisted he had no qualms with the squad at his disposal.“I’m very happy with all the signings we’ve made,” said the Liverpool head coach. “I know the next question: ‘Do you want more signings in other positions?’ At the end the club has decided those signings we have done are the ones that improved our team and our position.“There were other options we decided not to take, for different reasons: sometimes it is sporting reasons because they don’t improve what you have, sometimes it is economical reasons as it didn’t make sense in terms of the market to do those movements. But I’m happy now I know what we have, I have a lot of quality in the team and now it is the moment for us, for the players, for me to develop what we have.”Leoni has been sidelined with an anterior cruciate ligament injury since last September but is expected to resume first-team training during the international break, which starts this month. There is no date on Bradley’s and Ekitiké’s return from serious knee and achilles injuries respectively, but Iraola said the club had to plan for the long term and wait for all three to recover.Iraola said: “The club has decided not to sign someone because we need them for these two or three months and instead trust the players we have, us working with the players we have and thinking of the long term.“Yes, as a manager you need the players for today but if they [the club] explain to you the vision and the long-term project, you also have to understand the club. Sometimes it doesn’t make sense to pay crazy money – the market was the market – for players who maybe in the long term you don’t need. Then you will need this money to solve other problems in that position. Sometimes it’s better to look a little bit further than the next game and the next month.”Despite the absence of a natural right-winger – Liverpool explored deals for Yankuba Minteh at Brighton and Ismaïla Sarr at Crystal Palace – Iraola is confident Barcola, Victor Muñoz, Cody Gakpo and Rio Ngumoha will provide sufficient cover.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHe said: “I think we’ve preferred at the end to have the best players, probably, than a player that maybe is specifically for that [right-sided] position. I’m very used from my previous teams to demand for all the wingers to play both sides.“Probably all of them have played more on the left, but I would say I’ve seen them in a good place on the right. Probably Rio is more specific from the left side, but I think he has also showed the willingness to improve and play on the right. Even Bradley, he’s very open and I think he can play right and left. He started actually more on the right side when he started with Olympique Lyonnais. I’m happy with the four wingers we have and I’m sure we are going to be able to cover those two positions.”Explore more on these topicsLiverpoolAndoni IraolaTransfer windownewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s huge’: Nike deal breaks new ground in WSL for London City Lionesses | London City Lionesses | The Guardian
description: The Women’s Super League club have signed a record breaking front of shirt sponsorship deal with the American sportswear company
Author: Tom Garry
Headline: The Women’s Super League club have signed a record breaking front of shirt sponsorship deal with the American sportswear company
Content: London City Lionesses have announced a landmark multi-year front-of-shirt partnership with Nike.Photograph: London City LionessesView image in fullscreenLondon City Lionesses have announced a landmark multi-year front-of-shirt partnership with Nike.Photograph: London City LionessesLondon City Lionesses‘It’s huge’: Nike deal breaks new ground in WSL for London City LionessesClub owner says deal is largest in women’s gameClaimed to exceed some men’s Premier League shirt dealsTom GarryThu 3 Sep 2026 17.33 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 18.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Women’s Super League club London City Lionesses’ new front-of-shirt sponsorship deal with Nike is the largest in the women’s game, according to their American owner, Michele Kang.The length and value of the deal has not been disclosed but sources close to the WSL club are hailing it as a gamechanging moment and Kang claims that it even exceeds some men’s Premier League clubs’ shirt deals.Women’s Super League 2026-27 preview No 10: London City LionessesRead moreLondon City, who host Manchester United on Friday in the opening game of the new WSL campaign, are about to embark on only their second top-flight season, but this summer they have shocked the sport by signing a flurry of some of the biggest names in women’s football, including the formerBallon d’Or winner Alexia Putellas, the formerEngland goalkeeper Mary Earpsand Putellas’ Spain and Barcelona teammate, Mapi León.It has been reported that the largest current front-of-shirt sponsorship deal for a women’s football team is an approximately $4m per year agreement reached by the new NWSL franchise in Atlanta – who will begin competing in 2028, but Kang told BBC Sport: “I can absolutely confirm that this is the largest women-only front-of-shirt deal. It is higher than the Atlanta number.“I can absolutely also share that it is higher than some of the men’s Premier League front-of-shirt deals. It’s huge. That’s why it is landmark. There are so many other people who believe in the future of women’s football. They [Nike] didn’t make this decision lightly. They did not write a charity cheque. They believe in the future and they believe together we will invest and build this future together.”View image in fullscreenMichele Kang has been London City Lionesses owner since December 2023.Photograph: Charlotte Wilson/Offside/Getty ImagesThe deal will be a major boost to London City’s finances. In their most recent set of financial accounts, they posted an annual revenue of just £902,000 for the 2024-25 season, when they won promotion to the top flight. Their operating loss was over £10m, and more than 10 times that revenue.Their transfer business has attracted questions about how they can fit their lavish spending within the salary cap, as the WSL’s rules dictate that clubs cannot spend more on their player wage bills than 80% of their relevant revenue plus up to £4m of owner contributions. But it is understood this Nike deal will transform their annual revenue astronomically compared to previous seasons.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe popularity on social media of their biggest new signing Alexia Putellas – who has 3.4 million Instagram followers – and Earps and León is believed to have been a major driving factor in the supposedly high valuation from Nike. Putellas has helped Spain win 2023’s World Cup and won the Champions League four times with Barcelona. The Spaniard shared the news of the sponsorship on her Instagram account on Thursday.Explore more on these topicsLondon City LionessesWomen's Super LeagueFinancesBusinessWomen's footballnewsShareReuse this content

title: Daniel Kretinsky to become biggest West Ham shareholder in blow to Amanda Staveley | West Ham United | The Guardian
description: Daniel Kretinsky is to become the biggest shareholder at West Ham in a blow to Amanda Staveley
Author: Jacob Steinberg
Headline: Daniel Kretinsky is to become the biggest shareholder at West Ham in a blow to Amanda Staveley
Content: Daniel Kretinsky has been a shareholder at West Ham since 2021.Photograph: David W Černý/ReutersView image in fullscreenDaniel Kretinsky has been a shareholder at West Ham since 2021.Photograph: David W Černý/ReutersWest Ham UnitedDaniel Kretinsky to become biggest West Ham shareholder in blow to Amanda StaveleyRoyal Mail owner made agreement with David SullivanStaveley was pushing to buy  stake in the clubJacob SteinbergThu 3 Sep 2026 18.39 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 18.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDaniel Kretinsky is set to become the biggest shareholder at West Ham after striking an agreement withDavid Sullivan, dealing a blow to Amanda Staveley’s hopes of buying a stake in the Championship club.Staveley was a guest at the London Stadium for West Ham’s 4-2 win over Wolves earlier this week and was pushing to buy Vanessa Gold’s 25.1% stake in the club. The British businesswoman, previously a director at Newcastle, had struck a deal with the Gold family in July and was fronting a consortium looking for a way on to the east London club’s board.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWest Ham fight off Wolves as Divine Mukasa double eases pressure on NunoRead moreHowever that arrangement sparked a process allowing West Ham’s other shareholders to exercise their pre-emption rights over the Gold family’s stake before a 5.30pm deadline on Thursday evening. It is believed that Kretinsky, a Czech billionaire and the owner of Royal Mail, and Sullivan have come to an agreement that will see the former increase his 27% stake to 46%. Sources have said there is unlikely to be a way back for Staveley’s group.Sources have consistently said that Kretinsky, who will surpass Sullivan as the biggest shareholder, is determined to increase his interest in West Ham as they look to rebuild after their relegation from the Premier League last season. His plans were complicated by Staveley entering the picture.However it is understood that Sullivan rebuffed an inquiry from Staveley about buying his stake during the summer. The 77-year-old privately indicated a preference to deal with Kretinsky, who first bought a stake in West Ham in November 2021. The arrangement will see Sullivan increase his stake from 38.8% to 40%, making him the second largest shareholder. The American businessman Tripp Smith’s stake will go from 8% to 11% and the remaining shareholders will rise from 1.1% to 3%. Staveley would need shareholders not to take up their pre-emption rights to have a chance of making a separate offer for the Gold shares.Sullivan stepped down as a director and co-chair of West Ham in June, before a joint investigation by the Times and Panorama reporting on seven women abusing his power and preying on them for sex in claims that date back to the 1980s and 90s. The 77-year-old categorically denies the allegations. Sullivan has been present at West Ham’s home games this season but does not have a seat on the board and is no longer the most powerful person at the club.Explore more on these topicsWest Ham UnitedDavid SullivannewsShareReuse this content

title: World Cup wishlists, early movers, big clearouts: 2026 summer transfer window trends | Transfer window | The Guardian
description: At the end of a busy transfer window which spanned the World Cup, here are some of the subplots of the summer
Author: Billy Munday
Headline: At the end of a busy transfer window which spanned the World Cup, here are some of the subplots of the summer
Content: On the move: Real Madrid’s Yan Diomande, Sevilla signing Robbie Ure and new Liverpool winger Víctor Muñoz.Composite: Guardian picture deskView image in fullscreenOn the move: Real Madrid’s Yan Diomande, Sevilla signing Robbie Ure and new Liverpool winger Víctor Muñoz.Composite: Guardian picture deskTransfer windowWorld Cup wishlists, early movers, big clearouts: 2026 summer transfer window trendsAt the end of a busy transfer window which spanned the World Cup, here are some of the subplots of the summerBilly Munday,Will MageeandMarcus ChristensonThu 3 Sep 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 12.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn the World Cup wishlist …The World Cup is always a good shop window. Yan Diomande was already a rising star at RB Leipzig but shining for Côte d’Ivoire in the US helped push up his price tag before a £115.7m move to Real Madrid. There were other breakout stars: Switzerland’s Johan Manzambi, whose signature Aston Villa pipped Newcastle to; Bosnia and Herzegovina’s Kerim Alajbegovic, who went to Juventus; and Ghana’s Caleb Yirenkyi, who is now in the Premier League with Coventry. Cape Verde’s cult hero Vozinha now keeps net for the Chilean giants Colo-Colo and Morocco’s attacking dynamo, Ismael Saibari, has rocked up at Bayern.Billy MundayTime is of the essenceWhile Europe’s wealthiest clubs generally allowed the World Cup to run its course before moving for their main targets, there were some exceptions. Real Madrid announced the signing of Marc Cucurella for £52m as he was getting ready to start Spain’s opener against Cape Verde, then Bernardo Silva before Portugal began their campaign two days later. Liverpool spent heavily early on asthey signed Víctor Muñoz for £34.5min mid-June and completedtheir pre-agreed £60m deal for Jérémy Jacquetat the start of July. Tottenham had spent almost £230m on Jan Paul van Hecke, Mateus Fernandes and Sandro Tonali before the last 16 was over, also adding Andy Robertson and Marcos Senesi on free transfers. Other clubs seemed to treat the World Cup as an opportunity to do deals under the radar. Bayer Leverkusen moved quickly,just as they did in January, to sign promising youngsters in Kennet Eichhorn and Afonso Moreira for a combined £32.8m in June. Brighton were among the most proactive squad builders in the Premier League, spending just over £50m on Zadok Yohanna, Costinha and Pascal Struijk before the World Cup action had moved beyond the last 32.Will MageeView image in fullscreenZadok Yohanna was an early arrival for Brighton, who did not wait around to make signings.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersPremier League newcomers splash the cash“Think about us like a volcano,” Hull’s owner, Acun Ilicali, said in July. “It’s boiling right now and it’s going to erupt.” He was not wrong. In the end, the promoted Premier League side signed 18 players this summer for a combined sum of £156.5m. Ipswich went even further, splashing £194.7m on 15 additions, while Coventry spent £122.4m on 11 new signings. It is a far cry from a few years ago when many promoted teams were frugal, often relying on the players who took them to the promised land. As recently as 2021 the three promoted teams, Norwich, Watford and Brentford, spent a combined £98.8m – with the latter’s acquisition of Kristoffer Ajer from Celtic the most expensive signing at £13m. The fact that Premier League newcomers are spending so lavishly isa reminder of the division’s financial dominanceand the game’s increasingly extreme economic disparities.Marcus ChristensonFrench talent factory ups its outputIn sharp contrast to the Premier League, where eight clubs had a net spend over £100m and only six made a net gain, 15 out of 18 Ligue 1 clubs made money on player trading this summer. Paris Saint-Germain led the way thanks in no small part to the £123m deal which took Bradley Barcola to Liverpool, making a net profit of more than £150m overall. Lille, who made around £100m, sanctioned big-money departures for Ayyoub Bouaddi and Matias Fernandez-Pardo, who joined Manchester City and Newcastle for £85.7m and £51m respectively. Strasbourg, the smaller cog in BlueCo’s transfer machine, brought in almost £90m as they moved on Diego Moreira, Julio Enciso, Abdoul Ouattara, Guéla Doué, Valentín Barco and Emmanuel Emegha – the latter two moving to, that’s right, Chelsea. While Ligue 1 has been a conveyor belt of talent for some time, its output is reaching new levels. Of the 15 biggest fees ever received by French clubs, five have come in this window.WMView image in fullscreenBradley Barcola was the most expensive of numerous acquisitions from Ligue 1 clubs.Photograph: Liverpool FC/Getty ImagesFiorentina lead clubs in clearout modeThere has been plenty of upheaval this summer, but nowhere more so than at Fiorentina. After battling relegation for much of last season, eventually finishing 15th in Serie A, theViolahave moved on 34 players either permanently or on loan, with Moise Kean and Tariq Lamptey among the high-profile departees. No other club in Europe’s “big five” leagues can match that but Chelsea, with 33 leavers (18 on loan), are not far off. While Chelsea made a net profit of around £60m thanks tothe £125m deadline-day deal for Enzo Fernández, Fiorentina have spent more than £100m net on a rebuild from the ground up. Depending on interpretation, that’s either a sign ofPremier League money taking on a bizarre and irrational life of its own, or a lesson in the eye-watering cost of fixing a failed recruitment strategy.WMskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionInter order the full EnglishThere has been a steady stream of English players heading to Italy in recent years, but it’s not often three turn up at one club in quick succession. Inter have opened the floodgates this summer, signing John Stones from Manchester City on a free, Djed Spence from Tottenham for £25.6m and Curtis Jones from Liverpool for £25.7m. The pantheon of Inter cult heroes includes Paul Ince and Ashley Young, who won theScudettoin 2021, so the club has a longstanding Anglophile streak, but Serie A has also become an increasingly attractive destination. With Omari Hutchinson joining Fikayo Tomori and Ruben Loftus-Cheek at Milan, the derby will have a distinctly English flavour.WMView image in fullscreenCurtis Jones savours victory against Cagliari on his Inter debut.Photograph: Mattia Pistoia/Inter/Getty ImagesSeville forges links with Celtic nationsIt is Ireland v Scotland in the frontlines of Seville this season. Perhaps inspired by their pre-season trip to Dublin, Real Betis spent £17.1m to sign Troy Parrott from AZ, where he scored 31 goals in the Netherlands last season. Manuel Pellegrini said moving to La Liga is a “leap” for Parrott, but it’s not as big a jump as Robbie Ure has made. The £5.6m Glasgow-born striker, uncapped by Scotland, has become Sevilla’s new No 9 off the back of 15 goals in 15 games in the first half of the Swedish season for theunlikely Allsvenskan leaders, Sirius. “I wanted to be in top-class environments,” the 22-year-old said.BMTransfer tumbleweed and tight pocketsThey may have been the least active club in Europe’s top leagues this summer with zero new arrivals but, given their tradition of only signing players born or trained in the Basque Country, Athletic Bilbao have a good excuse.Marseille, not so much. Other than fulfilling their pre-agreed obligations to buy Timothy Weah and Hamed Traorè, OM have not brought in a single player while stripping their squad back to the bare bones in a drastic attempt to repair their finances. Then there are the clubs with modest budgets who have opted for a thrifty approach. Málaga, newly promoted to La Liga, have brought in seven players but not paid a single transfer fee. Le Mans, new arrivals in Ligue 1, have limited themselves to two undisclosed fees while making nine signings, also allowing five players to leave without receiving a fee in return.WMExplore more on these topicsTransfer windowfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Nick Kyrgios enters treatment program after accepting one-month ban for cocaine use | Nick Kyrgios | The Guardian
description: Fallen Australian tennis star Nick Kyrgios has entered a treatment program after accepting a one-month ban for testing positive to cocaine
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Fallen Australian tennis star Nick Kyrgios has entered a treatment program after accepting a one-month ban for testing positive to cocaine
Content: Nick Kyrgios is free to play tennis again after his ban for cocaine use was reduced by the International Tennis Integrity Agency.Photograph: Amr Alfiky/ReutersView image in fullscreenNick Kyrgios is free to play tennis again after his ban for cocaine use was reduced by the International Tennis Integrity Agency.Photograph: Amr Alfiky/ReutersNick KyrgiosNick Kyrgios enters treatment program after accepting one-month ban for cocaine useAustralian free to play again after having suspension reducedITIA accepts Kyrgios’s use of cocaine was outside of competitionAustralian Associated PressThu 3 Sep 2026 19.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFallen Australian tennis starNick Kyrgioshas entered a treatment program after accepting a one-month ban for testing positive to cocaine.After admitting his “huge mistake” wheninitially suspended for failing a drugs teston June 22 at an ATP 250 tournament in Spain, Kyrgios is allowed to compete again from Friday.Kyrgios, who had been provisionally suspended since 4 August, had faced a ban ranging from a baseline three-month period to up to four years.Stefanos Tsitsipas says Nick Kyrgios’s cocaine ban was ‘pretty much expected’Read moreDuring an interview with InternationalTennisIntegrity Agency (ITIA) investigators, Kyrgios explained his use of cocaine had occurred socially during a night out, days before he was due to play in Mallorca.The ITIA consulted an independent scientific expert at a World Anti-Doping Agency (Wada)-accredited laboratory, who stated the explanation was consistent with the level of cocaine found in his sample.As a result, the ITIA accepted Kyrgios’s use of cocaine was outside of competition.Under Wada rules, the default suspension for a breach of this type is three months, which can be further reduced to one month if the individual commits to a treatment program approved by the ITIA.The 2022 Wimbledon finalist also forfeited the 6570 euros he won in Mallorca for losing in the first round to countryman Adam Walton.But his suspension was reduced for agreeing to enter a treatment program.The International Tennis Integrity Agency (ITIA) said Kyrgios, whose career world ranking peaked at No 13, could appeal against the provisional suspension but he opted against doing so.“I recently failed a drug test in Mallorca after testing positive for cocaine,” Kyrgios posted on Instagram last month. “I made a huge mistake and I take full responsibility for it.“I’m sorry to my fans, my family, my sponsors and everyone close to me. Above all, I’m sorry to the kids who follow me. I know the example this sets and I’m deeply disappointed in myself.”Kyrgios, who played only four official singles matches on the elite ATP Tour this year, has battled knee and wrist injuries in recent years and has all but conceded he is finished as a singles force.The ITIA said Kyrgios was suspended for a ‌positive test for benzoylecgonine, a cocaine metabolite, with a World Anti-Doping Agency laboratory confirming the positive result on 17 July.The 31-year-old was banned from playing, coaching or attending any tournaments sanctioned by the men’s and women’s tennis tours worldwide and national-level events in Australia.Kyrgios last played in the men’s doubles at Wimbledon in London on July 2, when he and partner Alexander Bublik lost in the first round.Explore more on these topicsNick KyrgiosTennisAustralia sportnewsShareReuse this content

Alexei Popyrin fall in second roundAustralian Associated PressThu 3 Sep 2026 19.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDiminutive Dane Sweeny has won a real-life David-versus-Goliath battle to rock the US Open with a stunning second-round upset over dual grand slam semi-finalist Lorenzo Musetti.The unheralded Australian wildcard took down the 14th seed 3-6, 6-1, 6-2, 6-2 on Thursday (Friday AEST) for the biggest win of his career.Standing only 5ft 5in (170cm) tall, Sweeny rose to the occasion to reach the third round of a grand slam for the first time and earn a minimum pay day of $US290,000 ($A402,750).Naomi Osaka grinds it out to see off Siniakova’s stubborn US Open challengeRead moreFor a couple of heady hours it looked like his underdog countrymen Tristan Schoolkate and Alexei Popyrin would join Sweeny in round three.But Schoolkate’s inspired run from qualifying finally came to a halt at the hands of fifth-seeded French Open runner-up Flavio Cobilli.Schoolkate snatched the first set before the Italian showed his class to prevail 3-6, 6-3, 6-4, 7-5 after two hours and 41 minutes in New York’s scorching summer heat.And two years after upstaging Novak Djokovic in the US Open’s third round, Popyrin fell short of a place in the last 32 once again, losing a tense four-set battle with Chilean Alejandro Tabilo.Like Schoolkate, Popyrin took the opening set before the 25th-seeded South American claimed two pivotal tiebreakers, then the match 2-6, 7-6 (7-4), 7-6 (7-3), 6-2 to seal a likely third-round date with German top seed Alexander Zverev.But ranked more than 100 places below his world No 14 opponent, Sweeny is savouring a mighty breakthrough after bossing Musetti into submission.He ran the 14th seed ragged and had the Italian looking in particular distress when he required a medical time-out after falling behind a double break at 0-3 in the all-important third set.Even after clawing one break back, Musetti – who has made the Wimbledon and French Open semi-finals over the past two years – continued remonstrating animatedly to his courtside box.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDespite sporting a massive ice pack on his right elbow after his first-round win, Sweeny continued diving like Boris Becker for acrobatic winning volleys at the net.And the 25-year-old was duly rewarded with a last-32 shot at another Italian, world No 22 Luciano Daredri on Saturday (AEST) – and a rankings rise to a career-best No 115 in the world, or better.“I’m just grateful to be even able to compete in grand slams. The tennis journey is such a rollercoaster,” Sweeny said. “And to soak up the atmosphere and get a win, a couple of wins, in front of this crowd, is awesome.”Australia’s sixth seed Alex de Minaur was scheduled to plau Dutchman Botic van de Zandschulp on The Grandstand after Schoolkate’s match.Explore more on these topicsUS Open Tennis 2026US Open tennisTennisAustralia sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Scottish Premiership: McPake’s solo pearler seals Hearts’ cruise past 10-man Hibs | Scottish Premiership | The Guardian
description: Hearts eased to a 3-1 win over Hibernian on Thursday, after Celtic beat Aberdeen 3-0 on Wednesday, while Falkirk lost 1-2 to Rangers
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Hearts eased to a 3-1 win over Hibernian on Thursday, after Celtic beat Aberdeen 3-0 on Wednesday, while Falkirk lost 1-2 to Rangers
Content: Josh McPake of Hearts rounds off a brilliant run through the Hibs defence with a deflected shot off Grant Hanley to give his side a 3-1 lead.Photograph: Stuart Wallace/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenJosh McPake of Hearts rounds off a brilliant run through the Hibs defence with a deflected shot off Grant Hanley to give his side a 3-1 lead.Photograph: Stuart Wallace/ShutterstockScottish PremiershipScottish Premiership: McPake’s solo pearler seals Hearts’ cruise past 10-man HibsCamilo Durán inspires Celtic’s 3-0 win against AberdeenFalkirk 1-2 Rangers; Kilmarnock 0-1 St MirrenAgence France-PresseThu 3 Sep 2026 17.13 EDTFirst published on Wed 2 Sep 2026 18.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWouter Vrancken enjoyed a memorable first Edinburgh derby in charge ofHeartsas his rampant side cruised to a deserved 3-1 victory over 10-manHibernianat Easter Road.James Wilson and Laurent Mendy had the visitors two goals up at half-time before Hibs ralled early in the second half and pulled one back through substitute Adam Mayor.Their hopes of a fightback were dashed, however, when Josh McPake – in front of the watching Scotland manager Sebastien Pocognoli – scored a brilliant third for Hearts shortly after Hibs substitute Jack Iredale was sent off. McPake’s superb solo run was capped with a finish that deflected in off Grant Hanley.It was a seventh successive match unbeaten in all competitions for Hearts, who have recovered impressively after losing each of their first four matches under the ultra-cavalier Vrancken.Scottish Premiership: Shankland on the spot to ease pressure on McInnes and RangersRead moreTheCelticstriker Camilo Durán inspired the Scottish champions’ 3-0 win overAberdeen, whileRangerssnatched a 2-1 victory againstFalkirkon Wednesday.Durán has scored six goals in five matches for Martin O’Neill’s side after his latest eye-catching contribution at Parkhead. The Colombian netted in the 14th minute with the latest in his series of spectacular strikes since joining from Qarabag in the close-season. Durán collected Benjamin Nygren’s pass and unleashed a long-range drive that cannoned in off the crossbar.O’Neill may find it difficult to put the winger back on the flanks when the striker Kasper Høgh recovers from a thigh injury. Nygren and Yang Hyun-jun were also on target asCeltickilled off the game before the break.Although they suffered a humiliating Champions League exit against Lask, Celtic have made a perfect start to their title defence with four successive wins. It was an emotional night in Glasgow as Kenny Dalglish was given a warm ovation on the pitch before the match. Dalglish launched his iconic career with Celtic before joining Liverpool in 1977. The 75-year-old revealed earlier this year that he was receiving treatment for cancer.Celtic are two points clear of second-placeSt Mirren, whose 1-0 win atKilmarnock– their first at Rugby Park for 13 years – was secured by Fraser Taylor’s maiden goal for the club in the third minute.View image in fullscreenCamilo Durán starred again as Celtic swept aside Aberdeen.Photograph: Ian MacNicol/Getty ImagesLawrence Shankland’s double gave Rangers a dramatic win over Falkirk to ease the pressure on theirmanager, Derek McInnes. With McInnes serving the first of a two-matchtouchline ban(reduced from four matches) for comments made as Hearts manager last season, he watched from the stands as Shankland saved him from another chastening result.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenRangers’ captain, Lawrence Shankland, celebrates his second goal against Falkirk.Photograph: Kirk O’Rourke/Rangers FC/ShutterstockShankland, who scored from the spot in the 1-0 win at Aberdeen on Sunday, fired Rangers ahead with a fine strike in the seventh minute. Kosta Nedeljkovic, making his first Rangers start since signing on loan from Aston Villa, turned an Ethan Ross cross into his own net to giveFalkirkan unexpected equaliser just before the break. But Scotland star Shankland, who signed from Hearts in the close-season, reduced Rangers’ anxiety when he curled in the winner after 79 minutes.Motherwell’s Seb Palmer-Houlden, Alex Lowry and Dylan Levitt scored their first goals for the club in a 3-0 win againstDundee United. They ended Wednesday in third but were leapfrogged by Hearts on Thursday.St Johnstonesalvaged a 1-1 draw in the Tayside derby againstDundee. Dundee seemed to have sealed the points when Charlie Reilly scored in the 87th minute, but St Johnstone’s Josh Fowler levelled in the 90th minute.Explore more on these topicsScottish PremiershipCelticRangersAberdeenFalkirkSt MirrenKilmarnocknewsShareReuse this content

title: Naomi Osaka grinds it out to see off Siniakova’s stubborn US Open challenge | US Open Tennis 2026 | The Guardian
description: Naomi Osaka recovered from a mid-match slump to beat Katerina Siniakova 6-2, 5-7, 6-1 and reach the third round of the US Open
Author: Tumaini Carayol
Headline: Naomi Osaka recovered from a mid-match slump to beat Katerina Siniakova 6-2, 5-7, 6-1 and reach the third round of the US Open
Content: Naomi Osaka had some nervous moments on the way to victory.Photograph: Robert Deutsch/IMAGN IMAGES/ReutersView image in fullscreenNaomi Osaka had some nervous moments on the way to victory.Photograph: Robert Deutsch/IMAGN IMAGES/ReutersUS Open Tennis 2026Naomi Osaka grinds it out to see off Siniakova’s stubborn US Open challengeFormer champion into third round with 6-2, 5-7, 6-1 win‘I hope to continue making good memories here’Tumaini Carayolat Flushing MeadowsThu 3 Sep 2026 17.06 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 19.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor a second consecutive match at the US Open,Naomi Osakaappeared to be cruising. Everything was in hand as the two-time champion established a set and a break lead in her round two match against Katerina Siniakova, an uneventful return to the third round beckoning.Instead of carrying that great momentum forward until the end, though, Osaka was overcome by tension in the final stages of the second set and she soon found herself in a decider. It took a significant amount of resilience and restraint for her to reset and find a way through to the third round with a comprehensive final set to win 6-2, 5-7, 6-1.US Open 2026: Auger-Aliassime out; Keys, Osaka and Swiatek through; Sweeny and Popyrin in action – liveRead moreBefore the North American hard-court swing, a period that yielded US Open titles in 2018 and 2020, Osaka finally looked like a grand slam contender again. After years of struggling through the clay- and grass-court seasons, seemingly just waiting for the hard courts to return, this year Osaka produced career-best showings on those surfaces to the fourth round at the French Open and quarter-finals at Wimbledon.Her level on grass at Wimbledon, a surface she has toiled on for much of her career, was particularly impressive as she defeated the world No 1, Aryna Sabalenka, in round four. Osaka ran out of steam in the quarter-finals, fatigue seeping in after she reached the Bad Homburg final a week earlier, but it was some of the best tennis she had played since winning her last grand slam title at the Australian Open in 2021. She headed back to North America full of confidence.Elevated expectations can naturally lead to greater pressure and Osaka’s first two wins in New York this year are perhaps a reflection of the additional weight on her shoulders. In her 7-6 (6), 7-6 (3) first-roundwin over Anastasia Zakharova, a nervous Osaka squandered a break in both sets before barely dragging herself over the line in two tie-breaks. This time her nerves cost her a set. The most important thing about the early stages of the grand slam tournaments for the top players, though, is simply finding a way to win and offering themselves an opportunity to unleash their top form in later rounds.“I’m quite fortunate to have a lot of high-quality matches that went in my favour,” said Osaka. “Especially whenever I think of going into the third set and I need to regroup, I literally only specifically think of the [2019] Australian Open Final [a three-set win against Petra Kvitova]. Then it’s just like you can just pull from your memory bank for every certain situation that you need to get finished.“I think that’s the best thing about being a more experienced player. You’ve been able to play so many different matches in different situations. Here, obviously, I’ve had a lot of good memories, and I hope to continue making them.”It is increasingly difficult to speak only of tennis when discussing Osaka. At the same time that her overall form has improved, every grand slam appearance this year has featured dramatic walk-on outfits and match kit reveals that have generated their own headlines. Her outfits at the US Open this year are a homage to Allen Iverson, the former basketball player. Her elaborate outfit choices, and the discussion around them, have often been the source of conversation and also ample scorn.For such a reserved and inoffensive person, Osaka’s mere existence seems to enrage some of her detractors. Some describe her as an attention seeker who should focus only on her tennis. Her mental health difficulties in 2021, when she struggled with public scrutiny, are often referenced as hypocritical considering the way her choice of attire even though she is at a completely different stage in her life half a decade on. So much of the criticism she receives is in bad faith, driven by people who will never forgive her anti-racist activism during the early 2020s.View image in fullscreenIga Swiatek enjoyed a comfortable win against Nadia Podoroska.Photograph: Robert Prange/Getty ImagesAlthough Osaka has matured, growing in confidence and stature, she is introverted at heart. She believes fashion allows her a far easier avenue for her to express herself. Most of all, she is an entertainer who runs around a court and hits tennis balls for the pleasure of her audience. This is not a matter of life and death. Wearing elaborate dresses while playing tennis is no outrage.Osaka has been handed one of the toughest draws of the many title contenders, with the second seed, Elena Rybakina a potential fourth-round opponent. The first objective, though, is simply making it there.Meanwhile, Iga Swiatek, the eighth seed and 2022 champion, continued to build momentum in New York as she reached the second round with a 6-3, 6-2 win over Nadia Podoroska. British qualifier Harriet Dart was comprehensively defeated 6-2, 6-2 by the 25th seed, Marie Bouzkova. In the men’s draw, Félix Auger-Aliassime, the third seed and a semi-finalist last year, struggled with dizziness and illness as he was defeated 6-7 (5), 6-3, 6-2, 6-2 by Karen Khachanov.Explore more on these topicsUS Open Tennis 2026Naomi OsakaUS Open tennisTennisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Crocombe takes hat-trick for Sussex, Surrey skittled for 83: county cricket, day two – as it happened | County Championship | The Guardian
description: Matt Fisher and Henry Crocombe made hay for Surrey and Sussex respectively on a good day for bowlers
Author: Tanya Aldred
Headline: Matt Fisher and Henry Crocombe made hay for Surrey and Sussex respectively on a good day for bowlers
Content: 6h ago15.22 EDTFisher and Crocombe make hay on good day for bowlersTanya AldredMatt Fisher, left out of England’s squad for the third Test, scrawled his name in neon crayons with a career-best six for 25 asYorkshirewere bowled out for 82 in their second innings at the Oval. But that came only hours afterSurreyhad been bowled out for 83 in their first innings as 23 wickets fell in front of a startled crowd. It was the first time since 1950 that a day of first‑class cricket at the Oval contained elements of all four innings. Surrey, set 185 to win, creaked unhurt to reach 27 without loss at stumps.Henry Crocombe bagged his second hat-trick in two games, asEssexcollapsed like a teacup tower, losing seven wickets for six runs in 26 balls. With Simon Harmer, Zaman Akhter and Shane Snater in his pocket, Crocombe charged about Chelmsford, teammates in pursuit, and finished with five wickets – happy news indeed for his new masters at the Oval where he moves at the end of the season.Sussexthen stuttered to 90 for four in their second innings, but the lead is already 188. Sam Cook was withdrawn from the game midway through by England.The Derby-born debutant Mohammed Bin Naeem’s 71 leftDerbyshirethe happier side after they finished 162 for two at stumps, but James Bracey’s 113 had earlier propped up aGloucestershirefightback at Bristol.Jack Haynes’ career-best 159 and Liam Patterson-White’s 111 sailedNottinghamshirepast five batting points, whereupon they declared and Dillon Pennington removed bothLeicestershire’s openers.Somersetjust missed a fifth batting point at Taunton, but a hefty first innings lead of 247 overGlamorganleft little room for disappointment. Tom Lammonby, after being twice reprieved in the 90s from no balls of various flavours, dollied a caught and bowled for 95, and there were half-centuries for Josh Thomas, James Rew and Archie Vaughan. Mason Crane collected four wickets before, opening the batting forGlamorgan, he was caught off the last ball of the day.Half-centuries by James Sales and Saif Zaib turned the tables onDurhamwho had started the day in a dominant position but tumbled down the escalator, losing seven for 48, despite 81 from David Bedingham. The leg-spinner Yuzvendra Chahal twirled out four for 36.Northamptonshirefinished with a lead of 20.A first century of the season for Rob Yates putWarwickshirein a dominant position againstHampshire, Kyle Abbott became the first Division One bowler to tick off 50 wickets, and then Hampshire collapsed to 70 for six. There was four wickets forMiddlesex’s Tom Helm as Lancashire were inched out for 150 at Merchant Taylor’s school; while Sam Northeast’s unbeaten 96 put a spring inKent’s step againstWorcestershire.Somerset’s women pulled off a sensational win againstYorkshirein the one-day cup. Yorkshire needed just 10 to win off 25 overs with five wickets in hand, but proceeded to lose them all for four runs and come up five short.ShareUpdated at15.56 EDT

title: England beat Ireland by six wickets: second women’s cricket one-day international – as it happened | Cricket | The Guardian

Author: Taha Hashim
Headline: Issy Wong took her first five-fer at international level as England wrapped up a series victory with a game to spare
Content: 8h ago13.42 EDTRaf NicholsonEngland sealed victory in their one-day international series against Irelandwith a straightforward six-wicket win at Derby on Thursday, after seamer Issy Wong took a career-best five for 33.Wong, once again handed the new ball in the absence of Lauren Bell, bowled with accuracy and control to knock over Ireland captain Gaby Lewis’s leg stump, then ran rampant through the lower-middle order as they tried to hit out but instead were bowled out for 165.It was in marked contrast with Wong’s performance in the first ODI, when she sent down four consecutive wides in her opening spell, and sparked hopes she may be recovering some of the mojo she lost when originally discarded by England three summers ago.Wong’s five wickets lead England to rampant victory over Ireland and ODI series winRead moreShareUpdated at13.59 EDT

title: Columbia’s Michael Zheng comes full circle as Americans advance at US Open | US Open Tennis 2026 | The Guardian
description: The former Columbia University tennis star won on the same Flushing Meadows grounds where he trained as a child as Shelton, Tiafoe and Pegula also advanced
Author: Bryan Armen Graham
Headline: The former Columbia University tennis star won on the same Flushing Meadows grounds where he trained as a child as Shelton, Tiafoe and Pegula also advanced
Content: Michael Zheng hits a return during his straight-sets victory over Fabian Marozsan on Wednesday at the US Open in New York.Photograph: Darren Carroll/USTA/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMichael Zheng hits a return during his straight-sets victory over Fabian Marozsan on Wednesday at the US Open in New York.Photograph: Darren Carroll/USTA/Getty ImagesUS Open Tennis 2026Columbia’s Michael Zheng comes full circle as Americans advance at US OpenFormer Ivy League star wins US Open debutShelton and Tiafoe advance to third roundPegula cruises past Kenin in 56 minutesBryan Armen Grahamat Flushing MeadowsThu 3 Sep 2026 00.59 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 10.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMichael Zheng spent years making the long trek from northern New Jersey, first by bus across the Hudson River to the Port Authority bus terminal and then nearly the full length of the No 7 subway line, all for the opportunity to train at the USTA Billie Jean King NationalTennisCenter. On a rainswept Wednesday afternoon in Queens, the destination was the same but the purpose had changed entirely.The 22-year-old American wildcard and two-time NCAA champion from nearbyColumbia Universitybrushed aside Hungary’s Fabian Marozsan 6-4, 6-4, 6-2 to win his rain-delayed US Open debut, providing one of the more unlikely highlights on a busy day for the home contingent in New York.Katie Boulter crashes out of US Open after Karolina Muchova nightmareRead morePlaying before a vocal crowd of his college teammates and alumni who splashed the intimate confines of Court 10 with blue and white, Zheng needed only 1hr 51min to dispatch of the world No 63, breaking five times and dropping serve only once. He hit nearly twice as many winners (33) as unforced errors (17) and was especially ruthless on his first serve, winning all but three of 39 points (92.3%) over three sets.“It just felt like a college tennis match, really,” Zheng said. “My teammates came out. They had the ‘Let’s go, Michael’ chants, and I’m not sure my opponent was ready for it.”He added: “This is a place I grew up training. It was one of the first places that I kind of called home base, actually, the Billie Jean King National Tennis Center. So it’s really special to get that first main-draw win here and in front of my family, friends and teammates as well.”Long before Wednesday’s win, Zheng was a 10-year-old making the roughly two-hour commute from his home in Montville, New Jersey, several times a week to cut his teeth at the national center. His mother would collect him from school and drop him at a nearby bus stop, leaving him to travel alone through Manhattan into Queens to practice on the blue courts in the shadows of Arthur Ashe and Louis Armstrong stadiums.View image in fullscreenMichael Zheng in action against Fabian Marozsan on Court 10 during their first-round match at the US Open on Wednesday in New York.Photograph: Darren Carroll/USTA/Getty ImagesThe years since have brought handsome returns. Zheng, whose parents emigrated from China, became the first Columbia student-athlete since 1906to win the NCAA singles championshipin 2024, then became the first man in 13 years to successfully defend the title last November.His breakthrough on the professional tour quickly followed. Zheng began this year by qualifying for his first grand slam main draw at the Australian Open and beating Sebastian Korda over five sets in the opening round for his first tour-level victory. He followed that with another qualifying run into the French Open before reaching the third round at Wimbledon,seeing off British No 1 Cameron Norriealong the way. Somewhere in between, Zheng found time to graduate from Columbia with a degree in psychology.“If you told me at the end of last year that I would play the main draw at all four slams, I probably wouldn’t believe whoever told me that,” he said. “I think qualifying for the first time at a slam just gives you that confidence that you can do it again.”Wednesday marked another milestone in what’s been a remarkable rise from Ivy League tennis to the grand slam stage. The result lifted Zheng, who entered the tournament ranked 107th, to No 96 in the live rankings and into the top 100 for the first time.“It’s kind of that benchmark, I would say, that players who want to play professionally have,” said Zheng, whose ranking sat outside the top 700 little more than a year ago. “You break the top 100, you can make a living playing tennis now. So it’s definitely really special.”With rain having pushed his first-round match back a day, Zheng will have little time to celebrate. He returns on Thursday afternoon to face Yunchaokete Bu, the Chinese lucky loser ranked 124th, who stunned rising Spanish star Rafael Jodar 6-2, 6-1, 6-1 in one of the most lopsided scorelines of the tournament so far.View image in fullscreenBen Shelton celebrates after defeating Hubert Hurkacz in their second-round match at the US Open on Wednesday in New York.Photograph: Geoff Burke/IMAGN IMAGES/ReutersIf Zheng supplied Wednesday’s homegrown surprise, Ben Shelton provided the star power. The highest-ranked American in the men’s draw survived his first serious examination of the fortnight with a 6-3, 5-7, 7-6 (3), 7-5 win over Hubert Hurkacz beneath the closed roof on Ashe.The eighth-seeded Shelton needed nearly three hours to tame the former world No 6 in a match featuring two of the sport’s most formidable serves. After splitting the first two sets, the 23-year-old American seized control during the third-set tie-break, racing to a 3-0 lead before closing it out 7-3.Hurkacz threatened to force a decider when he earned two break points with Shelton serving at 4-all in the fourth, but Shelton escaped and soon turned the pressure back on his opponent. With Hurkacz serving at 5-6, Shelton pounded away with his forehand until the Pole sprayed one final forehand wide.Shelton flexed both arms and roared toward the stands after completing a victory that sent him into the round of 32 for a fourth straight year in New York.“I was super excited to get through that one and relieved obviously, because I thought he was serving lights out, moving well, not making errors from the baseline, and it was a tall task today,” Shelton said. “I’m kind of just running my own race and focusing on the next round.”Shelton, a semi-finalist here three years ago, arrived in New Yorkfresh off the Montreal titleand with perhaps his best chance yet at becoming the first American man to win a major singles championship since Andy Roddick at the 2003 US Open.Another aspirant to end that 23-year wait is 11th-seeded Frances Tiafoe, who defeated Japanese qualifier Rei Sakamoto 6-3, 7-6 (2), 7-5 to reach the third round for a seventh straight year, the longest active streak among men. The 28-year-old made only 18 unforced errors to Sakamoto’s 40, while dropping serve only twice in the 2hr 40min match.Jessica Pegula made considerably shorter work of her all-American encounter on Ashe, bundling out former Australian Open champion Sofia Kenin 6-3, 6-1 in only 56 minutes. The third seed raced away with the final seven games to progress into the third round, where she will face Canada’s Leylah Annie Fernandez.View image in fullscreenJessica Pegula serves against Sofia Kenin during their second-round match at the US Open on Wednesday in New York.Photograph: Kirsty Wigglesworth/APOn the Grandstand court, Alex Michelsen took out the 16th-seeded Brandon Nakashima 6-3, 6-3, 6-4 in another all-American tie, while Emma Navarro fought back from a set down to defeat Caty McNally 3-6, 6-2, 6-3. Tommy Paul also progressed there in the night session, overcoming a third-set wobble to beat Croatia’s Dino Prizmic 6-2, 6-3, 5-7, 6-4 in just over three hours.Taylor Townsend was among the day’s most emphatic American winners, trouncing Australia’s Taylah Preston 6-1, 6-1 to book a third-round date with French Open semi-finalist Diana Shnaider. Teenager Iva Jovic also went through, defeating Poland’s Magdalena Frech 7-5, 6-3, while Zachary Svajda beat Germany’s Daniel Altmaier 6-3, 6-1, 6-7 (5), 6-2.There was disappointment for Sloane Stephens, the 2017 champion, who was beaten 6-1, 7-5 by 11th-seeded Marta Kostyuk of Ukraine. The 33-year-old offered far more resistance after being overwhelmed in the opening set, reaching set point in the second but failing to convert it and force a decider.Also on Armstrong, Sebastian Gorzny’s debut US Open appearance came to an end against Daniil Medvedev. The 20-year-old wildcard was beaten 6-1, 6-3, 7-5 by the 2021 champion, although he pushed Medvedev throughout a competitive third set before the Russian finally broke through late.Elsewhere on the outer courts, Marcos Giron was edged by Peru’s Ignacio Buse 3-6, 6-3, 6-3, 6-7 (6), 6-1, while Ann Li rallied to win 5-7, 7-6 (4), 6-4 over Donna Vekic.Explore more on these topicsUS Open Tennis 2026Columbia UniversityTennisUS Open tennisUS sportsAndy RoddickShareReuse this content

title: Jordan Chiles announces comeback bid for third Olympics at LA 2028 | Gymnastics | The Guardian
description: The 25-year-old Olympic champion confirmed her return in a Michael Jordan-narrated video as she targets a third Games on home soil
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The 25-year-old Olympic champion confirmed her return in a Michael Jordan-narrated video as she targets a third Games on home soil
Content: Jordan Chiles of UCLA competes in the floor exercise during the NCAA women’s gymnastics championships at Dickies Arena in Fort Worth, Texas, on 19 April 2025.Photograph: C Morgan Engel/NCAA Photos/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJordan Chiles of UCLA competes in the floor exercise during the NCAA women’s gymnastics championships at Dickies Arena in Fort Worth, Texas, on 19 April 2025.Photograph: C Morgan Engel/NCAA Photos/Getty ImagesGymnasticsJordan Chiles announces comeback bid for third Olympics at LA 2028Olympic champion targets third Games in LAMichael Jordan narrates announcement videoChiles joins Lee and Carey on comeback trailAgenciesWed 2 Sep 2026 20.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJordan Chiles is returning for a run at her third Olympics, ⁠announcing Wednesday she intends to compete in the 2028 Games in Los Angeles.Chiles shared ⁠her decision ⁠in ​a video narrated by basketball legendMichael Jordan.‘I’m back’: Suni Lee announces return to gymnastics two years before LA 2028Read more“Why continue? Because there’s still more to ⁠give,” Jordan says in part. “Why now? Because not every chapter ends when people expect ⁠it to. Why her? Because she’s that girl. Some decisions ​don’t need permission. ‌Just one more ‌bet on herself.“Chiles, 25, owns a 2024 gold medal ‌from Paris and a 2021 silver from Tokyo in team competitions.She won an individual bronze in 2024 on floor exercise before the medal was taken away by the Court of Arbitration for Sport and ‌given to Romania’s Ana Barbosu after a score inquiry. Chiles appealed the decision to the ​CAS and awaits a ruling.Chiles starred at UCLA and won two NCAA titles in floor exercise (2023, 2026) and two others on bars (2023, 2025). She is a 23-time ⁠All-American who recorded 19 perfect-10s.Earlier this week, Chiles returned ​to ​UCLA as a student ​coach.Chiles isn’t the only former US Olympian ​on the ‌comeback trail. ​Six-time Olympic medalist ​Suni Leeannounced a comebackin July while three-time medalist Jade Carey resumed competing in June.Simone Biles, meanwhile, has yet to declare whether she’ll pursue more Olympic glory.Explore more on these topicsGymnasticsLA Olympic Games 2028Michael JordanUS sportsSimone BilesShareReuse this content

title: Apocalypse prep or pure pragmatism: what is behind Peter Thiel’s move to Argentina? | Peter Thiel | The Guardian
description: Relocation coincides with proposed laws that opponents say would entrench power of US tech billionaires in country
Author: Aisha Down
Headline: Relocation coincides with proposed laws that opponents say would entrench power of US tech billionaires in country
Content: Protesters marching to Peter Thiel’s mansion in Buenos Aires this week. There is broad unease about the tech magnate’s presence in the country.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenProtesters marching to Peter Thiel’s mansion in Buenos Aires this week. There is broad unease about the tech magnate’s presence in the country.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesPeter ThielApocalypse prep or pure pragmatism: what is behind Peter Thiel’s move to Argentina?Relocation coincides with proposed laws that opponents say would entrench power of US tech billionaires in countryAisha DownGlobal technology reporterThu 3 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 08.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDozens of protesters converged on Peter Thiel’s mansion in Buenos Aires this week after a congressional session raised questions about the billionaire’s presence in the country.In white masks, they held signs saying “Peter Thief” and “No to the Peter Thiel law” in front of the wrought-iron gates of the $12m (£8.9m) residence, which Thiel bought in April as he moved his family toArgentina.There is broad unease at the tech magnate’s presence in the country. His move has been characterised as part of a plan to hedge against world war three: Argentina, agriculturally rich and deep in the southern hemisphere, might just be the ideal place for a tech billionaire towait out the apocalypse.But recent developments in the country suggest Thiel could have more pragmatic considerations.View image in fullscreenProtesters marched to the gates of the $12m residence Peter Thiel bought when he moved his family to Argentina in April.Photograph: Tomás Cuesta/ReutersLast week, Argentina’s chamber of deputies held a six-hour debate on a set of sweeping regulatory changes put forward by Javier Milei’s rightwing government shortly after Thiel moved to Buenos Aires. They invited Thiel, Milei and an official linked to Argentina’s intelligence services to answer questions.“None of them answered, and none of them came to the meeting,” said Juan Marino, a member of the chamber of deputies and the leader of the Piquetero party.Marino said the new laws amounted to a “technofascist legislative package” aimed at entrenching the power of US tech billionaires in the country. Thiel has not publicly advocated for them, but Marino and others have said that their timing was suggestive.The meeting in the chamber of deputies came after Argentinian deputies from several parties made public requests to the government for information about Thiel, his meetings and his businesses. None have been answered.View image in fullscreenPeter Thiel held closed-door meetings with Javier Milei and key presidential advisers in the months after he moved to Argentina.Photograph: Gage Skidmore/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockOne of the laws, the “super RIGI”, would put in place an investment regime offering foreign companies a minimal tax rate and a 30-year guarantee against regulatory change. It specifically names AI datacentres among investments it hopes to attract.Another, which failed,aimed to eliminatemost of the restrictions around foreigners buying land in Argentina. A final decree would require some civilian government departments to share vast amounts of personal data on Argentinian citizens with the state intelligence services.There is no evidence that Thiel has advocated for these laws directly. But in the months after he moved to Buenos Aires, he held closed-door meetings with Milei and key presidential advisers. It is uncommon for a foreign investor to have this degree of access.In the regulatory package, Marino and others see the footprint of Thiel’s larger techno-libertarian interests.The decree that gives vast amounts of Argentinians’ personal data to state intelligence services comes as Argentinian deputies have asked increasinglypointedquestionsabout whether Palantir, the company Thiel co-founded, has undisclosed contracts with the state, which have gone unanswered.View image in fullscreenOne of the proposed laws protesters oppose would offer foreign companies a minimal tax rate and a 30-year guarantee against regulatory change.Photograph: Tomás Cuesta/ReutersThe land law, said Marino, could have paved the way for semi-autonomous “startup cities” – such as the controversialPróspera development in Honduras– that Thiel has advocated as a way for libertarians to carve out zones outside state control.“Argentina is kind of a laboratory,” said Cecilia Nicolini, who represents Argentina at the Mercosur regional parliament. US tech billionaires, she said, “are using Argentina as a laboratory, because they have a person in power, Milei, who is even more crazy than they are”.Over the summer Milei wrote an article in the Financial Times advocating the creation of “non-human corporations” – “entities operated by AI agents or robots”.It parallels a vision put forward by OpenAI’s chief executive, Sam Altman, whopredicted in 2024that the world could soon be run by AI-owned companies. It also raises dark, thorny questions about the legal liabilities of those entities.Nicolini said: “It’s not just that [Thiel] chose Argentina in terms of, it’s a secure place to live in a world that is facing a number of wars, etcetera.“But really, behind it, I think there is a clear plan. And it is related to reforms that Milei is trying to pass, with some success in some cases, and in others, backlash.”Thiel was approached for comment.Explore more on these topicsPeter ThielArgentinaJavier MileiPalantirAmericasData protectionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Nvidia to buy developer platform Hugging Face in $12.9bn deal | Nvidia | The Guardian
description: Semi-conductor giant bets that support for open AI models could offset potential slowdown in demand for chips
Author: Nick Robins-Early
Headline: Semi-conductor giant bets that support for open AI models could offset potential slowdown in demand for chips
Content: Nvidia’s acquisition of Hugging Face will give it direct access to platform developers use to collaborate, test and share tools.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersView image in fullscreenNvidia’s acquisition of Hugging Face will give it direct access to platform developers use to collaborate, test and share tools.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersNvidiaNvidia to buy developer platform Hugging Face in $12.9bn dealSemi-conductor giant bets that support for open AI models could offset potential slowdown in demand for chipsNick Robins-Earlyand agenciesThu 3 Sep 2026 12.59 EDTFirst published on Thu 3 Sep 2026 09.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNvidiawill buy the popular developer platform Hugging Face for nearly $13bn, betting that support for ⁠open AI models could offset a potential slowdown in demand for the semiconductor giant’s chips.Shares ⁠inNvidiawere ⁠slightly lower ​after the $12.93bn (£9.57bn) deal – which ranks among its biggest ever – was announced for the database of AI models on Thursday.Hugging Face, based in New York and backed by the likes of Intel, Advanced Micro Devices and Amazon, was founded in 2016 by the French entrepreneurs Clément Delangue, Julien Chaumond and Thomas Wolf.Nvidia is already a major open AI player in the US with ⁠its widely used Nemotron model and vocal support for the technology.Nvidia’s quarterly revenue doubles to nearly $100bn as CEO declares ‘golden age’Read moreAcquiring Hugging Face will give it direct access to a platform developers use to ⁠collaborate and test and share tools, potentially providing insight and data that could help it narrow the ​technology gap with top American and ‌Chinese labs.“Nvidia gains visibility into customer’s preferences and the AI models they use,” said Naveen Chhabra, principal analyst at Forrester. “They can see which models are trending, what datasets customers are downloading, and the architectures that are gaining traction weeks before they hit mainstream tech news.”Demand for open-weight models ‌has surged from businesses balking at the steep bill of deploying generative AI. Chinese companies ‌such as DeepSeek, Moonshot and Z.ai have emerged as crucial players with models that can match the best from the US in tasks including generating computer code at a lower cost.There are fears that some US firms could become reliant on Beijing’s models even as both countries race to dominate a technology they see as crucial to their future. The Trump administration hasscrambled to respondto the wave of open models from China, weighing whether to restrict their use while also worrying about stifling American businesses that have taken to using them.Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s chief executive, was a signatory of an open letter earlier this year from major tech firms that advocated for open models and warned against government regulation that would stifle their use. Huang pledged that Nvidia would keep Hugging Face open after acquiring it.“Hugging ‌Face will remain an open platform for the entire AI ecosystem,” said Huang, adding that his company’s chips would not be required to ​build on or deploy through Hugging Face.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUnder the deal, Nvidia will pay about $11.9bn to Hugging Face investors, while offering an equity-based retention program of up to $1bn for employees who join Nvidia.For Nvidia, building up its open source business may help it cushion a demand slowdown from customers such as ⁠Meta, OpenAI and Microsoft, which are developing their own AI chips to cut reliance ​on its costly and ​supply-constrained processors. Several Chinese chip-making firms have alsomade recent advancementsthat could further disrupt the balance of power within big tech, though they face strict international export controls.It has been a volatile year in the market for chipmakers, with a chip stockselloff in Julywiping $1tn from the market caps of leading firms. Nvidia shares bounced back in August, though, with a strong revenue forecast leading to the second-biggest one-day gain in market history – adding $442bn to the company’s market value.Hugging Face has also been ​in the news recently after ahack by rogue AI agentsthat ​escaped OpenAI’s testing ‌environment. Beyond hosting AI ​models, it offers datasets, ​software libraries and cloud services used to build and deploy AI applications.Explore more on these topicsNvidiaAI (artificial intelligence)ComputingTechnology sectornewsShareReuse this content
