title: Bring on the drones: how a technology revolution is being rolled out across Africa’s nature reserves | Global development | The Guardian
description: As graduates of an online training course gather from across the continent, the consensus is overwhelming: computers and saving animals go together
Author: Nick Dall
Headline: As graduates of an online training course gather from across the continent, the consensus is overwhelming: computers and saving animals go together
Content: Mabel Nokhuthula Piki from the Chinhoyi University of Technology in Zimbabwe takes part in the new conservation tech course at Lapalala reserve, South Africa.Photograph: Courtesy of CCFView image in fullscreenMabel Nokhuthula Piki from the Chinhoyi University of Technology in Zimbabwe takes part in the new conservation tech course at Lapalala reserve, South Africa.Photograph: Courtesy of CCFThe age of extinctionGlobal developmentBring on the drones: how a technology revolution is being rolled out across Africa’s nature reservesAs graduates of an online training course gather from across the continent, the consensus is overwhelming: computers and saving animals go togetherThe age of extinction is supported byAbout this contentNick DallThu 3 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 05.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn a bitingly cold night inLapalala Wildernessnature reserve in South Africa’s Limpopo province, Duncan Kanyakera watches as instructor Jacques Viljoen deploys a thermal drone in search of a lone cheetah. Once the drone has disappeared into the inky sky, Kanyakera, from Tsavo in Kenya, and 20 other conservation professionals from across Africa turn their attention to the open-air screen in anticipation.Many of the students – from 11 African countries as far flung as Benin, Liberia, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Madagascar – witnessing the demonstration have earned their places at Lapalala after performing well on an online training programme for protected area technicians (PAT) run by the Connected Conservation Foundation (CCF). Also on the course, are five members ofPeace Parksstaff in training.“Data and technology are critical to modern conservation,” says CCF’s Sophie Maxwell. “Cameras and collars and software like EarthRanger have transformed the fight against poaching … But then an elephant knocks over a pole and you are back to square one.”View image in fullscreenStudents learn how to use, maintain and repair a range of technology used in protecting wildlife.Photograph: Courtesy of CCFSince 2015, the CCF hasinstalled state-of-the-art tech systems in parks across Africawith remarkable success, helping to protect nearly 10m hectares (25m acres). “Parks with tech solutions are safer and more biodiverse and they have better relationships with communities,” says Maxwell.Over the years, the CCF has “identified a critical gap”, says Carien Soldatos who oversees the PAT training programme: “Tech is fantastic, but it all depends on having trained technicians on the ground. Without people who know how to use, repair and maintain them, the fanciest gizmos in the world aren’t much use.” While there are such people in some parks, they are sorely lacking in many parts ofAfrica.After searching everywhere for a tech course aimed at conservation professionals, the CCF decided tocreate its own. Their 10-module course, which launched in July 2025, was a global first. In the first year, 680 people from all over the world finished at least one module. Those who completed all 10 modules were invited to interviews, with the top 16 chosen to attend the practical component at Lapalala.In less than 10 minutes, the heat sensor technology in the drone launched by Viljoen locates the cheetah resting with her cubs. Once he has locked its location, the operator sends a pin to the park’s on-duty field rangers, who rush to the scene. “I was stunned,” says Kanyakera. “There was no moon and the cheetah was miles away from us. But we could see exactly what was happening as the rangers got out of their vehicle and checked up on her.”Kanyakera, who works for the Taita Taveta Wildlife Conservancies Association (TTWCA) to support a network of 35 conservancies and ranches in Kenya’s vast Tsavo landscape, recognised immediately how handy a drone would be back home. Human-wildlife conflict is a challenge in Tsavo: “If an elephant gets into a corn field, it causes havoc,” he says. “And then you have the problem of humans retaliating.”View image in fullscreenSixteen people were chosen from across Africa to attend this year’s practical course, with a second planned for early next year.Photograph: Courtesy of CCFThe aim, says Kanyakera, is to keep humans and animals apart via designated wildlife corridors. But this gets tricky in the dry season when animals and humans alike are drawn towards water. Currently, if Kanyakera gets reports of an elephant near a village, he has to first work out where the elephant is and which direction it is moving in, before deploying rangers to intervene. This can take hours.“With a drone, we could find the elephant in minutes,” he says. “The noise of the drone alone would probably be enough to scare the animal off. And if that doesn’t work, I can deploy rangers much more accurately.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every fortnightSign up toGlobal DispatchGet a different world view with a roundup of the best news, features, opinion and photography, curated by our global development teamEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe course featured guest lectures and practicals on subjects including connectivity, communication and monitoring sensors.Photograph: Courtesy of CCFWhile a night-vision drone is the most exciting item on Kanyakera’s Christmas list, the course has also shown him how simple changes could drastically improve the tech “stack” back in Tsavo. This has a lot to do with the course design, explains Maxwell: “Each day, they build a new element of the stack,” she says, “before breaking it down at the end of each day and building it again the next morning to add another layer. It’s all about building muscle memory.”And it seems to be working. “As soon as I get home, I’ll reconfigure our camera traps to make the most of AI,” says Kanyakera who also has his sights set on re-equipping the ops room in Tsavo. “In the past, we would just Google and make a decision. Now I know so much more, I can target what I really want. The learnings from this course can make a big difference to the people and animals of Tsavo.”The course – which featured guest lectures and practicals from nine experts on topics including connectivity, communication, power systems, monitoring sensors, hardware integration and GIS visualisation tools – is having an impact far beyond Tsavo.Effort Zivengwa, who works at theZimbabwe Parks and Wildlife Management Authorityhead office in Harare, is part of a tech team responsible for 11 national parks. “We were content with what we were doing,” he says. “But, after completing this course, I think we have to do more. We are already usingEarthRangerand we do have sensors, but they are not integrated.“We have park headquarters and lodges that don’t have internet access,” he adds. “Using point-to-point internet can fix that problem easily.” The learning module on solar power further shifted his understanding of what is possible. “We have a lot of remote stations,” he says. “But the sun shines everywhere.”View image in fullscreenMabel Nokhuthula Piki plans to use what she has learned to teach her own students how computers can help save animals.Photograph: Courtesy of CCFMabel Nokhuthula Piki, who teaches wildlife monitoring skills at the Chinhoyi University of Technology in central Zimbabwe, has also found the course empowering. “My students didn’t comprehend that tech was important. They couldn’t get the link between saving animals and computers. But now I am going to change their minds,” she says. “It is impossible to understand the value of tech until you have seen it.”The CCF is planning to run a second practical course with another batch of students in the first quarter of 2027. What is more, says Soldatos, “we will be supporting five participants from the first course with internships and/or hardware donations”. The lucky five have not yet been chosen, but Kanyakera, Zivengwa and Piki are all in the running.Find moreage of extinction coverage here, and follow the biodiversity reportersPhoebe WestonandPatrick Greenfieldin the Guardian app for more nature coverageExplore more on these topicsGlobal developmentThe age of extinctionConservationSouth AfricaAfricafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Ruin and decay bring a chance of rebirth’: Hidetaka Miyazaki on uniting players in a damaged world | Games | The Guardian
description: As FromSoftware’s new multiplayer game The Duskbloods nears release, the legendary game director behind Dark Souls talks connection, pessimism and of course, feet
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: As FromSoftware’s new multiplayer game The Duskbloods nears release, the legendary game director behind Dark Souls talks connection, pessimism and of course, feet
Content: ‘Of all the things Miyazaki and his team do well, creating a sense of mystery is the greatest’ … The Duskbloods.Photograph: NintendoView image in fullscreen‘Of all the things Miyazaki and his team do well, creating a sense of mystery is the greatest’ … The Duskbloods.Photograph: NintendoGamesInterview‘Ruin and decay bring a chance of rebirth’: Hidetaka Miyazaki on uniting players in a damaged worldKirk McKeandAs FromSoftware’s new multiplayer game The Duskbloods nears release, the legendary game director behind Dark Souls talks connection, pessimism and of course, feetThu 3 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 12.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSince 2009’s Demon’s Souls, Japanese video game director Hidetaka Miyazaki has shown the world a different way to think about game design. His games defy convention with punishing fights, obscure rules, and unknowable, inhospitable worlds. The “Soulslike” genre – named afterDemon’s Soulsand its sequelDark Souls– is now ubiquitous, influencing multimillion-sellers from God of War and Star Wars: Jedi to Hollow Knight. Miyazaki’s most recent success, 2022’sElden Ring, which credited Game of Thrones author George RR Martin as a co-creator, sold over 30m copies and inspired Alex Garland to adapt it for the big screen at A24. It earned Miyazaki a spot on Time magazine’s “most influential” list, an accolade he shares with just one other game developer: Mario creator Shigeru Miyamoto.Miyazaki is now 51 and has been FromSoftware’s president since 2014, elevated from game designer to CEO after the success of the Souls series. He has a cherubic face that could pass for 35. He rarely speaks publicly, and never on camera. When he does speak, he answers questions like one of his characters – softly, sadly, his head bowed, making eye-contact only when I am speaking. Outside the studio where we speak is the sprawl of Tokyo’s Shinjuku, an ever-changing maze where tourists get lost and pop-up stores appear and vanish without a trace. Today, a J-pop band performs in the square as the cicadas scream from the trees. A gilded statue of Malania, one of Elden Ring’s toughest bosses, looms over this dimly lit conference room inside From’s headquarters, a bonfire checkpoint away from the chaos.View image in fullscreenHe creates an ‘atmosphere of wonder’ … Hidetaka Miyazaki accepts a Bafta games award for Elden Ring in 2023.Photograph: Stuart Wilson/Bafta/Getty Images for BaftaFromSoftware’s in-game universes are filled with clues – enemies, places and scraps of information from item descriptions paint a vague image of the world, and the player fills the blank space. You never fully understand these domains, although countless YouTube video game theorists have tried – as have other developers in awe of his work. “Of all the many things Miyazaki and his team do well, creating a sense of mystery is the greatest,” explains Dishonored directorHarvey Smith, who has more than 40 days’ playtime in Elden Ring. “It’s so incredibly hard to do in video games, which are technical systems … But Miyazaki somehow creates an atmosphere of wonder. Even when finishing, you are left ruminating on fun, murky elements that feel half understood. It’s a delicious sense of intrigue.”Rather than the single-player action game that Miyazaki’s audience craves (fans are desperate for a sequel to his 2015 gothic masterpiece Bloodborne,for instance), hislatest project The Duskbloodsis a multiplayer Switch 2 exclusive. Eight players face off against ghoulish horrors, fighting each other to avoid being culled at the end of each round. The survivors are whittled down over three phases culminating in a final three-way battle. The Duskbloods is releasing to an audience with shifting tastes and trends, and it is certainly a risk. “I’m very nervous,” Miyazaki says. “With every title we release there is this mounting tension.”The game opens with an arresting image: one hand reaching out for another. A male character is slumped on a chair, dejected; the shot moves in close to focus on their draped fingers. From below the frame, a pale hand slowly reaches out and caresses them before gently clasping his wrist. Hands are a recurring motif in Miyazaki’s games; in Elden Ring, massive crawling hands burrow up from underground to attack you, and hand-like giants are revered as deities.“It’s not necessarily something I’m consistently aware of – maybe it’s something subconscious coming through,” Miyazaki says when I ask about this imagery. “Take a look online and there’s a rumour that I have a bit of a thing for feet, but I’m not honestly sure where this comes from. I feel like I’m trying to depict some side of human nature or the human existence that is difficult to describe.” (His games have featured, by my count, at least six barefoot female characters.)View image in fullscreen‘It’s rumoured I have a bit of a thing for feet’ … Elden Ring Nightreign.Photograph: Bandai NamcoPerhaps all the hands and feet are symbolic of human connection. One hand reaches for another; bare feet connect skin with earth.Miyazaki has been exploring that theme since Demon’s Souls, whose novel, stranger-centric multiplayer was inspired by a time his car slipped on an icy hill and a stranger helped to push him to safety. In Demon’s Souls and the Dark Souls series, players paint runes on the ground, which other players can then use to summon help in a fight, creating moments of spontaneous togetherness before an inevitable parting.While The Duskbloods primarily puts players in opposition, it also explores temporary alliances and conflicting objectives, buoyed by Miyazaki’s love for tabletop role-playing games and board games. Players can even become betrothed to each other, forming an alliance. “I feel it’s less a traditional romance and more a sense of secure trust with a character in the world, and that’s something I personally yearn for,” he says. “It’s not necessarily a romantic pairing – it’s having someone that you can ultimately rely on. This concept is carried through from characters like the maidens in Elden Ring … it’s a transient, ephemeral love, which is maybe a motif I’m striving for.”The Duskbloods is preoccupied with ruin and rebirth, a thematic cornerstone of From’s games – much as Godzilla was a product of nuclear paranoia in Japan. Even as Miyazaki and I talk, a deadly magnitude 6.8 earthquake hits the Kumamoto prefecture on Kyushu island, a thousand miles away. If the very ground beneath your feet is unreliable, that can shape your outlook on life, a concept explored extensively in Japanese literature and entertainment, recently on the hit television showShōgun.“[Ruin and rebirth] is an ongoing theme in a lot of my games, I realise,” Miyazaki says. “That theme on a cosmological scale applies to The Duskbloods as an interesting philosophical area to explore.”View image in fullscreen‘If we have two ideas of a brighter or dark future, I would tend to sway towards the darker one,’ …Bloodborne.Photograph: Sony Computer EntertainmentMiyazaki describes himself as a pessimist, a tendency that he believes comes across in his output. That should be obvious to anyone who’s finished any of his games, in which you keep throwing body and blade against seemingly impossible odds, reborn each time you die at a bonfire checkpoint, to try again. Even when you triumph, nothing ultimately seems to change: these games culminate in bleak, morally ambiguous gut-punches, leaving you not as a conquering hero but as the perpetuator of a hopeless cycle. “If we have two ideas of a brighter or dark future, I would tend to sway towards the darker one,” Miyazaki says. “[But] if you explore the ruin and the decay in those worlds, it also lets you explore some chance of rebirth, and I think having that tiny pinprick of light or hope can be something beautiful, something fleeting.”Sekiro, Dark Souls, Bloodborne, and Elden Ring are all separate series, but they share the same bones. They’re reborn in different forms, to explore fresh ideas, places and perspectives while still playing, feeling and sounding like a FromSoftware game. While it’s immediately clear The Duskbloods is a Miyazaki game, it too wears a different skin, inspired by extraction shooters like Escape from Tarkov and those tabletop role-playing games the director loves. “There’s no intentional FromSoftware [mantra] – ‘this is the way we make our games’ – because if you start to do that it becomes stale and conservative, and you start having to adhere to a set of rules and philosophies, and it just doesn’t become interesting, you can’t make anything that’s as fun,” Miyazaki says.“So I feel like at least what’s worked for us philosophically is trying to adhere to what we find interesting first. I think that has created a good throughline through our games, and that’s what we concentrate on to [conceive] a new title.”Back in his early days at the studio, when he was only a coder on the Armored Core series of games, Miyazaki volunteered to take on a struggling project at From – the game that would become Demon’s Souls. (The game was already in trouble, so he felt he had nothing to lose.) He changed everything about the game, and then the game changed everything about his life, as he climbed from coder to company president. From failure was born a game that changed the landscape of video games. Ruin and rebirth.But does Miyazaki think he has changed? “I don’t intend to,” he says, a smile curling on his lips. “But I probably have.”This article was amended on 3 September 2026 to correct the release year of the original Demon’s Souls.Explore more on these topicsGamesAction gamesRole playing gamesinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Women are giving their partners the ‘Illiterate Boyfriend’ test: ‘Do your best to pronounce these words’ | TikTok | The Guardian
description: People online are distressed at men butchering words such as ‘hyperbole’ and ‘hors d’oeuvres’ – highlighting a gender reversal in ‘intelligence gaps’
Author: Alaina Demopoulos
Headline: People online are distressed at men butchering words such as ‘hyperbole’ and ‘hors d’oeuvres’ – highlighting a gender reversal in ‘intelligence gaps’
Content: ‘It’s not necessarily that someone needs a specific degree or to know every word in the dictionary,’ said Robin Hamilton, a couples therapist. ‘It’s more: are you able to communicate with me?’Illustration: Rita Liu/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘It’s not necessarily that someone needs a specific degree or to know every word in the dictionary,’ said Robin Hamilton, a couples therapist. ‘It’s more: are you able to communicate with me?’Illustration: Rita Liu/The GuardianTikTokWomen are giving their partners the ‘Illiterate Boyfriend’ test: ‘Do your best to pronounce these words’People online are distressed at men butchering words such as ‘hyperbole’ and ‘hors d’oeuvres’ – highlighting a gender reversal in ‘intelligence gaps’Alaina DemopoulosThu 3 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 07.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere are common non-negotiables we look for in a prospective partner. They should be kind, caring and thoughtful. Having a shared interest helps. So does remembering important dates and anniversaries. But how much does it matter if they know how to pronounce the word “gnocchi”?Turns out that’s a potential dealbreaker, at least according to a (rather judgy) cohort onTikTok. See: the “Illiterate Boyfriend” trend, which is testing some couples on the app. Users have compiled a list of what are essentially SAT words for women to ask their male partners to read. Many of these men – this is an overwhelmingly heterosexual activity – fail to finish the list unscathed. They trip over entries such as “hyperbole”, “cynicism”, “diaphragmatic” and the oft-butchered French term, “hors d’oeuvres”.“I want you to do your best to pronounce these words,” one woman asks her boyfriend in aclipviewed more than 8.8m times. He gamely nails his first attempt, reading off the herb “thyme”. But he’s less successful with “epitome”, “challah” and “fuchsia”. (“Foo-chia?” he guesses). “Conscientious” and “faux pas” also prove tricky. He ends up with a score of five out of 17, or 29% – very much a failing grade.Is it, like, OK to say ‘like’ now?Read moreThe couple laughed through the exercise, but viewers were not as charmed by an adult man struggling through what they considered basic vocabulary. “The fact that his vote matters just as much as mine is really pissing me off,” one woman wrote in the comments section. “I’m gonna be honest girl, this is worth breaking up with him over,” read another comment.Two of the words the man correctly identified were “colonel” and “regime”, which, to one user, was evidence of ared flag: “he’s obviously a Republican”. (Maybe he just has an interest in military history, a time-honored hobby of boyfriends everywhere.) Regardless of political affiliation, it seemed fair game to dunk on Mr Foo-chia. One final quip from a viewer: “He’d be so upset if he could read these comments.”The test made its way around TikTok, with more young couples joining in, to similarly bleak results. Even those men who did well got caught up in the pop-misandry circus. One man zipped through the list, ending with a perfect score and a self-satisfied grin. It was not the flex he might have hoped for. “This is the barest fckn minimumest [sic] of bare minimums,” one woman commented. “The men are being praised for literacy we’re in hell,” wrote another.double quotation markWe do have in our mating market an oversupply of educated women and an undersupply of formally educated menDr Wendy WalshDistress over so-called “intelligence gaps” brings to mind a phenomenon that reverses decades of dating precedent: women are nowmore likelyto marry less-educated men than men are to marry less-educated women. This is not necessarily by women’s choice; it is the new dating pool. According to a 2024 Pew Researchreport, in 1995, young men and women were equally likely to hold a bachelor’s degree. Now, 47% of women ages 25 to 34 have one, compared with 37% of their male counterparts.“We do have in our mating market an oversupply of educated women and an undersupply of formally educated men – I’m talking academically, not necessarily in their skill set, emotional or social intelligence,” said Dr Wendy Walsh, a clinical psychologist and expert atDatingNews.com.Dr Jess Carbino is a former sociologist for Tinder and Bumble who studies dating apps. When she polls people on what they look for in a partner, “intelligence” is rarely in the top three desired traits. “They say things like humor, kindness, attractiveness, typically,” she said. “Maybe people on the coasts – New York, Los Angeles, San Francisco – might say intelligence. But by and large, that’s not one of the top things being measured.” And there are so many different ways to consider intelligence, spelling being a way to formally test fourth-graders, not romantic partners.One thing people do want is an equal. “It’s not necessarily that someone needs a specific degree or to know every word in the dictionary,” said Robin Hamilton, a couples therapist. “It’s more: are you able to communicate with me, are you able to meet me halfway with the subjects that I’m talking about?”One of those subjects might bereading, an indicator ofvocabulary range. Men’srates of book readinghave slipped over the past decade; nearly half of all women read just one novel or short story in 2022, but only one in four men did. According to data from Tinder, mentions of books in bios on the dating app jumped 40% this year among women, but only 23% among men. Women believe they see this disparity playing out on TikTok, even if it is through an ultimately meaningless list.It is elitist – and naive – to draw any real conclusions about what makes a good partner based on a reading test. This “Illiterate Boyfriend” list contains words that may be more indicator of class than intelligence, conflating education with one trait women have prioritized for hundreds of years, mostly due to necessity: having money.But the trend also reflects awider disillusionment among straight women, who are significantly less likely towant to datethan men are, partly because they say it’s hard to find someone who checks all their boxes. “He looks at the word ‘queue’ and pronounces it ‘qwi-wee’?” onewomansaid in avideoresponding to the test. “And youstillhave sex with him?”“It’s rage bait for women who are frustrated and angry with the mating marketplace that is slanted unfairly” against women, Walsh said, adding: “It’s OK to date a guy who can’t say epitome or niçoise. I have a PhD, but I need spellcheck for hors d’oeuvres.”Explore more on these topicsTikTokLanguageRelationshipsWomenMenLiteracyUS educationfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Gloria Steinem personified America’s feminist movement | Moira Donegan | The Guardian
description: The activist made the movement mainstream – and became a receptacle for its hopes and disappointments
Author: Moira Donegan
Headline: The activist made the movement mainstream – and became a receptacle for its hopes and disappointments
Content: ‘Steinem stood in for a large swath of feminists – intellectuals and activists, writers and organizers, liberals and radicals, lesbians and Playboy bunnies – and did her best to respect them all.’Photograph: Granger/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘Steinem stood in for a large swath of feminists – intellectuals and activists, writers and organizers, liberals and radicals, lesbians and Playboy bunnies – and did her best to respect them all.’Photograph: Granger/ShutterstockOpinionGloria SteinemGloria Steinem personified America’s feminist movementMoira DoneganThe activist made the movement mainstream – and became a receptacle for its hopes and disappointmentsGloria Steinem, groundbreaking feminist campaigner, dies aged 92‘We badly need to raise our boys more like our girls’: Gloria Steinem – a life in quotesThu 3 Sep 2026 15.47 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 16.26 EDTShareBy the time she died on Wednesday, at 92 years old at her home in New York,Gloria Steinemwas synonymous with feminism, a kind of human mascot for the movement. So it can be easy to forget that when she was born, feminism was over. It was something that had been faddish years before, among women who were now old ladies; something that seemed, in retrospect, like it might have been a bit overwrought and out of touch. To the girl Gloria Steinem, growing up in Ohio in the 1930s and 40s, the suffrage movement that had gained women the right to vote less than two decades prior probably seemed remote – especially to a girl like her, growing up itinerant and poor under the care of a single mother who was plagued by a violent and debilitating mental illness. You might say that growing up, Steinem had worries that were more immediate than the status of women.But experience has a way of radicalizing women about their own gendered condition. Steinem attended Smith, and her education opened up previously unhoped for possibilities. En route to a postgraduate fellowship in India in 1957, when she was in her early 20s, she had an illegal abortion in London. Later, in 1969, while she was working as a journalist for New York magazine, she attended an “abortion speak-out” put on by a group of radical women from the emergent fringe of what was then called the Women’s Liberation movement.Gloria Steinem obituaryRead moreThe women, crowded into a church near Washington Square Park, talked about being blindfolded in the backs of cars as the mobsters drove them to motels, where illegal abortions were performed by drunk, lascivious or simply cruel doctors. They talked about having to threaten suicide, over and over, to get a legal exemption; they talked about lying in hospital wards, hemorrhaging or riddled with sepsis, unsure that they would live. Their rage at the pain and humiliation struck something in Steinem. She had already been writing about women’s status – her famous article “A Bunny’s Tale”, in which she went undercover at the Playboy Club, ears and all – had been published six years before. But the woman Steinem would become was born on that March day, in that church.The woman who walked out would become one of the most successful and visible faces of the second wave, a figurehead who came to personify the feminist movement itself. The former journalist, keenly aware of both the dynamics of mass media and of the potential uses of her own willowy good looks, deployed stardom and glamour in the service of the feminist cause. She was not the first famous feminist, but she might be said to have been the first famous feminist of the celebrity era, forging a public persona halfway between Madonna and Joan of Arc. Her magazine Ms, launched in 1972, brought the women’s liberation movement, once largely confined to the hip downtowns of major cities such as New York and Chicago, to newsstands across America. But Steinem’s work was not exclusive to the media: she also campaigned relentlessly, and sometimes successfully, to make the feminist movement a power player within the Democratic party, brokering her own support in exchange for policy commitments from candidates.Steinem’s image – powerful, beautiful and connected – lent feminism an allure and mass appeal. Few accomplished so much in making women’s rights and dignity a mainstream American concern, but Steinem’s aim, to her credit, was always to use her own more palatable image to direct attention to other people’s work, to more expansive visions for justice and to more challenging ideas. Not everyone followed her; not everyone took her up on her work’s invitation to move from feminism’s more gentle demands to its more radical ones. Some did.double quotation markSteinem’s position as an embodiment of women’s struggle meant that her public persona became a receptacle for all its hopes and disappointmentsWhat does it mean to be a figurehead and a human symbol for a movement that aspires to represent fully half of the human race? Steinem’s position as an embodiment of women’s struggle meant that her public persona became a receptacle for all its hopes and disappointments; she was both credited with feminism’s achievements and blamed for its failures, even when these achievements and failures were not hers. Critics have blasted Steinem’s move to insert herself as the representative of feminism as a kind of savvy and opportunistic ambition. I prefer to think of it as a kind of generosity. She stood in for a large swath of feminists – intellectuals and activists, writers and organizers, liberals and radicals, lesbians and Playboy bunnies – and did her best to respect them all.Both at the peak of the second wave and in the latter decades of her life, this role was one of dedicated coalition building. The feminist movement, in the second wave era as now, was amorphous and internally fractious, deeply divided by disagreements over priorities, tactics, and even ultimate aims. Perhaps it was because of the power of Steinem’s celebrity, or her formidable gifts as a fundraiser, that when Steinem took a side in these rifts, that side tended to win.Hillary Clinton leads tributes to Gloria Steinem: ‘Her activism was rooted in optimism’Read moreBut in a movement, like many others, where political differences often became personal vendettas, Steinem was an uncommonly gracious opponent – unusually willing to engage in self-criticism, to engage across deeply felt difference, and to encourage younger feminists whose visions did not exactly match her own. She lent her advice and imprimatur to feminist initiatives ranging from the anodyne and corporate to the incendiary and radical. From her perch on the Upper East Side, she acted as an elder stateswoman and patron saint for a movement that had changed beyond what her younger self would have recognized. Feminists of all different generations made pilgrimages uptown to kneel beside her chair. For years, she seems to have answered every email, taken every meeting, and met everyone’s little daughter.What will the feminist movement be without her? Any honest account of the status of women in Steinem’s life would have to admit that feminism, as a political movement for women’s liberation, is in a moment of precipitous retreat. In the decades after she founded Ms, at the height of the second wave, the movement’s grassroots activist energy diminished. Both the academy and the organized radical left largely lost interest in women’s status. If the rise of social media briefly looked like it might channel women’s ongoing discontent with the violence and indignity of their lives into measurable political action, it quickly proved to be more effective in mobilizing mass male resentment and spreading viral misinformation about birth control. Roe was struck down.Organized feminism, now, is largely the province of a few liberal NGOs, righteous but battered, which are coming in for more and more persecution from the Trump regime and its allies. If feminism is to be revived, now, it will have to be rebuilt. Without Steinem, the task will be that much harder.Moira Donegan is a Guardian US columnistExplore more on these topicsGloria SteinemOpinionFeminismActivismWomenCivil rights movementcommentShareReuse this content

title: In 2016, Trump pledged to erase the federal debt. It just hit $40tn | Steven Greenhouse | The Guardian
description: The trillions in tax cuts going to the rich and corporations could have instead been used to address the affordability crisis
Author: Steven Greenhouse
Headline: The trillions in tax cuts going to the rich and corporations could have instead been used to address the affordability crisis
Content: ‘It would be a very different thing if Trump were borrowing money to build a better future.’Photograph: Annabelle Gordon/EPAView image in fullscreen‘It would be a very different thing if Trump were borrowing money to build a better future.’Photograph: Annabelle Gordon/EPAOpinionUS economyIn 2016, Trump pledged to erase the federal debt. It just hit $40tnSteven GreenhouseThe trillions in tax cuts going to the rich and corporations could have instead been used to address the affordability crisisThu 3 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 12.44 EDTShareDear reader, I recognize that your eyes might glaze over at any mention of the nation’s$40tnfederal debt. But your reaction to this mind-boggling number shouldn’t be ennui; it should be outrage and dismay.Outrage is in order because the nation’s debt has climbed to more than $40tn under Donald Trump, even though back in 2016, when the debt wasless than half what it is today, candidate Trump insisted that he’dtotally eliminate the debt within eight years. That was yet another example of the Demagogue-in-Chief’s willingness to say anything, no matter how insincere or untrue, to woo voters.Not only has Trump failed to reduce the debt, he has spectacularly increased it. Take Trump’s “big, beautiful bill” and thehuge tax cutsit lavished upon the very rich and corporations. That legislation is expected toincrease the nation’s debtby a whopping $3.4tn over the next decade. Worse, during Trump’s time as president, including his first term, the federal debt hasclimbed by a colossal $11.6tn.Outrage is also in order because the trillions in tax cuts going to the rich and corporations could have instead been used to address the affordability crisis that is squeezing so many Americans. Those trillions could have gone to creating more affordable childcare for every family or increasing subsidies to hold down soaring healthcare premiums or expanding government aid to make college more affordable.We surveyed 6,000 Americans. Here is the winning message for Democrats | Dustin GuastellaRead moreTrump’s tax cuts for the rich and the $40tn debt have worsened the affordability crisis in one important and painful way. They have helped push up long-term interest rates to their highest level in nearly two decades, and that has pushed up mortgage rates, too. The unhappy result: housing has become less affordable, when housing affordability has already been a big problem for young Americans. Higher mortgage rates often mean that homebuyers have to pay several hundred dollars more in interest each month.Interest rates have climbed not only because investors are dismayed that the national debt has hit a record, but also because Trump’s tariffs and war against Iran have fueled inflation and because investors are unsettled by all the chaos Trump has created at home and abroad.Outrage is also called for because of the way Trump and his Republican yes-men in Congress jumped to enact giant tax cuts when their super-wealthy donors and friends said jump. In a move that shows how rigged the system is, Trump and the GOP legislated these tax cuts for the rich and corporations even though the wealthy and corporations were already doing perfectly well and would continue doing just fine, with their mansions, yachts and private jets, even without those tax cuts. Of the $4.4tn in tax cuts in the “big, beautiful bill”,nearly half go to the richest 5%of Americans.If any further evidence is needed to show that Republicans in Congress have sold their souls to billionaires, millionaires and corporations, the increased debt caused by the big, unbeautiful bill’s tax cuts will be a burden on our children and grandchildren for decades to come. By the mid-2030s, the nation will have topay more than $2tn in interest paymentseach year to finance the federal debt. That’s double the $1tn a year we are paying now – $1tn is slightly less than what thegovernment spends on Medicare, is higher thanthis year’s Pentagon budgetand is more than five times what the federal governmentspends on education each year.All this is maddening for another reason. In recent decades, Republicans held themselves out as the party of “fiscal responsibility”. But they’ve really become the party of fiscal irresponsibility. During George W Bush’s two terms, with his tax cuts tilted toward the wealthy and his expensive, ill-fated war against Iraq, the federal debtballooned by 85%(by $4.9tn). In Trump’s first term, the debtsoared by $7.8tn(a 39% increase), stemming from his initial big tax cuts for the rich as well as increased Pentagon spending – and then there wasmore than $2tn in emergency spendingto stabilize the economy during the first year of the Covid-19 pandemic.During Trump’s second term, the debt is likely to soar by nearly $8tn once again. Trump ispushingfor a record $1.5tn annual defense budget, far higher than any previous year, even though it will send our country’s debt further into the stratosphere. Some of that money will go to redesigning aircraft carriersmerely becauseTrump dislikes how the current ones look.Bill Clinton was the last president to have an annual budget surplus, but Democratic presidents have also pushed up the federal debt. During Biden’s four years as president, the debt rose $8.4tn, partly because of the annual budget deficits he inherited from Trump and partly because of his$2tn-plus pandemic-era emergency spending packageto stabilize families’ finances and ensure the US didn’t sink into a deep economic downturn.Trump has made our K-shaped economy even worse | Steven GreenhouseRead moreThe federal debt has grown even larger than the country’s overall gross domestic product. Indeed, the ratio of the debt to GDP will soon be higher than the record 106% where it stood when the second world war ended. Franklin D Roosevelt ran up huge debts for an urgent reason: to defeat Nazi Germany and its allies. In sharp contrast, under Trump, the US is running big deficits, of approximately $2tn a year, for the opposite of urgent reasons: to finance a disastrous war in Iran and to give big tax giveaways to two powerful groups that were already prospering, eg the ultra-wealthy and corporations.It would be a very different thing if Trump were borrowing money to build a better future, as people do to build a new house or pay for college. But Trump is not jacking up the country’s debt to improve our future; he’s not spending to improve education, childcare or our country’s infrastructure or to fix the housing crisis.I am not a fiscal conservative and nor are many Democrats, but it is a real concern that for the first time in US history, other countries and many investors seem truly worried about the record size of the federal debt. Those worries have spooked financial markets and pushed up interest rates.As the midterm elections heat up, the Democrats should attack Trump and the Republicans over the huge, fast-growing federal debt. Democrats need to make clear that Republicans have become the party of fiscal irresponsibility.We can agree that the $40tn debt isn’t a sexy issue, but the Democrats can and should turn it into a hard-hitting and winning campaign issue that they can use to hammer Trump and the Republicans, along with the affordability crisis and Trump’s calamitous war against Iran.Steven Greenhouse is a journalist and author, focusing on labor and the workplace, as well as economic and legal issuesExplore more on these topicsUS economyOpinionDonald TrumpTrump administrationUS domestic policyUS-Israel war on IranUS politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: Ben-Gvir posts Palestinians on conveyor belts to detention camps. The world is silent | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: Ben-Gvir did not come into power in a vacuum: he was helped into his position by an international community that has afforded Israel complete impunity
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: Ben-Gvir did not come into power in a vacuum: he was helped into his position by an international community that has afforded Israel complete impunity
Content: ‘Ben-Gvir is no aberration; he is the international community’s creation.’Photograph: Amir Levy/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Ben-Gvir is no aberration; he is the international community’s creation.’Photograph: Amir Levy/Getty ImagesOpinionIsraelBen-Gvir posts Palestinians on conveyor belts to detention camps. The world is silentArwa MahdawiBen-Gvir did not come into power in a vacuum: he was helped into his position by an international community that has afforded Israel complete impunityThu 3 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 06.01 EDTShareLet me introduce you to Itamar Ben-Gvir, the leader of Israel’s far-right Jewish Power (Otzma Yehudit) party, the minister of national security, and an almost cartoonishly evil man. You’ll have heard his name before: he made international news when hefilmed himselftaunting bound activists who had been detained trying to deliver humanitarian aid to Gaza. But you might not be familiar with many of his recent shocking comments, because they haven’t been widely covered by much of the US media.Let’s start with an AI-generated video that Ben-Gvir posted on Twitter/X on Sunday and thendeleted. It shows portly Palestinian prisoners being loaded on to a conveyor belt and going into a detention camp, then emerging emaciated. The caption is “we promised – we delivered!” which seems to be a reference to the national security minister’s promise toworsenconditions for Palestinian prisoners. An ambitious goal, considering conditions are already hellish: Israeli human rights group B’Tselem has likened the prisons where Palestinians are kept to “torture camps”.I’m being diplomatic with my summary of this latest video, by the way. I suggest you gowatch ityourself to fully take in how awful it is. (It may have been deleted, but it lives on online). If the podcaster Hasan Piker had tweeted something similar, with Israelis as the subject rather than Palestinians, it would be front-page news. US lawmakers, all of whom seem to be obsessed with Piker, would be demanding that the podcaster be punished.Ben-Gvir, by the way, has some imaginative ideas for punishment. One of his sick fantasies is to put crocodiles in moats around prisons where Palestinians are held to stop prison breaks. The plan is nowon holdbecause Israeli rights groups have said it is cruel to crocodiles.I can’t stress enough that, in any discussion of Palestinian “prisoners”, it’s important to remember that many of these people have not gone through any sort of due process. Thousands of prisoners, including about200 children, are held under “administrative detention”: a technocratic name for a dystopian practice.To quote the B’Tselemdefinition: “In administrative detention, a person is held without trial without having committed an offense, on the grounds that he or she plans to break the law in the future. As this measure is supposed to be preventive, it has no time limit. The person is detained without legal proceedings, by order of the regional military commander, based on classified evidence that is not revealed to them.”In other words: if you are Palestinian, heavily armed Israeli soldiers can come into your house in themiddle of the night, drag you into a de facto torture chamber despite the fact that you haven’t committed a crime, and hold you there indefinitely without telling you why you’re being held or informing your family where you are.When you hear the word “prisoner”, people like Ben-Gvir want you to think of dangerous terrorists who deserve everything they get. In reality, many are people like Layan Nasir: a23-year-old womanwho was taken away at gunpoint from her parents’ home for no clear reason and only made international news because she is a Christian.But back to Ben-Gvir, who presides over prisoners. One of the minister of national security’s greatest achievements is a racist death penalty law that, because of the way it is worded, exclusivelyapplies to Palestinians. Last month Ben-Gvir posted a video of a gallows complex where Palestinians convicted of terror offenceswill be hanged. For his birthday in June, he celebrated with anoose-themed cake.Ben-Gvir doesn’t just want to hang his enemies; he wants more bloodshed in Gaza – which is still very much a killing field despite a so-called ceasefire. “I think we should be doing 30 to 40 targeted assassinations [in Gaza] per night,”Ben-Gvir recently saidon a podcast. “Not just those who pose an immediate threat. There are people there who don’t deserve to live … They are not even people.”I could go on and on: Ben-Gvir is a busy man. He recently filmed himself entering prison cells containingPalestinian womenandtauntingthem. On the same podcast where he urged nightly killings in Gaza, he went on to say that he thought Israel should occupy the entirety of Gaza. And, on Monday, hestormedthe al-Aqsa mosque compound in East Jerusalem, accompanied by extremist settlers and with the protection of the Israeli military.This is something he does regularly: it is a blatant provocation and a contravention of an agreement that gives Muslims exclusive rights to worship at al-Aqsa while Jews pray at the Western Wall.Ben-Gvir and others like him, however, want to change the decades-old status quo and have Israel control everything. “We are in charge here in Jerusalem and all of the land of Israel,” Ben-Gvir said during a2023 visitto the compound.Ben-Gvir is so shameless that there is no way to spin his conduct. He has been condemned and sanctioned by politicians and governments around the world. Nevertheless, Israel’s apologists have tried to cast him as a fringe figure. “Ben-Gvir’s statements do not reflect the policy of the State of Israel and should be condemned by all who care about Israel’s future,” the American Jewish Committeestatedin August, after the politician’s comments about settlement in Gaza.Some of Ben-Gvir’s peers have also tried to distance themselves from the extremist. The foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, condemned the video where Ben-Gvir taunts foreign activistssaying: “You are not the face of Israel.”Make no mistake: Ben-Gvir may be an embarrassment, but he is no anomaly. He is very much the face of modernIsraeland his vision for the country accurately reflects the reality on the ground.“Israeli policy is directed toward making life unbearable for Palestinians wherever they live, so that their emigration can be described as an act of free will,” the Israeli journalist Amira Hasswrote in Haaretzthis week. “‘Erasure’ is the nightmare solution being written into reality every day.” Settler violence is escalating, more land in the West Bank and Gaza is being seized, and there has been widespread dehumanization of Palestinians inIsraeli society.Hass writes: “Together, these and similar forces are creating the material, ideological and psychological infrastructure within Israeli-Jewish society for another mass expulsion of Palestinians and for what might accompany it: mass slaughter.”I’m quoting Hass because she is a brilliant journalist. But, I’ll be honest, I’m also quoting her because I’m part-Palestinian and she’s Israeli. I’m quoting Hass because, by virtue of being Israeli, she is seen as someone worth listening to. The world has made it very clear that it doesn’t want to listen to Palestinians, that we are barbarians who should not be believed.And it is this sort of widespread dehumanization that has resulted in the complete shamelessness of a man like Ben-Gvir. He did not come into power in a vacuum: he was helped into his position by an international community which has afforded Israel complete impunity. He has been aided and abetted by international media organizations that have helpeddemonize Palestinians, cast doubt on our claims, and manufacture consent for erasure and expulsion.He has been bolstered by lawmakers who tell us that we must defend Israel at all costs. And now, in the wasteland that is Gaza, in thenightlypogromsby Israeli settlers in the West Bank, and in Ben-Gvir’s brazen bloodlust, we are seeing the inevitable outcome of this unconditional support. Ben-Gvir is no aberration; he is the international community’s creation.Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian US columnistExplore more on these topicsIsraelOpinionGazaPalestinecommentShareReuse this content

title: The wars in Ukraine and Iran are becoming dangerously enmeshed | Christopher S Chivvis | The Guardian
description: As the Trump administration refuses to end its war in Iran, it is steering into the storm, not out of it
Author: Christopher S Chivvis
Headline: As the Trump administration refuses to end its war in Iran, it is steering into the storm, not out of it
Content: ‘Ratcliffe’s trip was necessary, especially in light of Russia’s reckless grey-zone operations in Europe. But it will not be enough.’Photograph: Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Ratcliffe’s trip was necessary, especially in light of Russia’s reckless grey-zone operations in Europe. But it will not be enough.’Photograph: Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc/Getty ImagesOpinionUkraineThe wars in Ukraine and Iran are becoming dangerously enmeshedChristopher S ChivvisAs the Trump administration refuses to end its war in Iran, it is steering into the storm, not out of itThu 3 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 11.12 EDTShareRussia hasn’t yet killed large numbers of Europeans outside Ukraine, but it’s getting closer. The night of 4-5 August, an airport bus driverdiscoveredan armed drone lying near the tarmac of the Leipzig-Halle airport, which is a central hub of Europe’s logistical support to Ukraine’s war effort. A cargo jet, meanwhile, may have struck a second drone shortly after takeoff, forcing an abrupt landing, and investigators founda third droneladen with military explosives nearby.In 2024, incendiary devices hidden in parcelsignited in DHL cargoat the same airport. Had these detonated in the air, a major air catastrophe and large-scale civilian casualties would have ensued, probably resulting in a broader war.The most recent incident may be what prompted the CIA director, John Ratcliffe, to get on a plane for Moscow last week. There, according to reports, hewarnedhis counterparts against attacks on Nato territory, urged them tocurb supportfor Iran, argued that escalation in Ukraine would backfire, and pressed fora dealwith Ukraine to end the war.Patriot missiles have been a godsend for Ukraine against Putin, but they’re running out. Kyiv needs help and fast | Jack WatlingRead moreRatcliffe’s trip is unlikely to have much impact on the Kremlin’s plans for an escalation againstUkrainein the coming months – but it is further evidence of the dangerous and growing enmeshment of the Iran and Ukraine wars.Sending Ratcliffe to Moscow is a logical choice for the White House, given the substantial role the intelligence services play in Putin’s government and justifiable concern that he may be getting too-rosy assessments of the war from his own team. The attempt at diplomacy is to be applauded. Nevertheless, the Trump administration’s refusal to end the war with Iran is working at cross purposes with their effort to end the war in Ukraine. They are steering into the storm, not out of it.One of the reasons for Ratcliffe’s visit to Moscow, according to the Washington Post, was todispel the Kremlin’s beliefthat the Trump White House was distracted from Ukraine by Iran. Good luck with that. The reporting on thesevere depletionof US interceptor stocks from the war on Iran is so extensive it can only haveencouragedVladimir Putin to launch even more deadly missile strikes against Ukraine’s defenseless population.Ukraine, for its part, hassent228 specialists and truckloads of drones to assist the Gulf states in their defense against Iranian missile strikes, prompting at least one Iranian lawmaker todeclare Ukraine fair gamefor its own attacks. And Ukrainestruck an Iranian commercial vesselin late July. Russia has meanwhileprovidedIran with battlefield intelligence that make its strikes more deadly. Moscow has, of course, also long benefited from Iranian-designed drones to attack Ukraine.Both conflicts are getting worse and going nowhere at the same time. True, Putin is in a pinch, with aneconomy badly damagedby Ukrainian strikes against Russian oil refineries and logistics hubs, but the pinch will just as easily prompt Russia’s leader toward escalation as it will restraint – especially if he sees the US distracted again in the Middle East and believes he has a window of opportunity to deal a crushing death blow to Kyiv.Putin, like Zelensky, like Trump, and like the Iranian leadership, faces the same sunk-cost dilemma that has led so many of history’s wartime leaders to double down on fruitless military operations – from Alcibiades in Sicily, to Napoleon inRussia, to LBJ in Vietnam. If today’s leaders follow suit, the costs and escalation risks will mount while the conflicts fuse further.Meanwhile, Xi Jinping and Putin met onMondayand will join Iran’s leaders in Bishkek this week for the annual summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization. They will discuss their plan to link their energy markets even more closely and probably condemn the new “economic offensive” that the US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, announcedlast weekto intensify pressure on Iran. Beijing may not want to see either war continue, but it also does not want to see Russia or Iran lose outright, and it is still in a strong position to avoid this outcome by helping the Iranians and Russians stave off the worst effects of the war on their economies and populations.Iran accuses US of ‘war crime’ after missile blast kills four people at weddingRead moreRatcliffe’s trip was necessary, especially in light of Russia’s reckless grey-zone operations inEurope. But it will not be enough. His predecessor, Bill Burns, once went to Moscow in an effort to warn Russia against attacking Ukraine. That intervention fell on deaf ears, as Ratcliffe’s also will.Clearer plans to end both wars through more positive inducements are badly needed.To start, Washington should settle withIranby unfreezing assets and offering sanctions relief in exchange for a real ceasefire and a framework arrangement for joint control of the strait by the littoral powers. It can then work to mitigate the consequences of this loss with a major push to diversify energy supplies – through alternative routes out of the region, alternative sources such as Venezuela, and a push on renewables. Ukraine, meanwhile, needs to become more serious about neutrality. It also needs a real debate about whether hanging on to the remainder of the Donbass it controls is worth indefinitely perpetuating the war.In the conclusion to his recent book, The Coming Storm, which traces the parallels between today’s world and the world on the eve of the first world war, the historian Odd Arne Westad writes: “A key lesson of the world before 1914 is that regional conflicts, long left unresolved, can be the powder kegs that set off a global conflagration.” As the Iran and Ukraine conflicts intertwine without an end in sight, the world’s leaders should take such warnings far more seriously. But without real pressure from their citizens, they may not.History is not doomed to repeat itself. But you don’t need to be a renowned historian to recognize the dangers the world is throwing up before us, nor to lament the failure of our leaders to calm these storms.Christopher S Chivvis is a senior fellow and director of the American Statecraft Program at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. He served as the United States national intelligence officer for Europe from 2018 to 2021Explore more on these topicsUkraineOpinionRussiaUS-Israel war on IranIranTrump administrationMiddle East and north AfricaEuropecommentShareReuse this content

title: Unlike Keir Starmer, Andy Burnham promises us that things will get better. And we must believe they can | Polly Toynbee | The Guardian
description: The PM’s warmth and feelgood policies, such as scrapping VAT on energy bills and a taskforce looking at political donations, offer something rare: hope, says Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee
Author: Polly Toynbee
Headline: The PM’s warmth and feelgood policies, such as scrapping VAT on energy bills and a taskforce looking at political donations, offer something rare: hope, says Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee
Content: Andy Burnham leaves 10 Downing Street, 2 September 2026.Photograph: Thomas Krych/APView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham leaves 10 Downing Street, 2 September 2026.Photograph: Thomas Krych/APOpinionLabourUnlike Keir Starmer, Andy Burnham promises us that things will get better. And we must believe they canPolly ToynbeeThe PM’s warmth and feelgood policies, such as scrapping VAT on energy bills and a taskforce looking at political donations, offer something rare: hopeThu 3 Sep 2026 12.36 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 13.48 EDTShareOf all the epithets thrown at a new prime minister, “people-pleaser” bounces off Andy Burnham. After all, the polls have him witha favourability rating of +13, making him the only party leader who scores above zero. His manner as he responded to all 125 of his questioners on his first Commons appearance this week had a warmth and empathy that his predecessor lacked. It’s a natural timbre, a good bedside manner for an uneasy country.Keir Starmer’s rating as he left officewas-36. He was defenestrated precisely because of his unpopularity. That baffled his allies, but his ratings crashed early into an electoral death zone from which no leader returns. His revenge comes in giving Labour a potentially awkwardbyelection confrontation with Zack Polanski: although, just as Burnham defeated the right in Makerfield, any candidate under his leadership stands a good chance of defeating the Greens in Holborn and St Pancras.Starmer’s fall began soon after Labour’s landslide victory in July 2024 with his message of foreboding gloom in the Downing Street garden. The country faced an economic and societal “black hole”, he said, adding that “things will get worse before they get better”.Burnham has avoided that kind of misery, on Tuesday making a promiseto “unlock a feeling of positivity and possibility” in every part of the country. And why not? Hope is always better than despair. It has its own elevating power that can stimulate growth, social optimism and investment. Even in the face of coming storms, it’s better by far to have a leader who raises spirits in adversity.The strongestEl Niño on record, exacerbated bythe stresses of the climate emergency, will hit the UK with tempestuously alarming weather through to early 2027. Equally alarming was that, even as Burnham spoke, thebond marketsset off their own El Niño with their global sell-off raising interest rates across the world, especially on UK debt. Their preference for investing in AI companies over governments may be the wrong bet, amid warnings of this bubble bursting to the devastation of the global economy. And still there is no sign that Donald Trump will end his calamitous war with Iran and free the world from its economic blight.Burnham, well-seasoned in the ways of politics, is fully armed against the cannonades from right and left. He’s all too familiar with the particular poison of most of the British press, for ever hostile to Labour. But the extra lashings of vitriol suggests the right are alarmed by his popularity. Here’s Tim Stanley, the Telegraph’s parliamentary sketch writer,on Burnham’s first Commons outing: “What a relief! The PM’s a dud. For a horrid moment I thought Labour had found a man who could flog socialism to simpletons, but Our Andy’s debut at the Dispatch Box – billed as make-or-break for the British Left – was met by embarrassed silence.”Presumably, it reassures Telegraph readers to be fed exaggeration when both Reform UK and the Conservatives are on the slide. Farage is not recovering from the scrutiny over his astounding £5m gift, while the Tories languish even below their 2024 election result, which was their lowest since 1832.They perk up at Kemi Badenoch becoming a little less unpopular. She is indeed more confident at PMQs, but her negative rating suggests she’s no people-pleaser. She leads her party downwards. My hunch is it’s not terminal: the Tories always resurrect, but only by shape-shifting to catch up with changing times, from which they periodically disconnect. But it won’t happen under her. Burnham is lucky to have an opponent swimming hard against the modern tide. Until the Tories repent, or at least recognise the catastrophic consequences of their Brexit, they won’t revive. Their anti-net zero climate extremism is bizarrely out of tune with a country that has just seenrecord heatwavesand which,Tory voters included, backs the zero emissions target.Her“slashing” Britain’s welfare billmay be what people want, but it also acts as a reminder of the sheer cruelty of the Tories’ austerity years. And she is prone to tumbling into her own elephant traps. She thought she had a gotcha when she challenged Burnham as a spendthrift: what had he cut? “Tax is the simple answer,” he said, quick as a flash, citingtwo tax cuts in his first week.His summer of goodwill defied Labour’s enemies, who enjoyed little success opposingcapping bus fares at £2, scrapping the 5%VAT on energy billsor the creation of No 10 North, all of which were well received by the public. They will hope hispledge to end rough sleeping in England by Christmasfails. When faced with the prison overcrowding crisis, he did the unpopular thing and released prisoners. Unwelcome public advice from friends, including his former economic adviserJim O’Neill, warning he must make cutsor tax rises has been picked up with glee by Badenoch. But oddly, she failed to mention his solution: end the ruinous triple lock on pensions.Many people are pleased that he will set aboutcapping political donations. Stella Creasy withdrew her strongly backed amendment to the representation of the people bill calling for a £500,000 cap, signalling her confidence in Burnham’s promised taskforce to draw up a plan. That’s a people-pleaser for a public disgusted with the squalor of cash swirling around Westminster. Another strongly backed amendment from Alex Sobel, to set up a national commission on electoral reform, was ruled out of the scope of the bill by the speaker, but the government confirmed it supports reform: it will be back and in the next manifesto.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThat’s a good start. You couldn’t hope for better. Can he buck the trend of prime ministers haemorrhaging popularity within months?Storms ahead are threatening. But facing into the wind with optimism is the way to go.Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
