title: Badly parked ebikes in London are a menace – but other cities have shown us the solution | Agustin Guilisasti | The Guardian
description: Paris converted tens of thousands of on-street parking spaces into docking stations, fundamentally changing its approach to public space, says Agustin Guilisasti, founder and CEO of the London ebike operator Forest
Author: Agustin Guilisasti
Headline: Paris converted tens of thousands of on-street parking spaces into docking stations, fundamentally changing its approach to public space, says Agustin Guilisasti, founder and CEO of the London ebike operator Forest
Content: Ebikes block a traffic island on Piccadilly, London, 13 November 2024.Photograph: Jeff Gilbert/AlamyView image in fullscreenEbikes block a traffic island on Piccadilly, London, 13 November 2024.Photograph: Jeff Gilbert/AlamyOpinionEbikesBadly parked ebikes in London are a menace – but other cities have shown us the solutionAgustin GuilisastiParis converted tens of thousands of on-street parking spaces into docking stations, fundamentally changing its approach to public spaceAgustin Guilisasti is founder and CEO of the London ebike operator ForestThu 3 Sep 2026 11.43 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 13.59 EDTShareShared ebikes have become a key part of London’s transport network. From Hounslow to Greenwich, it’s rare to step on to the street without seeing one, and they now facilitate millions of journeys every month. Forest recorded 3m rides this July alone, a new high. Demand keeps rising, and operators are logging ever-higher ride-per-bike ratios, a key measure of how intensively fleets are being used.This is good news for London, which gains a cleaner, healthier and more sustainable way to get around – one that eases reliance on private car ownership. And, with new research revealing that air-quality improvements driven by the ultra-low emission zone (Ulez)have led tobetter lung healthin children, the benefits of reducing polluting journeys are increasingly clear.But shared ebikes also draw real criticism. Poorly parked bikes make near-daily headlines, and with good reason. I’m acutely aware of the criticism directed at us and I know this is a problem. Misparked bikes, and the cluttered pavements they leave behind, cause understandable frustration. It’s a nuisance, and – at worst – a genuine hazard for pedestrians and other road users. Especially disabled pedestrians or those with access needs.But the solution doesn’t lie in fewer bikes – it lies in answering the crucial question around parking. Other European cities have shown that, with the right infrastructure and planning, shared ebikes can be woven into existing transport systems. They’ve done it by answering one key question: where should bikes go when they’re not moving?London’s cycling infrastructure has come a long way – theCycleway network now covers 450km(280 miles) – but our roads are still asked to accommodate buses, taxis, pedestrians, scooters, cyclists, private vehicles and mopeds within the same finite space. If London is serious about making shared ebikes part of its transport network, policymakersneed to rethink how that space is allocated, particularly when it comes to parking.Paris offers the clearest case study. The administration of the former mayor, Anne Hidalgo, didn’t just build cycle lanes; it fundamentally reconsidered how public space should be used once the pedalling stops. Her administrationconverted tens of thousands of on-street car parking spacesinto Vélib’ docking stations (Paris’s version of Transport for London’s Santander bike scheme) and dedicated bays for bikes and shared micromobility. These, incidentally, also made room for wider pavements and more trees.Hidalgo’s approach was informed by a simple insight: a single car parking spacecan hold about 10 bicycles. Repurposed, that space now serves hundreds of people a day instead of storing one stationary vehicle.London hasn’t yet had this conversation, but the timing has never been better, for two key reasons. First, car ownership in the capital is declining.Almost half of London households no longer own a car, rising to nearly two-thirds in inner London. Yet about 18% of households in inner London still own two or more vehicles.And, second, as part of the recently passed English Devolution and Community Empowerment Act, TfL has been tasked with designing a pan-London licensing framework for shared micromobility that will finally bring regulation to a market that has grown rapidly over the past five years. It is inevitable that parking for shared mobility schemes will be a key part of that framework’s design.I see this scheme’s design as a real opportunity to question whether one of the world’s best-connected cities should keep prioritising scarce street space for second cars, over transport that serves thousands of people every day.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFor example, if the mayor and TfL converted even 15% of the on-street parking currently taken up by second cars into dedicated micromobility bays, this would create space for almost 1m shared ebikes – far more than the estimated 50,000 already in London and far more than we would ever conceivably need – with every one of them parked on the carriageway, not the pavement.With help from operators, boroughs, TfL and the mayor, London could solve its ebike parking conundrum in an instant and get on with the most urgent task: integrating them into the transport system safely, sustainably and for the benefit of all Londoners.Agustin Guilisasti is founder and CEO of the London ebike operator ForestExplore more on these topicsEbikesOpinionTransport policyPublic transportLondonEnglandTransportcommentShareReuse this content

title: Billionaires hoarding wealth while the rest of us struggle need to ask themselves: what would Dolly do? | Rebecca Shaw | The Guardian
description: Every story about Dolly Parton’s generosity should shame the super-rich, who could easily make the world a better place for all
Author: Rebecca Shaw
Headline: Every story about Dolly Parton’s generosity should shame the super-rich, who could easily make the world a better place for all
Content: Dolly Parton performs at Glastonbury in 2014. ‘She had a deeply ingrained understanding that there are more important things than watching your bank balance grow,’ writes Rebecca Shaw.Photograph: Cathal McNaughton/ReutersView image in fullscreenDolly Parton performs at Glastonbury in 2014. ‘She had a deeply ingrained understanding that there are more important things than watching your bank balance grow,’ writes Rebecca Shaw.Photograph: Cathal McNaughton/ReutersOpinionThe super-richBillionaires hoarding wealth while the rest of us struggle need to ask themselves: what would Dolly do?Rebecca ShawEvery story about Dolly Parton’s generosity should shame the super-rich, who could easily make the world a better place for allThu 3 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 20.00 EDTShareSince the moment the news broke that the greatDolly Parton had died, we have been inundated with all manner of Feelings. The internet is flooded with tributes to Dolly by people from all walks of life, who knew her personally or only from afar. There seems no end to the sharing of stories and thoughts about her, and in what feels like a miracle in this divided world, it has only been positive. Even on social media, where people tear down nice things like it’s their full-time job, I’ve seen nothing but adoration. She is not only beloved for her musical genius, but also for her generosity, her sense of humour, her support for other artists, her active care for marginalised communities, her attitude to living, her truly kind spirit.I am one of these enthusiasts, of course. I have loved Dolly since I was a kid. I remember going to the Nashville country music museum in my 20s and seeing her handwritten lyrics for Jolene. A shiver went down my spine at the thought of 27-year-old Dolly writing that song, not knowing how far she would go, and the great good she would do for the world.‘It’s sad to lose a really nice person’: mourners flock to Dollywood after death of Dolly PartonRead moreBut after she died, and after a few days of reading every tribute with tears in my eyes, and both fists pumping, I decided that there was actually one important Feeling that has been missing from the discussion. That feeling is shame – and it is the shame that other millionaires, billionaires and (excuse me while I vomit a little in my mouth) trillionaires should be feeling.We live in a world where the gulf between the rich and the poor has never been greater. We understand that the Earth and the majority of people on it are suffering more and more while an enormous amount of wealth and power is concentrated in the hands of a tiny elite. The wealthiest 10% of the global populationowns 75% of all wealth. The poorest 50% holds only 2%. The individuals at the top could use tiny portions of their own fortunes to make the world so much better for everyone, and overwhelmingly they choose not to.Dolly Parton’s life as a self-made millionaire was the antithesis of this. She has shown them all up with the power of her legacy. Every story about her kindness and generosity is an indictment on people who hoard their wealth. Those who use their resources to accelerate environmental destruction, escalate nonsensical culture wars, and invest in actual wars. Those who do everything they can to get richer with no consideration for the rest of humanity.double quotation markShe has shown us that humanity and grace and generosity can be real priorities for wealthy peopleI suspect that a lot of Dolly’s desire to make life better for others came from the fact that she grew up in poverty. That experience provides perspective that you can’t have if you are born into wealth. She had a deeply ingrained understanding that there are more important things than watching your bank balance grow.She knew that money is the means, not the end. I can’t help but wonder if those who value profits over people saw this global outpouring of love for Dolly and thought about how they themselves might be remembered. I wonder if any had a brief moment of reflection, thinking about who would mourn their loss, or whether they had ever used their own privilege for good.I know the answer is no. I know that you generally don’t become a billionaire by caring that much about other people. I’ve seen people say that Dolly didn’t hate anyone, and wouldn’t judge others like this. That she would keep her heart open to them. Well, I’m not Dolly Parton. Nobody is, but definitely not me. I do judge these people, and I think we all should. Dolly has shown us what is possible. She has shown us that humanity and grace and generosity can be real priorities for wealthy people.Dolly had enough money to do whatever she wanted in life. She didn’t need more. This is true for all of the richest people on the planet. But Dolly saw the needs of others, and she responded. There are people who have enough to literally change huge aspects of society for the better, to make our world an easier place to live for everyone. But they don’t. If they don’t feel shame about that, we need to make them feel shame. We must not let them luxuriate in apathy as the world burns. We must demand more. The people hoarding wealth and resources need to start asking themselves: what would Dolly do?Rebecca Shaw is a writer based in SydneyExplore more on these topicsThe super-richOpinionDolly PartoncommentShareReuse this content

title: The Ceuta border breach was leapt on by Europe’s right. That doesn’t absolve Spain | María Ramírez | The Guardian
description: The government’s sluggish response has been disastrous for everyone involved – and for Sánchez’s message on immigration, says María Ramírez, deputy managing editor of Spanish news outlet elDiario.es
Author: María Ramírez
Headline: The government’s sluggish response has been disastrous for everyone involved – and for Sánchez’s message on immigration, says María Ramírez, deputy managing editor of Spanish news outlet elDiario.es
Content: Dozens of people by makeshift tents on the beach, a day after a violent protest during which some tents were set alight.Photograph: Antonio Sempere/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDozens of people by makeshift tents on the beach, a day after a violent protest during which some tents were set alight.Photograph: Antonio Sempere/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionSpainThe Ceuta border breach was leapt on by Europe’s right. That doesn’t absolve SpainMaría RamírezThe government’s sluggish response has been disastrous for everyone involved – and for Sánchez’s message on immigrationThu 3 Sep 2026 09.29 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 09.32 EDTShareMore than a month after an estimated 72,000 people suddenly crossed from Morocco into the Spanish territory of Ceuta, the city remains in chaos and the damage inflicted on the Spanish government is becoming clearer. Most of those who made the crossing have returned to Morocco. The scale of the incident was nevertheless extraordinary, and about 140 peopleare thought to have died.Also extraordinary was the response of the22 EU governmentsthat rounded on the Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, rather than demonstrate the solidarity one might expect from allies. Perhaps less surprising was the exploitation of the crisis by rightwing and far-right parties in Spain and beyond,Donald Trump’s attacksand the interventions ofRussian state-linked actorsandIsraeli criticson social media tofuel division.But this opportunism by Europe’s rightwing governments – Italy suspended its Schengen arrangements with Spain for no good reason – does not absolve Spain of blame. What has unfolded since 30 July is tragic for Ceuta, which has a permanent population of only about 84,000 people, and for the thousands of people, including an estimated 1,200 unaccompanied children, left on its streets and beaches. Sánchez’s government must take responsibility for some of the damage it is now belatedly trying to mop up.Ceuta was a carnival of anti-migrant content for hateful opportunists on the right – and a lesson for the left | Jonathan LiewRead moreOn 1 August, in the aftermath of the border breach, Sánchez reassured the EU that“virtually all”of the people who had arrived in Ceuta had returned to Morocco. The overwhelming majority did indeed leave, but thousands did not – and they are still in the city. Official numbershave fluctuated. The Spanish government’s estimate is that 5,000 of those who arrived are still in Ceuta; the region’s local governmenthas suggestedit could be double that. For weeks, there was no accommodation available, and hundreds are still camped on beaches or near the overcrowded migrant centres.View image in fullscreenWomen and children picking from donated clothes in a sports field set up by local residents as an improvised shelter.Photograph: Violeta Santos Moura/ReutersPeople living near these centrescomplainthey cannot leave their apartments out of fear, and that their children are unable to play on the beach or in the street. Businesses have had to close for days on end, incurring losses. Summer festivities had to be cancelled. Many migrants, including women and children, have survived on charity from local NGOs, the Red Cross and neighbours, and have little food, water and shelter.Yet as the situation deteriorated, the Spanish government failed for weeks to appoint anyone to coordinate a response. This would have been essential in Spain’s decentralised system, with powers divided between the central government and local and regional authorities. Now Madrid is finally funnelling resources and money into the matter, but only after the situation had deteriorated dangerously.Tensions have been evident in recent days, with local people crying in front of TV cameras, and politicians pleading for help. Protests directed against migrants have been constant. They have been mostly peaceful, but there have been outbreaks of violence. In one incident, a group of protesterstried to drive migrants off the beachand burned their tents before they were dispersed by the police with teargas. In another, military police were allegedly assaulted by a group from Morocco. At least 23sexual assaultsagainst migrants have been reported, including nineagainst children.View image in fullscreenCeuta residents protesting in late August by the beach where migrants have made makeshift camps.Photograph: REDUAN/EPACeuta was already fragile. The city, smaller than the site of Madrid airport, is home to a multicultural community that has been part of Spain since the 17th century. But even before this,its citizens complainedabout feeling abandoned. And now Morocco isreviving claims of sovereignty.Sánchez’s defence of Morocco –telling parliamenton Thursday that there was “no evidence” that Rabat had orchestrated events at the border – is at odds with popular sentiment in Ceuta and with most of the parties in parliament, including hisleftwing allies Sumar, the minority partner in the governing coalition.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Spanish government’s slow response and state of denial are damaging not only for Ceuta, but for Madrid’s own message on immigration. Spain has quite successfully promoted immigration as a force for good in recent years, even as most governments in Europe have moved in the opposite direction. What happened in Ceuta should not diminish the case for immigration as a factor driving economic growth and social dynamism, as Spain has shown over the past decade. But the mismanagement of Ceuta on the ground will inevitably impair that message.Even now, the Spanish government is backtracking, tightening its migration rules and pointing to disinformation around asupreme court decisionthat protected migrants’ rights against speedy returns as a cause for the rush on Ceuta. It has said it will stop transferring unaccompanied minors out of the territory and distributing them around the country for their protection, and isapproving restrictionsin line with the hardlineEU pact on migration and asylumpushed by rightwing governments.Regional politicians, who are mostly conservative, refuse to help out. The conservative People’s party (PP), which is leading inthe pollsbefore next year’s general election, is always better at attacking the government than clarifying what it would do differently. But even some local politicians from theSocialist Workers’ partyhave recently joined demonstrations in solidarity with Ceuta.The Ceuta episode has landed Spain with an almost impossible situation to resolve. But a combination of passivity and blaming everyone butMoroccohas not helpedthe city’s residents, Sánchez’s political position or the positive case for immigration in Spain and beyond.María Ramírez is a journalist and deputy managing editor of elDiario.es, a news outlet in SpainDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: China’s demise was gleefully predicted by the west – meanwhile, it built an AI revolution | Larry Elliott | The Guardian
description: Free AI models that are as good as the investment-hungry US versions will disrupt global markets, and offer Britain a lesson, says Guardian columnist Larry Elliott
Author: Larry Elliott
Headline: Free AI models that are as good as the investment-hungry US versions will disrupt global markets, and offer Britain a lesson, says Guardian columnist Larry Elliott
Content: China's first fully domestically produced 100,000-card AI supercluster Sugon 8000 at the World Artificial Intelligence Conference in Shanghai, 20 July 2026.Photograph: VCG/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenChina's first fully domestically produced 100,000-card AI supercluster Sugon 8000 at the World Artificial Intelligence Conference in Shanghai, 20 July 2026.Photograph: VCG/Getty ImagesOpinionChinese economyChina’s demise was gleefully predicted by the west – meanwhile, it built an AI revolutionLarry ElliottFree AI models that are as good as the investment-hungry US versions will disrupt global markets, and offer Britain a lessonThu 3 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 12.03 EDTShareAlmost from the moment it began, the end of the Chinese economic miracle has been much anticipated. Thick and fast, the books have come explaining how it will end badly. Overinvestment. A country wallowing in debt. Thecollapse of the property market. Political repression. The demand for democracy from a growing middle class. All have been put forward as reasons for the inevitable terminal crisis.Even those impressed by the country’s rapid growth took comfort from the notion that the west would continue to dominate advanced manufacturing whileChinawould be stuck assembling TVs. And while the wait for its much-predicted demise has gone on and on, China has become the workshop of the world.This process has come in two distinct phases. Initially, it is true, there was a concentration on low-cost manufactured goods because cheap labour costs provided a competitive advantage. Firms left for east Asia in search of higher profits. Without China 1.0, Donald Trump would have remained a New York property developer and Brexit might never have happened.Yet, the Chinese were not content to remain solely the producers of low-cost consumer goods and began to invest heavily in higher-end manufacturing. China 2.0 shattered the illusion that it would forever remain a developing economy destined to produce low-grade products and little else.The market in solar panels was captured. It became theworld leader in batteries and electric vehicles. It no longer has to import machine tools from Germany because it is now capable of making its own. The rise of the far-right Alternative für Deutschland is in no small measure due to the threat posed by China to German manufacturing jobs.Of course, China’s critics have a point. The model relies too heavily on investment and has much excess capacity. The country produces far more goods than it can consume domestically, particularly given the low level of wages and a relatively ungenerous welfare system. As a result, China can only keep growing at a rate that prevents rising unemployment from leading to social unrest if it exports its surfeit of goods to the rest of the world. China found itself isolated at the recent meeting of finance ministers of the G20 group of leading developed and developing countries, facing criticism from all sides forfailing to boost domestic demand for its products.Perhaps this means the rest of the world has finally woken up to the threat. If it has, that would not be a moment too soon because China is now competing with the US for dominance in the race to develop artificial intelligence. Welcome to China 3.0.In July, a Chinese startup calledMoonshot unveiled its Kimi K3 modeland it was an instant success. Just two days after its launch, the company suspended new subscriptions because demand was too great for its computing capacity. That was not surprising given that Kimi K3 was marketed as being able to match the models of its US rivals – such as the latest versions of OpenAI’s ChatGPT – at no cost. This was not a fluke or a random event.As Edoardo Campanella of UniCredit notes, Beijing is pursuing a clear AI strategy: staying close to the technological frontier, diffusing its models throughout the global economy, and setting standards across international markets. “If this strategy succeeds, the third China shockmight not just disrupt the global economy, but also the global balance of power,” says Campanella.Beijing’s strategy might not succeed but even so there are three things that are striking about the AI development race. The first is that this would appear to be the worst possible time for Washington toantagonise its traditional alliesby whacking them with punitive tariffs. The US needs all the friends it can muster.The second is that the arrival on the scene of free Chinese AI models could spell big trouble for global markets. Until now, the US has been confident its technological prowess will give it the upper hand in the AI development race and that has justified massive investment in technology companies.Despite rising oil prices, share prices on Wall Street have reflected confidence not just that AI will transform economies but that the US will be the main beneficiary. But if China can develop its AI models at a lower cost and offer them for nothing, investors will soon start to question whether the massive investment in the US justifies the sky-high share prices of tech companies. China’s success in AI couldprick the stock market bubble.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionInside China’s robotics revolutionRead moreFinally, there are lessons that countries such as Britain need to learn from China if it is to re-industrialise. When China began to build up its manufacturing strength almost 50 years ago, it saw itself as a developing country. It had no illusions about the scale of the challenge but had a plan and stuck to it.There was no aversion to picking winners. Nor would the strategy be left exposed to the whims of speculators. Instead, there was a willingness to use all the policy tools available: subsidies, tariffs, exchange controls and state investment.The result is what we see now: a China that has shifted through the gears from an industrial policy dominated by cheap goods to an industrial policy of everything. Sure, China’s model has its flaws but there is a stark contrast with Britain’s negligent approach since the late 1970s. One country is serious about manufacturing and the other isn’t.Larry Elliott is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsChinese economyOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)EconomicsAsia PacificIndustrial policyManufacturing sectorChinacommentShareReuse this content

title: The September reset is real. I’m about to become a better person, flaxseed by flaxseed | Emma Brockes | The Guardian
description: Small changes are what I’m aiming for – 10-minute workouts, cleaning out my handbag. Then I’m less likely to have failed come October, says Guardian columnist Emma Brockes
Author: Emma Brockes
Headline: Small changes are what I’m aiming for – 10-minute workouts, cleaning out my handbag. Then I’m less likely to have failed come October, says Guardian columnist Emma Brockes
Content: ‘September triggers good feelings of renewal’.Photograph: Geoffrey Swaine/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘September triggers good feelings of renewal’.Photograph: Geoffrey Swaine/ShutterstockOpinionAutumnThe September reset is real. I’m about to become a better person, flaxseed by flaxseedEmma BrockesSmall changes are what I’m aiming for – 10-minute workouts, cleaning out my handbag. Then I’m less likely to have failed come OctoberThu 3 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 03.28 EDTShareAre you a January resolutions or a September reset person? The latter has always felt more propitious to me, light of the exhaustion of Christmas and with the weather still on our side. Last week, when the Pavlovian response to buying new stationery (for my kids) kicked in, I found myself following a rote impulse to sort my life out by replacing the bag in the vacuum cleaner and committing to an unsustainable course of personal change. This is it! The beginning of a new way of life, driven by sharp pencils and the crispness of autumn.I mean, it won’t last. But while most of us have read enough advisories cautioning againstnew year resolutionsas durable, somehow September still promises the earth. I can’t shake it. As soon as the breeze picks up and the leaves start to turn, I feel my pilot light ignite – and the urge to sign up to unaffordable personal training sets in. It feels like an ancient response. I’m not writing this while leaning on a dry stone wall or managing my sheepdogs, but still; the sensory changes brought in by autumn surely activate latent energies in all of us. If you can avoid pumpkin spice and survive the costume search for Halloween, September triggers good feelings of renewal via the psychic memory of our serf forebears bringing in the harvest.Or, in my case, attempting to do 10 minutes of squats and move last night’s dishes from the sink to the dishwasher before lunchtime. As ever when trying to implement new habits, the question is how you trick yourself into making them stick. It’s like that classic scene from Road Runner, when, running out beyond the edge of the cliff, Wile E Coyote keeps going until he looks down and drops like a stone. Will a magnetised whiteboard, stuck to the fridge, keep me running on thin air for a bit longer? What about a new trainer, texting me motivational messages – “let’s go soldier mode!” – at 7am every day? After all these years of failed resolutions, has the answer to fixing my life really resided in buying sandwich bags for the efficient storage of leftovers?This is part of the problem, of course: that any commitment to change is used by most of us as a pretext to spend money. I assume that, in medieval times, the serf stockpiling for winter didn’t believe that the key to surviving til spring lay in a trip to the Container Store or buying a bar-grade blender. We can’t buy our way into new habits (although, I have to say, my new blender is amazing) unless it’s backed up with behavioural changes that come from – who knows?Panic, probably. Which is why, in spite of all the scepticism, it still feels to me as if theSeptember reset is real. As someone pointed out to me yesterday, it marks the entry point into the spookiest season, which means different things as we age. Influencers can run the clock on our finite number of summers, but as you get older it’s the onset of autumn that really turns up the burner on our sense of time passing. Foreshadowing death, the urge to get an arsing move on at this time of year is strong, and although it’s a line or argument that worries me – not least because it means I share psychological traits with eg notoriouslycrisis-surfing ex prime minister Boris Johnson– I’ve always considered panic a much underrated motivational force.And so, this year, I’ve gone to the literature for help in utilising the September force and discovered there’s a whole movement around it. Contrary to new year, when we tank our chances of success before we’ve even started by creating goals that are too large to achieve, September offers a lower pressure context in which to implement small change.Small change is good!Small change is, they say, where it all happens. Ten-minute workouts. Going to bed an hour earlier. Being more open to popular life hacks such as, “keep a gratitude journal” (no).If it feels like deckchairs on the Titanic, given the way the world is right now, we can control only what we can control. Will acollapse in the bond marketcrash all our futures, if the climate crisis doesn’t get us first? While I think about that, there’s a small chance that if I chip off the crust around the base of the kitchen tap, clear the drift of receipts from the bottom of my bag and put flaxseed into everything I eat, maybe all will be well.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEmma Brockes is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsAutumnOpinionNew yearHealth & wellbeingMental healthHealthcommentShareReuse this content

title: The people of France are in an extraordinary funk about their future – here’s why | Paul Taylor | The Guardian
description: The race to succeed Emmanuel Macron is looming, but rarely has the mood been so gloomy or the lure of extremist solutions so alarming, says Paul Taylor, of the European Policy Centre
Author: Paul Taylor
Headline: The race to succeed Emmanuel Macron is looming, but rarely has the mood been so gloomy or the lure of extremist solutions so alarming, says Paul Taylor, of the European Policy Centre
Content: A protester holding a French flag at a ‘gilets jaunes’ demonstration, Paris, 8 December 2018.Photograph: SOPA Images/LightRocket/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA protester holding a French flag at a ‘gilets jaunes’ demonstration, Paris, 8 December 2018.Photograph: SOPA Images/LightRocket/Getty ImagesOpinionFranceThe people of France are in an extraordinary funk about their future – here’s whyPaul TaylorThe race to succeed Emmanuel Macron is looming, but rarely has the mood been so gloomy or the lure of extremist solutions so alarmingThu 3 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 10.33 EDTShareFrance, as the French travel writer Sylvain Tesson once noted, “is a paradise inhabited by people who think they live in hell”. As the campaign for next year’s presidential election hits its stride withever more wannabes declaringtheir candidacies, the country is in a particularly sullen mood.If the vote were held now, the anti-immigration populistMarine Le Penwould have a strong chance of romping into the Élysée palace, riding a wave of voter disillusionment with the entire political class and a sense that “we’ve tried everything else”. But a lot can happen between now and 18 April 2027, the date of the first round. France is also a country of sudden shocks.In spring 2011, Dominique Strauss-Kahn, the then head of the IMF and an admired former finance minister, was hot favourite to become the Socialist party candidate who would beat the incumbent conservative Nicolas Sarkozy in the 2012 race. But Strauss-Kahn was felled by asexual harassment scandaland the unfancied socialist politician François Hollande ended up in the Élysée. In 2016, the former conservative prime minister François Fillon was well ahead in the race to succeed Hollande, then he was exposed as having arranged taxpayer-fundedphoney parliamentary jobsfor his wife. He finished third and a young centrist outsider without a party machine, Emmanuel Macron, went on to triumph.To understand the backdrop to next year’s election – with huge stakes forEuropeand the western alliance as well as for France – it’s worth examining the unique features that distinguish the French funk from the crisis facing other advanced democracies. After all, politics has become more raw and polarised in many countries. Other big European economies are stagnating. Mainstream parties are shrinking and fragmenting across Europe under growing challenges from insurgent rightwing national populists as well as a new radical, often ecologist, left. Political instability is accelerated everywhere by social-media frenzy and the 24/7 news cycle.But several historical factors make the French malaise special, as I explored in a recent conversation with Michel Wieviorka, an eminent sociologist and author of numerous studies on French society, includingOù va la France: Métamorphose ou Déchéance? (Where is France Headed: Metamorphosis or Decline?).France was Europe’s first centralised state, with a culture ofdirigisteeconomic development harking back to Cardinal Richelieu, Louis XIV and his minister Jean-Baptiste Colbert in the 17th century. That tradition was revived by Charles de Gaulle and postwar governments that used a powerful national economic planning commissariat to drive industrial modernisation, including the nuclear programme, the aerospace sector and massive public infrastructure investment.This helps explain why French people have great expectations of the state and accept some of the highest levels of taxation, income redistribution and public spending as a proportion of economic output of any major economy. It also helps explain why France’sdebt-to-GDP ratio of 118%is among the highest and fastest rising in Europe.“The French are very attached to public services and anxious about their degradation, which is spectacular in public education but also in the justice system, the police, the tax system and health services, as revealed by the Covid-19 pandemic,” Wieviorka said. “They have the feeling that we used to be a great country at the forefront of modernity, but it is now falling apart.”Another unique characteristic is a multi-century tradition of often violent protest. From the peasantjacqueriesand Paris barricades of the 16th and 17th centuries to the landmark upheaval of the 1789 French revolution, revolt against authority has long been seen as legitimate by a large part of society. As Jean-Paul Sartre put it, “It is right to rebel.” The French labour movement, too, was rooted in anarcho-syndicalism before being dominated by the communist party, and lacks the British or German trade unions’ tradition of reformist compromise.Like the English did in the 17th century, the Frenchexecuted their kingin the 18th century, but it took almost another century to finally abolish monarchy after two royal restorations and two emperors. The French left fought for the republican principle, prevailing over authoritarian forces backed by the Catholic church in theDreyfus affairat the end of the 19th century. That led to a strict separation of church and state and the principle of secularism that enjoys consensus support today.However, as Wieviorka noted, the decline of France’s Christian identity and religious observance has coincided with the rise of Islam, mostly among people of immigrant origin. This has stirred anxieties fanned by mainstream conservative and hard-right politicians and the new-right media empire of the billionaireVincent Bolloré.These fears explain the rise of the extreme-right Front National founded byJean-Marie Le Pen in 1972, which Wieviorka called “the pioneering national-populist party in Europe”, putting the fight against immigration at the centre of its agenda. Rebranded in 2018 as the National Rally (RN) by his daughter, Marine, in a quest for respectability, the party hasroots in the Vichy regimethat collaborated with Nazi Germany but swapped antisemitism for anti-Islamism, advocating “national priority” for French citizens in welfare, housing and healthcare.Another distinguishing feature is France’s political and administrative elite, rebuilt on meritocratic lines after the second world war with the creation of L’École nationale d’administration (ENA) to train top civil servants and captains of nationalised enterprises, many of whom made a career in politics. The system has become ossified and spawned a self-perpetuating elite – the so-calledénarques–increasingly seen as remote from ordinary French people’s concerns.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThese factors combined explain the state of public opinion on the eve of the campaign – deeply pessimistic about the state of the country, anxious about identity, declining public services and the cost of living, and disillusioned with a political establishment seen as having failed on all these fronts.To Wieviorka’s matrix of factors underlying the political malaise, I would add a widespread lack of economic realism and a belief that what the French call “public money”, which in the UK or Germany is known as “taxpayers’ money”, is infinitely extendable.Economic unrealism makes France particularly susceptible to magic money solutions such as RN’s fantasy that the debt and deficit would melt away if the government only stopped welfare payments to immigrants and slashed its EU contribution, or the radical leftist Jean-Luc Mélenchon’s claim that France just needs to write off “cost free”18% of its debtheld by the European Central Bank and confiscate all inheritances of more than €12m.No wonderthere’s little time for politicians who propose dreary real-world solutions such as raising the retirement age or curbing some welfare benefits. A famous slogan in the student uprisings of May 1968 proclaimed: “Be realistic, demand the impossible”.The big risk now is that the French vote with their gut rather than with their head. At a time of such geopolitical and fiscal peril for France and Europe, that is an alarming prospect.Paul Taylor is a senior visiting fellow at the European Policy CentreExplore more on these topicsFranceOpinionMarine Le PenEmmanuel MacronFrançois HollandeEuropeNicolas SarkozycommentShareReuse this content

title: An Unexpected Life by Gloria Steinem review – a fitting tribute to a feminist icon | Autobiography and memoir | The Guardian
description: The activist’s memoir, due to be published this month, now stands as a posthumous testament to her remarkable life
Author: Emma Brockes
Headline: The activist’s memoir, due to be published this month, now stands as a posthumous testament to her remarkable life
Content: Gloria Steinem at Ms magazine in 1980.Photograph: New York Daily News Archive/NY Daily News/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGloria Steinem at Ms magazine in 1980.Photograph: New York Daily News Archive/NY Daily News/Getty ImagesAutobiography and memoirReviewAn Unexpected Life by Gloria Steinem review – a fitting tribute to a feminist iconThe activist’s memoir, due to be published this month, now stands as a posthumous testament to her remarkable lifeEmma BrockesThu 3 Sep 2026 10.16 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 16.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGloria Steinem was due to speak at a women’s lunch in New York at the end of this month and at more events in October, illustrating the central theme of An Unexpected Life, her new memoir, which, when it’s published a few weeks from now, will stand as posthumous testament to the 92-year-old icon: just keep going. So it is, after herdeath on Wednesday, that the book’s opening pages unfold with a deep, added poignancy and when Steinem expresses gratitude for a life that has been both happier and longer “than I ever imagined”, one is struck by the greater gratitude we probably owe her.An Unexpected Life is a follow-up of sorts toMy Life on the Road, the activist’s memoir of a decade ago, and as the tributes pour in, the book offers us an opportunity to go back over Steinem’s hardscrabble origins in Toledo, Ohio, and the roots of her activism. This is where it all happened, the formation of a woman who would come to define second wave feminism by combining a tough-as-they-come stance with something that looked a lot like serenity. Reading the first half of the book, one is reminded of Steinem’s original power and the improbability and iconoclasm of her journey, in which a childhood governed by poverty and dysfunction turned into a lifelong mission to resist the narrow templates laid out for her.It’s a cracking backstory. Steinem’s rackety father was a travelling salesman of sorts, touring the country with a dance pavilion that saw Steinem spend long stretches of her childhood with him on the road, which, she writes, conditioned her to enjoy a similarly unconventional existence in adulthood. When she was at home, the young Steinem was a carer for her increasingly mentally unwell mother, who was frequently to be found wandering the town in her nightdress, and Steinem writes movingly about what it is to grow up ashamed of your house and your family. “I learned I could survive almost anything,” she writes, “including a sad mother who was called the Crazy Lady of the neighborhood. We are all one human family, and we are responsible for one another.”Raised on instability, Steinem grew up remarkably free of the pressure weighing on most of her female peers to knuckle down into conventional marriage and motherhood, leaving her free to pursue a life as a freelance writer and, later, an activist. After college, she went to India for two years, a defining period that informed her outlook to the very end, and on return, began her career as a campaigning journalist, which culminated in her co-founding of Ms magazine in 1971 and eventual ascent to the head of the women’s movement.These periods of her life are well documented. What I found interesting in the book were Steinem’s asides about the cost of pursuing the life she chose. “Though I managed to support myself,” she writes, “I didn’t save money until I was past fifty. I was sure that I’d end up as a bag lady, like women I saw sleeping in subway stations. I used to handle that fear by thinking, It’s a life like any other. I’ll organize the other bag ladies.” She eventually became somewhat financially secure, largely thanks to buying part of a 19th-century brownstone on the Upper East Side of Manhattan, the beloved home in which she died this week – although a throwaway line towards the end of the book suggests she was still paying off her mortgage well into her 80s, an astonishing fact given her fame.double quotation markIt is useful to be reminded by Steinem of how bad things were so very recentlySteinem is the real thing, of course; she was never in it for the money. She makes a strong case that she wasn’t in it for the attention, either, although, as a talented speaker and organiser, she drew on great reserves of magnetism that over the years caused her a lot of problems with jealousy from within the movement, and condescension from without. Right until the end, Steinem was stewarding large groups of women – famous and otherwise – at “talking circles” in her house and putting herself at the centre of a conversation she had in some ways begun.A big strand of these debates was the shoe-horning of women into flat, unfulfilled lives, which they are conditioned to believe are the only desirable option. This is where the book’s startling honesty comes into play, a habit Steinem seems to have had from the get-go. Some years after graduating, she wrote to her Smith College classmates in an alumni newsletter: “I’m quite broke, not at all who I thought I would be – and consciously happy.”She writes powerfully about women who made different, unhappier choices under pain of social death: “I remember one woman, married to a socially acceptable man much older than she, who explained, ‘After he dies, I’ll be free.’ The cost of freedom seemed to mean she was able to live only in the future.” It is useful to be reminded of how bad things were so very recently. As the book informs us, “in the 1960s Columbia Law School had a 5% quota for women” – in an era in which American women were earning, on average, 59 cents on each dollar earned by men. (“Now,” she writes, “they typically earn 82 cents for every dollar earned by men. At the going rate, it will be fifty years before we reach parity overall, and seventy-five years for African American women to reach parity with African American men.”)There are glowing, drive-by sketches of some of the famous figures Steinem encountered on the road, including James Baldwin and Annie Leibovitz. She is disinclined to offer anything but praise for the people she admires and so the book’s only waspish assessment is reserved for Andy Warhol, whose smirking sensibility really flies up Steinem’s nose and sits poorly alongside her earnestness. I like her for this – having a crack at the immensely irritating Warhol, about whom, she sniffs, “It seems a low point of the art world that Andy Warhol’s is considered valuable.”As we enter the post-Steinem era – a statement that seems outlandish, given the length and ardour of her service – it’s a pleasure, simply, to spend time in her company, and her role as an elder is one she takes seriously, evoking her deep relationship with Native Americans as the basis for many of her insights. “The patriarchal nuclear family, the one that we are supposed to think is the only kind of family, is really only about 150 years old, and almost entirely a function of industrialization and capitalism.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt wasn’t until she was much older, she writes, that she realised so much of her life “was spent doing what was expected of me, and not enough doing what I loved”. Counterintuitively, this included her hard line on marriage, which she set herself against as a matter of principle, only marrying her great love, David Bale, at 66 and staying with him until he died three years later. This is the old Steinem we love, the combination of absolute force and, hard on its heels, admission of error.After all the doubt and indecision, Steinem at 92 had a very clear idea of what she was supposed to be doing, and my God she did it right to the end. “My role as an older person is to remind us how far we have come, and with age comes the responsibility to keep learning. As Robert Browning wrote: ‘The best is yet to be, / The last of life, / for which the first was made.’” Or as Steinem put it, with a hard-won smile it’s impossible to resist, “Now even my jeans are much older than many people I work with.” We should all be so lucky; what a life.An Unexpected Life by Gloria Steinem is published by Ebury in the UK and Random House in the US. title: The Bayeux tapestry: a stupefying, thrilling, horrifying masterpiece that shakes the earth | Art | The Guardian
description: The greatest battle ever depicted in art is here at last – and it hurtles along, making your heart pound with its sense of doom and destiny, culminating in fires and corpses on a battlefield full of pathos
Author: Jonathan Jones
Headline: The greatest battle ever depicted in art is here at last – and it hurtles along, making your heart pound with its sense of doom and destiny, culminating in fires and corpses on a battlefield full of pathos
Content: ‘It beats almost everything else’ … the Bayeux tapestry.Photograph: Isogood_patrick/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘It beats almost everything else’ … the Bayeux tapestry.Photograph: Isogood_patrick/ShutterstockArtReviewThe Bayeux tapestry: a stupefying, thrilling, horrifying masterpiece that shakes the earthBritish Museum, LondonThe greatest battle ever depicted in art is here at last – and it hurtles along, making your heart pound with its sense of doom and destiny, culminating in fires and corpses on a battlefield full of pathosJonathan JonesThu 3 Sep 2026 10.51 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 14.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt should not work. It should not even exist. Nothing about theBayeux tapestrymakes sense according to any norms of art: its creators couldn’t do proper portraits or pictorial depth or landscapes or any of the sophisticated things we associate with timeless masterpieces. When they depict a church, they have to write what it is: Ecclesia. But these artists – or who knows, perhaps she was a single artist – created something so stupefying and delightful, so abundant in visual thrills, horrors and humour, it beats almost everything else ever painted or carved – let alone embroidered on a strip of linen.And now here it is, in front of my eyes, close enough to touch if it wasn’t behind a glass screen of such high quality you never catch a reflection. The British Museum’s display of this wonder is perfect. It’s laid out in its case, the length of a gallery, which you reach after some archaeological foreplay involving armour, quotes from chronicles and info screens. Then you see the colours of the tapestry below you from a parapet – russets, greens, yellows – after which you simply start at the beginning and follow the story rightwards. Surrounded by darkness and picked out by finely adjusted lighting, the Bayeux tapestry shines. My only quibble is the ethereal soundtrack – shouldn’t there be drums, oliphants, troubadours?I managed a pretty satisfying eyeful in under an hour, although more than the allotted 40 minutes. This is pacy art: it hurtles along. In fact, that’s how it embraces you. Your heart pounds with a sense of doom and destiny. This is, you realise, the greatest battle in art.View image in fullscreenDetails to savour … the Bayeaux tapestry.Photograph: David Levene/the GuardianIt has plenty of competition. Battles and war have engrossed artists down the millennia, from Trajan’s Column to Picasso’s Guernica, usually in scenes of hopeless chaos. So one thing that’s unique about the Bayeux tapestry, and key to its dramatic zip, is the clear and definitive nature of the battle it depicts.On 14 October 1066, Harold, recently crowned king of Anglo-Saxon England, and his army faced the newly landed forces of William, Duke of Normandy, near Hastings. By the end of the day, Harold was dead, along with devastating numbers of his soldiers and nobles – and the Normans had conquered England. They never left. This battle changed a nation and William succeeded where those later would-be cross-Channel invaders – Philip II of Spain, Napoleon and Hitler – would all fail.So a big battle with a very clear conclusion. As you pad along the British Museum display, savouring lovely details like a servant eavesdropping on a conversation, or one of Harold’s people carrying his hunting dog to a ship so it doesn’t get its paws wet, you are led through the buildup to the big fight with mounting excitement.When hell is finally unleashed, the Norman cavalry pound with such force you can almost hear hooves shake the earth. Norman archers fire continuous volleys that send arrow shafts straight into Saxon bodies. Meanwhile, the Saxons stand manfully in hauberks with their axes and take it. They give it, too, to the point that William seems for a moment to be losing the day, horses tipping over, knights falling.It’s in such images that the Bayeux tapestry transcends everything you could reasonably expect of a medieval artwork. The scene where the Norman cavalry seems to falter is simultaneously realistic and nightmarish. One horse is completely upended, its face to the earth, rear legs in the sky. Another tips over as its rider slides forward, his armoured body suddenly a helpless rag.View image in fullscreen‘A universal depiction of the madness that is war’ … the Bayeaux tapestry.Photograph: David Levene/the GuardianAs you move along the strip, what hits you is its brilliant sense of momentum. Early on, two messengers race across the French countryside, their hair flying out behind them in straight black threads: it’s a thrilling way to convey speed. Such bone-shaking velocity is shown again and again in superbly simple ways. At Hastings, you see the Norman knights gradually gather pace. Their horses calmly prance, riders bolt upright with lances aloft, then one rider tilts forward as his horse lowers its head and bends its front legs in a run. Soon the legs of all the horses are flying in rhythm as the knights hold their lances ready to throw, adding to the sense of forward thrust.It’s the 11th-century answer to Eadweard Muybridge’s motion photograph sequences. We follow the change in speed as if it was happening to a single figure. The Normans are so disciplined they seem be to one single, lethal horseman – and that is why they will win.While you are dragged forward, you are also led up and down, to meander in a marginal world of monsters and myths. Bizarre goings-on in the borders above and below the action constantly interrupt the drive of the story. The gryphons, dragons and square-winged, hieratic birds of prey seem much bigger and bolder in life than reproduction and harder to ignore.I thought I’d detected some structure to it all: the top margin is more ordered and sublime, suggesting the heavenly sphere (Halley’s Comet speeds through it like a rocket), while the creatures below look earthy and sinful. Then I saw two bare-chested female centaurs at the top spreading their arms out as if to say: “Lo and behold!” So much for logic.The great thing about a border is that you can break it. When William’s ships speed across the Channel, their bulging, wind-filled, multicoloured sails fill the upper space. As the Battle of Hastings gets bloodier, bodies and body parts pile up in the lower one.View image in fullscreenLisa Nandy views the tapestry with George Osborne (chair of the British Museum) and Michael Lewis, co-curator of the exhibition.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianIn both the borders and central strip, the Bayeux tapestry always set its action in a wider world, and even, when it shows the comet, a larger cosmos. As the armoured elite go to war, peasants plough and sow the fields. They are portrayed in distracting, vibrant detail and this workaday scene as the battle approaches is pointed and poignant: whoever wins, whoever rules England, country people will still work the soil. That same sudden cutaway from the rulers’ perspective happens when a woman and her child watch the Normans set their house on fire. But what you can see here, close to the stitches in such good light, is that one of the men torching the house also seems sad and conflicted.It’s that honesty that makes this not just a fascinating medieval relic but a universal depiction of the madness that is war. If the violence is stunningly real, so are its consequences. The dead bodies pile up in mounds as Saxon after Saxon falls. King Harold didn’t really get killed by an arrow in his eye we are told, but seeing the tapestry so close, it sure looks like it. Anyway, his royal body just joins the rest. In the final scenes, the peasants, the churls, get their revenge. Little shabby figures pull the mailed hauberks off dead knights, leaving them naked.It’s a final flourish of the precocious artistic brilliance of these 11th-century artists and craftspeople. Naked bodies emerge from their armour, pale and oddly beautiful – the complete ones, at least – as these medieval geniuses show they can depict, through embroidery, incredibly gentle, intimate nudes whose dead flesh fills the battlefield with pathos.It ends there. But, although there’s a lost later section, this anticlimax looks perfect to me. By then, I had been drained by this epic in all its tragedy and comedy. Bodies and body parts. That’s where the war talk was heading all along.At theBritish Museum, London, 10 September-11 JulyExplore more on these topicsArtBritish MuseumBayeux tapestryreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I have an obsession with barber shops’: kd lang on her prairies upbringing, Patsy Cline and being shaved by Cindy Crawford | Pop and rock | The Guardian
description: The Canadian singer-songwriter answers your questions about her trailblazing career, her spirituality, and collaborations with the likes of Neko Case, Laura Veirs and Pee-wee Herman
Author: Laura Snapes
Headline: The Canadian singer-songwriter answers your questions about her trailblazing career, her spirituality, and collaborations with the likes of Neko Case, Laura Veirs and Pee-wee Herman
Content: ‘The sky was very important to me’ … kd lang.Photograph: Jeri HeidenView image in fullscreen‘The sky was very important to me’ … kd lang.Photograph: Jeri HeidenFilm & Music reader interviewPop and rockInterview‘I have an obsession with barber shops’: kd lang on her prairies upbringing, Patsy Cline and being shaved by Cindy CrawfordAs told toLaura SnapesThe Canadian singer-songwriter answers your questions about her trailblazing career, her spirituality, and collaborations with the likes of Neko Case, Laura Veirs and Pee-wee HermanThu 3 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 11.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI left the Canadian prairies many years ago, but they remain my home. How do you feel about that part of westernCanada, where the prairies meet the Rockymountains, whichshaped us both? What does Alberta mean to you now?NicholasLittleAll of my artistic preferences were formed by the minimalism of the prairies, by the affordable space and the stillness. There weren’t many things around, so a field with bales would be this incredibly graphic moment, or a tree or a certain hill – very small increments of beauty placed in vast amounts of space. The sky was very important and a feeling of – I wouldn’t say loneliness, but solace, perhaps. That’s my bottom line, my basic instinct. It’s the frame that that informs all of my art, the way I decorate my house, the way I sing, the way I dress. That sort of minimalist nature is embedded in me.Many people can sing a song well, but you’re a vocalist who emotes raw vulnerability. Do you work like a method actor – entering, or reliving, the reality of the song during the practice period?verdantearthI try to sink myself into the lyrics for sure. I try to create visuals, sort of an emotional internal movie of what the lyrics possess, to relive it emotionally. With [Case/Lang/Veirs track] Honey and Smoke, for example, I imagine watching somebody I’m in love with dancing with somebody else and feeling jealousy.How proud are you of that infamous Vanity Fair cover shoot [in which Cindy Crawford“shaves”kd in a barber’s chair]?TrumansdadView image in fullscreen‘It was magical’ … Herb Ritts’ Vanity Fair cover.Photograph: Herb Ritts/Vanity FairVery. I was friends with Herb [Ritts] and somehow I got the opportunity to do the Vanity Fair cover, and he was shooting it. I was obsessed with a French movie called The Hairdresser’s Husband at the time. I have kind of an obsession with cutting hair and barber shops. I don’t know where that came from – actually, I just realised why, and I’ve never told anyone this! My dad’s drugstore in the really small town I grew up in – the next business over was a barber shop, so I used to watch the barber cutting hair all the time. It must be some sort of childhood visualisation imprint or something. I suggested to Herb, maybe we can do it in a barber’s chair. He phoned me a few days later and said, “I have Cindy Crawford.” I was like, “OK!” We shot it on the roof of his building in downtown Hollywood, up on the roof at golden hour. It was magical. Cindy was super professional, as you can imagine. She’s a model, so it was her realm. I was trying to behave and not be an idiot. It was incredible, and I knew that it had a certain gravity to it. After all these years, I feel like we made a piece of art and a significant social statement, and I really have such pride about it.LS: You have a very cheeky look on your face on the cover.Yeah. I mean, come on!Could you name some of your favourite visual artists and explain why you love them?Do you own art?SimotherI can’t afford to be a collector, but I’m certainly a fan. I love everything; some of my favourite painters areFranz Kline, because I love the confidence with which he painted, andAgnes Martinbecause I love patterns and simplicity. She’s also from Alberta. I really gravitate towards abstract expressionism just because I love that the emotion is driving it. That’s how I relate to art, emotionally rather than intellectually.View image in fullscreen‘They’re both incredible songwriters’ … (from left) Laura Veirs, kd lang and Neko Case in 2016.Photograph: Don Ryan/APLooking back 10 years on, what do you remember most about Case/Lang/Veirs? And would you be tempted to work with Neko Case and Laura Veirsagain if the stars aligned?VerulamiumParkRangerI remember how excited I was when I had the idea to collaborate with them. When I texted them, they both answered within half an hour. And then the work began. I remember it being quite difficult in terms of having three major artists, who had been bosses their whole lives, coming together – we had to navigate and reformulate how we worked, the structure of writing and creativity. They’re both incredible songwriters. I’m in awe of their songwriting ability, and I had to stay out of the way because I felt like they were so much more prolific than I was. We ended up being real good friends, and we had an exciting but short tour.What was it like being part of the Vancouver music scene and performing at the Railway Club in the 80s?budthespudYou must be a Canadian. The Railway Club and the Savoy Club in Vancouver were extremely important to my career. They were both really great small alternative independent music venues. The person who booked the music, Janet Forsyth, booked me very early, and the buzz started happening. It was an incredibly vibrant and buzzy time for me. The shows were extremely formative because I was trying out a lot of different material, learning how to be a stage performer. To this day, Janet Forsyth is my best friend.View image in fullscreenPee-wee’s Playhouse Christmas Special.Photograph: Everett Collection/AlamyWhat was it like to be a part of thePee-wee’s Playhouse Christmas Special(AKA the greatest, gayest Christmas special ever made)? My little brother and I have watched it together every year since 1988!AlexisHidellIt was amazing – it was magical because it was so unbridled. I just sang a Christmas carol – it was all carols, but he had really contrasting artists like Grace Jones and Doris Day. It was like he had all these different kites and he was flying them all at once. You could do whatever you wanted and it was joyful and wise and sardonic – it contained everything. It’s not unlike the paintings we were talking about: it’s emotional expression without any constraints, artistic freedom. Paul [Reubens, AKA Pee-wee Herman] and I became friends. I lovedthe documentary Matt Wolf made on him. Paul was serious and very deliberate.Would you ever consider a follow-up to [lang’s 2004 album of cover versions]Hymns of the 49th Parallel? Hearing Canadian music treated with that kind of deep respect and understanding – the individual songs and the way they exist in conversation with each other – changed something for a lot of people, I think.MarnaNightingaleI have been asked that by my record company and my manager, but I really try to honour my muse and my instincts. It hasn’t happened yet, but maybe it will. Certainly the material is there. There’s an embarrassment of riches of great Canadian songwriting.kd lang on Tony Bennett: ‘It was a salve for society to see an older man and a young dyke in a happy relationship’Read moreWhat was it like appearing on the Larry Sanders show?CaptainLibIt was fun. He was a beautiful guy. [The show was] an intense niche to be put into because they have their own vernacular and rhythm and way of being. I tried to inhabit my own space with it and be natural, but man, the energy there was kind of like being placed in the middle of a football game, and somebody’s vacuuming naked … I don’t totally remember what happened.You’ve described your connection withPatsy Clineas “otherworldly”. What is it about her – and the emotional landscapes of songs such asLeavin’ on Your Mind– that gives her such enduring appeal?Bopalena_now_JohnnyThe emotional connection is inexplicable. Emotion is something ethereal and indescribable. Patsy contained an empathy, an earthiness, a vulnerability, a sense of humour – all the essential parts of humanity. She just sang from an open place, and let people feel comfortable immersing themselves in her.View image in fullscreenStage presence … lang with accordionist Teddy Borowiecki in 2006.Photograph: Mark Mainz/Getty ImagesThe accordion is prominent not just in thebeautiful Constant Craving but in multiple other recordings of yours. Can you tell us more about your accordionist, Teddy Borowiecki, and do you have a particular fascination with this instrument?BirtyDankersIt was around in my upbringing because in the Canadian prairies there were a lot of German and Polish eastern Europeans who had migrated to Canada, so it was prevalent in dance bands and so forth. And Teddy, who is Polish, was a very good accordion player, so I wanted to utilise his talent.What can you share about your meditation practice, and how ithas affected you, the living of your life, and your music?SillyputtyMy spiritual practice is inseparable from anything I do, and is of utmost importance. It’s taken precedence over all things in my life. So I don’t even know where to start or how to describe it. It’s given me a different point of reference that has anchored me in motivation and purpose. Just taking my contribution to the universe very seriously – not self-righteously, but the desire to be authentic and uncontrived.The 10th anniversary edition of Case/Lang/Veirs is released via Anti- on 4 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsPop and rockFilm & Music reader interviewCountryCanadainterviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Finally, a victory for the middle-aged white man!’ Chris Cantrill on winning the Edinburgh comedy award | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: The ex-marketing manager’s win, for his spoof Sycamore Gap-inspired whodunnit Rewilding, arrives just as he’s gearing up for a new season of hit sketch show SNL UK – which he calls ‘the hardest job of my life’
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: The ex-marketing manager’s win, for his spoof Sycamore Gap-inspired whodunnit Rewilding, arrives just as he’s gearing up for a new season of hit sketch show SNL UK – which he calls ‘the hardest job of my life’
Content: ‘In my head, I’m a plucky young upstart still’ … Chris Cantrill.Photograph: Rebecca Need-MenearView image in fullscreen‘In my head, I’m a plucky young upstart still’ … Chris Cantrill.Photograph: Rebecca Need-MenearEdinburgh festival 2026Interview‘Finally, a victory for the middle-aged white man!’ Chris Cantrill on winning the Edinburgh comedy awardBrian LoganThe ex-marketing manager’s win, for his spoof Sycamore Gap-inspired whodunnit Rewilding, arrives just as he’s gearing up for a new season of hit sketch show SNL UK – which he calls ‘the hardest job of my life’Thu 3 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 09.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor the last month, Chris Cantrill has been performinghis fringe show Rewildingdaily in a lunchtime slot. And yet, when we plan to speak about hisvictory in the Edinburgh comedy awards, the interview is arranged – on the festival’s penultimate day – for lunchtime. Can he really have won the fringe’s major prize, and – hell of a mic drop, this – immediately sacked off his last two shows? “I couldn’t be happier not to be at the festival today,” he says, on video call from his Northumberland home. But the cancellation, it transpires, is long-standing, because work starts immediately post-fringe on the new series ofSNL UK, for which he writes.“But I’m absolutely over the moon not to be doing my show right now,” he admits. “I’ve got a lot of adrenaline in my body slowly seeping out, and I feel like I’ve been hit by a train.” The Edinburgh comedy award (it used to be the Perrier, and was won in the past by Steve Coogan, The League of Gentlemen and Frank Skinner) has been a long time coming for Bradford-born Cantrill. This year’s was his fourth nomination, twice as a solo act, and twice as part of his duoThe Delightful Sausage, alongside2024 winner Amy Gledhill. He is, as I tease him when we speak, a comparatively senior winner, the oldest since Bridget Christie, also 42, 13 years ago. “Finally, a victory for the middle-aged white man!,” he retorts, then bursts into laughter. “Common sense at last!”View image in fullscreenChris Cantrill performing Rewilding at the 2026 Edinburgh fringe.Photograph: Jack Kirby“But in my head, I’m a plucky young upstart still.” And you can see why. Cantrill didn’t take up comedy until he was 28, having “worked in an office as a marketing manager. I wasn’t a good fit for that.” He sidelined as a comedian, but was going nowhere fast when in 2016 his first child was born. By way of a last resort, he then asked Gledhill whether she fancied “trying something a little bit different” – and The Delightful Sausage came into being. This raucous and surreal double act, a slacker northern Mighty Boosh, was Cantrill’s unlikely meal ticket, a mates-having-a-laugh confection that went unexpectedly mainstream. “We used to come to Edinburgh and hang out with comics we knew from Glasgow, Newcastle, the regions. Then we started getting nominated [for the award] and found ourselves in the orbit of switched-on, ruthlessly ambitious, twentysomethings. I remember thinking, ‘oh God, that’s a bit intense, isn’t it?’”Cantrill has always styled himself an outsider, speaking (whenthe Guardian interviewed The Delightful Sausage in 2022) about his hard-to-shake impostor syndrome. One might think winning the award, againstfellow nominees including Lara Ricote and upcoming Last One Laughing star Harriet Dyer, would put paid to that self-image. But Cantrill doesn’t see it that way. Edinburgh’s comedy awards, he says, “have undoubtedly altered the trajectory of my life. Being nominated took me from part-time while working in an office to doing comedy full-time.” But winning won’t be transformative. “What this means is that when I send an email, there’s 30% more chance someone will respond to it. If I’m working on other stuff, it might move that stuff forward slightly more favourably.”View image in fullscreen‘Oh God, that’s a bit intense’ … Cantrill performing with Amy Gledhill as The Delightful Sausage.Photograph: James Darcey / J Darcey imagesThe show for which Cantrill won the prize, meanwhile, seems designed to confirm the Yorkshireman as a fish out of water. Rewilding continues the story of his move to rural Northumberland, first related in2024’s Easily Swayed. In this year’s show, we meet fellow residents of the fictionalised “Gaskill village” as an act of vandalism is perpetrated on a local landmark. The tale, a thinly veiled take on the global outrage caused bythe felling of the Sycamore Gap tree, becomes a spoof whodunnit, in which Cantrill, a city boy still adapting to countryside life – not to mention a child trapped in a grown man’s body – plays a key role.Rewilding is about “how I observed that [Sycamore Gap story] at a grassroots WhatsApp level,” says Cantrill. “I just thought it was fascinating.” How do such incidents affect communities – and why do we care so much about trees? “One of them [ie the two men convicted of the crime] was obsessed with it. From when he was a kid, he had a string that measured the circumference of it. Then when he got arrested, he said, ‘it’s just a tree’. And I was like, you wouldn’t have driven through the night in a storm to cut it down if you thought it was just a tree that had a no effect on anyone.”Cantrill trialled the show in front of his fellow villagers, many of them depicted in it. “They like laughing at themselves,” he reports. “Hopefully the comedy award doesn’t change their perspective on it, and I’ll be hearing from their lawyers soon.” Taken as a pair, the two city-boy-in-the-country shows feel like a sitcom in utero – but Cantrill is cautious of that thinking. (A long-planned Delightful Sausage sitcom has yet to come to fruition.) One benefit of being older when success comes your way, he says, is that you enjoy the moment rather than fret about next steps. “There’s this award. There’s me and Amy working on a show for BBC Radio 4 [Icklewick FM] and it’s the most joy of my life. So I’m just trying to be like: this is happening now for a bit, let’s savour it.”View image in fullscreen‘This needs to end, whatever the decision’ … Chris Cantrill, seventh from left, with the writers for Saturday Night Live UK in March.Photograph: Saturday Night Live UK/PAThere’s also SNL UK, whose success has been a huge boon to British comedy – and to which Sky TV recently committed long-term. When the creative team was first assembled, Cantrill recalls, “I went in for a casting, I went in as a writer, I submitted a tape. Then I did a showcase in Soho theatre, then several screen tests. And they kept going, ‘Can you come back and do it again?’ Eventually I said to the producer, ‘it’s been lovely seeing you every three weeks for the last six months. But this needs to end, whatever the decision.’” It ended with a writing job that he now describes as “great”, but also “the hardest of my life”.“They started by giving us ‘corporate resilience training’,” says Cantrill, wrinkling his nose: “about how to stay resilient in a pressured environment. And I remember saying toJonno [head writer Daran Johnson], ‘I’m a veteran performer. I donotneed resilience training.’ And then we did the first read-through, and my sketch either was cut or completely died. I’ve had both happen to me. And I turned to Jonno and said, ‘Please, can I have a top-up of the resilience training?’” It’s a competitive environment, in short, with no guarantee your work will ever make it to the screen.“I’ve always been hard on myself. At no point do Amy and I ever think we’re good and comfortable with our comedy. So SNL has been challenging.” But it’s also been “the closest thing I’ve done to what you think in your head the job [of comedy writing] will be. It’s sort of magical.” And off he goes on a rhapsody about filming SNL, the glamour of “storming around Television Centre, dressed as Victorians”, changing Riz Ahmed’s lines at the last minute, arranging cue cards, conferring with the director. “It feels like you’re in a film. It’s a rush.”View image in fullscreen‘Just surreal’ … Cantrill collects his Edinburgh comedy awardPhotograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianSNL also changed his experience of the fringe – in ways that surely spell the end for his outsider self-image. “I was part of a two-person team for years, and it was a closed shop. We’d work relentlessly and never see anyone else’s shows. But suddenly because of SNL, I’ve got all these wayward children all over the city. I’m going to see [SNL co-writers]Bella [Hull]andAyo [Adenekan]andOmar [Badawy], and I’m so invested in their success. It’s a really nice feeling.”In one of the funniest sections of Rewilding, Cantrill makes indiscreet jokes about SNL, teasing that its cast may not be “one big happy family”, and that his relationship is strained with the “private schoolboys” who run the show. But that’s just him being “a little cheeky boy”, he now tells me. “I do still feel on the outside of things. When I meet the upper echelons of the taste-makers, to those people, with my accent, I do sound basically like Kes.”“But I’m old enough to know what an opportunity looks like. So, when something like this pops up, it’s time to knuckle down and make the most of it.” That knuckling down, on season two of SNL, begins the day after we speak – leaving just 24 hours more to process the dream-come-true of winning the Edinburgh comedy award. “On no level have I processed it yet. It just happened yesterday. My phone has melted. My wife is keeping an eye on all the messages. I completely lost it on stage at my last performance and it all caught up with me. It was just surreal.” But Cantrill has been round the block too many times to get carried away. “I’ll be back in SNL dying on my arse on Wednesday, having a script read to silence,” he says. “And I can’t wait.”This article was amended on 3 September. A caption wrongly described Chris Cantrill’s comedy partner Amy Gledhill as his wife.Explore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Comedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)Edinburgh festivalinterviewsShareReuse this content
