title: ‘My work has always been serious’: Maurizio Cattelan on his $6m banana, his gold toilet – and bringing Hitler to Berlin | Maurizio Cattelan | The Guardian
description: He is famed for creating a golden loo that was stolen and a $6m banana that was eaten. But, says the sculptor ahead of a major new show in Germany, there’s more to his work than pranks and provocation
Author: Deborah Cole
Headline: He is famed for creating a golden loo that was stolen and a $6m banana that was eaten. But, says the sculptor ahead of a major new show in Germany, there’s more to his work than pranks and provocation
Content: ‘The problem is, people often stop at the joke’ … Maurizio Cattelan at the Neue Nationalgalerie in Berlin.Photograph: Christian Jungeblodt/the GuardianView image in fullscreen‘The problem is, people often stop at the joke’ … Maurizio Cattelan at the Neue Nationalgalerie in Berlin.Photograph: Christian Jungeblodt/the GuardianMaurizio CattelanInterview‘My work has always been serious’: Maurizio Cattelan on his $6m banana, his gold toilet – and bringing Hitler to BerlinDeborah Colein BerlinHe is famed for creating a golden loo that was stolen and a $6m banana that was eaten. But, says the sculptor ahead of a major new show in Germany, there’s more to his work than pranks and provocationThu 3 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 11.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMaurizio Cattelan, the art world’s merriest prankster, pauses when asked which object in his sprawling new Berlin show is most likely to be defaced, stolen or eaten, then emits a foghorn of a laugh. “There is no need to vandalise anything,” says the trim, soulful Italian, explaining that he has already taken care of all that, given how the work cuts villains, imposters and straw men down to size. “But,” he says, referring to the show’s more daring works, “maybe we need someone to resuscitate people.”Cattelan, who speaks in a lilting English, grins broadly, a mischievous glint in his brown eyes. Speaking on the subterranean level of Mies van der Rohe’s weightlessNeue Nationalgalerie(NNG) in Berlin, he darts between the impish and the profound in conversation, mirroring the dizzying range of his work. The silver-haired sculptor is best known for duct-taping a banana to a wall in 2019 and calling it Comedian, in a droll commentary on the excesses of the art market. The joke became even funnier when it sold for $6.2m, then hilarious when its buyer took abite out of his purchase and swallowed it.View image in fullscreenComedian, 2019, the $6.2m banana.Photograph: © 2025 Maurizio CattelanThere was also the gold toilet, called America, that was installed in New York’s Guggenheim in 2016, its curatorslater offering the piece to Donald Trump’s White Houseinstead of the Van Gogh that it requested.Thieves later made off withthe 18-carat loo when it went on display at Blenheim Palace, Winston Churchill’s Oxfordshire birthplace.“It’s rare to be with an artist who’s recognised on the street,” says NNG director Klaus Biesenbach. “He reached a level of accessibility with these very easy-to-communicate ideas: ‘Oh God, a person puts a banana on the wall and it’s sold for six million!’ He is a very deep thinker who camouflages seriousness with humour, and who camouflages the sublime with irony.”Night, Cattelan’s first major solo exhibition in Germany, was granted to him as winner of this year’s Neue Nationalgalerie prize honouring influential contemporary artists. Cattelan collaborated with curator Lisa Botti on new commissions, as well as selecting historic works from the past three decades, noticeably skipping over his greatest hits. “They were part of a different conversation,” he says. “My work has always been serious. The problem is people often stop at the joke.”The show spotlights the wax and wane of power, the contentiousness of collective memory, and the horror and hope of history, as symbolised by its scarred and vibrant host city. “Night,” he says, “is a beautiful title. We sleep, we love, we dream, we fear. It’s a moment where things get fuzzy. And after night, there is dawn and another day. But it’s definitely a suspended moment – a magic moment.”double quotation mark‘I suffer when making a show – but I love the rush. It’s a fix, a dependency’At the entrance, peering down from the roof, the 2003 work Never features Oskar, Günter Grass’s eerie child witness to the Nazi era from his novelThe Tin Drum, silently beating out his warning. Purgatory, created for the show, presents a stunted-scale version of Berlin’s Brandenburg Gate as an ambivalent landmark, a portal for visitors to rethink their engagement with European history.View image in fullscreenKneeling for $17m … Him, from 2001, is Cattelan’s most controversial – and lucrative – sculpture.Photograph: Attilio Maranzano/Maurizio CattelanHim, from 2001, features a diminutive kneeling man who is revealed to be Adolf Hitler in a prayer-like pose, facing off against 2007’s Dawn, a female figure with real human hair, her hands pinned in a crucifixion pose. Overhead, thousands of stuffed pigeons are absorbed by the black ceiling. They, for Cattelan, are “a menacing presence”, though Botti adds: “It’s also about the holy spirit, about looking up. It’s a bit of optimism.” It all calls to mind La Nona Ora, or The Ninth Hour, an infamous work from 1999 (sadly not in the show) depicting Pope John Paul II resplendent in ceremonial garb, having been struck down by a meteorite.The Hitler piece Him has been Cattelan’s most lucrative, selling for $17.2m in 2016. It had courted controversy in Warsaw, where it was displayed on the site of the wartime ghetto, recallingthe day in 1970 when West German chancellor Willy Brandt dropped to his kneesin front of the city’s Monument to the Ghetto Heroes to beg forgiveness for the crimes of the Nazi era. The Simon Wiesenthal Centercalled Cattelan’s work“a senseless provocation”.Cattelan is satisfied the Night exhibition is in the right place at the right time, lending the works fresh power. He confesses to a certain obsession with the darkest chapters of German history, but primarily for the universality of their nightmarish resonance. “Hitler in this case represents evil,” he says. “It could have been Genghis Khan or another very popular, very famous leader.” He is unafraid of the possibility of a Berlin audience questioning his right to borrow from German iconography, “like if I was wearing rasta hair or something”. Cultural appropriation, he believes, is a “very American” accusation.View image in fullscreen‘My Catholicism comes out when I don’t want it to!’ … The Ninth Hour (1999).Photograph: Dominik Pluess/APCattelan calls the NNG “an incredible building” and considers this modernist masterpiece with its famously windswept plaza “a major contributor” to the show. “There is no separation between inside and outside here,” he says. “I had to find a way not to dominate it, not to be dominated but to have a conversation. I connected with the idea of a church. My Catholicism comes out when I don’t want it to! But this time it came out as a structure, on this idea of central axes through the exhibition.” Botti describes Cattelan’s work as “comic existentialism”, saying: “You laugh about something, but then the laugh gets stuck in your throat.”His work comments on an era of crumbling social structures and disinformation, created by an artist who divides his time between Trump’s US and Italy under hard-right prime ministerGiorgia Meloni, choosing New York and Milan as his bases. “Internationally, there is now a resurgence of people asking for more strong leadership: Meloni is a very cunning and astute politician.” Expressing a grudging admiration for her unusual staying power, he says: “It’s disappointing to think that the left weren’t able to produce, in all the occasions they had, such stability. What didn’t they have that she has?” He suggests an answer: scapegoats. “We have always these enemies that are offered to us. They give us problems that probably we don’t have. But nobody has the magic wand.”Cattelan was born to a working-class family in Padua, a historic city 40km west of Venice, and famously had no formal art training. Having Berlin put on one of his most ambitious exhibitions in years has felt like a kind of homecoming, given it’s now 20 years since he co-curated thefourth Biennale, a barn-burner of a show that made the most of the now-restored capital’s“poor but sexy” era.“Maurizio really participated in Berlin becoming Berlin,” says Klaus Biesenbach, director of the NNG, calling that 2006 biennale “a watershed moment for this city” and its creative scene. Cattelan believes Berlin “still carries scars, history, contradictions – it’s a sort of outdoor experiment”. He credited it with helping him recapture part of his youth, his days spent as a postman, a mortuary attendant and a sperm donor. “Berlin definitely was about clubbing,” he says. “It was very interesting because in Berlin stuff can grow overnight, last like a mushroom for a few days and then disappear. [Clubbing] was something I didn’t experience during my 20s or 30s. I had a serious … well, four or five years of taking back lost time. It was beautiful, it was very raw. Now it’s over again. The city became more mature.”View image in fullscreenNovecento (1997), showing in the Castello di Rivoli in Torino.Photograph: Paolo Pellion di Persano/Maurizio CattelanFor Cattelan, the 2010s brought a highly publicised retirement, then a ferocious comeback. “At that time, it was like that pressure, the anxiety, the making of the shows we were producing – you reach a level where it’s like” – he makes a drowning sound – “where you have to raise a white flag.”Each major exhibition sends him on a rollercoaster of exhilaration and panic, he says, admitting to being “extremely desperate” while planning Night. “Do I suffer? Yes, I don’t like it. It’s always a challenge. I still need the rush. It’s a contradiction, but I love the hate of making a show. It’s a fix. It’s a dependency. Maybe a therapist would say, ‘We can solve your addiction problem.’ And I’d say, ‘No, no, I love it.’”I wonder, given the death ofDavid Hockney, another epochal figure of the art world, if Cattelan has given any thought to his own legacy, but he does not seem to envision a future in which his work endures. “I don’t have a foundation,” he says. “I don’t have a studio, never had. I also don’t have a family. A legacy would be like being so conscious about yourself that you have these constructions.”However, now being in his 60s, he says: “Maybe I should think about who I want to pass my problems to. I’m super lucky. I did have doubts [as an artist]. But I jumped into the void and said, ‘If we overcome fear, there will be a fantastic dawn. A fantastic dawn.’”Maurizio Cattelan: Night is atNeue Nationalgalerie, Berlin, from 10 September to 7 MarchExplore more on these topicsMaurizio CattelanArtSculptureExhibitionsInstallationinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Adéla: Prima review – Slovakian star smashes the fourth wall to bask in pop’s cynicism and seduction | Music | The Guardian
description: The 22-year-old is impressively frank about indulging industry sleaze in her pursuit of fame on a debut that puts a distinctive spin on the best of 00s hedonism
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: The 22-year-old is impressively frank about indulging industry sleaze in her pursuit of fame on a debut that puts a distinctive spin on the best of 00s hedonism
Content: ‘Meta commentary on what it is to be a female pop star’ … Adéla.Photograph: Ryley  PaskalView image in fullscreen‘Meta commentary on what it is to be a female pop star’ … Adéla.Photograph: Ryley  PaskalAlexis Petridis's album of the weekMusicReviewAdéla: Prima review – Slovakian star smashes the fourth wall to bask in pop’s cynicism and seduction(Polydor)The 22-year-old is impressively frank about indulging industry sleaze in her pursuit of fame on a debut that puts a distinctive spin on the best of 00s hedonismAlexis PetridisThu 3 Sep 2026 10.30 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 12.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere’s something very striking about hearing a pop star in 2026, their voice larded with Auto-Tune, opening a song with the line “I can’t really sing”. We live in an era where fans seem more aware than ever of the nefarious music business machinations that lurk within the star-making process, one where you’re never far away from online outrage decrying some artist or other as an industry plant. Nevertheless, admitting that the ubiquitous audio processing software is sometimes deployed for a helping hand, not a futuristic aesthetic, feels strangely jarring. On one hand, well of course it is. On the other, actually announcing that without it, you might be honking like a despondent goose, in the first line of a song, still amounts to a dramatic breaking of the fourth wall.View image in fullscreenThe artwork for Prima.Photograph: PR IMAGEThat said, it’s very much on brand for Adéla Jergová, who started her career as a contestant on a TV talent show – she failed to make the cut for crumbling “global girl group” Katseye, as documented on Netflix’s Pop Star Academy – before established names alighted on her as a more left-field solo proposition: Grimes co-produced her early single Machine Girl. New artists are well advised to have a USP, something that helps them cut through the mass of peers vying for public attention on streaming services. The 22-year-old Slovakian has chosen to differentiate herself from the serried ranks of post-Brat female pop stars by spiking her songs about hedonism and messy sexual encounters (“no bed frame, we can do it on the carpet … you eat real good for a starving artist”) with a kind of meta commentary on what it is to be a female pop star.Her debut EP, 2025’s The Provocateur, came in a sleeve that featured Jergová urinating in the street and boasted a selection of songs that depicted the cynicism of the music business and Jergová’s willingness to indulge it in her pursuit of fame. “I bring you body and my energy / Calculate my attitude and my identity … you found your monetary fantasy / Stop, pose, drop, I’ll make your wallet sing,” offered Superscar. There’s plenty more where that came from on Prima. Songs about smoking weed then having it off in a car (Marijuana) coexist with stuff like KGB – “you want a pop star with a big bra for them big hits”; songs that flippantly compare a budding romance to a pair of Christian Louboutin heels (Red Bottoms) with Therapy, home to the aforementioned line about Auto-Tune. “I’ll have to talk to the people I have to talk to,” it continues. “They are old white men / They’re so annoying, but they hold the keys to my future / So I have to do it anyway because that’s how life works.”Adéla: Ain’t in LA – videoYou could decry all this as hopelessly cynical, or place it in a longstanding lineage of pop stars revealing the industry’s workings. The Monkees decried their career as “a manufactured image with no philosophies” on the soundtrack of the 1968 film Head; boyband ‘NSync depicted themselves as puppets on the sleeve of 2000’s No Strings Attached. Although perhaps Jergová’s most pertinent spiritual forebear, given how often she drops her name in the lyrics, is mid-80s Madonna, who was happy to wear a belt-buckle that read BOY TOY if it aided her stated ambition to “rule the world”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSleeve NotesGet music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTrash hits! Why a wave of hedonistic, feral female pop stars are rejecting respectabilityRead moreIf it’s an old trick, it still feels impressively bracing and frank, its effect amplified by the fact that it’s set to sharply written melodies and music that frequently evokes the 00s, a decade that apparently seems like a hedonistic pre-social media nirvana to those too young to remember it first-hand. Nicole Kidman revolves around the kind of sped-up old soul sample that automatically evokes Kanye West’s productions circa The College Dropout and Late Registration; the rattling tabla-driven rhythm of Boys has a distinct flavour of Timbaland’s productions for Missy Elliott; KGB is co-produced by Harrison Smith, better known as the Dare, the sometime Charli xcx collaborator praised and reviled in equal measure for his role in the indie sleaze revival.Prima was apparently made in a hurry so that Jergová would have enough material to warrant a support slot with Demi Lovato. It definitely feels like a debut album. There are moments where it sinks into boilerplate pop: Hitachi is a standard-issue piano ballad about a failing relationship; Fantasize isn’t particularly interesting beyond the fact that its hook is played on a trombone and the opening line unexpectedly features the word “reciprocity”. But failing to be a perfectly turned finished product on arrival is hardly a crime: rather, it suggests an artist who has room to grow and develop. On the basis of what’s here – which is frequently sharp, funny and daring – watching Adéla do just that should be fascinating.This week Alexis listened toAlabama Shakes – GardenNew album I Must Be Dreaming more or less picks up where Alabama Shakes left off a decade ago: not a problem at all if the results are like Garden’s distorted, gently psychedelicised southern soul.Explore more on these topicsMusicAlexis Petridis's album of the weekPop and rockreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I don’t chase the dollar. I never did’: the astonishing hidden life of Mr T | Culture | The Guardian
description: He grew up in the ghetto, became a global superstar – then gave it all up. Why did he step away from the spotlight?
Author: Simon Hattenstone
Headline: He grew up in the ghetto, became a global superstar – then gave it all up. Why did he step away from the spotlight?
Content: ‘My job is to love people’ … Mr T.Photograph: Nolis Anderson/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘My job is to love people’ … Mr T.Photograph: Nolis Anderson/The GuardianThe big interviewCulture‘I don’t chase the dollar. I never did’: the astonishing hidden life of Mr THe grew up in the ghetto, became a global superstar – then gave it all up. Why did he step away from the spotlight?Simon HattenstoneThu 3 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 07.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMr T explains why he’s late, but he wants to make one thing clear – this is not an apology. “You caught me in my devotion, and nothing comes before God. So I won’t say I apologise for the delay. I just want you to know that God comes first in all my life. For allowing my success, I give God the glory.”He is here to discuss a new Netflix documentary, Untold Mr T: I Pity the Fool. At 74, he rarely gives interviews. But when Mr T decides to talk, he really does talk. What Mr T thinks, Mr T says. And I’ve never heard anyone trash the very thing they’re here to promote quite like Mr T does today.The actor, former wrestler and cultural icon is full of surprises. Perhaps the most surprising is that he’s still famous. As he says, he has no right to be. It’s more than 32 years since he participated in a wrestling match. Thirty-five years since he had a significant acting role in a TV show. Thirty-nine years since he starred as BA Baracus in The A-Team, and 44 years sinceRockyIII – the only TV show and movie he’s really remembered for. And yet, somehow, he’s still a household name.View image in fullscreen‘I don’t need gold now.’Photograph: Nolis Anderson/The GuardianIn the 80s, many boys and girls wanted to grow up to be Mr T. The A-Team was shown all over the world. This action-adventure TV series about four US army special forces commandos turned mercenaries became a huge hit and helped define the era.The movie star George Peppard was supposed to be the show’s headliner. But much to Peppard’s chagrin, Mr T proved far more popular. His BA (Bosco Albert or Bad Attitude, take your pick) Baracus was a mechanical genius and problem-solver; a peerless brawler and human battering ram, who wore an African Mandinka-style haircut, rattled with gold chains and had a pain threshold second to none. In some ways, BA Baracus and Mr T were similar. In others, they couldn’t have been more different.Born Lawrence Tureaud, Mr T grew up on the south side of Chicago, in poverty. His minister father left home when he was five, leaving his mother, Willie, to bring up their 12 children. The family survived on her work scrubbing floors for the wealthy, and welfare. Lawrence was known to his brothers and sisters as Little T. When he was growing up, everyday racism had a devastating impact on him. He was horrified by the disrespect most white people showed his family.View image in fullscreenThe A-Team. From left standing: Dwight Schultz, Melinda Culea, Dirk Benedict. Front: Mr T, George Peppard.Photograph: Pictorial Press Ltd/AlamyAged 18, he changed his name to Mr T. “Let me explain that,” he says. “See, everything I do there is a reason behind it. My father was a minister and I watched him being called Boy. And I watched my uncle being called Boy. I watched one of my brothers who was a marine come home from Vietnam in his beret and uniform, and some white guys were calling him Boy. So at 18 I had to register for the draft. I said, if I’m old enough to fight and die for my country, I’m old enough to be respected as a man, so I self-ordained myself Mr T at first. Then I legally changed my name to Mr T later on, so the first word out of everyone’s mouth would be Mr.”We meet on a video call. At 74, he looks wonderful. He’s wearing a stars and stripes bandana and a T-shirt that says Lord’s Gym, illustrated with a picture of Jesus doing press-ups with the crucifix on his back. His face, less full than it once was, is magnificently creased and creviced, with laughter lines galore.double quotation markMy mother taught me to take the high roadMr T is part preacher, part poet, part pugilist. Close your eyes and you could be chatting to Muhammad Ali in his prime. It’s all there in the rhythm of his speech, the wit and wisdom, the fighting talk. And yet, over the decades, he has often been portrayed as a muscle-bound meathead. He says if he had been that, his mother would never have forgiven him.He takes me back to his earlier years at school. Sure, he wanted to be tough like his bigger brothers, and hoped to be a successful footballer or boxer. But even more importantly, he wanted to pass his exams, because Willie had taught him the importance of education. She told him how the abolitionist Frederick Douglass, who was born into slavery, had been taught to read by the wife of his enslaver, “and then his slave master told her: ‘Don’t teach a slave to read, because if you do, he won’t be a slave much longer.’” Education was the route to freedom.What did he study? “Philosophy and theology. A teacher in high school said, there’s no money in that, and I said: ‘Sir, that’s disrespectful. That’s insulting, because not everybody’s about money.’ They didn’t take the time to know who I am.” I tell him I’ve been reading a lot about him, but it’s the first I’ve heard of him studying philosophy and theology. “See, that’s the problem. I’ve told journalists the same thing I’ve told you, but they don’t print that. They didn’t want people to know what Mr T is like. I was born and raised in the ghetto, but the ghetto was not born and raised in me. We was poor financially, but we was rich spiritually. I never robbed nobody, I never raped nobody, I never broke into nobody’s house. I never snatched a purse.”By the age of 15, he was a celebrated school athlete and looked like an adult bodybuilder. But his peers mocked him. “Growing up in the ghetto, even though I played football and wrestled, the thugs called me a sissy. You know why? Because I never robbed nobody.” He talks louder and louder. Soon he’s shouting. “They called me a sissy for listening to my mother, for listening to the teachers, for doing my homework. They didn’t go to school. They was dropouts. They was thugs. They’re in jail now or dead. They didn’t become nothing. As the Bible says, ‘Unless two agree, they can’t walk together.’ I told my mother I was going to be something in life. I was going to buy her a house and pretty dresses. They wasn’t going anywhere.” At times like this, he reminds me less of Ali and more of Samuel L Jackson’s Jules Winnfield in Pulp Fiction. Except Mr T’s Bible quotes are for real, and they focus on the loving aspect of the Old Testament rather than the hellfire and damnation.Despite all this, the new Netflix film zeroes in on a violent incident that happened when Mr T was in his teens. In the documentary, he describes how some local thugs robbed his mother of her welfare money, and he knocked their teeth out with the butt of a rifle, and told them that was just the start of it. He leaves the story hanging.View image in fullscreenIn the Netflix documentary, Untold Mr T: I Pity the Fool.Photograph: Courtesy of NetflixI mention this and he scowls. “There is too much emphasis on that scene. These thugs kept on robbing poor black women, who didn’t have no recourse. So we did what we was supposed to do. We’ll leave it like that. We don’t have to get into gory detail. You touch my mother, you got to pay. Bottom line. Then I would have been a real sissy if Ididn’ttake care of it.” But he’s not proud of what he did. “Revenge on the guys went against my God’s teaching, because Jesus said, vengeance is mine. But then we wasn’t dealing with the Bible stuff. It’s Dodge City. Somebody got to pay. Case closed. There’s nothing else to talk about. We’re going on to the next thing.”Did the guys live to tell the tale? “We’re going on to the next thing.” Silence.After college, he won a football scholarship to Prairie View A&M University, a predominantly Black college in Texas, where he majored in maths and was deputy president of the freshman year. But he was thrown out in 1971 for being part of a protest and uprising against the expulsion of the editor of the student newspaper, The Prairie View Panther. Photographs from the timeshow a very different Mr T– a smart-suited, clean-shaven student.View image in fullscreenA yearbook photo of Mr T.Photograph: AlamyHe returned to Chicago, did manual jobs (janitor at a local bank; housekeeping at a hotel) while attending local colleges on athletic scholarships. In 1975, he joined the military police corps of the US army and was named top trainee out of 6,000 recruits. He left the army in 1978 with an honourable discharge and, after a knee injury destroyed his dream of playing in the National Football League, he started working as a bouncer.This is when he developed his look. He was working at Dingbats nightclub, and accumulated gold chains from patrons who dropped jewellery or left it behind after late-night fights. His image was carefully cultivated. The gold, he says, was his way of reclaiming history. Instead of wearing chains of steel, as his forefathers had, he’d wear chains of gold. “People were concerned that I had too much gold and they asked me if it was too heavy. Nobody said to my ancestors: ‘That pregnant lady shouldn’t be in chains.’ Nobody cared about that, but all of a sudden they’re worried about this Black man, Mr T.”The jewellery and haircut were a way to attract attention, he says. “See, my mother and father taught me it takes a smart man to play dumb. In order to catch a rat, you gotta have cheese,so they want to see this man with the gold, with this funny haircut. Who is this guy? So they give me a chance, and I slip my message in. Maybe he looks crazy, but he’s not crazy. Now I’ve got your attention, I can tell you about me.”He explains why he used to wear seven earrings – three in his right ear, four in the left. “The three is symbolic of the father, son and the holy ghost; the three wise men; the three Hebrew boys – Shadrach, Meshach and Abed-nego; the three parts of the day – morning, noon and night; the three graces – faith, hope and love; the three civil rights workers that was killed in Mississippi trying to register blacks – James Chaney, Mickey Schwerner and Andrew Goodman. And the four in my left ear are symbolic of the four seasons – spring, winter, summer and fall; the four directions – north, east, south and west; the four gospel writers – Matthew, Mark, Luke and John. You put the three and the four together, it’s seven. There were seven times the Israelites marched around the walls of Jericho, Samson had seven locks of hair, there are seven colours in the rainbow, there are seven musical notes, God made heaven and Earth in six days, and rested on the seventh. I am the seventh son. So everything I do, there is a reason behind it.”Mr T became a personal bodyguard to the stars, including Michael Jackson, Diana Ross, Steve McQueen and Ali. I ask who he was closest to. He gives me an I’d-have-to-kill-you-if-I-told-you look. “No, I don’t want to name names. Everybody protected was important to me, ’cos it’s a life. If there was a gun, I’d take the bullet; if there was a knife, I’d be stabbed.” Did he ever have to take a bullet or knife for anybody? “No, no, no, it didn’t come to that. But if it had, I was ready.”He had first met Ali as a 16-year-old. “I was a sophomore in high school. One of my teachers knew Muhammad Ali, and told him about me and he came to my school. He said, ‘I want the baddest kid in the school to meet me in the gym’, because I’d just won the city wrestling championship. Ali became my hero because he stood up during the Vietnam war and said: ‘I have no quarrel with the Viet Cong, they never called me nigger, so why are we fighting the Viet Cong?’”View image in fullscreenAs Clubber Lang in Rocky III in 1982.Photograph: Collection Christophel/AlamyIn 1980, Mr T won an NBC show called America’s Toughest Bouncer. The thing is, he says, there were tougher men than him in the competition, but they didn’t have the right motivation. “I didn’t win because I was the roughest or toughest or baddest – there were sometoughguys there. True, you had to be a little tough, a little physical, but I won because I had a greater cause than the other guys. One guy said, if I win I’m gonna buy a car, another said he was gonna party. I said, when I win I’m gonna feed the homeless in the community.”It was on this show that casting director Rhonda Youngspotted him and suggested him to Sylvester Stallone for Rocky III as his antagonist Clubber Lang. Mr T’s performance is astonishing, not least because he had never acted before and many of his lines were improvised. (Most famously, when he taunts Rocky by telling his wife, “Bring your pretty little self over to my apartment tonight, and I’ll show you a real man.”) It was in Rocky III that he first said “I pity the fool,” which became his catchphrase. The film was the second highest grossing movie of 1982, ranking only behind ET the Extra-Terrestrial.View image in fullscreenIn character as BA Baracus in The A-Team.Photograph: NBC/NBCUniversal/Getty ImagesMr T was on a mission, but he insists it had nothing to do with stardom. “My pastor, Reverend Henry Hardy, said: ‘When you are in Los Angeles filming Rocky III find a place that you can minister to.’ So when I was out there I got connected to this homeless centre called the Midnight Mission.” Half a century on, he can still reel off the names of the other shelters he worked with when making Rocky – the Fred Jordan centre and Union Rescue Mission. “I brought them food and clothes. They didn’t know who I was. Because we were filming Rocky III, I brought a lot of Nike stuff. I left it at the door. Eventually at the Midnight Mission they found out who I was and they asked if I’d come in and pray and deliver a sermon, so I started preaching there.”A year later, in 1983, the A-Team started and Mr T became a global superstar. It was shown in more than 70 countries, and he soon became the best paid cast member, much to Peppard’s annoyance. He then became a global superstar twice over as the figurehead for the US’s most high-profile anti-drugs campaign.“The president and his wife, Nancy Reagan, hear about me telling the kids ‘don’t do drugs’, telling the kids ‘don’t rob and steal’, and Nancy Reagan says ‘Mr T would be good for my programme Just Say No’. So they check your background. And when they check my background, it blew them away. They said ‘Wow! He grew up in the ghetto, his mother brought them up on welfare and food stamps and they have no police record! Run that check again!’ They run that check again. ‘And one of his brothers is a Chicago police officer, another brother is a Chicago fireman, how do they do that?’” Mr T answers his own question for me. “Because we love and respected our mother.” There is a famous campaign photograph, taken in December 1983 at the White House, with Mr T dressed as Father Christmas, while Nancy Reagan sits on his knee and kisses his forehead.View image in fullscreenNancy Reagan with Mr T in December 1983.Photograph: Diana Walker/Getty ImagesIn 1985, he became a global superstar thrice over when he starred in the first WrestleMania with Hulk Hogan at Madison Square Garden. Liberace was the guest timekeeper and Ali was the special “outside” referee. By now, you couldn’t move for Mr T merchandise. There were Mr T dolls, Mr T fancy dress sets, Mr T cereal, Mr T lunchboxes, and a Mr T cartoon series.Does he think Peppard, who reportedly called him “the worst actor on the set” and refused to address Mr T by his name, was jealous of him? “My mother taught me to take the high road. I don’t want to get into that. My job is to love people, and I did. I always respected him. See, I don’t have to hate nobody. How can I claim to be a man of God if I’m hating somebody?”I was surprised, before our interview, when Netflix told me how much Mr T loved the documentary and how keen he was to promote it. The film suggests that his descent was as rapid as his rise, fuelled by poor decisions and bad behaviour. When I mention this, he tells me it’s a fake narrative. The truth is, he says, he didn’t want to act any more. “I don’t want to sound cocky or conceited, but if I never made another dollar, if I was never on TV again, all I ever wanted to do is done.” What was that? “All I wanted to do was buy my mother a beautiful house and pretty dresses. I done that in the 80s, so the game was over. It was done. I was already walking away. When they called me for the A-Team, I was at the wrap party for Rocky III. I was told, ‘the producer wants to meet you’, and I was like ‘I’m going home, my work is done. I’ve done Rocky III, I’m going back to what I did.’ My mother told me, ‘Son, there are some things that money just can’t buy.’ Like the poem says, if you can walk with kings and queens and not lose your common touch then you will be a man my son. How many people have sold their soul to the devil, chasing money? I’m not chasing the dollar. I never did.”The problem with the Netflix film, he says, is it focuses on the hardman stereotype and ignores the real Mr T. “The documentary pissed me off, because they didn’t cover a lot of stuff. When I saw it I was like: ‘What the heck?’ It’s garbage. You build me up, then you try to punk me out. I said: ‘Wow man, I’m more than that.’ Two days they interviewed my pastor, and he gets 30 seconds [on screen].” In his view, “That’s what we call, in the black community, a white man wanting to change the story and control the narrative. If you don’t know me, you’re gonna think I’m some monster.”View image in fullscreenMr T and Hulk Hogan backstage during WrestleMania 1 at Madison Square Garden on 31 March 1985.Photograph: WWE/Getty ImagesMr T appears most unhappy about the prominence given to his former agent, Peter Young. He says they fell out and claims he sued him after discovering that Young was allegedly putting his name to contracts Mr T knew nothing about.Meanwhile, in the documentary, Young says Mr T made terrible decisions, citing the film Freaked, a comedy set in a sideshow, in which he played the Bearded Lady. Young says Mr T walked away three days before the film wrapped.“I didn’t have no problem playing Freaked, because we were going against the typecast,” Mr T insists. “Brooke Shields was in it, Keanu Reeves was in it, Randy Quaid was in it. It was a fine role, but he’s putting me down for being in it. He wants to cut Mr T down. The time that it took to put that part [of the documentary] on, you could have had my pastor speaking about the people I changed in the community, but you don’t show that.” To be fair, the documentary does show a bit of that. He starts addressing me as if I made the film. “You see what I mean? Why don’t you show Mr T working with the Make-A-Wish kids, why don’t you show Mr T being in the army? So we show Mr T tough, and then you show Mr T as the Bearded Lady. See, that’s an agenda. It was a hidden agenda, they had to undercut what I’m about. What a joke!”He’s not done yet. “Here’s the bit that really pisses me off. Me and my manager did a conference call with Scott [Weintrob, the director] and he says, ‘what about Peter Young?’ and I said, ‘we had to sue him, so no, nothing to do with him’. Then we started to ask Scott, ‘OK, we wanna see some footage of what we’re doing, because when we do a movie we see dailies’. But he didn’t show it to me. We started filming last year at Easter. I didn’t see the finished product until a month ago. I didn’t see nothing on film. So now I see it, I say: ‘Goddammmmmmmmnmn, ain’t this something.’ We told them ‘Don’t put Peter in my doc’, but he did.”View image in fullscreen‘I’m doing what my calling is.’Photograph: Nolis Anderson/The GuardianWhen he finally saw the film, he says he had to pray for self-control. “I said: ‘Lord, don’t let me go off.Don’t let me go off.’’Cos I wanted to go off on Netflix. And I thought: ‘If I go off in here, it’s not going to be pretty.’ I said: ‘Take the high road.’ So I took the high road.”A message is flashing on my screen from the Netflix rep, who is listening in on the interview, pleading with me to change the subject. But Mr T isn’t quite done. I’ve asked about the comment in the film that he would only turn up to events if a white limousine was booked for him. “What’s wrong with white limousines? Shouldn’t I have a choice of colour? I wear white underwear. That makes me a bad guy? Let’s get real here. I wear white T-shirts sometimes, does that make me a bad person? I wear white socks. So what’s the beef about that? Sure, I like a white limousine. When Elvis Presley died he had a white limousine, so why can’t I have one while I’m living? But Mr T’s a bad guy. We don’t care about him feeding the homeless, but, you know, ‘He wanteda white limousine,he wanted acertainkind of soap in his hotel room.Wow, he’s a bad guy.’”Mr T is spitting with fury. “I’m not supposed to tell you what I like? I’m just supposed to take what you give me? No, no, no, no, brother, it don’t go like that. ‘When he became successful, he told ’em if they don’t fly his whole family, he ain’t flying,’” he says, as if quoting his critics. “That’s what I told them, too. My family is coming along. If they’re not part of it, I don’t do the deal.” Sure, he got the best deal he could, he says, because he was in a position to, and he knew his worth.We asked Netflix, Weintrob and Young whether they wanted to comment on the views Mr T has expressed about the film. Young replied: “Please give Mr T my best, and let him know I forgive him.” Netflix and Weintrob have so far declined to comment.I try to change the subject, and I tell him I love his daughter Erica’s comedy. (She is one of his three children, and a former teacher.) “I don’t go to see the comedy because it’s got four letter words in it and stuff,” he says. He’s still seething at Netflix. I ask him what he’s doing at the moment, and he tells me he’s visiting family in Chicago and spending time with the Pacific Garden Mission. “Once or twice a week I take them hand and foot warmers, ’cos it’s so cold. See, my life is like a rose. You gotta get past the thorns to get to the beautiful rose. So I take all the garbage, the lies, the lawsuits. As my brother would say, in a fight, ‘That’s all you got?’” Somehow the anger has dissipated and calm is restored.He says he’s so grateful for the difficulties he has faced in life – his childhood poverty and the T-cell lymphoma that almost did for him in the 1990s. And there’s been plenty worse than a film that doesn’t treat him with sufficient respect. “You ain’t gonna hear me crying the blues about ‘we was treated rough’. Life ain’t supposed to be easy. That made me who I am. I think of Maya Angelou’s poem. She said: ‘Still I rise.’ So, whatever you throw at me, I gonna rise from that. If you give me lemons, I’m gonna make lemonade. If you give me crap, I’m gonna make fertiliser.”I ask him if it’s true that he stopped wearing gold after Hurricane Katrina in 2005. Yes, he says. After helping with relief work in Louisiana, he felt it would be disrespectful to display his wealth while thousands of people had lost everything. Has he started wearing it again? “Sometimes I wear gold. Maybe one earring. I don’t need gold now. My heart is gold. You know why I don’t need to wear gold? The gold got you attention. Like making an announcement ‘Attention! Attention! Attention!’” And now he’s grinning like a little boy. “So, now you got the attention, slowly people know about this guy Mr T. They know his rap; they know what he stands for.”I tell him I’m going to expose him for having a cute smile, and it will ruin his reputation. I get another flash of it before it turns into a hammy snarl. “Then I’m gonna say: ‘Don’t believe what they say.’”Netflix asks me to wind up, though it seems as if he could chat for ever. He’s barely taken a breath in almost two hours. I’ve never met a septuagenarian with a set of lungs like Mr T. OK, just a few more questions I say.Is there a lady in his life at the moment? (In the mid-80s he and Phyllis Clark, the mother of his three children, divorced.) “Oh, there are a lot of ladies in my life. There’s my daughter, my sisters, my nieces. And then there’s the ladies at church.” I ask Mr T if he is teasing me? “Yes, I am. Actually, there is a lady in my life, yes. We’re about to get married. Yes. Now, go with that.” What’s her name? “I ain’t gonna tell you. I gave you enough now.”If you got offered a decent role in the next Rocky film would you take it? “No, no, no. I’m doing what my calling is. The money I made allowed me to have this free time.”Has he got much money left? “No. Let’s say I’m broke, because that sells better. People want to hear, he’s broke and he’s run out of money. It works better.” I tell him I don’t want to say it if it’s not true. He’s grinning. “You have no choice. I’m not going to open my wallet to you. See, if I’ve got God I’ve got all I need anyway. All I wanted to do is done – buy my mother a house and pretty dresses. I am complete. I. Am. Complete. All right brother, God bless you.”Untold Mr T: I Pity the Fool premieres globally on Netflix on 8 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsCultureThe big interviewTelevisionRockyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I was never taught Welsh history’: Michael Sheen on reclaiming rebel leader Owain Glyndŵr  | Michael Sheen | The Guardian
description: Actor will play 15th-century hero in sweeping production about Welsh rebellion against English crown
Author: Steven Morris
Headline: Actor will play 15th-century hero in sweeping production about Welsh rebellion against English crown
Content: Michael Sheen at the Wales Millennium Centre, Cardiff. One of the actor’s main reasons for staging Owain & Henry is because Glyndŵr’s story has never been told on an epic scale.Photograph: Dimitris Legakis/Athena PicturesView image in fullscreenMichael Sheen at the Wales Millennium Centre, Cardiff. One of the actor’s main reasons for staging Owain & Henry is because Glyndŵr’s story has never been told on an epic scale.Photograph: Dimitris Legakis/Athena PicturesMichael SheenInterview‘I was never taught Welsh history’: Michael Sheen on reclaiming rebel leader Owain GlyndŵrSteven MorrisActor will play 15th-century hero in sweeping production about Welsh rebellion against English crownThu 3 Sep 2026 02.17 EDTFirst published on Thu 3 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere are myriad films, plays and books focusing on heroes of English, Scottish and Irish history but far fewer that tell the stories of the great figures ofWales.A major new play about the Welsh nobleman Owain Glyndŵr’s early 15th-century rebellion against the English crown will help redress the balance this autumn.Michael Sheen, who will play Glyndŵr, said one of the main rationales for staging the show was simply that the rebel leader’s story had never before been told on such a large scale.“We’re talking about a figurevoted the second most important Welsh person of all time, only behind Aneurin Bevan [the architect of the NHS],” Sheen said. “But nobody’s ever done anything about him on this scale before. That tells a story in itself.”Sheen said when growing up in south Wales he had not been taught about Glyndŵr’s rebellion against Henry IV. “He meant absolutely nothing. I was never taught about him. He’s in the cultural collective consciousness so at some point I became aware of his name but I knew nothing about his story,” he said.“I was never taught Welsh history. It wasn’t on the curriculum. And again, that tells you something.”View image in fullscreenMichael Sheen said Owain Glyndŵr was in the cultural collective consciousness but he had known little about his story.Photograph: Dimitris Legakis/Athena PicturesOwain & Henry, will be performed at the Donald Gordon theatre atWales Millennium Centre, the second biggest stage in Europe, by Sheen’s fledgling company,Welsh National Theatre.The Millennium Centre is also co-producing the play.Sheen said there were very few ambitious, large-scale Welsh plays written for big theatre spaces. “For most Welsh playwrights, the reality of getting your play produced is that you probably have to write for a studio space. Maybe a couple of weeks’ run. And maybe a cast of maybe two or three. Beyond that, it becomes very difficult.”Sheen said the Olivier award-winning Welsh playwright Gary Owen had only felt able to create a sweeping version of the Glyndŵr story when the pandemic seemed to make it unlikely that it would ever be produced.He said: “During Covid, during the lockdown, he thought, no one’s going to ever see this play anyway, so I might as well write it the way I want to write it.”View image in fullscreenA painting of Owain Glyndŵr in battle by AC Michael.Photograph: Lordprice Collection/AlamySheen described Glyndŵr as a very unlikely rebel. “He was born into privilege. He inherited estates. He worked in the service of English noblemen. Fought on behalf of the English king, Richard II, in Scotland. Fought against the French. He was taught at the Inns of Court.“But then he got into a land dispute with his neighbour [the Englishman Reginald de Grey]. And this land dispute grew and grew and grew until eventually he was essentially being called a traitor.“He wasn’t the big crusading rebel leader. He found himself in a position where he had to fight back, otherwise really bad things were going to happen for him and his family. So he was sort of forced into it.”Sheen said he thought the Glyndŵr story, which will be performed in English, was relevant today. “Just putting it on is important, I think, but also the story is a kind of catalyst for a conversation that we very much need to have at the moment.”Earlier this year, the Welsh nationalist partyPlaid Cymru won the Welsh Senedd electionsin spectacular fashion, ending 100 years of Labour rule in Wales.It means that two governments – the devolved Plaid Welsh administration and the Labour UK government – have a say in the life of Welsh citizens.Sheen said: “The old has been swept away. And the immediate future of Wales is essentially in the hands of two very different visions of what it is to be Welsh, what Welsh identity is, what Welsh nationhood can be.“This play speaks to that absolutely. Even though we’re talking about events in the early 1400s, it speaks to us right now in a more urgent way than I could ever have imagined.View image in fullscreenOwain & Henry will be staged at the Donald Gordon theatre at the Wales Millennium Centre from 5 November.Photograph: Geography Photos/Universal Images Group/Getty“But also beyond Wales, it’s looking at what is it to be a leader? What is leadership? What is a responsible use of power? Is might right? They’re all things that feel very, alive right now.”Sheen said Glyndŵr’s world was a brutal one. “It was a world where everything was changing. You’ve got a man on the throne [Henry IV] where there are questions of legitimacy around him. And therefore there is a kind of febrile nature to the politics of that time. It feels very of now where the political floor is shifting all the time.”Sheen said it was “early days” for the new Plaid government. He has invited the Welsh administration toengage with him over the dumping of toxic waste in Wales, a subject the actor has highlighted in a documentary.Buried With Michael Sheen review – this vital look at a toxic waste scandal is deeply enraging TVRead more“But as yet, that has not happened. There’s also been a lot of talk about wanting to support the arts. But, you know, we’ll see what happens. This is the thing, isn’t it? When you actually get into power, then it’s not about talk any more, it’s about doing stuff.”Does he hope that Welsh ministers will come and watch the play? “Oh, they will come and watch it. It’ll ask a lot of questions. This is not in any way a sort of cloaked support for any particular party. It’s about values and beliefs, but they’ll come and watch it.”Owain & Henry is atWales Millennium Centre, 5-28 NovemberExplore more on these topicsMichael SheenWalesHeritageTheatreCardiffActinginterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Martin McDonagh says CIA has ‘done awful things all around the world’ | Movies | The Guardian
description: McDonagh’s new film, Wild Horse Nine, stars John Malkovich as an agent in 1970s Chile who feels ‘guilt and regret’ over his role in global interventions
Author: Philip Oltermann
Headline: McDonagh’s new film, Wild Horse Nine, stars John Malkovich as an agent in 1970s Chile who feels ‘guilt and regret’ over his role in global interventions
Content: ‘We don’t question the CIA’s activity as much as we ought to’ … Martin McDonagh, centre, in Venice with Wild Horse Nine stars Sam Rockwell and John Malkovich.Photograph: Anthony Harvey/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘We don’t question the CIA’s activity as much as we ought to’ … Martin McDonagh, centre, in Venice with Wild Horse Nine stars Sam Rockwell and John Malkovich.Photograph: Anthony Harvey/ShutterstockMoviesMartin McDonagh says CIA has ‘done awful things all around the world’McDonagh’s new film, Wild Horse Nine, stars John Malkovich as an agent in 1970s Chile who feels ‘guilt and regret’ over his role in global interventionsPhilip Oltermannin VeniceThu 3 Sep 2026 10.21 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 10.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US’s history of intervening in democratic processes around the world deserves more attention in the light of current political developments, playwright and film-makerMartin McDonaghhas said, as his Oscar-tipped film about a rueful CIA agent premieres at the Venice film festival.“I’ve been very interested in the truth of what the CIA has been doing over the last 60 years, and the awful things they’ve done all around the world,” McDonagh said about Wild Horse Nine, his first film since his 2022 tragicomedyThe Banshees of Inisherin.“I think maybe something that’s not talked about enough. We know what the KGB are like, but we probably don’t question the CIA’s activity as much as we ought to.”In Wild Horse Nine,John Malkovichplays Chris, a veteran agent for the foreign intelligence service who is stationed in Santiago, Chile, on the eve of the US-supported coup against Salvador Allende – Latin America’s first democratically elected Marxist president – in 1973. Recently diagnosed with cancer and acting erratically, Chris is dispatched to Easter Island with his protege Lee (Sam Rockwell), where he starts to reflect critically on his role in other CIA interventions, including the Guatemalan coup d’état of 1954, the 1961 assassination of revolutionary Congolese prime minister Patrice Lumumba and – according to the film’s telling – the killing of John F Kennedy.View image in fullscreen‘Sadder and darker’ … John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell in Wild Horse Nine.Photograph: Diego Araya Corvalán/Searchlight PicturesMcDonagh said he had originally set out writing a screenplay about a father and son who were both actors, but the story had only started to gel when he tied the story to theCIAoverthrow of Allende. “I realised that the story could be about a guy who [feels] guilt and regret about the things he has done,” he said. “It took it away from something a bit corny to somewhere much sadder and darker.”As well as Rockwell and Malkovich, who has already been tipped as an Oscar contender for his leading turn, Wild Horse Nine stars Steve Buscemi, Parker Posey and Tom Waits.double quotation markOne of the frightening things is that they don’t seem to be making it covert any moreMcDonagh on US in VenezuelaAsked at the press conference what they thought of the Trump administration’s illegal capturing of Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro in January, the US members of the cast looked reluctant to answer. “I can’t think any more,” said Malkovich.London-born Irish national McDonagh took over the mic instead. “I think, for me, one of the frightening things is that they don’t seem to be making it covert any more, which is very strange,” he said. “Like in the 70s, at least these horrible people had the intelligence to keep their acts secret, but it just feels like things are getting stupider and stupider and stupider.”“When I wrote the film and we made it, it was to talk about 1973 and Chile at that point,” McDonagh added. “But watching it now, it does feel like it does seem to have a bit of a commentary on present day geopolitics.”Explore more on these topicsFilmVenice film festivalMartin McDonaghJohn MalkovichCIASam RockwellFestivalsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Guitar used by George Michael in Faith video goes up for auction | George Michael | The Guardian
description: Gretsch Synchromatic 160 acoustic guitar expected to sell for as much as £120,000, as star lot in auction of items owned by late personal assistant Siobhan Bailey
Author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
Headline: Gretsch Synchromatic 160 acoustic guitar expected to sell for as much as £120,000, as star lot in auction of items owned by late personal assistant Siobhan Bailey
Content: Striking a chord … George Michael in the video for Faith.Photograph: Vevo/YouTubeView image in fullscreenStriking a chord … George Michael in the video for Faith.Photograph: Vevo/YouTubeGeorge MichaelGuitar used by George Michael in Faith video goes up for auctionGretsch Synchromatic 160 acoustic guitar expected to sell for as much as £120,000, as star lot in auction of items owned by late personal assistant Siobhan BaileyBen Beaumont-ThomasThu 3 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 16.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne of the most iconic items in George Michael’s career, the acoustic guitar he energetically strummed in the video for 1987’s Faith, is going up for auction.The guitar, a Gretsch Synchromatic 160 with a sunburst finish to the body, has an estimated sale price of £60,000-£120,000. It comes with a case featuring the words Rockabilly Rebel pasted on it – a reference to the twangy, 1950s-referencing sound of Faith, which topped the US charts for four weeks and became a foundation stone of Michael’s post-Wham! solo career.The guitar is part of a broader auction from the archive of Michael’s former personal assistant, Siobhan Bailey, who died in 2014 aged 56. It is being arranged via her widower.Bailey worked for Michael for more than 20 years, and amassed a sizeable trove of memorabilia. The star lot is the Gretsch guitar, but there are 31 others spanning everything from gold and platinum discs to tour programmes – and a metal lighthouse statue presented to Michael by Malaga city council in 1989 (estimated price £200-£400).‘I thought it didn’t stand a cat’s chance in hell’: Andrew Ridgeley on Wham’s surreal trip to ChinaRead moreThere are glimpses into the machinations for George Michael and Wham! tours via private itinerary documents, including one of Bailey’s handwritten notebooks, and a running order document for 1985’s Live Aid. Another itinerary details Wham!’s 1985 tour of China, when they became the first western act to tour the country. The trip was documented –in fractious circumstances– by director Lindsay Anderson in the film Wham! in China: Foreign Skies, recently reissued in an altered form asWham! 10 Days in China.The auction also features the ultimate version of Michael’s album Older – a promotional box set not made available to the public, expected to sell for £300-600 – and invitations that Michael received to various events including a reception by TV soap EastEnders, and a lunch with David and Victoria Beckham in 2002 (“rickshaws at nightfall, dress: white tie and diamonds”). Another lot features 49 photos, some of them taken by Bailey and previously unseen.Coincidentally, another Faith-era item is going up for sale at a separate auction announced this week: Ray-Ban sunglasses worn by Michael on the Faith tour are expected to sell for £15,000 to £30,000 at the upcoming Music Memorabilia Live auction held in London on 1 and 2 October.The auctions arrive as the 10th anniversary of Michael’s death approaches in December, along with a broader re-appreciation of the Faith era.A new film, George Michael: The Faith Tour, will be released on 6 November, drawn from rediscovered footage of a 1988 concert in Paris. The film is co-directed by Andy Morahan, who directed the Faith music video, and is assembled from footage generated by 14 35mm cameras which captured Michael’s performance. It will be preceded by a short film by Mary McCartney, pairing unseen images of Michael by acclaimed photographer Herb Ritts with an unheard interview with Michael. An 18-track live album, also titled George Michael: The Faith Tour, is being released alongside it.The Siobhan Bailey auction takes place 29 October, both online and in person at Sworders in Stansted Mountfitchet, Essex. The items go on display at Sworders’ London branch from 20-27 October.Explore more on these topicsGeorge MichaelPop and rocknewsShareReuse this content

title: Public given rare access as Thomas More painting goes under microscope | Art | The Guardian
description: Visitors to Nostell in West Yorkshire will get to see cutting-edge research into work considered the only faithful copy of Holbein masterpiece
Author: Mark Brown
Headline: Visitors to Nostell in West Yorkshire will get to see cutting-edge research into work considered the only faithful copy of Holbein masterpiece
Content: On-site research into the painting, expected to last eight days, will be the first time macro X-ray fluorescence scanning has been done in public in the UK.Photograph: Annapurna Mellor/National TrustView image in fullscreenOn-site research into the painting, expected to last eight days, will be the first time macro X-ray fluorescence scanning has been done in public in the UK.Photograph: Annapurna Mellor/National TrustArtPublic given rare access as Thomas More painting goes under microscopeVisitors to Nostell in West Yorkshire will get to see cutting-edge research into work considered the only faithful copy of Holbein masterpieceMark BrownNorth of England correspondentThu 3 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA spectacular, internationally important painting of Thomas More and his family is to have its secrets explored as the public look on.The open heritage science project, scheduled to begin on Thursday, is a UK first and will deploy techniques used at the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam during its famous public restoration ofRembrandt’s masterpiece The Night Watch.Visitors toNostell, a Palladian mansion near Wakefield in West Yorkshire, will be able to watch cutting-edge research normally undertaken behind closed doors in labs, the National Trust said.Simon McCormack, Nostell’s curator, said they wanted to take the public on a deeper dive into what is a prized and fascinating painting.“Why are we doing all these things behind the scenes when we are looking after and caring for heritage which ultimately belongs to everybody?” he asked.The painting is considered “one of the glories” of the National Trust collections. At 2.5 metres by 3.4 metres, its size meant that for most of the 18th century it stayed in its packing case, as it was too big to get through doors to hang it.View image in fullscreenSimon McCormack, the project’s curator, hopes it will have the same ‘buzz and drama’ as the Rijksmuseum’s restoration of Rembrandt’s The Night Watch.Photograph: Annapurna Mellor/National TrustIt shows three generations of the More family, Henry VIII’s lord chancellor who was executed for not supporting the annulment of the king’s first marriage to Catherine of Aragon.Encountering the painting in person is quite something. McCormack said: “It’s lifesize and it is that trompe l’oeil effect where you might feel you’re almost walking into the painting. It’s very visceral, very realistic.”The work is regarded as the only faithful, lifesize copy of the painting by Holbein, which was destroyed in a fire during the 18th century.Holbein, widely considered the most important artist working in 16th-century England, was introduced to More by their mutual friend Erasmus.Mystery sitter in Holbein portrait could be Anne Boleyn, AI analysis findsRead moreMore commissioned Holbein to paint him and his family, with the result being considered by art historian Roy Strong as “arguably the greatest and most innovative work of Holbein’s English period” and “at least a century ahead of its time”.McCormack said the Holbein was “arguably the first family portrait in a domestic setting in British art history”.The Holbein was destroyed in fire in 1752 but a preparatory sketch survives in Basel, Switzerland. Five copies are known about at present, including one in theNational Portrait Galleryand a miniature in the V&A’s collection.McCormack saidthe Nostell versionis “understood to be the most faithful to Holbein’s original and the only same-size version that survives”.It depicts More with his family, pets, books and musical instruments in their Chelsea home. As with most Tudor-era paintings, it is filled with symbolism and hidden meanings. A tethered monkey next to More’s second wife Alice has been seen as representing discipline and her ability to control the household. More was believed to have owned a pet monkey.The many books refer to the family’s scholarly reputation and three-petalled irises in the painting allude to faith, valour and wisdom.The on-site research, expected to last eight days, is being carried out by the Fitzwilliam Museum’s Hamilton Kerr Institute. It will be the first time that macro X-ray fluorescence scanning has been done in public in the UK. Researchers are hoping to uncover any hidden under-drawing as well as discovering and dating later additions to the painting.Erma Hermens, the institute’s director, said: “We are very excited to use our technical equipment in situ for the first time, taking it from Cambridge to Yorkshire, to help the National Trust in their understanding of this amazing family portrait.”Money to help fund the project has been provided by theCenter for Thomas More Studies at Dallas university.McCormack is hoping the project will have the same “buzz and drama” as the Rijksmuseum’s Night Watch conservation.“There are lots of myths and legends around our painting which heritage science may be able to help answer,” he said.“It may have been at the house for 300 years but we don’t know for certain who painted the Nostell portrait.”Explore more on these topicsArtHistoryWest YorkshireMuseumsRembrandtShareReuse this content

title: New musical to give intimate portrait of Marilyn Monroe and Arthur Miller’s marriage | Stage | The Guardian
description: Misfits Together, by Bastille’s Dan Smith and To Kill a King’s Ralph Pelleymounter, is set amid the 1950s’ ‘red scare’
Author: Chris Wiegand
Headline: Misfits Together, by Bastille’s Dan Smith and To Kill a King’s Ralph Pelleymounter, is set amid the 1950s’ ‘red scare’
Content: Marilyn Monroe with her husband Arthur Miller in New York in 1957.Photograph: New York Daily News Archive/NY Daily News/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMarilyn Monroe with her husband Arthur Miller in New York in 1957.Photograph: New York Daily News Archive/NY Daily News/Getty ImagesStageNew musical to give intimate portrait of Marilyn Monroe and Arthur Miller’s marriageMisfits Together, by Bastille’s Dan Smith and To Kill a King’s Ralph Pelleymounter, is set amid the 1950s’ ‘red scare’Chris WiegandStage editorThu 3 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 07.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was lampooned as the union of the “hourglass” and the “egghead” – the marriage, in the summer of 1956, between Hollywood superstarMarilyn Monroeand Pulitzer-winning playwright Arthur Miller. Now, a new stage musical is to give a nuanced and intimate portrait of that famous relationship, treat each as trailblazers in their own way and reveal parallels between the volatile state of the US during the 50s “red scare” and now.The production, which opens next autumn atLeicester’s Curve, is called Misfits Together, a reference to the film Miller wrote for Monroe that was released shortly after their divorce in 1961. It is a foray into musical theatre by two indie musicians, Dan Smith of the band Bastille and Ralph Pelleymounter from To Kill a King, who have recorded the score as a studio album. The first track, Oh America, is out on Thursday.Smith and Pelleymounter had originally envisaged it as a musical about 50s America. They shared their songs with Charlotte Bogard Macleod, who has written the book, and had long been fascinated by the relationship that caught the public’s imagination.View image in fullscreenArthur Miller, Laurence Olivier and Marilyn Monroe at the Savoy hotel, London, in 1956.Photograph: PA“I’d always wanted to exploreArthur Millerand how he had this integrity that cut through everything,” she said. “He refused to name names [before the House Un-American Activities Committee] and he stood up at a huge personal cost. When we started doing research, we just couldn’t believe that Marilyn was so central to this. She was supporting him. She had her own production company. And we were thinking, why hasn’t this been talked about or celebrated?” Each empowered the other, she added – “fighting [the anti-communist senator Joe] McCarthy or fighting misogyny”.Smith said that the musical would deal with how Monroe was pigeonholed. “Here’s a working-class woman who was in foster care and created the persona of Marilyn Monroe and became one of the most successful and known people ever in the world,” he said. “And still at the height of her success and fame, she was constantly questioned and denigrated and patronised.”Despite her many achievements, Monroe had been “reduced and reduced and reduced” to the image of a bombshell, Pelleymounter said. The musical, he added, would look at how her fame eclipsed Miller’s.Presented with Tila Arts, Misfits Together will be staged by Curve’s artistic director, Nikolai Foster, who said the company had been watching Monroe’s films for research. He praised her “innate understanding of the art of film-making” and “the craft of acting”. Foster said the musical showed the couple’s lives in such closeup that at times during the workshops they almost forgot that the main characters were two of the 20th century’s most famous cultural figures.View image in fullscreenFrom left, Curve chief executive Chris Stafford, librettist Charlotte Bogard Macleod, Dan Smith, Ralph Pelleymounter and Curve artistic director Nikolai Foster.Photograph: Phil TragenPelleymounter said he had returned to the phrase “history doesn’t repeat, but it rhymes” throughout their work on the project. Seventy years after the red scare, othering was still being used to create “fear and anger in order to maintain the status quo” in the US, he said. One song written for the musical expresses Miller and film directorElia Kazan’s frustration at “seeing politicians say things on the news that are so blatantly not true, that are manipulative and scaremongering”.Other famous figures in the musical include Laurence Olivier, Monroe’s co-star in The Prince and the Showgirl. “He says: ‘Stop trying to act, just be sexy,’” said Bogard Macleod. “His one note is: ‘Be sexy!’ He was frustrated with her wanting lots of takes, and she was just trying to get it right. But then when you see the film, she’s the one that shines.”Marilyn Monroe and Arthur Miller: a year in their lives - in picturesRead moreSmith and Pelleymounter wrote more than three dozen songs for the musical and have been whittling them down to under half that number. The pair, longtime friends, “have always loved writing narrative songs and using songwriting to dive into character and story and history and culture”, said Smith. “I want the songs to be epic and instant and nuanced and move the story along, to sweep across history and then zoom into someone’s psychology.”One song takes surprising inspiration from Eminem’s hit Stan, as it tells an “incredibly complex story via their correspondence”. Pelleymounter said they had also drawn inspiration from famous photos of the pair. “Bicycle rides have definitely made it into at least one song.”Pelleymounter and Smith will be following in the footsteps of fellow indie musician Passenger (Michael David Rosenberg), who recently had a musical theatre success with theOlivier award-nominatedThe Unlikely Pilgrimage of Harold Fry. Smith has also written the music and lyrics for Young Romantics, a musical in development whose characters include Mary Shelley and Lord Byron.Misfits Together will run at Curve’s Studio theatre from 4 September until 2 October 2027.Explore more on these topicsStageTheatreMusicalsArthur MillerMarilyn MonroeCurve theatreBastillenewsShareReuse this content

title: Berlin Philharmonic/Petrenko review – insightful Elgar and Tchaikovsky holds Proms audience in thrall | Proms 2026 | The Guardian
description: Elgar’s Enigma Variations sounded fresh and striking in the German orchestra’s reading, while Tchaikovsky’s fourth symphony was thrilling and monumental
Author: Erica Jeal
Headline: Elgar’s Enigma Variations sounded fresh and striking in the German orchestra’s reading, while Tchaikovsky’s fourth symphony was thrilling and monumental
Content: Freshness… Kirill Petrenko conducts the Berlin Philharmonic at the BBC Proms.Photograph: Lena LaineView image in fullscreenFreshness… Kirill Petrenko conducts the Berlin Philharmonic at the BBC Proms.Photograph: Lena LaineProms 2026ReviewBerlin Philharmonic/Petrenko review – insightful Elgar and Tchaikovsky holds Proms audience in thrallRoyal Albert Hall, LondonElgar’s Enigma Variations sounded fresh and striking in the German orchestra’s reading, while Tchaikovsky’s fourth symphony was thrilling and monumentalErica JealThu 3 Sep 2026 10.31 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 10.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIs the Berlin Philharmonicthe best orchestra in the world? Quite possibly. The only potential disappointment about the first of their two Proms under their chief conductor Kirill Petrenko was that there were just two works. Elgar’s Enigma Variations and Tchaikovsky’s Symphony No 4 made an insightful pairing, though, sharing an autobiographical aspect that, in different ways, reveals much about their composers.The Elgar – bread-and-butter repertoire for UK orchestras but not yet for German ones – was approached with a freshness that made these portraits of the composer’s friends and family seem particularly affectionate. The opening can sound like merely a warm-up for what’s to come; here, though, from the very start the string tone was sumptuous and pregnant with possibility, the phrasing meaningful. This attention to detail continued throughout a performance that gloried in the richness of the orchestra’s sound and the full extent of its range, from the softest of melancholy cello solos to the floor-shaking throb of the Royal Albert Hall organ in the finale. A particularly striking moment came with the stark timpani rolls in the penultimate variation, conjuring the sound of a ship’s engine to honour a friend who was then on a long sea voyage – or, reading deeper, perhaps a lost love who had emigrated years before.There is no room for friends and family in the Tchaikovsky – just implacable Fate breathing down the composer’s neck during an especially turbulent time in his life. The Fate theme came at us like a juggernaut at the opening thanks to the Philharmonic’s outstanding brass section. This work was where Petrenko’s mastery of the long view paid off – in each movement Tchaikovsky’s repetitious figurations were sculpted into long lines that built and receded to create something huge. The third movement had similar scope but came as a kind of light relief: its long passages of gossamer plucked strings were dispatched with pinpoint accuracy, and Petrenko seemed barely to need to conduct it at all. When Fate thundered back in to disrupt the finale, the quality of the silence in the pauses afterwards spoke volumes: this was an orchestra holding its audience in thrall.Available on BBC Soundsuntil 12 October. The Promscontinue until 12 September.Explore more on these topicsProms 2026Classical musicBerlin PhilharmonicreviewsShareReuse this content
