title: Fun, flirty and fried to perfection: farewell to Chicken Shop Date, the YouTube show that helped kill off TV  | Television | The Guardian
description: Amelia Dimoldenberg’s series helped turn YouTube into a world-beating phenomenon. As it bows out, we remember its best bits – from mocking MC Ghetts to that sizzling tension with Billie Eilish and Andrew Garfield
Author: Stuart Heritage
Headline: Amelia Dimoldenberg’s series helped turn YouTube into a world-beating phenomenon. As it bows out, we remember its best bits – from mocking MC Ghetts to that sizzling tension with Billie Eilish and Andrew Garfield
Content: It finally came to pass … Andrew Garfield and Amelia Dimoldenberg on Chicken Shop Date.Photograph: YouTubeView image in fullscreenIt finally came to pass … Andrew Garfield and Amelia Dimoldenberg on Chicken Shop Date.Photograph: YouTubeTelevisionFun, flirty and fried to perfection: farewell to Chicken Shop Date, the YouTube show that helped kill off TVAmelia Dimoldenberg’s series helped turn YouTube into a world-beating phenomenon. As it bows out, we remember its best bits – from mocking MC Ghetts to that sizzling tension with Billie Eilish and Andrew GarfieldStuart HeritageThu 3 Sep 2026 08.42 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 14.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Amelia Dimoldenberg posted a video to social media this week, telling an unknown companion “we need to talk”, it felt like a monumental announcement was on the horizon. And so it came to pass. Chicken Shop Date,Dimoldenberg’s YouTube series, is coming to an end.The press release covering the announcement came packed with superlatives. Chicken Shop Date has generated 34m hours of views over the years, and has reached 97% of all countries on the planet. What it didn’t mention is that Chicken Shop Date helped to legitimise YouTube as a platform that has taken on – and perhaps beaten – television. The very fact that the Guardian is covering the end of a YouTube video series in the first place is, in part, down to Chicken Shop Date.Nevertheless, the writing has clearly been on the wall for some time. Dimoldenberg is moving on to bigger and better things – she hosts red carpet interviews for several major awards and is writing a romcom film, plus a YA show for the BBC – but Chicken Shop Date has also started to ossify. What began as a fun and flirty interview show, which thrived on the genuine tension that sometimes occurred between host and guest, has gradually become just another stop on the promotional cycle. It’s hard to try to flirt with someone who has quite clearly just been shoved in front of you by a publicist, as has been the case in some recent episodes (Ben Stiller,Elmo).View image in fullscreenBlast from the past … Louis Theroux prepares to rap on Chicken Shop Date.Photograph: YoutubeStill, it’s easy to see why the show was so popular. Dimoldenberg’s entire demeanour, simultaneously needy and passive aggressive, has made for compelling viewing over the years. In terms of sheer pop culture heft, it’s worth remembering that it was Dimoldenberg who first goadedLouis Theroux into reprising a raphefirst performed in a documentary 26 years ago. It immediately went viral.Shakira danced to it on Jimmy Fallonand, despite the Chicken Shop Date redux happening four years ago, Theroux still references it approximately once every 45 seconds on his podcast.There is also the tidal wave of interest generated by her romance (showmance? Fauxmance?) with Andrew Garfield, with whom she had shared some conspicuous chemistry on various red carpets. When he finally appeared on Chicken Shop Date in 2024, public intrigue was so high that the episode ended up getting 13m views. What’s most fascinating about this is how quickly the chemistry turned to ash as soon as the cameras started rolling. The pair looked stilted and awkward, as if they’d just realised the world expected them to be its performing monkeys. It was one of the show’s biggest moments, but also a timely reminder that not all dates are dead certs.Other, smaller moments are just as indelible. In 2022, Matty Healy treated his appearance as an actual romantic opportunity, teasing Dimoldenberg, holding her hand and, right at the end,pestering her for a kissfor an uncomfortable length of time. In 2024, Billie Eilish played the same trick, holding Dimoldenberg’s gaze for so long thatthe host became visibly flustered.Of course, purists will prefer the earlier episodes, when Dimoldenberg would use the show to deliberately weird out some much more niche British musicians. An early video, before Chicken Shop Date had established its visual identity, saw Dimoldenberg pull a variety of increasingly disgusted facesat grime MC Ghettsas he discussed the physical side of his love life.Another, slightly later one, with Raleigh Ritchie (real name Jacob Anderson) perhaps saw the moment when the show’s potential came into clearest focus.She spent the interview chiding Ritchie for his poor posture, then seemingly provoked him into unwittingly stumbling into an immediately retracted Jimmy Savile impersonation.It’s this essence, far more than the format or the guests, that have propelled Amelia Dimoldenberg to fame. As long as she can maintain what made her so special – the flirtiness, the awkwardness, the sense that she changed her mind about being wherever she is as soon as she got there – then she’s bound to have a long career ahead of her. If not, well … we’ll always have the chicken.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionSocial mediafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: La Mesías review – this utterly bizarre TV show is unforgettable  | Television | The Guardian
description: Finally landing on Mubi, this Spanish mega-hit about six sisters drilled into becoming viral Christian pop stars is wildly ambitious, blackly funny and a true triumph. Oh, and there are UFOs too
Author: Hannah J Davies
Headline: Finally landing on Mubi, this Spanish mega-hit about six sisters drilled into becoming viral Christian pop stars is wildly ambitious, blackly funny and a true triumph. Oh, and there are UFOs too
Content: Holy pop … La Mesías on Mubi.Photograph: MubiView image in fullscreenHoly pop … La Mesías on Mubi.Photograph: MubiTV reviewTelevisionReviewLa Mesías review – this utterly bizarre TV show is unforgettableFinally landing on Mubi, this Spanish mega-hit about six sisters drilled into becoming viral Christian pop stars is wildly ambitious, blackly funny and a true triumph. Oh, and there are UFOs tooHannah J DaviesThu 3 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 11.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt Primavera Sound festival in Barcelona in 2024, nestled alongside the likes of Pulp and Charli xcx was an unusual addition to the bill. Stella Maris arrived on stage as haunting home movies, religious iconography and glittery gifs popped up on the screen behind them. Part-Haim, part-Heaven’s Gate, the six sisters performed their hits: “Christian electronic dance music” that their late mother, apparently, believed would help them to save the world.The performance was very real, but the band was not. It was a stunt for the Spanish TV mega-hit La Mesías or The Messiah, which was released there in 2023. Its seven episodes centre on an estranged brother and sister, Enric and Irene, who discover that their siblings have become a viral pop band. Cue a soft-focus, flashback-heavy trip into the family’s past, thick with emotional neglect, parental narcissism and religious fanaticism. Oh, and there are UFOs, too.La Mesías is nothing if not singular in its vision, and was masterminded by Los Javis, the Spanish duo who won best director at Cannes film festival earlier this year for their upcoming queer drama film La Bola Negra. Certainly, this isn’t a series you will forget in a hurry. As well as being incredibly long (some episodes clock in at close to an hour and 20 minutes, making it less of an outlier on the usually cinema-focused streamer Mubi), it is – and I mean this lovingly – truly bizarre. Sometimes, it feels like two or three different series have been smooshed together, with timelines that jostle for your attention. There are the early years, with a young Enric and Irene played with poise and maturity by child actors Bruno Núñez Arjona and Carla Moral, plus Ana Rujas as Montserrat – part Cher in Mermaids, part Mommie Dearest who drunkenly tells her kids that “mamá tiene que vivir” (“mum needs a life, too”). Then there are the sheltered adolescent years, with the siblings now played by Biel Rossell and Irene Balmes and known by the names Isaías and Resurrección. They’re coerced by their mother into performing religious music in the 90s, while wearing clothes that look as if they’re from the 1920s. Finally, we have Enric and Irene in the present (Roger Casamajor and Macarena García), traumatised by their childhood but also determined to save their younger sisters.View image in fullscreenA rather ambitious feat … La Mesías.Photograph: sophiekoehler/MubiIf this wasn’t already clear, it is a rather ambitious feat. And if you thought Pedro Almodóvar had a lot to say about mothers, then just wait to see what Los Javis have in store here as Montserrat (also played by Lola Dueñas and Carmen Machi) inflicts all of her own psychic chaos and religious mania on to her children. The pairing of Dueñas as the middle Montserrat and Albert Pla as her super-conservative husband, Pep, is a casting coup, as they play some of the most horrendous (but also often the most farcical) parents imaginable. For all its horrors, La Mesías is blackly funny, finding its humour in unexpected places, like a visit from social services, or the aforementioned performance by the two teenage siblings, who are met with a horrible mixture of indifference and laughter on stage. The Stella Maris tunes are funny, too, but they’re also rather catchy thanks to some canny writing from the Catalan pop band Hidrogenesse.There are some aspects of La Mesías that don’t quite work. The apparent internet ubiquity of Stella Maris is never quite squared with just how sheltered the sisters apparently are (although, in fairness, they were heavily inspired by the real-life group Flos Mariae). There are about 10 plotlines too many, and some of the episodes drag. And while the music budget was clearly high, some of the needle-drops – among them Hozier’s Take Me to Church and Everytime You Go Away by Paul Young – can feel rather on-the-nose (an exception should probably be made for Pink Floyd’s Mother (“mama’s gonna make all your nightmares come true”) which is spot-on but also chilling here). But as a work of art, this series is a triumph – a nightmare-inducing thriller with the kind of ambition that shows exactly why Los Javis would go on to win at Cannes. Enric and Irene’s aunt tells them that “your mum met many men, but the worst of them was God”, which feels too simplistic an explanation for what we see here. This isn’t a show that critiques religion, so much as the dogma, destruction – and sometimes even the poppy indoctrination – that mere mortals bring to it.La Mesías is on Mubi now.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewMubireviewsShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: Richard Ayoade brings maximum contempt to new Taskmaster | Television | The Guardian
description: The brilliantly deadpan comic joins Nina Conti, Chloe Petts and Isy Suttie. Plus: A House Through Time reaches the present day. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Ali Catterall
Headline: The brilliantly deadpan comic joins Nina Conti, Chloe Petts and Isy Suttie. Plus: A House Through Time reaches the present day. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Effortlessly enjoyable … Richard Ayoade in Taskmaster.Photograph: Andy Devonshire/Avalon Television/Channel 4View image in fullscreenEffortlessly enjoyable … Richard Ayoade in Taskmaster.Photograph: Andy Devonshire/Avalon Television/Channel 4TV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: Richard Ayoade brings maximum contempt to new TaskmasterThe brilliantly deadpan comic joins Nina Conti, Chloe Petts and Isy Suttie. Plus: A House Through Time reaches the present day. Here’s what to watch this eveningAli Catterall,Phil Harrison,Jack Seale,Hannah VerdierandSimon WardellThu 3 Sep 2026 01.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTaskmaster9pm, Channel 4Taskmaster is often funnier when one contestant has stagey contempt for the whole project. Step forwardRichard Ayoade, who makes his intention to do the bare minimum very clear in this opener. A mere 22 seasons in, the show remains an effortlessly enjoyable way to spend an hour – the other comics making up the cohort are Chloe Petts, Isy Suttie, Nina Conti and Matt Lucas.Phil HarrisonRenovation Rescue8pm, Channel 4This latest variation on the home improvement show continues with more renovation wrongs being righted by Vogue Williams and Luke Mabbott. They’re in Nottingham, where they learn from Sylvia and Dave that even minimalist designs can go wrong. Worse still, Sylvia has been diagnosed with a serious health issue.PHThe Yorkshire Vet8pm, Channel 5Who knew bulls could get sunburns? Clearly, as temperatures soar across the UK, nothing is off the table. The latest episode of this cheerfully entertaining series sees Shona Searson looking after a breeding animal who has forgotten to slap on the suncream. Meanwhile, Julian Norton is wary when a 12ft Burmese python arrives at the practice.PHA House Through Time9pm, BBC TwoView image in fullscreenPast lives … David Olusoga in A House Through Time.Photograph: Richard Ranken/Twenty Twenty ProductionsDavid Olusoga wraps up the history of a beautiful Georgian home in Edinburgh from the 1930s through to the present day. Current residents Morag and Henrietta are delighted to hear it was once “a house of ill fame”, but there’s sadness as Olusoga traces the poverty and war, then the threat of demolition in the 1960s.Hannah VerdierFightland9pm, Sky AtlanticThe pulp boxing gangland thriller continues, with Duke (Howard Charles) in a tighter spot than ever since his promoter and drug-dealer nemesis Kingsley (Nicholas Pinnock) has proved elusive. As he hurtles towards a disastrous meeting with some tough Russians, drastic action is required.Jack SealeHit Point9pm, U&DaveThe gritty west London crime thriller continues as the two fugitives do a runner with the missing millions, while their dangerous rivals (including Peter Serafinowicz in a cuddly hat) close in to claim their share. Elsewhere, framed, innocent Kieran threatens to spill the beans, putting Leo’s double life in jeopardy. What’s a bent cop meant to do?Ali CatterallFilm choiceView image in fullscreenManic … Mark Eydelshteyn and Mikey Madison in Anora.Photograph: Anora Productions/PAAnora (Sean Baker, 2024),Thursday, NetflixSean Baker’s brilliant indie drama and surprise Oscar winner showcases the writer and director’s ability to immerse us fully in the lives of society’s most marginal characters. His focus here is the titular Brooklyn stripper and sex worker, played by Mikey Madison from Better Things. When a Russian oligarch’s son, Ivan (Mark Eydelshteyn), falls impetuously in love with her, Anora seizes the chance of a better life. But she is up against some formidable in-laws. Veering skilfully from slapstick comedy to gritty drama, it’s a superbly acted, manic treasure.Simon WardellExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV tonightRichard AyoadefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Gentlemen season two review – these geezers in tweed are irritating, stupid and extremely funny  | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: Guy Ritchie’s crime caper is back with the usual hijinks, swearing and men shaking their fists. But its ridiculousness is strangely comforting – and Theo James’s beefcake Eddie is so bland that he is fascinating to observe
Author: Sarah Dempster
Headline: Guy Ritchie’s crime caper is back with the usual hijinks, swearing and men shaking their fists. But its ridiculousness is strangely comforting – and Theo James’s beefcake Eddie is so bland that he is fascinating to observe
Content: ‘A wardrobe of beef in cufflinks’ … Theo James as Eddie.Photograph: NetflixView image in fullscreen‘A wardrobe of beef in cufflinks’ … Theo James as Eddie.Photograph: NetflixTV reviewTelevision & radioReviewThe Gentlemen season two review – these geezers in tweed are irritating, stupid and extremely funnyGuy Ritchie’s crime caper is back with the usual hijinks, swearing and men shaking their fists. But its ridiculousness is strangely comforting – and Theo James’s beefcake Eddie is so bland that he is fascinating to observeSarah DempsterThu 3 Sep 2026 03.02 EDTFirst published on Wed 2 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHe lives in a house, a very big house in the country. He has pectorals the size of Bentleys and wears plus-fours so voluminous they could accommodate his fleet of gundogs and still provide room for snarling groundskeeper Geoff (“I would do anyfink for you an’ this famlee”). And yet! Edward “Eddie” Horniman, 13th Duke of Halstead (Theo James), is sad. And aggrieved. A moment’s silence, please, as this powerful hunk pontificates on the unbearable lightness of being the millionaire protagonist in Guy Ritchie’s The Gentlemen.“Four hundred years ago, this estate spread out as far as the eye could see,” he tells Geoff (Vinnie Jones) as the camera swoops over his verdant playpen, a lavish patchwork of abundant hedges and cap-doffing deer. “But it’s been diminished. Year after year. Generation after generation. First came the apologies, then came the shame, then came the contraction. I want it back, Geoff,” he growls, hexagonal jaw stiff with emotion. “I want it all back!”Well, of course he does. For what is The Gentlemen if not Ritchie’s ode to the enterprising zeal of the Empire, a time when toffs like Eddie spread their buttocks across the map, and lowborn bruisers provided them with endless bleedin’ bog roll? The series is also an ode of sorts to Ritchie’s own empire, in the sense that it is a facsimile of everything else the director has ever made. Which is to say; an action caper composed primarily of fists, shouting and men made of fists shouting “faaackin’ ’ell” in tweed. Only here, the energy that fizzed through his early stuff has been replaced with a clock-watching aimlessness that suggests a wariness – if not an active fear – of the running time. Anyway, here is series two, and it is precisely as irritating, beautifully shot, overlong, extravagantly stupid and fitfully funny as its predecessor.View image in fullscreenThey want more. More, by Jove! … Theo James and Kaya Scodelario in The Gentlemen.Photograph: NetflixThe last time we joined Eddie, he was up to his cravat in cash, having joined forces with frosty Susie Glass (Kaya Scodelario) to help head the cannabis operation that the latter’s crime family had been running from a bunker on the aristo’s estate. And now? He wants more. More, by Jove. First, he wants to shake off Susie and bulbous paterfamilias Bobby (Ray Winstone), the duo having held him in a debt-shaped headlock due to their having bailed out Eddie’s financially incontinent brother Freddy (Daniel Ings, who remains the best thing in this bunkum by a country mile). Second, our muscular hero wants to venture into the world of international arseholery via an Italian drug deal with “boss of bosses” Marco Moretti (Sergio Castellitto). Plus! He wants to become a hereditary peer. This will allow him to a) determine the outcome of a bill to decriminalise marijuana and b) parade around his grounds in a cape the size of Sussex.Elsewhere, there is a motorcycle chase, some cobblers re a coveted Botticelli and a gloriously full-bodied turn from Hugh Bonneville as the eminently bribable Lord Hawthorne (“I am being greased!”). Meanwhile, the perpetually semi-naked Bobby continues to bark orders from between his sauna and hot tub; an effort, presumably, to become the world’s first fully amphibious cockney.In the middle of all this is Theo James’s Eddie, a thick-armed enigma wrapped in a yawn. Why does his face never move? Maybe he was born with it. Maybe it’s Maybelline. Or maybe it’s the realisation that Eddie isn’t so much a character as a wardrobe of beef in cufflinks, his main contribution to proceedings being to drawl about profit margins while blankly reducing the local partridge population to soup (“I shot another one, Geoff!”)There’s a certain comfort in Ritchie’s commitment to the bit, a sense of reassurance in the knowledge that in these restless times, his fetishisation of the gentry and preoccupation with uninhibited wide-boys remains immutable. But it ain’t half slow, ma’am. For all its international hijinks, its oi-oi-saveloy geezerisms, you may still find yourself wishing the whole thing would, in the words of Bobby, “gerra faaackin’ move on”.The Gentlemen is on Netflix nowExplore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV reviewTelevisionGuy RitchiereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Chad Powers season two review – Glen Powell’s sweet sports comedy scores a touchdown | Television | The Guardian
description: The Hollywood hottie is back as the quarterback in disguise, in an oddball comedy that is naughty, lovable and disarmingly unique
Author: Jack Seale
Headline: The Hollywood hottie is back as the quarterback in disguise, in an oddball comedy that is naughty, lovable and disarmingly unique
Content: The man behind the mask … Colton Ryan as Gerry in a Chad Powers mask.Photograph: DisneyView image in fullscreenThe man behind the mask … Colton Ryan as Gerry in a Chad Powers mask.Photograph: DisneyTV reviewTelevisionReviewChad Powers season two review – Glen Powell’s sweet sports comedy scores a touchdownThe Hollywood hottie is back as the quarterback in disguise, in an oddball comedy that is naughty, lovable and disarmingly uniqueJack SealeThu 3 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 11.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the first episode of season two of Chad Powers, there is but one concern: the main character’s nose has fallen off.The TV outlet for the wacky side of movie hottieGlen Powell, Chad Powers presents itself to us having willingly taken on the burden of a ludicrous premise. Powell is Russ Holliday, a former hotshot college-football quarterback who, eight years ago, committed a career-cancelling faux pas during the televised game that was meant to make him a star. With his sporting dreams suddenly vaporised, he became an obnoxious playboy. But then, just as he felt his feet starting to scrape rock bottom, he heard that a university in Georgia was holding open tryouts for a new quarterback. Donning prosthetic whiskers, teeth, hair and an occasionally unreliable nose – a slightly more sophisticated version of a joke-shop disguise – Russ became “Chad Powers”, a southern oddball and the new star of the team, while constantly dealing with the threat of being found out and sent home.The series has been compared toEastbound & Down, on account of its love of cartoonish characters being crass in a sporting context, and to the show that surely influenced its commissioning,Ted Lasso. Both Powers and Lasso feature a main character who is winging it, and both play off a naughty sense of humour against a weakness for sweet, folksy wisdom. In its overall structure, though, Powers most recallsSuits, the legal drama where one of the lawyers was secretly an unqualified impostor, and where the narrative was destined to destroy itself: the only thing that could really happen was someone finding out, but the more people who found out, the less room the story had to breathe.View image in fullscreenAn underdog to cheer for … Glen Powell is Chad Powers.Photograph: DisneyBy the end of season one, the Chad/Russ deception was known to team mascot Danny (Frankie Rodriguez), who recognised Russ on day one but vowed to assist him, because it suited his thwarted theatrical flair; and assistant coach Erika, AKA “Ricky” (Perry Mattfeld), a potential love interest who went cold on adorable Chad when toxic, selfish Russ made a reappearance and had sex with Ricky’s stepmother in his Tesla Cybertruck. (Incidentally, the show’s prominent featuring of the Cybertruck might make you think it was paid product placement, but instead it is visual shorthand for Russ being an agonisingly embarrassing loser, and one of its best gags.)What next? The task for Chad Powers is to not be the TV equivalent of a bad Adam Sandler/Will Ferrell movie, with a funny first act and then a long, boring plateau as the novelty of the premise wears off. Season two has a few solutions.One is just Chad carrying on being Chad, who, because his creator is frantically making everything up as he goes along, has a disarmingly unique imagination: he tries to get out of attending an event by claiming his Venus flytrap needs attention, and asks philosophical questions like: “What if balloons were afraid of heights?” Another is the looming threat of displaced and now dangerously disgruntled wannabe quarterback Gerry (Colton Ryan). Suits fans will spot that Gerry is the Louis Litt of the piece, as he tries to bring Chad down with increasingly manic recklessness, despite being a softie at heart.View image in fullscreenClue’s in the name … the South Georgia Catfish football team’s stars, Chad (Powell) and coach ‘Ricky’ (Perry Mattfeld).Photograph: Disney+There is also an attempt to lean into the serious dramatic potential of the mask Russ wears. Are all of us not, Chad Powers asks, wearing a mask in the workplace, and in relationships? And since everything Chad says and does is really Russ, which is the fiction and which the real man? That question gets more complex when we glimpse the damaged soul behind the crass preening of Russ, and we see that Russ’s overconfidence was a fake trait to hide behind long before Chad came along.‘I don’t know how anyone takes themselves seriously in this job’: Hollywood hotshot Glen Powell talks to Marina HydeRead moreCelebrities, meanwhile, have another layer of artifice that they place between themselves and the world. Picking up on this, the show has the college capitalise on Chadmania by selling Chad face masks. To hide his temporary lack of a nose, Chad himself ends up wearing a mask for a heart-to-heart with Ricky, which means Powell has to act with just his eyes through solid plastic. He manages it, though he’s at his best when Chad removes all his disguises and reverts to Russ: Powell’s face mixes matinee-idol looks with a boyish vulnerability that’s perfect for showing us that Russ is not awful at all, just lost.None of that is allowed to weigh heavily on what is still a stupid sports comedy peopled by charming doofuses, but this slightly more serious Chad Powers has given itself a shot at surviving for longer than it really should. It’s an underdog that’s worth cheering for.Chad Powers is on Disney+Explore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewGlen PowellTV comedyreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Hillary Clinton leads tributes to Gloria Steinem: ‘Her activism was rooted in optimism’ | Gloria Steinem | The Guardian
description: Former secretary of state joins Nancy Pelosi, Jill Biden, Roxane Gay and others in heralding groundbreaking feminist
Author: Richard Luscombe
Headline: Former secretary of state joins Nancy Pelosi, Jill Biden, Roxane Gay and others in heralding groundbreaking feminist
Content: Gloria Steinem at a rally outside the United Nations in New York City in 1978.Photograph: Bettye Lane/Photo Researchers/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGloria Steinem at a rally outside the United Nations in New York City in 1978.Photograph: Bettye Lane/Photo Researchers/Getty ImagesGloria SteinemHillary Clinton leads tributes to Gloria Steinem: ‘Her activism was rooted in optimism’Ex-secretary of state joins Nancy Pelosi, Jill Biden, Roxane Gay and others in heralding groundbreaking feministGloria Steinem, groundbreaking feminist campaigner, dies aged 92‘We badly need to raise our boys more like our girls’: Gloria Steinem – a life in quotesRichard LuscombeThu 3 Sep 2026 14.08 EDTFirst published on Thu 3 Sep 2026 09.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLeading figures from politics, entertainment and wider society led glowing tributes toGloria Steinemon Thursday, with Hillary Clinton hailing the American feminist icon whodied at 92at home in New York City as “one of the architects of the entire structure of women’s equality”.Clinton, a former US secretary of state, presidential candidate and first lady, was among the first to jump in with praise early on Thursday when she appeared on the CBS Mornings TV show to share her respect and gratitude for Steinem.Clinton urged younger generations to use Steinem as a role model in supporting each other in promoting the causes she championed.“I’m hoping that young women realize that the fight is worth it,” she said. “It is exhilarating.”Kamala Harris, the former US vice-president, hailed Steinem as a “trailblazing activist, organizer, and journalist – an icon in so many ways”, in a poston X.“To know her as a person is to know someone who was kind, sharp, and witty. She was invested in young women and keeping the door open for the next generation of leaders,” Harris wrote.“I will always be grateful for her encouragement and support in my campaign for the presidency. A campaign that was made possible, in no small part, because of her activism and so many other giants upon whose shoulders we stand.”Others who eulogized Steinem included Nancy Pelosi, the Democratic former House speaker, who called her “a fearless trailblazer who transformed the fight for equality in America”. Meghan Markle, the Duchess of Sussex, added her voice to call Steinem her “friend and mentor”, while the music icon Patti Smith referred to her as “the greatest”.Broadcaster Oprah Winfrey called Steinem a “formidable reformer who shaped American thought and culture”. And Billie Jean King, the athlete who led the fight for equality for female tennis players, said in aFacebook postthat “the world has lost a true giant and a dynamic voice”.“She lit a torch many years ago. It is now our responsibility to keep it lifted into the future. May she rest in power,” King wrote.Jill Biden, another former first lady, released a statement in which she said she and former US president Joe Biden “are holding Gloria’s loved ones in our hearts”.Biden wrote: “Gloria Steinem understood that women’s equality begins with the freedom to make decisions about our own bodies, health, and futures. For decades, she fought to make that freedom real for generations of women and girls.“She spoke up when it was difficult, listened to those whose voices too often went unheard, and never stopped pushing our country forward. Her voice changed our country, and her courage will continue to inspire us to keep fighting for the freedoms she spent her life defending.”Steinem had supportedHillary Clinton’s 2016 presidential campaign as the Democratic nominee running against Republican Donald Trump, which was ultimately unsuccessful as Trump prevailed in an election that would have given the United States its first female president. Clinton said on Thursday she was “heartsick” at news of the death of her feminist friend and ally.“Everyone who not only knew her but followed her, was inspired and challenged by her,” she said.“I think back to my first awareness of Gloria way back in the 1960s into the 70s, when all of a sudden this incredibly smart, beautiful, talented woman began talking about how women should have equal opportunity, how we should aim for the stars, be able to pursue our own dreams.“I knew there were, back when I was a young woman, schools that wouldn’t take women, jobs that wouldn’t take women, scholarships that weren’t open to women. I lived it.“But the lived experience became much more real and applicable to our entire society when Gloria began to point it out.”Clinton noted Steinem’s distaste at what politics had become in recent years, and said she had “the most incredible conversation” with her during a visit to Steinem’s home last year.“Even though we’re facing some challenges and pushback here in this country and around the world to women’s full participation and equality, Gloria was at heart an optimist,” she said. “Her activism was rooted in optimism, and that’s a moral choice, and she made it every day.”Pelosi paid tribute in a poston Xthat said: “Gloria Steinem was a fearless trailblazer who transformed the fight for equality in America and inspired generations of women to know their power.“Her voice, courage and relentless advocacy helped break down barriers and open doors once firmly closed to women. May it be a comfort to all of us who loved Gloria that her extraordinary legacy will live on in every generation that carries her fight forward.”Markle posted her memorieson Instagram. “Celebrating the life and legacy of my friend and mentor, and also grateful to know that in these last few weeks and days she knew exactly how loved and admired she was,” she wrote.“My very favorite story about GLO is when she was out one day in NY, and a woman approached her in absolute awe and said she wanted to introduce her young daughter to her (though she was embarrassed to say the young girl may not know who she was).”The post continued: “Gloria replied: ‘It doesn’t matter if she knows who I am. What matters is that she knows who SHE is’. Rest in peace, and rest in pride.”Smith, who shared a similar path to Steinem as a cultural revolutionary icon emerging from New York in the 1960s and 70s, posted a brief tributeon Instagram. “This is the greatest Gloria. All are grateful for her revolutionary spirit; a lifetime of service,” she wrote.The Oscar-winning actor Julianne Moore played Steinem in the 2020 biopic The Glorias. Shesaidon Instagram: “The time I spent studying Gloria in order to play her was one of the most edifying of my life.“Everything I watched, everything I read, everything I observed about her gave me a template for how I wanted to behave. Her honesty, her tolerance, her patience, and her insistence on humanism and inclusion as she moved through the world offers us all a moral roadmap.”Others who paid tribute on Thursday also recalled Steinem’s trailblazing.“Gloria was one of a kind. Genuine, generous, curious, thoughtful. She lived a staggering life and her passing is a staggering loss tempered only by the ferocity of her legacy,” Roxane Gay, the prominent social commentator and author of Bad Feminist, commented on theInstagram postannouncing Steinem’s death.Winfrey, on her own Oprah Dailywebsite, said Steinem “challenged a culture that often told us who we could be, what we could do, and how much space we were allowed to take up, and then spent her life making that space wider for all of us”.Alongside a picture of Winfrey and Steinem together, the TV host added: “She never wanted the movement to be about her. She understood that real change happens when one woman finds her voice and then uses it to help another woman find hers.”Explore more on these topicsGloria SteinemFeminismWomen (Society)CelebrityGenderWomen (Life and style)newsShareReuse this content

title: What we’re reading: Irvine Welsh, Janice Hallett and Guardian readers on the books they enjoyed in August | Books | The Guardian
description: Writers and Guardian readers discuss the titles they have read over the last month. Join the conversation in the comments
Author: Irvine Welsh
Headline: Writers and Guardian readers discuss the titles they have read over the last month. Join the conversation in the comments
Content: Photograph: PRView image in fullscreenPhotograph: PRWhat we're readingBooksWhat we’re reading: Irvine Welsh, Janice Hallett and Guardian readers on the books they enjoyed in AugustWriters and Guardian readers discuss the titles they have read over the last month. Join the conversation in the commentsIrvine Welsh,Janice Hallettand Guardian readersThu 3 Sep 2026 08.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIrvine Welsh, authorI’ve been enjoyingContrappostobyDave Eggers. The premise that love and art are the only things that make life worthwhile pulses beautifully through this novel and its two protagonists, spanning decades of their obsession with both, and each other. The tragedy is they are not sufficient alone for a relationship to survive to the exclusion of everything else (namely capitalism, which always has a place at the table), but they remain essential and enduring. Nowhere is this better evoked than here. Think John Williams’s Stonerbut with art instead of literature and stuffed with more memorable characters.View image in fullscreenIrvine Welsh.Photograph: Europa Press News/Europa Press/Getty ImagesInRaveheart, Graeme Armstrong confronts the twin promises of utopia and madness in a time before the internet’s colonisation of the mind, when people still dared to dream and lived to party. This book made me want to call some heads, rent a farmhouse, get a sound system and neck several pills. In fact, I might just do that.Finally, another one for creatures of the night in all their disparate glory.Overnightby Dan Richards is more than a tribute to the people (and other critters) who operate in the hours of darkness to ensure we have everything we need – it’s a discourse on the very nature of night-time itself, and its essential relationship to our humanity. This is a beautifully written work of startling brilliance, astonishing the reader page after page.Can Nothing Save Us? by Irvine Welsh is published by Jonathan Cape (£20). To support the Guardian, buy a copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Jean, Guardian readerI am readingThe Shampoo Effectby Jenny Jackson. My only regret is not saving this book until my late summer beach vacation, because this book is best read with sand betwixt your toes. The story follows a group of lifelong friends in their thirties in their Massachusetts home town as they navigate marriage, parenthood, and careers. A newcomer from New York City arrives to work on what she hopes will be her big break as a writer and becomes irrevocably interwoven in the group’s complicated dynamics. It’s funny, sharp, and has me wondering as a child-free woman if many parents are self-medicating with weed on a regular basis to get through the day.Janice Hallett, authorI’ve been diving deep into true crime lately.London Fallingby Patrick Radden Keefe is a book that examines so much more than its central crime story: that of a young man whose big dreams and relentless drive took him in a deadly direction. Keefe elevates the tragedy by placing it in the context of our capital’s criminal history. I’ve also revisited Carol Ann Lee’s exceptionally researched and presentedThe Murders at White House Farm.For someone fascinated by criminal psychology and the legal system, this book is without a doubt a core text on the Jeremy Bamber case. Meanwhile, I was hooked for a whole weekend onDead Fashion Girlby Fred Vermorel. Described as “a situationist detective story” it starts with the 1954 murder of a young fashion designer in Ruislip, not far from where I live, and splays outwards and downwards into London’s postwar criminal underbelly.The Silent Appeal by Janice Hallett is published by Profile (£20). To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Barbara, Guardian readerYou wouldn’t think that an account of a ten-month long legal process would be a page-turner, but that is exactly what Emmanuel Carrère has achieved inV13,the book based on his weekly magazine columns covering the trial of the surviving perpetrators of the terror attacks in Paris on Friday (ie Vendredi) 13, 2015. He delves into the lives of the victims, the perpetrators, the lawyers, and produces an all-round picture of the human beings involved in this horrific event. It is written with compassion, empathy, and a genuine curiosity about motivation.Light-years away (or perhaps not) is the deceptively simple tale told by Iain Crichton Smith inConsider the Lilies,a short novel about an elderly woman’s treatment at the hands of the Duke of Sutherland as he evicted tenants during the Highland Clearances – one woman, representing the fates of 150,000. A note at the front of the book tells me that I bought it on North Uist more than half-a-century ago, and now that I’m older I find it possibly even more moving than it was then.Explore more on these topicsBooksWhat we're readingIrvine WelshDave EggersfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: New Cemetery by Simon Armitage audiobook review – the poet laureate’s meditations take flight | Books | The Guardian
description: The building of a cemetery during the pandemic inspires the Huddersfield-born author to reflect on childhood memories and the changing local landscape
Author: Fiona Sturges
Headline: The building of a cemetery during the pandemic inspires the Huddersfield-born author to reflect on childhood memories and the changing local landscape
Content: Simon Armitage.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSimon Armitage.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianAudiobook of the weekBooksReviewNew Cemetery by Simon Armitage audiobook review – the poet laureate’s meditations take flightThe building of a cemetery during the pandemic inspires the Huddersfield-born author to reflect on childhood memories and the changing local landscapeFiona SturgesThu 3 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Huddersfield council proposed turning some local grazing land into a cemetery during the Covid lockdown, some nearby residents were unhappy. Not poet laureate Simon Armitage, who also lived close to the site. In the introductory essay to his poetry collection, New Cemetery, he notes how the dead would be ideal neighbours for a writer who enjoys quiet. He also “figured that once the departed had taken up residence in the soil, they were unlikely to be evicted to make way for some other form of public amenity or private eyesore”.From his home, Armitage watched as the cemetery took shape, the pastures giving way to walkways, parking bays and neatly arranged burial plots. The verse is rooted in his ruminations around the cemetery’s creation, which coincided with the death of his father who had taught him how to win a fight and the best way to hold an axe (“You’re holding it all wrong / It’s not a pen”). Each poem is named after a species of moth, among them Common Quaker, Dark Brocade, Pine Beauty and May Highflyer, and written in three-line stanzas.Armitage is the reader, his delivery instantly recognisable in its gentle lugubriousness. We find him observing the changing landscape or remembering scenes from his past such as his mother doing the washing in the sink and “manhandling shirts, / hauling drowning sailors / from sea to deck”, or his father playing the “pantomime grinch” on Christmas Eve. Elsewhere, he wryly reflects on the absurdities of his working life, stationed in his shed, where he’ll dither a while / poem-less under / trepanned tiles, stalled // in the anglepoise / of heaven / and desk”.Available via Faber, 1hr 10minFurther listeningLeaving HomeMark Haddon, Vintage Digital, 5hr 8minThe Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time’sauthor’s darkly funny and candid memoir details his difficult childhood in 1970s Northampton, his years at boarding school and his time looking after his elderly parents who had shown him little love while raising him. Read by the author.Talking Classics: The Shock of the OldMary Beard, Profile Audio, 5hr 38minDrawn from series of lectures delivered in Chicago in 2023, Talking Classics finds the acclaimed classicist and historian explaining why we should care what Greeks and Romans got up to 2000 years ago and the ways the past informs the present.Explore more on these topicsBooksAudiobook of the weekPoetryreviewsShareReuse this content

title: A Death of One’s Own by Terry Eagleton review – meditations on arriving at a full stop | Terry Eagleton | The Guardian
description: The literary critic brings his vast reading to bear on life’s most inescapable fact
Author: Kathryn Hughes
Headline: The literary critic brings his vast reading to bear on life’s most inescapable fact
Content: Terry Eagleton in 2018.Photograph: Tracey Paddison/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenTerry Eagleton in 2018.Photograph: Tracey Paddison/ShutterstockBook of the dayTerry EagletonReviewA Death of One’s Own by Terry Eagleton review – meditations on arriving at a full stopThe literary critic brings his vast reading to bear on life’s most inescapable factKathryn HughesThu 3 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 02.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTerry Eagleton is not a fan of sloppy thinking, especially when it comes to the granite fact of death. He particularly doesn’t like the attitude ofDylan Thomaswho famously urged his ailing father to “not go gentle into that good night”. If the “night” – death – is so “good” then why, asks Eagleton reasonably, would Thomas want his dad to dawdle? Shouldn’t DJ Thomas, rather, be encouraged to trot towards his lovely end like an ecstatic marathon runner on the home straight?Eagleton’s reproach to Thomas’s doublethink should not be read as panicky denial about the reality of his own mortality. To the contrary, Eagleton, who at 83 admits that he wasn’t sure whether this book would end up being published posthumously, finds it hard to think or write about much else. After a 60-year academic career spent tussling with Marxist literary theory, not to mention the epistemological void at the heart of postmodernism criticism, these days Eagleton is more interested in pondering death and how it “lacks a sense of occasion”. It might visit, for example, while you happen to be dressed in a giraffe outfit.Not, Eagleton clarifies, that it would really matter being found dead disguised as a long-necked ungulate since you would be beyond all caring. Indeed, this not mattering is, as he sees it, one of the great pleasures of being deceased. You’re beyond the reach of moral and social obligation: you can cheat your creditors, fail to turn up at your mother’s funeral and ignore increasingly hysterical demands to pay a parking fine. There might even be something sexy about being dead, a certain “pornographic pleasure” in decomposition, what Eagleton calls “the erotic bliss of yielding to an impregnable power”. Practically speaking, you’re no longer required to hold it all together.Until that moment of blessed release, though, we are obliged to trundle on as best we can. Eagleton mildly advocates trying to live each day in the full knowledge that death is just around the corner. Done right, this should in theory release us “from the mortal anxiety that compels us to clutch, seize and despoil”. Instead, we would experience the world around us with the visionary intensity of a William Blake, savouring every raindrop, ray of sunlight and crunch of apple to the point of almost painful lucidity. Lovely in principle, but as Eagleton puts it with a typically bathetic side-swipe, the mental contortion required to attain this state of ecstasy may end up being “more trouble than it’s worth”.For the fact remains that we are time-trapped creatures, forever casting back to the past and projecting forward to an imagined future, refusing to live in the reality of now. For this reason, our meagre deaths tend to arrive like an unexpected insult, a monstrous unfairness that we weren’t expecting. Eagleton is consoling here about the fact that when death arrives we probably won’t say the right or splendid thing. Thomas’s final words were apparently “the End is in Eden” which, as Eagleton tartly points out, is just one more of the old windbag’s “metaphysical vacuities”.As far as deathbed utterance goes, better instead to recall Steve Jobs’s less prescriptive “Oh wow. Oh wow. Oh wow”, which doesn’t strain for “sham grandeur” and leaves the listener free to fill in the blank according to their own fantasies. Personally, I’ve always liked to imagine that Jobs was being shown a vision of a heavenly Apple store, with serried ranks of angels in cobalt-coloured T-shirts tip-tapping away on futuristic Macs.A Death of One’s Own is in no sense an argument about its subject or even a sustained inquiry into death’s terrors and odd consolations. Instead, Eagleton lets his capacious mind, vast reading and wicked wit loose over the whole business of arriving at a full stop. In his introduction he explains that he has included ideas and individuals that have been central to his “spiritual and intellectual life” of the past six decades. Marx, Freud and cradle Catholicism are all invited to troop on stage to take a final bow “before the curtain comes down”. I found that the best way to read this book, which is undeniably dense, is to take in a bit each night before going to sleep, that “little death” from which, God willing, we awake refreshed each morning.A Death of One’s Own: Reflections on Mortality by Terry Eagleton is published by Yale (£18.99). To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com.
