title: Bucking Fastard review – Herzog’s starry twins soap provokes a syncing feeling  | Movies | The Guardian
description: Venice film festival: Rooney and Kate Mara play the real-life Chaplin sisters who spoke in unsettling unison in this silly, pointless drama
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Venice film festival: Rooney and Kate Mara play the real-life Chaplin sisters who spoke in unsettling unison in this silly, pointless drama
Content: Double trouble … Rooney and Kate Mara in Bucking Fastard.Photograph: Courtesy Venice Film FestivalView image in fullscreenDouble trouble … Rooney and Kate Mara in Bucking Fastard.Photograph: Courtesy Venice Film FestivalMoviesReviewBucking Fastard review – Herzog’s starry twins soap provokes a syncing feelingVenice film festival:Rooney and Kate Mara play the real-life Chaplin sisters who spoke in unsettling unison in this silly, pointless dramaPeter BradshawThu 3 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 11.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWerner Herzog is such a unique film-maker that even a dud from him has some interest, but sadly a dud is what this is. It is a fiction feature based on a true story which – despite a few laughs – systematically wastes the audience’s time, as well as the talents of its formidable female leads, real-life sisters Rooney and Kate Mara. You can almost feel this pointless, aimless film making it up as it goes along, losing its way, line by line, scene by scene.It is inspired by the story oftwins Freda and Greta Chaplinfrom York in the UK; they eerily spoke in unison and in the 1980s were the subject of a highly publicised court case for harassing a neighbour. Herzog’s movie transplants their story to Ireland, in which the Maras play weirdly but comically interdependent sisters Jean and Joan Holbrook whose lives are sent in all sorts of loopy directions. Orlando Bloom plays the roguish neighbour who breaks the women’s hearts (Herzog imagines them as a short-lived throuple), and Domhnall Gleeson is a caring social worker who tries to make them less dysfunctional by taking their case after they move away from the scene of their sexual resentment and legal shame. (During the trial they shout out the spoonerism of the title.)Eventually the Holbrooks live with an aunt in the country where they (bafflingly) conceive a desire to extend a tunnel they find in a hillside cave, believing it will take them fromIrelandto the supposed utopia of Orkney where they will be happy. There is a (sort of) entertaining touch of Jules Verne in the outcome to all this. But when the film finally fades to black, after an eventful but also dull story, it’s almost difficult to credit how inconsequential and throwaway it’s all been. The women’s lives are theoretically poignant and fascinating and the Mara sisters show that they are more than capable of showing something like this. But the characters they’re given to play are essentially just silly. Perhaps Herzog could have made a fascinating documentary about the real Chaplin sisters while they were still alive. But Bucking Fastard is a Dumping Thisappointment.Bucking Fastard screened at the Venice film festivalExplore more on these topicsFilmVenice film festivalWerner HerzogRooney MaraKate MaraDomhnall GleesonYorkreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Falling House review – fierce tale of an Iranian prison guard holding his family hostage | Movies | The Guardian
description: Venice film festival: Mohsen Gharaei’s powerfully acted domestic drama watches as the failing patriarch attempts to contain family rebellion
Author: Xan Brooks
Headline: Venice film festival: Mohsen Gharaei’s powerfully acted domestic drama watches as the failing patriarch attempts to contain family rebellion
Content: Thinly veiled parable … Farhad Aslani and Laleh Marzban in Falling House.Photograph: @mehdidelkhastehView image in fullscreenThinly veiled parable … Farhad Aslani and Laleh Marzban in Falling House.Photograph: @mehdidelkhastehMoviesReviewFalling House review – fierce tale of an Iranian prison guard holding his family hostageVenice film festival:Mohsen Gharaei’s powerfully acted domestic drama watches as the failing patriarch attempts to contain family rebellionXan BrooksThu 3 Sep 2026 08.15 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 08.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIran is a prison and everybody is inside: cons and non-cons; parents and their children. That’s the message hammered home, never subtly but with terrific force and conviction, throughout the course of Mohsen Gharaei’s hothouse domestic drama, which plays in the Orizzonti section in Venice. It’s about a low-level jailer, crushed by life, who returns from the day job and proceeds to incarcerate his own family. He does so out of love and to reassert his authority, to protect his wife and kids from the world and from their own foolish notions. For him, it’s a bone-headed busman’s holiday. For his family, it’s a nightmarish tragicomic staycation.Veteran Iranian actor Farhad Aslani is perfectly cast as Rashid Hafizhi, Gharaei’s misguided prison guard. Rashid is a burly bear of a man who nonetheless carries an air of bewilderment and defeat, as though he’s smart enough to know that everyone in the vicinity is just that little bit smarter than him. He’s been falsely accused of aiding and abetting a jailbreak and is facing imminent eviction from his rented family home. Then, just when it seems his day can’t get any worse, Rashid learns that his cherished eldest daughter, Ensi (Laleh Marzban), is planning to run off to seek work as a model in Turkey. Modelling in Iran is a non-starter, she explains. Ensi has to cover her arms and neck for each job, while the power supply is so unstable and the lights have a tendency to cut out in the middle of a photoshoot.Gharaei’s previous picture, Without Everything, was a major box office hit in Iran in 2021, and was lavished with awards at the Fajr film festival in Tehran. This one looks set for a rather rockier reception, assuming it is permitted to land safely at all. It’s an angry, cornered beast of a movie, a rugged piece of old-school social realism and a thinly veiled parable of life in the Islamic Republic. Escape, it suggests, is the only reasonable option. But for that one needs money, a passport and a key to open the door.One fears for the inhabitants of Falling House. Outside the Hafizhi family home, bulldozers are raking the earth to prepare for a new housing estate. Inside, the jailer has become a one-man wrecking ball, goaded into a fury by the sight of Ensi’s modelling portfolio and doubling down at every turn. First Ensi is imprisoned; then his wife, Zitab (Rina Raminfar); finally his plucky youngest daughter. “This is my prison,” he says. “And I make the rules.”Some of the dialogue is perhaps a little on the nose. “Rashid, I know you’re in a bad place,” wails Zitab just as the house goes into lockdown. “How unlucky are we?” says Ensi a little later. “The people coming to demolish our house are our only hope.” Or wait, might these lines in fact be intentional jokes, judiciously deployed to lighten the glowering mood? Falling House spins an anguished, brutal tale, but it could play just as well as an absurdist black comedy and Gharaei leaves the door ajar for an alternative parallel reading. He whips up a robust, potent, powerfully acted affair, a film that’s altogether more sturdy than the Hafizhis’ frail house on the landfill. Sturdier, too, than the broken family inside.Falling House screened at theVenice film festival.Explore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsIranVenice film festivalFestivalsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Star Trek IV: The Voyage Home review – Kirk, Spock and co on semi-intentionally hilarious save-the-whale mission | Movies | The Guardian
description: Our heroes travel back through time to San Francisco in 1986 so they can commune with aliens threatening future Earth – it’s preposterously good fun
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Our heroes travel back through time to San Francisco in 1986 so they can commune with aliens threatening future Earth – it’s preposterously good fun
Content: High minded discussion about the potty-mouthed vulgarity of 20th-century America … William Shatner and Leonard Nimoy in Star Trek IV: The Voyage Home.Photograph: Paramount Pictures/AllstarView image in fullscreenHigh minded discussion about the potty-mouthed vulgarity of 20th-century America … William Shatner and Leonard Nimoy in Star Trek IV: The Voyage Home.Photograph: Paramount Pictures/AllstarMoviesReviewStar Trek IV: The Voyage Home review – Kirk, Spock and co on semi-intentionally hilarious save-the-whale missionOur heroes travel back through time to San Francisco in 1986 so they can commune with aliens threatening future Earth – it’s preposterously good funPeter BradshawThu 3 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 05.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHere is the fourth and silliest movie in the Star Trek franchise, now on rerelease for its 40th anniversary. Directed byLeonard Nimoy, it’s a film of pure shark-jumping or rather whale-jumping absurdity. The film’s opening credits proclaim, with sublime confidence in its own unquestioned pop-cultural importance in the field of space travel, that Star Trek IV is dedicated to the crew of the space shuttle Challenger, which had that year catastrophically exploded midair, killing all seven of them.Spock has been brought back to life, as the apparent end result of all the bizarre metempsychotic plot contortions of the previous film. But the permanent and irrevocable death of Kirk’s son seems to be passed over remarkably casually. The eerie boyishness of Shatner’s Kirk, with that beaming smile, almost makes you forget that he has been through an agonising bereavement. Hasn’t he?Now the crew of the USS Enterprise, in official disgrace after the highly irregular commandeering of their craft during their “search for Spock”, are heading for home in a cranky old Klingon ship which Mr Scott (James Doohan) has fixed up with his customary self-pitying bluster. But on nearing Earth, they find that it is being threatened by a vast and mysterious ship which is transmitting a weird hailing – or rather wailing, or indeed whaling – frequency. In short order, our heroes work out that these are whale noises, and the menacing ship could well be placated with some answering calls, but whales are now extinct. So the obvious answer is to travel back in time by arriving at warp speed with a “slingshot” circuit around the planet, whoosh back to San Francisco circa 1986, teleport a couple of whales into a specially created tank, bring them back to the 23rd century and let those moaning, keening animals soothe the aggressor and send it on its way.Huh? Wha …? Excuse me? WTF? The pure goofiness of this idea, with its half-baked environmentalism and semi-intentional comedy, is enjoyable, while the scenes in which the Enterprise crew stumble like whales out of water around the streets of San Francisco are funny in their entirely ridiculous way. Nimoy’s bass-voiced Spock is always entertaining to watch, and there is an uproarious scene in which Kirk and Spock discuss the potty-mouthed vulgarity of 20th-century America, which they attribute to the popularity of Jacqueline Susann and Harold Robbins. (The fact that they were talking about writers shows how high-minded Kirk and Spock always are.) The scene in which Spock swims with the whales, ecstatically communing with them, makes the whole thing worth it.Star TrekIV: The Voyage Home is in UK and Irish cinemas from 4 September.Explore more on these topicsFilmScience fiction and fantasy filmsStar TrekWilliam ShatnerLeonard NimoyUS televisionTelevisionreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Lomu review – fascinatingly nuanced tribute to rugby’s first superstar | Movies | The Guardian
description: His destructive pace and power changed the game for ever, but behind the fame and impassive exterior of this gentle giant was a life of chaos and emotional discord
Author: Andrew Pulver
Headline: His destructive pace and power changed the game for ever, but behind the fame and impassive exterior of this gentle giant was a life of chaos and emotional discord
Content: Wreaking havoc … Jonah Lomu.Photograph: Dean Treml/PHOTOSPORTView image in fullscreenWreaking havoc … Jonah Lomu.Photograph: Dean Treml/PHOTOSPORTMoviesReviewLomu review – fascinatingly nuanced tribute to rugby’s first superstarHis destructive pace and power changed the game for ever, but behind the fame and impassive exterior of this gentle giant was a life of chaos and emotional discordAndrew PulverThu 3 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 09.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere’s an inevitable air of melancholy overhanging this profile ofNew Zealandrugby star Jonah Lomu; we all know how the story ended for this magnificent human specimen, who died in 2015 aged 40 as a result of a longterm kidney disorder. Lomu, of course, became a legend of the game after breaking into the All Blacks side – the ferociously high-achieving New Zealand national team, for anyone outside the rugby-appreciating universe – at the scarcely believable age of 19; his special combination of a tank-like physique, electric pace and ability to slalom at high speed gave him an almost unstoppable force in what is arguably the toughest contact sport of all. Lomu had the bulk and power of a forward (I liked the detail that he was sometimes drafted into the back of the scrum when they needed “more power”) but he was set loose on the wing, where he was twice the speed and three times the size of everyone else, and where his destructive instincts could wreak havoc.Well, modern rugby appears to have learned the Lomu lesson; everyone has bulked up – so its arguable whether he would have the same impact today. But as this film underlines, there was a lot more to Lomu’s story than steamrolling the hapless English backline; he had a complicated relationship both with his Tongan heritage and his superstar status, the combination of which seemed to overwhelm him. Interestingly, this film (directed by Gavin Fitzgerald and Vea Mafile’o) initially appears to push the by-now customary idea that Lomu’s Indigenous heritage was an ineffable source of strength, wisdom and insight; however it soon becomes clear that this wasn’t entirely the case.Born in New Zealand to Tongan immigrants, as a kid Lomu was sent to Tonga to live with an aunt for several years; this seems to be the trigger for an early sense of displacement. On returning to New Zealand he clashed with his preacher father Semisi over the latter’s strict religious observance even as he became a schoolboy rugby star; it’s a real Chariots of Fire moment when Lomu asserts that his sporting gifts are God-given. The father’s disciplinarian toughness turned into domestic violence; Lomu was kicked out of the house at 15 afterstepping in to defend his mother. Later on, Lomu’s marriages – all three – were to women of whom his family disapproved; and it becomes clear that some part of Lomu actively resented the constrictions of tradition. Meanwhile, rugby union’s sudden conversion to out-and-out professionalism – in part spurred by Lomu’s stellar showing at the 1995 World Cup – meant that the ins and outs of management took their toll, with much jostling over the big money that Lomu could command. And the third element in Lomu’s plangent progress arrived at almost the exact moment his career hit its height: a diagnosis of nephrotic syndrome, the kidney disorder that would eventually fatally compromise his health.All these factors come together in the extraordinary final sequence: Lomu’s memorial service at Auckland’s Eden Park which, we understand, was riven by behind-the-scenes tension and discord, disputes over funerary rituals, wife and mother exchanging frozen smiles, Indigenous-language chants roaring from the stands. If Lomu himself remained an enigma – as he readily admitted, talking about himself was not his forte – the chaos and emotion that swirled around him to the end makes fascinating viewing.Lomu is in cinemas on 7 September onlyExplore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsJonah LomuNew ZealandTongaRugby unionAsia PacificreviewsShareReuse this content

title: A Month in the Country review – delicate, tragicomic tangle of desire and disappointment | Stage | The Guardian
description: Brian Friel’s version of Turgenev treads lightly between humour and hurt as wayward passions rock a country house
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: Brian Friel’s version of Turgenev treads lightly between humour and hurt as wayward passions rock a country house
Content: Raw deal … (from left) Amanda Wilkin, Susan Brown and Mark Hadfield in A Month in the Country at the Donmar Warehouse.Photograph: Helen MurrayView image in fullscreenRaw deal … (from left) Amanda Wilkin, Susan Brown and Mark Hadfield in A Month in the Country at the Donmar Warehouse.Photograph: Helen MurrayStageReviewA Month in the Country review – delicate, tragicomic tangle of desire and disappointmentDonmar Warehouse, LondonBrian Friel’s version of Turgenev treads lightly between humour and hurt as wayward passions rock a country houseArifa AkbarThu 3 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 10.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAbored hausfrau languishing in her marriage. A confidante who secretly loves her. A charge that falls for the handsome new tutor and an assortment of ancillary characters mirroring the cross-crossing drama of suddenly flaring passions and unrequited love. Add a drawing room in a summer-house and it becomes clear to see how Ivan Turgenev’s mid-19th century play, set in the heart of the Russian countryside, might have served as a blueprint for Anton Chekhov’s tragicomedies some decades later.Now add Brian Friel, whose sparkling script “after Turgenev” is spun so delicately that it appears both of its time and a universal story of pained love and marriage. The drama is simultaneously a comedy and a quiet – yes, Chekhovian – tragedy in which broad, entertaining characters rub alongside anguish and rejection (you can see the subtle influence of Turgenev’s play, in its pining mood, onDancing at Lughnasa, written by Friel just two years later, in 1990).The fine line between humour and hurt is as delicately trodden by directorLyndsey Turnerand an able ensemble, headed up by Sophie Okonedo who playsNatalya. She feels stifled in her marriage to Arkady (Thomas Arnold) and rebuffing the love that family friend Michael (Alistair Petrie) professes to her, she falls for her son’s young tutor, Aleksey (Patrick Gibson, Irish-accented, almost childlike in his awe of her sophistication). Jealousy rises up between Natalya and her 17-year-old charge, Vera (Rachelle Diedericks, wonderfully guileless) who falls for him too, and the plot thickens with class resentments, manipulations and marriage proposals.View image in fullscreenManipulations and marriage proposals … Patrick Gibson, Sophie Okonedo and Alistair Petrie in the background.Photograph: Helen MurrayLight relief against the intoxicating passions comes through the constant card-playing of Arkady’s mother, Anna (Susan Brown), amusing shenanigans between servant couple, Katya and Matvey, and a German employee, Herr Schaaf (Mark Hadfield) who uses vocabulary like a Mr Malaprop.This runs the risk of resembling a restoration play but the pace never becomes frenzied or farce-like. Okonedo is nuanced as always, playing Natalya as a haughty, controlling snob but still retaining compassion for her. There are a couple of strangely melodramatic moments of psychological exposition (using a disembodied voice on audio) in which characters speak to themselves in a heightened state of emotional turmoil. It is how we learn of Natalya’s intentions, and she sounds like a drawing room Lady Macbeth, although it does not jar as much as it could.Lesley Travers’ stunning set design covers the stage with a glass box filled with foliage, which appears like a verdant bell-jar and lifts to reveal the drawing room, the green around it almost as alive as the grassy verge inMike Bartlett’s play, Juniper Blood, staged at the Donmar last year.Despite the many unhappy couples here, the notion of loving someone unreservedly is endorsed in its closing note, even if, or especially if, they don’t love you back. Anna speaks of her late husband’s infidelity and her decision to quietly accept it. Her son too averts his gaze from the fact that his wife may not love him and it appears, in its own way, an act of enduring love.AtDonmar Warehouse, London,until 3 OctoberExplore more on these topicsStageTheatreDonmar WarehouseSophie OkonedoLyndsey TurnerBrian FrielreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Present Laughter review – gender-switched Coward comedy dazzles in 70s New York | Stage | The Guardian
description: Antihero actor Garry becomes a magnificent new kind of beast as Gerri, played with blistering hilarity by Tracy-Ann Oberman
Author: Mark Lawson
Headline: Antihero actor Garry becomes a magnificent new kind of beast as Gerri, played with blistering hilarity by Tracy-Ann Oberman
Content: Peter McKintosh’s Manhattan loft design has walls decorated with  mock-Warhols.Photograph: Simon AnnandView image in fullscreenPeter McKintosh’s Manhattan loft design has walls decorated with  mock-Warhols.Photograph: Simon AnnandGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.StageReviewPresent Laughter review – gender-switched Coward comedy dazzles in 70s New YorkTheatre Royal BathAntihero actor Garry becomes a magnificent new kind of beast as Gerri, played with blistering hilarity by Tracy-Ann ObermanMark LawsonThu 3 Sep 2026 08.08 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 08.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe reputation of Noël Coward’s plays has involved escaping restrictions: his recorded clipped, waspish tone in key roles and a perception that, at a time when gay men’s careers and lives were at risk, the dramatist could not be socially and emotionally truthful.Seven years ago, in an Old Vic revival of Coward’s 1942 off-stage comedy Present Laughter, Andrew Scott – as actor Garry Essendine, a gorgon of priapic self-importance – memorably banished the parodic playing style and probed forbidden subtext. Changing Joanna, one of Garry’s love interests, into Joe made characters bisexual or in sham marriages.That seemed the limit of new life to be found in the play, especially as Matthew Warchus’s production survives in the NationalTheatreat Home archive. But the Coward estate has authorised a differently radical transformation directed by Lindsay Posner, starting an appetising national tour in Bath.View image in fullscreen‘The adaptation’s primary purpose is expanding the classical canon for women’ … Tracy-Ann Oberman and Seb Carrington.Photograph: Simon AnnandGarry is now Geri, an actress-singer played by Tracy-Ann Oberman, who previously feminised Shylock in The Merchant of Venice. Whereas Garry had a fantasy of playing Peer Gynt, Geri’s Ibsen vanity is being cast as Hedda Gabler. As dramaturg, Oberman reverses six other characters, with Essendine’s secretary morphing from Monica to Monty, and the ex-spouse being Len not Liz.These re-gendered characters also have a new calendar and atlas, moving from mid 20th century London to New York in the 1970s (Studio 54 has just opened). Peter McKintosh’s Manhattan loft design has walls decorated with mock-Warhols of the star and a poster for a cabaret show called Geri With a G, a nod to Ms Minnelli’s recent Liza With a Z. Coward’s ghastly avant garde playwright Roland Maule is here Rosina, an intense cross-genre experimentalist for whose work no theatre is far enough off-Broadway.View image in fullscreen‘Oberman poignantly recalls 70s American power women Dolly Parton and Farrah Fawcett’.Photograph: Simon AnnandMultiple line revisions interestingly reflect the sexism of language. Whereas Garry was rather admired as a “cad”, Geri is denigrated as a “cow”, although, stingingly, his disparagement of women as “bitches” stays in her mouth. Local and time references are smoothly retooled: Maule comes not from Uckfield but Yonkers and Essendine’s impending trip to take culture to the colonies bypasses Coward’s rather patronised “Africa” for “Australia”. The equivalent of Garry’s terror of soon requiring toupees is Geri’s fear of needing work on her face.These translations are not as politically powerful as allowing Garry to be gay, although the time shift is vital because no 1940s showbiz woman could have been as sexually ruthless as Geri.The adaptation’s primary purpose, though, is expanding the classical canon for women. Oberman, playing an actor less good than she thinks, makes it hard to think of many better than her, surpassing even last year’s Hampstead turn as a rude, ruthless matriarch over 20 years in Richard Greenberg’sThe Assembled Parties.In a sequinned pantsuit fighting teeth for maximum dazzle – blond tresses piled as high as the platform shoes that make even funnier the running in the farcical finale – Oberman poignantly recalls 70s American power women Dolly Parton and Farrah Fawcett (both painted by Warhol) in a performance that vocally samples Coward’s clicky diction. James Dreyfus’s enjoyable Monty is, like Lear’s Fool, alone licensed to speak truth to the tyrant. The show is, paradoxically, a daring Coward.AtTheatre Royal Bathuntil 5 September,then touring.Explore more on these topicsStageTheatreTheatre Royal BathNoel CowardreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘The myth is constantly being told’: creating a live album on stage as tribute to New York | US theater | The Guardian
description: In an ambitious new project, a cast of New Yorkers will help to create a one-of-a-kind tribute to New York City on stage in Central Park
Author: Juan A Ramírez
Headline: In an ambitious new project, a cast of New Yorkers will help to create a one-of-a-kind tribute to New York City on stage in Central Park
Content: ‘One of the big things about New York is that if you decide it’s your home and you respect the city, it’s gonna respect you.’Photograph: Marc J FranklinView image in fullscreen‘One of the big things about New York is that if you decide it’s your home and you respect the city, it’s gonna respect you.’Photograph: Marc J FranklinUS theater‘The myth is constantly being told’: creating a live album on stage as tribute to New YorkIn an ambitious new project, a cast of New Yorkers will help to create a one-of-a-kind tribute to New York City on stage in Central ParkJuan A RamírezThu 3 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 11.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLast year, theatre-makers Emily Lim and Dan Canham spent time in Sunderland developing a three-night live performance that sought to capture the north-east city’s essence and history through music, dance and spoken word. It was Lim’s final coup as the director of the National Theatre’s now defunct, UK-wide community programme, Public Acts, and the result was Public Record – a title that nods to both physical media (the audio is stored at the British Library and Sunderland Museum) and to the institutional archive.Hollywood encore: how ‘pro-shot’ Broadway shows became a major draw on the big screenRead more“It’s very full-circle,” Lim says, now doing the same forNew YorkCity’s Public Theatre, whose own Public Works branch inspired the National’s initiative. “The key difference is that instead of serving the country and national profile, our responsibility here is to serve the city.”For five nights starting Friday, Lim and Canham will gather a cast of over 100 – including a handful of professional musicians and dancers, but mostly community members from across the five boroughs – at the open-air Delacorte Theater in Central Park to attempt that same archival feat for a radically different city.“It’s not just a remake, it’s a complete reinvention,” says Canham, who acts as co-director and choreographer. “Sunderland was about civic pride, belonging, the reclaiming of a narrative. In New York, you don’t have to reclaim it; the myth of New York is constantly being told.”With a population almost 30 times larger and drastically different cultural footprints, he says the project has become “much more focused on the people and the community as opposed to trying to tell the story of the whole city, which is an impossible feat”.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Marc J FranklinAbout 350 New Yorkers were engaged nearly a year ago, through the Public Works programme, to participate in workshops and surveys describing their experiences in the city. The process “begins and ends with deep listening”, says Lim, to find “the right people who were steeped in life here and culture here to lead and help curate these stories”. (The final cast ranges from ages seven to 84.)She and Canham worked with playwright Lisa Sanaye Dring, whose play Sumo was produced at the Public last year, to sharpen that research into the piece’s “12-track” structure, which Canham says they intentionally developed in Sunderland as “a blueprint version, able to fit different contexts”. Rather than coming in with ideas of what this New York record would include, Dring was motivated “not by what I was excited to say, but by what our community is saying”.Tracks are titled after types of public record, like Birth Certificate (where performers detail their “origin stories”), or broader musical terms repurposed for the city in sections like Karaoke, which for New York will substitute I Wanna Dance with Somebody (Who Loves Me) to the original’s Dancing Queen.The number Tribute Act initially honored Faye Fantarrow, a Sunderland singer-songwriter who died in 2023, aged 21, who Canham says “was beloved by the whole city and represented a lot for its people. In a city the size and breadth of New York, that’s kind of impossible.” This Public Record, Lim notes, has “become a different interpretation of how we hold collective grief and every city’s particular relationship to death”.For the After Dark track, meant to honor the city’s nightlife, the team tapped Papi Juice, a Brooklyn-based collective that centers queer and trans people of color, to live mix the dancier section. The three-person operation has been organizing parties since 2013 and has recently branched into more theatrical spaces like Little Island and Lincoln Center. Lim says they “feel like they’re speaking to a very specific moment in the city”.Its resident DJ, Oscar Nñ, is producing the collective’s first complete song for Public Record, co-written and performed with the artist Maya Margarita, another multi-disciplinarian who moves fluidly from opening for Beyoncé’s Renaissance tour to acting off-Broadway.“It is a very high-energy, clubby, bouncy song, but also there is a certain level of romance, dreaminess, longing,” Nñ says. “A queer dancefloor is something that is so important. We always undermine what it can do or has done for culture, so it’s cool that Emily and Dan were so excited to have a moment just dedicated to the New York City dance.”Michael Thurber, a longtime Public collaborator and the production’s music director, enlisted local artists across varied scenes to create original compositions, including the Carnatic violinist Arun Ramamurthy and Louis Cato, who led the house band for The Late Show with Stephen Colbert.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Marc J FranklinWhen it came to the Love Song, the team kept finding themselves in the shadow of an enduring monument. Sunderland’s slot was taken up by the classic Elvis ballad Can’t Help Falling in Love, which functions as its football club’s unofficial anthem. “For ages, we were kicking around, ‘What is the love song for New York?’ and New York, New York kept coming and going as a thing that, ‘No, no, it can’t be that,’” says Lim, referencing the theme from Martin Scorsese’s film of the same name, originated by Liza Minnelli and popularized by Frank Sinatra.Eventually, Thurber says it became “the most exciting story, musically. We didn’t want to be too on the nose, but then it was Knicks in five” – the basketball team’s improbable win this summer – “and we came up with this idea of, what if it was sung in Spanish as a statement about the city’s Spanish-speaking population, and to subversively put a new lens on this song we all know and love?”The track, now titled Nuevayol as a wink to Bad Bunny’s own ode to the city, features new arrangements by Latin jazz legend Arturo O’Farrill, and will be sung live by Puerto Rican musician Mireya Ramos.“It introduces the idea of people’s migration stories,” Lim says of the track, which echoes the piece’s multilingual nature. “In so many ways, what makes a New Yorker is the idea of how we hold multiplicity and difference, and the political notion of who gets to call this place home and who gets to belong?”That richness is reflected in the track Marriage Certificate, which Thurber says includes snippets of music which, “whenever a certain song comes on, it’s like a whole culture of people know exactly what to do. Highlighting that on a stage like the Delacorte, which normally only does Shakespeare, says these kinds of things are art and culture, and they’re incredibly bonding forces.”“It’s sort of beautiful that people that are not from New York are helping us tell its story because that is New York,” he adds. “One of the big things about New York is that if you decide it’s your home and you respect the city, it’s gonna respect you.”Public Record will be performed at the Delacorte Theater in New York from 4-8 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsUS theaterNew YorkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I want to go further’: Justin Broadrick on retiring Godflesh, playing with Phoebe Bridgers – and his new band | Music | The Guardian
description: A hernia may mean his screaming days are over, but the Napalm Death alum’s influence on metal echoes on in unexpected places – and with ‘heavy, ugly’ experiments in the pipeline, his passion for ‘outsider music’ remains strong
Author: Matt Mills
Headline: A hernia may mean his screaming days are over, but the Napalm Death alum’s influence on metal echoes on in unexpected places – and with ‘heavy, ugly’ experiments in the pipeline, his passion for ‘outsider music’ remains strong
Content: ‘We were being exposed to a metal audience that had never experienced anything like us’ … (from left) Ben Green and Justin Broadrick of Godflesh.Photograph: Kim SølveView image in fullscreen‘We were being exposed to a metal audience that had never experienced anything like us’ … (from left) Ben Green and Justin Broadrick of Godflesh.Photograph: Kim SølveMusicInterview‘I want to go further’: Justin Broadrick on retiring Godflesh, playing with Phoebe Bridgers – and his new bandMatt MillsA hernia may mean his screaming days are over, but the Napalm Death alum’s influence on metal echoes on in unexpected places – and with ‘heavy, ugly’ experiments in the pipeline, his passion for ‘outsider music’ remains strongThu 3 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn 4 October 2024, Justin Broadrick felt a pop. The singer and guitarist of pioneering industrial metal duo Godflesh had felt pain in his groin for several years. After a coughing fit following a show in Sofia, Bulgaria, he knew he had a hernia. “It was a small knob in my groin,” says Broadrick. “I got back home and told my partner, and she was like, ‘Let’s watch how it goes.’” He continued to perform live for another year, wearing up to two hernia belts at a time. By the time he got it surgically treated in February this year, it was 13cm long.The next month, Broadrick shared a picture of himself in hospital and announced that Godflesh’s near-four-decade career will soon end. His condition had been caused by the physicality of shouting over their music since he was 18; he just turned 57. If he were to do so again, he would risk blowing out his abdominal wall entirely. There will be two more studio albums – starting with this autumn’s reliably crushing Decay, recorded pre-surgery – and possibly some archival releases and remixes. But beyond that? Nothing.“I’m still in a lot of discomfort, even now,” says Broadrick, talking to me by phone in mid-August. “I’m not the toughest guy in the world, I’m very sensitive to pain, so it’s going to be nine to 12 months [after surgery] before potentially feeling no negative sensations whatsoever.”Godflesh: Living/Ending – videoBroadrick received support from all over the heavy metal world, including current or former members of Megadeth, Slipknot, Fear Factory, Neurosis, Sunn O))) and Killing Joke. It was just a small glimpse of the impact Godflesh have made. When Broadrick and bassist Ben “GC” Green formed the band in 1988, their cacophonous beats, programmed on a £500 drum machine, were unprecedented in the genre. Broadrick’s riffs were immediate, dense and unsettling. From top to bottom, they were the heaviest band ever.Metallica were fans: guitarist Kirk Hammett got Andres Serrano to design their Load and Reload album covers after Broadrick showed him a Godflesh video directed by the provocative artist. Mike Patton praised them as “ridiculously heavy” and invited Broadrick to audition for Faith No More in 1993. He turned the offer down. “There’s no way I can join someone else’s band,” he reasons today. And many of nu metal’s frontrunners idolised Godflesh. Founding Slipknot drummer Joey Jordison once blared their music during an interview at his house; when Broadrick first heard Korn’s debut single Blind, he thought: “I quite like it, but it sounds like Godflesh meets Faith No More.”View image in fullscreen‘Among the distress [of touring] and the feeling of wanting to kill everyone, there is transcendence’ … Broadrick and Green in 1992.Photograph: Johnny Greig/AlamyDespite his widespread influence, Broadrick eschews the limelight. Born in Birmingham, he now lives with his partner, 15-year-old son and many, many pets in a north Wales village so remote that it doesn’t have as much as a pub. He avoids social situations, rarely granting interviews, but gives long, sometimes meandering answers. He says that these are symptoms of his autism, which went undiagnosed until 2022, when he was in his early 50s.“I’m generalising, but the psychiatrist pretty much said to me that there are two types of autistic people,” he explains in his undiluted Brummie accent. “A lot of people who used to get diagnosed with Asperger’s generally have the cold, don’t speak, sit-in-a-corner type of autism. My autism is the other one, where, they said, people can get hyperemotional and hypersensitive and talk all the time, trying to get themselves understood.”Broadrick’s hypersensitivity shaped Godflesh’s music. Their beats echo the clanging he heard from nearby factories while growing up on a council estate, and his anguished shouts and misanthropic lyrics are rooted in childhood trauma. His mum and stepdad were punk musicians who hosted wild parties with drugs and alcohol while he was home. “I was exposed to all manner of shit,” he says, “but at school, I was totally isolated. I couldn’t communicate with kids. I was virtually mute. Two very different, polarising existences there. As soon as I became obsessive about music at the age of eight, that’s all I could communicate about.”He began making music under the pseudonym Final when he was 13. At 15, he walked out of his first exam and never went back to school. After meeting Nicholas Bullen of West Midlands grindcore agitators Napalm Death at a market, he joined the band and wrote “90%” of the music on side A of their debut album, Scum. It became a cult classic, inspiring a legion of copycats. The 1.3-second track You Suffer holds the Guinness world record for the shortest song ever recorded.Godflesh: Crush My Soul – videoCome the release of Scum in 1987, however, Broadrick had already grown bored and left. “I love what we created, but I felt restricted. We said, ‘Let’s play as fast as we can.’ I remember saying to [drummer] Mick Harris, ‘Faster! Faster!’, and he was laughing, and we just got faster and faster. It was very momentary – very temporary, almost.”In 1988, Broadrick and Green, who grew up on the same estate, started Godflesh. They were both signing on at the time, and talked Green’s mum into taking out a bank loan to cover that £500 drum machine. Their formula of playing distorted guitar over huge beats was inspired by Run-DMC’s single King of Rock, which Broadrick heard on The Old Grey Whistle Test. The angular riffs were pulled from Killing Joke, while the discordance and rhythmic vocal patterns evoked early Swans. That unique blend resonated widely, getting the pair off the dole “relatively quickly”. Their 1989 debut album, Streetcleaner, was released by popular death metal label Earache (then also home to Napalm). After initially only reaching No 19 on the UK indie chart, it became a sleeper hit and seminal release.Godflesh proved especially popular in the US, where they scored their breakthrough by supporting Napalm in 1991. However, the tour triggered Broadrick’s hypersensitivity. From his first gig, he had used drink or substances to cope with the sensory overload of performing. Still, he had to play. Music is the only job he’s ever had, and, “among the distress and the feeling of wanting to fucking kill everyone, there is transcendence”, he says.“I hated the overwhelm, everything about it. Two-and-a-half months, that fucking tour! I spent two-and-a-half months trying to get off,” he admits. “But here’s the thing: you could tell we were being exposed to a metal audience that had never experienced anything like us.”View image in fullscreenBanned … Broadrick on the set of the video for Crush My Soul in 1994.Photograph: Karjean Levine/Getty ImagesThanks to a deal by Earache, Sony-backed juggernaut Columbia Records agreed to distribute Godflesh’s 1994 album Selfless in the US. But then MTV banned the Serrano-directed Crush My Soul video – not only did it contain religious imagery and end with red liquid being poured on to Broadrick, but the artist had previously flared tempers with his 1987 photographPiss Christ, which depicted a crucifix submerged in urine. Broadrick believes that the rise of nu metal not long after Selfless “buried” Godflesh: “Labels that wanted to sign Godflesh two years before were not interested any more. They just wanted anyone who sounded like Korn or Slipknot.”He also expresses his frustration over certain high-profile artists not acknowledging him. He claimed in a 90s interview that Metallica’s Hammett never publicly gave him the credit for introducing him to Serrano’s work. “Kirk promptly fell out with me and got friends of his to write me nasty letters and shit,” he alleges today. “That was the end of that.”Were you ever able to mend that relationship? “Eventually, he admitted that it was taken from the influence of Godflesh. It’s now public knowledge that it was inspired by a Godflesh video, but he didn’t say that for many, many years. And I got made the bad guy for daring to suggest that that concept was taken from the band. I’m pretty upset now, to be honest, that people turned on me about it.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSleeve NotesGet music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGodflesh suffered another, ultimately fatal blow when Green left in 2001, two weeks before a tour. After rushing to replace his longtime partner and once again hitting the road, Broadrick collapsed. He ended Godflesh in April 2002, ahead of a scheduled North American run, and put together a new shoegaze project, Jesu.More ambient and melodic than Godflesh, Jesu broadened Broadrick’s influence. Heremixed Julien Baker’s song Favorin 2021. Baker’s Boygenius bandmate Phoebe Bridgers did backing vocals. Recently, Bridgers emailed Broadrick about doing some “Jesu-style stuff” on her chart-topping new album,Lost Weekend. “I thought I was being scammed,” he admits, but he played guitar on the tracks Bobby and Best Dressed.Was it intimidating, collaborating with a pop star? “The fact that she was so personable and we were immediate friends was brilliant for me, but I was overwhelmed by how big she is. I was literally sending music to Taylor Swift’s personal engineer! I’m catapulted into this huge, mainstream world, and I’m like, ‘How the fuck am I here?!’” They’re still working together, as recently as three weeks before we speak. “She wanted me to play guitar and bass on a song for a film. She said to me a few months ago, ‘I’m just going to keep hitting you up.’”View image in fullscreen‘It will always be a beacon’ … Broadrick playing in Norway in 2023.Photograph: Gonzales Photo/AlamyAfter performing across Europe and North America as Jesu in 2007, Broadrick quit drink and drugs and gave up touring. “I ended up drinking a bottle of Jack Daniel’s every night,” he says. “Total self-destruction. I was killing myself, so I had to address it. I had to stop touring.”Two years later, craving a heavier counterpart to Jesu, he restarted Godflesh with Green. They’ve experimented plenty since the early days: they’ve done dub remixes, some of their later beats took from hip-hop and breakbeat, and new album Decay contains two of their longest, most claustrophobic compositions in Master and Slave and Consume Me.But Broadrick feels trapped by the band’s framework. His hernia didn’t cause their impending split as much as confirm it.“The Godflesh template has become dated to me,” he says. “It’s very 80s and 90s, like a noise rock band. For want of a better analogy, it’s very meat and potatoes. I always wanted to go much further than that. You can step outside the template, but it won’t be Godflesh any more.”‘I don’t want to die in a hotel room somewhere’: Black Sabbath on reconciling for their final gig – and how Ozzy is living through hellRead moreHe hopes to record Godflesh’s final album, aptly entitled The End, in November and December and release it as soon as possible. It’ll feature vocals, but they’ll be higher-pitched screams and spoken-word sections that he can handle safely. He reveals that the music will mark a “sideways step” for the band, as he plans to use a guitar with a tremolo arm: something Godflesh haven’t touched since their debut album.After Godflesh are put to bed, Broadrick, as well as continuing with Jesu and his electronic solo project JK Flesh, will form a new “brutal, industrial, heavy” solo band called White Light District. There’ll be sampled percussion and electronic textures. Live, he’ll be joined by a session drummer.“I wouldn’t dare call it a Godflesh replacement,” he says. “Because it’s heavy, ugly music, people may venture that it is, but it will be less rock based. It’s not confined by that instrumentation. It will sound like Glenn Branca with metal guitars, except it’s not metal: 15 layers of guitar that create this ultra-cluster of fucking hallucinatory dissonance, which could not be created by a band.”As he readies The End and this new pursuit, Broadrick admits that Godflesh’s retirement hasn’t sunk in yet. He believes, in a way, that the band will live for ever. “I’m not saying this arrogantly, but I think it will always be a beacon. It was a vehicle for my alien way of writing things, and I will still be writing shit like that. It’s outsider music. It doesn’t belong, and I don’t belong, and I’m happy to not belong. I don’t want to belong.”Decay is released via Relapse on 25 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsMusicMetalPop and rockinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Queens of the Stone Age’s Josh Homme kicked a woman and his ex-wife alleged domestic abuse. Why the cosy makeover? | Josh Homme | The Guardian
description: Like Johnny Depp and Chris Brown before him, Homme has got past his chequered history to retain an adoring fanbase. Almost a decade post-#MeToo, audiences no longer seem to care
Author: Laura Snapes
Headline: Like Johnny Depp and Chris Brown before him, Homme has got past his chequered history to retain an adoring fanbase. Almost a decade post-#MeToo, audiences no longer seem to care
Content: Josh Homme performing with Queens of the Stone Age last year.Photograph: Mondadori Portfolio/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJosh Homme performing with Queens of the Stone Age last year.Photograph: Mondadori Portfolio/Getty ImagesJosh HommeQueens of the Stone Age’s Josh Homme kicked a woman and his ex-wife alleged domestic abuse. Why the cosy makeover?Laura SnapesLike Johnny Depp and Chris Brown before him, Homme has got past his chequered history to retain an adoring fanbase. Almost a decade post-#MeToo, audiences no longer seem to careThu 3 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 07.02 EDTShareAs part of the promo for Queens of the Stone Age’s new album Perfecth, the band has set up a novelty complaints hotline for fans to call. “No bitching too big, no whiny too tiny,” it promises. I’ll bite: how about the fact that frontman Josh Homme’s ex-wife Brody Dalle testified in court that hehead-butted her so hard that she “saw stars”and said he had fantasised about killing her? Or that hekicked a female photographer in the face? It’s certainly not what anyone’s talking about as part of Homme’s friendly neighbourhood rock star image rehabilitation: duetting on Shania Twain’s new album, taking the couch on Celebrity Gogglebox, teatime BBC 6 Music interviews.Homme and Dalle clearly had a complicated relationship: he allegedly tried to throw her boyfriend off a balcony; he claims that she was violent towards him; both have taken outrestraining orders against one another; Homme has full custody of their kids after Dalle’s boyfriend was found to have forged her signature on an application for a restraining order. Homme has recently talked about coming through a dark period, includingsuccessful treatment for cancer, and getting a handle on his vices. Nevertheless, there is clear footage of him brutally kicking the camera of photographer Chelsea Lauren back into her face, which he acknowledged in an apology video, and court testimony from Dalle alleging that a drunk Homme told her “I want to fucking strangle you right now” on one occasion, and head-butted her on another.Their situation shares resonances with Johnny Depp and Amber Heard’s messy relationship breakdown, which prompted a British judge to deem that the Sun was in fact accurate inlabelling Depp a “wife-beater”despite his libel claim against them; althougha US jury ruled in his favour against Heard, who was found guilty of defamation. You only have to see the grim trailer for Ebenezer, Depp’s forthcoming Scrooge trauma plot movie, to see how much any of this really damaged his career. “It’s good to be back,” Depp-as-Scrooge tee-hees in his first spoken scene. Subtext, as Garth Marenghi told us, is for cowards. Text appears proclaiming “the master of misfits returns”; the entire aesthetic seems skimmed from former Depp hits Sweeney Todd, Pirates of the Caribbean and Edward Scissorhands. As someone says in the comments: “This entire trailer is just, ‘You like Johnny Depp right?’” You could sum up most of the rest of the comments as: we sure do! Nothing says future Christmas classic like big-budget reputation laundering.You get the hopeless feeling that none of this matters any more. Chris Brown is currently on a high-profile US tour with Usher that has had guest appearances from trailblazing female artists such as Alicia Keys and Mary J Blige – despite him beating then-girlfriend Rihanna in 2009 and another ex being granted a five-year restraining order after he threatened her. “For years, traditional media has been tiptoeing around the popularity of Chris Brown, and in reality, that benefits nobody but him,” critic Alphonse Pierre wrote ina pan of Brown’s latest album, Brown. “The lack of critical engagement with his music has allowed him to contextualise his own redemption with statistic and sob stories.” And yet, as Doreen St Felixwrote in the New Yorker, the tour’s audience is full of adoring women.Almost a decade after the mainstream#MeToo movement, it’s clear that audiences’ nostalgia for artists who made art that meant something to them at a formative age overrides the inconvenience of violence against women. Couple that fondness with an expensive publicity campaign and the counternarrative never stands a chance, easily dismissed as the shrill cries of cranks. I believe firmly in rehabilitation and second chances, but haven’t been able to shake a sense of horror that millions of people can apparently look past allegations and evidence of violence against women when engaging in supposedly feelgood pop culture.Last month, Homme made headlines during a Detroit show where he flouted the venue’s smoking ban, risking a $10,000 fine to take a stand against“fuckin’ corporate assholes”who “tell you what to do” (while his band, um, voluntarily play those corporate assholes’ corporate venue for a fat pay cheque). This sort of limp rock’n’roll cosplay is just as cosy in its own way as reviewing crap British TV on primetime Channel 4: vanilla rebellion figures offering the comforting reassurance that rock stars still walk among us, boldly reminding us that rules are made to be broken.The notion of so-called rock’n’roll behaviour, many have theorised, was partly why music never had much of a “#MeToo moment”, that hopeless relic of a phrase. When bad behaviour isn’t just accepted but venerated, real wrongdoing can be brushed under the same whisky-stained rug. Blind eyes are turned, offenders are remade as outlaws, myths are upheld, party lines toed: “It’s so safe to play along / Little soldiers in a row,” as Homme sang in Go With the Flow. The jokey complaints hotline might be the most honest part of QOTSA’s return: a grim reflection of the fact that nobody is taking this shit seriously any more.Explore more on these topicsJosh HommePop and rockQueens of the Stone AgeJohnny Depp#MeToo movementcommentShareReuse this content

title: The Excursions of Mr Brouček review – Rattle’s illuminating touch lets Janáček’s sozzled antihero soar | Classical music | The Guardian
description: In this beautifully balanced live recording Simon Rattle, the London Symphony Orchestra and an outstanding cast make the music sing and dance
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: In this beautifully balanced live recording Simon Rattle, the London Symphony Orchestra and an outstanding cast make the music sing and dance
Content: A performance so ripe you can almost smell the garlic on his breath… Peter Hoare (Brouček) with Simon Rattle and the London Symphony Orchestra at the concert performance in the Barbican Hall, May 2025.Photograph: Mark AllanView image in fullscreenA performance so ripe you can almost smell the garlic on his breath… Peter Hoare (Brouček) with Simon Rattle and the London Symphony Orchestra at the concert performance in the Barbican Hall, May 2025.Photograph: Mark AllanClassical musicReviewThe Excursions of Mr Brouček review – Rattle’s illuminating touch lets Janáček’s sozzled antihero soarHoare/Briscein/Crowe/LSO/Rattle(LSO Live)In this beautifully balanced live recording Simon Rattle, the London Symphony Orchestra and an outstanding cast make the music sing and danceClive PagetThu 3 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 12.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJanáček’s comedy can be a charmer on stage but it’s a devil to get your head around on disc. Based on satirical stories by Svatopluk Čech – who even puts in an appearance in Act II – Mr Brouček (or Mr Beetle in Czech) is a petty minded, puffed-up landlord with an insatiable appetite for beer and sausages. The first half propels our sozzled antihero on an imaginary flight to the moon where he proceeds to puncture the pretensions of the artsy-fartsy inhabitants. The second half deposits him in the thick of the 15th-century Hussite wars where, cowardly to the core, he singularly fails to cover himself in glory. Amid the fun and games, the conversational text flies by at a discombobulating rate of knots.View image in fullscreenJanáček: The Excursions of Mr Brouček, London Symphony Orchestra album coverPhotograph: LSO LiveThis recording takes pride of place in the catalogue thanks in part to Simon Rattle’s illuminating way with the music. Not only does he make it sing and dance – bagpipes and all – he brings out every quirk and colour of Janáček’s imaginative score. By giving the opera room to breathe, listeners have the best chance yet of appreciating the composer’s fertile wit and gift for musical storytelling.Peter Hoare leads an outstanding cast in a performance so ripe you can almost smell the garlic on his breath. Aleš Briscein is peerless as an earthbound painter and a preening moon poet with Lucy Crowe radiant as a lunar goddess. The LSO play like fiends, and the live recording is beautifully balanced.Allow content provided by a third party?This article includes content hosted onembed.music.apple.com.
