title: ‘Ruin and decay bring a chance of rebirth’: Hidetaka Miyazaki on uniting players in a damaged world | Games | The Guardian
description: As FromSoftware’s new multiplayer game The Duskbloods nears release, the legendary game director behind Dark Souls talks connection, pessimism and of course, feet
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: As FromSoftware’s new multiplayer game The Duskbloods nears release, the legendary game director behind Dark Souls talks connection, pessimism and of course, feet
Content: ‘Of all the things Miyazaki and his team do well, creating a sense of mystery is the greatest’ … The Duskbloods.Photograph: NintendoView image in fullscreen‘Of all the things Miyazaki and his team do well, creating a sense of mystery is the greatest’ … The Duskbloods.Photograph: NintendoGamesInterview‘Ruin and decay bring a chance of rebirth’: Hidetaka Miyazaki on uniting players in a damaged worldKirk McKeandAs FromSoftware’s new multiplayer game The Duskbloods nears release, the legendary game director behind Dark Souls talks connection, pessimism and of course, feetThu 3 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 12.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSince 2009’s Demon’s Souls, Japanese video game director Hidetaka Miyazaki has shown the world a different way to think about game design. His games defy convention with punishing fights, obscure rules, and unknowable, inhospitable worlds. The “Soulslike” genre – named afterDemon’s Soulsand its sequelDark Souls– is now ubiquitous, influencing multimillion-sellers from God of War and Star Wars: Jedi to Hollow Knight. Miyazaki’s most recent success, 2022’sElden Ring, which credited Game of Thrones author George RR Martin as a co-creator, sold over 30m copies and inspired Alex Garland to adapt it for the big screen at A24. It earned Miyazaki a spot on Time magazine’s “most influential” list, an accolade he shares with just one other game developer: Mario creator Shigeru Miyamoto.Miyazaki is now 51 and has been FromSoftware’s president since 2014, elevated from game designer to CEO after the success of the Souls series. He has a cherubic face that could pass for 35. He rarely speaks publicly, and never on camera. When he does speak, he answers questions like one of his characters – softly, sadly, his head bowed, making eye-contact only when I am speaking. Outside the studio where we speak is the sprawl of Tokyo’s Shinjuku, an ever-changing maze where tourists get lost and pop-up stores appear and vanish without a trace. Today, a J-pop band performs in the square as the cicadas scream from the trees. A gilded statue of Malania, one of Elden Ring’s toughest bosses, looms over this dimly lit conference room inside From’s headquarters, a bonfire checkpoint away from the chaos.View image in fullscreenHe creates an ‘atmosphere of wonder’ … Hidetaka Miyazaki accepts a Bafta games award for Elden Ring in 2023.Photograph: Stuart Wilson/Bafta/Getty Images for BaftaFromSoftware’s in-game universes are filled with clues – enemies, places and scraps of information from item descriptions paint a vague image of the world, and the player fills the blank space. You never fully understand these domains, although countless YouTube video game theorists have tried – as have other developers in awe of his work. “Of all the many things Miyazaki and his team do well, creating a sense of mystery is the greatest,” explains Dishonored directorHarvey Smith, who has more than 40 days’ playtime in Elden Ring. “It’s so incredibly hard to do in video games, which are technical systems … But Miyazaki somehow creates an atmosphere of wonder. Even when finishing, you are left ruminating on fun, murky elements that feel half understood. It’s a delicious sense of intrigue.”Rather than the single-player action game that Miyazaki’s audience craves (fans are desperate for a sequel to his 2015 gothic masterpiece Bloodborne,for instance), hislatest project The Duskbloodsis a multiplayer Switch 2 exclusive. Eight players face off against ghoulish horrors, fighting each other to avoid being culled at the end of each round. The survivors are whittled down over three phases culminating in a final three-way battle. The Duskbloods is releasing to an audience with shifting tastes and trends, and it is certainly a risk. “I’m very nervous,” Miyazaki says. “With every title we release there is this mounting tension.”The game opens with an arresting image: one hand reaching out for another. A male character is slumped on a chair, dejected; the shot moves in close to focus on their draped fingers. From below the frame, a pale hand slowly reaches out and caresses them before gently clasping his wrist. Hands are a recurring motif in Miyazaki’s games; in Elden Ring, massive crawling hands burrow up from underground to attack you, and hand-like giants are revered as deities.“It’s not necessarily something I’m consistently aware of – maybe it’s something subconscious coming through,” Miyazaki says when I ask about this imagery. “Take a look online and there’s a rumour that I have a bit of a thing for feet, but I’m not honestly sure where this comes from. I feel like I’m trying to depict some side of human nature or the human existence that is difficult to describe.” (His games have featured, by my count, at least six barefoot female characters.)View image in fullscreen‘It’s rumoured I have a bit of a thing for feet’ … Elden Ring Nightreign.Photograph: Bandai NamcoPerhaps all the hands and feet are symbolic of human connection. One hand reaches for another; bare feet connect skin with earth.Miyazaki has been exploring that theme since Demon’s Souls, whose novel, stranger-centric multiplayer was inspired by a time his car slipped on an icy hill and a stranger helped to push him to safety. In Demon’s Souls and the Dark Souls series, players paint runes on the ground, which other players can then use to summon help in a fight, creating moments of spontaneous togetherness before an inevitable parting.While The Duskbloods primarily puts players in opposition, it also explores temporary alliances and conflicting objectives, buoyed by Miyazaki’s love for tabletop role-playing games and board games. Players can even become betrothed to each other, forming an alliance. “I feel it’s less a traditional romance and more a sense of secure trust with a character in the world, and that’s something I personally yearn for,” he says. “It’s not necessarily a romantic pairing – it’s having someone that you can ultimately rely on. This concept is carried through from characters like the maidens in Elden Ring … it’s a transient, ephemeral love, which is maybe a motif I’m striving for.”The Duskbloods is preoccupied with ruin and rebirth, a thematic cornerstone of From’s games – much as Godzilla was a product of nuclear paranoia in Japan. Even as Miyazaki and I talk, a deadly magnitude 6.8 earthquake hits the Kumamoto prefecture on Kyushu island, a thousand miles away. If the very ground beneath your feet is unreliable, that can shape your outlook on life, a concept explored extensively in Japanese literature and entertainment, recently on the hit television showShōgun.“[Ruin and rebirth] is an ongoing theme in a lot of my games, I realise,” Miyazaki says. “That theme on a cosmological scale applies to The Duskbloods as an interesting philosophical area to explore.”View image in fullscreen‘If we have two ideas of a brighter or dark future, I would tend to sway towards the darker one,’ …Bloodborne.Photograph: Sony Computer EntertainmentMiyazaki describes himself as a pessimist, a tendency that he believes comes across in his output. That should be obvious to anyone who’s finished any of his games, in which you keep throwing body and blade against seemingly impossible odds, reborn each time you die at a bonfire checkpoint, to try again. Even when you triumph, nothing ultimately seems to change: these games culminate in bleak, morally ambiguous gut-punches, leaving you not as a conquering hero but as the perpetuator of a hopeless cycle. “If we have two ideas of a brighter or dark future, I would tend to sway towards the darker one,” Miyazaki says. “[But] if you explore the ruin and the decay in those worlds, it also lets you explore some chance of rebirth, and I think having that tiny pinprick of light or hope can be something beautiful, something fleeting.”Sekiro, Dark Souls, Bloodborne, and Elden Ring are all separate series, but they share the same bones. They’re reborn in different forms, to explore fresh ideas, places and perspectives while still playing, feeling and sounding like a FromSoftware game. While it’s immediately clear The Duskbloods is a Miyazaki game, it too wears a different skin, inspired by extraction shooters like Escape from Tarkov and those tabletop role-playing games the director loves. “There’s no intentional FromSoftware [mantra] – ‘this is the way we make our games’ – because if you start to do that it becomes stale and conservative, and you start having to adhere to a set of rules and philosophies, and it just doesn’t become interesting, you can’t make anything that’s as fun,” Miyazaki says.“So I feel like at least what’s worked for us philosophically is trying to adhere to what we find interesting first. I think that has created a good throughline through our games, and that’s what we concentrate on to [conceive] a new title.”Back in his early days at the studio, when he was only a coder on the Armored Core series of games, Miyazaki volunteered to take on a struggling project at From – the game that would become Demon’s Souls. (The game was already in trouble, so he felt he had nothing to lose.) He changed everything about the game, and then the game changed everything about his life, as he climbed from coder to company president. From failure was born a game that changed the landscape of video games. Ruin and rebirth.But does Miyazaki think he has changed? “I don’t intend to,” he says, a smile curling on his lips. “But I probably have.”This article was amended on 3 September 2026 to correct the release year of the original Demon’s Souls.Explore more on these topicsGamesAction gamesRole playing gamesinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I show how energetic it can be’: the photographer capturing Britain’s golden age of jazz  | Photography | The Guardian
description: Temi Adegbayibi started out taking pictures of the Ezra Collective and other British musicians as a hobby, then found his work exhibited at the Royal Albert Hall. He discusses Black joy and the movement and stillness of jazz
Author: Emma Loffhagen
Headline: Temi Adegbayibi started out taking pictures of the Ezra Collective and other British musicians as a hobby, then found his work exhibited at the Royal Albert Hall. He discusses Black joy and the movement and stillness of jazz
Content: ‘I’m always trying to figure out how to capture the energy of a drum solo.’Photograph: Temi AdegbayibiView image in fullscreen‘I’m always trying to figure out how to capture the energy of a drum solo.’Photograph: Temi AdegbayibiPhotography‘I show how energetic it can be’: the photographer capturing Britain’s golden age of jazzTemi Adegbayibi started out taking pictures of the Ezra Collective and other British musicians as a hobby, then found his work exhibited at the Royal Albert Hall. He discusses Black joy and the movement and stillness of jazzEmma LoffhagenThu 3 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen I speak to Temi Adegbayibi on the phone, the 26-year-old photographer is on the move. He is travelling across London, then running up the stairs to his desk, fitting our conversation into the interstitial spaces of a life split between freelance photography, film production and working at the Royal Albert Hall.His glittering portfolio includes photographs of Jorja Smith, Basement Jaxx, Fireboy DML andEzra Collective, but like many in the creative industries, he oscillates between the glamour of the stage and the reality of making a living. “I’ve always had day jobs,” he says. “Most photographers back in the day weren’t shooting for money, they were shooting for passion.”Adegbayibi grew up in Enfield, north London, and first picked up a camera when his cousin TJ Koleoso – Ezra Collective’s bassist – asked him to photograph theirchurch’s worship band before the service. He shot there for a couple of years before graduating to local gigs, building a body of work by approaching small artists and asking if he could photograph them. “The more I shot, the more confident I felt,” he says. “Then more people reached out to me, based on my Instagram.”His work with Ezra Collective has been a key part of that trajectory. In 2022, Adegbayibi went to Lewes’s Love Supreme jazz festival to watch the band play one of their first major headline shows. One photo in particular, of TJ leaning back on his bass, and another of the whole band that was subsequently used on an album sleeve, convinced him that photography could become more than a hobby: “I was like: ‘Damn, I can actually do something with this.’”double quotation markI think my photography serves as an example of Black joy and the truth behind Black communitiesSince then, he has photographed Ezra on tour and at increasingly large shows, including theirperformanceat the Royal Albert Hall in November 2023. That led to a solo exhibition of his work celebrating British jazz, and eventually to his becoming one of the venue’s in-house photographers. Adegbayibi’s freelance work largely focuses on music, and has taken him to gigs and festivals across the UK, including Glastonbury and Recessland, the London festival celebrating Black music and culture.What distinguishes Adegbayibi’s photography is its sense of movement, intimacy and joy, particularly in his images of Black musicians. “I’ve always loved shooting Black people,” he says. “You’re spoiled for choice with the amount of beautiful smiles flying around.” He is interested in that split-second smile, the release in someone’s face, whether that’s on stage or in the crowd. There is a conscious resistance behind that approach: “Black people and musicians are often portrayed as aggressive, violent or angry,” he says. “I think my photography serves as an example of Black joy and the truth behind Black communities; what we are actually like.”His interest in movement has also become a technical fascination. Inspired by visual artist Kat Anderson, he began experimenting with slow shutter speeds, light and layering to create photographs that “almost feel like you’re painting with light”. His Albert Hall exhibition explored movement and stillness within jazz – “how energetic, but also still, jazz moments can be while I’m taking pictures”.The competitive nature of photography does not escape him. London is full of talented photographers, he says, and consistent work can be difficult to secure. But rather than seeing that as a reason to retreat, he sees the competition as motivation. “I use it as a driving force,” he says. “Having that community in London is inspiring and pushes me to do more.” He was struck by seeing his work’s wider lineage at the V&A East’sinaugural exhibitionThe Music Is Black, which features decades of images of Black British musicians, and the photographers who documented them. It made him think about the place his own photographs might occupy in that archive. “Maybe someday someone can look at an image and think: ‘That’s what jazz gigs were like back then.’ Or: ‘That’s what Black musicians were doing, and how they were dressed,’” he says. “That’s the hope.”‘We just went for it’: five of Temi Adegbayibi’s best shotsAyo Salawu (main picture)“This was the main image in my Royal Albert Hall exhibition. I’m always trying to figure out how to capture the energy of a drum solo in a still image; I’d been researching slow shutters, layering and double exposures. We shot it in a blackout studio in Greenwich, set up the drums, ordered some pizza and just went for it.”View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Temi AdegbayibiDavid Kayode and Anna Adetiba“David is leading on saxophone and Anna is supporting him,” says Adegbayibi of this studio shot. “I asked Anna to keep walking back and forth behind David while he played. I used a slow shutter to blur Anna’s movement while keeping David as still and sharp as possible. I wanted the picture to show those two different kinds of movement happening at the same time.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Temi AdegbayibiJai Amore and Blu“These two were basically the energy drivers throughout the show. Their job was to keep everything going. There was a screen effect behind them that delayed their movements and created copies of them. I framed it so it looked like this deliberate doubling effect. It’s one of my favourite pictures because it came from just paying attention to everything happening around me.”View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Temi AdegbayibiFelix Buxton“There’s so much going on at a Basement Jaxx gig – dancers, people in monkey costumes, DJs, hype men. At one point Felix was singing by himself, and I was following him when he put his hand up in a way that made him look as if he was floating. I just captured it. The white background is actually a bunch of LED lights that I blew out so it looked like a backdrop.”View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Temi AdegbayibCKTRL“I shot this about two months ago in the Elgar Room at the Royal Albert Hall. I love CKTRL as an artist, so when I was asked to shoot him it was an immediate yes. The gig was really dark, which can be difficult for a photographer, so I used a low shutter speed and moved with him to create this softer blur. With some post-processing, it ended up feeling almost like a painting.”Explore more on these topicsPhotographyJazzEzra CollectivefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: I camped in one of Britain’s last remaining rainforests | Devon holidays | The Guardian
description: After years of conservation work, this campsite on the edge of Dartmoor now offers the opportunity to pitch next to a fragile ecosystem
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: After years of conservation work, this campsite on the edge of Dartmoor now offers the opportunity to pitch next to a fragile ecosystem
Content: Ancient woodland surrounds the Wray Valley campsite.Photograph: Greydog ImagesView image in fullscreenAncient woodland surrounds the Wray Valley campsite.Photograph: Greydog ImagesDevon holidaysI camped in one of Britain’s last remaining rainforestsA fragment of temperate rainforest lies on the edge of Dartmoor, and following years of conservation work, its owners have now opened up a sustainable campsite next to this fragile ecosystemKirsten AmorThu 3 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 04.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMist blankets the valley as I wheel my camping gear down the small hill towards a clearing ringed by trees and shrubs. A picnic bench sits at its edge, angled towards the reason why I’m here: one of the last remaining fragments of temperate rainforest in Britain. I’m pitching my tent at Wray Valley Camping, a low-impact site on Dartmoor’s eastern edge between Lustleigh and Moretonhampstead, where I’ll spend five days on one of the site’s “nearly wild” pitches.Also known as Atlantic woodland, temperate rainforests depend on a rare combination of high humidity, rainfall and consistently mild coastal temperatures where the sea moderates the climate. They once stretched from the western Highlands of Scotland down to Cornwall,covering 20% of the UK, and sheltering rare and delicate lichens and plants. Today more than 95% of our temperate rainforest cover is gone, but Devon’s near-constant dampness and its exposure to the Atlantic make it one of the last strongholds for this rare habitat.Wray Valley Camping owners Michelle Grist and her partner Kevin Chamberlain have spent seven years restoring this fragile ecosystem while developing the adjacent campsite.View image in fullscreenHound Tor is an easy cycle from the campsite.Photograph: Paul Biggins/Alamy“We always intended to run a sustainable campsite from here,” says Michelle, a retired environmental consultant, admitting that neither she nor Kevin (a member of the Dartmoor search and rescue Ashburton team) had ever run one previously. “We did not take it over,” she adds. “We built it from scratch.” Years of camping, both in the UK and abroad, gave them enough experience to know what they liked and what they didn’t. The valley’s topography dictated their designs from the start, Kevin explains – tents only, nothing driven in.The early years were slow-going: Kevin built a compost toilet by hand before a shower block and other facilities arrived. Running alongside it all was the harder, longer graft of coaxing the temperate rainforest back to life.“It was actually difficult getting on to the land,” Michelle tells me. “While the drains upland had been cleared, our land was completely flooded.” Michelle and Kevin worked along with several other organisations to restore the woodland, adding 1,200 native plants, 200 metres of new hedgerow and 45 native saplings as well as removing invasive species.double quotation markIf you’re asking people to make a bit more effort to protect this environment, it tends to attract those who appreciate itTheir efforts culminated in February this year, when Wray Valley Camping saw six acres of its 4-hectare (10-acre) estate designated a Devoncounty wildlife site (CWS), recognising its importance as one of Dartmoor’s fragile remnants of temperate rainforest and wet woodland. The campsite now offers a unique opportunity to sleep beside this rare ecosystem in one of its four Nearly Wild camping pitches.A short signposted sustainability trail around the campsite and woodland explains the restoration work. Along the way, I spot a pied flycatcher between the oaks, hazels, rowans and willows while stonechats call to each other and an oil beetle meanders across a mossy stone in search of food.In the distance, the whiz of bike chains and children’s voices echo from theWray Valley Trail. This 7-mile (11km) walk and cycle track snakes along the edge of the temperate rainforest, retracing where the Moretonhampstead and South Devon Railway steam train once ran. Today it links the historic villages of Moretonhampstead and Lustleigh, and beyond to Bovey Tracey.View image in fullscreenKirsten Amor and her husband John Higgins camping at Wray Valley.Photograph: Kirsten AmorAs I walk along the old trackbeds of the valley trail, I imagine iron cleaving the valley and clouding it with steam and soot. When once the scream of the train whistle heralded fallen timber and quarried stone, today it’s given way to the shrill call of the treecreeper. It’s a small measure of how fast this corridor has recovered since industry nearly gutted it in the 19th century.double quotation markWithout the white noise of everyday life, every splash and wingbeat becomes audibleThe Wray Valley Trail acts as a low-impact gateway for exploring eastern Dartmoor, and it is worth building a few days’ itineraries around it. From the Wray Valley campsite, it’s an easy cycle or walk to Lustleigh and on towards Hound Tor, where towering granite boulders guard the low moss-strewn walls of abandoned medieval settlements. Waymarked paths from here weave between Dartmoor’s scattered prehistoric monuments and weatherworn waycrosses.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA 40-minute drive away, Dartmoor’smost popular temperate rainforest, Wistman’s Wood, is a cautionary lesson on what happens when these fragile environments go viral: eroded paths, damaged mosses and trampled roots from footfall they were never intended to sustain. Even as conservationists work there to double the woodland’s size, it remains under pressure from its popularity.For Michelle and Kevin, restoring the woodland is only part of the challenge. The harder task is ensuring that welcoming visitors help protect the landscape rather than putting it under pressure. Their approach is simple: keep visitor numbers low and deliberately limit the impact they have on the landscape, even if that means sacrificing some of the conveniences of modern camping. There are no electric hookups, cars are left in the parking area and campers wheelbarrow their kit to their pitch. Kevin admits that the arrangements can divide opinion but says the extra effort is intentional: “If you’re asking people to make a bit more effort to protect this environment, it tends to attract those who appreciate it.”View image in fullscreenDartmoor is a rare UK stronghold of Atlantic woodland.Photograph: Nigel Hicks/AlamyThat philosophy runs through the rest of the carbon-negative site, from borehole water and solar power to discounts for guests arriving on foot, by bike or by public transport. The result feels as close to wild camping as you can get with a hot shower.Both Michelle and Kevin say they’re surprised by the enthusiasm of the campsite guests. One horticulturist recently helped catalogue its plants, while scout groups have joined woodland management activities.The dying embers of sunlight fade behind our tent as we position our chairs towards the rainforest and sit, whisky in hand, and wait. A stoat dashes past liverworts into the undergrowth. An owl hoots in the distance and bats swoop and dart in the starlight above us. Without the white noise of everyday life, every splash and wingbeat becomes audible.Wray Valley may only be a small site, but it sits in a much larger mosaic of habitats. Ancient woodland lies on either side, while the nearby site of special scientific interest (SSSI) at Bovey Tracey supports species such as adders and ground-nesting birds. Camping here offers more than a place to pitch a tent – it provides a glimpse of how a small patch of land can contribute to the wider recovery of Dartmoor’s nature.Nearly Wild stays atWray Valley Campinginclude small pitches at£10/£8 (adult/child) per personor large pitches priced per pitch (from £40 forfour people). Both includehot showers and toilets. title: Jam season is here - bottle that sunshine now to brighten up the winter | Food | The Guardian
description: September’s preserving season is a race to capture the heady flavours of summer fruit
Author: Itamar Srulovich
Headline: September’s preserving season is a race to capture the heady flavours of summer fruit
Content: Sunshine in a jar … Felicity Cloake's strawberry jam.Photograph: The GuardianView image in fullscreenSunshine in a jar … Felicity Cloake's strawberry jam.Photograph: The GuardianFeastFoodJam season is here - bottle that sunshine now to brighten up the winterSeptember’s preserving season is a race to capture the heady flavours of summer fruitSign up here for our weekly food newsletter, FeastItamar SrulovichandSarit PackerThu 3 Sep 2026 07.35 EDTLast modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 07.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe ideal time to make lemonade, when lemons are juicy and plentiful and cheap, is in the dead of winter, when the last thing you want is a cooling glass of lemonade. Similarly, jam-making is best done on a grey November afternoon, when the windows are steamed up and the kitchen is the warmest place in the house. Winter is exactly when you want to be standing over a great pot of bubbling fruit and boiling sugar, but much less so in summer, which is when all the good fruit is in season. From May until mid-October, our fruit supplier bills spike exponentially as boxes and boxes of seasonal fruit in its absolute prime make their way to our kitchen for a jam session, and the practice of turning them into a sweet spread is part profession, part obsession. Jam is very much our jam.Early in the season, we can just about cope. Thesoft fruitsstart to come in when the weather is still behaving itself, and we love giving them a little seasonal accent – elderflower comes with the last rhubarb, as well as with the first strawberries and apricots, and it pairs wonderfully with all of them (if you are starting there, Felicity Cloake has a very thorough guide tothe perfect strawberry jam). Cherries, meanwhile, go with just about anything, while young bay leaves often find themselves heading into the blackcurrant pot. Fennel fronds and peaches are another favourite, and we make some whenever we can get those two at the same moment. It is an amazing combination: sweet, perfumed and just a little bit green.View image in fullscreenIntriguing … Lillie O’Brien’s fig and earl grey jam.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianFor us, the realpreserving frenzybegins round about now, at the deep, sticky end of summer. In fact, September may well be the best jam month of all. The days are not too hot and the produce – figs, plums, grapes – are the ultimate jammers. Plums offer near endless possibilities and, depending on the variety, can take a surprising amount of spice: cassia bark, star anise, perhaps a clove or two. Nigel Slater’s collection oflate-summer jams and picklesis exactly the sort of thing to read when the fruit bowl begins to look threatening.Grapes, meanwhile, are a bit of a challenge, not least because most of the varieties grown commercially are chosen for their sweetness, whereas you want something else for jam: there needs to be some acidity, some funk, some flavour in there. Fragola grapes, with their musky, intoxicating, wild strawberry flavour, are a rare treat – we usually get only one delivery of them each year, which makes them all the more special, and all the more worthy of preserving for the rest of the year.Figs, especially those beautiful, black bursa ones, make the best jam of all, and the one that we and our customers crave the most. The fruit hardly needs any help, either, although its honeyed sweetness loves nothing more then a few pods of cooling cardamom for balance (that said, we are more than a little intrigued byLillie O’Brien’s earl grey combo).Our annual September challenge, then, is simple: make enough fig jam to last until Christmas. Every year, we make what looks like an absurd quantity. And every year it disappears far too quickly, which is exactly the point – spend a bit of the summer sweating over the pots so that in winter, when we aren’t sweating at all, there’s a little bit of jarred sunshine ready for us when it is most desperately needed.Our month in foodView image in fullscreenHappy new year … Claudia Roden’s honey cake.Photograph: Romas Foord/The ObserverThe sweet spot|Jams aside, our pastry kitchen currently smells heavily of honey and spice as we get busy baking loaves and loaves of honey cake in readiness for the Jewish new year next week, which this year is coming round earlier than usual. It is traditional to start the year with something sweet, be that an apple dipped in honey, dates,sweet challah breadand, of course,honey cake. You don’t need to be Jewish to enjoy this delicious tradition: on the 11th, wish your Jewish friends a happy new year, and have something sweet for yourself.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFeastRecipes from all our star cooks, seasonal eating ideas and restaurant reviews. Get our best food writing every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLocal attraction|Our love for Jackson Boxer’s cooking knows no bounds, and even though hisBrunswick Houseis so close to our home in south London that we are there more often that is OK to admit, whenever he opens a new place, we go.Vesperis on Exmouth Market in the centre of London, and it made us question our loyalty not only to Brunswick House, but also to our own home and our beloved neighbourhood, because the fried potato pizzette is something we need to live closer to.Book marks|We got a sneak preview of two new books that are already making our autumn look much more delicious, and both of which are published today.Simple Too by Yotam Ottolenghiis full of mouthwatering recipes that look and taste as good as they are easy to make, and promises to add a touch of glamour to our midweek meals. The second is the new one by Fuchsia Dunlop, a perennial favourite of ours, andFive Tastes: The Magic of Flavour in a Chinese Kitchenis a deep and delicious dive into the flavours that are the cornerstones of Chinese cooking. We are into all of them.If you want to read the complete version of this newsletterplease subscribeto receive Feast in your inbox every Thursday.Explore more on these topicsFoodFeastPickling, fermenting and preservingFruitVegetablesSummer food and drinkAutumn food and drinknewslettersShareReuse this content

title: Are there any drinkable canned cocktails?  | Food | The Guardian
description: Palatable premix cocktails – well, ones that adults like, at least – are far and few between
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Palatable premix cocktails – well, ones that adults like, at least – are far and few between
Content: Moth is one of the drinkable brands – try the mango one in our recs.Photograph: Moth/PRView image in fullscreenMoth is one of the drinkable brands – try the mango one in our recs.Photograph: Moth/PRGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.FoodAre there any drinkable canned cocktails?Palatable premix cocktails – well, ones that adults like, at least – are far and few betweenMina HollandThu 3 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor somebody whose children recently learned how to crack open a tinnie, this week’s tasting was a perilous one. Cans covered in seductive, brightly coloured pictures of parasols, palm trees and their favourite fruits filled the kitchen, and both the seven- and the five-year-old tried to take a swig. Premix cocktails are disproportionately marketed to young drinkers – gateway booze, if you will, as the likes of Bacardi Breezer pineapple was for me – and often have a one-note, cloying taste.Absolut’s passionfruit martiniandMalibu’s piña coladaare cases in point: both have sugary, synthetic fruit flavours that mask, or even eliminate, the taste of the base spirits. Is it any wonder that, in 2024, Britain had theworst rate of child alcohol consumption in the world? These drinks make it easy to forget that you’re even drinking alcohol.Perhaps more than any other theme, writing about premix cocktails has made me confront the very question of why we drink alcohol. Take me as an example. My Bacardi Breezer years were undoubtedly a question of booze for function; it loosened my teenage inhibitions and I had a laugh. The fact that this so-called “alcopop” was so saccharine chimed with my childish predilection for sweetness, and conveniently masked the flavour of the rum, which may at the time have offended my uninitiated palate. Twenty-five years on, and my palate is a different place, and I welcome the notes and nuances of a well-mixed drink. I now drink alcohol to savour it, and I like what I’m drinking to give me pause; it doesn’t need to be hard work, but I do like it to make me think.That’s not to say there aren’t premix cocktails out there that can do this, and I tasted several that I found interesting. The Reina Mezcalita in today’s pick, for instance, is delicious – smoky mezcal meets zippy lime soda – and I’d happily sip it from the can in the park or, even better, from a glass rimmed withTajìnat home.Whitebox and Moth both produce good iterations of premix drinks (and in reassuringly small, potent formats) and are widely available in supermarkets; they feel a bit more grown up, too, both on the sugar front and because their ABVs skew higher, which you can taste (in the premix realm, quality seems to align with a higher ABV).Marks & Spencer has the widest own-brand selection, some of them better than others, but, on the whole, its premium Served range has more character and acidity (a good thing) than you’ll find elsewhere – I enjoyed the mojito and the lychee martini especially.Spritz cocktails, meanwhile, work particularly well in cans.M&S’s limoncello oneis a crowdpleaser, while Aperol Spritz To Go is everything you want and need it to be: a failsafe, bittersweet symphony.Five canned cocktails worth cracking openWhitebox Cosmo£5 (100ml) Ocado, 16.8%. Vodka, cranberry, lime and triple sec: cosmopolitans are making a comeback, and this one has me here for it.Reina Mezcalita£4.99 (200ml) Mex Grocer, 10%. A smoky, citrussy delight, and my favourite of the lot.M&S Served Mojito£3.35 (250ml) Ocado, 8%. Unlike this store’s cheaper premixes, this one has some complexity. Rum, mint and lime.Aperol Spritz To Go£3 (250ml) Waitrose, 5%. Inarguably good and utterly dependable. Literally does what it says on the tin.Moth Mango Margarita£4.15 (125ml) Waitrose, 14.9%. Ripe mangoes meet Tequila Enemigo and triple sec: 100% toothsome.Explore more on these topicsFoodCocktailsSpiritsFruitMexican food and drinkItalian food and drinkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Rachel Roddy’s summer minestrone with pesto – recipe | Food | The Guardian
description: A fresh, seasonal vegetable soup that can be made in advance and only improves in texture and flavour over time
Author: Rachel Roddy
Headline: A fresh, seasonal vegetable soup that can be made in advance and only improves in texture and flavour over time
Content: Rachel Roddy’s summer minestrone with pesto.Photograph: Rachel Roddy/The GuardianView image in fullscreenRachel Roddy’s summer minestrone with pesto.Photograph: Rachel Roddy/The GuardianA kitchen in RomeFoodRachel Roddy’s summer minestrone with pesto – recipeA fresh, seasonal vegetable soup that can be made in advance and only improves in texture and flavour over timeRachel RoddyThu 3 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNow that I am an accomplished sourdough maker, soon to start my own micro-bakery and YouTube channel … Only joking! Now that I can make half-decent, variable loaves of sourdough, I have become more aware of how the temperature in the kitchen affects food. Not that I was completely unaware, of course – I have curdled enough milk and neglected enough eggs – but feeding, then watching the sourdough starter in a jar, and then the dough itself, seeing how the process takes hours in winter, speeds up in spring, then takes on a foaming, bubbling and at times terrifying life of its own in summer, are lessons in living microorganisms and fermentation.It is a shame, then, that I didn’t give the same attention to the pan of summer minestrone I had felt so pleased with myself for cooking, cutting the courgettes carefully so they looked like Trivial Pursuit scoring wedges, while drinking tea and listening for the bottle bank lorry to drop the glass into its box, and before the sun (or anyone else) was up. Even though the combined taste of minestrone and milky Yorkshire tea is interesting, I knew it had turned out particularly well. I put on the lid, left the pan at the back of the stove and went out.It must have been 11am by the time I got back home with a plant of basil quietly suffocating behind its plastic cone. The kitchen was already hot and the minestrone was only slightly, but unequivocally, fizzy. A spoonful of pesto did not balance it out – but please don’t let my neglect put you off making this abundantly fresh-green and creamy-white courgette, green and white bean minestrone, inspired by three recipes in Laura Ragoni’s Profumi e Sapori di Liguria.If you are eating the minestrone straight away, leave it to sit for 10 minutes before serving. If you have prepared the minestrone in advance, not only will it sit for hours, but resting improves the flavour and texture.That said, learn from my mistake: if you are experiencing hot weather and the rest is longer than an hour, that rest needs to take place in a cool spot, or in the fridge to avoid a spoiled, fizzy soup. The minestrone can then be reheated gently until warm rather than hot.Summer minestrone with pestoServes65 tbspolive oil1 onion, peeled and diced small1 stick celery, trimmed and diced1 small bunch flat-leaf parsley, stems separated from the leaves (save the leaves for the pesto), and mincedSalt6 cherry tomatoes, quartered2 large courgettes, trimmed, cut into quarters lengthwise, then into quarter-moons200g green beans, cut into 2½cm lengths1 large potato, peeled and cut into cubes1 parmesan rind2400g tinswhite beans, drainedFor the pesto1garlic clove, peeled20g pine nuts, or almonds50gparsley leaves and basil100g olive oil50g cheese(pecorino, grana padano, parmesan, or a mixture), gratedHeat the olive oil in a heavy-based pan or casserole dish and gently fry the onion, celery, minced parsley stems and a pinch of salt, stirring often, until soft – about eight minutes.Add the tomatoes, stir for a minute or two, then add the courgettes, green beans and potatoes, and a pinch of salt, stirring to prevent sticking and so each chunk glistens with oil. Add one and a half litres of water and a parmesan rind, if you have one, then raise the heat so the soup nearly boils. Reduce to a simmer for 30 minutes, or until the vegetables are tender.Meanwhile, make the pesto. Pulse or pound the garlic, nuts and a pinch of salt, until they form a rough paste. Add the parsley and basil leaves, and pulse again until creamy. Gradually stir in the cheese and oil.About 10 minutes before the end of the cooking time, add the drained white beans, then leave the minestrone to sit for at least 10 minutes before serving, passing around the pesto so everyone can add the amount they like.Explore more on these topicsFoodA kitchen in RomeItalian food and drinkVegetablesSoupMain courseStarterCheeserecipesShareReuse this content
